status: Every section of Seneca’s Moral Letters that the Stoic Constitution quotes: 304 sections from 94 letters. Each was translated from the Latin alone by one model, checked against the Latin by a second, and each point was settled in writing by a third reading. None has been read by the owner or checked by a person who reads Latin.

edition.latin: The Latin Library, Seneca, Epistulae morales ad Lucilium (https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/sen.html), an older public-domain text
edition.checked_against: Latin Wikisource, Epistulae morales ad Lucilium (a copy of the same text with section markers)
edition.numbering: letter and section, as in the standard editions
edition.hand_splits: Both sources run 22.13–17, 30.1–4 and 41.8–9 together; those were split at the Latin sentence each section begins with.

method: A first translator (Claude Fable 5.2) worked from the Latin alone, with a short glossary that keeps shared Stoic terms in the same English as the project’s Marcus, and wrote notes where the Latin is open.
A second reader saw only the Latin and the English and listed every place where the English says more, less or other than the Latin.
A third reading settled each point in writing (Accepted, Partly accepted or Declined, with the reason from the Latin) and gave the final English.

No reader saw any published translation of Seneca. Gummere’s 1917–25 English is kept privately and used only to measure similarity (as the 1634 English is for Marcus); none of its words are published.
Letter titles are the project’s own, written from each letter’s Latin.
limits: The Latin is an unattributed older text, not a modern critical edition; doubtful readings are noted where a reader saw them.
All three readings were made by language models; no person who reads Latin has checked the English.
Only the quoted sections are translated, so a section may begin in the middle of an argument; its notes say so where it matters.
footer: Latin: The Latin Library. The English and the letter titles are this project’s own translation.

passages.latin: Quem mihi dabis qui aliquod pretium tempori ponat, qui diem aestimet, qui intellegat se cotidie mori? In hoc enim fallimur, quod mortem prospicimus: magna pars eius iam praeterit; quidquid aetatis retro est mors tenet. Fac ergo, mi Lucili, quod facere te scribis, omnes horas complectere; sic fiet ut minus ex crastino pendeas, si hodierno manum inieceris.
passages.english: Who will you give me who sets any price on time, who puts a value on a day, who understands that he is dying every day? For we are deceived in this, that we look ahead to death: a great part of it has already gone by; whatever of our lifetime lies behind us, death holds. So do, my Lucilius, what you write you are doing: take hold of every hour. In this way it will come about that you depend less on tomorrow, if you lay hands on today.

notes.note: Literally “whom will you give”, an idiom for “name a man”. The English keeps the verb “give” and the form of a question.
notes.other_reading: Name me a man who sets any price on time

notes.note: The present infinitive can be heard as a process (“is dying”) or as a repeated act (“dies”). The English takes the process, since the next sentence says part of death is already behind.
notes.other_reading: that he dies every day

notes.note: The verb means to see ahead, in front of one. The point is that death is placed only in the future.
notes.other_reading: that we see death as lying ahead of us

notes.note: The pronoun refers to death, not to life. The verb as spelled can be a present (“is going by”) or a contracted perfect (“has gone by”); the English takes the perfect, because the next clause speaks of what already lies behind. Some editions may print the perfect in full (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: a great part of it is already going by

notes.note: An imperative of the verb “to embrace, to clasp”. “Take hold of” is used because the sentence ends with a hand laid on today.
notes.other_reading: embrace all your hours

notes.note: Literally “hang from tomorrow”, the ordinary Latin way of saying “depend on”. The English gives the plain sense, since “hang on tomorrow” would read as waiting.
notes.other_reading: that you hang less on tomorrow

notes.note: To lay a hand on something is an act in Roman law by which one claims a thing or a person as one’s own. “Lay hands on” is the English phrase for seizing and keeps the hand; the Latin has a single hand.
notes.other_reading: if you have claimed today as your own

check.note: As spelled the verb is a present, “is already going by”. The English reads it as a contracted perfect, and that choice should be confirmed.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps “has already gone by”. The perfect fits “already” and the next clause, which speaks of what lies behind, and the note records the present as the other reading.

check.note: The Latin verb is “give”, in the sense of produce or name, not “show”, and “Whom” at the head of the sentence is stiff.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the opening now reads “Who will you give”, which restores the Latin verb and keeps its future tense. The suggested “is there you can give” adds a “can” that the Latin does not have.

check.note: “What you write that you are doing” is correct but awkward English.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “what you write you are doing”, which says the same thing more plainly.

check.note: The Latin phrase means “depend on”. “Hang on tomorrow” is not clear in the English of today.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “you depend less on tomorrow”. The Latin phrase is the ordinary one for depending, and “hang on tomorrow” reads in English as waiting; the note keeps the literal “hang from”.

check.note: The Latin phrase is the legal gesture of seizing something as one’s own. “Lay your hand on” can read as a mere touch.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “if you lay hands on today”. “Lay hands on” is the English phrase for seizing and keeps the hand of the Latin, where “lay hold of” would drop it and would echo “take hold of” in the sentence before, which stands for a different Latin verb.

passages.latin: Hoc cotidie meditare, ut possis aequo animo vitam relinquere, quam multi sic complectuntur et tenent quomodo qui aqua torrente rapiuntur spinas et aspera. Plerique inter mortis metum et vitae tormenta miseri fluctuantur et vivere nolunt, mori nesciunt.
passages.english: Practise this every day, so that you can leave life with an even mind: life, which many clasp and hold on to in the way that people being swept away by rushing water clasp thorns and jagged edges. Most people are tossed about, wretched, between the fear of death and the torments of life, and they do not want to live, they do not know how to die.

notes.note: The verb covers both thinking a thing over and rehearsing it as an exercise. “This” may point back to the thought of the section before or forward to the clause that follows; the English leaves “this” open and takes the clause as purpose.
notes.other_reading: Rehearse this every day: to be able to leave life with an even mind

notes.note: A set phrase, literally “with a level mind”, meaning without distress or resentment. “Mind” is kept for animus as the glossary prefers, and “calm” is left for tranquillitas.
notes.other_reading: calmly, without complaint

notes.note: The second word can be a participle (“rushing water”) or part of a noun phrase (“a torrent of water”). The sense is much the same.
notes.other_reading: by a torrent

notes.note: The second word is a bare neuter plural, “rough things”, whatever is harsh to grasp; “jagged edges” narrows it a little. The Latin has no second verb, and “clasp” is repeated to make the English run.
notes.other_reading: thorns and rough things

notes.note: In classical Latin “most people”; in writers of Seneca’s time it often means only “very many”. The English keeps the stronger sense.
notes.other_reading: A great many people

notes.note: The verb is from the word for a wave and carries on the water image: they are tossed like something afloat. The adjective “wretched” describes the people, not the manner.
notes.other_reading: drift miserably back and forth

notes.note: With an infinitive this verb means “do not know how to”. The two clauses stand side by side in the Latin with no “and” or “but” between them.
notes.other_reading: they are unwilling to live and unable to die

check.note: The English takes “this” as pointing back and the clause as purpose. “This” can equally point forward, with the clause saying what is to be practised, and the verb can also be “think over, rehearse”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the purpose reading is kept, “Practise this every day, so that you can leave life with an even mind”, as a deliberate choice, since the Latin clause has the ordinary form of a purpose and “this” can gather up the thoughts of the section before. The note records the other reading, in which the clause says what is to be rehearsed.

check.note: “With an even mind” is word for word and not current English; “calmly” is suggested.
check.decided: Declined: “with an even mind” stands. The glossary gives “mind” for animus and keeps “calm” for tranquillitas, a different word, so “calmly” would blur two settled renderings; the note explains the set phrase.

check.note: “Rough things” is literal but limp and a little unclear for whatever is harsh to grasp.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “thorns and jagged edges”. The note records that the Latin has only a bare “rough things”.

passages.latin: asperum cultum et intonsum caput et neglegentiorem barbam et indictum argento odium et cubile humi positum et quidquid aliud ambitionem perversa via sequitur evita. Satis ipsum nomen philosophiae, etiam si modeste tractetur, invidiosum est: quid si nos hominum consuetudini coeperimus excerpere? Intus omnia dissimilia sint, frons populo nostra conveniat.
passages.english: Rough dress, an uncut head of hair, a rather neglected beard, hatred declared on silver, a bed laid on the ground, and whatever else seeks attention by a perverse route: avoid them. The very name of philosophy, even if it is handled with restraint, draws enough ill will: what if we begin to withdraw ourselves from the customs of people? Inside, let everything be different; let our outward face fit in with the people.

notes.note: The section as given starts in the middle of a sentence: the list is the object of this one imperative at its end, and it continues the warning in the section before against doing conspicuous things. The English puts the list first and the command last, as the Latin does.
notes.other_reading: Avoid rough dress, an uncut head of hair (and so on)

notes.note: The noun covers dress, grooming and style of living generally. It is narrowed to dress because hair, beard and bed follow separately.
notes.other_reading: a harsh style of living

notes.note: The comparative can mean “rather careless” or “too careless”.
notes.other_reading: a beard too carelessly kept

notes.note: The participle is the word used for declaring war, and “declared on” is meant to keep that sound. “Silver” may be silver tableware or money; the next section speaks of silver plate, and “silver” is kept for the same word in both sections.
notes.other_reading: open war declared on silverware

notes.note: The noun here is not political ambition but the courting of notice and admiration. The road is “turned the wrong way”: display is sought through seeming to reject display.
notes.other_reading: chases after show by a road turned back to front

notes.note: The word means attracting ill will or resentment, not “invidious” in the modern English sense.
notes.other_reading: is resented enough

notes.note: The noun can mean custom and habits, or company and dealings with people. The English takes custom, because the list before it is of habits of dress and living and the next sentence speaks of the outward face.
notes.other_reading: what if we begin to withdraw ourselves from the company of people

notes.note: The verb is “to pick out, to remove”, with the speakers themselves as its object. The tense is future perfect, literally “shall have begun”, given here as a plain present.
notes.other_reading: what if we shall have begun to pick ourselves out of the common habit of mankind

notes.note: The noun is literally the forehead or brow, and then the front or outward face of a thing; it is set against “inside”. “The people” could also be “the crowd” or “the public”.
notes.other_reading: let our front agree with the crowd

check.note: The verb is the one for declaring war, and that colour is faint in “a declared hatred”. The silver is most likely silver plate, which “silver” alone leaves unclear.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “hatred declared on silver”, where “declared on” brings back the sound of declaring war. “Silver” is kept, not “silverware”, because the same Latin word is “silver” in the next section and the Latin leaves plate or money unsaid; the note records this.

check.note: The noun is the courting of attention or admiration, which is wider than “show”, and “chases after” is a little stronger than the Latin verb.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “chases after show” becomes “seeks attention”. “Attention” is the wider word the point asks for, and “seeks” is used instead of “pursues” because “seeks attention” is the current English phrase for this.

check.note: A road cannot be wrong-headed; the Latin is a perverse way, turned back to front.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “by a perverse route”. “Perverse” gives the Latin’s sense of a way turned the wrong way round, and the note explains it.

check.note: The Latin word means arousing ill will or resentment, which is stronger than “unpopular”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “draws enough ill will”. The Latin word speaks of resentment aroused, which is more than not being liked.

check.note: The noun can be custom and habits or company and dealings with people. The English takes the first without saying so.
check.decided: Accepted: the reading “custom” is kept and the English now reads “from the customs of people”, because the list before it is of habits of dress and living. A note is added giving the other reading, “from the company of people”.

check.note: “Unlike” with nothing after it is unclear English.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Inside, let everything be different”.

check.note: The noun is the face one shows. “Front” is not clear to a reader of today, and “agree with the people” reads as agreeing in opinion.
check.decided: Accepted: “front” becomes “outward face” and “agree with” becomes “fit in with”, as suggested. The Latin noun is the brow or the face one shows, and the verb means to suit or match, not to share an opinion.

passages.latin: Non splendeat toga, ne sordeat quidem; non habeamus argentum in quod solidi auri caelatura descenderit, sed non putemus frugalitatis indicium auro argentoque caruisse. Id agamus ut meliorem vitam sequamur quam vulgus, non ut contrariam: alioquin quos emendari volumus fugamus a nobis et avertimus; illud quoque efficimus, ut nihil imitari velint nostri, dum timent ne imitanda sint omnia.
passages.english: Let the toga not gleam, nor be dirty either. Let us not own silver with engraved work of solid gold sunk into it, but let us not think it a sign of frugality to have gone without gold and silver. Let us make it our aim to follow a better life than the crowd, not a contrary one: otherwise we drive from us and turn away the people we want to see reformed. We also bring it about that they want to imitate nothing of ours, for fear that everything has to be imitated.

notes.note: The construction is “not … either”. The verb covers both being dirty and being shabby or mean-looking.
notes.other_reading: but let it not be shabby either

notes.latin: in quod solidi auri caelatura descenderit
notes.note: Literally “into which the engraving of solid gold has gone down”: silver plate with ornament in solid gold sunk or inlaid into it. The exact technique is not certain; “sunk into it” keeps the downward movement.
notes.other_reading: silver inlaid with reliefs of solid gold

notes.note: A perfect infinitive, “to have gone without”. It may be only a general perfect with the force of “to go without”.
notes.other_reading: to do without gold and silver

notes.note: The first noun is wider than thrift: it is sober, plain living. “Frugality” is used here and in Ep. 5.5 so that the two sections match.
notes.other_reading: a sign of plain living

notes.note: The common mass of people, with a slighting tone. “The crowd” is used here, and “the people” is kept for populus in the section before.
notes.other_reading: than the common run of people

notes.note: The first verb is “to put to flight”, not “to flee”. The second is “to turn away”, which could mean turning them from the speakers or turning them from the better life.
notes.other_reading: we frighten them off and put them against us

notes.note: The last word can be a genitive going with “nothing”, as translated, or a nominative plural that names the philosophers’ own people as the subject. The genitive is taken because the subject is the people to be reformed.
notes.other_reading: that our own people want to imitate nothing

notes.note: Literally “while they fear”, with a shade of cause. “For fear that” gives that shade without a bare “because”.
notes.other_reading: while they fear that everything has to be imitated

check.note: “Let in” and “chased work” are craft terms most readers will not catch. The verb is literally “has sunk down into”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “silver with engraved work of solid gold sunk into it”. The craft terms are gone, and “sunk into” is used instead of “inlaid” because the Latin verb is “has gone down into”.

check.note: The noun is a sign or indication; “proof” is stronger than the Latin.
check.decided: Accepted: “proof” becomes “sign”, which is what the Latin noun says.

check.note: The English can be misread as the speakers wanting to be corrected, and “corrected” is schoolroom English for a verb that means made better, reformed.
check.decided: Accepted: “to be corrected” becomes “to see reformed”, which cannot be misread as the speakers wishing to be corrected and is closer to the Latin sense of being freed of faults.

check.note: The verb here is to turn people away, to alienate them. “Turn aside” is weaker and vague.
check.decided: Accepted: “turn aside” becomes “turn away”, the plain sense of the Latin verb here. “Drive away from” is shortened to “drive from” so that “away” is not said twice.

check.note: The Latin “while” with a present here has causal force. A bare “while” reads as only temporal and makes the sentence hard to follow.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “for fear that everything has to be imitated”. The Latin “while they fear” carries a shade of cause that a bare “while” loses; the note keeps the literal wording.

passages.latin: Quemadmodum desiderare delicatas res luxuriae est, ita usitatas et non magno parabiles fugere dementiae. Frugalitatem exigit philosophia, non poenam; potest autem esse non incompta frugalitas. Hic mihi modus placet: temperetur vita inter bonos mores et publicos; suspiciant omnes vitam nostram sed agnoscant.
passages.english: Just as it is a mark of luxury to long for refined things, so it is a mark of madness to run from things that are in ordinary use and can be had at no great price. Philosophy demands frugality, not punishment; and there can be a frugality that is not unkempt. This is the mean I favour: let life be balanced between good conduct and the conduct of people in general; let everyone look up to our life, but let them find it recognisable.

notes.note: A genitive of characteristic: “it is the mark of”. The noun is self-indulgent, extravagant living; “luxury” is used here and again in Ep. 7.7.
notes.other_reading: is a mark of self-indulgence

notes.note: The adjective means choice, refined, pampering. The same word describes the self-indulgent housemate of Ep. 7.7.
notes.other_reading: dainty and costly things

notes.note: Literally “obtainable at no great”, with “price” understood.
notes.other_reading: cheap to get

notes.note: The noun is a penalty or punishment. The section before spoke of torturing one’s own body, so self-punishment is meant, but the Latin says only “punishment”.
notes.other_reading: not self-punishment

notes.note: The adjective is used first of hair that is not dressed, then of anything left unadorned. The English keeps the Latin’s double negative.
notes.other_reading: frugality need not be slovenly

notes.note: The noun can be a measure, a limit, a mean, or simply a manner. “Mean” is used because what follows is a balance between two things.
notes.other_reading: This is the way I think best

notes.latin: temperetur vita inter bonos mores et publicos
notes.note: The verb means to mix in due proportion. The noun, used once for both adjectives, covers ways, habits and morals: the life is to be blended between the ways of a good man and the ways of people at large. No possessive is expressed with “life”.
notes.other_reading: let our life be a blend of good morals and common morals

notes.latin: suspiciant omnes vitam nostram sed agnoscant
notes.note: The first verb is literally “look up at”, so admire. The second is to recognise something as known or as one’s own: people should find the life familiar, not alien.
notes.other_reading: let everyone admire our life, but let them recognise it

check.note: The Latin form means “is a mark of”. “It belongs to luxury … it belongs to madness” is Latin in English dress.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “it is a mark of luxury” and “it is a mark of madness”, which is what the Latin form means.

check.note: “Dainty” is dated and suggests small and pretty; the adjective is “luxurious, refined”.
check.decided: Accepted: “dainty things” becomes “refined things”, which is current English and does not suggest small and pretty.

check.latin: potest autem esse non incompta frugalitas
check.note: “Frugality can be not unkempt” is faithful but clumsy English.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “and there can be a frugality that is not unkempt”. This is plain English and keeps the Latin’s “can be” and its double negative, where “need not be” would change “can” to “need”.

check.note: The noun is the mean or limit, and “measure” can be read as a step taken. The verb is “pleases, is what is favoured”, not quite “approve”.
check.decided: Accepted: “measure” becomes “mean” and “approve” becomes “favour”, as suggested. “Measure” could be read as a step taken, and the Latin says that the thing pleases the writer, which is nearer to “favour”.

check.latin: temperetur vita inter bonos mores et publicos
check.note: The verb is to blend or strike a balance, and “tempered between” is not English. “Public ways” is obscure for the customs of people in general.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “let life be balanced between good conduct and the conduct of people in general”. “Balanced” and “conduct” follow the suggestion; the passive is kept, no possessive is added because the Latin has none, and “the conduct of people in general” is used because “common conduct” can read as vulgar conduct.

check.note: The verb is to recognise as familiar or as one’s own kind. A bare “recognise it” leaves the reader unsure what is meant.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “but let them find it recognisable”. “Also” is left out because the Latin has no word for it.

passages.latin: Ferae pericula quae vident fugiunt, cum effugere, securae sunt: nos et venturo torquemur et praeterito. Multa bona nostra nobis nocent; timoris enim tormentum memoria reducit, providentia anticipat; nemo tantum praesentibus miser est. Vale.
passages.english: Wild animals run from the dangers they see, and when they have escaped they are free from care: we are tormented both by what is coming and by what is past. Many of our good things do us harm: for memory brings back the torment of fear, and foresight takes it ahead of time. No one is wretched from present things alone. Farewell.

notes.note: The second word is a short form of the perfect, “they have escaped”, not an infinitive. The Latin has no “and” before it; one is added to join the clauses.
notes.other_reading: once they have got away

notes.note: “Free from care” matches the glossary’s rendering of securitas. The word describes a state of mind, not safety.
notes.other_reading: they are untroubled

notes.note: The verb is from the same root as the noun “torment” in the next sentence, so “tormented” and “torment” keep the link. Both nouns are neuter singulars, “what is to come” and “what is past”.
notes.other_reading: we are tortured by the future and by the past alike

notes.note: Bona is the plural of bonum, the glossary’s “the good”. “Good things” is used because “goods” alone reads as possessions; what is meant is the advantages of being human, memory and foresight, and the section before calls foresight the greatest good of the human condition.
notes.other_reading: Many of our blessings

notes.note: The noun is human foresight, not divine providence. The verb is “to take beforehand”: foresight takes the torment of fear before its time.
notes.other_reading: foresight anticipates it

notes.note: The second word here means “only”. The ablative gives the cause and is taken as neuter (“present things”); “present troubles” could be understood, less probably.
notes.other_reading: no one is made wretched only by what is present

check.note: “Goods” reads first as possessions. What is meant is good things that people have, such as memory and foresight.
check.decided: Accepted: “goods” becomes “good things”, since “goods” alone reads as possessions. The note records that the Latin word is the plural of the glossary’s “the good”, and Ep. 7.12 is brought into line.

check.note: Found while settling: “takes it up ahead of time” could be read as “resumes it”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “takes it ahead of time”, the literal sense of the Latin verb, “to take beforehand”.

passages.latin: Mittam itaque ipsos tibi libros, et ne multum operae impendas dum passim profutura sectaris, imponam notas, ut ad ipsa protinus quae probo et miror accedas. Plus tamen tibi et viva vox et convictus quam oratio proderit; in rem praesentem venias oportet, primum quia homines amplius oculis quam auribus credunt, deinde quia longum iter est per praecepta, breve et efficax per exempla.
passages.english: So I will send you the books themselves, and so that you do not spend much effort chasing here and there after what will be of use, I will put marks in them, so that you can go straight to the very things I approve of and admire. Yet both the living voice and a shared life will do you more good than a set discourse. You ought to come to the thing itself, on the spot, first because people trust their eyes more than their ears, and then because the road is long by way of precepts, short and effective by way of examples.

notes.note: “The books themselves”, as against a report or extracts from them. The section does not say which books.
notes.other_reading: the actual books

notes.note: Literally “while you chase here and there after things that will be of use”. The clause is folded into “chasing”.
notes.other_reading: while you hunt everywhere for the useful parts

notes.note: The noun is most likely marks or signs set against passages. It could also mean written notes or comments.
notes.other_reading: I will add notes

notes.note: A set phrase, “the living voice”, for teaching heard in person as against reading. It is kept literally.
notes.other_reading: the spoken word

notes.note: Living with someone: daily company, especially sharing a table. “A shared life” is used, which keeps the echo of “living” that this word has with “living voice” in the Latin.
notes.other_reading: daily companionship

notes.note: The noun is speech or a composed discourse. Set against the living voice, and following the sending of books, it seems to mean discourse on the page, but the Latin does not say “written”; “set” marks it as composed.
notes.other_reading: than the written word

notes.note: A legal idiom: to go to the very spot where the thing in dispute is, so as to judge it at first hand. The English keeps both “the thing” and “the spot”; seeing is left to the next clause, as in the Latin.
notes.other_reading: you must come and see for yourself on the spot

notes.note: Precepts are rules or instructions given in words, set against examples, which are patterns seen in a person. “Precepts” and “examples” are kept as a fixed pair.
notes.other_reading: by way of instructions

check.note: The Latin “both … and” is dropped. “Living together” today suggests a couple sharing a home; the noun is sharing someone’s daily life and company.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “both” is restored and the English now reads “both the living voice and a shared life”. “Daily” is left out because the Latin noun says only living with someone, and “life” keeps the echo of “living” that the two Latin words share.

check.note: “A discourse” is dated and leaves unclear what is set against the living voice. The noun here is composed, set language as against talk face to face.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “than a set discourse”. “Set” marks the composed language the point describes; “set words” alone is not current English, and “written” is left to the note because the Latin does not say it.

check.note: The Latin is an idiom for coming to the spot and judging the matter at first hand. “The place itself” leaves the reader asking what place.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “You ought to come to the thing itself, on the spot”. This answers the question of what place; “and see” is not added because the Latin leaves seeing to the next clause, about eyes and ears.

passages.latin: Unum exemplum luxuriae aut avaritiae multum mali facit: convictor delicatus paulatim enervat et mollit, vicinus dives cupiditatem irritat, malignus comes quamvis candido et simplici rubiginem suam affricuit: quid tu accidere his moribus credis in quos publice factus est impetus?
passages.english: A single example of luxury or of greed does a great deal of harm: a self-indulgent housemate little by little weakens and softens, a rich neighbour stirs up craving, a spiteful companion rubs his own rust off on a man however spotless and straightforward. What do you think happens to a character on which the attack has been made by the people as a body?

notes.note: “Luxury” is used as in Ep. 5.5, and “greed” for the love of money.
notes.other_reading: of extravagance or of avarice

notes.note: The noun is someone who lives with you day to day and shares your table. The adjective is “pampered, self-indulgent”, the same word as the “refined things” of Ep. 5.5.
notes.other_reading: a pampered companion at table

notes.note: Literally “takes out the sinews”. The two verbs have no object in the Latin, and none is supplied.
notes.other_reading: unstrings and softens us

notes.note: The noun is the general word for desire, here the wish to have what the rich neighbour has, which answers the greed named at the start. “Craving” is used so that “greed” stays for avaritia, a different word.
notes.other_reading: stirs up greed

notes.note: The adjective can be “ill-natured, spiteful” or “grudging, mean”. The English takes the first.
notes.other_reading: a mean-spirited companion

notes.note: The first adjective is “shining white”, and of character “frank, clean”. “Spotless” is chosen so that the image of rust on a clean surface holds; “a man” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: on even the most honest and straightforward person

notes.note: The noun is rust, and by extension blight or ill will. The verb is a perfect stating a general truth among present tenses, given here as a present.
notes.other_reading: has rubbed his own rust onto him

notes.note: The noun is character or morals. “These” is vague: it may mean such a character as was just described, or the characters of people like Seneca and Lucilius; the English reads “a character”.
notes.other_reading: to those morals of ours

notes.latin: in quos publice factus est impetus
notes.note: The adverb can mean “by the people as a body” or “in public, openly”. The English takes the first, which sets the whole people against the single example at the start; “attack” picks up the “attack of the vices” in the section before.
notes.other_reading: on which the attack has been made openly

check.note: The noun is someone one lives with day to day, not only a table companion. “At table” narrows it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a self-indulgent housemate”. The Latin noun is someone one lives with, not only a guest at table.

check.note: Two different figures in the list of three, the one who shares the house and the one who goes about with a man, are both given as “companion”.
check.decided: Accepted: “companion” is kept for comes only, and convictor is now “housemate”, so the three figures stay distinct.

check.note: The Latin has no object, so the object in the English is added. “Unstrings” is archaic.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “little by little weakens and softens”, with no object, as in the Latin. The note keeps the literal “takes out the sinews”.

check.note: The noun here answers the greed named at the start, as the pampered housemate answers luxury; it is the wish to have more. Bare “desire” loses that link.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “desire” becomes “craving”, a word for wanting to have. “Greed” is not used because it already stands for avaritia at the start of the sentence, and the Latin has a different word here.

check.note: “Bright” reads as clever and “simple” as simple-minded. The first adjective is clean, unstained and frank; the second is straightforward, without guile.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “a man however spotless and straightforward”. “Straightforward” is taken as suggested; “spotless” is used instead of “clean” because it fits both a character and a surface that rust can mark.

check.note: The Latin is a perfect among presents. The English makes it present, which is defensible as a perfect of general truth, but the change should be marked.
check.decided: Accepted: the present “rubs” is kept, and the note states that the Latin is a perfect expressing a general truth among present tenses.

check.note: The adverb can mean “by the people as a body” or “in public, openly”. The English chooses the first, which fits, but it is a choice.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “by the people as a body”, and the note records the other sense of the adverb, “in public, openly”. The passive of the Latin is kept.

passages.latin: Necesse est aut imiteris aut oderis. Utrumque autem devitandum est: neve similis malis fias, quia multi sunt, neve inimicus multis, quia dissimiles sunt. Recede in te ipse quantum potes; cum his versare qui te meliorem facturi sunt, illos admitte quos tu potes facere meliores. Mutuo ista fiunt, et homines dum docent discunt.
passages.english: You are bound either to imitate or to hate. But both are to be avoided: do not become like the bad because they are many, and do not become an enemy to many because they are unlike you. Withdraw into yourself as far as you can; keep company with those who will make you better, and let in those whom you in your turn can make better. This works both ways, and people learn while they teach.

notes.note: Neither verb has an object in the Latin; the crowd of the section before is understood. The English leaves the object out as the Latin does.
notes.other_reading: You must either copy them or hate them

notes.latin: neve similis malis fias, quia multi sunt
notes.note: The “because” clause gives the reason one might be tempted, not Seneca’s reason for the warning. English leaves this as open as the Latin does.
notes.other_reading: do not grow like the bad just because there are many of them

notes.note: The Latin plays on “many” twice: the bad are many, and many are unlike. “To many” could also be heard as “to the many”, the same crowd; “you” after “unlike” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: nor an enemy to the many because they are different

notes.note: The last word is nominative and stresses the subject, “you yourself”. English cannot easily carry it beside “into yourself”, so it is not separately rendered.
notes.other_reading: Withdraw, you yourself, into yourself

notes.note: The verb form is an imperative of the deponent verb “to move among, to spend time with”, not an infinitive.
notes.other_reading: spend your time with those

notes.note: The verb is used of letting visitors into one’s house or presence, and “let in” keeps that.
notes.other_reading: welcome those

notes.note: The pronoun “you” is expressed in the Latin, which it need not be, and sets this clause against the one before. “In your turn” carries that stress.
notes.other_reading: those whom you can make better

notes.note: Literally “these things are done mutually”: the making better goes both ways.
notes.other_reading: These things are done in both directions

notes.note: This has the ring of a proverb and is often cited as one. No earlier source for it is known here (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: men learn by teaching

check.note: The expressed pronoun sets “you” against the “you” of the clause before: those who make you better, those whom you in turn can make better. The emphasis is lost.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “those whom you in your turn can make better”. The Latin expresses the pronoun, which it need not, and so sets this clause against the one before.

check.note: The Latin is simply “to many”. “The many” adds an article and a slightly political ring.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “an enemy to many”. The Latin has no article, and the note records “the many” as the other way to hear it.

check.note: “These things are done in both directions” is accurate but stiff.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “This works both ways”; the note keeps the literal wording.

passages.latin: Bene et ille, quisquis fuit - ambigitur enim de auctore -, cum quaereretur ab illo quo tanta diligentia artis spectaret ad paucissimos perventurae, 'satis sunt' inquit 'mihi pauci, satis est unus, satis est nullus'. Egregie hoc tertium Epicurus, cum uni ex consortibus studiorum suorum scriberet: 'haec' inquit 'ego non multis, sed tibi; satis enim magnum alter alteri theatrum sumus'.
passages.english: That man too put it well, whoever he was (for it is disputed who said it): when he was asked what was the aim of such great care over an art that would reach very few, he said, “A few are enough for me, one is enough, none is enough.” Epicurus put this third one excellently, when he was writing to one of the partners in his studies: “I write these things,” he said, “not for many, but for you; for we are a large enough theatre, each for the other.”

notes.note: The Latin has no verb: “well, that man too”. “Put it” is supplied. “Too” looks back to the saying of Democritus quoted in the section before.
notes.other_reading: Well said, too, by that man

notes.note: The Latin sets this aside between dashes; the English uses brackets. The noun is the author or originator of the saying.
notes.other_reading: for the author is uncertain

notes.latin: quo tanta diligentia artis spectaret ad paucissimos perventurae
notes.note: Literally “where such great care over an art that would reach very few was looking”. The noun can be an art, a craft or a skill; the future participle goes with “art”, not with “care”.
notes.other_reading: what was the point of taking such pains over a craft that only a handful would ever come to know

notes.note: Literally “no one is enough”. The paradox is in the Latin and is meant.
notes.other_reading: not even one is enough

notes.note: Again there is no verb: “excellently, this third one, Epicurus”; “put” is supplied, as with “well” above. It is the third of the three sayings promised in the section before. It survives as a fragment of Epicurus, known perhaps chiefly from this passage (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: This third saying, an excellent one, is Epicurus’s

notes.note: The noun is someone who shares a lot or a property with you, so a partner. The studies are his philosophical pursuits.
notes.other_reading: one of his fellow students

notes.note: No verb is expressed; “write” is supplied from the context of a letter. “These things” keeps the plural of the Latin, and “not for many” could also be “not for the many”.
notes.other_reading: these things are meant not for the many, but for you

notes.latin: satis enim magnum alter alteri theatrum sumus
notes.note: The noun is a theatre, and so the audience that fills one. The image is kept as “theatre”.
notes.other_reading: for each of us is audience enough for the other

check.note: “The author is in doubt” can be read as “the author doubts”. The Latin says there is dispute about who the author is.
check.decided: Accepted: the bracket now reads “for it is disputed who said it”, which cannot be taken to mean that the author doubts.

check.note: The first word is an adverb answering “well” earlier in the passage. Turning it into “an excellent one” loses the parallel and the step up.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Epicurus put this third one excellently”. So that the adverb answers “well”, the opening is changed to “That man too put it well”, and the same supplied verb serves both.

check.note: The Latin has no verb, and the pronoun at the head of the saying is plural, “these things”. “Write” is a fair supplement but is supplied, and “this” flattens the plural.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the plural is restored as “these things”. The supplied verb “write” stays, because the Latin clause has no verb and the saying comes from a letter; the note says that it is supplied.

passages.latin: Ista, mi Lucili, condenda in animum sunt, ut contemnas voluptatem ex plurium assensione venientem. Multi te laudant: ecquid habes cur placeas tibi, si is es quem intellegant multi ? introrsus bona tua spectent. Vale.
passages.english: These things, my Lucilius, are to be stored away in your mind, so that you may despise the pleasure that comes from the approval of the greater number. Many praise you: have you any reason to be pleased with yourself, if you are the kind of man whom many understand? Let your good things face inward. Farewell.

notes.note: The verb is used of laying up stores. “These things” are the three sayings just quoted in the letter.
notes.other_reading: must be laid up in your heart

notes.note: The first word is a comparative, “of more people”: the greater number, the majority, or simply a good many. “The greater number” is kept so that it stays distinct from the “many” that follows, a different Latin word. The noun is assent or approval, including applause.
notes.other_reading: from the applause of the many

notes.note: The opening word marks an open question, “have you anything”, with a hint that the answer is no. The phrase “to please oneself” means to be satisfied with oneself.
notes.other_reading: what reason have you to be satisfied with yourself

notes.latin: si is es quem intellegant multi
notes.note: The subjunctive describes a type: “the kind of man whom many understand”. Being understood by many is treated as a bad sign.
notes.other_reading: if you are a man the many can understand

notes.note: “Your good things” is taken as the subject of the verb “face, look”, as a house is said to face a direction: they should be turned inward, not toward an audience. The words could also mean “let them look at your good things within”, with people as the subject. The input has a stray space before the question mark and a small letter after it; a new sentence is read here.
notes.other_reading: let them look at your good things on the inside

check.note: The first word can be “of the majority” or simply “of a larger number of people, of many”. The English takes the first.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “the approval of the greater number” is kept as a deliberate choice. The Latin word is a comparative, “of more people”, and differs from the “many” of the next sentence, so the two are kept apart in English; the note gives “of the many” as the other reading.

check.latin: si is es quem intellegant multi
check.note: The Latin construction describes a type, “the kind of man whom many can understand”. The English states it as plain fact and loses that shade.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “if you are the kind of man whom many understand”. “The kind of man” gives the force of the Latin mood; “can” and “the many” are not added because the Latin has neither.

check.note: “Your goods” reads as possessions, and the sentence then makes little sense. What is meant is his good qualities, which should face inward and not towards an audience.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “Let your good things face inward”. “Face” is taken as suggested; “good things” is used, as in Ep. 5.9, because the Latin is the plain plural of “the good” and has no word for “qualities”.

passages.latin: 'Se contentus est sapiens.' Hoc, mi Lucili, plerique perperam interpretantur: sapientem undique submovent et intra cutem suam cogunt. Distinguendum autem est quid et quatenus vox ista promittat: se contentus est sapiens ad beate vivendum, non ad vivendum; ad hoc enim multis illi rebus opus est, ad illud tantum animo sano et erecto et despiciente fortunam.
passages.english: “The wise man is content with himself.” Most people, my dear Lucilius, interpret this wrongly: they push the wise man back on every side and force him inside his own skin. But a distinction must be drawn about what that saying promises and how far. The wise man is content with himself for living happily, not for living, since for living he has use for many things, and for living happily he has use only for a mind that is sound and held high and looks down on fortune.

notes.note: The Stoic claim that the wise man is enough for himself. “Contentus” means both satisfied and contained within. “Content with himself” is kept so that the same words can return in the next two sections; it means that he is enough for himself, not that he is pleased with himself.
notes.other_reading: The wise man is self-sufficient.

notes.note: A plain affectionate address. The English uses the ordinary form of address in a letter of today, which adds “dear”.
notes.other_reading: my Lucilius

notes.note: “Submovere” is to make someone move back, as a crowd is cleared out of the way, and “undique” is from or on every side. The English has him pressed back from every direction, which the image of the skin then completes. The words can also be read as removing him from everything around him.
notes.other_reading: they cut the wise man off from everything

notes.latin: quid et quatenus vox ista promittat
notes.note: “Vox” is a saying or phrase, and “promittat” is what it holds out or undertakes. “Promises” is kept.
notes.other_reading: what that phrase claims, and within what limits

notes.latin: ad hoc enim multis illi rebus opus est, ad illud tantum
notes.note: “Hoc” points to the nearer term (simply living) and “illud” to the further one (living happily). The English names each instead of writing “the latter” and “the former”, and gives “enim” as “since”.
notes.other_reading: for the latter he has use for many things, for the former only for

notes.note: “Opus est” is “has use for” here and in 9.14 and 9.15, because 9.14 sets “opus est” against “egere” and ties it to knowing how to use things. “Needs” would be more natural in this sentence alone, but in 9.14 it would run into “nothing is necessary to the wise man”.
notes.other_reading: he needs many things

notes.latin: animo sano et erecto et despiciente fortunam
notes.note: “Erecto” is raised up, unbowed, and can also mean alert; “held high” is used because “upright” would be heard as honest. “Despiciente” is literally looking down on. Fortune has no capital, since nothing here makes it a person.
notes.other_reading: a mind that is healthy, alert and scornful of fortune

check.note: “Erectus” here means raised up, lofty, unbowed. A reader of today takes “upright” of a mind to mean honest, which is a different quality.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a mind that is sound and held high and looks down on fortune”. “Erecto” describes a mind that is raised and unbowed, not an honest one, and “held high” also sits well beside “looks down on”.

check.latin: ad hoc enim multis illi rebus opus est
check.note: “Enim” is dropped: the Latin gives this clause as the reason for the distinction. The “For” of the draft is the “for” of purpose, and a reader may be unsure which it is.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “enim” is now “since”, and the sentence reads “not for living, since for living he has use for many things, and for living happily he has use only for a mind”. “For living” is kept throughout, where the suggestion changed to “in order to live”, so that the two terms of the distinction are named in the same words each time.

check.note: “Undique” is from every side, and “submovent” is move away, push back. “Cut off from everything” is stronger and names things, not directions.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “they push the wise man back on every side and force him inside his own skin”. The Latin speaks of directions and of moving him back, and this leads straight into the skin. The note keeps the other reading.

check.note: “Dear” is not in the Latin.
check.decided: Declined: the address keeps “dear”. Latin “mi” with a name is the everyday affectionate address in a letter, and the everyday English for that carries “dear”; without it the address is not English of today. The note records the literal form.

check.note: Found while settling: the Latin is impersonal (a distinction is to be drawn), and the draft gave it a first person plural subject.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a distinction must be drawn about what that saying promises and how far”. This keeps the impersonal form, and “distinction” is heard again when 9.14 speaks of the distinction of Chrysippus.

passages.latin: Volo tibi Chrysippi quoque distinctionem indicare. Ait sapientem nulla re egere, et tamen multis illi rebus opus esse: 'contra stulto nulla re opus est - nulla enim re uti scit - sed omnibus eget'. Sapienti et manibus et oculis et multis ad cotidianum usum necessariis opus est, eget nulla re; egere enim necessitatis est, nihil necesse sapienti est.
passages.english: I want to point out to you Chrysippus’s distinction as well. He says that the wise man is in want of nothing, and yet has use for many things: “on the other hand there is nothing the fool has use for, since he does not know how to use anything, but he is in want of everything.” The wise man has use for hands and eyes and many things necessary for daily use; he is in want of nothing. For to be in want is a matter of necessity; nothing is necessary to the wise man.

notes.note: Chrysippus was the third head of the Stoic school, in the third century BC (from memory, unchecked). “Quoque” adds his distinction to the one drawn in 9.13.
notes.other_reading: a distinction of Chrysippus too

notes.latin: sapientem nulla re egere, et tamen multis illi rebus opus esse
notes.note: The whole section rests on two Latin expressions for need: “egere” (to be in want, to feel a lack) and “opus est” (there is use or occasion for). “Is in want of” is kept for the first and “has use for” for the second throughout 9.13 to 9.15. English “need” would fit either and so blur the distinction.
notes.other_reading: the wise man lacks nothing, and yet needs many things

notes.note: Literally, for the fool there is use for nothing. The English turns it as “there is nothing the fool has use for” so that it is not heard as the idiom “has no use for”, which today means scorns.
notes.other_reading: the fool needs nothing

notes.note: This parenthesis explains why the fool has no “opus”: he cannot use anything. “Opus est”, “uti” here and “usum” below are different Latin words that all become “use” in the English; the link is in the thought and is kept on purpose. The Latin sets the words off as a parenthesis; the English uses commas.
notes.other_reading: since he knows how to make use of nothing

notes.note: The quotation marks are the editor’s. It is open whether the words of Chrysippus end here or whether the next sentence about hands and eyes is still his; the English follows the marks as given.
notes.other_reading: but he lacks everything

notes.note: Seneca calls these things “necessary” for daily use and then says nothing is necessary to the wise man. The tension is in the Latin and is not softened.
notes.other_reading: many things required for everyday use

notes.latin: egere enim necessitatis est, nihil necesse sapienti est
notes.note: The genitive says that being in want belongs to, or is a mark of, necessity, which can also mean compulsion. “Necessity” and “necessary” are kept so that the echo stays.
notes.other_reading: for to be in want is to be under compulsion, and nothing compels the wise man

check.note: In English of today “has no use for” means scorns, so “the fool has use for nothing” can be heard as the fool despising everything. The Latin says there is nothing he needs for any purpose.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the clause now reads “there is nothing the fool has use for, since he does not know how to use anything”, which is further from the idiom of scorn. “Has use for” is kept, and not “is of any use to”, because the same Latin phrase has the same English in the sentences on either side.

check.note: “Opus est” and “uti” (with “usum” below) are different Latin words, and all become “use”. The sentence about the fool then reads almost as saying the same thing twice, where the Latin explains one notion by another; the choice should be made openly.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “has use for” stays the fixed rendering of “opus est” throughout 9.13 to 9.15, as the suggestion allows, and “use” is kept for “uti”. The Latin gives not knowing how to use a thing as the reason for having no “opus” for it, so the link is in the argument; the note now says that three Latin words share the one English word.

passages.latin: Ergo quamvis se ipso contentus sit, amicis illi opus est; hos cupit habere quam plurimos, non ut beate vivat; vivet enim etiam sine amicis beate. Summum bonum extrinsecus instrumenta non quaerit; domi colitur, ex se totum est; incipit fortunae esse subiectum si quam partem sui foris quaerit.
passages.english: So, although he is content with himself, he has use for friends. He desires to have as many of them as possible, not in order to live happily, for he will live happily even without friends. The highest good does not look for equipment from outside; it is cultivated at home, it comes wholly from itself. It begins to be subject to fortune if it looks for any part of itself outside the house.

notes.note: The same “opus est” as in 9.13 and 9.14, so the same English. “Has use for friends” sounds more calculating in English than the Latin does; the next clause corrects it.
notes.other_reading: he needs friends

notes.note: “Cupit” is a strong word for wishing. “Desires” is used, not “wants”, so that it does not collide with “is in want of” (egere) in the section before.
notes.other_reading: he wants to have as many of them as he can

notes.note: “Instrumenta” are tools, gear or means. The English has “equipment”.
notes.other_reading: does not seek tools from outside

notes.note: “Colitur” can mean is tended or cultivated, or is worshipped, as a household god is worshipped at home. The English takes the first and keeps “at home” as the image.
notes.other_reading: it is worshipped at home

notes.note: Either it derives entirely from itself or it is a whole made of itself. The English takes the first, which answers “from outside” just before.
notes.other_reading: it is complete in itself

notes.latin: si quam partem sui foris quaerit
notes.note: “Foris” is outside the house and answers “domi”, at home. “Outside the house” keeps the image; “out of doors” would be heard today as in the open air.
notes.other_reading: if it looks for any part of itself outside

check.note: “Colitur” can also mean is worshipped or honoured, as in a household cult, not only is tended or cultivated. The English has to choose one.
check.decided: Accepted: “it is cultivated at home” is kept, as the suggestion allows, and the note on these words gives “it is worshipped at home” as the reading not taken. “Cultivated” fits a good that is grown at home and comes wholly from itself.

check.note: “Out of doors” today means in the open air. The Latin is the plain opposite of “domi”: outside the house.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “if it looks for any part of itself outside the house”. This keeps the answer to “at home” without the sense of open air.

check.note: The emphatic “ipso”, which is not in the “se contentus” of 9.13, is not rendered. A very small point.
check.decided: Declined: “content with himself” stands. “Se ipso” is the fuller form of the same reflexive as “se” in 9.13, and English “himself” already carries it; “alone” would say “solo”, which the Latin does not have, and the phrase has to match 9.13.

passages.latin: 'Quid ergo?' inquis 'si beatum se dixerit ille turpiter dives et ille multorum dominus sed plurium servus, beatus sua sententia fiet?' Non quid dicat sed quid sentiat refert, nec quid uno die sentiat, sed quid assidue. Non est autem quod verearis ne ad indignum res tanta perveniat: nisi sapienti sua non placent; omnis stultitia laborat fastidio sui. Vale.
passages.english: “What then?” you say. “If that man who is rich to his shame calls himself happy, and that one who is master of many but slave of more, will he become happy by what he himself thinks?” What matters is not what he says but what he thinks, and not what he thinks on one day but what he thinks constantly. But there is no reason for you to fear that so great a thing may come to someone unworthy: what is his own pleases no one but the wise man; all folly suffers from disgust with itself. Farewell.

notes.latin: ille turpiter dives et ille multorum dominus sed plurium servus
notes.note: The repeated “ille” points to two familiar types. “Turpiter dives” may mean rich by shameful means or rich in a shameful way; “rich to his shame” leaves both open and cannot be heard as merely very rich. “Multorum” and “plurium” can be people or things (slaves owned, or masters and passions served); “many” and “more” are left as open as the Latin.
notes.other_reading: the man whose wealth was basely won, and the man who owns many slaves but is a slave to more masters

notes.note: “Sententia” is an opinion held or delivered, a vote or a verdict, and “sentiat” in the reply is from the same root. The English gives both with “think” so that the reply can be heard to answer the question.
notes.other_reading: will he become happy by his own verdict?

notes.latin: Non quid dicat sed quid sentiat refert
notes.note: “Sentire” covers both to feel and to think or hold a view. “Thinks” is used all three times: the line of comedy quoted just before this section is about what a man thinks himself to be, and “feels” would suggest a passing mood.
notes.other_reading: What matters is not what he says but what he feels

notes.note: The great thing is being happy, carried over from the line of comedy quoted just before this section.
notes.other_reading: so great a prize

notes.note: “Sua” is neuter plural: his own things, which may be his possessions, his condition or his lot. The English keeps it as wide as the Latin.
notes.other_reading: no one but the wise man is satisfied with what he has

notes.note: “Laborat” is to be sick with something. “Fastidium” ranges from squeamish distaste to weariness. “Sui” is its object: disgust at itself.
notes.other_reading: all folly is sick with weariness of itself

check.note: “Sua sententia” in the question is answered by “sentiat” twice: the root is the same and the answer turns on it. The draft gives “verdict” and then “feels”, so the link is lost, and “feels” suggests mood where the Latin means to think or judge.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the question now ends “will he become happy by what he himself thinks?” and the reply reads “not what he says but what he thinks, and not what he thinks on one day but what he thinks constantly”. One English verb now serves “sententia” and “sentiat”, so the reply is heard to answer the question. “Thinks” is used and not “judges”, because the glossary keeps “judgment” for “iudicium” and “thinks” is the plainer word.

check.note: “Turpiter” says how he is rich: by base means, or in a disgraceful way. “Shamefully rich” can be heard in English as merely excessively rich.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “that man who is rich to his shame”. “Shame” is kept, to match “most shameful” for the same Latin root in Ep. 10.5, and the phrase can no longer be heard as very rich.

passages.latin: Sed ut more meo cum aliquo munusculo epistulam mittam, verum est quod apud Athenodorum inveni: 'tunc scito esse te omnibus cupiditatibus solutum, cum eo perveneris ut nihil deum roges nisi quod rogare possis palam'. Nunc enim quanta dementia est hominum! turpissima vota dis insusurrant; si quis admoverit aurem, conticiscent, et quod scire hominem nolunt deo narrant. Vide ergo ne hoc praecipi salubriter possit: sic vive cum hominibus tamquam deus videat, sic loquere cum deo tamquam homines audiant. Vale.
passages.english: But, to send this letter with some small gift as is my habit, what I found in Athenodorus is true: “Know that you are released from all desires at the point when you have come to ask god for nothing except what you can ask for openly.” For as things are, how great is the madness of people! They whisper the most shameful prayers to the gods; if anyone brings his ear close, they will fall silent, and what they do not want a human being to know they tell to god. See, then, whether this might not be a wholesome precept to give: live with people just as if god saw, speak with god just as if people heard. Farewell.

notes.note: A diminutive: a little present. In these early letters Seneca usually closes with a saying borrowed from another writer, and that is the gift.
notes.other_reading: with some little present

notes.note: A Stoic philosopher. More than one Athenodorus of Tarsus is known, and which is meant is not clear (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: in the writings of Athenodorus

notes.latin: verum est quod apud Athenodorum inveni
notes.note: The English keeps the literal statement that what was found in Athenodorus is true. It could be smoothed into an introduction of the saying.
notes.other_reading: here is a true saying that I found in Athenodorus

notes.note: “Solutum” is loosed or untied, as from bonds. “Cupiditates” are desires or cravings.
notes.other_reading: set free from all cravings

notes.note: The singular “deum” can be god or a god. The passage moves between the singular and the plural “dis”; each is kept as it stands, with “god” in lower case as the glossary has it.
notes.other_reading: you ask a god for nothing

notes.note: “Vota” are vows or wishes addressed to a god, so prayers in the sense of requests. “Turpissima” is most shameful or most foul.
notes.other_reading: they whisper the foulest wishes into the gods’ ears

notes.latin: quod scire hominem nolunt deo narrant
notes.note: “Homo” is a human being as against a god. The English has “human being” here and “people” for the plural, not “man” and “men”.
notes.other_reading: what they do not want a man to know they tell to a god

notes.latin: Vide ergo ne hoc praecipi salubriter possit
notes.note: “Vide ne” with the subjunctive can mean “take care that it does not” or, as a polite way of proposing something, “consider whether it does not”. The English takes the second, since Seneca goes on to give the precept.
notes.other_reading: So take care that this cannot be laid down as a healthy rule

notes.latin: sic vive cum hominibus tamquam deus videat
notes.note: “Sic” answers “tamquam” in both halves of the precept: in such a way, as if. English “as if” does most of that work, and “just” is added to carry the repeated “sic”. “Videat” and “audiant” are plain seeing and hearing, so “saw” and “heard”.
notes.other_reading: live with people in such a way as if god were watching, speak with god in such a way as if people were listening

check.latin: sic vive cum hominibus tamquam deus videat
check.note: The repeated “sic”, in such a way, which shapes the precept, is dropped in both halves. “As if god sees” is also slightly off as English.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the precept now reads “live with people just as if god saw, speak with god just as if people heard”. “Just” carries the repeated “sic”, since “in such a way as if” is not English of today, and the verbs are now “saw” and “heard”. “Watching” and “listening” are not used because the Latin verbs are plain seeing and hearing.

passages.latin: Iam clausulam epistula poscit. Accipe, et quidem utilem ac salutarem, quam te affigere animo volo: 'aliquis vir bonus nobis diligendus est ac semper ante oculos habendus, ut sic tamquam illo spectante vivamus et omnia tamquam illo vidente faciamus'.
passages.english: Now the letter calls for its close. Take one, and a useful and wholesome one at that, which I want you to fix in your mind: “We must hold some good man dear and keep him always before our eyes, so that we live just as if he were looking on and do everything as if he saw it.”

notes.note: A term from rhetoric for the close of a sentence or speech. Here it is the closing saying Seneca habitually adds to a letter.
notes.other_reading: its closing sentence

notes.latin: Accipe, et quidem utilem ac salutarem
notes.note: “Accipe” is “take” or “receive”, with “clausulam” understood, so the English supplies “one”. “Salutarem” is giving health or saving; the English has “wholesome”.
notes.other_reading: Here it is, and a useful and salutary one too

notes.note: Literally to fasten or nail to the mind.
notes.other_reading: to fasten to your mind

notes.latin: aliquis vir bonus nobis diligendus est
notes.note: The saying is that of Epicurus, as the next section says. “Diligere” is to esteem and love; its root sense is to pick out, and 11.10 goes on to say “choose” (elige). Some editors may print “eligendus” here (from memory, unchecked); the English translates the word as given, with “hold dear”.
notes.other_reading: We must choose some good man

notes.latin: tamquam illo spectante vivamus et omnia tamquam illo vidente faciamus
notes.note: Two different verbs, “spectare” (to watch, look on) and “videre” (to see), are kept distinct. “Just” carries the “sic” that stands before the first “tamquam”, as in the similar precept at Ep. 10.5.
notes.other_reading: so that we live as if he were watching and do everything as if he were looking at us

check.note: “Diligere” is to single out and hold in esteem, to love by choice. “Cherish” is warmer and more tender, and it hides the link with “choose” in 11.10; some editors have suspected “eligendus” here (from memory, unchecked).
check.decided: Partly accepted: “cherish” gives way to “hold dear”, which is esteem as much as tenderness. “Single out some good man to love” would give two verbs for the one Latin word, so the link with “choose” in 11.10 and the possible other text are left to the note.

check.note: “Poscere” is to demand or call for; “asks for” is weaker.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Now the letter calls for its close.”

check.note: Found while settling: “sic” before the first “tamquam” was not rendered, the same point the second reader raised on the similar precept at Ep. 10.5.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “so that we live just as if he were looking on”, with “just” for “sic” as in Ep. 10.5. The second “tamquam” has no “sic” and stays “as if”.

passages.latin: Hoc, mi Lucili, Epicurus praecepit; custodem nobis et paedagogum dedit, nec immerito: magna pars peccatorum tollitur, si peccaturis testis assistit. Aliquem habeat animus quem vereatur, cuius auctoritate etiam secretum suum sanctius faciat. O felicem illum qui non praesens tantum sed etiam cogitatus emendat! O felicem qui sic aliquem vereri potest ut ad memoriam quoque eius se componat atque ordinet! Qui sic aliquem vereri potest cito erit verendus.
passages.english: This, my dear Lucilius, is Epicurus’s precept. He gave us a guardian and a minder, and not without reason: a great part of wrongdoing is removed if a witness stands beside those who are about to do wrong. Let the mind have someone to revere, by whose authority it may make even its privacy purer. How fortunate is the man who corrects not only when he is present but even when he is thought of! How fortunate is the man who can revere someone in such a way that he composes and orders himself even at the memory of him! One who can revere someone in this way will soon be someone to be revered.

notes.note: Literally Epicurus prescribed this, or gave this as a precept. The verb is turned into a noun to match “precept” in Ep. 10.5.
notes.other_reading: This is what Epicurus taught

notes.note: A plain affectionate address, given in the ordinary English form, which adds “dear”, as at Ep. 9.13.
notes.other_reading: my Lucilius

notes.note: A “paedagogus” was the slave who escorted a boy to school and watched over his behaviour, not a teacher. “Tutor” would mislead, so the English has “minder”, the plain word for someone who looks after a child.
notes.other_reading: he gave us a guardian and a tutor

notes.latin: magna pars peccatorum tollitur, si peccaturis testis assistit
notes.note: The same word appears twice (“peccatorum”, “peccaturis”), so “wrongdoing” and “do wrong” are kept. “Sins” would bring in a Christian tone.
notes.other_reading: a great share of sins is done away with if a witness stands by those about to sin

notes.note: “Vereri” is respect tinged with awe or fear, which is why a witness deters. The word comes four times and ends in “verendus”, so one English word, “revere”, is kept throughout.
notes.other_reading: someone to stand in awe of

notes.note: “Secretum” is a place or state of being alone and unobserved, or the hidden inner part. “Sanctius” is purer, more blameless, or more holy and inviolable; the English takes the moral sense.
notes.other_reading: it may make even its solitude more holy

notes.note: “Felix” is lucky or blessed by fortune. “Fortunate” keeps “happy” for “beatus”, as the glossary has it.
notes.other_reading: O happy the man

notes.note: “Emendat” (corrects, makes better) has no object in the Latin, and the English leaves it without one. Those corrected are the people who have him before them or think of him.
notes.other_reading: but even when he is only in our thoughts makes us better

notes.latin: ad memoriam quoque eius se componat atque ordinet
notes.note: “Ad memoriam” may be “at the memory of him” or “by the standard of his memory”, as “ad regulam” is used in 11.10. The English takes the first.
notes.other_reading: that he shapes and orders himself even by the memory of him

check.note: “Emendat” has no object in the Latin; “others” is supplied. It is a likely reading, but the Latin leaves it open.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the supplied object is removed and the English now reads “the man who corrects not only when he is present but even when he is thought of”. The suggested “makes people better” would also supply an object, so the verb is left bare as in the Latin and the note says who is meant.

check.note: “Sanctus” of conduct is pure, blameless, inviolate. “Holy” gives a religious colour that the Latin need not have.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “it may make even its privacy purer”. “Purer” gives the moral sense without the religious colour and is plainer than “more blameless”; “privacy” is kept because “secretum” is the state of being unobserved, which is the point after the witness.

check.note: “Vereri” carries awe, a respectful fear, which is why a witness deters. “Respect” is consistent across all four uses but weak.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “respect” becomes “revere” in all four places, ending “will soon be someone to be revered”. “Revere” carries the awe, and unlike “stand in awe of” it has a plain passive for “verendus”, so one word can serve throughout.

check.note: A “paedagogus” is the slave who escorts and supervises a boy. “Minder” today may suggest a bodyguard or handler.
check.decided: Declined: “minder” stands. “Paedagogus” is one noun for the slave who both looked after a boy and watched his behaviour, and “minder” is the plain word of today for someone who looks after a child. “Attendant” alone drops the watching, and the suggested added clause about keeping in order is not in the Latin; the note explains the role.

check.note: “Dear” is not in the Latin.
check.decided: Declined: the address keeps “dear”, as at Ep. 9.13. Latin “mi” with a name is the everyday affectionate address in a letter, and the everyday English for that carries “dear”; a note records the literal form.

passages.latin: Elige itaque Catonem; si hic tibi videtur nimis rigidus, elige remissioris animi virum Laelium. Elige eum cuius tibi placuit et vita et oratio et ipse animum ante se ferens vultus; illum tibi semper ostende vel custodem vel exemplum. Opus est, inquam, aliquo ad quem mores nostri se ipsi exigant: nisi ad regulam prava non corriges. Vale.
passages.english: So choose Cato. If he seems to you too stiff, choose Laelius, a man of a more relaxed mind. Choose the man whose life and speech and very face, which carries his mind in plain view, have pleased you. Show him to yourself always, either as guardian or as example. Someone is needed, I say, against whom our character may measure itself: you will not straighten what is crooked except against a ruler. Farewell.

notes.note: Seneca does not say which Cato. It may be the younger Cato, the Stoic who died at Utica and whom Seneca often holds up, or the elder Cato the Censor, who is nearer in time to Laelius (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: So choose a Cato

notes.note: “Rigidus” is stiff, unbending or stern. The physical word is kept because it is set against “relaxed” (remissioris).
notes.other_reading: too stern

notes.note: Gaius Laelius, the friend of Scipio Aemilianus, known as “the Wise” (from memory, unchecked). “Animus” here is disposition or temper; the English keeps the glossary’s “mind”, so that the word is the same as in the next sentence.
notes.other_reading: Laelius, a man of gentler temper

notes.latin: ipse animum ante se ferens vultus
notes.note: Literally the face itself carrying the mind in front of it. “Ante se ferre” is an idiom for showing openly; “carries his mind in plain view” keeps the carrying and gives the sense.
notes.other_reading: the face itself, which shows his mind openly

notes.note: The same “opus est” that is “has use for” in Ep. 9.13 to 9.15. There is no contrast with “egere” here, so the English has plain “is needed”, and it keeps the impersonal form of the Latin. “Inquam” marks a point being repeated.
notes.other_reading: There is use, I repeat, for someone

notes.latin: ad quem mores nostri se ipsi exigant
notes.note: “Exigere ad” is to test or measure against a standard. “Mores” is character, habits or conduct. “Se ipsi” stresses that the character does the measuring itself.
notes.other_reading: by whom our habits may themselves be tested

notes.latin: nisi ad regulam prava non corriges
notes.note: A play on words. “Regula” is a straight edge and also a rule. “Prava” is crooked and also morally wrong. “Corrigere” is to straighten and also to correct; the English keeps the carpenter’s image.
notes.other_reading: you will not correct what is wrong except by a rule

check.latin: ipse animum ante se ferens vultus
check.note: “Ante se ferre”, like “prae se ferre”, is to display openly. The word for word English is hard to follow.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “and very face, which carries his mind in plain view”. This gives the sense of open display that the suggestion asks for and still keeps the image of carrying, which the brief asks to be kept.

check.note: Found while settling: “animus” was “temper” here and “mind” in the next sentence, where the glossary gives “mind” and the passage does not need another word.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a man of a more relaxed mind”. The glossary word serves here, and “mind” is now the same in this sentence and the next; the note gives “temper” as the other reading.

check.note: Found while settling: “opus est” is impersonal, and the draft gave it a first person plural subject.
check.decided: Accepted: the sentence now begins “Someone is needed”, which keeps the impersonal form of the Latin. The first person plural stays only where the Latin has it, in “nostri”.

passages.latin: Debeo hoc suburbano meo, quod mihi senectus mea quocumque adverteram apparuit. Complectamur illam et amemus; plena voluptatis, si illa scias uti. Gratissima sunt poma cum fugiunt; pueritiae maximus in exitu decor est; deditos vino potio extrema delectat, illa quae mergit, quae ebrietati summam manum imponit;
passages.english: I owe this to my country place near the city: my old age showed itself to me wherever I turned. Let us embrace it and love it; it is full of pleasure, if you know how to use it. Fruit is most welcome when it is slipping away; the beauty of boyhood is greatest at its close; those given over to wine are delighted by the last drink, the one that sinks them, the one that puts the finishing touch to drunkenness;

notes.note: A “suburbanum” is an estate or house in the country close to Rome. “Suburban” would mislead today.
notes.other_reading: my suburban villa

notes.note: A pluperfect with no object expressed (eyes or attention is understood). The English uses the simple past.
notes.other_reading: wherever I had turned my eyes

notes.note: A general “you” in the subjunctive (if one knows). The second person is kept as the Latin has it.
notes.other_reading: if one knows how to use it

notes.note: Literally “when they are fleeing”: the fruit is nearly over for the year, or is just going over. “Slipping away” keeps the image of flight without speaking of supply.
notes.other_reading: Fruit is most welcome when it is fleeing

notes.latin: pueritiae maximus in exitu decor est
notes.note: “Decor” is grace, charm or good looks. “In exitu” is as boyhood goes out.
notes.other_reading: boyhood has its greatest charm as it ends

notes.note: “Mergit” is plunges under or drowns. The object (the drinkers) is understood.
notes.other_reading: the one that drowns them

notes.note: An idiom from the workshop: to put the last hand to a work is to finish it off.
notes.other_reading: that lays the last hand on drunkenness
