notes.note: The section as given ends on a semicolon. The sentence runs on into section 5, which is not in the input, so the English ends on a semicolon too and is not rounded off.
notes.other_reading: the same words closed with a full stop

check.note: “Fugiunt” is are fleeing, are going: the season is ending or the fruit is passing. “Running out” speaks of supply and loses the image of flight; the Latin could also mean fruit just going over.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “Fruit is most welcome when it is slipping away”. This drops the talk of supply and keeps the flight in “fugiunt”, which the suggested “when it is going” would flatten; the note records both ways of taking it.

passages.latin: Itaque sic ordinandus est dies omnis tamquam cogat agmen et consummet atque expleat vitam. Pacuvius, qui Syriam usu suam fecit, cum vino et illis funebribus epulis sibi parentaverat, sic in cubiculum ferebatur a cena ut inter plausus exoletorum hoc ad symphoniam caneretur: 'bebiotai, bebiotai'.
passages.english: So every day must be ordered as if it were bringing up the rear of the column, and were completing and filling out life. Pacuvius, who made Syria his own by right of possession, whenever he had made the offerings for the dead to himself, with wine and those funeral feasts, used to be carried from dinner to his bedroom in such a way that, amid the applause of his kept men, this was sung to music: “Life has been lived, life has been lived.”

notes.note: A military idiom: “agmen cogere” is to close the marching column, to be the rearguard. The day is pictured as the last in the line of days.
notes.other_reading: as if it closed the series

notes.note: “Consummare” is to add up to a total and so to finish. “Explere” is to fill up to the full measure.
notes.other_reading: and rounded off and made up the full sum of life

notes.note: A legal joke. “Usus” is the continued possession by which a thing becomes one’s property, so “by right of possession”. Pacuvius is thought to have run Syria for years under Tiberius as deputy for a governor kept at Rome (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: who made Syria his own by long use

notes.latin: cum vino et illis funebribus epulis sibi parentaverat
notes.note: “Cum” with the pluperfect indicative marks a repeated act, hence “whenever”. “Parentare” is to make the yearly offerings to one’s dead; “sibi” says he made them to himself, as if already dead. “Illis” may mean the customary funeral feasts or those notorious feasts of his.
notes.other_reading: each time he had sacrificed to his own ghost with wine and the usual funeral banquet

notes.note: “Exoleti” were male slaves past boyhood kept for sex. “Kept men” is the nearest plain English, though it does not say that they were slaves.
notes.other_reading: amid the clapping of his male prostitutes

notes.note: “Symphonia” is a band of musicians or their playing: to an accompaniment.
notes.other_reading: to the accompaniment of a band

notes.note: The chant is Greek, written in Latin letters in this copy, and the English translates it. It is an impersonal perfect passive, literally “it has been lived”, that is, the life is over. “Life has been lived” keeps the impersonal form and the verb “live”, so that the link to “vixi” in the next section is plain.
notes.other_reading: He has lived, he has lived.

check.note: “Sibi” is to himself: he made the offerings for the dead to himself, as if already dead. “His own rites for the dead” can be read as rites of his own devising for other dead people, so the point may be missed.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “whenever he had made the offerings for the dead to himself, with wine and those funeral feasts”. “To himself” is what “sibi” says, and it is the point of the story.

check.note: The Latin gives Greek here, an impersonal perfect passive: life has been lived. The draft makes it personal and does not show that the chant was in Greek, though it keeps the link with “vixi” in 12.9.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the chant now reads “Life has been lived, life has been lived”, impersonal as the Greek is, and the note says that the words are Greek. “Has been lived” is used, not “is lived”, so that the tense is a finished past and the verb still answers “vixi” in 12.9.

check.note: “Long” is added. “Usu” is the legal term for ownership gained by continued possession, a sour joke about his tenure in Syria, and “by long use” does not convey it.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “who made Syria his own by right of possession”. “Long” is gone and “by right of” gives the legal tone; “possession” is used and not “occupation”, which in a province could be taken as military occupation.

check.note: “Exoleti” are grown male prostitutes or kept men. “Favourites” is a euphemism that softens the Latin.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “amid the applause of his kept men”. The note says exactly who they were.

passages.latin: Nullo non se die extulit. Hoc quod ille ex mala conscientia faciebat nos ex bona faciamus, et in somnum ituri laeti hilaresque dicamus, vixi et quem dederat cursum fortuna peregi. Crastinum si adiecerit deus, laeti recipiamus. Ille beatissimus est et securus sui possessor qui crastinum sine sollicitudine exspectat; quisquis dixit 'vixi' cotidie ad lucrum surgit.
passages.english: There was no day on which he did not carry himself out for burial. What he used to do from a bad conscience let us do from a good one, and as we go to sleep let us say, glad and cheerful: “I have lived, and I have finished the course that Fortune had given.” If god adds a tomorrow, let us receive it gladly. The happiest man, and the untroubled owner of himself, is the one who waits for tomorrow without anxiety; whoever has said “I have lived” rises every day to a gain.

notes.note: “Efferre” is the usual verb for carrying a body out to burial. The double negative “nullo non die” means on every single day. “Se efferre” can also mean to exalt oneself, which may be a second sense heard underneath.
notes.other_reading: Every single day he held his own funeral.

notes.note: “Conscientia” is awareness of what one has done, so conscience. The pair bad and good is kept as in the Latin.
notes.other_reading: out of a guilty awareness of himself

notes.latin: vixi et quem dederat cursum fortuna peregi
notes.note: A line of Vergil: the words of Dido before her death, Aeneid 4.653 (from memory, unchecked). This copy does not mark it as a quotation; the English puts it in quotation marks as the words to be said. Fortune has a capital because she is spoken of here as a giver.
notes.other_reading: I have lived, and I have run the course that fortune had assigned

notes.note: “Deus” is singular: god or a god. “Adiecerit” is throws in or adds, as an extra.
notes.other_reading: If a god throws in tomorrow as well

notes.note: “Sui” is taken with “possessor” (owner of himself) and “securus” as describing that owner: untroubled, secure. The glossary’s “free from care” is not used here because it cannot stand before “owner” without becoming unclear. “Securus sui” could also be read together, as unworried about himself.
notes.other_reading: and is untroubled about himself, his own master

notes.note: “Cotidie” (every day) can go with “rises” or with “has said”; the English takes it with “rises”. “Lucrum” is a term from accounts: each further day is entered as gain over and above what was counted on.
notes.other_reading: whoever has said “I have lived” every day gets up to pure gain

check.note: The Latin is an untroubled owner of himself. The draft can be misread as admitting to being free from care, and it is unclear what “free from care” attaches to.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “The happiest man, and the untroubled owner of himself, is the one who waits for tomorrow without anxiety”. “Securus” describes the owner, and the new wording cannot be taken as an admission; the note says why the glossary’s “free from care” is not used here.

check.note: “Cotidie” stands between the saying and the rising and can go with either: has said it every day, or rises every day. The English has to choose.
check.decided: Accepted: “rises every day” is kept, as suggested, and the note on these words records the other reading, in which the saying is what happens every day.

check.note: “Lucrum” here is a gain over and above what was reckoned on. “Rises to a profit” is not clear English.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “rises every day to a gain”. “A gain” is plainer than “a profit” and stays a noun as “lucrum” is, where “something gained” is looser; the note explains that each further day counts as gain.

check.latin: vixi et quem dederat cursum fortuna peregi
check.note: The Latin as given has no quotation marks here and the English adds them, reasonably after the verb of saying. The words are a line of Vergil, Aeneid 4.653, the last words of Dido (from memory, unchecked), which a note should name; a pronoun is supplied after “given”.
check.decided: Accepted: the quotation marks stay, the note names the source, and the line now ends “the course that Fortune had given”, without the supplied pronoun.

passages.latin: Non potest athleta magnos spiritus ad certamen afferre qui numquam suggillatus est: ille qui sanguinem suum vidit, cuius dentes crepuere sub pugno, ille qui subplantatus ad versarium toto tulit corpore nec proiecit animum proiectus, qui quotiens cecidit contumacior resurrexit, cum magna spe descendit ad pugnam.
passages.english: An athlete who has never been beaten black and blue cannot bring great courage to the contest. The one who has seen his own blood, whose teeth have rattled under a fist, the one who has been tripped and has taken his opponent on the whole of his body, who, thrown down, has not thrown away his spirit, who has got up more defiant every time he has fallen: he goes down to the fight with great hope.

notes.note: Literally “great breaths”, that is, high mettle or confidence. “Great” is used here and again for magna spe at the end so that the echo can be heard, and “courage” keeps this word apart from animum, which is “spirit” later in the sentence.
notes.other_reading: high spirits; great confidence

notes.note: The word means bruised by blows, with a second sense of being insulted or jeered at. The English takes the physical sense, which the rest of the sentence supports.
notes.other_reading: who has never been bruised; who has never been jeered at

notes.note: The verb is a sound word: to rattle, crack or clatter. “Rattled” leaves open whether the teeth broke.
notes.other_reading: whose teeth have cracked under a fist

notes.latin: subplantatus ad versarium toto tulit corpore
notes.note: The copy splits one word in two: the second and third words here are read as a single word meaning “opponent”. The phrase is literally “bore his opponent with whole body”. The English takes the body as the athlete’s own, flat on the ground under the other man; it can also be the opponent’s, coming down with all his weight.
notes.other_reading: who has been tripped and has taken his opponent’s full weight on his body

notes.note: A play on one verb: proiectus is thrown to the ground and proiecit is threw away, gave up. “Thrown down” and “thrown away” keep the echo. Animum is “spirit” here, as the glossary allows where the sense is courage.
notes.other_reading: who, flung to the ground, did not give up his spirit

notes.note: The verb form can be present or perfect; the English takes it as a general present. “Goes down” is the set phrase for entering the arena or the ring, and the literal verb is kept.
notes.other_reading: he has gone down to the fight; he enters the fight

check.note: The Latin as given splits one word in two, and it should be read as adversarium. The English already reads it so; the point is only that the slip was seen.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps “his opponent”, reading the two words as one, and the note on the phrase records the slip in the copy.

check.note: The whole body can be the athlete’s own or can go with the opponent, whose whole weight he takes. “Borne with his whole body” is hard to picture and “his” can be either man.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “has taken his opponent on the whole of his body”. The words for “whole body” go most simply with the verb, so the body is the athlete’s own; the other reading, the opponent’s full weight, is given in the note.

check.note: The “great” of the first words is answered by the “great hope” of the last, and “high” followed by “great” loses the echo.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “great courage” at the start and keeps “great hope” at the end, since the Latin uses one adjective in both places.

check.note: The play on words is kept, but “throw down his spirit” is not natural English, and the tenses shift from “has seen” to “was thrown, got up, fell” though the Latin perfects are one series.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “who, thrown down, has not thrown away his spirit, who has got up more defiant every time he has fallen”. “Thrown” still comes twice for the one Latin verb, and all the verbs are in one tense as in the Latin.

passages.latin: Quaedam ergo nos magis torquent quam debent, quaedam ante torquent quam debent, quaedam torquent cum omnino non debeant; aut augemus dolorem aut praecipimus aut fingimus. Primum illud, quia res in controversia est et litem contestatam habemus, in praesentia differatur. Quod ego leve dixero tu gravissimum esse contendes; scio alios inter flagella ridere, alios gemere sub colapho. Postea videbimus utrum ista suis viribus valeant an imbecillitate nostra.
passages.english: So some things torment us more than they ought, some torment us before they ought, some torment us when they ought not to torment us at all; we either increase our pain, or anticipate it, or invent it. The first of these, since the matter is in dispute and we have a case formally before the court, should be put off for the present. What I call slight you will insist is very grave; I know that some people laugh under the lash and others groan at a blow of the fist. Later we will see whether those things are strong by their own strength or by our weakness.

notes.note: The word is the one for torture on the rack. It comes three times, and “torment” is used each time so that the threefold division can be followed.
notes.other_reading: torture us

notes.latin: aut augemus dolorem aut praecipimus aut fingimus
notes.note: The three verbs answer the three kinds just listed. Praecipimus is literally “take beforehand”, here “anticipate”. Dolorem is “pain” by the glossary, though here it covers distress of mind as well as of body.
notes.other_reading: we either enlarge our distress, or take it in advance, or make it up

notes.note: “That first thing” is the first of the three kinds: the things that torment more than they ought. “The first of these” makes the reference plain.
notes.other_reading: That first point

notes.note: A term of Roman court procedure: the stage at which both parties have formally stated the issue before a judge. Seneca jokes that he and Lucilius are parties to a pending lawsuit on this question. The English gives the sense in plain words.
notes.other_reading: we have a suit in which issue has been joined

notes.note: Literally light and heavy, in the sense of slight and serious; “slight” and “grave” are used because English does not call a suffering light or heavy in this way. The first verb is a future perfect, and the superlative can be “very grave” or “gravest”.
notes.other_reading: What I call light you will maintain is the heaviest of all

notes.note: Literally “among whips”, that is, while being flogged. “Under the lash” is the English phrase for it.
notes.other_reading: some people laugh among the whips

notes.note: A blow with the fist or a box on the ear, a lesser thing than the whips just mentioned.
notes.other_reading: at a punch; at a slap

notes.latin: suis viribus valeant an imbecillitate nostra
notes.note: The Latin sets being strong by one’s own forces against being strong by another’s weakness. The paradox of the second is kept.
notes.other_reading: whether those things owe their power to their own strength or to our weakness

check.note: The Latin is a legal term for an issue formally stated before a judge. “A suit formally joined” is lawyers’ English that a reader of today will not follow, and “over it” is added.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “a case formally before the court”, with “over it” removed. “Already” and “on it” from the suggestion are left out because the Latin has neither.

check.note: “Among the whips” is word for word but odd English; the sense is laughing while being flogged. “Men” is not in the Latin, which says only “some”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “some people laugh under the lash”. The note gives the literal “among whips”.

check.note: “Cuff” for a blow is dated and can be misread as a handcuff or a shirt cuff. The Latin word is a blow with the fist or a box on the ear.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “groan at a blow of the fist”. “Single” in the suggestion is not in the Latin and is left out.

check.latin: Quod ego leve dixero tu gravissimum esse contendes
check.note: “Light” and “heavy” are literal, but English does not speak of a light or heavy suffering in this way, so the sentence reads oddly.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now has “slight” and “very grave” for the two adjectives, and “insist” for the verb. “Grave” still carries the idea of weight, and the note gives the literal light and heavy.

passages.latin: Illud praesta mihi, ut, quotiens circumsteterint qui tibi te miserum esse persuadeant, non quid audias sed quid sentias cogites, et cum patientia tua deliberes ac te ipse interroges, qui tua optime nosti, 'quid est quare isti me complorent? quid est quod trepident, quod contagium quoque mei timeant, quasi transilire calamitas possit? est aliquid istic mali, an res ista magis infamis est quam mala?' Ipse te interroga, 'numquid sine causa crucior et maereo et quod non est malum facio?'
passages.english: Do this for me: whenever people stand around you trying to persuade you that you are wretched, think not about what you hear but about what you feel, and take counsel with your own power to endure, and be the one to question yourself, you who know your own affairs best: “Why is it that these people are lamenting over me? Why is it that they are alarmed, that they even fear infection from me, as if misfortune could jump across? Is there any evil in that, or is that thing ill spoken of rather than evil?” Be the one to question yourself: “Am I perhaps in torment and grieving without cause, and making an evil of what is not one?”

notes.note: The verb means to make good, guarantee or perform something for someone. The English takes the plain “do this for me”.
notes.other_reading: Guarantee me this

notes.note: The word covers both wretched and pitiable. The English takes “wretched”.
notes.other_reading: that you are miserable; that you are to be pitied

notes.note: The verb can mean what you feel (by sense) or what you think (your own view). Set against “what you hear”, it is taken as “feel”.
notes.other_reading: but about what you yourself think

notes.note: Literally “deliberate with your own patientia”. The noun can be the power to endure or the fact of undergoing something, so the sense is either to consult your own power to bear the thing or to consult what you are in fact going through. The English takes the first.
notes.other_reading: consult what you are yourself going through

notes.note: The pronoun ipse stresses that the questioner is to be Lucilius and not the bystanders. The same words come again in the command at the end, and “be the one to question yourself” is used both times.
notes.other_reading: and ask yourself

notes.note: Literally contagion from the speaker’s own person: he is treated as a source of infection by touch, which prepares the image of misfortune jumping across.
notes.other_reading: that they even fear catching it from me

notes.note: Infamis is “of ill repute”. “Evil” is kept for mala and for the word for evil just before and after, so that the one word runs through the passage.
notes.other_reading: is that thing more notorious than bad?

notes.note: The form is passive, of one who is tortured, and can also be used of one who tortures himself. “In torment” leaves both open, as the Latin does. The verb is not the one rendered “torment” in Ep. 13.5.
notes.other_reading: Am I perhaps tormenting myself and grieving without cause

notes.note: Literally to make evil what is not. It can mean turning something into an evil or treating it as one; “making” is kept.
notes.other_reading: and treating as an evil what is not one

check.note: The word ipse stands first and is emphatic: Lucilius himself, not the bystanders, is to put the questions. The English drops it here and in the same phrase earlier in the passage.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “be the one to question yourself” in both places, so that the stress on who is asking is kept and the repeated Latin phrase has one English phrase.

check.note: The Latin word is infection passed on by touch, which prepares the image of misfortune jumping across. “Contact” keeps the touch and loses the disease.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “that they even fear infection from me”. This names the disease, as the point asks, and keeps a noun where the Latin has a noun.

check.note: The noun can be the power to endure or what is in fact being undergone, set against what is heard from others. The English takes the first and is opaque as it stands.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “take counsel with your own power to endure”, which keeps the first reading and makes it plain. The second reading is given in the note.

check.latin: res ista magis infamis est quam mala
check.note: The English is clumsy for a plain contrast of two adjectives, and the Latin “that thing” is flattened to “the thing”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “or is that thing ill spoken of rather than evil?”, without the hyphens of the suggestion. “Evil” is kept so that the one word runs through the passage.

check.note: The form can be passive or reflexive in sense, being tormented or tormenting oneself. The reflexive suits the active verbs that follow, and the English has chosen the passive without saying so.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “in torment”, which does not say who does the tormenting, since the Latin form does not say either. A note gives both readings.

passages.latin: 'At enim futurum est.' Primum dispice an certa argumenta sint venturi mali; plerumque enim suspicionibus laboramus, et illudit nobis illa quae conficere bellum solet fama, multo autem magis singulos conficit. Ita est, mi Lucili: cito accedimus opinioni; non coarguimus illa quae nos in metum adducunt nec excutimus, sed trepidamus et sic vertimus terga quemadmodum illi quos pulvis motus fuga pecorum exuit castris aut quos aliqua fabula sine auctore sparsa conterruit.
passages.english: “But it is to come.” First look carefully at whether there are sure proofs of an evil to come. For most of the time we are troubled by suspicions, and we are made fools of by rumour, the thing that so often finishes a war, but finishes individuals far more. That is how it is, my Lucilius: we are quick to side with opinion. We do not refute the things that lead us into fear, nor do we search them, but we panic, and turn and run like those whom dust raised by a herd in flight has driven from their camp, or whom some tale spread about with no source has terrified.

notes.note: An imagined objection from Lucilius. No subject is stated: “it” is the trouble he fears, which the next sentence names as an evil to come. The words can be a claim that it will happen or a reminder that it lies ahead; “it is to come” allows both.
notes.other_reading: “But it is going to happen.”

notes.note: The noun covers proofs, evidence and signs. The English takes “sure proofs”.
notes.other_reading: reliable signs; definite evidence

notes.latin: conficere bellum solet fama, multo autem magis singulos conficit
notes.note: A play on one verb used twice: to finish (settle, decide) a war, and to finish off (wear out, destroy) a person. “Finishes” is used both times. “Far more” is a matter of degree in the Latin, not of frequency.
notes.other_reading: rumour, which often decides a war but much more surely destroys individuals

notes.note: The verb is to go over to a side, and so to assent. “Opinion” follows the glossary: it is what is supposed or believed as against the fact, and it could be a person’s own unexamined belief or what people are saying.
notes.other_reading: we are quick to agree with what is commonly believed

notes.latin: non coarguimus illa quae nos in metum adducunt nec excutimus
notes.note: The first verb is a court word, to prove false or convict. The second is literally to shake out, as a garment is shaken out to see what is hidden in it, and so to search or examine; “search” gives the sense.
notes.other_reading: we do not show up as false the things that bring us into fear, nor shake them out

notes.note: Literally to turn the back, the soldier’s phrase for running away. In English that phrase suggests ignoring something, so “turn and run” is used.
notes.other_reading: and turn our backs

notes.latin: pulvis motus fuga pecorum exuit castris
notes.note: The last two words are a soldier’s phrase, literally “stripped of the camp”: troops are made to abandon their camp and lose it. The picture is of soldiers who take a dust cloud raised by fleeing animals for an enemy. Pecorum is any herd or flock, cattle or sheep.
notes.other_reading: whom dust raised by cattle in flight has stripped of their camp

notes.note: Literally “without an author”: a story no one will answer for. “Source” is used here and for the same noun in Ep. 13.13.
notes.other_reading: with no one to vouch for it

check.note: The objector may mean that the trouble is still to come, not that it will certainly happen, and the English leans to the second. “It” has nothing to refer to when the section stands alone.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “But it is to come”, which fits both senses. “The trouble” is not supplied, because the Latin states no subject and the next sentence at once names the evil to come.

check.note: Bare “opinion” is unclear to a reader of today; the Latin means what is supposed as against fact. The verb with this case is to side with or assent to.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “quick to side with opinion”. “Opinion” stays because the glossary settles it for this Latin word, and the note explains it as what is supposed as against fact.

check.note: The Latin verb is stronger than testing: it is to show something up as false, to refute or convict it. “Put to the proof” only says that no test is made.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “do not refute”, one plain word with the strength the point asks for.

check.note: The Latin idiom, shaking out a garment to search it, means to examine thoroughly. “Shake them out” is literal and does not carry that sense in English.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now has “search them” for the second verb, without “through”. “Search” keeps the picture of going through someone’s clothes, and the note gives the literal shaking out.

check.note: The Latin “but” is dropped, and the contrast between not examining and panicking is left to a semicolon.
check.decided: Accepted: “but” is restored before “panic”, so that the contrast the Latin states is stated in the English.

check.note: In English, turning one’s back suggests ignoring something. The Latin is the military phrase for running away.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “turn and run”, and the note gives the literal phrase.

check.latin: pulvis motus fuga pecorum exuit castris
check.note: The Latin is the standard military phrase for making soldiers abandon their camp, and “stripped of their camp” is literal and strange. The animals are any herd or flock, wider than “cattle”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “dust raised by a herd in flight has driven from their camp”. The note gives the literal “stripped of the camp”.

passages.latin: Ergo spem ac metum examina, et quotiens incerta erunt omnia, tibi fave: crede quod mavis. Si plures habebit sententias metus, nihilominus in hanc partem potius inclina et perturbare te desine ac subinde hoc in animo volve, maiorem partem mortalium, cum illi nec sit quicquam mali nec pro certo futurum sit, aestuare ac discurrere. Nemo enim resistit sibi, cum coepit impelli, nec timorem suum redigit ad verum; nemo dicit 'vanus auctor est, vanus [est]: aut finxit aut credidit'. Damus nos aurae ferendos; expavescimus dubia pro certis; non servamus modum rerum, statim in timorem venit scrupulus.
passages.english: So weigh hope and fear, and whenever everything is uncertain, favour yourself: believe what you prefer. If fear has more votes, lean rather to the other side all the same, and stop disturbing yourself, and keep turning this over in your mind: that the greater part of mortals, though they have nothing evil upon them and nothing evil that is certain to come, seethe and run this way and that. For no one resists himself once he has begun to be pushed, and no one brings his fear down to the truth; no one says “The source is worthless, worthless: he either made it up or believed it.” We give ourselves to the breeze to be carried; we take fright at doubtful things as though they were certain; we do not keep things in proportion: a slight unease at once turns into fear.

notes.note: The verb comes from the tongue of a balance, so “weigh” keeps the image. It can also mean simply “examine”.
notes.other_reading: So examine hope and fear

notes.note: The image is of a jury or a senate voting: fear “will have more votes”. The noun can also mean opinions or considerations. The Latin verb is future; the English has a present after “if”.
notes.other_reading: If fear has more arguments on its side

notes.note: The Latin says “to this side” and does not name it: it is the side just recommended, hope and what one would prefer to believe. Straight after fear’s votes, “this side” would read in English as fear’s, so the English has “the other side”.
notes.other_reading: lean rather to this side all the same

notes.latin: cum illi nec sit quicquam mali nec pro certo futurum sit
notes.note: The pronoun is singular, agreeing with “the greater part”; the English has a plural. The second half is literally “nor is going to be for certain”, and it can mean either that nothing evil is certain to come or that it is certain none will come. The English takes the first.
notes.other_reading: though nothing evil has befallen them and it is certain none will

notes.note: The first verb is to seethe or boil, used of water and of an anxious mind; here it is agitation, not anger. The second is to run in different directions. Both images are kept.
notes.other_reading: are in a fever and rush about

notes.note: The verb can be “bring back to” or “bring down to, reduce to”. The English takes the second, which suits the talk of proportion at the end of the section.
notes.other_reading: and no one brings his fear back to the truth

notes.note: The square brackets are the editor’s mark for a word he thinks should be deleted, and the second “is” is left out. The adjective is literally “empty”, and so idle or untrustworthy. “Source” is the same noun so rendered in Ep. 13.8.
notes.other_reading: “The man who reports it is empty, empty”

notes.note: The second verb is bare: “he believed”. The sense is that he either invented the story or took it on trust from someone else.
notes.other_reading: either he invented it or he was taken in by it

notes.note: The noun is a light wind, and is also used of a breath of rumour or popular favour. The plain image is kept.
notes.other_reading: We let ourselves be carried along by every breath of rumour

notes.note: Literally “the measure of things”: the true scale of each thing. “Keep things in proportion” is the English phrase for it.
notes.other_reading: we do not keep the measure of things

notes.note: The last word is literally a small sharp stone, such as one in a shoe, and so a nagging unease. The English “scruple” now means a moral qualm, so it is avoided, and the image of the stone is given up. Literally the unease “comes into fear”.
notes.other_reading: a pebble of doubt at once becomes a fear

check.note: Coming straight after “If fear has more votes”, “this side” reads in English as fear’s side. The Latin points back to the side just recommended, believing what one prefers.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “lean rather to the other side all the same”, and no words are added to name the side. The note says that the Latin has “this side” and what it points to.

check.note: “In a ferment” is dated, and “run about” is weak for the frantic movement to and fro that the second verb describes.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “seethe and run this way and that”. “Run” is kept from the draft because the Latin verb is the plain word for running.

check.latin: nec timorem suum redigit ad verum
check.note: The verb can be “bring back to” or “reduce to, cut down to”. The second fits the talk of measure at the end of the section, and the English has taken the first.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “brings his fear down to the truth”. This takes the sense of reducing without adding the image of cutting, which the Latin verb does not have; the other reading is in the note.

check.note: The square brackets are an editor’s sign that the second “is” should be deleted, and the English leaves it out. The bare repetition is in the Latin, though “unreliable, unreliable” reads awkwardly.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “The source is worthless, worthless”, which is nearer to the literal “empty” and reads more easily when repeated.

check.note: “The measure of things” is literal and opaque. The sense is that the true scale of things is lost.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “do not keep things in proportion”, the ordinary English phrase for the same thought, which keeps both “keep” and “things” from the Latin.

passages.latin: Pudet me ibi sic tecum loqui et tam lenibus te remediis focilare. Alius dicat 'fortasse non veniet': tu dic 'quid porro, si veniet? videbimus uter vincat; fortasse pro me venit, et mors ista vitam honestabit'. Cicuta magnum Socratem fecit. Catoni gladium assertorem libertatis extorque: magnam partem detraxeris gloriae.
passages.english: I am ashamed to be talking with you like this, and to be reviving you with such mild remedies. Let someone else say “Perhaps it will not come.” As for you, say: “And what if it does come? We will see which of the two wins. Perhaps it is coming on my side, and that death will bring honour to my life.” Hemlock made Socrates great. Wrest from Cato the sword that championed freedom: you will have taken away a great part of his glory.

notes.note: This word, “there”, has nothing clear to point to in the opening sentence, and editors have doubted it (from memory, unchecked). The English leaves it untranslated and does not guess at a sense.
notes.other_reading: I am ashamed, at that point, to be talking with you like this

notes.note: The verb is to revive someone by warmth, to nurse back to life. “Reviving” is used; the word can carry a note of coddling.
notes.other_reading: to be nursing you with such gentle remedies

notes.note: A command to Lucilius, set against what someone else may say. “As for you” is added so that “say” reads as a command and not as a statement.
notes.other_reading: You say:

notes.note: “Which of the two”: the speaker and the thing that is coming.
notes.other_reading: We will see which of us wins

notes.note: The verb form can be present (“comes”) or perfect (“has come”), and the phrase can be “on my side” or “for my benefit”. The English takes the present and “on my side”, which suits the contest in the clause before.
notes.other_reading: perhaps it has come for my benefit

notes.note: Only here does the passage say that the feared thing is death. The verb is from the family of the word the glossary renders “what is honourable”; “bring honour to” is used. “My” is supplied: the Latin says only “life”.
notes.other_reading: that death will make life honourable

notes.note: Socrates was put to death at Athens by being made to drink hemlock.
notes.other_reading: It was the hemlock that made Socrates great

notes.note: The middle word is a legal one: the person who formally lays claim to someone as free in court. “Championed” gives that sense of acting for another. Cato the Younger killed himself with his sword rather than submit to Caesar; the Latin says only “of freedom”, which can be his own or that of Rome.
notes.other_reading: the sword that made good his claim to freedom

check.note: The word means “there”, not “here”, and has nothing clear to point to in this sentence; it may be corrupt (the second reader says this from memory, unchecked). The draft writes “here” and smooths the difficulty over.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “to be talking with you like this”, with no word for ibi. The note says that the word does not make clear sense in the Latin as given and that editors have doubted it (from memory, unchecked).

check.note: The Latin word is the legal one for a person who formally claims someone as free. “Claimed his freedom” can be read today as “took his freedom away”, the opposite of the Latin, and “his” is added.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the sword that championed freedom”, to the same effect as the second suggestion. It can no longer be read as taking freedom away, and “his” is gone because the Latin has no possessive.

check.note: “Of us” is supplied. The Latin is “which of the two”, the speaker and the thing that is coming.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “which of the two wins”.

check.note: The phrase can be “for my benefit” or “on my side”, which suits the image of a contest just before. The verb can also be perfect, “it has come”, though the present fits better.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “it is coming on my side”, which continues the contest of the clause before. The other sense and the other tense are in the note.

check.note: “Man” is not in the Latin and the phrase is stiff.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Let someone else say”.

check.note: Found while settling: “You say:” reads in English as a statement, but the Latin is a command to Lucilius.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “As for you, say:”. The three added words make the command plain and are recorded in a note.

passages.latin: Fateor insitam esse nobis corporis nostri caritatem; fateor nos huius gerere tutelam. Non nego indulgendum illi, serviendum nego; multis enim serviet qui corpori servit, qui pro illo nimium timet, qui ad illud omnia refert.
passages.english: I admit that it is planted in us to hold our own body dear; I admit that we hold it in our guardianship. I do not deny that it should be indulged; I deny that we should be its slaves. For the man who is a slave to his body, who fears too much for it, who measures everything by it, will be a slave to many.

notes.note: The noun is “dearness”: affection, holding something precious. “Hold dear” is used so that the link with the word “dear” in the next section of the letter (Ep. 14.2) can be heard.
notes.other_reading: a fondness for our own body is planted in us

notes.note: A legal phrase: to act as guardian, as of a ward who cannot look after himself. The image is kept.
notes.other_reading: that we are charged with looking after it

notes.note: The verb is to be kind to, to make allowances for, to humour. “Indulged” is meant without the modern sense of spoiling.
notes.other_reading: that we should be kind to it

notes.note: The verb is the one for being a slave, and it comes three times in the sentence; “slave” is used each time. The Latin is impersonal, and the English gives it the first person plural of the first sentence.
notes.other_reading: I deny that it should be served

notes.note: “Many” can be masculine (many masters, many people) or neuter (many things). The English leaves it as open as the Latin.
notes.other_reading: will be a slave to many masters; will be a slave to many things

notes.note: Literally “refers everything to it”: makes the body the standard by which everything is judged.
notes.other_reading: who refers everything to it

check.note: This word is picked up by the word for “dear” in the next section of the letter (Ep. 14.2), and “fondness” hides the link.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “it is planted in us to hold our own body dear”, so that “dear” answers “dear” in Ep. 14.2.

check.note: “Refers everything to it” is a Latinism and says little in English. The sense is making the body the standard by which everything is judged.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “who measures everything by it”, and the note gives the literal wording.

check.note: The word for “many” can be masculine, many masters, or neuter, many things, and “many” alone reads as many people. The Latin leaves it open.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps “will be a slave to many”, as the point allows, because the Latin does not choose between masters and things. The note gives both.

passages.latin: Sic gerere nos debemus, non tamquam propter corpus vivere debeamus, sed tamquam non possimus sine corpore; huius nos nimius amor timoribus inquietat, sollicitudinibus onerat, contumeliis obicit; honestum ei vile est cui corpus nimis carum est. Agatur eius diligentissime cura, ita tamen ut, cum exiget ratio, cum dignitas, cum fides, mittendum in ignes sit.
passages.english: This is how we ought to conduct ourselves: not as though we ought to live for the sake of the body, but as though we could not live without the body. Too great a love of it unsettles us with fears, loads us with anxieties, exposes us to insults. What is honourable is cheap to the man to whom his body is too dear. Let it be cared for with the greatest diligence, but in such a way that, when reason demands it, when dignity demands it, when good faith demands it, it must be thrown into the flames.

notes.note: Literally “to carry ourselves thus”. “This is how” gives the “thus”, which the two “as though” clauses then explain.
notes.other_reading: We ought to conduct ourselves not as though

notes.note: The verb “live” is understood from the clause before and is supplied.
notes.other_reading: but as though we could not do without the body

notes.note: The noun covers insults and humiliating treatment. The verb is to throw in the way of, to expose to.
notes.other_reading: lays us open to humiliations

notes.latin: honestum ei vile est cui corpus nimis carum est
notes.note: A play on price: vile is cheap and carum is dear, both of cost and of affection. English “cheap” and “dear” keep both senses, and “dear” answers “hold dear” in Ep. 14.1. Honestum is “what is honourable”, by the glossary.
notes.other_reading: the man who values his body too highly sets little value on what is honourable

notes.note: The first noun is standing or self-respect; the second is good faith, loyalty or one’s pledged word. The English takes “dignity” and “good faith”. The verb “demands” is given once in the Latin (in the future tense) and is repeated.
notes.other_reading: when self-respect, when loyalty demands it

notes.note: Literally “it is to be sent into fires”, in the plural. The image is of giving the body up to burning, and it is kept as an image.
notes.other_reading: it must be sent into the fire

check.note: The first word, “in this way”, is not translated, though nothing is lost in sense.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now begins with “This is how”, followed by a colon and the two “as though” clauses.

check.note: “Sent” is weak for the Latin verb here and “it is to be” is stiff.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “it must be thrown into the flames”. “Flames” is kept for the Latin plural, where the suggestion has “the fire”.

check.note: The noun can be loyalty to a person or cause, or keeping one’s word. “Good faith” has a legal ring in English and narrows it.
check.decided: Declined: the Latin noun covers both keeping one’s word and being true to a person, and “good faith” still allows both, while “loyalty” would drop the first. The note gives “loyalty” as the other reading.

passages.latin: Denique consilium rerum omnium sapiens, non exitum spectat; initia in potestate nostra sunt, de eventu fortuna iudicat, cui de me sententiam non do. 'At aliquid vexationis afferet, aliquid adversi.' Non damnat latro cum occidit.
passages.english: Finally, in everything the wise man looks to the intention, not the outcome. The beginnings are in our power; on the result Fortune passes judgment, and I do not allow her a verdict on me. “But she will bring some harassment, some adversity.” A robber does not condemn when he kills.

notes.note: Literally “the plan of all things”. The first noun is plan, considered intention or deliberate purpose; “intention” is used, and “of all things” is given as “in everything”.
notes.other_reading: the wise man looks to the plan of every action

notes.note: “Beginnings”: how a thing is set about, as against how it turns out.
notes.other_reading: the first steps are in our power

notes.note: Fortune sits as a judge here, so she has a capital and “she”, as the glossary allows where she is personified. “Passes judgment” begins the court image that “verdict” and “condemn” continue.
notes.other_reading: the result is decided by fortune

notes.latin: cui de me sententiam non do
notes.note: A court phrase, literally a refusal to give her a verdict about the speaker. It is taken to mean that he does not allow Fortune the right to pronounce on him. The construction is unusual and could be read otherwise.
notes.other_reading: to whom I do not allow a vote on my case

notes.note: The verb has no stated subject. The English takes it to be Fortune, from the clause before, and the reply about the robber suits that; it could also be the course of action being recommended.
notes.other_reading: “But it will bring some harassment, some adversity.”

notes.note: The first verb is the court word for finding guilty. The point, left unstated, is that a blow from Fortune is violence and not a verdict on the man. The bare image is kept.
notes.other_reading: A robber does not pass sentence on a man when he kills him

check.note: The Latin is “of all things, in everything”, not specifically actions. The first noun is the considered intention behind a thing, and “plan” is thinner.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “in everything the wise man looks to the intention, not the outcome”.

check.latin: cui de me sententiam non do
check.note: The Latin must mean that he does not allow Fortune a verdict on himself. The word for word English can be read as handing her a verdict, which makes little sense.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “do not allow her a verdict on me”. The note keeps the warning that the construction is unusual.

check.note: The verb has no expressed subject. It may be Fortune, or “it”, the course of life under discussion or the outcome, and the English has chosen Fortune.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps “she”, as the point allows, and the note states the choice. Fortune is the nearest subject, and the reply about the robber answers a charge against her.

check.note: The court image runs through three words, for judging, for a verdict and for finding guilty. “Pass sentence” blurs the third with “passes judgment” two lines above.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “A robber does not condemn when he kills”, so that the three court words have three English words.

check.note: Fortune has a capital here, but the same word is in lower case in Ep. 16.5. The Latin gives no capital in either place, and one spelling is asked for across the project.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the capital stays here, where Fortune sits as a judge, and Ep. 16.5 now has a capital too, since there she is obeyed like a master. The glossary keeps lower case where fortune is not personified, so a single spelling for every passage is not adopted.

passages.latin: Liquere hoc tibi, Lucili, scio, neminem posse beate vivere, ne tolerabiliter quidem, sine sapientiae studio, et beatam vitam perfecta sapientia effici, ceterum tolerabilem etiam inchoata. Sed hoc quod liquet firmandum et altius cotidiana meditatione figendum est: plus operis est in eo ut proposita custodias quam ut honesta proponas. Perseverandum est et assiduo studio robur addendum, donec bona mens sit quod bona voluntas est.
passages.english: I know that this is clear to you, Lucilius: that no one can live happily, or even tolerably, without the study of wisdom, and that the happy life is brought about by wisdom made complete, but a tolerable life even by wisdom begun. But this, which is clear, must be made firm and fixed deeper by daily practice: there is more work in keeping to what you have resolved than in resolving on what is honourable. One must persevere and add strength by constant study, until what is a good intention becomes a good mind.

notes.note: A word from the courts, used when a case is clear enough to decide. It returns in the next sentence and “clear” is used both times.
notes.other_reading: I know you are satisfied of this

notes.note: Literally “zeal for wisdom” or “pursuit of wisdom”, a Latin way of saying philosophy. The same noun returns at the end of the section, so “study” is used in both places, though the Latin word is wider than study from books.
notes.other_reading: without the pursuit of wisdom; without philosophy

notes.note: “Completed” or “perfected” wisdom, set against wisdom merely begun. “Made complete” keeps the pair of finished and started.
notes.other_reading: by perfect wisdom

notes.note: The noun is practice, rehearsal or exercise as much as reflection. The English takes “practice”.
notes.other_reading: by daily reflection

notes.latin: ut proposita custodias quam ut honesta proponas
notes.note: A play on one verb: proposita are things resolved on, and proponas is to resolve on. “Resolved” and “resolving” keep it. Honesta is plural, “honourable things”, here “what is honourable”.
notes.other_reading: in keeping your resolutions than in making honourable ones

notes.note: The same noun as in the first sentence; here it could equally be effort or application. “Study” is kept. The verbs are impersonal, hence “one must”.
notes.other_reading: by constant effort

notes.latin: donec bona mens sit quod bona voluntas est
notes.note: The word for mind here is mens, not the animus of the glossary; bona mens is a set phrase for a sound, good state of mind. The other noun is will, wish or intention; “intention” is used because “a good will” can be misread. The Latin has the plain verb “is” in both halves, and “becomes” brings out the change after “until”.
notes.other_reading: until what is a good will is a good mind

check.latin: donec bona mens sit quod bona voluntas est
check.note: The verb after “until” means “comes to be”, and a second “is” loses the change that the sentence is about. “A good will” is also odd today and can even be read as a testament.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “until what is a good intention becomes a good mind”. “Good” still stands in both halves, as in the Latin.

check.note: The noun is eager pursuit or devotion, not only study in the book sense. The draft keeps “study” for both places where it occurs, which is consistent, but takes the narrower sense.
check.decided: Declined: the Latin has the same noun twice, and “study” is the one English word that works in both places. The suggested “pursuit” and “effort” would give two words for one, and “constant pursuit” cannot stand in English without an object. The wider sense is recorded in the note.

passages.latin: Quidquid est ex his, Lucili, vel si omnia haec sunt, philosophandum est; sive nos inexorabili lege fata constringunt, sive arbiter deus universi cuncta disposuit, sive casus res humanas sine ordine impellit et iactat, philosophia nos tueri debet. Haec adhortabitur ut deo libenter pareamus, ut fortunae contumaciter; haec docebit ut deum sequaris, feras casum.
passages.english: Whichever of these is the case, Lucilius, or even if all of them are, one must do philosophy. Whether the fates bind us by an inexorable law, or god, the arbiter of the universe, has arranged everything, or chance drives and tosses human affairs about without order, philosophy ought to protect us. It will urge us to obey god willingly, and Fortune defiantly; it will teach you to follow god and bear chance.

notes.note: “These” are the three possibilities raised by an objector in the section before: fate, a ruling god, or chance.
notes.other_reading: Whatever is true among these

notes.note: Literally “or if all these are”. It is taken as “even if all of them hold together”.
notes.other_reading: or if all these things exist

notes.note: An impersonal form, “there must be philosophising”. It is kept impersonal with “one must”.
notes.other_reading: we must be philosophers

notes.note: The adjective is literally “not to be moved by entreaty”; the English uses the same word, “inexorable”. The noun is plural, “the fates”, and the plural is kept.
notes.other_reading: whether the fates bind us by a law that no prayer can move

notes.note: The first noun is a judge or umpire with full discretion, and so a ruler or master; “arbiter” is kept. “God” is lower case and has no article, here and in the next sentence, so that one being is meant throughout; Latin has no articles, and “a god” is equally possible.
notes.other_reading: or a god who rules the universe has arranged everything

notes.note: The verb “obey” has to be carried over from the clause before, giving the paradox of obeying Fortune defiantly: giving way to what she does without giving in. The adverb is stubbornly or unyieldingly. Fortune has a capital because she is obeyed like a master, as in Ep. 14.16 where she judges.
notes.other_reading: and to submit to fortune without yielding

notes.note: The Latin moves from the first person plural in the clause before to “you” (singular) here, and the change is kept.
notes.other_reading: it will teach you to follow god and put up with chance

check.note: One adjective is unpacked into a clause and “prayer” is brought in by name. That is true to the make-up of the word, but it is more than the Latin says and a little ornate.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “by an inexorable law”, one adjective for one adjective, with no prayer named. The suggested “a law that cannot be moved” would lose the sense of pleading that the Latin word has and the English word keeps.

check.note: The same word is “a god” here and then “god” twice in the next sentence, so a reader may think two different beings are meant. “Arbiter” is also a Latinism.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “or god, the arbiter of the universe, has arranged everything”, so that “god” is the same throughout. “Arbiter” is kept because it is an English word and carries the sense of one who decides, which “ruler” would lose.

check.note: Found while settling: “fortune” is in lower case here, though she is obeyed like a master and has a capital in Ep. 14.16.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Fortune” with a capital, as the glossary asks where she is personified.

passages.latin: Sed non est nunc in hanc disputationem transeundum, quid sit iuris nostri si providentia in imperio est, aut si fatorum series illigatos trahit, aut si repentina ac subita dominantur: illo nunc revertor, ut te moneam et exhorter ne patiaris impetum animi tui delabi et refrigescere. Contine illum et constitue, ut habitus animi fiat quod est impetus.
passages.english: But now is not the time to cross over into this discussion: what is ours to decide if providence is in command, or if the chain of the fates drags us along bound, or if the sudden and the unforeseen are the masters. I return now to this: to warn you and urge you not to let the impulse of your mind slip away and grow cold. Keep hold of it and set it firm, so that what is an impulse becomes a settled state of mind.

notes.note: A legal phrase, literally “what is of our right”: what falls under a person’s own authority. “Ours to decide” gives the sense.
notes.other_reading: what lies within our own right

notes.note: Literally “the series of the fates drags (us) tied on”. The first noun is a row or linked sequence; “chain” suits the dragging. “Us” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: if the sequence of the fates pulls us along in bonds

notes.note: Two words of nearly the same meaning for what comes suddenly, standing for chance. Two different English words are used so that neither is dropped.
notes.other_reading: if sudden and unexpected events hold sway

notes.note: The first noun is a rush, drive or onset; “impulse” is used, and “mind” for the second noun by the glossary, though “spirit” would also suit. Both words return in the last sentence with the same English.
notes.other_reading: the ardour of your spirit

notes.note: Literally “slip down and cool off”. Both images are kept.
notes.other_reading: to sink and go cold

notes.note: The first verb is to hold together, hold in or keep hold of; the second is to set up, make stand, settle. It is open whether the first means restraining the impulse or keeping it from escaping; the English takes the second.
notes.other_reading: Hold it in check and settle it

notes.note: A technical term (the Latin for the Greek hexis): a lasting condition of the mind, as against a passing movement. The English “habit” would suggest mere custom, so “settled state” is used.
notes.other_reading: a habit of the mind

check.note: “Within our own right” is a literal version of a legal phrase and is not clear English. The sense is what remains for a person to decide.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “what is ours to decide”, and the note gives the literal legal phrase.

check.note: The Latin word is “this”, pointing forward to the question then stated, and “that” slightly suggests a discussion already mentioned.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “into this discussion”. The opening is turned to “now is not the time” so that “this” does not come twice in the clause.

passages.latin: Si vis vacare animo, aut pauper sis oportet aut pauperi similis. Non potest studium salutare fieri sine frugalitatis cura; frugalitas autem paupertas voluntaria est. Tolle itaque istas excusationes: 'nondum habeo quantum sat est; si ad illam summam pervenero, tunc me totum philosophiae dabo'. Atqui nihil prius quam hoc parandum est quod tu differs et post cetera paras; ab hoc incipiendum est. 'Parare' inquis 'unde vivam volo.' Simul et parare disce: si quid te vetat bene vivere, bene mori non vetat.
passages.english: If you want to have time for your mind, you must either be poor or be like a poor man. Wholesome study cannot be carried on without a concern for frugality; and frugality is voluntary poverty. So away with those excuses: “I do not yet have as much as is enough; if I reach that sum, then I will give myself wholly to philosophy.” And yet nothing should be acquired before this thing that you put off and acquire after everything else; one must begin with this. “I want,” you say, “to acquire something to live on.” At the same time learn to acquire as well: if something forbids you to live well, it does not forbid you to die well.

notes.note: The noun can be dative (“be free for the mind”, have leisure to attend to it) or ablative (“be free in mind”). The English takes the dative.
notes.other_reading: If you want to be free in mind

notes.note: The Latin word for poor means of small means, not destitute; the next section sets it against a stronger word. “Poor” and “poverty” are kept.
notes.other_reading: you must either be a man of small means

notes.note: This construes two ways: “wholesome study cannot be carried on”, with the adjective attached to the noun, or “study cannot become wholesome”, with the adjective as predicate. The English takes the first, since the adjective stands beside the noun and the pair names philosophy as the study that heals. The adjective is giving health or saving.
notes.other_reading: Study cannot do you good without a concern for frugality

notes.note: One verb runs through the rest of the section in four forms: to get, acquire or provide. “Acquire” is used each time so that the reply to the objector can be followed. What is to be acquired first is philosophy.
notes.other_reading: nothing should be got ready before this

notes.note: Literally something to live from: the means of living.
notes.other_reading: the means to live

notes.note: The sentence is very compressed and not certain. Literally “at the same time also learn to acquire”, and the verb has no object: it may be a living, got alongside philosophy, or philosophy itself, of which the same verb has just been used, or the art of acquiring, which philosophy teaches. The English supplies no object.
notes.other_reading: Learn to get that too, at the same time; or: Learn while you acquire

notes.latin: si quid te vetat bene vivere, bene mori non vetat
notes.note: “Live well” can mean live comfortably or live rightly, and the first sense seems to be turned against the objector’s wish for a living. “Live well” and “die well” leave the play open.
notes.other_reading: if anything prevents you from living in comfort, it does not prevent you from dying well

check.note: The adjective can go with the noun, wholesome study cannot take place, or with the verb, study cannot be made wholesome and cannot do good. The English takes the first.
check.decided: Declined: the draft stands. In the Latin the adjective sits next to its noun, and the two together name philosophy, the study that heals; the other reading is given in the note in the words suggested.

check.note: The Latin gives the verb no object, and the English supplies “that”, a living. The same verb has just been used of philosophy itself, so what is to be got is open, and the reader should not be given a resolved version without a note.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “At the same time learn to acquire as well”, with no object supplied. The note sets out what the missing object could be.

check.note: The chain on one verb is kept as “get” throughout, but “getting after” can be read as a phrasal verb and the clause stumbles.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now has “acquire” for all four uses of the verb, and the clause reads “this thing that you put off and acquire after everything else”.

check.note: English says “begin with”, not “begin from”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “one must begin with this”.

passages.latin: Non est quod nos paupertas a philosophia revocet, ne egestas quidem. Toleranda est enim ad hoc properantibus vel fames; quam toleravere quidam in obsidionibus, et quod aliud erat illius patientiae praemium quam in arbitrium non cadere victoris? Quanto hoc maius est quod promittitur: perpetua libertas, nullius nec hominis nec dei timor. Ecquid vel esurienti ad ista veniendum est?
passages.english: There is no reason for poverty to call us back from philosophy, or even destitution. For those who hurry towards this must bear even hunger. Some have borne it in sieges, and what other reward was there for that endurance than not falling into the conqueror’s power? How much greater is this that is promised: unending freedom, and fear of no one, neither man nor god. Should one not come to these things even hungry?

notes.note: A stronger word than the one for poverty: actual want, lacking the necessities. The English takes “destitution”.
notes.other_reading: not even real want

notes.note: “This” is neuter and unnamed: the goal just spoken of, philosophy and what it promises.
notes.other_reading: those who are hastening to this goal

notes.note: The noun is the will or discretion of someone who may do with a person as he pleases. The English takes “power”.
notes.other_reading: not to be at the victor’s mercy

notes.note: The adjective is unbroken or continuous, and so lasting. The English takes “unending”.
notes.other_reading: lasting freedom; unbroken freedom

notes.latin: nullius nec hominis nec dei timor
notes.note: Literally “fear of no one, neither of man nor of god”. The word for no one can also be neuter, “of nothing”. It is taken of persons, as the two nouns suggest.
notes.other_reading: fear of nothing, neither of man nor of god

notes.latin: Ecquid vel esurienti ad ista veniendum est
notes.note: The opening word marks an urgent question and carries no negative. The English adds “not” to show that the answer expected is yes, because a bare “must one” would read in English as a protest. The verb is impersonal and the participle is literally “to one who is hungry”.
notes.other_reading: Must one, then, come to these things even hungry?

check.note: The opening word only marks a question and the Latin has no negative. The English adds “not” to show that the answer expected is yes; the force is probably right, but it is a choice.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English keeps “Should one not come to these things even hungry?”, as the point allows, because a bare “Must one” would read in English as a protest and reverse the force. The note now says that “not” is supplied and gives the closer wording as the other reading.

passages.latin: Ceterum adeo mihi placet temptare animi tui firmitatem ut e praecepto magnorum virorum tibi quoque praecipiam: interponas aliquot dies quibus contentus minimo ac vilissimo cibo, dura atque horrida veste, dicas tibi 'hoc est quod timebatur?'
passages.english: But I am so much in favour of testing the firmness of your mind that, following the precept of great men, I shall give a precept to you as well: set some days in between on which, content with the scantiest and cheapest food and with coarse and rough clothing, you say to yourself, “Is this what was feared?”

notes.note: Placet can express liking or a settled decision. The English takes it as approval, which is the weaker of the two senses.
notes.other_reading: so resolved on testing

notes.latin: e praecepto magnorum virorum tibi quoque praecipiam
notes.note: The noun and the verb share a root, so “precept” is used twice. Quoque goes with tibi: what the great men laid down for others is now laid down for Lucilius as well. The great men are not named in this section; Epicurus is named later in the letter (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: following the teaching of great men, to instruct you as well

notes.note: Interponere is to put something in between other things: the days are set into ordinary life.
notes.other_reading: set aside a number of days

notes.note: Minimo is least in amount; vilissimo is cheapest or commonest.
notes.other_reading: the smallest amount of the commonest food

notes.note: Durus of cloth is stiff or coarse; horrida is rough, bristly, shaggy to the touch.
notes.other_reading: stiff and shaggy clothing

notes.note: The verb is an impersonal passive in the imperfect: no one is named as the one who feared. The English keeps it impersonal.
notes.other_reading: Is this what you were afraid of?

check.note: Placet can be liking or a decision. “So set on” takes the second sense and sounds more determined than the Latin need be.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “so much in favour of testing”, which states approval without adding resolve. The note records the stronger sense.

check.note: Quoque follows tibi, so the sense is “to you as well”. With “too” at the end the English can be read as “a precept as well as something else”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “give a precept to you as well”, so that “as well” attaches to Lucilius. “Precept” is kept, not “prescribe”, because the Latin noun and verb share a root and the echo should be heard.

check.note: “At intervals” is not a separate word in the Latin. It repeats what the verb (“put in between”) already says.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “set some days in between”, and “at intervals” is gone.

check.note: “Hard clothing” is not natural English, since durus of cloth means coarse or stiff. The atque is also reduced to a comma.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “coarse and rough clothing”, with the “and” of the Latin restored.

passages.latin: Non est nunc quod existimes me dicere Timoneas cenas et pauperum cellas et quidquid aliud est per quod luxuria divitiarum taedio ludit: grabattus ille verus sit et sagum et panis durus ac sordidus. Hoc triduo et quatriduo fer, interdum pluribus diebus, ut non lusus sit sed experimentum: tunc, mihi crede, Lucili, exultabis dipondio satur et intelleges ad securitatem non opus esse fortuna; hoc enim quod necessitati sat est dabit et irata.
passages.english: There is no reason now for you to think that I mean dinners in the style of Timon and poor men’s rooms and whatever else there is by which luxury plays, out of boredom with riches: let that pallet be a real one, and the rough cloak, and the bread hard and coarse. Bear this for three or four days, sometimes for more days, so that it is not play but a test: then, believe me, Lucilius, you will leap for joy, filled for two coppers, and you will understand that for freedom from care there is no need of Fortune; for this, which is enough for necessity, she will give even when angry.

notes.note: An adjective from Timon, the Athenian known for hating mankind and living apart. It seems to name a fashionable meal of mock austerity (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: Timon’s dinners

notes.note: Said to be small rooms in rich houses fitted out like a poor man’s room, for playing at poverty (from memory, unchecked). Cella is any small plain room.
notes.other_reading: paupers’ cells

notes.note: Taedio is taken as a cause (“out of boredom”) with divitiarum depending on it. Divitiarum could instead go with luxuria. Ludit is echoed by lusus below, so the English has “plays” and “play”.
notes.other_reading: the luxury of riches plays out of boredom

notes.latin: grabattus ille verus sit et sagum
notes.note: A grabattus is a low, cheap bed; a sagum is a coarse woollen cloak worn by soldiers and by poor men. “Rough” is used for the cloak because “coarse” serves for the bread in the same sentence.
notes.other_reading: let the camp bed be a real one, and the soldier’s cloak

notes.note: Sordidus is dirty, mean, low. Of bread it is taken as the dark loaf of the lowest grade, not as literally soiled.
notes.other_reading: bread that is hard and dirty

notes.note: Literally “for three days and for four days”. The English gives the sense, stretches of three or four days, with “or”.
notes.other_reading: for three days and for four days

notes.note: A dupondius was a small coin worth two asses. The ablative is price or means. Satur is a bare adjective, “full”, so no “at being” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: fed full on two pennies’ worth

notes.latin: ad securitatem non opus esse fortuna
notes.note: Fortune is personified here, since she is “angry” in the next clause, so the capital is used. Securitas is “freedom from care” as in the glossary.
notes.other_reading: that peace of mind does not need good fortune

notes.latin: hoc enim quod necessitati sat est
notes.note: Hoc can point back to the meal just described (“this, which is enough”) or simply lead into the relative clause (“that which is enough”). The English takes the first. “Necessity” is kept for necessitas because “need” already renders opus esse in the clause before.
notes.other_reading: for what is enough for need

check.note: Timoneas is an adjective: dinners of the Timon kind. The possessive suggests dinners that Timon himself gave.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “dinners in the style of Timon”.

check.note: “Cells” suggests a prison or a monastery, and “paupers” is stronger than pauperes, people of small means. The reader will not see that these are rooms.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “poor men’s rooms”.

check.note: Divitiarum is taken with taedio but could go with luxuria. The English choice is the likelier, but it is a choice.
check.decided: Accepted: the English stands as “luxury plays, out of boredom with riches”, and the note records the other reading, “the luxury of riches plays out of boredom”.

check.note: A sagum is a coarse woollen cloak, often but not only a soldier’s. “Soldier’s” is an explanation folded into the text.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “soldier’s” is removed and the English now reads “the rough cloak”. “Rough” is used and not “coarse” because “coarse” already describes the bread in the same sentence.

check.note: “At a time” is added. “Three and four” copies the Latin et where English says “or”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “for three or four days”. The note keeps the literal “for three days and for four days”.

check.latin: hoc enim quod necessitati sat est
check.note: Hoc is dropped: the sense is “this much, namely what is enough for need”. “Necessity” is also stiffer than the plain “need”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “this” is restored and the English now reads “for this, which is enough for necessity”. “Necessity” stays because “need” already renders a different Latin phrase (opus esse) in the clause just before, and one English word for two Latin words would blur the sentence.

check.note: Found while settling: “at being filled” turned a bare adjective (satur, “full”) into a stated cause of the joy.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “you will leap for joy, filled for two coppers”, which adds no reason that the Latin does not give.

passages.latin: In omnes personas hic exardescit affectus; tam ex amore nascitur quam ex odio, non minus inter seria quam inter lusus et iocos; nec interest ex quam magna causa nascatur sed in qualem perveniat animum. Sic ignis non refert quam magnus sed quo incidat; nam etiam maximum solida non receperunt, rursus arida et corripi facilia scintillam quoque fovent usque in incendium. Ita est, mi Lucili: ingentis irae exitus furor est, et ideo ira vitanda est non moderationis causa sed sanitatis. Vale.
passages.english: This passion flares up against all persons; it is born of love as much as of hatred, no less in serious matters than in play and jokes; and what matters is not how great the cause it is born from but what kind of mind it reaches. So with fire: it does not matter how great it is but what it falls on; for solid things do not take even the greatest fire, while things that are dry and catch fire easily nurse even a spark all the way to a blaze. So it is, my Lucilius: the outcome of enormous anger is madness, and therefore anger is to be avoided not for the sake of moderation but for the sake of sanity. Farewell.

notes.note: “This passion” is anger, the subject of the saying of Epicurus quoted just before. “Passion” for affectus follows the glossary.
notes.other_reading: this emotion blazes up

notes.note: Persona is a person in a given role or standing, so the phrase may mean people of every kind. The English keeps the plain “all persons”.
notes.other_reading: against persons of every kind

notes.note: Quo is “to what place”: what the fire lands on.
notes.other_reading: where it falls

notes.note: The perfect states a general truth from experience, so the English uses the present. Solida is neuter plural, “solid things”, such as sound timber or stone; it is kept general.
notes.other_reading: solid timbers have been known to resist even the largest fire

notes.note: Corripi is “to be seized”. The Latin does not say by what, and the English supplies “fire” from the sentence.
notes.other_reading: things that are dry and easy to seize

notes.latin: scintillam quoque fovent usque in incendium
notes.note: Fovere is to keep warm, to cherish. “Nurse” keeps the image.
notes.other_reading: feed even a spark until it becomes a conflagration

notes.note: Furor is raving madness; the saying of Epicurus just before uses a different word for madness. Exitus is the way out, the end or outcome.
notes.other_reading: the end of huge anger is frenzy

notes.note: Sanitas is both health and soundness of mind. “Sanity” is chosen because it answers “madness”. Moderatio is keeping within measure.
notes.other_reading: not for the sake of self restraint but for the sake of health

check.note: The Latin says “against all persons”. “Of every kind” is an interpretation of personas (roles, characters) that may be right but is not stated.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “against all persons”, and the note records “persons of every kind” as the other reading.

check.note: This is a perfect of general truth, parallel to the present fovent. The English perfect reads like a report of past cases, and “taken in” is unclear for catching fire.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “solid things do not take even the greatest fire”, a present to match “nurse” in the second half.

check.note: Two qualities joined by et (“dry and easy to seize”) become one restricting the other. “Easily caught” does not say by what.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “things that are dry and catch fire easily”, two qualities side by side as in the Latin.

check.note: “Huge anger” is not a natural English pairing.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “enormous anger”.

passages.latin: Aliud propositum est declamantibus et assensionem coronae captantibus, aliud his qui iuvenum et otiosorum aures disputatione varia aut volubili detinent: facere docet philosophia, non dicere, et hoc exigit, ut ad legem suam quisque vivat, ne orationi vita dissentiat vel ipsa inter se vita; unus sit omnium actio[dissentio]num color [sit]. Maximum hoc est et officium sapientiae et indicium, ut verbis opera concordent, ut ipse ubique par sibi idemque sit. 'Quis hoc praestabit?' Pauci, aliqui tamen. Est enim difficile [hoc]; nec hoc dico, sapientem uno semper iturum gradu, sed una via.
passages.english: Those who declaim and angle for the approval of a ring of listeners have one purpose, those who hold the ears of young men and men of leisure with varied or rapid discussion have another: philosophy teaches doing, not saying, and it demands this, that each person live by his own law, that his life not be at odds with his speech, nor his life itself at odds with itself; let all actions be of one colour. This is both the greatest duty of wisdom and its greatest sign: that deeds agree with words, that the man himself be everywhere consistent with himself and one and the same. “Who will achieve this?” Few, but some all the same. For it is difficult; and I am not saying that the wise man will always go at one pace, but that he will go by one road.
