notes.note: “One purpose, another” can mean that the two groups differ from each other, or more loosely that both differ from philosophy, which follows after the colon. The English keeps the literal shape and adds no link.
notes.other_reading: Declaimers have a different aim, and so do those who hold the ears of the young: philosophy, though, teaches doing

notes.note: Corona is the ring of bystanders around a speaker. Captare is to hunt or fish for.
notes.other_reading: fishing for the applause of the crowd standing round

notes.note: Otiosi are people with leisure, with time on their hands. The word can carry blame but need not, so the English has “men of leisure”.
notes.other_reading: of young men and idlers

notes.note: Varia is changing or wide ranging. Volubilis is rolling, rapid, and can be heard as praise (“fluent”) or as blame (“glib”); “rapid” leaves that open.
notes.other_reading: with wide ranging or glib argument

notes.note: Suam with quisque normally means “each his own”. The reflexive could instead point back to philosophy, the subject of “demands”. The English takes the first.
notes.other_reading: that each person live by its law (philosophy’s law)

notes.note: The square brackets are an editor’s deletions carried into the copy; the English reads “unus sit omnium actionum color”. As given the words stand after a semicolon with no “that”, so they are translated as a fresh wish, though they could be one more thing that philosophy demands. The wording of this sentence is disturbed in the tradition and other editions print it differently (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: that all his actions be of one colour

notes.note: The two nouns nearly rhyme in Latin. Officium is duty, task or function; indicium is a sign or proof.
notes.other_reading: the greatest task of wisdom and the greatest proof of it

notes.note: Par sibi is literally “equal to himself”, a match for himself, and idem is “the same”. The English gives the sense in current words.
notes.other_reading: equal to himself and the same

notes.note: The bracketed word is marked for deletion and is left out. “For” explains why only a few achieve it.
notes.other_reading: For this is difficult

notes.latin: uno semper iturum gradu, sed una via
notes.note: Gradus is a step or pace. The contrast is between the same speed and the same road. “Will go” is repeated in the second half for English grammar.
notes.other_reading: will always walk with the same step, but along the same road

check.note: Otiosi are people with leisure, with time on their hands. “Idlers” adds blame that the word does not carry.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “men of leisure”.

check.note: Volubilis is rapid, rolling, glib. “Fluent” is praise, where Seneca is being dismissive of this kind of talk.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “fluent” is replaced, but by “rapid”, not “glib”. The Latin word means rolling or fast flowing and does not itself blame, so “glib” would add a judgment just as “fluent” added praise. The note records “glib”.

check.note: Suam is taken with quisque. It could also refer to philosophia, the subject of exigit, giving “that each live by its law”, and the English chooses without saying so.
check.decided: Accepted: the English stands as “his own law”, since suam beside quisque normally means “each his own”, and the note records “its law”, meaning philosophy’s.

check.note: The square brackets are an editor’s deletions carried into the copy, and the English translates the cleaned wording. As given it is a fresh wish, not a further clause after ut and ne, and “his” is added; the wording is disturbed in the tradition (from memory, unchecked).
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “let all actions be of one colour”, a separate wish with no “his”. The note says that the brackets are deletions and that the text is doubtful (from memory, unchecked), and it gives the dependent reading.

check.note: “Equal to himself and the same” is a word for word copy that a reader of today will stumble on.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “consistent with himself and one and the same”. “Consistent with himself” is taken from the suggestion; “man” is not added, since idem is simply “the same”.

check.latin: nec hoc dico, sapientem uno semper iturum gradu, sed una via
check.note: The words “do not say this, that” copy the Latin construction and are awkward in English. The sense is right.
check.decided: Accepted: the clause now runs “not saying that the wise man will always go at one pace, but that he will go by one road”. “Go” is kept for iturum, which is the plain verb of going.

passages.latin: Invideas licet, etiam nunc libenter pro me dependet Epicurus. 'Magnificentior, mihi crede, sermo tuus in grabatto videbitur et in panno; non enim dicentur tantum illa sed probabuntur.' Ego certe aliter audio quae dicit Demetrius noster, cum illum vidi nudum, quanto minus quam [in] stramentis incubantem: non praeceptor veri sed testis est.
passages.english: Begrudge it if you like: even now Epicurus will gladly pay on my behalf. “Your talk, believe me, will seem grander on a pallet and in rags; for those things will not only be said but proved.” I at least hear in a different way what our Demetrius says when I have seen him naked, lying on something far less than straw bedding: he is not a teacher of the truth but a witness to it.

notes.note: A concession: “though you may grudge it”. Invidere is to envy or begrudge. What Lucilius might grudge is not stated; perhaps that the payment again comes from Epicurus.
notes.other_reading: You may be envious

notes.note: Dependere is to pay down what is owed, and the form is future. It continues the joke of these letters that the saying attached to each one is a payment due.
notes.other_reading: will settle the account for me

notes.note: Literally “even now” or “still”. With the future verb it can also be narrowed to “this time too”: Epicurus will pay once more.
notes.other_reading: this time too

notes.latin: in grabatto videbitur et in panno
notes.note: The quoted words are given as those of Epicurus; their place in his remains is not identified here (from memory, unchecked). Grabattus is a low, cheap bed; pannus is a rag or patch of cloth.
notes.other_reading: will seem grander on a camp bed and in a rag

notes.note: Probare is to prove or test, and also to win approval. The section before asks for words to be proved by deeds, with the same verb, so “proved” is kept.
notes.other_reading: but will be believed

notes.note: Cum with the perfect indicative beside a present main verb says what holds whenever the thing has happened; it could also point to one occasion. Nudus can be naked or merely without an outer garment, and the English chooses “naked”. Demetrius is the Cynic philosopher, a friend of Seneca (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: ever since seeing him without a cloak

notes.note: The edition brackets “in” for deletion. The phrase is compressed and does not construe strictly: literally “lying on, by how much less than, straw bedding”. The English takes it to say that his bed was far poorer than straw; with “in” kept it could mean that he was not even lying on straw.
notes.other_reading: and, what is more, not even lying on straw

notes.latin: non praeceptor veri sed testis est
notes.note: Praeceptor is one who gives precepts, a teacher; testis is a witness in court.
notes.other_reading: he does not teach the truth, he gives evidence for it

check.note: Dependo (“pay”) is third conjugation, so dependet is future, “will pay”. The present would be dependit.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “will gladly pay on my behalf”. The form is a future, and the note on the verb says so.

check.note: Etiam nunc can also mean “still” or “this time too”. With the future verb, “this time too” fits a writer who has been paying the debts of these letters from Epicurus.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “even now”, which is what the two Latin words say and which still makes sense with the future “will pay”. “This time too” narrows the phrase to one of its senses, and the note records it as the other reading.

check.note: Cum with the perfect indicative is plainly temporal, a “when” or a “since”. “Now that” adds a causal colour.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “now that” is removed and the clause now begins with a plain “when” and a perfect (“have seen him”). “Since” is not used because in English it can also be heard as giving a reason, and because a perfect indicative after cum beside a present main verb describes what holds each time.

check.note: “Bare” is not said of a person in English. Nudus can mean naked or without an outer garment, and the English should choose one openly.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “naked”, and the note records “without a cloak” as the other sense.

check.note: The English copies a compressed exclamation and is hard to follow. The Latin itself is awkward here (the bracketed in is an editor’s deletion), which should be said and not smoothed over; stramenta is straw bedding, not just straw.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “lying on something far less than straw bedding”, without the added “and”, since the Latin sets the two descriptions side by side. The note says that the phrase does not construe strictly and that “in” is bracketed for deletion.

passages.latin: Profunda super nos altitudo temporis veniet, pauca ingenia caput exserent et in idem quandoque silentium abitura oblivioni resistent ac se diu vindicabunt. Quod Epicurus amico suo potuit promittere, hoc tibi promitto, Lucili: habebo apud posteros gratiam, possum mecum duratura nomina educere. Vergilius noster duobus memoriam aeternam promisit et praestat: fortunati ambo! si quid mea carmina possunt, nulla dies umquam memori vos eximet aevo, dum domus Aeneae Capitoli immobile saxum accolet imperiumque pater Romanus habebit.
passages.english: A fathomless depth of time will come over us; few talents will lift their heads out and, though bound to go off some day into the same silence, will hold out against oblivion and will long assert their freedom. What Epicurus was able to promise his friend, this I promise you, Lucilius: I shall have favour with those who come after; I can bring out with me names that will last. Our Vergil promised everlasting memory to two men, and he is making it good: “Fortunate pair! If my songs have any power, no day shall ever take you out of time that remembers, so long as the house of Aeneas dwells beside the immovable rock of the Capitol and the Roman father holds the empire.”

notes.latin: Profunda super nos altitudo temporis veniet
notes.note: Altitudo is depth as well as height, and profunda, from a different root, deepens it. The image is deep water closing over everyone, with a few heads rising above it.
notes.other_reading: The deep flood of time will roll over us

notes.note: Quandoque is “at some time, some day”. The future participle concedes that even these will go in the end.
notes.other_reading: though sooner or later they will pass into the same silence

notes.note: Vindicare is a legal word: to claim something as one’s own, or to claim a person into freedom. Here the talents claim themselves back from oblivion, and “assert their freedom” gives that sense.
notes.other_reading: will long keep their claim to themselves

notes.note: The friend is Idomeneus, named in the sentences just before this section.
notes.other_reading: his own friend

notes.note: Gratia is favour, credit or influence with someone.
notes.other_reading: shall have credit with posterity

notes.note: Educere is to lead out, here out of the depth of time. The names are those taken along by being written to.
notes.other_reading: carry out with me names that will endure

notes.latin: fortunati ambo! si quid mea carmina possunt
notes.note: Vergil, Aeneid 9, on Nisus and Euryalus (from memory, unchecked). The Latin as given has no quotation marks; they are supplied because the colon introduces the words of Vergil. The verse is given as prose.
notes.other_reading: Happy both! If my poems can do anything

notes.note: Literally “from the mindful age”: time that keeps a memory.
notes.other_reading: shall ever erase you from the memory of the ages

notes.note: Who “the Roman father” is has been disputed: Jupiter of the Capitol, the ruler, or the Roman head of a house (from memory, unchecked). It is kept literal. Imperium is command, rule or empire, and “the empire” is the widest of these.
notes.other_reading: and the father of Rome holds command

check.latin: Profunda super nos altitudo temporis veniet
check.note: The Latin uses two different roots (profunda, altitudo). “Deep depth” repeats one word and jars.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “A fathomless depth of time”, two different words for the two Latin ones.

check.note: Se vindicare is a legal image: to assert one’s own freedom, to claim oneself. The English can be read as “keep their claim private”, which is not the sense.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “will long assert their freedom”. “Assert” is used and not “defend” because vindicare is to lay a claim, not to stand guard.

check.note: Imperium here is rule or empire, wider than “command”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “holds the empire”, and the note records “command”.

passages.latin: 'Nemo' inquit 'aliter quam quomodo natus est exit e vita.' Falsum est: peiores morimur quam nascimur. Nostrum istud, non naturae vitium est. Illa nobiscum queri debet et dicere, 'quid hoc est? sine cupiditatibus vos genui, sine timoribus, sine superstitione, sine perfidia ceterisque pestibus: quales intrastis exite'.
passages.english: “No one,” he says, “goes out of life otherwise than as he was born.” That is false: we die worse than we are born. That fault is ours, not nature’s. She ought to remonstrate with us and say: “What is this? I gave birth to you without desires, without fears, without superstition, without treachery and the other plagues: go out such as you came in.”

notes.note: “He” is Epicurus, whose saying is quoted in other words just before this section. Seneca restates it here and then contradicts it.
notes.other_reading: it is said

notes.note: Literally “otherwise than in the way he was born”.
notes.other_reading: in any other state than the one he was born in

notes.note: “Goes out” is used so that it is heard again in “go out” at the end, where the Latin repeats the verb and sets it against “came in”.
notes.other_reading: leaves life

notes.latin: Nostrum istud, non naturae vitium est
notes.note: The glossary gives “vice” for vitium. Here the point is whose defect it is that people die worse than they were born, so “fault” is used.
notes.other_reading: That vice is ours, not nature’s

notes.note: Queri cum aliquo is to bring a complaint to someone about his conduct, to remonstrate with him. It does not mean to complain alongside him.
notes.other_reading: to complain to us

notes.note: Gignere is used of a father begetting and of a mother bearing. Nature is feminine here, so the English has “gave birth”.
notes.other_reading: begot you

notes.note: A plural command to everyone. Literally “of what kind you entered, go out”.
notes.other_reading: leave as you were when you entered

check.note: Exit here is picked up by exite at the end, and intrastis answers it. The English has “leaves” first and “go out” later, so the echo is lost.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “goes out of life”, so that “go out” at the end repeats it.

check.note: Queri cum aliquo is to remonstrate with someone, to bring a complaint against him. “Complain to” can be read as if those addressed were only the listeners.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “remonstrate with” in place of “complain to”, which makes those addressed the ones at fault.

check.note: “Brought forth” is archaic.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “gave birth to you”, which suits nature spoken of as “she”.

passages.latin: Hoc ante omnia fac, mi Lucili: disce gaudere. Existimas nunc me detrahere tibi multas voluptates qui fortuita summoveo, qui spes, dulcissima oblectamenta, devitandas existimo? immo contra nolo tibi umquam deesse laetitiam. Volo illam tibi domi nasci: nascitur si modo intra te ipsum fit. Ceterae hilaritates non implent pectus; frontem remittunt, leves sunt, nisi forte tu iudicas eum gaudere qui ridet: animus esse debet alacer et fidens et supra omnia erectus.
passages.english: Do this before all else, my Lucilius: learn to feel joy. Do you now think that I am taking many pleasures away from you, I who clear away the things of chance, who think that hopes, the sweetest of delights, are to be avoided? No, on the contrary: I do not want gladness ever to be lacking to you. I want it to be born for you at home: it is born if only it comes about within yourself. The other kinds of cheerfulness do not fill the breast; they smooth the brow, they are slight, unless perhaps you judge that a man who laughs is feeling joy: the mind ought to be lively and confident and raised up above all things.

notes.note: Gaudere is the verb of gaudium, “joy”, which the Stoics set apart from pleasure (from memory, unchecked). “Joy” is kept for gaudium and gaudere, “pleasure” for voluptas, “gladness” for laetitia and “cheerfulness” for hilaritas.
notes.other_reading: learn how to rejoice

notes.note: Fortuita are things that come by chance. Summovere is to move something out of the way.
notes.other_reading: pushing aside the gifts of chance

notes.note: Oblectamenta are things that delight or divert.
notes.other_reading: hopes, the sweetest of amusements

notes.note: “At home” is the image of something grown in one’s own house, not brought in from outside. The image is kept.
notes.other_reading: to be grown at home for you

notes.latin: nascitur si modo intra te ipsum fit
notes.note: The Latin has no “there”: “at home” is understood from the clause before. Fit is “comes about” or “is made”. Some editions may read a different verb here (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: it is born there, provided it is produced inside you yourself

notes.note: Remittere is to relax or unbend. Leves is light, slight, shallow, and can also be fickle.
notes.other_reading: they unknit the brow, they are lightweight

notes.latin: alacer et fidens et supra omnia erectus
notes.note: Alacer is brisk, lively, in good spirits. Erectus is upright or lifted.
notes.other_reading: eager and confident and standing upright above everything

check.note: Oblectamenta are delights. “Amusements” makes hopes sound trivial, which weakens what Seneca admits he is taking away.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the sweetest of delights”.

check.latin: nascitur si modo intra te ipsum fit
check.note: “There” is added. The Latin says only “it is born, if only it comes about within yourself”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “it is born if only it comes about within yourself”. The note says that “at home” is understood from the clause before.

check.note: Alacer is brisk, lively, in good spirits. “Eager” suggests wanting something, which sits badly beside the removal of hopes.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “lively and confident”.

passages.latin: Mihi crede, verum gaudium res severa est. An tu existimas quemquam soluto vultu et, ut isti delicati loquuntur, hilariculo mortem contemnere, paupertati domum aperire, voluptates tenere sub freno, meditari dolorum patientiam? Haec qui apud se versat in magno gaudio est, sed parum blando. In huius gaudii possessione esse te volo: numquam deficiet, cum semel unde petatur inveneris.
passages.english: Believe me, true joy is a stern thing. Or do you think that anyone with a relaxed and, as those pampered people say, “cheery little” face despises death, opens his house to poverty, holds pleasures under the bridle, rehearses the endurance of pains? The man who turns these things over within himself is in great joy, but a joy with little charm. It is this joy that I want you to be in possession of: it will never fail, once you have found where it is to be got from.

notes.note: Severus is stern, grave, serious.
notes.other_reading: a serious matter

notes.note: Solutus is loosened, relaxed, unbent.
notes.other_reading: with a carefree look

notes.note: Hilariculus is a diminutive of the word for cheerful, quoted as a pet word of a pampered set. It is very rare and the text may be an editor’s correction (from memory, unchecked). Delicati are the pampered or self indulgent.
notes.other_reading: and, as those spoilt people put it, a “blithe little” one

notes.note: Frenum is the bridle or bit of a horse.
notes.other_reading: keeps pleasures on a tight rein

notes.note: Meditari is to think something over, or to practise it as an exercise. The English takes the second. “Pains” is plural in the Latin.
notes.other_reading: thinks over the bearing of pain

notes.note: Literally “turns these things over with himself”. “These things” are the four acts just listed.
notes.other_reading: Whoever keeps turning these thoughts over in his mind

notes.note: Parum is “too little”, often a mild way of saying “not”. Blandus is coaxing, caressing, charming.
notes.other_reading: but a joy that is not at all soft

notes.note: Literally “from where it is to be sought”: the place it is fetched from.
notes.other_reading: where it is to be sought

check.latin: soluto vultu et, ut isti delicati loquuntur, hilariculo
check.note: The et is dropped, so the second adjective becomes a gloss on the first and not a second quality. The sense is “with a relaxed and, as they say, cheery little face”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “with a relaxed and, as those pampered people say, ‘cheery little’ face”, two qualities joined by “and”.

check.note: “Dainty people” is dated and unclear. Delicati are the pampered, the self indulgent.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “those pampered people”.

check.note: Parum is “too little, not very”, weaker than “not at all”. Blandus is coaxing, charming, agreeable, which is not “soft”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “but a joy with little charm”.

check.note: Unde is “from where”: the place it is fetched from, not the place where one looks.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “where it is to be got from”.

passages.latin: Fac, oro te, Lucili carissime, quod unum potest praestare felicem: dissice et conculca ista quae extrinsecus splendent, quae tibi promittuntur ab alio vel ex alio; ad verum bonum specta et de tuo gaude. Quid est autem hoc 'de tuo'? te ipso et tui optima parte. Corpusculum quoque etiam si nihil fieri sine illo potest, magis necessariam rem crede quam magnam; vanas suggerit voluptates, breves, paenitendas ac, nisi magna moderatione, temperentur, in contrarium abituras. Ita dico: In praecipiti voluptas , ad dolorem vergit, nisi modum tenuit; modum autem tenere in eo difficile est, quod bonu esse credideris: veri boni aviditas tuta est.
passages.english: Do, I beg you, dearest Lucilius, the one thing that can make a person happy: scatter and trample those things that shine on the outside, that are promised to you by someone else or from something else; look to the true good and take your joy from what is your own. But what is this “from what is your own”? From yourself, and from the best part of you. As for the little body too, even though nothing can be done without it, believe it to be a necessary thing rather than a great one; it supplies empty pleasures, short ones, ones to be regretted and, unless they are tempered with great moderation, bound to pass into their opposite. This is what I say: pleasure is on a steep slope; it tilts towards pain unless it has kept within bounds; but to keep within bounds is difficult in a thing that you have believed to be good: greed for the true good is safe.

notes.note: The Latin names no person: “make (someone) happy”. “A person” is supplied; “you” is as possible, since the command is to Lucilius. Felix is lucky or fortunate as well as happy; the glossary keeps “happy” for beatus, and it is used here too for want of a better plain word.
notes.other_reading: that can make you fortunate

notes.note: Extrinsecus can be “on the outside”, an outward shine, or “from without”, a borrowed light. The English takes the first.
notes.other_reading: that shine with a light from outside

notes.note: “By someone else” is the one who promises; “from something else” is the source the thing is to come from. Alio in the second place could also be a person.
notes.other_reading: by another or from another

notes.note: “De tuo” is a money idiom: from your own property, at your own cost. That sense is kept, since the next sentence asks what “your own” is.
notes.other_reading: rejoice in what is yours

notes.note: A diminutive of “body”, said slightingly. “Too” is hard to place: perhaps the body also counts as one’s own, but only as a necessity. It is left as it stands.
notes.other_reading: This poor body as well

notes.note: The comma in the digitised text is a slip; the words are read together. Moderatio shares a root with modus, the “bounds” of the next sentence.
notes.other_reading: unless they are kept in check by great restraint

notes.latin: In praecipiti voluptas , ad dolorem vergit
notes.note: The capital and the spacing are slips in the copy. “In praecipiti” is on a sheer drop or steep slope; “slope” is chosen because the next verb is “tilts”. It is taken as two clauses with “is” supplied; it could be one.
notes.other_reading: Pleasure, on the brink, tilts towards pain

notes.note: Modus is measure or limit. The verb is perfect: “unless it has kept”.
notes.other_reading: unless it has kept to measure

notes.note: “bonu” is a slip for bonum. The “you” is general, and the perfect subjunctive is “have come to believe”.
notes.other_reading: in anything one has come to think good

notes.note: Aviditas is greed or keen appetite. The strong word is kept, since the point is that here even greed does no harm.
notes.other_reading: eagerness for the true good is without danger

check.note: The Latin gives no object. “A person” is supplied, and “you” is just as possible.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “make a person happy”. The Latin names no one and English needs an object; “make one happy” would follow “the one thing” awkwardly, and the note records “you” as the other reading.

check.note: Extrinsecus can be “on the outside” (an outward glitter) or “from without” (a borrowed light). “Shine from outside” is unclear and settles neither.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “shine on the outside”, keeping “shine” for the plain verb splendent. The note records the other sense.

check.note: The English copies the words and is hard to follow. Ab alio is “by someone else”; ex alio is “from another source”, and alio may be neuter (“from something else”).
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “by someone else or from something else”. “Source” is not added, since the Latin has only the bare word “another”.

check.note: The diminutive belittles. “Poor” adds pity that is not in it.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the little body”. “This” is not used because the Latin has no word for it.

check.latin: etiam si nihil fieri sine illo potest
check.note: With the indicative potest this is a fact conceded, not a supposition.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “even though nothing can be done without it”.

check.latin: magis necessariam rem crede quam magnam
check.note: The English is stiff and copies the Latin order.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “believe it to be a necessary thing rather than a great one”. “Believe” is kept for crede because the same verb returns at the end of the section (“have believed to be good”).

check.note: A verb is supplied (“stands”), and “steep edge” is an odd phrase for in praecipiti, “on the brink”. As punctuated in the Latin given, the words could also run on into vergit as one clause.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “pleasure is on a steep slope”, with the plain “is” that English needs. “Slope” is preferred to “brink” because the next verb (vergit) means “tilts” or “slopes”; the note records “brink” and the reading as one clause.

check.note: “Kept to measure” is not current English. The same phrase recurs in the next clause and should be changed there in the same way.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “kept within bounds” and “to keep within bounds”, the same words in both clauses.

passages.latin: Quod sit istud interrogas, aut unde subeat? Dicam: ex bona conscientia, ex honestis consiliis, ex rectis actionibus, ex contemptu fortuitorum, ex placido vitae et continuo tenore unam prementis viam. Nam illi qui ex aliis propositis in alia transiliunt aut ne transiliunt quidem sed casu quodam transmittuntur, quomodo habere quicquam certum mansurumve possunt suspensi et vagi?
passages.english: Do you ask what that is, or where it comes up from? I will tell you: from a good conscience, from honourable plans, from right actions, from contempt for the things of chance, from the peaceful and unbroken course of a life that keeps to one road. For those who leap from one set of purposes to another, or do not even leap but are carried across by some accident, how can they have anything certain or lasting, when they are suspended and wandering?

notes.note: “That” points back to what the letter has just named, most likely the true good at the end of the section before, possibly the joy that goes with it. The answer that follows replies to “where from” and not to “what”.
notes.other_reading: what this thing is

notes.note: Subire is to come up from below or to steal in.
notes.other_reading: where it arises from

notes.note: Conscientia is knowledge shared with oneself. It is wider than the modern “conscience” but includes it.
notes.other_reading: from a good awareness of oneself

notes.note: Consilia are plans, intentions or decisions. “Honourable” follows the glossary’s word for honestum.
notes.other_reading: from honourable intentions

notes.note: The same word as in 23.3, so the same English: “the things of chance”. Casu below is a different word and is given as “accident”.
notes.other_reading: from scorn of what chance brings

notes.latin: ex placido vitae et continuo tenore unam prementis viam
notes.note: Placidus is quiet, peaceful; “calm” is avoided because the glossary keeps it for tranquillitas. Prementis agrees with vitae: a life that treads, or keeps to, one road.
notes.other_reading: from the quiet, unbroken tenor of a life that treads a single path

notes.note: The verb is passive: they are sent or carried across, and do not move themselves.
notes.other_reading: are thrown across by a kind of chance

notes.note: Suspensus is hanging, and so in suspense, unsettled. The image is kept with “suspended”, and “when they are” is added for English grammar.
notes.other_reading: unsettled and drifting

check.note: Fortuitorum is “the things of chance” and casu is also given as “chance”: two Latin words, one English word. A reader may link them where Seneca does not.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “by some accident”, so that “chance” is kept for the one Latin word.

check.note: “In the air” is supplied. Suspensi is “in suspense, unsettled”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “in the air” is removed and the English now reads “suspended and wandering”. The literal sense of suspensi is hanging, and the image is kept, with “unsettled and drifting” in the note.

passages.latin: Non est quod existimes paucos.esse hos: propemodum omnes sunt. Quidam vero tunc incipiunt cum desinendum est. Si hoc iudicas mirum, adiciam quod magis admireris: quidam ante vivere desierunt quam inciperent. Vale.
passages.english: There is no reason for you to think that these are few: they are nearly everyone. Some, indeed, begin at the time when they must stop. If you judge this a wonder, I will add something for you to wonder at more: some have stopped living before they began. Farewell.

notes.note: The full stop is a slip in the copy; the words are read together. “These” are the people of the section before, who are only now beginning to live.
notes.other_reading: that such people are few

notes.note: Literally “they are almost all (people)”.
notes.other_reading: it is almost all of mankind

notes.note: “Begin” has no object; “to live” is understood from the context. The second verb is impersonal, “when there must be a stopping”; the English gives it the subject “they”.
notes.other_reading: begin to live only when it is time to leave off

notes.note: The verb shares a root with mirum in the clause before, so the English has “a wonder” there and “wonder at” here.
notes.other_reading: something that will surprise you more

notes.note: The subjunctive in the “before” clause may carry “before they could begin”. The plainer form is kept.
notes.other_reading: have left off living before they could begin

check.note: “Very” strengthens a plain tunc with cum, “then, when”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “begin at the time when”, without “very”.

check.note: The form says that stopping has to happen: “when they must stop”, “when it is time to stop”. “Right” turns a necessity into a matter of propriety.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “when they must stop”, which states the necessity outright.

check.note: Admireris picks up mirum in the clause before, but the English has “strange” there and “wonder at” here.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “If you judge this a wonder” and “something for you to wonder at more”. “Judge” is kept for iudicas.

passages.latin: Securus itaque inimici minas audi; et quamvis conscientia tibi tua fiduciam faciat, tamen, quia multa extra causam valent, et quod aequissimum est spera et ad id te quod est iniquissimum compara. Illud autem ante omnia memento, demere rebus tumultum ac videre quid in quaque re sit: scies nihil esse in istis terribile nisi ipsum timorem.
passages.english: So, free from care, listen to your enemy’s threats; and although your own conscience gives you confidence, still, because many things outside the case carry weight, hope for what is fairest and also prepare yourself for what is most unfair. But above all remember this, to take the uproar away from things and to see what is in each thing: you will find that there is nothing terrible in those things except the fear itself.

notes.note: The adjective belonging to securitas, which the glossary renders as freedom from care. That phrase is kept so the link shows, and it stands first, as in the Latin.
notes.other_reading: Listen to your enemy’s threats without anxiety

notes.note: A personal enemy. The words about the case that follow suggest an opponent at law, but the Latin word is the general one and is kept general.
notes.other_reading: your opponent’s threats

notes.note: Conscientia is knowledge shared with oneself, here the knowledge of being in the right. English “conscience” is a little narrower.
notes.other_reading: although your knowledge of your own innocence gives you confidence

notes.note: Legal language: causa is the case being tried, and things outside it can still sway the result. The legal word is kept.
notes.other_reading: many things that have nothing to do with the merits have power

notes.note: Aequus can mean just, fair or favourable, and iniquissimum is its opposite. “Fairest” and “most unfair” keep the two words as plainly opposite as they are in the Latin, and suit a verdict.
notes.other_reading: hope for the most favourable outcome and prepare yourself for the most unfavourable

notes.note: Tumultus is noise, commotion, alarm. The verb demere returns in the next section for taking off a mask, so a plain “take away” is used.
notes.other_reading: to strip things of their commotion

notes.note: Istis is the pronoun that points at what belongs to the person addressed: here the threats Lucilius is facing. “Those things” keeps the pointing without suggesting his possessions.
notes.other_reading: in those things of yours

notes.note: Ipsum can point to the fear of these particular things or to fear in general. The English takes the first.
notes.other_reading: except fear itself

check.latin: et quod aequissimum est spera et ad id te quod est iniquissimum compara
check.note: After the comma, “both hope” is first read as a noun phrase before it is seen to be a command. In this courtroom setting the pair is better taken as the fairest and the most unfair outcome.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “hope for what is fairest and also prepare yourself for what is most unfair”, which removes the stumble and makes the two words plain opposites, as aequissimum and iniquissimum are. “Outcome” is not added because the Latin says only “what is”.

check.note: Istis points at the things Lucilius himself is facing; “them” flattens this into a vague reference back.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “in those things”, which keeps the pointing of istis. “Of yours” is not added, because in English it would suggest Lucilius’s possessions and not the threats he faces; a note records the fuller sense.

check.note: After the command, scies means “you will find out”; “you will know” is flat and slightly odd English here.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “you will find”, since the future of scire after a command means coming to know.

check.note: Found while settling: “free from care” stood after “threats” and could be read as describing the threats.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now begins “So, free from care, listen to your enemy’s threats”, with the phrase first, where Securus stands in the Latin, so that it can only describe Lucilius.

passages.latin: Quod vides accidere pueris, hoc nobis quoque maiusculis pueris evenit: illi quos amant, quibus assueverunt, cum quibus ludunt, si personatos vident, expavescunt: non hominibus tantum sed rebus persona demenda est et reddenda facies sua.
passages.english: What you see happen to children happens to us too, who are slightly bigger children: the people they love, the people they are used to, the people they play with, if they see them wearing masks, they take fright. The mask must be taken off not only people but things, and their own face given back to them.

notes.note: Pueri can be boys or children in general. The general sense is taken.
notes.other_reading: What you see happen to boys

notes.note: Maiusculus is a diminutive of the comparative: somewhat bigger. The phrase stands in apposition to the pronoun before it.
notes.other_reading: us too, boys who are only a little older

notes.latin: illi quos amant, quibus assueverunt, cum quibus ludunt
notes.note: The Latin starts with “they” (the children) and then piles up three relative clauses before the verb. That loose order is kept.
notes.other_reading: they take fright if they see in masks the very people they love, are used to and play with

notes.note: Wearing a persona, the mask of the stage.
notes.other_reading: disguised

notes.latin: persona demenda est et reddenda facies sua
notes.note: Sua refers back to the people and things: their own face. The Latin has no word for “each”. Demenda repeats the verb of the section before, where the uproar is taken away from things.
notes.other_reading: the mask must be removed and their true appearance restored

check.note: “Each” is not in the Latin, which says only that their own face must be given back.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and their own face given back to them”, with no “each”; “to them” only repeats the people and things already named.

check.note: The verb describes the onset of fear; “are terrified” makes it a state.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “they take fright”, because expavescunt is a verb of beginning: the fright comes on at the sight of the mask.

passages.latin: Quid mihi gladios et ignes ostendis et turbam carnificum circa te frementem? Tolle istam pompam sub qua lates et stultos territas: mors es, quam nuper servus meus, quam ancilla contempsit. Quid tu rursus mihi flagella et eculeos magno apparatu explicas? quid singulis articulis singula machinamenta quibus extorqueantur aptata et mille alia instrumenta excarnificandi particulatim hominis? Pone ista quae nos obstupefaciunt; iube conticiscere gemitus et exclamationes et vocum inter lacerationem elisarum acerbitatem: nempe dolor es, quem podagricus ille contemnit, quem stomachicus ille in ipsis delicis perfert, quem in puerperio puella perpetitur. Levis es si ferre possum; brevis es si ferre non possum.
passages.english: Why do you show me swords and fires and a crowd of executioners roaring around you? Take away that parade you hide behind and frighten fools with: you are death, which a slave of mine recently scorned, which a slave girl scorned. And you in turn, why do you lay out whips and racks before me with great display? Why the separate devices fitted to separate joints to wrench them out, and a thousand other instruments for torturing a man piece by piece? Put away those things that stun us; order the groans to fall silent, and the cries, and the harshness of voices forced out while the body is being torn. You are pain, after all, which that man with gout scorns, which that man with a bad stomach endures in the very midst of his luxuries, which a girl endures to the end in childbirth. You are light if I can bear you; you are short if I cannot bear you.

notes.note: Carnifex is the public executioner, who also carried out torture. With swords and fires, in a scene that turns out to be death’s, “executioners” is used. Fremere is to roar, growl or mutter.
notes.other_reading: a mob of torturers snarling around you

notes.note: Pompa is a ceremonial procession, so the image is of death arriving with a train of attendants.
notes.other_reading: Take away that pageantry

notes.note: This may point to a real recent death in Seneca’s household or be a general example; the Latin does not say. The possessive can be read as pointing to one particular slave or to any slave of the household, and the English takes the second.
notes.other_reading: which my own slave scorned not long ago

notes.note: Contemnere is to think little of, to hold cheap. “Scorn” is used here, for contemnit below and for contemnunt in 24.25, so that the repetition shows; “despise” is avoided because it now suggests loathing.
notes.other_reading: made light of

notes.note: The address turns from death to a second figure, named only later as pain. The English does not name it early.
notes.other_reading: And you, pain, why do you in your turn

notes.note: Literally “little horses”, the name of a torture frame on which the body was stretched.
notes.other_reading: the wooden horse

notes.note: Excarnificare is built on carnifex, the word behind “executioners” in the first sentence: to do the executioner’s work on someone to the end, to torture or tear to pieces. English cannot keep the echo without calling death’s attendants torturers, so the echo is recorded here.
notes.other_reading: for butchering a man piece by piece

notes.note: Elidere is to squeeze or crush out, so the voices may be forced out of the victim or choked off; the English takes the first. The Latin says only “amid the tearing”, and “the body” is supplied so that the English says what is torn. Acerbitas could also be bitterness or shrillness.
notes.other_reading: the shrillness of voices choked off amid the tearing

notes.note: Nempe marks something as obvious: of course, to be sure.
notes.other_reading: Why, you are only pain

notes.note: Delicis stands for deliciis: luxuries, pleasures, indulgences in general, which for this man may well be those of the table. “His” is supplied. Ille here and with the gouty man points to a familiar type, not one person.
notes.other_reading: which the dyspeptic puts up with in the very midst of his delicacies

notes.latin: Levis es si ferre possum; brevis es si ferre non possum
notes.note: The Latin rhymes levis and brevis. The thought that pain is either light or short is Epicurean (from memory, unchecked). The second half implies that unbearable pain ends the sufferer, but the Latin leaves that unsaid and so does the English.
notes.other_reading: You are slight if I can bear you; you are brief if I cannot

check.note: Contemnere is to think little of; “despise” today mostly means to loathe, so a reader may think the slave hated death. Whatever is chosen should be the same here, for contemnit below and in 24.25.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “scorned” here, “scorns” for contemnit below and “scorn” in 24.25, since contemnere is to hold cheap, not to hate.

check.note: The word picks up carnificum in the first sentence, and the English uses two unrelated words and loses the echo.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “butchering” becomes “torturing”, which is what the word means in a scene of whips and racks, but “executioners” stays for carnificum, because that crowd stands around death with swords and fires. The argument does not turn on the echo, so it is recorded in a note instead of being forced into the English.

check.note: Pone answers Tolle above and means lay aside; “put down” suggests something held in the hand.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Put away those things”, since the command is to lay the display aside, not to set it down.

check.note: Elisarum can mean forced out or choked off, and acerbitatem may be bitterness or shrillness. “The tearing” with no object is hard to follow.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “forced out” is kept, since groans and cries wrung from the victim are what the sentence lists, and the English now reads “while the body is being torn” so that the tearing has an object. The note records the other senses of elisarum and acerbitatem.

check.note: Delicis means pleasures or luxuries in general; “delicacies” narrows it to fine food, and “his” is supplied.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “in the very midst of his luxuries”, the wider sense of the word. “His” stays, because English wants a possessive where the Latin leaves the owner to be understood, and the note says so.

check.note: “Lately despised” is dated wording and word order.
check.decided: Accepted: “lately” becomes “recently”, placed before the verb, which is the plain form in English of today.

passages.latin: Haec in animo voluta, quae saepe audisti, saepe dixisti; sed an vere audieris, an vere dixeris, effectu proba; hoc enim turpissimum est quod nobis obici solet, verba nos philosophiae, non opera tractare. Quid? tu nunc primum tibi mortem imminere scisti, nunc exilium, nunc dolorem? in haec natus es; quidquid fieri potest, quasi futurum cogitemus.
passages.english: Turn over in your mind these things, which you have often heard and often said; but whether you have truly heard them, whether you have truly said them, prove in action. For this charge that is commonly thrown at us is a most shameful one: that we handle the words of philosophy, not its deeds. What? Have you learned now for the first time that death hangs over you, now exile, now pain? You were born to these things. Whatever can happen, let us think of it as going to happen.

notes.note: Voluta is the imperative of volutare (turn over and over), though it looks like a participle. It is taken as the command, which the following proba supports.
notes.other_reading: These things, turned over in the mind

notes.note: Effectus is the carrying out as well as the outcome. With the contrast of words and deeds that follows, the carrying out is taken.
notes.other_reading: prove by the result

notes.latin: hoc enim turpissimum est quod nobis obici solet
notes.note: The superlative can mean “a most shameful thing” or “the most shameful of the things thrown”. The English takes the first. The Latin does not say who is charged: philosophers in general, or the Stoics.
notes.other_reading: For this is the most shameful of the charges commonly thrown at us

notes.latin: verba nos philosophiae, non opera tractare
notes.note: Tractare is to handle or deal in; “handle” is used here and again in 24.24. Opera are deeds, set against words.
notes.other_reading: that we deal in the words of philosophy, not its works

notes.note: A shortened form of scivisti: have come to know.
notes.other_reading: Did you find out now for the first time

notes.note: In with the accusative: born into these things, or born for them.
notes.other_reading: You were born for this

notes.note: The Latin moves from the second person singular to a first person plural exhortation. The shift is kept.
notes.other_reading: let us think of whatever can happen as something that will happen

check.note: Effectus is the carrying out as well as the outcome; “by the result” suggests waiting to see how things turn out, where the contrast of words and deeds points to practice.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “prove in action”, because the next clause sets words against deeds and effectus can mean the carrying out.

check.latin: hoc enim turpissimum est quod nobis obici solet
check.note: The English reads as “of all the things thrown, the most shameful”; the Latin can equally be “a most shameful thing, this charge”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the superlative is now read as “a most shameful one”, said of the charge itself, so the English no longer ranks it among other charges. The suggested “a great disgrace” is not used because it gives up the superlative form; a note records the reading not taken.

check.note: Opera here are deeds; “the works of philosophy” can be read as its books, nearly the opposite of the point.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “not its deeds”. “Handle” is kept for tractare and not changed to “deal in”, so that the same verb has the same English in 24.24.

check.note: “Only” is not in the Latin and is then repeated twice more, where the Latin has plain nunc each time.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “now for the first time”, then “now exile, now pain”, with no “only”.

check.latin: Haec in animo voluta, quae saepe audisti, saepe dixisti
check.note: Found while settling: in “Turn these things over in your mind, which you have often heard”, the “which” could be taken with “mind”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Turn over in your mind these things, which you have often heard and often said”, so that the relative clause follows the word it belongs to.

passages.latin: Pauper fiam: inter plures ero. Exul fiam: ibi me natum putabo quo mittar. Alligabor: quid enim? nunc solutus sum? ad hoc me natura grave corporis mei pondus adstrinxit. Moriar: hoc dicis, desinam aegrotare posse, desinam alligari posse, desinam mori posse.
passages.english: I will become poor: I will be among the greater number. I will become an exile: I will think myself born in the place I am sent to. I will be bound: what of it? Am I unbound now? Nature has bound me fast to this heavy weight of my body. I will die: what you are saying is this, I will cease to be able to be ill, I will cease to be able to be bound, I will cease to be able to die.

notes.note: Fiam and moriar can be future or subjunctive (a supposition). Alligabor is plainly future, so all four are put as futures.
notes.other_reading: Suppose I become poor

notes.note: Plures is a comparative: the more numerous, the majority. The poor outnumber the rich.
notes.other_reading: I will have more company

notes.note: To be tied up, that is, chained or imprisoned. “Bound” is kept so that solutus (unbound) and adstrinxit (bound fast) answer it in English.
notes.other_reading: I will be put in chains

notes.note: A short idiom of dismissal.
notes.other_reading: Well, what then?

notes.latin: ad hoc me natura grave corporis mei pondus adstrinxit
notes.note: Ad hoc is taken with pondus: to this heavy weight. Ad hoc could also stand alone, with the weight in apposition.
notes.other_reading: Nature has tied me to this: the heavy weight of my body

notes.note: “You” is whoever is making the threat, an imagined speaker; the Latin does not say whether Lucilius is meant. The sense is “what your words amount to is this”.
notes.other_reading: You mean this:

notes.note: A deliberate paradox, kept literally.
notes.other_reading: I will no longer be liable to death

check.note: The formal future auxiliary comes nine times in this short passage and is stiff for plain English of today. The future tense itself is right, as alligabor shows.
check.decided: Accepted: every future in the passage now has “will”, the plain form in English of today. The tense is unchanged.

passages.latin: Non sum tam ineptus ut Epicuream cantilenam hoc loco persequar et dicam vanos esse inferorum metus, nec Ixionem rota volvi nec saxum umeris Sisyphi trudi in adversum nec ullius viscera et renasci posse cotidie et carpi: nemo tam puer est ut Cerberum timeat et tenebras et larvalem habitum nudis ossibus cohaerentium. Mors nos aut consumit aut exuit; emissis meliora restant onere detracto, consumptis nihil restat, bona pariter malaque summota sunt.
passages.english: I am not so silly as to go through the Epicurean refrain at this point and say that the fears of the underworld are empty, that Ixion is not turned on a wheel, that no rock is pushed uphill by the shoulders of Sisyphus, that no one’s entrails can both grow back and be torn at every day. No one is so much a child as to fear Cerberus and the darkness and the ghostly look of those whose bare bones hang together. Death either consumes us or strips us bare. For those who are let out, better things remain, with the burden taken off; for those who are consumed, nothing remains: good things and bad alike have been removed.

notes.note: Silly, out of place. “Foolish” is avoided because the glossary keeps “fool” for stultus.
notes.other_reading: I am not so foolish

notes.note: Cantilena is a song sung over and over, a stale tune. The Epicureans argued at length that the tales of punishment after death are false.
notes.other_reading: the old Epicurean song

notes.note: Inferi are those below: the dead and their world.
notes.other_reading: fears of the dead below

notes.latin: nec Ixionem rota volvi nec saxum umeris Sisyphi trudi in adversum
notes.note: Two sinners of myth: Ixion bound to a turning wheel, Sisyphus pushing a rock up a slope for ever. In adversum is “against the slope”.
notes.other_reading: nor a stone shoved up the hill on the shoulders of Sisyphus

notes.latin: nec ullius viscera et renasci posse cotidie et carpi
notes.note: No name is given. The allusion is probably to Tityus, whose liver is eaten by vultures in the underworld (from memory, unchecked). Viscera is entrails or flesh; carpi is to be plucked or torn at bit by bit, and “every day” is taken with both verbs.
notes.other_reading: nor can anyone’s liver grow again every day and be pecked at

notes.note: The many-headed dog that guards the entrance to the underworld.
notes.other_reading: the hound of the underworld

notes.note: Larvae are hostile ghosts, pictured as skeletons. Literally: the larva-like appearance of those holding together with bare bones. Habitus could also be dress or bearing.
notes.other_reading: the spectral shape of skeletons

notes.note: Exuere is to strip off clothing: death either uses a person up entirely or takes the body off like a garment. The English adds “bare” to complete the clothing image; the release it implies comes in the next clause.
notes.other_reading: Death either destroys us or sets us free

notes.note: Emissis is a participle in the dative, “for those sent out or released”, as from a prison. The burden is the body.
notes.other_reading: if we are released, better things await us once the load is lifted

notes.note: Plural: good things and bad things. The glossary’s “the good” is for the singular bonum; the plural “goods” would read as merchandise, so “good things” is used.
notes.other_reading: goods and evils alike have been removed

check.latin: et renasci posse cotidie et carpi
check.note: Cotidie most naturally covers both verbs, but the English ties it to “grow back” only; carpi is to be plucked or pecked at, not “torn away”; and “nor can” breaks the English construction.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “that no one’s entrails can both grow back and be torn at every day”, with “every day” covering both verbs and the clause in line with the two before it. “Torn at” is used instead of “pecked at” because the Latin names no bird.

check.note: Exuere is to take off a garment. The bare verb leaves the reader asking stripped of what, and sounds like a loss, not the release that emissis shows it to be.
check.decided: Accepted: “bare” is added after the verb, so the clothing image of exuere is complete: death takes the body off like a garment.

check.note: “Hold together by bare bones” is hard to picture; the image is of spectres shown as skeletons, whose bare bones hang together.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the ghostly look of those whose bare bones hang together”. “Ghostly” is kept from the draft, to the same effect as “spectral”.

check.note: “Goods” in the plural reads as merchandise to a reader of today.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “good things and bad alike”.

passages.latin: Cotidie morimur; cotidie enim demitur aliqua pars vitae, et tunc quoque cum crescimus vita decrescit. Infantiam amisimus, deinde pueritiam, deinde adulescentiam. Usque ad hesternum quidquid trans;t temporis perit; hunc ipsum quem agimus diem cum morte dividimus. Quemadmodum clepsydram non extremum stilicidium exhaurit sed quidquid ante defluxit, sic ultima hora qua esse desinimus non sola mortem facit sed sola consummat; tunc ad illam pervenimus, sed diu venimus.
passages.english: We die every day; for every day some part of life is taken away, and even at the time when we are growing, life is growing less. We have lost infancy, then childhood, then youth. Right up to yesterday, whatever time has passed has perished; this very day that we are living we share with death. Just as it is not the last drop that empties a water clock but whatever has run out before, so the last hour, in which we cease to be, does not alone make death but alone completes it. That is when we come to it, but we have been coming for a long time.

notes.note: The Latin plays on crescere (grow) and decrescere (grow less). The English keeps “grow” in both halves so the play can be heard.
notes.other_reading: even while we grow, life is shrinking

notes.note: Pueritia covers childhood in general as well as boyhood. With a general subject, “childhood” is used.
notes.other_reading: then boyhood

notes.note: Roman adulescentia runs later than English “adolescence”, to about thirty.
notes.other_reading: then young manhood

notes.note: A slip in the digitised text. It is read as transit or transiit, “has passed”.
notes.other_reading: whatever time passes

notes.note: Perit can be present (“perishes”) or a shortened perfect (“has perished”). With “right up to yesterday” the perfect is taken.
notes.other_reading: whatever time goes by, up to yesterday, is lost

notes.note: Dividere cum is to share out with someone: death takes its part of today.
notes.other_reading: we divide with death

notes.note: A clepsydra is a clock that measures time by dripping water. Stilicidium (for stillicidium) is a drip.
notes.other_reading: it is not the final trickle that drains the water clock

notes.latin: non sola mortem facit sed sola consummat
notes.note: Consummare is to bring to a total, to finish off. The repeated sola (alone) is kept.
notes.other_reading: is not the only one that causes death, but the only one that finishes it

notes.latin: tunc ad illam pervenimus, sed diu venimus
notes.note: Pervenire (to come all the way) is built on venire (to come), and the English keeps “come” for both. Both forms can be present or perfect; they are taken as presents, and the present with diu is what English puts as “have been coming”.
notes.other_reading: we reached it then, but we were a long time on the way

check.note: A digitising slip for transit, the short perfect; the English reads it so. Perit after it can be perfect or present, and the English has chosen the perfect.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps “has passed” and “has perished”. One note records the slip and another the choice of tense.

check.note: The Latin plays crescimus against decrescit; “growing” and “shrinking” lose the echo.
check.decided: Accepted: “is shrinking” becomes “is growing less”, so that “grow” is heard twice, as the root of crescere is in the Latin.

check.note: The subject is general; “boyhood” narrows it to males where the Latin word also covers childhood.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “childhood”, since the subject is general and pueritia covers both.

check.latin: tunc ad illam pervenimus, sed diu venimus
check.note: Both verbs can be present or perfect, and the English mixes the two; the echo of venimus in pervenimus is also lost in “arrive” and “coming”.
check.decided: Accepted: “arrive at” becomes “come to”, so that “come” is heard in both halves as venire is. Both verbs are read as presents; the Latin present with diu is what English puts as “have been coming”.

passages.latin: Video quo spectes: quaeris quid huic epistulae infulserim, quod dictum alicuius animosum, quod praeceptum utile. Ex hac ipsa materia quae in manibus fuit mittetur aliquid. Obiurgat Epicurus non minus eos qui mortem concupiscunt quam eos qui timent, et ait: 'ridiculum est currere ad mortem taedio vitae, cum genere vitae ut currendum ad mortem esset effeceris'.
passages.english: I see what you are looking for: you are asking what I have packed into this letter, what spirited saying of someone’s, what useful precept. Something will be sent from this very subject, the one that has been in hand. Epicurus rebukes those who long for death no less than those who fear it, and says: “It is ridiculous to run to death out of weariness of life, when it is by your way of life that you have made it necessary to run to death.”

notes.note: Literally, where Lucilius is looking, that is, what he has his eye on.
notes.other_reading: I see where you are looking

notes.note: From infulcire, to stuff or cram in. It refers to Seneca’s habit of enclosing a saying in each letter.
notes.other_reading: what I have stuffed into this letter

notes.note: Animosus is full of spirit, courageous.
notes.other_reading: what brave saying of someone’s

notes.note: Idiom: literally “which has been in the hands”, the matter being handled. The Latin names no handler, and the English keeps it so.
notes.other_reading: the subject we have had in our hands

notes.note: A passive with no sender named. It is kept so.
notes.other_reading: I will send you something

notes.note: Taedium is weariness shading into disgust.
notes.other_reading: out of disgust with life

notes.latin: cum genere vitae ut currendum ad mortem esset effeceris
notes.note: A saying of Epicurus (a known fragment, from memory, unchecked). Cum can be “when” or “although”; genus vitae is kind or manner of life. The saying turns on “run” being repeated, so it is repeated.
notes.other_reading: although it is your manner of living that has brought you to the point of having to run to death

check.note: The sense is right, but “from this very subject that has been in hand” is stiff and a little unclear.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “from this very subject, the one that has been in hand”, which separates the two halves and is easier to follow. The suggested wording is not used because it brings in a first person that the Latin, with its passive and its “has been in hand”, does not have.

passages.latin: Quidquid horum tractaveris, confirmabis animum vel ad mortis vel ad vitae patientiam; [at] in utrumque enim monendi ac firmandi sumus, et ne nimis amemus vitam et ne nimis oderimus. Etiam cum ratio suadet finire se, non temere nec cum procursu capiendus est impetus.
passages.english: Whichever of these you handle, you will strengthen your mind to endure either death or life; for we need to be warned and strengthened in both directions, both not to love life too much and not to hate it too much. Even when reason advises making an end of oneself, the leap is not to be taken rashly or at a run.

notes.note: “These” are the sayings just quoted in the section before. Tractare is to handle, work at, think over; “handle” is used, as in 24.15.
notes.other_reading: Whichever of these you ponder

notes.latin: vel ad mortis vel ad vitae patientiam
notes.note: Patientia is the bearing or endurance of something. The noun is turned into a verb.
notes.other_reading: for the endurance either of death or of life

notes.note: The square brackets are taken as the editor’s sign that the word should be deleted, which is the usual convention (from memory, unchecked). “But” does not fit beside enim (“for”), so the English follows the deletion.
notes.other_reading: but in both directions we need to be warned and strengthened

notes.note: Firmandi echoes confirmabis earlier in the sentence, so “strengthen” is used for both. Monere is to warn or advise.
notes.other_reading: we need to be advised and steadied

notes.note: Literally “reason advises to end oneself”. By strict grammar se would point back to reason, but the sense is the person; the Latin names no person and no “life”, so the English has “making an end of oneself”. Ratio is “reason”, as in the glossary.
notes.other_reading: Even when reason urges us to put an end to our life

notes.latin: non temere nec cum procursu capiendus est impetus
notes.note: Procursus is a running forward, a run before a jump. Impetum capere can be to take a spring or gather momentum, which fits the run, or to form an impulse, impetus being also the Stoic word for impulse. The English keeps the bodily image with “leap”.
notes.other_reading: the impulse is not to be formed rashly or in a rush

check.latin: non temere nec cum procursu capiendus est impetus
check.note: Impetum capere is to take a run, to launch oneself, which fits procursu; the English makes impetus a mental impulse, and “taken up” is unclear.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the leap is not to be taken rashly or at a run”, taking the phrase as the bodily image of a spring with a run before it. “Leap” is used instead of the suggested “launch into it” so that impetus stays a noun and the image stays whole; the note records “impulse” as the other reading.

check.note: “Work over” today chiefly means to beat up, and the same verb is “handle” in 24.15.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “Whichever of these you handle”, the word already used for tractare in 24.15, instead of the suggested “turn over”, which is kept for voluta there.

check.note: “Ending oneself” is literal but not English; the Latin has no word for “life”, so a close alternative is needed.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “making an end of oneself”, which is English and still adds no “life”.

check.note: The brackets mark a word the editor deletes, since at and enim cannot stand together; the English leaves it out, and this should be said.
check.decided: Accepted: the English stands without “but”, and the note says that this follows the editor’s deletion.

passages.latin: Vir fortis ac sapiens non fugere debet e vita sed exire; et ante omnia ille quoque vitetur affectus qui multos occupavit, libido moriendi. Est enim, mi Lucili, ut ad alia, sic etiam ad moriendum inconsulta animi inclinatio, quae saepe generosos atque acerrimae indolis viros corripit, saepe ignavos iacentesque: illi contemnunt vitam, hi gravantur.
passages.english: A brave and wise man ought not to flee from life but to go out of it. And above all, that passion too should be avoided which has taken hold of many: the lust for dying. For there is, my Lucilius, as towards other things, so also towards dying, an unconsidered leaning of the mind, which often seizes men who are noble and of the keenest character, and often the spiritless and the downcast. The former scorn life; the latter find it a burden.

notes.note: Sapiens is here an adjective beside fortis. It is the same word the glossary renders “the wise man”.
notes.other_reading: The brave man and the wise man

notes.latin: non fugere debet e vita sed exire
notes.note: The contrast is between running away and walking out. Exire is the plain word for leaving.
notes.other_reading: should not run away from life but take his leave of it

notes.note: Affectus is the Stoic term for a passion, a disordered movement of the mind. “Passion” is used, as in the glossary.
notes.other_reading: that feeling too must be avoided

notes.note: Libido is craving or lust, a word with a bad sense.
notes.other_reading: a craving to die

notes.note: Inconsulta: without deliberation. Inclinatio: a leaning or bent.
notes.other_reading: an unreflecting bent of the mind

notes.note: Generosus can mean of noble birth or of noble spirit. Acerrima indoles is a very keen, energetic nature. The two are joined by “and” in the Latin and are taken as describing character.
notes.other_reading: men of high birth and the fiercest temperament

notes.note: Ignavus is idle, spiritless or cowardly; set against men of keen character, “spiritless” is taken. Iacentes is literally “lying down”, said of those who are sunk and without energy; “downcast” keeps something of the image.
notes.other_reading: the cowardly and the prostrate

notes.note: Contemnere is to think little of, to hold cheap. “Scorn” matches 24.14.
notes.other_reading: The former make light of life

notes.note: Gravari is to feel something as a burden; the form could also be a plain passive.
notes.other_reading: the latter are weighed down by it

check.note: Ignavus is idle or spiritless as well as cowardly, and against men of the keenest character “spiritless” fits better; “prostrate” for iacentes is literal and unclear.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the spiritless and the downcast”. “Spiritless” is taken as suggested; “downcast” is used instead of “listless” because it keeps something of the lying-down image in iacentes and does not repeat the sense of the first word.

check.note: Gravari with a thing commonly means to find it burdensome; the English takes it as a plain passive.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the latter find it a burden”, the usual sense of gravari, which also answers the active “scorn” before it.

check.note: As in 24.14, “despise” now suggests loathing, where contemnere is to hold cheap; the two passages should match.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “The former scorn life”, the same word as in 24.14.

check.note: Found while settling: “noble men of the keenest character” ran two descriptions into one and dropped the “and” of atque.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “men who are noble and of the keenest character”, two descriptions joined as in the Latin.

passages.latin: Quosdam subit eadem faciendi videndique satietas et vitae non odium sed fastidium, in quod prolabimur ipsa impellente philosophia, dum dicimus 'quousque eadem? nempe ex pergiscar dormiam, esuriam, algebo aestuabo. Nullius rei finis est, sed in orbem nexa sunt omnia, fugiunt ac sequuntur; diem nox premit, dies noctem, aestas in autumnum desinit, autumno hiemps instat, quae vere compescitur; omnia sic transeunt ut revertantur. Nihil novi facio, nihil novi video: fit aliquando et huius rei nausia.' Multi sunt qui non acerbum iudicent vivere sed supervacuum. Vale.
passages.english: Some people are overcome by having had their fill of doing and seeing the same things, and by not hatred of life but distaste for it. We slide into this with philosophy itself pushing us, while we say: “How long the same things? Of course I will wake, I will sleep, I will be hungry, I will be cold, I will be hot. Nothing has an end, but all things are linked in a circle; they flee and they follow. Night presses on day, day on night; summer ends in autumn, winter bears down on autumn, and is checked by spring. All things pass in such a way that they come back. I do nothing new, I see nothing new: at some point there comes nausea at this too.” There are many who judge living to be not bitter but superfluous. Farewell.

notes.note: Satietas is fullness, having had enough. “Having had their fill” keeps the food image, which continues in fastidium and nausia.
notes.other_reading: A weariness of doing and seeing the same things comes over some people

notes.note: Fastidium is the distaste of someone who is overfed, a squeamishness.
notes.other_reading: not hatred of life but disgust with it

notes.note: An ablative absolute. Philosophy itself gives the push, by teaching that everything returns.
notes.other_reading: driven on by philosophy itself

notes.note: The Latin has no verb. The English is kept as bare.
notes.other_reading: How long must it be the same things?

notes.latin: nempe ex pergiscar dormiam, esuriam, algebo aestuabo
notes.note: Ex pergiscar is expergiscar split in two. The verbs go in opposed pairs (wake and sleep, be cold and be hot), but esuriam (be hungry) has no partner in the Latin as given; editors supply a word here (from memory, unchecked). The English translates what stands.
notes.other_reading: Of course I will wake and sleep, eat and be hungry, be cold and be hot

notes.note: Nexa: tied or woven together. In orbem: into a ring.
notes.other_reading: all things are bound into a ring

notes.note: Premit just before is “presses on”; instare is to stand close upon, to threaten. The two verbs are given different English, as Seneca varies them.
notes.other_reading: winter follows close on autumn

notes.note: Vere is here the ablative of ver, “by spring”, not the adverb “truly”.
notes.other_reading: which is held in by spring

notes.latin: fit aliquando et huius rei nausia
notes.note: Nausia is seasickness, nausea. Aliquando can be “at some point” or “sometimes”; the first is taken, in answer to “how long?”. “This” is the endless return.
notes.other_reading: sometimes there comes nausea at this too

notes.latin: Multi sunt qui non acerbum iudicent vivere sed supervacuum
notes.note: Acerbus is bitter or harsh. Supervacuum is superfluous, not needed. “Judge” is kept for iudicent, as in the glossary.
notes.other_reading: There are many who think living not painful but pointless

check.latin: ex pergiscar dormiam, esuriam, algebo aestuabo
check.note: Ex pergiscar is expergiscar split in two, and esuriam has no partner in a run of opposed pairs; editions supply one (from memory, unchecked). The English translates what is there, but the gap should be recorded.
check.decided: Accepted: the English stands, now with “will”, and the note records that esuriam lacks its pair in the Latin as given.

check.note: Premit just before is “presses on”, so two different Latin verbs get nearly the same English where Seneca varies.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “presses on” stays for premit, which it translates closely, and instat now reads “bears down on”, so the two verbs differ in English as in Latin.

check.latin: fit aliquando et huius rei nausia
check.note: Aliquando can be “sometimes” as well as “at some point”; “a sickness” for nausia is vague and could be taken for an illness.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “at some point there comes nausea at this too”. “Nausea” is taken as suggested; “at some point” is kept, as the answer to the opening “how long?”, and the note records “sometimes”.

check.note: “Surfeit” is a dated word that many readers will not know.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “overcome by having had their fill”, plain words that keep the food image which runs on into fastidium and nausia. The suggested “having had enough” would lose that image.

passages.latin: 'Sic fac' inquit 'omnia tamquam spectet Epicurus.' Prodest sine dubio custodem sibi imposuisse et habere quem respicias, quem interesse cogitationibus tuis iudices. Hoc quidem longe magnificentius est, sic vivere tamquam sub alicuius boni viri ac semper praesentis oculis, sed ego etiam hoc contentus sum, ut sic facias quaecumque facies tamquam spectet aliquis: omnia nobis mala solitudo persuadet.
passages.english: “Do everything,” he says, “as though Epicurus were watching.” It is without doubt useful to have set a guard over oneself and to have someone you look to, someone you judge to be present at your thoughts. This is indeed far grander, to live as though under the eyes of some good man who is always present; but I am content even with this, that you do whatever you do as though someone were watching. Solitude persuades us to every evil.

notes.note: “He” is Epicurus, named at the end of the section before. The saying is a fragment of Epicurus addressed to a pupil (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: “Act in everything,” says Epicurus, “as if Epicurus were looking on.”

notes.note: Custos is a guard, keeper or watcher. The verb custodi in the next section picks it up, so “guard” is used in both places.
notes.other_reading: to have appointed a guardian over oneself

notes.note: Respicere is to look back at, and so to look to or have regard for. The Latin moves here from the impersonal to “you”; the shift is kept.
notes.other_reading: to have someone you look back to

notes.note: Interesse is to be present at, or to take part in.
notes.other_reading: someone you regard as a witness of your thoughts

notes.note: This first “this” looks forward to living under a good man’s eyes. The second “this” (what Seneca is content with) is the lesser thing: acting as though anyone at all were watching.
notes.other_reading: It is certainly far nobler

notes.latin: alicuius boni viri ac semper praesentis
notes.note: Literally “of some good man, and one always present”.
notes.other_reading: of some good man who is always at your side

notes.note: Persuadere with the thing in the accusative: to talk someone into something.
notes.other_reading: solitude urges every kind of evil on us

check.note: Respicere here is to look to, to have regard for; “look back to” suggests looking into the past.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “someone you look to”. The second person of respicias is kept, so the wording is “you look to”, not “to look to”.

passages.latin: Cum iam profeceris tantum ut sit tibi etiam tui reverentia, licebit dimittas paedagogum: interim aliquorum te auctoritate custodi - aut Cato ille sit aut Scipio aut Laelius aut alius cuius interventu perditi quoque homines vitia supprimerent, dum te efficis eum cum quo peccare non audeas. Cum hoc effeceris et aliqua coeperit apud te tui esse dignatio, incipiam tibi permittere quod idem suadet Epicurus: 'tunc praecipue in te ipse secede cum esse cogeris in turba'.
passages.english: When you have made so much progress that you have respect even for yourself, you may dismiss your minder. Meanwhile guard yourself by the authority of certain men: let it be the famous Cato, or Scipio, or Laelius, or another at whose coming even depraved men would suppress their vices, while you are making yourself the man in whose company you would not dare to do wrong.
