When you have made yourself that, and have begun to have some standing in your own eyes, I will begin to allow you what the same Epicurus advises: “Withdraw into yourself most of all at the time when you are forced to be in a crowd.”

notes.note: Reverentia is respect mixed with awe or shame before someone.
notes.other_reading: a sense of shame before yourself

notes.note: The paedagogus was the slave who went about with a boy and watched his behaviour. He was a minder, not a teacher, and the image is of a child who has outgrown him.
notes.other_reading: you may send away your tutor

notes.note: Custodi picks up custodem in the section before, so “guard”. Aliquorum is plural: some people.
notes.other_reading: keep yourself under the authority of certain men

notes.latin: aut Cato ille sit aut Scipio aut Laelius
notes.note: Ille marks Cato as the well-known one, hence “the famous Cato”. The Latin does not say which Cato (the Elder or the Younger) or which Scipio. Laelius is presumably Gaius Laelius, the friend of the younger Scipio (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: let it be that Cato, or Scipio, or Laelius

notes.latin: cuius interventu perditi quoque homines vitia supprimerent
notes.note: Interventus is a coming in upon the scene. Perditi are men morally lost, not men who have lost their money. The verb is “would suppress”, not “did suppress”.
notes.other_reading: at whose appearance even abandoned men would hold their vices in

notes.latin: dum te efficis eum cum quo peccare non audeas
notes.note: Dum with the present indicative is “while”. Cum quo is “with whom”, that is, with yourself as the witness. Peccare is to do wrong.
notes.other_reading: until you make yourself someone before whom you would not dare to go wrong

notes.note: Effeceris repeats efficis from the clause before, so “make yourself” is repeated. Hoc is a plain “this”: the thing just described.
notes.other_reading: When you have achieved this

notes.latin: aliqua coeperit apud te tui esse dignatio
notes.note: Dignatio is esteem, the standing one has with someone. Apud te is “with you, in your judgment”. The English makes “you” the subject where the Latin has the esteem.
notes.other_reading: and some esteem for yourself has begun to exist with you

notes.latin: tunc praecipue in te ipse secede cum esse cogeris in turba
notes.note: A saying of Epicurus (a known fragment, from memory, unchecked). Secedere is to go apart, to withdraw.
notes.other_reading: Retire into yourself above all when you are compelled to be in a crowd

check.note: The paedagogus is the slave who minds a boy; the image is of a child who has grown out of needing him. “Attendant” loses that and suggests a servant.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “you may dismiss your minder”, which keeps the picture of a child and his keeper. “Dismiss” stays for dimittas.

check.note: Perditi are the morally lost; “ruined” suggests men who have lost their money.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “even depraved men”.

check.note: Effeceris picks up efficis in the clause before; “done this” hides the link and leaves “this” unclear.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “When you have made yourself that”, repeating “make yourself” as the Latin repeats its verb.

check.note: Ille with a name is “the famous, the well-known”; “great” adds a judgment the Latin does not quite make.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the famous Cato”.

check.latin: aliqua coeperit apud te tui esse dignatio
check.note: The wording is clumsy, and apud te is “in your own eyes”, not “in you”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and have begun to have some standing in your own eyes”, which gives apud te its sense of “in your judgment” and dignatio its sense of esteem enjoyed.

passages.latin: Dissimilem te fieri multis oportet, dum tibi tutum [non] sit ad te recedere. Circumspice singulos: nemo est cui non satius sit cum quolibet esse quam secum. 'Tunc praecipue in te ipse secede cum esse cogeris in turba' - si bonus vir , si quietus, si temperans. Alioquin in turbam tibi a te recedendum est: istic malo viro propius es. Vale.
passages.english: You need to become unlike the many, until it is safe for you to withdraw to yourself. Look around at people one by one: there is no one for whom it is not better to be with anyone at all than with himself. “Withdraw into yourself most of all at the time when you are forced to be in a crowd”: if you are a good man, if you are untroubled, if you are self-controlled. Otherwise you must withdraw from yourself into the crowd: there, with yourself, you are closer to a bad man. Farewell.

notes.note: Multis can be “the many” (the crowd) or simply “many people”. The first is taken.
notes.other_reading: You ought to become unlike most people

notes.note: The brackets are taken as the editor’s sign to delete non, which is the usual convention (from memory, unchecked). The English follows the deletion. With non kept, the clause says how long Lucilius must go on becoming unlike the many.
notes.other_reading: as long as it is not safe for you to withdraw to yourself

notes.note: With non deleted, dum with the subjunctive can be “until” or “provided that”. “Until” is taken, since the section before makes withdrawal something to be allowed later.
notes.other_reading: provided that it is safe for you to withdraw to yourself

notes.latin: nemo est cui non satius sit cum quolibet esse quam secum
notes.note: Satius is “better, preferable”. Cum quolibet is “with anyone you please”.
notes.other_reading: there is no one who would not be better off with anybody at all than with himself

notes.latin: si bonus vir , si quietus, si temperans
notes.note: The Latin as given has no verb here and does not construe as it stands; the stray space before the comma suggests that a word such as es has dropped out in copying. “You are” is supplied three times.
notes.other_reading: if you will be a good man, untroubled, self-controlled

notes.note: At rest, untroubled. “Quiet” would suggest not talking, and the glossary keeps “calm” for tranquillitas, so “untroubled” is used.
notes.other_reading: if you are calm

notes.latin: in turbam tibi a te recedendum est
notes.note: This reverses the saying: away from yourself, into the crowd. The Latin has recedere here and secedere in the saying; “withdraw” is used for both so the reversal is plain.
notes.other_reading: you must retreat from yourself into the crowd

notes.note: Istic is “there where you are”, that is, with yourself, not in the crowd. The bad man is Lucilius himself. Propius is a comparative with nothing stated to compare against, and “closer” is left hanging in the same way.
notes.other_reading: there you are too close to a bad man

check.latin: dum tibi tutum [non] sit ad te recedere
check.note: The brackets mark a word the editor deletes, and the English follows the deletion and reads dum as “until” without saying so. With non kept the clause means “so long as it is not safe”; with non deleted, dum could also be “provided that”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps “until it is safe for you to withdraw to yourself”, following the deletion, because the section before treats withdrawal as something to be allowed once progress is made. Two notes now state the choice and give both other readings.

check.note: The Latin as given has no verb, and the stray space suggests a word lost in digitising; the English supplies “you are” three times without saying so.
check.decided: Accepted: the English stands with “you are” supplied, and the note says that the verb is missing in the Latin as given.

check.note: Istic means there where Lucilius is, alone with himself; after the mention of the crowd, “where you are” can be read as “in the crowd”, which reverses the point.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “there, with yourself, you are closer to a bad man”, so that the place cannot be taken for the crowd. “Closer” is kept from the draft, to the same effect as “nearer”.

check.note: “Quiet” suggests not talking; quietus is calm, at peace.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “quiet” is replaced, but by “untroubled”, not “calm”, because the glossary keeps “calm” for tranquillitas and this is a different Latin word.

check.note: “Them” is added and points back to “the many”; the Latin just says to look at individuals, and the next clause is about everyone.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Look around at people one by one”.

passages.latin: Gratias tamen mihi apud te ago: non sentio in animo aetatis iniuriam, cum sentiam in corpore. Tantum vitia et vitiorum ministeria senuerunt: viget animus et gaudet non multum sibi esse cum corpore; magnam partem oneris sui posuit. Exsultat et mihi facit controversiam de senectute: hunc ait esse florem suum. Credamus illi: bono suo utatur.
passages.english: Still, I thank myself in your presence: I do not feel the injury of age in my mind, though I feel it in my body. Only the vices and what waits on the vices have grown old: the mind is vigorous and is glad that it has not much to do with the body; it has laid down a great part of its burden. It exults and disputes with me about old age: it says that this is its flowering. Let us believe it: let it make use of its own good.

notes.latin: Gratias tamen mihi apud te ago
notes.note: The idiom is “to give thanks to someone before a third party”, here to himself with Lucilius as the audience. It is kept literal; “tamen” answers the section before, where he counts himself among the worn out.
notes.other_reading: Still, I congratulate myself, and I tell you so

notes.note: “Iniuria” is a wrong done by someone as well as the damage it leaves. “Injury” keeps both, where “harm” kept only the damage.
notes.other_reading: the harm of age

notes.note: “Ministeria” are services, or the staff who perform them. They are taken as the bodily parts and powers that serve the vices, and “what waits on” keeps the image of service without suggesting people. The Latin has no possessive with “vitia”, and the English has none.
notes.other_reading: the servants of my vices

notes.note: “Animus” is “mind” throughout, as the glossary prefers. It is set against the body here, but not as what survives death, so “soul” is not used.
notes.other_reading: the spirit is vigorous

notes.note: A legal idiom: to raise a dispute or bring a contested case against someone. The mind contests Seneca’s claim that this is old age.
notes.other_reading: it takes me to court over old age

notes.note: “Hunc” is masculine by attraction to “florem” and points to old age, or to this present time of life. “Flos”, flower, is the Latin image for the prime of life; “flowering” keeps the image in a form English uses of a time of life.
notes.other_reading: it says that this is its prime

notes.note: “Uti” is to use and also to enjoy; the English keeps the first sense. “Bonum” is “good” as in the glossary, and the subjunctive is a permission.
notes.other_reading: let it enjoy its own good

check.note: “Iniuria” is a wrong or injury done to someone, not just damage. “Harm” loses the sense of being wronged by age.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “the injury of age”. “Injury” carries both the damage and the wrong, as the Latin word does.

check.note: A possessive is added twice with the vices. The Latin has none and speaks more generally.
check.decided: Accepted: The possessive is dropped both times, and the sentence now begins “Only the vices and what waits on the vices”. The Latin names the vices without saying whose they are.

check.note: “Ministeria” are services or instruments, the things that wait on the vices, most likely the bodily powers. “Servants” makes the reader think of people.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “what waits on the vices”, one of the two wordings suggested. It keeps the image of service, which “tools” would turn into a different image, and no longer suggests persons.

check.note: The Latin sets what has aged against what has not in one sentence, with only a colon between. The full stop weakens the contrast.
check.decided: Accepted: The two halves are joined again by a colon: “have grown old: the mind is vigorous”. The contrast now stands in one sentence as in the Latin.

check.note: “Its flower” is not clear to a reader of today. The sense is the time of bloom, the prime, and “this” is this time of life.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “it says that this is its flowering”. This keeps the Latin image of the flower, as the brief requires, in a form English uses of a time of life, without adding “time”.

check.note: “Utor” is first of all “use, make use of”. “Enjoy” is possible but chooses pleasure over use without saying so.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “let it make use of its own good”. The note records “enjoy” as the other sense of the verb.

passages.latin: 'nihil est' inquam 'adhuc quod aut rebus aut verbis exhibuimus; levia sunt ista et fallacia pignora animi multisque involuta lenociniis: quid profecerim morti crediturus sum. Non timide itaque componor ad illum diem quo remotis strophis ac fucis de me iudicaturus sum, utrum loquar fortia an sentiam, numquid simulatio fuerit et mimus quidquid contra fortunam iactavi verborum contumacium.
passages.english: “What we have shown so far, whether in deeds or in words,” I say, “is nothing. Those are slight and deceptive guarantees of what the mind is, and wrapped in much flattering ornament. As to what progress I have made, I shall take death’s word. So it is not timidly that I am readying myself for that day on which, with the tricks and the paint set aside, I shall pass judgment on myself: whether I say brave things or mean them, whether all the defiant words I have flung at fortune were a pretence and a piece of acting.

notes.note: This is Seneca addressing himself, as the section before announces. The quotation opens here and does not close until the end of 26.6, so the English of this section ends with the quotation still open.
notes.other_reading: I say to myself

notes.note: First person plural, though the rest of the speech is in the singular. The plural is kept as the Latin has it; it may be the plural of a speaker talking of himself.
notes.other_reading: What I have shown so far

notes.note: “Pignus” is a pledge or security handed over as proof, and it goes with “crediturus” (to give credit, to believe) in the next clause. “Guarantees of what the mind is” spells out the bare genitive. “Animus” could lean towards “courage” here, but “mind” is kept to match “robur animi” in 26.6.
notes.other_reading: pledges of my courage

notes.note: “Lenocinium” is literally a pimp’s trade, hence adornment that makes a thing look better than it is. “Flattering ornament” gives the sense and loses the sordid colour.
notes.other_reading: and wrapped up in much pandering finery

notes.note: “Credere” with the dative is read as “believe”: he will believe death on the question of his progress. It could also be “entrust”: he will leave that question to death to settle.
notes.other_reading: what progress I have made, I am going to leave to death to decide

notes.note: “Componor” is passive with a middle sense, to compose or prepare oneself. “Non timide” is an understatement and is kept as “not timidly”, since “timidissimis” returns in 26.6.
notes.other_reading: So I am composing myself without fear

notes.note: “Stropha” (a Greek word) is a twist or dodge; “fucus” is red dye or face paint, hence disguise. Both are kept as images. “Set aside” renders the same verb as at the start of 26.6.
notes.other_reading: with all dodges and face paint removed

notes.note: “Sentire” is both to feel and to think or mean. Set against mere speaking, it is rendered “mean”.
notes.other_reading: whether I speak brave things or feel them

notes.note: A “mimus” is the Roman mime, a low stage piece with spoken parts, or an actor in one. “A piece of acting” keeps the stage; “farce” and “mime” both mislead in English of today.
notes.other_reading: were a pretence and a farce

notes.note: “Iactare” is to throw about and also to boast; the English keeps the throwing. “Fortune” has no capital, though as the opponent defied it is close to being personified.
notes.other_reading: all the stubborn words I have boastfully thrown out against Fortune

check.note: “Pignora” are pledges in the sense of securities or tokens that vouch for something. “Pledges of the mind” is hard to understand as it stands, and “animus” here leans towards spirit or courage.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “guarantees of what the mind is”. A guarantee is still a security offered as proof, and the bare “of the mind” is spelled out; “mind” is kept so that the word matches 26.2 and 26.6.

check.note: “Lenocinia” are a pander’s arts: embellishment that makes a thing look better than it is. “Allurements” suggests temptations, which is not the point.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “wrapped in much flattering ornament”. The note records the literal sense of the word.

check.note: “Sentire” can mean “really think, mean” as well as “feel”, and the English picks “feel” without saying so. “Speak brave things” is also stiff English.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “Speak brave things or feel them” becomes “say brave things or mean them”. Set against mere speaking, “sentire” is what a man really thinks; the suggested “only” and “really” are not in the Latin, and its “words” would blur the “verba” that comes later in the sentence.

check.note: A “mimus” is a stage piece played by an actor. “Farce” today mostly means something absurd, which shifts the point from “acted” to “ridiculous”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “a pretence and a piece of acting”. The question in the Latin is whether the defiance was acted, not whether it was absurd.

check.note: “Iactare” is “throw out” but also “boast, brag”. The English keeps only the throwing.
check.decided: Declined: “Flung at fortune” stands. The suggested “tossed out” also keeps only the throwing, and no single English verb both throws and boasts; the note records the boasting sense of “iactare”.

passages.latin: Remove existimationem hominum: dubia semper est et in partem utramque dividitur. Remove studia tota vita tractata: mors de te pronuntiatura est. Ita dico: disputationes et litterata colloquia et ex praeceptis sapientium verba collecta et eruditus sermo non ostendunt verum robur animi; est enim oratio etiam timidissimis audax. Quid egeris tunc apparebit cum animam ages. Accipio condicionem, non reformido iudicium.'
passages.english: Set aside the estimate people make: it is always uncertain and is split both ways. Set aside the studies you have pursued all your life: death is going to pronounce on you. This is what I say: debates, literary conversations, words collected from the teachings of the wise, and learned talk do not show the true strength of the mind; for even the most timid have bold speech. What you have done will be seen at the moment when you breathe your last. I accept the terms; I do not shrink from the judgment.”

notes.note: The second person is Seneca still addressing himself: this section continues the speech opened in 26.5 and closes it at the end. “Existimatio hominum” is the estimate people form of a man, his reputation; “opinion” is avoided because the glossary keeps it for “opinio”.
notes.other_reading: Set aside what people think of you

notes.note: Literally “is divided into each of two sides”, as of a vote or a split jury.
notes.other_reading: it is divided between the two sides

notes.note: “Pronuntiare” is the word for a judge delivering a verdict. “Pronounce on you” keeps the courtroom sense that “iudicium” picks up at the end.
notes.other_reading: death is going to deliver the verdict on you

notes.note: “Litteratus” is lettered, educated. “Literary” is the nearest word of today, though the talk need not be about books.
notes.other_reading: cultivated conversations

notes.note: “Sapientium” is plural, so “the wise” and not the glossary’s singular “the wise man”. “Verba” is “words”, as twice in 26.5, so that the contrast of words with real strength can be followed across both sections.
notes.other_reading: sayings gathered from the precepts of wise men

notes.note: “Robur” is oak, hence hard strength. “Animus” is kept as “mind”, though “spirit” or “courage” would also fit the context.
notes.other_reading: the real toughness of one’s spirit

notes.latin: est enim oratio etiam timidissimis audax
notes.note: Dative of possession: even the most timid have bold speech. “Oratio” is speech in general, not a formal oration.
notes.other_reading: for speech is bold even in the greatest cowards

notes.latin: Quid egeris tunc apparebit cum animam ages
notes.note: A play on “agere”: “quid egeris” is “what you have done” or “achieved”, and “animam agere” is the idiom for being at the last breath, literally “driving out the soul”. English cannot keep one verb for both, so the sense is translated.
notes.other_reading: What you have accomplished will appear when you are giving up your soul

notes.note: “Condicio” is the terms of an agreement or of a trial. “Iudicium” is “judgment” as in the glossary, and here also the court hearing itself.
notes.other_reading: I accept the condition; I do not dread the trial

check.note: “Of you” is supplied. It is reasonable, since “de te” follows, but it is not in these words.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “Of you” is dropped and the English now reads “Set aside the estimate people make”. The suggested “opinion” is not used, because the glossary keeps that word for “opinio” and “existimatio” is a valuing, an estimate.

check.note: The estimate is uncertain and wavering. “Doubtful” in English of today suggests “questionable”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “it is always uncertain”.

check.note: “Lettered” is old-fashioned.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “literary conversations”. A note says that the Latin word means educated talk, not only talk about books.

check.latin: ex praeceptis sapientium verba collecta et eruditus sermo
check.note: Without commas the English can be read as “the teachings of the wise and learned”, with “talk” left hanging. The Latin has four separate items.
check.decided: Accepted: The four items are now set off by commas: “debates, literary conversations, words collected from the teachings of the wise, and learned talk”. Nothing is dropped; the repeated “and” of the Latin becomes the commas of an English list.

check.note: “Verba” was “words” twice in 26.5 and becomes “sayings” here. The contrast of words with real strength runs through both sections.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “words collected from the teachings of the wise”, so that one Latin word has one English word across the two sections.

check.latin: Quid egeris tunc apparebit cum animam ages
check.note: The Latin plays on one verb, used for “what you have done” and for breathing the last breath. The English gives the sense and loses the play, so a note is needed.
check.decided: Accepted: The rendering is kept, as the first suggestion allows, and the note on the play on “agere” stays. English has no single verb for both “do” and “breathe out the soul”.

passages.latin: Hoc tibi soli putas accidisse et admiraris quasi rem novam quod peregrinatione tam longa et tot locorum varietatibus non discussisti tristitiam gravitatemque mentis? Animum debes mutare, non caelum. Licet vastum traieceris mare, licet, ut ait Vergilius noster, terraeque urbesque recedant, sequentur te quocumque perveneris vitia.
passages.english: Do you think this has happened to you alone, and do you wonder at it as something new, that by so long a journey and so great a variety of places you have not shaken off the sadness and heaviness of your mind? It is your mind you must change, not your sky. Though you have crossed the vast sea, though, as our Vergil says, “lands and cities fall away,” your vices will follow you wherever you arrive.

notes.note: “Mens” here and “animus” in the next sentence are both rendered “mind”: the Latin has two words, but no difference seems to be meant. “Gravitas” is heaviness, and “gravia” in 28.6 is used of oppressive places.
notes.other_reading: the gloom and weight on your spirits

notes.note: “Varietas” is variety. It is kept apart from “change”, which is saved for “mutare” in the next sentence and “mutatio” in 28.4.
notes.other_reading: so many changes of place

notes.note: “Mutare” is to change or exchange, and “caelum” is sky, hence climate or region. In English “change your mind” usually means to alter an opinion, which is not meant: the sense is a different mind, not a different sky.
notes.other_reading: You need a different mind, not a different climate

notes.note: Perfect subjunctive after “licet”: the crossing is already done when the vices follow, so “though you have crossed”.
notes.other_reading: Though you may cross the vast sea

notes.note: From Vergil, Aeneid 3.72, where the verb is “recedunt” (from memory, unchecked); Seneca fits it to his own sentence with a subjunctive. The Latin marks it only by naming Vergil; the quotation marks are added in the English.
notes.other_reading: though lands and cities drop back out of sight

notes.note: The Latin has no “your”; it is supplied, since the vices that follow him are his own. “Vitia” is “vices” as in the glossary, though “faults” would also fit sadness and heaviness of mind.
notes.other_reading: faults will follow you wherever you get to

check.note: “Varietas” is variety, not change. “Changes” runs together with “change” for “mutare” in the next sentence and “change of place” in 28.4, so two Latin words share one English word.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “so great a variety of places”. “Change” is left for “mutare” and “mutatio” alone.

check.note: “Mens” here and “animus” in the next sentence are both “mind”. This is fine if no difference is meant, but the Latin has two words.
check.decided: Accepted: “Mind” is kept for both, as the suggestion allows, because the two sentences speak of the same thing. The note now says plainly that the Latin has two words.

check.note: “Caelum” is sky and also climate. “Sky” is the literal choice and the possessive is supplied.
check.decided: Declined: “Not your sky” stands. “Caelum” is first of all “sky” and the image is kept, with “climate” in the note; Latin leaves the possessive out with both nouns alike, and English needs it with both for the sentence to be understood.

check.note: The verb is perfect: the crossing is already done when the vices follow.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “Though you have crossed the vast sea”.

check.note: “Behind” is added; the verb is just “recede, fall back”. Seneca has fitted Vergil’s verb to his own sentence.
check.decided: Accepted: The quotation now reads “lands and cities fall away”, with nothing added to the verb. The note keeps the reference to Vergil, from memory and unchecked.

passages.latin: Hoc idem querenti cuidam Socrates ait, 'quid miraris nihil tibi peregrinationes prodesse, cum te circumferas? premit te eadem causa quae expulit'. Quid terrarum iuvare novitas potest? quid cognitio urbium aut locorum? in irritum cedit ista iactatio. Quaeris quare te fuga ista non adiuvet? tecum fugis. Onus animi deponendum est: non ante tibi ullus placebit locus.
passages.english: To someone who made this same complaint Socrates said: “Why do you wonder that your journeys do you no good, when it is yourself you carry around? The same cause that drove you out is pressing on you.” What help can the newness of lands be? What help is getting to know cities or places? That tossing about of yours comes to nothing. Do you ask why that flight of yours does not help you? You flee with yourself. The burden of the mind must be laid down: until then no place will please you.

notes.note: Seneca gives the remark as a saying of Socrates; an earlier source for it could not be named (from memory, unchecked). It is translated as quoted speech, as the Latin marks it.
notes.other_reading: Socrates replied

notes.note: Literally “when you carry yourself around”: he takes on every journey the self he is trying to leave behind. “Cum” could be “when”, “since” or “although”; “when” is used.
notes.other_reading: seeing that you take yourself about with you

notes.latin: premit te eadem causa quae expulit
notes.note: “Premit” is presses, weighs on or pursues; “pressing on” leaves both the weight and the pursuit open. “Expulit” is “drove out”, that is, from home; the Latin has no “you” with it, and it is supplied.
notes.other_reading: the same cause that drove you away is at your heels

notes.note: “Iactatio” is a tossing about, used of ships at sea and of the sick in bed; the letter goes on to use the same word of shifting cargo. The physical image is kept, and “of yours” gives the force of “ista”, which points at the person addressed.
notes.other_reading: all that restless moving about is wasted

notes.note: Two words in the Latin: “you flee with yourself”, that is, in your own company. It is kept as short as English allows.
notes.other_reading: you take yourself along when you run away

notes.note: The genitive can mean the burden that lies on the mind or the burden that the mind is. The plain “of” leaves it as open as the Latin.
notes.other_reading: the load on your mind

notes.latin: non ante tibi ullus placebit locus
notes.note: Literally “not before will any place please you”; “before” looks back to laying the burden down.
notes.other_reading: no place will please you before that

check.note: The same word was “journey” in 28.1 and is “travels” here. The two sections are one argument.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “your journeys”, matching “journey” in 28.1.

check.note: “Premere” can mean “presses hard on, is at your heels”, which fits “drove you out”, as well as “weighs on”, which fits the burden later. The English has chosen one.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “is pressing on you”, which can be heard both of a weight and of a pursuer, as the Latin verb can. The note gives both senses.

check.note: “Iste” points at the person addressed: “that tossing about of yours”. The same applies to “fuga ista” in the next sentence.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “That tossing about of yours” and “that flight of yours”. Both phrases have the same pointing word in the Latin.

check.note: Found while settling: “iuvare” here and “adiuvet” two sentences later are one verb, “help”, but the draft had “what good” here, the phrase it also used for “prodesse” in the saying of Socrates.
check.decided: Accepted: The two questions now read “What help can the newness of lands be? What help is getting to know cities or places?”. “Help” answers “does not help you” below, and “do you no good” is left for the other verb.

passages.latin: At cum istuc exemeris malum, omnis mutatio loci iucunda fiet; in ultimas expellaris terras licebit, in quolibet barbariae angulo colloceris, hospitalis tibi illa qualiscumque sedes erit. Magis quis veneris quam quo interest, et ideo nulli loco addicere debemus animum. Cum hac persuasione vivendum est: 'non sum uni angulo natus, patria mea totus hic mundus est'.
passages.english: But once you have removed that ill, every change of place will become pleasant. Though you are driven out to the farthest lands, though you are set down in whatever corner of barbarian country, that dwelling, whatever it is like, will be hospitable to you. Who you are when you come matters more than where you come to, and for that reason we ought not to sign our mind over to any place. One must live with this conviction: “I was not born for one corner; this whole world is my country.”

notes.note: “Malum” is any ill; here it is the weight sitting on him in the section before, where he is called a sick man, so “ill” and not the moral “evil”. “Eximere” is to take out or remove, as a doctor does.
notes.other_reading: once you have taken that evil out

notes.note: “Licebit” is the conceding “licet” of 28.1 in the future tense, so “though”, as there. It governs “colloceris” as well.
notes.other_reading: You may be driven out to the farthest lands

notes.note: “Barbaria” is the world that is neither Greek nor Roman; “quolibet” is “any you like”.
notes.other_reading: though you are settled in any corner of the uncivilised world you please

notes.latin: hospitalis tibi illa qualiscumque sedes erit
notes.note: “Sedes” is a seat, hence a place to stay or live. “Dwelling” is used so that “place” can be kept for “locus”, which runs through the section.
notes.other_reading: that seat, such as it is, will welcome you

notes.latin: Magis quis veneris quam quo interest
notes.note: Very compressed: literally “it matters more who you have come than where to”. It is expanded just enough to be English.
notes.other_reading: It matters more as who you arrive than where you arrive

notes.note: “Addicere” is a legal word: to adjudge or sign over property, or a debtor to his creditor as a bondsman. “Sign over” keeps the legal sense; the Latin says literally “to no place ought we to sign over the mind”.
notes.other_reading: we ought not to bind our mind in bondage to any place

notes.note: “Persuasio” is a settled conviction; “opinion” is avoided, since the glossary keeps it for “opinio”. The gerundive is impersonal, so “one must”.
notes.other_reading: We must live in this belief

notes.latin: patria mea totus hic mundus est
notes.note: “Patria” is the native country; “mundus” is the world or the whole universe. The thought is the Cynic and Stoic one of being a citizen of the world; Seneca gives it here as a motto without naming a source.
notes.other_reading: this whole universe is my fatherland

check.note: “Malum” is any ill or trouble, and the section before speaks of a sick man, so an ailment is in view. “Evil” has a moral ring the context may not want.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “once you have removed that ill”. “Ill” is taken from the suggestion; “removed” is used and not “got rid of”, because the Latin verb is the plain one for taking a thing out.

check.note: This is the conceding “licet” that was “Though” in 28.1. “You may” reads at first as possibility or permission.
check.decided: Accepted: The sentence now reads “Though you are driven out to the farthest lands, though you are set down in whatever corner of barbarian country”, and runs on into the main clause. “Are” is used where the suggestion had “be”, which is an old form.

check.note: “Seat” for a place to live is odd in English of today.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “that dwelling, whatever it is like”. The suggested “place to live” is not used, because “place” is the word for “locus” three times in this section and “sedes” is a different word.

check.note: “Addicere” is a legal word: to assign a person or thing to an owner or creditor. “Make over” is right but may not be understood.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “sign our mind over to any place”. The legal image is kept in a phrase readers of today know.

passages.latin: Num quid tam turbidum fieri potest quam forum? ibi quoque licet quiete vivere, si necesse sit. Sed si liceat disponere se, conspectum quoque et viciniam fori procul fugiam; nam ut loca gravia etiam firmissimam valetudinem temptant, ita bonae quoque menti necdum adhuc perfectae et convalescenti sunt aliqua parum salubria.
passages.english: Can anything be as turbulent as the forum? Even there one may live quietly, if it should be necessary. But if one might place oneself, I would flee far from even the sight and the neighbourhood of the forum; for just as oppressive places test even the strongest health, so for a good mind too, one that is not yet perfected and is recovering, there are some places that are not wholesome enough.

notes.latin: Num quid tam turbidum fieri potest quam forum?
notes.note: “Num” expects the answer no, as the English question does. The forum is the public square of Rome, the place of the law courts, business and politics.
notes.other_reading: Surely nothing can be as turbulent as the forum?

notes.note: Literally “if it were allowed to dispose oneself”, that is, to station oneself by choice. “Liceat” repeats “licet” from the sentence before, so “may” is answered by “might”. The Latin is impersonal and then switches to the first person; the switch is kept.
notes.other_reading: if one were free to arrange one’s own life

notes.note: The form is either future indicative or present subjunctive. After “si liceat” it is read as subjunctive.
notes.other_reading: I shall flee

notes.note: “Gravis” is heavy, and of a place or its air oppressive and unhealthy. “Oppressive” keeps it apart from “valetudinem” (health) and “salubria” (wholesome), and nearer to the heaviness of mind in 28.1.
notes.other_reading: unhealthy places

notes.note: “Temptare” is to put to the test and, of illness, to attack. “Test” is used.
notes.other_reading: attack even the strongest health

notes.latin: bonae quoque menti necdum adhuc perfectae et convalescenti
notes.note: “Bona mens” is a good or sound mind; “good” is kept, because this mind is said to be only now regaining its health. “Necdum adhuc” is a doubled “not yet” and goes with “perfectae” alone; “convalescenti” keeps the medical picture of a patient regaining strength.
notes.other_reading: for a sound mind too, as yet unfinished and gaining strength

notes.note: “Aliqua” is neuter plural and can pick up “loca” (“some places”) or stand alone (“some things”). The English takes it with “loca”, since the sentence gives the reason for fleeing a place. “Parum” is “too little”, “not enough”.
notes.other_reading: some things are far from wholesome

check.latin: Num quid tam turbidum fieri potest
check.note: “Num” expects the answer no. The English question is neutral.
check.decided: Declined: “Can anything be as turbulent as the forum?” stands. The Latin is a question about “anything”, and the English question already expects the answer no; the suggestion would turn it into a statement about “nothing”. The note records the force of “num”.

check.note: “Disponere se” is to place or station oneself, and “one’s own life” expands it. “Liceat” also repeats “licet” from the sentence before, and that link is lost; the jump from the impersonal to the first person is awkward.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “But if one might place oneself”, which drops “one’s own life” and lets “might” answer “may” in the sentence before. The Latin clause is impersonal and only the main verb is first person, so the suggested first person in the clause with “if” is not taken.

check.note: The English uses unhealthy, health and healthy where the Latin has three different words. “Gravis” is “oppressive, heavy”, and echoes the heaviness of mind in 28.1.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “oppressive places”, and “salubria” at the end becomes “wholesome”, so that the three Latin words have three English words.

check.note: “Try” in this sense is a little old-fashioned. The verb means attack or put to the test.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “test even the strongest health”. “Test” is one of the two senses the point itself gives for the verb, and it is plainer than the suggested “put a strain on”, which brings in a different image.

check.note: “Bona mens” can also be “a sound mind”, which suits the image of health. The English has taken the moral sense.
check.decided: Declined: “A good mind” stands. “Bona” is “good”, and this mind is described in the same phrase as not yet perfected and recovering, which “sound” would contradict. The note records “sound mind”.

check.note: “Still” is not in the Latin: the doubled “not yet” goes with “perfected” only.
check.decided: Accepted: “Still” is removed and the phrase now reads “one that is not yet perfected and is recovering”. The second “is” keeps “not yet” from being read with “recovering”.

check.note: “Aliqua” is neuter plural: “some things” in general, or “some places”. “Some that” makes the reader supply “places”, and the English has to choose openly.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “there are some places that are not wholesome enough”. The choice is made openly, but for “places”: the word follows “loca” in the same sentence, and the sentence gives the reason for fleeing a place. A note records “some things”.

passages.latin: De Marcellino nostro quaeris et vis scire quid agat. Raro ad nos venit, non ulla alia ex causa quam quod audire verum timet, a quo periculo iam abest; nulli enim nisi audituro dicendum est. Ideo de Diogene nec minus de aliis Cynicis qui libertate promiscua usi sunt et obvios monuerunt dubitari solet an hoc facere debuerint. Quid enim, si quis surdos obiurget aut natura morbove mutos?
passages.english: You ask about our Marcellinus and want to know how he is doing. He seldom comes to us, for no other reason than that he is afraid to hear the truth; and that is a danger he is now clear of, for it should be spoken to no one unless he is going to hear it. That is why, about Diogenes and no less about the other Cynics who spoke freely to all alike and admonished whoever came their way, it is commonly doubted whether they ought to have done this. For what if someone were to rebuke the deaf, or those who are mute by nature or by illness?

notes.note: “Noster” marks him as a shared acquaintance, as it marks Vergil as a shared author in 28.1. The same English is used in both places.
notes.other_reading: our friend Marcellinus

notes.note: The everyday idiom for “how he is” or “what he is up to”; with what follows it also asks how he is getting on morally.
notes.other_reading: what he is doing

notes.note: “Nos” may be a true plural (Seneca and those around him) or the plural an author uses for himself. The plural is kept.
notes.other_reading: He seldom comes to me

notes.note: Literally “from which danger he is now away”. With the next clause it is taken that Seneca has stopped telling him the truth, since he will not listen; it could also mean only that he is safe by staying away.
notes.other_reading: though he is by now far from that risk

notes.latin: nulli enim nisi audituro dicendum est
notes.note: “Audituro” is “one who is going to hear”, with the sense of listening. “Hear” is kept to match “afraid to hear the truth” before it and the deaf after it; the “it” (the truth) is supplied.
notes.other_reading: for one should speak only to a man who will listen

notes.note: Diogenes of Sinope, the best known of the Cynic philosophers, famous for accosting people in the street with blunt reproofs.
notes.other_reading: about Diogenes the Cynic

notes.note: “Libertas” here is freedom of speech, frankness; “promiscua” is used on all alike, without choosing. The English turns the noun into “spoke freely” so that the kind of freedom is plain.
notes.other_reading: who used an indiscriminate freedom

notes.note: “Solet” is “it is usual”, so “commonly”. The Latin is impersonal and the English keeps it so.
notes.other_reading: people often question

notes.note: “Obvii” are those met in the road; “monere” is to advise, warn or admonish.
notes.other_reading: gave advice to anyone they met

notes.note: The mute are added beside the deaf, presumably because those mute from birth are usually deaf as well; the Latin does not say so. “Obiurget” is stronger than “monuerunt”, so “rebuke”.
notes.other_reading: or people dumb from birth or from disease

check.note: “Friend” is added. The same Latin word is rendered without it for Vergil in 28.1.
check.decided: Accepted: “Friend” is removed, so that “noster” is rendered here exactly as it is with Vergil in 28.1.

check.note: This can be the idiom “how he is” or the literal “what he is doing, what he is up to”. The English chooses the first.
check.decided: Declined: “How he is doing” stands. “Quid agat” is the everyday Latin for asking after someone, and the English phrase keeps the verb “do” and can be heard both ways; the note records the literal reading.

check.note: “Libertas” here is freedom of speech, frankness. Bare “freedom” does not tell the reader that, and the sentence is about speaking the truth to people.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “who spoke freely to all alike”. The note gives the more literal wording.

check.latin: dubitari solet an hoc facere debuerint
check.note: The English word order is hard to follow, and “solet” is “commonly, as a rule” more than “often”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The sentence is reordered and “often” becomes “commonly”: “That is why, about Diogenes and no less about the other Cynics who spoke freely to all alike and admonished whoever came their way, it is commonly doubted whether they ought to have done this”. The impersonal “it is doubted” is kept, as the brief asks, where the suggestion had “people question”.

passages.latin: Hoc, mi Lucili, non existimo magno viro faciendum: diluitur eius auctoritas nec habet apud eos satis ponderis quos posset minus obsolefacta corrigere. Sagittarius non aliquando ferire debet, sed aliquando deerrare; non est ars quae ad effectum casu venit. Sapientia ars est: certum petat, eligat profecturos, ab iis quos desperavit recedat, non tamen cito relinquat et in ipsa desperatione extrema remedia temptet.
passages.english: This, my Lucilius, I do not think a great man should do: his authority is watered down and does not have enough weight with those whom it could set right if it were less cheapened. An archer ought not to hit now and then, but to miss now and then; that is not an art which comes to its result by chance. Wisdom is an art: let it aim at what is sure, let it choose those who will make progress, let it draw back from those of whom it has despaired, yet let it not abandon them quickly, and in despair itself let it try remedies of last resort.

notes.note: “This” is the practice defended in the section before: admonishing many people at random in the hope that some of it works. “Mi” is “my”; an English letter would say “my dear”, which adds a word.
notes.other_reading: That, my dear Lucilius

notes.note: “Diluere” is to dilute, as wine with water; the image is kept.
notes.other_reading: his authority is weakened

notes.note: “Obsolefacta” is made common, worn by overuse, like a coin or a garment. It agrees with “auctoritas”: authority that had been made less common.
notes.other_reading: if it had not grown so stale

notes.latin: non aliquando ferire debet, sed aliquando deerrare
notes.note: The point lies in the repeated “aliquando” (“sometimes”, “now and then”): hitting should be the rule and missing the exception. The repetition is kept, and “now and then” is used because “ought not to hit sometimes” can be misread as “ought sometimes not to hit”.
notes.other_reading: ought not to hit the mark only now and then, but to miss it only now and then

notes.note: “Ars” is a skill or craft with a method, as against luck. “Art” is used to match the “arts” of 29.11 and 29.12.
notes.other_reading: Wisdom is a skill

notes.note: “Certum” is something definite or sure: a fixed mark for the archer, or a result that can be counted on. The English takes “what is sure”, against “by chance” just before, and lets “aim” carry the archer on.
notes.other_reading: let it aim at a definite mark

notes.note: The participle could come from “proficere” (to make progress, to benefit) or from “proficisci” (to set out). The sense requires the first.
notes.other_reading: let it pick out those who will benefit

notes.latin: ab iis quos desperavit recedat, non tamen cito relinquat
notes.note: Wisdom is to draw back from the hopeless, yet not abandon them quickly; “recedat” and “relinquat” are kept apart as “draw back” and “abandon”. The “them” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: let it withdraw from those it has given up on, but not be quick to desert them

notes.latin: in ipsa desperatione extrema remedia temptet
notes.note: “Extrema” can go with “remedia” (the last and most drastic remedies a doctor has) or with “desperatione” (“in utmost despair itself”). It is taken with “remedia” and rendered “of last resort”.
notes.other_reading: and even in utter despair let it try remedies

check.note: English of today says “my dear Lucilius”.
check.decided: Declined: “My Lucilius” stands. The Latin has only “mi”, “my”, and “dear” would add a word; the note records “my dear Lucilius” as the other rendering.

check.latin: Sagittarius non aliquando ferire debet, sed aliquando deerrare
check.note: The word for word English can be read as “an archer ought sometimes not to hit”. The point is that hitting now and then is not the standard; missing now and then is.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “An archer ought not to hit now and then, but to miss now and then”. “Now and then” is taken from the suggestion because it cannot be misread as the draft’s “sometimes” could; “ought” is kept for “debet” where the suggestion had “business”.

check.note: “Certum” can be “a fixed, definite mark”, carrying on the archer image, and not only “what is sure”. The English has chosen without saying so.
check.decided: Declined: “Let it aim at what is sure” stands. “Certum” is a bare “something sure”, set against “by chance” in the sentence before, and the Latin has no word for a mark; “aim” already carries the archer on. The note records “a definite mark”.

check.note: “Relinquere” is “abandon”, a stronger step than the “draw back” just before. “Leave” blurs the difference between the two.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “yet let it not abandon them quickly”, so that drawing back and abandoning are two clearly different steps.

check.note: “Moment” is added.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “Moment” is removed and the English now reads “in despair itself”. The suggested “even” is not taken, since the Latin has only “and”.

check.note: “Extrema” is “last” in the sense of last resort, extreme. “The last remedies” could be read as the final ones in a series.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “let it try remedies of last resort”. The note keeps the other way of construing “extrema”.

passages.latin: ÔQuis hoc?' inquis, tamquam nescias cui imperem. Epicurus; sed idem hoc omnes tibi ex omni domo conclamabunt, Peripatetici, Academici, Stoici, Cynici. Quis enim placere populo potest cui placet virtus? malis artibus popularis favor quaeritur. Similem te illis facias oportet: non probabunt nisi agnoverint. Multo autem ad rem magis pertinet qualis tibi videaris quam aliis; conciliari nisi turpi ratione amor turpium non potest.
passages.english: “Who said this?” you ask, as if you did not know whom I order to pay. Epicurus. But all of them, from every house, will shout this same thing to you together: Peripatetics, Academics, Stoics, Cynics. For who can please the people if virtue pleases him? The favour of the people is sought by bad arts. You must make yourself like those people: they will not approve of you unless they recognise you. But what you seem to yourself matters far more than what you seem to others; the love of base people cannot be won except by base means.

notes.note: The Latin has no verb: “Who this?”; “said” is supplied. “This” is the saying quoted in the section before, that he never wished to please the people. In the Latin as given a stray character stands before “Quis” where an opening quotation mark belongs, a slip of the digitised copy.
notes.other_reading: “Whose is this?”

notes.note: “Imperare” with a dative is to give orders to someone and also to levy on him, to demand payment or supplies. The section before is all in the language of debt and instalments, so the levy sense is taken; the one made to pay is Epicurus.
notes.other_reading: as if you did not know whom I give my orders to

notes.note: “House” is the household of a philosophical school; it is kept as an image, since the list of schools follows at once. “Conclamabunt” is to shout all together.
notes.other_reading: from every school

notes.latin: Quis enim placere populo potest cui placet virtus?
notes.note: The sentence turns on “placere” twice, so “please” is used both times, and “the people” for “populus” to match the next sentence.
notes.other_reading: For who that likes virtue can be liked by the public?

notes.note: “Artes” are arts, skills or practices; “bad arts” is the Latin phrase for dishonest methods. “Arts” is kept because 29.3 calls wisdom an art and 29.12 sets philosophy above all “arts”.
notes.other_reading: by dishonest means

notes.note: “Illis” is plural by sense after the singular “populus”: the people whose favour is sought, not the philosophers just listed. The English writes “those people” so that this cannot be mistaken.
notes.other_reading: You must make yourself like them

notes.note: Neither verb has an object in the Latin; English needs them, and “you” is supplied twice. “Agnoscere” is also to acknowledge as one of one’s own, which is the point: they must find their own likeness in him.
notes.other_reading: they will not approve of you unless they recognise themselves in you

notes.note: “Ratio” here is a way or method, not “reason”; the glossary allows this. “Turpis” is base or shameful, and it is repeated in “turpium”, so “base” is used twice.
notes.other_reading: except in a shameful way

notes.note: “Turpium” is taken as persons: the love that base people give. Grammatically it could be neuter, “love of base things”, but that does not fit “conciliari” (to win over).
notes.other_reading: the affection of shameful people

check.note: In the Latin as given a stray character stands before “Quis” where an opening quotation mark belongs, a digitising slip. The English rightly treats the words as a quoted question and has to supply “said”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English is kept, as suggested, and the note now records the slip in the digitised Latin.

check.note: “Imperare” with a dative also means to levy on someone, to demand payment or supplies from him. The section before is all in the language of payment and debt, so that sense may be the point, and the English drops it without saying so.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The verb is now rendered “order to pay”. The section before speaks of a debt and its last instalment, so the levy sense is taken; “order” is kept where the suggestion had “call on”, because the Latin verb commands. The note records the plainer reading.

check.note: “Domus” here is a philosophical school. “House” is literal and a reader may stumble.
check.decided: Declined: “From every house” stands. “Domus” is “house”, an image for a school and its household, and the brief keeps images; the four schools are named in the same sentence, and the note gives “school”.

check.note: “Bad arts” is not natural English; the sense is dishonest practices. Against changing it, “ars” is “art” in 29.3 and 29.12.
check.decided: Declined: “Bad arts” stands. “Malus” is simply “bad”, and “dishonest” would narrow it to one kind of badness; “arts” stays to match 29.3 and 29.12, as the point itself allows. The note records “dishonest means”.

check.note: “Illis” means the people. In the English, “them” follows a list of four schools and “bad arts”, so a reader can take it to mean the philosophers, which reverses the point.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “You must make yourself like those people”, so that the pronoun can only mean the people whose favour is sought.

check.note: Latin can leave the objects out; English cannot, and the sentence reads as broken. The object is “you”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “they will not approve of you unless they recognise you”. The note says that both objects are supplied and gives the fuller sense of the second verb.

check.note: “The base” is old-fashioned, and “the love of the base” can be read as love for them and not love from them.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “the love of base people cannot be won except by base means”. “People” removes the old-fashioned “the base”, and with “won” the love can only be theirs; “base” is kept for both forms of “turpis” and “love” for “amor”, since “shameful” sits badly with persons and “affection” is weaker than the Latin.

passages.latin: Quid ergo illa laudata et omnibus praeferenda artibus rebusque philosophia praestabit? scilicet ut malis tibi placere quam populo, ut aestimes iudicia, non numeres, ut sine metu deorum hominumque vivas, ut aut vincas mala aut finias. Ceterum, si te videro celebrem secundis vocibus vulgi, si intrante te clamor et plausus, pantomimica ornamenta, obstrepuerint, si tota civitate te feminae puerique laudaverint, quidni ego tui miserear, cum sciam quae via ad istum favorem ferat? Vale.
passages.english: What, then, will that philosophy deliver, which is praised and is to be preferred to all arts and all things? This, of course: that you would rather please yourself than the people, that you assess judgments and do not count them, that you live without fear of gods and men, that you either overcome evils or end them. But if I see you celebrated by the approving voices of the crowd, if when you come in there is a din of shouting and applause, the honours of a pantomime dancer, if throughout the whole city women and children praise you, why should I not pity you, since I know what road leads to that favour? Farewell.

notes.note: “Praestare” is to deliver, provide or make good on what was promised.
notes.other_reading: What, then, will that philosophy do for you

notes.note: “Illa” points to philosophy as something well known and much spoken of; “laudata” is a bare “praised”.
notes.other_reading: that much praised philosophy

notes.note: “Artibus” echoes the “bad arts” of 29.11, so “arts” is kept. “Rebus” is simply “things”; the second “all” is repeated in English for clarity.
notes.other_reading: to be ranked above every skill and every possession

notes.note: “Scilicet” is “of course”, “namely”, sometimes with irony. It is taken here as a plain answer to his own question.
notes.other_reading: Why, this

notes.note: “Aestimare” is to assess the worth of a thing; “numerare” is to count. What matters is how good the judgments passed on a man are, not how many there are.
notes.other_reading: that you weigh judgments and do not count them

notes.latin: ut aut vincas mala aut finias
notes.note: “Finias” (“end them”) probably looks to ending troubles by ending life, a thought common in these letters, but the Latin says only “end”. The English is left as open as the Latin.
notes.other_reading: that you either conquer your ills or put an end to them

notes.note: “Secundus” is favourable, like a following wind. “Vulgus” is the crowd or common mass, a more contemptuous word than “populus” above, so “people” is not used.
notes.other_reading: by the cheers of the mob

notes.note: In apposition to “shouting and applause”: these are the distinctions that belong to a pantomime, the solo stage dancer who was the popular star of Seneca’s Rome. “Ornamenta” are trappings or marks of honour.
notes.other_reading: the trappings of a stage dancer

notes.note: “Pueri” can be boys or children in general. The pair is taken as the usual Latin way of naming all who are not grown men, so “women and children”; they stand for those whose praise carried least weight in Roman eyes.
notes.other_reading: women and boys

notes.note: “Cum” with the subjunctive gives the reason here, so “since”.
notes.other_reading: when I know

check.note: “For you” is added. “Praestare” is to deliver, to make good on a promise.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “What, then, will that philosophy deliver”, with nothing added.

check.note: “Scilicet” is “of course, namely”. “Just” adds the idea of “only this”, which the Latin does not say.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “This, of course:”.

check.note: “Celeber” is “much talked of, thronged, celebrated”. “Made famous” adds a result.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “celebrated by the approving voices of the crowd”. “By” is used where the suggestion had “in”, since the voices are what do the celebrating.

check.note: “Pueri” can mean children in general, not only boys. The English has chosen the narrower sense.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “women and children”. The Latin pair is the usual one for all who are not grown men, and the note records “women and boys”.

check.note: “Cum” with the subjunctive here gives the reason: “since”, not “when”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “since I know what road leads to that favour”.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft’s “so praised” adds an intensifier. The Latin has only “praised”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “which is praised and is to be preferred to all arts and all things”. “Laudata” is a bare “praised”, with no word for “so”.

check.note: Found while settling: “weigh” brings in the image of a balance, which the Latin does not have. “Aestimare” is to assess the worth of a thing.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “that you assess judgments and do not count them”. The note records “weigh” as the other rendering.

passages.latin: Magna res est, Lucili, haec et diu discenda, cum adventat hora illa inevitabilis, aequo animo abire. Alia genera mortis spei mita sunt: desinit morbus, incendium exstinguitur, ruina quos videbatur oppressura deposuit; mare quos hauserat eadem vi qua sorbebat eiecit incolumes; gladium miles ab ipsa perituri cervice re vocavit: nil habet quod speret quem senectus ducit ad mortem; huic uni intercedi non potest. Nullo genere homines mollius moriuntur sed nec diutius.
passages.english: This is a great thing, Lucilius, and one that has to be learned over a long time: to go away with an even mind when that hour which cannot be avoided draws near. Other kinds of death are mixed with hope: an illness comes to an end, a fire is put out, a falling building has set down the people it seemed about to crush; the sea has thrown out unharmed those it had swallowed, with the same force with which it was sucking them down; a soldier has drawn his sword back from the very neck of the man who was about to die. The man whom old age is leading to death has nothing to hope for; against this alone no one can step in. By no kind of death do people die more gently, but by none more slowly either.

notes.note: The Latin form carries obligation: the thing must be learned, and over a long time. The English says both.
notes.other_reading: one that takes a long time to learn

notes.note: Aequo animo is literally “with a level or even mind”. “Mind” is kept for animus as the glossary prefers, and “even” leaves “calm” free for tranquillitas. Abire is the plain verb for leaving, used here of dying, and the image is kept.
notes.other_reading: to depart calmly; to leave without complaint

notes.note: Mita is not a Latin word. It is read as a copying slip for mixta (“mixed”), which the sense requires.
notes.other_reading: have hope mingled with them

notes.note: Ruina is the collapse of a building, or the fallen mass itself. Deposuit is “has set down”, as one sets down a load, so the picture is of the wreck lowering people gently instead of crushing them.
notes.other_reading: a collapse has let down safely those it seemed about to bury

notes.note: Sorbere is to suck in or gulp down. The phrase is taken with the throwing out: the same force that was drawing them in threw them out.
notes.other_reading: as violently as it had been swallowing them

notes.note: A word split in two in the copy, read as revocavit, literally “has called back”. With a sword as its object the English says “drawn back”. The soldier is an executioner who stops at the last moment.
notes.other_reading: has called his sword back

notes.note: Intercedere is the public-law word for lodging a veto, and the form here is impersonal. The English takes “this” as the thing a veto would block, the death that old age brings. It can also be the old man, on whose behalf no one can step in.
notes.other_reading: for him alone no one can step in

notes.note: Diutius is “for a longer time”. It is taken of the dying itself being long drawn out.
notes.other_reading: but in none do they take longer over it either

check.note: “This” can be the thing against which no veto can be lodged or the man for whom no one can intervene. The English takes it as the thing without showing the choice.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “against this alone no one can step in”, taking the Latin “this” as the death that old age brings, the thing a veto would be lodged against. The note gives the other reading, in which it is the old man on whose behalf no one can step in.

check.note: The split word is revocavit. In English a sword is drawn back, not called back, so the literal version reads oddly.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “has drawn his sword back”. The Latin verb is literally “called back”, but with a sword as its object it means withdrawing the blade.

check.note: The Latin form carries obligation: it must be learned, and over a long time. The English gives only the length of time.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “one that has to be learned over a long time”, because the Latin form says that the thing must be learned, not only how long the learning takes.

check.note: Mita is a slip in the copy for mixta. The English reads it correctly and nothing needs to change.
check.decided: Accepted: “mixed with hope” stands. The copy’s mita is read as mixta and the note says so.

passages.latin: Inter hos Bassum licet numeres, qui nos decipi noluit. Is ait tam stultum esse qui mortem timeat quam qui senectutem; nam quemadmodum senectus adulescentiam sequitur, ita mors senectutem. Vivere noluit qui mori non vult; vita enim cum exceptione mortis data est; ad hanc itur. Quam ideo timere dementis est quia certa exspectantur, dubia metuuntur.
passages.english: You may count Bassus among these, a man who did not want us to be deceived. He says that a man who fears death is as much a fool as one who fears old age; for just as old age follows youth, so death follows old age. Whoever does not want to die did not want to live; for life was given with death as its proviso; it is towards death that one goes. To fear it is what a madman does, for this reason: what is certain is waited for, what is doubtful is feared.

notes.note: “These” are the people of the section before: those who have stood close to death, seen it coming and received it. The pronoun is left as it is.
notes.other_reading: Among such witnesses

notes.note: Noluit can be a plain “did not want” or a stronger “refused to let”. The plain sense is kept.
notes.other_reading: who refused to let us be deceived

notes.note: Roman adulescentia runs from the mid teens to about thirty, so it is wider than English “adolescence”. The English says “youth”.
notes.other_reading: young manhood

notes.note: Exceptio is a legal term: a reserving clause or proviso attached to a grant. The literal “with the exception of death” would say the opposite of what is meant, so the English gives the legal sense.
notes.other_reading: life was granted subject to the reservation of death

notes.note: An impersonal form, literally “there is a going towards this”. “This” is most naturally death, the nearest noun, and the English names death so that the pronoun is clear. It could conceivably point to the proviso.
notes.other_reading: it is towards this proviso that one goes

notes.note: Literally “is of a madman”, that is, the act or mark of one. The English says “is what a madman does”.
notes.other_reading: is the mark of a madman

notes.note: A general maxim in the passive. The point rests on the contrast between waiting for and fearing, so both verbs are kept plain.
notes.other_reading: certain things are expected, uncertain things are dreaded

check.note: The sense is right, but “a madman’s part” is old-fashioned English.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “To fear it is what a madman does, for this reason: what is certain is waited for, what is doubtful is feared.” The Latin says only “is of a madman”, and “part” was an old turn of English.

passages.latin: Mors necessitatem habet aequam et invictam: quis queri potest in ea condicione se esse in qua nemo non est? prima autem pars est aequitatis aequalitas. Sed nunc supervacuum est naturae causam agere, quae non aliam voluit legem nostram esse quam suam: quid quid composuit resolvit, et quidquid resolvit componit iterum.
passages.english: Death has a necessity that is fair and cannot be overcome: who can complain of being in a condition that no one is not in? And the first part of fairness is equality. But at this point it is needless to plead the case of nature, who wanted our law to be no other than her own: whatever she has put together she takes apart, and whatever she has taken apart she puts together again.

notes.note: Aequus means both “fair” and “equal, the same for all”. “Fair” is used so that it leads into “fairness” (aequitas) in the next sentence; the other sense is what the question about everyone’s condition goes on to state. Invictam is literally “unconquered”, in the usual sense of what cannot be conquered.
notes.other_reading: Death brings a necessity that is the same for all and invincible

notes.note: A double negative, literally “in which no one is not”, meaning that everyone is in it. The negative form is kept, since the translator’s rules ask that every “not” be kept.
notes.other_reading: a condition that everyone shares

notes.latin: prima autem pars est aequitatis aequalitas
notes.note: A play on two words from one root: aequitas (fairness) and aequalitas (equality), both echoing aequam above. English cannot keep the echo. Prima pars may be “first part” or “chief part”.
notes.other_reading: and the chief element of fairness is equality

notes.note: Causam agere is the courtroom idiom for pleading a case as an advocate. The legal colour continues in lex (“law”) and condicio (“condition, terms”).
notes.other_reading: to act as counsel for nature

notes.note: Quid quid is a split quidquid, “whatever”. Resolvit can be present or past in form. The first is taken as present (“takes apart”), answering componit, and the second, which sits inside its “whatever” clause as composuit does, as past (“has taken apart”).
notes.other_reading: and whatever she takes apart she puts together again

check.note: The Latin is a plain relative clause, “who wanted”. The English turns it into a reason with “since”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the case of nature, who wanted”, a plain relative clause as in the Latin, with no “since”.

check.note: Resolvit can be present or past. By the parallel with composuit in the first half it is more likely past here: “whatever she has taken apart”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “whatever she has taken apart she puts together again”. In the Latin this verb sits inside the “whatever” clause, where the first half has the past form “has put together”, so the past is the better reading. The note records the double form.

check.note: Aequam can also mean equal, the same for everyone, which is what the next clause says. “Fair” keeps the link to “fairness” and is defensible, but the other sense is not heard.
check.decided: Accepted: “fair” is kept, the first of the two courses offered, so that one English word runs from this adjective into “fairness” in the next sentence. The note gives the sense “equal for all”.

check.note: Literal, but hard to take in at first reading. The double negative means everyone.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “a condition that no one is not in”, which is shorter and easier to take in. The suggested “that no one is outside” would drop the Latin’s second “not”, which the translator’s rules say must be kept.

check.note: “For now” suggests the pleading is put off until later. The Latin says only now, at this point.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “But at this point”. The Latin word means “now” and promises nothing for later.

check.note: The word is split in the copy and should be read quidquid. The English reads it correctly.
check.decided: Accepted: “whatever she has put together” stands, and the note says that the split word is read as quidquid.

passages.latin: Iam vero si cui contigit ut illum senectus leviter emitteret, non repente avulsum vitae sed minutatim subductum, o ne ille agere gratias diis omnibus debet quod satiatus ad requiem homini necessariam, lasso gratam perductus est. Vides quosdam optantes mortem, et quidem magis quam rogari solet vita. Nescio utros existimem maiorem nobis animum dare, qui deposcunt mortem an qui hilares eam quietique opperiuntur, quoniam illud ex rabie interdum ac repentina indignatione fit, haec ex iudicio certo tranquillitas est. Venit aliquis ad mortem iratus: mortem venientem nemo hilaris excepit nisi qui se ad illam diu composuerat.
passages.english: And further, if it has been anyone’s lot that old age should let him go gently, not torn suddenly from life but drawn away little by little, oh, that man truly ought to give thanks to all the gods that, having had his fill, he has been brought through to a rest that is necessary for a human being and welcome to a tired one. You see some people wishing for death, and indeed more than life is usually begged for. I do not know which of the two I should think give us more courage, those who demand death or those who wait for it cheerful and quiet, since the first sometimes comes from frenzy and sudden indignation, while this calm comes from a settled judgment. Someone has come to death angry: no one has received death cheerfully when it came, except a man who had long made himself ready for it.

notes.note: Emittere is to send out or release; it is also used of freeing a slave and of discharging a soldier. The plain “let go” is kept. Leviter is “lightly, gently”.
notes.other_reading: should release him gently; should discharge him gently

notes.note: Ne here is the affirming particle (“truly, indeed”), not the negative. It is translated “truly”.
notes.other_reading: oh, he indeed

notes.note: Literally “sated, filled full”, as after a meal. The picture is of a guest who has had enough.
notes.other_reading: having had enough of life

notes.note: Magis is simply “more”, and the English adds nothing to it. Rogari is to be asked or begged for, as a condemned man begs for his life.
notes.other_reading: more than people usually ask for life

notes.note: Animus is “mind” in the glossary, but here the sense is courage or heart, which the glossary allows.
notes.other_reading: give us greater spirit; put more heart into us

notes.latin: haec ex iudicio certo tranquillitas est
notes.note: The Latin sets a neuter “that” (the demanding of death) against “this calm”. “Calm” is the glossary’s word for tranquillitas and “judgment” for iudicium. Certo is “fixed, settled, sure”.
notes.other_reading: the latter is a calm that comes from firm judgment

notes.note: Venit can be present (“comes”) or past (“has come”); the spelling does not show which. The English takes it as past, to match the past forms in the second half of the sentence. The sentence plays on the man coming to death and death coming to the man, kept by “come” and “came”.
notes.other_reading: Someone comes to death angry

notes.note: Se componere is to compose, settle or arrange oneself. It is taken as making oneself ready over a long time.
notes.other_reading: had long been composing himself for it

check.note: The Latin has only “more than”. “Keenly” is added.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and indeed more than life is usually begged for”. The Latin has only “more than”.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “when death comes, no one has received it”, a present set against a past in one clause, and took venit as present though the verbs that follow it are past.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Someone has come to death angry: no one has received death cheerfully when it came, except a man who had long made himself ready for it.” Venit can be present or past in form, and the past matches the other verbs of the sentence. The note gives the present.

passages.latin: Illud quidem aiebat tormentum nostra nos sentire opera, quod tunc trepidamus cum prope a nobis esse credimus mortem: a quo enim non prope est, parata omnibus locis omnibusque momentis? 'Sed consideremus' inquit 'tunc cum aliqua causa moriendi videtur accedere, quanto aliae propiores sint quae non timentur.'
passages.english: He used to say that this torment at least we feel by our own doing: that we tremble just when we believe death is near us. For who is there that it is not near, ready as it is in every place and at every moment? “But let us consider,” he said, “just when some cause of dying seems to be approaching, how much nearer other causes are that are not feared.”

notes.note: No subject is expressed. From the run of the letter the speaker is Bassus, the old man whose talk Seneca is reporting; the section does not name him, so the English has “He”.
notes.other_reading: Bassus used to say

notes.note: The phrase says that the effort or agency is the sufferers’ own: the torment is self-made.
notes.other_reading: that we have ourselves to thank for feeling this torment

notes.note: Quod can explain what the torment is (“namely that”) or give a cause (“because”). It is taken as explaining. Trepidare is to be in a flurry of fear; the English says “tremble”.
notes.other_reading: because we panic just when

notes.note: Tunc with cum is “then, when”, pointing at the moment. “Just when” is used in both places where the pair occurs.
notes.other_reading: at the time when

notes.latin: a quo enim non prope est
notes.note: Literally “for from whom is it not near?”. The question is in direct form, so it may be Seneca’s own aside or part of what Bassus said. It is left outside the quotation marks, as in the Latin.
notes.other_reading: (still reported speech) for, he said, who is there that it is not near

notes.note: The form serves as present and as past. Since the reporting verb before it is past, the English has “he said”.
notes.other_reading: he says

check.latin: a quo enim non prope est
check.note: “For whom is it not near” can be read as “for the benefit of whom”, so either “for” or “near to whom” seems lost and the sentence is unclear.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “For who is there that it is not near, ready as it is in every place and at every moment?” This gives both the Latin “for” and “near to whom”.

check.note: “Are in alarm” is stiff English for a plain verb.
check.decided: Partly accepted: a plain verb is now used, but it is “tremble”, not “panic”. The Latin verb is of fearful agitation, which “panic” overstates.

check.note: “At the time when” is used twice for the Latin pair. It is consistent but heavy; “just when” says the same.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “just when” in both places where the Latin pair occurs.

passages.latin: Generosos animos labor nutrit. Non est ergo quod ex illo vetere parentum tuorum eligas quid contingere tibi velis, quid optes; et in totum iam per maxima acto viro turpe est etiam nunc deos fatigare. Quid votis opus est? fac te ipse felicem; facies autem, si intellexeris bona esse quibus admixta virtus est, turpia quibus malitia coniuncta est.
