Quemadmodum sine mixtura lucis nihil splendidum est, nihil atrum nisi quod tenebras habet aut aliquid in se traxit obscuri, quemadmodum sine adiutorio ignis nihil calidum est, nihil sine aere frigidum, ita honesta et turpia virtutis ac malitiae societas efficit.
passages.english: Hard work feeds noble minds. So there is no reason for you to pick out, from that old prayer of your parents, what you would want to come to you, what you would wish for; and altogether, for a man who has already passed through the greatest things, it is shameful still to be wearying the gods. What need is there of prayers? Make yourself fortunate, you yourself; and you will, if you understand that those things are good which have virtue mixed into them, and those shameful which have wickedness joined to them. Just as nothing is bright without a mixture of light, and nothing is black unless it has darkness in it or has drawn something dark into itself; just as nothing is hot without the help of fire, and nothing cold without air; so it is partnership with virtue and with wickedness that makes things honourable and shameful.

notes.note: Labor is toil, exertion, hardship; the section before has just said it is not itself a good. Generosus is “well-born” and so “noble”. “Minds” is kept for animos, though “spirits” is possible.
notes.other_reading: Toil nourishes spirits of good stock

notes.note: As given, the Latin has no noun for illo vetere (“that old one of your parents”) to agree with. “Prayer” is supplied in the English because the next sentence asks what need there is of vota (“prayers”); printed texts are believed to read voto here (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: from that old (thing) of your parents

notes.note: Literally “for a man already driven through the greatest things”. Maxima may be the highest offices, a full public career, or great affairs and trials generally. The English leaves that open and turns the passive into the plainer “passed through”.
notes.other_reading: for a man who has already been taken through the highest offices

notes.note: The phrase is “even now” in the sense of “still”: he goes on doing it. The English says “still”.
notes.other_reading: even now

notes.note: The stock phrase for pestering the gods with prayers. The image of tiring them is kept.
notes.other_reading: to keep importuning the gods

notes.note: Felix is “fortunate, favoured, prosperous”, the thing people pray for, and it can also be “happy”. “Fortunate” is used so that “happy” stays with beatus, as in the glossary. Ipse stresses that Lucilius, not the gods, is to do it.
notes.other_reading: Make yourself happy by your own doing; make your own good fortune

notes.note: Malitia is the opposite of virtus here, the Stoic term for badness of character, not “malice” in the English sense. “Wickedness” is used throughout the passage and “vice” is left for vitium, as in the glossary.
notes.other_reading: with which vice is combined; with which badness is joined

notes.note: In Stoic physics air is the cold element as fire is the hot one (from memory, unchecked), so cold things are cold by having air in them. The translation is literal.
notes.other_reading: nothing is cold without (an admixture of) air

notes.note: Societas is partnership or association. The two nouns are taken as what a thing is associated with (virtue makes it honourable, wickedness shameful), not as virtue and wickedness associating with each other. “Honourable” follows the glossary’s rendering of honestum.
notes.other_reading: the company of virtue and of wickedness is what produces the honourable and the shameful

check.note: As given, the Latin has no noun for “that old” to agree with. The English supplies “prayer”, which is probably right but is a supplement and should be marked as one.
check.decided: Accepted: “prayer” is kept, since the next sentence speaks of prayers, and the note states that the noun is supplied and that the Latin as given lacks it.

check.note: Felicem can be “fortunate” or “happy”, and “by yourself” can be read as “alone”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “Make yourself fortunate, you yourself”, which removes the sense “alone”. “Fortunate” is kept so that “happy” stays with the glossary’s beatus and because good fortune is what the prayers just mentioned ask for. The note gives “happy”.

check.note: The phrase here means “still”. “Even now” can be read as “at this very moment”, which is weaker than the Latin.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “it is shameful still to be wearying the gods”.

check.note: Literal but vague. Maxima may be the highest positions or the greatest affairs of a career, and the participle need mean no more than “who has passed through”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “who has already passed through the greatest things”. “Greatest” is kept and not “highest”, because the Latin word does not say whether rank or great affairs are meant. The note sets out the choice.

passages.latin: Propera ergo, Lucili carissime, et cogita quantum additurus celeritati fueris, si a tergo hostis instaret, si equitem adventare suspicareris ac fugientium premer vestigia. Fit hoc, premeris: accelera et evade, perduc te in tutum et subinde considera quam pulchra res sit consummare vitam ante mortem, deinde exspectare securum reliquam temporis sui partem, nihil sibi, in possessione beatae vitae positum, quae beatior non fit si longior.
passages.english: So hurry, dearest Lucilius, and think how much you would add to your speed if an enemy were bearing down on you from behind, if you suspected that cavalry were coming up and pressing on the tracks of those in flight. This is happening: you are being pressed. Speed up and get away, bring yourself through to safety, and consider again and again what a fine thing it is to complete one’s life before death, and then to wait free from care for the remaining part of one’s time, waiting for nothing for oneself, settled in possession of the happy life, which does not become happier if it is longer.

notes.note: A future participle with fueris, standing for an unreal “would add” inside an indirect question. It could also be heard as “would have added”.
notes.other_reading: how much you would have added to your speed

notes.note: Instare is to press hard upon, to threaten at close quarters. “Bearing down on” is used so that “press” is kept for premere alone, the verb that the next sentence repeats.
notes.other_reading: if an enemy were pressing on you from behind

notes.note: Singular, which can mean one horseman or, collectively, the cavalry. It is taken collectively.
notes.other_reading: that a horseman was coming up

notes.note: Premer is a slip for premere (a letter dropped). Premere vestigia is to tread close on someone’s tracks. “Press” is used because the next sentence repeats the verb (premeris, “you are being pressed”).
notes.other_reading: and was hard on the heels of the fugitives

notes.note: Can mean “repeatedly”, “from time to time” or “immediately after”. The first is taken.
notes.other_reading: and from time to time consider; and then at once consider

notes.note: Consummare is to bring to its full sum, to finish off or complete. The thought is of a life made whole before it ends.
notes.other_reading: to bring life to its full sum before death

notes.note: Glossary: securitas is freedom from care. The word describes the unnamed subject of “to wait”, a general “one”, which is kept.
notes.other_reading: to wait without anxiety

notes.note: As given, these two words have no verb or participle to govern them and do not construe. The English repeats “wait” from exspectare as a stopgap (“waiting for nothing for oneself”). A word has probably fallen out, and printed editions are believed to mark or mend the text here (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: (literally) nothing for oneself; (with a word supplied) promising oneself nothing, or relying on oneself

check.latin: nihil sibi, in possessione beatae vitae positum
check.note: As given, the two words have no verb or participle to govern them, and the English supplies “looking for” silently. The gap should be reported and, if the verb “wait” is understood again, the English should repeat it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “waiting for nothing for oneself”, repeating the verb of the clause before. The note says that the Latin as given has no verb here and that the rendering is a stopgap.

check.note: Two Latin verbs are both given “press”, though the point of “you are being pressed” rests on the second only, so the echo is blurred.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “if an enemy were bearing down on you from behind”, so that “press” belongs to one Latin verb only. “Bearing down” is used and not “close behind”, because the Latin verb is of an enemy pressing hard, not only of nearness.

check.note: A letter is dropped in the copy and the word should be read premere. The English reads it correctly.
check.decided: Accepted: “pressing on the tracks” stands. The copy’s premer is read as premere and the note says so.

check.note: The singular can be collective, “cavalry”, or one horseman. The English chooses cavalry, which is likely but not certain.
check.decided: Accepted: “cavalry” is kept, the first course offered, and the note gives “a horseman”.

passages.latin: Opto tibi tui facultatem, ut vagis cogitationibus agitata mens tandem resistat et certa sit, ut placeat sibi et intellectis veris bonis, quae simul intellecta sunt possidentur, aetatis adiectione non egeat. Ille demum necessitates supergressus est et exauctoratus ac liber qui vivit vita peracta.
passages.english: I wish for you to have yourself at your own disposal: that your mind, driven about by wandering thoughts, may at last come to a stand and be settled; that it may be content with itself and, once it has understood the true goods, which are possessed the moment they are understood, may have no need of added years. That man alone has got beyond necessities, and is discharged from service and free, who lives with his life completed.

notes.note: Facultas is having something available, the means or free disposal of it. It answers the abundance of things that Lucilius’s parents prayed for: the wish is that he should have himself. “Command of yourself” is avoided because it suggests self-control.
notes.other_reading: possession of yourself; access to yourself; command of yourself

notes.note: Resistere here is to halt, to stand still, not to resist. Certa, set against the “wandering” thoughts, is “fixed, settled”.
notes.other_reading: may at last stop and be sure

notes.note: Literally “may please itself”, that is, be satisfied with itself. The English “pleased with itself” suggests smugness, which is not meant.
notes.other_reading: may be pleased with itself

notes.note: Literally “an addition of lifetime”. The English says “added years”.
notes.other_reading: may not need any extension of its span

notes.note: Demum marks the one case that at last qualifies: “he and only he”, “he at length”. The English says “That man alone”.
notes.other_reading: He at last

notes.note: Necessitates may be needs, or the compulsions and constraints of life. The wider “necessities” is kept.
notes.other_reading: has risen above all needs

notes.note: A military term: released from the soldier’s oath, discharged from service. “From service” is added in the English so that the image is heard.
notes.other_reading: released from his oath

notes.note: A deliberate paradox: he lives when his life has already been carried through to the end. Peracta is “finished, played through”, as of a play or a task.
notes.other_reading: who lives after his life has been finished

check.note: The Latin noun is having something available, at one’s disposal. “Command of yourself” suggests self-control, which is a different idea.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now says “to have yourself at your own disposal”. The Latin noun means having a thing available, and it answers the abundance of things that the parents wished for.

check.note: Certa is set against the “wandering” thoughts: fixed, settled. “Be sure” suggests being certain of an opinion.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “come to a stand and be settled”. The Latin word is the opposite of “wandering” here, so it means fixed, not certain of an opinion.

check.note: The word is the soldier’s release from service. “Discharged” alone may not carry that image for a reader of today.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “discharged from service”, so that the soldier’s release is heard.

passages.latin: Propera ad me, sed ad te prius. Profice et ante omnia hoc cura, ut constes tibi. Quotiens experiri voles an aliquid actum sit, observa an eadem hodie velis quae heri: mutatio voluntatis indicat animum natare, aliubi atque aliubi apparere, prout tulit ventus. Non vagatur quod fixum atque fundatum est: istud sapienti perfecto contingit, aliquatenus et proficienti provectoque. Quid ergo interest? hic commovetur quidem, non tamen transit, sed suo loco nutat; ille ne commovetur quidem. Vale.
passages.english: Hurry to me, but to yourself first. Make progress, and before all else take care of this: that you be consistent with yourself. Whenever you want to test whether anything has been achieved, watch whether you want the same things today as yesterday: a change in what one wants shows that the mind is adrift, turning up now in one place and now in another, as the wind has carried it. What is fixed and set on a foundation does not wander: that falls to the perfect wise man, and to some extent also to the one who is making progress and has advanced. What then is the difference? The latter is indeed shaken, yet he does not shift his ground, but sways in his own place; the former is not even shaken. Farewell.

notes.note: Constare sibi is to stand firm with oneself, to be consistent. It is the verb behind constantia, which the glossary gives as “steadiness”; “be steady with yourself” is not natural English, so the English says “consistent”.
notes.other_reading: that you stay steady and true to yourself

notes.note: Literally “whether anything has been done”, that is, whether any ground has been gained.
notes.other_reading: whether you have got anywhere

notes.note: Voluntas is the noun of velle, “to want”, which has just been used (velis). The English keeps “want” for both so that the link is heard. The Latin noun is general and not in the second person, hence “one”.
notes.other_reading: a change of will

notes.note: Natare is to swim or float; here to float about with nothing to hold it, as the wind in the next clause shows. “Adrift” keeps the image.
notes.other_reading: that the mind is afloat; that the mind is at sea

notes.note: Fundatum is “set on a foundation”. The image of a building is kept.
notes.other_reading: fixed and firmly grounded

notes.note: Proficiens is the Stoic term for the person who is making progress but is not yet wise; it picks up the command Profice at the start. Provectus is “carried forward, advanced”. One person is meant, not two.
notes.other_reading: to the one who is progressing and well advanced

notes.note: Hic is the nearer of the two just named (the one making progress), ille the wise man. Commovetur is “is set in motion, shaken”; “shaken” is used for both occurrences.
notes.other_reading: the one is moved, to be sure

notes.note: Transire is to go across. It is taken as leaving the spot where he stands, in contrast with swaying in his own place.
notes.other_reading: yet he does not cross over; yet he does not go over (to the other side)

notes.note: Nutare is to nod, sway or totter. He rocks but stays where he is.
notes.other_reading: he wavers where he stands

check.note: The Latin noun picks up the verb “want” just before. The English moves from “want” to “will”, so the link is lost, and “a change of will” is not natural English.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “a change in what one wants”, keeping “want” for the one Latin root. It has “one” and not “you” because the Latin noun is general and not in the second person.

check.note: “Afloat” in English sounds like a good thing, not sinking. The Latin means floating about with nothing to hold it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the mind is adrift”. The Latin is of floating about with nothing to hold it, and “adrift” keeps the water.

check.note: “Founded” on its own is odd English for something set on a foundation.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “fixed and set on a foundation”. This gives the Latin image exactly; the suggested “firmly” has no word in the Latin.

check.note: The Latin is simply “advanced”. “Some way” is added, and “to some extent” has already been said.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and has advanced”. “Some way” was not in the Latin.

check.note: “Cross over” leaves the reader asking where to. The sense is that he does not shift from where he stands.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “yet he does not shift his ground”. The Latin verb is “go across”, and the next words, “sways in his own place”, show that leaving his spot is meant. The note gives “cross over”.

check.note: “Moved” may be read as emotionally touched. The image is physical: set in motion, shaken.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “is indeed shaken” and, at the end, “is not even shaken”, one word for the one Latin verb. The Latin image is of being set in motion.

passages.latin: Quod si tanta cupiditas te longioris aevi tenet? cogita nihil eorum quae ab oculis abeunt et in rerum naturam, ex qua prodierunt ac mox processura sunt, reconduntur consumi: desinunt ista, non pereunt, et mors, quam pertimescimus ac recusamus, intermittit vitam, non eripit; veniet iterum qui nos in lucem reponat dies, quem multi recusarent nisi oblitos reduceret.
passages.english: But if so great a desire for a longer life has hold of you, consider that none of the things that go out of sight and are put back into the nature of things, from which they came out and will soon come forth, is used up: these things stop, they do not perish, and death, which we dread and refuse, interrupts life, it does not snatch it away; a day will come again to put us back into the light, a day that many would refuse if it did not bring them back with their memory gone.

notes.note: The copy puts a question mark after the if-clause. The English sets it aside and reads the clause as a condition leading into “consider”, which is believed to be the usual punctuation (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: But what if so great a desire for a longer life has hold of you? Consider that

notes.note: “The nature of things” is the glossary’s rendering of rerum natura. Here it means nature as the store from which things come and to which they return.
notes.other_reading: into nature; into the universe

notes.note: Two different verbs of coming out stand side by side, prodierunt and processura sunt, given as “came out” and “come forth”. The Latin has no “again”.
notes.other_reading: and from which they will soon come out again

notes.note: Recondere is to put back in store, to lay away again. Consumi is to be used up or destroyed; “used up” keeps the store image.
notes.other_reading: are laid away again; is destroyed

notes.note: Desinere is to leave off, to cease. The contrast is between stopping and being lost for good.
notes.other_reading: they cease, they are not lost

notes.note: The same verb returns at the end (recusarent), so “refuse” is used both times. It is the word for declining or objecting to something offered.
notes.other_reading: which we dread and shrink from

notes.latin: veniet iterum qui nos in lucem reponat dies
notes.note: The Stoic teaching that the world and everything in it returns (from memory, unchecked). The Latin says that once again a day will come, a day such as to put people back, not that the same day returns. Reponat is “put back”, as into a place once held.
notes.other_reading: the day will come again that restores us to the light

notes.note: Oblitos is “having forgotten”, with no object stated; what is forgotten is presumably the earlier life. The English says “with their memory gone” and adds no object. The word agrees with an unexpressed object, either the many or the people put back into the light.
notes.other_reading: if it did not bring us back with no memory of the past

check.latin: Quod si tanta cupiditas te longioris aevi tenet?
check.note: The Latin as given ends this clause with a question mark. The English runs it on as a condition, which is the natural construction, but the copy’s punctuation should not be set aside without notice.
check.decided: Accepted: the conditional is kept, and the note says that the copy’s question mark is set aside.

check.note: “Again” is not in the Latin. Two different verbs are also given the same English.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “from which they came out and will soon come forth”. The Latin has no “again” and uses two different verbs.

check.note: In English “the nature of things” means how things are. Here the Latin phrase is nature, the natural world, as a place things go back into.
check.decided: Declined: “the nature of things” stands. It is the rendering the glossary settles for rerum natura, kept so that the phrase reads the same from passage to passage, and the note says that here it means nature as the store things go back into.

check.note: “Having forgotten” with no object is unclear English.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “with their memory gone”, which is clearer than a bare “having forgotten”. The suggested “everything” is not used because the Latin names no object of the forgetting.

check.latin: veniet iterum qui nos in lucem reponat dies
check.note: “The day will come again” sounds like the same day returning. The Latin says that once again a day will come, and its verb form marks purpose: a day to put people back.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now has “a day” in place of “the day” and “to put” in place of “that puts”. The Latin says that once more a day will come, one that is to put people back, not that the same day returns.

passages.latin: Sed postea diligentius docebo omnia quae videntur perire mutari. Aequo animo debet rediturus exire. Observa orbem rerum in se remeantium: videbis nihil in hoc mundo exstingui sed vicibus descendere ac surgere. Aestas abit, sed alter illam annus adducet; hiemps cecidit, referent illam sui menses; solem nox obruit, sed ipsam statim dies abiget. Stellarum iste discursus quidquid praeterit repetit; pars caeli levatur assidue, pars mergitur.
passages.english: But later I will show more carefully that all the things that seem to perish are changed. A man who is going to come back ought to go out with an even mind. Watch the circle of things as they return upon themselves: you will see that nothing in this world is extinguished, but that things go down and rise by turns. Summer has gone, but another year will bring it; winter has fallen away, its own months will bring it back; night has buried the sun, but day will at once drive night itself away. That running about of the stars comes back to whatever it has passed; one part of the sky is continually being lifted, one part is being sunk.

notes.note: Simply “are changed”. The Latin has no “only” or “merely”, so none is added.
notes.other_reading: undergo change

notes.note: Aequo animo as in Ep. 30.4, “with an even mind”. Exire is to go out, to leave, used of dying; rediturus is “one who is going to return”.
notes.other_reading: He who will return should depart calmly

notes.note: Orbis is a ring or circuit. Remeare is to travel back; in se is “into, upon themselves”.
notes.other_reading: the cycle of things returning on their own tracks

notes.note: Mundus is the ordered world, the universe, not just the earth.
notes.other_reading: in this universe

notes.note: Literally to be quenched or put out, as a flame. “Extinguished” keeps the image.
notes.other_reading: is put out; is annihilated

notes.note: Abit as written is a present (“goes”); it can also be a shortened past form (“has gone”). The English takes it as past, beside cecidit (“has fallen”), and treats obruit (“has buried”) the same way.
notes.other_reading: Summer goes; night buries the sun

notes.note: Literally “winter has fallen”, that is, dropped away or ended, matching the going down and rising of the sentence before. “Away” is added because in English “winter has fallen” would be heard as “has arrived”, the opposite of the sense.
notes.other_reading: winter has gone down

notes.note: Discursus is a running in different directions, here the stars moving on their several courses. “Running about” is used; the return is said by the verb that follows.
notes.other_reading: That running to and fro of the stars; that coursing of the stars

notes.note: Praeterit can be present (“passes”) or a shortened past form (“has passed”). Repetere is to make for again, to return to: the stars come round again to the points they have passed.
notes.other_reading: returns to whatever it passes; fetches back whatever has gone by

check.note: In English “winter has fallen” is heard like “night has fallen”, meaning it has arrived. The Latin means the opposite: winter has dropped away.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “winter has fallen away”, which cannot be heard as winter arriving. “Fallen” is kept for the Latin verb, and “go down” is left to the different verb of the sentence before.

check.note: The form as given is a present, “goes”; it can be a shortened past, and the English takes it so, in line with “has fallen”. The same doubt holds for the verb of night and the sun.
check.decided: Accepted: “Summer has gone” is kept, the second course offered, because the unambiguous past “has fallen” stands beside it in a matched set of three. The note records the present for this verb and for “has buried”.

check.note: “To and fro” suggests the stars go back and forth. The Latin noun is their running about on their courses, and the return is said by the verb.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “That running about of the stars”, which no longer suggests going back and forth. “Coursing” is not used because the Latin noun says running in different directions, not only running.

check.note: “Nothing is put out” may not be understood at once as a light being put out.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “nothing in this world is extinguished”, which keeps the image of a flame and is understood at once.

check.note: Found while settling: “goes back over whatever it has passed” suggests the stars reversing along their path, where the Latin verb is of making for a place again.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “comes back to whatever it has passed”.

passages.latin: Neminem mihi dabis qui sciat quomodo quod vult coeperit velle: non consilio adductus illo sed impetu impactus est. Non minus saepe fortuna in nos incurrit quam nos in illam. Turpe est non ire sed ferri, et subito in medio turbine rerum stupentem quaerere, 'huc ego quemadmodum veni?' Vale.
passages.english: You will not show me anyone who knows how he began to want what he wants: he was not led to it by deliberation but flung into it by impulse. Fortune collides with us no less often than we with it. It is shameful not to go but to be carried, and suddenly, in the middle of the whirlwind of things, to ask in a daze, “How did I get here?” Farewell.

notes.note: Literally “you will give me no one”, the idiom for producing an example.
notes.other_reading: You will not find me a single person

notes.note: Illo can be the adverb “to that point” (led there by deliberation), which is the reading taken, or go with consilio (“by that plan”).
notes.other_reading: he was not brought by that plan

notes.note: A play of sound, and both words are of violent motion: impetus is a rush or impulse, impingere to dash one thing against another. He did not walk to his wish; he was flung at it.
notes.other_reading: but was hurled into it by a rush

notes.note: Incurrere is to run into, to collide with or charge at. Fortune stands first in the English sentence and is then “it”, since nothing here treats it as a person; the glossary allows “Fortune” and “her” where it is one.
notes.other_reading: Fortune charges at us no less often than we at her

notes.note: Ire is to go on one’s own feet; ferri to be borne or swept along.
notes.other_reading: not to walk but to be swept along

notes.note: Turbo is a whirlwind or spinning eddy; res is “things, affairs, events”. Stupentem is “stunned, dazed”.
notes.other_reading: dumbfounded in the middle of the whirl of events

check.note: The Latin verb is flung or dashed into something. “Driven against it” reads as if he were set against what he wants.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “flung into it by impulse”. The Latin verb is of dashing one thing into another, and “driven against” could be read as opposed to it.

check.note: Fortune is “it” here while nature is “she” in Ep. 30.11, and “runs into” can sound like a chance meeting where the Latin is a collision.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now uses “collides with” for the Latin verb. “It” is kept, because here fortune is something people run into as much as something that runs into them, with no will or act of a person given to it as nature has in Ep. 30.11. The note gives “her”.

passages.latin: Facis rem optimam et tibi salutarem si, ut scribis, perseveras ire ad bonam mentem, quam stultum est optare cum possis a te impetrare. Non sunt ad caelum elevandae manus nec exorandus aedituus ut nos ad aurem simulacri, quasi magis exaudiri possimus, admittat: prope est a te deus, tecum est, intus est.
passages.english: You are doing a very good thing, and one that is healthy for you, if, as you write, you keep on making your way towards a sound mind. It is foolish to pray for this when you can obtain it from yourself. There is no need to lift hands to heaven, or to beg the temple-keeper to admit us to the ear of the statue, as if we could be heard better: god is near you, he is with you, he is within.

notes.note: A superlative with no article: it can be “the best thing” or “a very good thing”. The English takes the weaker sense, since nothing is being compared.
notes.other_reading: You are doing the best thing

notes.note: Salutaris covers “healthy”, “wholesome” and “saving”. The English keeps the medical image, which returns at the end of the letter (ad salutem, 41.9).
notes.other_reading: one that will save you

notes.note: Bona mens is a set phrase for a right state of mind. Mens, like animus, is “mind”, and the English reads “a sound mind”.
notes.other_reading: a good mind; good sense

notes.note: Optare is “to wish for” and also “to pray for”. Since the next sentence is about prayer in a temple, the English reads “pray for”. The relative clause is made a separate sentence.
notes.other_reading: which it is foolish to wish for

notes.latin: Non sunt ad caelum elevandae manus
notes.note: The gerundive with non can mean “need not be” or “must not be”. The English takes it as “there is no need” and keeps it impersonal, as the Latin has it.
notes.other_reading: Hands must not be lifted to heaven

notes.note: The attendant who keeps a temple and controls access to the cult statue.
notes.other_reading: the sacristan; the temple warden

notes.note: Latin has no article, so this can be “god”, “a god” or “the god”. The English reads “god” with a small letter, following the glossary. The last clause has no “you” in the Latin, so the English reads “within”.
notes.other_reading: a god is near you, with you, inside you

check.note: The Latin has no word for “that way”, and “up” is likewise added to the verb of admitting.
check.decided: Accepted: the clause now ends at “heard better”, and “admit” replaces the phrase with “up”. The Latin has no word for “that way” or for “up”.

passages.latin: Ita dico, Lucili: sacer intra nos spiritus sedet, malorum bonorumque nostrorum observator et custos; hic prout a nobis tractatus est, ita nos ipse tractat. Bonus vero vir sine deo nemo est: an potest aliquis supra fortunam nisi ab illo adiutus exsurgere? Ille dat consilia magnifica et erecta. In unoquoque virorum bonorum [quis deus incertum est] habitat deus.
passages.english: This is what I say, Lucilius: a sacred spirit sits within us, the observer and guardian of the bad and the good that are ours. As it has been treated by us, so it treats us in its turn. And indeed no one is a good man without god: or can anyone rise above fortune unless helped by him? It is he who gives advice that is grand and lofty. In each and every good man (which god is uncertain) a god lives.

notes.note: Spiritus is “breath” as well as “spirit”, and may stand for the Stoic breath that runs through things. The English reads “sacred spirit” and avoids “holy spirit” because of its Christian ring.
notes.other_reading: a holy breath sits within us

notes.note: Literally “of the bad things and good things that are ours”. It can mean what is done badly and well, or the bad and good that befall a person. The English leaves it open.
notes.other_reading: of our bad and good deeds

notes.note: Custos is one who keeps watch over something, whether to protect it or to hold it to account. The English reads “guardian”.
notes.other_reading: watcher and keeper

notes.note: Again no article: “without god” or “without a god”. The English keeps “god” so that “by him” in the next clause has a clear reference.
notes.other_reading: without a god

notes.note: Consilia can be advice given or plans and purposes formed. Erecta is literally “standing upright”, here in the sense of raised high, so the English reads “lofty”; “upright” would suggest honesty.
notes.other_reading: He gives purposes that are great and high-minded

notes.note: These words are from Vergil (Aeneid 8.352, said there of a grove and hill; from memory, unchecked), where “which god is uncertain” is a parenthesis. Square brackets in this copy elsewhere mark words an editor cuts; here they are taken to stand for Vergil’s parenthesis, since the words construe and belong to the line. The Latin has no quotation marks, so the English has none.
notes.other_reading: In each and every good man a god lives. (Bracketed words left out as a deletion.)

check.note: The Latin says only “bad things and good things” that are ours. “Deeds” is added and settles the sense as what is done, when it may also be what befalls.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “deeds” is dropped and the English now reads “the bad and the good that are ours”. The Latin has only the two adjectives and a possessive, and the suggested “in us” would narrow it the other way; the note keeps “deeds” as the other reading.

check.note: Erecta means raised up, lofty. “Upright” in English today means honest, and “counsels” is old-fashioned.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “advice that is grand and lofty”. Erecta is “raised up”, and “upright” today means honest; “counsels” is an old form.

check.note: The Latin has square brackets, not quotation marks, and the English moves the marks, reverses the order and adds “though”. Brackets are treated differently in Ep. 49.10, so one rule is needed.
check.decided: Partly accepted: one rule is set for square brackets: bracketed words are translated only where they construe and the sentence needs them, and each case has a note. Here they are taken as a parenthesis inside the line of Vergil, so the English reads “(which god is uncertain) a god lives” in the Latin order, without “though”. Quotation marks are dropped because the Latin has none.

check.note: Custos is one who watches over and keeps. “Guard” suggests a sentry or jailer.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “guard” becomes “guardian”, since custos is one who watches over and keeps. “Observer” stays, because it is the plain English of observator.

passages.latin: Lauda in illo quod nec eripi potest nec dari, quod proprium hominis est. Quaeris quid sit? animus et ratio in animo perfecta. Rationale enim animal est homo; consummatur itaque bonum eius, si id implevit cui nascitur.
passages.english: Praise in him what can neither be snatched away nor given, what is man’s own. You ask what that is? The mind, and reason made perfect in the mind. For man is a reasoning animal; and so his good is brought to completion if he has fulfilled what he is born for.

notes.note: “Him” is the man of the section before, who is praised for his household, house and wealth, things that are around him and not in him.
notes.other_reading: Praise in that man

notes.note: Proprium is “one’s own” and also “peculiar to”. Hominis can be “of the man” in question or “of man” as a kind. The English reads “man’s own”, with no article so that humankind is meant, and keeps the link with the section before, where what is praised is what is the thing’s own.
notes.other_reading: what is peculiar to a human being

notes.latin: animus et ratio in animo perfecta
notes.note: Animus is “mind” and ratio is “reason”, as in the glossary. Perfecta agrees with ratio only: it is reason that is perfected, not the mind.
notes.other_reading: mind, and complete reason in the mind

notes.note: Rationale comes from ratio. The English reads “reasoning” so that a reader sees the link with “reason” in the sentence before. Animal is any living creature.
notes.other_reading: For man is a rational living creature

notes.note: Consummatur is “is brought to its full sum”, “is completed”. Bonum is “the good”, here “his good”, meaning man’s.
notes.other_reading: and so his good is made complete

notes.note: Literally “if he has filled up that for which he is born”. The subject is man. Nascitur is present tense, a general truth.
notes.other_reading: if he has carried out the thing he is born to

check.note: The Latin means what belongs to the human being as such, as fruitfulness belongs to the vine. “Man’s own” could be read as what this one man owns.
check.decided: Declined: “man’s own” stays. Proprium is first “one’s own”, which answers “can neither be snatched away nor given”, and “man” without an article already means humankind, as in “man is a reasoning animal” in the next sentence. “Peculiar” today suggests oddness; the other reading is in the note.

passages.latin: Quid est autem quod ab illo ratio haec exigat? rem facillimam, secundum naturam suam vivere. Sed hanc difficilem facit communis insania: in vitia alter alterum trudimus. Quomodo autem revocari ad salutem possunt quos nemo retinet, populus impellit? Vale.
passages.english: And what is it that this reason demands of him? A very easy thing: to live according to his own nature. But the madness shared by all makes it hard: we push one another into vices. And how can people be called back to health when no one holds them back and the crowd drives them on? Farewell.

notes.note: “Him” is man, the reasoning animal of the sentence before.
notes.other_reading: demands of a man

notes.note: A superlative: “the easiest thing” or “a very easy thing”. The English takes the second, as it does for the same construction at the start of the letter (41.1).
notes.other_reading: The easiest thing of all

notes.note: The Stoic formula of living according to nature, here with suam, “his own”. Suam refers to the one who lives, that is man, not to reason.
notes.other_reading: to live in agreement with its own nature

notes.note: Communis is “shared”, “held in common”. The English reads “shared by all”, because “common” can be heard today as “ordinary”.
notes.other_reading: the common madness

notes.note: Salus is “health”, “safety” and “rescue”. The English reads “health” to match “healthy” (salutarem) at the start of the letter.
notes.other_reading: called back to safety

notes.note: Populus is “the people” as a whole. The English reads “the crowd” because the image is of being pushed. The Latin sets the two clauses side by side with no “and”.
notes.other_reading: whom no one holds back, whom the people push on

check.note: Communis means shared by all. “Common” can be read today as ordinary or frequent.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the madness shared by all”, since communis is “shared”, not “ordinary”.

check.note: The superlative can be “very easy” or “the easiest thing”. The stronger reading would sharpen the contrast with “makes it hard”.
check.decided: Declined: “A very easy thing” stays. The superlative stands alone, with no “of all” or other comparison in the Latin, which is the pattern of “very”, and the same choice is made for rem optimam in 41.1. The stronger reading is in the note.

passages.latin: Patricius Socrates non fuit; Cleanthes aquam traxit et rigando horto locavit manus; Platonem non accepit nobilem philosophia sed fecit: quid est quare desperes his te posse fieri parem? Omnes hi maiores tui sunt, si te illis geris dignum; geres autem, si hoc protinus tibi ipse persuaseris, a nullo te nobilitate superari.
passages.english: Socrates was not a patrician. Cleanthes drew water and hired out his hands for watering a garden. Philosophy did not receive Plato as a noble; it made him one. What reason is there for you to despair of being able to become the equal of these men? All of these are your ancestors, if you conduct yourself in a way worthy of them; and you will, if you persuade yourself of this at once: that you are surpassed by no one in nobility.

notes.note: A Roman word for the old hereditary aristocracy, applied here to an Athenian. The English keeps it as “patrician”.
notes.other_reading: Socrates was not of high birth

notes.latin: Cleanthes aquam traxit et rigando horto locavit manus
notes.note: Cleanthes was the second head of the Stoic school, said to have earned his living by drawing water at night (from memory, unchecked). Locavit manus is literally “let out his hands for hire”.
notes.other_reading: Cleanthes hauled water and hired himself out as a labourer to water a garden

notes.latin: non accepit nobilem philosophia sed fecit
notes.note: Nobilem goes with both verbs: philosophy did not take him in already noble but made him noble. “Noble” and “nobility” stand for nobilis and nobilitas through the passage. Plato was in fact of high birth by ordinary reckoning (from memory, unchecked), so the claim is pointed.
notes.other_reading: Philosophy did not find Plato noble but made him so

notes.note: Maiores is the ordinary word for ancestors, literally “those greater” or “older”.
notes.other_reading: All these are your forefathers

notes.note: “At once” or “straight away”, taken with “persuade yourself”. It could also be “from the outset”.
notes.other_reading: if from the very start you persuade yourself of this

notes.note: Passive in the Latin and kept passive. “No one” is absolute and is kept.
notes.other_reading: that no one outdoes you in nobility

passages.latin: Quis est generosus? ad virtutem bene a natura compositus. Hoc unum intuendum est: alioquin si ad vetera revocas, nemo non inde est ante quod nihil est. A primo mundi ortu usque in hoc tempus perduxit nos ex splendidis sordidisque alternata series. Non facit nobilem atrium plenum fumosis imaginibus; nemo in nostram gloriam vixit nec quod ante nos fuit nostrum est: animus facit nobilem, cui ex quacumque condicione supra fortunam licet surgere.
passages.english: Who is well born? The man who is well made by nature for virtue. This is the one thing to look at. Otherwise, if you go back to ancient times, there is no one who does not come from that point before which there is nothing. From the first beginning of the world down to this time we have been led all the way by a line in which the splendid and the lowly alternate. A hall full of smoke-darkened images of ancestors does not make a man noble. No one has lived for our glory, and what was before us is not ours. It is the mind that makes a man noble, and the mind may rise above fortune from any station whatever.

notes.note: From genus, “stock”: of good birth. It is a different word from nobilis (“noble”) later in the passage, so it has a different English word.
notes.other_reading: Who is of good stock?

notes.note: Compositus is “put together”, “arranged”. The English reads “well made by nature”.
notes.other_reading: well fitted by nature for virtue

notes.note: Literally “if you call back to old things”, with no object in the Latin. The English supplies none and reads “go back”.
notes.other_reading: if you call the matter back to antiquity

notes.latin: nemo non inde est ante quod nihil est
notes.note: A double negative, kept as one: everyone goes back to the very first beginning. Inde is “from there”, given as “from that point”.
notes.other_reading: everyone comes from the place before which nothing exists

notes.note: Active in the Latin: the line “has led” the speaker and his reader the whole way. The English is passive so that the sentence can keep the Latin order, from the beginning of the world to the line.
notes.other_reading: a line in which the splendid and the lowly alternate has led us all the way from the first beginning of the world down to this time

notes.note: The adjectives can be of persons (illustrious and low-born ancestors) or of states. Splendidus is “shining”, “distinguished”, and sordidus is “dirty”, “of low rank”. “The splendid and the lowly” leaves both open.
notes.other_reading: a chain alternating between distinguished and mean conditions

notes.note: Imagines are literally “likenesses”. In the main hall of a noble Roman house they were the portrait masks of ancestors, darkened by smoke over the years (from memory, unchecked). The English reads “images of ancestors”.
notes.other_reading: a hall full of smoky ancestor masks

notes.note: Animus is “mind”, as in the glossary. “Spirit” would also fit here, where the point is what a person is in himself.
notes.other_reading: it is the spirit that makes a man noble

notes.note: Condicio is one’s station or lot in life, such as slave, freedman or knight. The English reads “station”.
notes.other_reading: from whatever condition

check.note: The verb has no object in the Latin, and the object in the English is added. It can as well mean simply “if you go back”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “if you go back to ancient times”. The verb has no object in the Latin and none is supplied.

check.note: Imagines in a Roman hall are the masks or busts of ancestors. “Portraits” suggests paintings and loses the point that these are ancestors.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “smoke-darkened images of ancestors”. Imagines in a Roman hall are the family’s ancestors, so that is said, but the word itself means “likenesses”. That they were masks is left to the note (from memory, unchecked).

check.latin: cui ex quacumque condicione supra fortunam licet surgere
check.note: The Latin relative ties the clause to the mind, but “it is allowed” can be read as impersonal. “Condition” for station in life is also unclear.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and the mind may rise above fortune from any station whatever”. The Latin relative ties the rising to the mind, and “station” is clearer than “condition” for a person’s place in life.

check.latin: perduxit nos ex splendidis sordidisque alternata series
check.note: The sentence ends on the verb with nothing after it and is hard to follow. Perduxit means has led all the way.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the sentence is recast in the passive so that it ends on the “line in which the splendid and the lowly alternate”, and perduxit is given as “led all the way”. The Latin order, from the beginning of the world to the line, is kept and not reversed as suggested.

passages.latin: 'Servus est.' Sed fortasse liber animo. 'Servus est.' Hoc illi nocebit? Ostende quis non sit: alius libidini servit, alius avaritiae, alius ambitioni, , omnes timori. Dabo consularem aniculae servientem, dabo ancillulae divitem, ostendam nobilissimos iuvenes mancipia pantomimorum: nulla servitus turpior est quam voluntaria. Quare non est quod fastidiosi isti te deterreant quominus servis tuis hilarem te praestes et non superbe superiorem: colant potius te quam timeant.
passages.english: “He is a slave.” But perhaps free in mind. “He is a slave.” Will that harm him? Show who is not one: one man is a slave to lust, another to greed, another to ambition, [gap in the Latin] all to fear. I will give you a man of consular rank who is a slave to a little old woman, I will give you a rich man who is a slave to a slave girl, I will show you young men of the noblest birth who are the bought slaves of pantomime dancers: no slavery is more shameful than voluntary slavery. So there is no reason why those disdainful people should deter you from showing yourself cheerful to your slaves, and superior without being arrogant: let them honour you rather than fear you.

notes.note: The words of an imagined objector, said twice. The English puts them in quotation marks as the Latin does.
notes.other_reading: “But he is a slave.”

notes.note: Animus is “mind”, as in the glossary. “Free in spirit” is the other natural English.
notes.other_reading: But perhaps free in spirit

notes.note: Literally “Will this harm him?”. It can also be heard as “Is this to be held against him?”.
notes.other_reading: Is that to count against him?

notes.note: Servire is “to serve” and “to be a slave”. The English reads “is a slave to” each time, because the argument depends on the same word as servus and servitus. Libido is “lust” or more widely “desire”.
notes.other_reading: one man serves his desire

notes.note: The doubled comma shows that something has fallen out of this copy, and the English marks the place in square brackets. From memory, unchecked, editions print a supplement here meaning “all to hope”. The sentence construes without it.
notes.other_reading: another to ambition, all to hope, all to fear

notes.note: Consularis is a man who has been consul. Anicula is a slighting diminutive, given as “little old woman”; ancillulae, “slave girl”, is a diminutive of the same kind.
notes.other_reading: a former consul enslaved to some little old woman

notes.note: Mancipium is a slave as a piece of bought and owned property, a harsher word than servus. Pantomimi were solo stage dancers with a large following; the English keeps the name and reads “pantomime dancers”.
notes.other_reading: the chattels of stage dancers

notes.note: An idiom, “there is no reason why”, followed by what should not happen. The point is that Lucilius should not be put off, not that these people lack a motive.
notes.other_reading: So do not let those disdainful people deter you

notes.note: Fastidiosus is one who turns up his nose at something. “Fastidious” today means careful over detail, so the English reads “disdainful”.
notes.other_reading: those squeamish people

notes.note: A play on sound between superbe (“arrogantly”) and superiorem (“superior”). The English keeps the sense, not the sound.
notes.other_reading: their superior, but not haughtily so

notes.note: Colere is “to cultivate”, “to honour”, “to show regard for”, and is used of the gods and of patrons. The English reads “honour”. The Latin names no subject; “them” is the slaves.
notes.other_reading: let your slaves respect you rather than fear you

check.note: The doubled comma shows that something has dropped out of the Latin as given. The English passes over the gap without saying so.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now marks the place with “[gap in the Latin]”, the same sign used in Ep. 48.9. The words thought to be lost are given in the note (from memory, unchecked).

check.note: Fastidiosus here means disdainful. “Fastidious” today means careful about detail, so the reader gets the wrong idea of these people.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “those disdainful people”. Fastidiosus is one who looks down on something, which “fastidious” no longer means.

check.note: The idiom means there is no reason why they should deter you, that is, do not let them. The English reads as if these people have no reason to do so.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “there is no reason why those disdainful people should deter you”. This keeps the Latin’s “there is no reason” and makes plain that the point is Lucilius not being put off, without adding “you have” or “let”.

check.note: Anicula is a diminutive with contempt in it. “Old woman” is neutral.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a little old woman”, which gives the slighting diminutive.

check.note: Mancipia are bought slaves, and “property” weakens the word in a passage built on slave words. “Pantomime” misleads today: a pantomimus was a solo stage dancer.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the bought slaves of pantomime dancers”. Mancipia is a slave word and is given as one; “pantomime” is kept as the name of the art, with “dancers” for “actors” and a note.

check.note: “Them” could be taken as the disdainful people, when the Latin means the slaves. Colere is also warmer than “respect”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “honour” replaces “respect”, since colere is the regard paid to a patron or a god. “Them” stays: the Latin names no subject, and “your slaves” is the nearest plural before it.

check.note: Found while settling: “free in his mind” could be heard as “free only in his own imagination”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “free in mind”, which is what the two Latin words say.

passages.latin: Iterum ego tamquam Epicureus loquor? mihi vero idem expedit quod tibi: aut non sum amicus, nisi quidquid agitur ad te pertinens meum est. Consortium rerum omnium inter nos facit amicitia; nec secundi quicquam singulis est nec adversi; in commune vivitur. Nec potest quisquam beate degere qui se tantum intuetur, qui omnia ad utilitates suas convertit: alteri vivas oportet, si vis tibi vivere.
passages.english: Am I talking like an Epicurean again? But in fact the same thing is in my interest as is in yours: or else I am no friend, if whatever matter concerns you is not mine. Friendship makes between us a partnership in all things. Nothing favourable and nothing adverse belongs to one alone; life is lived in common. And no one can live happily who looks only at himself, who turns everything to his own advantage: you must live for another, if you want to live for yourself.

notes.note: This looks back to the end of the section before, where Seneca said that one thing was in Lucilius’s interest and another in his own. He now takes that back as Epicurean talk. The copy punctuates it as a question; it could be an exclamation.
notes.other_reading: There I go again, talking like an Epicurean!

notes.note: Vero corrects the question just asked. The English reads “But in fact”.
notes.other_reading: No: in truth the same thing is in my interest

notes.note: “Is expedient”, “is in the interest of”. It repeats the verb of the sentence before this section and is kept distinct from utilitates (“advantage”) later.
notes.other_reading: the same thing is expedient for me as for you

notes.latin: aut non sum amicus, nisi quidquid agitur ad te pertinens meum est
notes.note: Aut is “or else” and nisi is “unless”, so the Latin states the condition twice. The English gives nisi as “if … not” to make one condition of it. Agitur can be “is being done” or “is at stake”, and “whatever matter” leaves that open.
notes.other_reading: or else I am not a friend, unless whatever is at stake that concerns you is mine

notes.note: Consortium is a legal word for holding property jointly and undivided, as heirs might (from memory, unchecked). The English reads “partnership”.
notes.other_reading: a joint ownership of everything

notes.latin: nec secundi quicquam singulis est nec adversi
notes.note: Literally “neither is anything favourable for individuals singly, nor anything adverse”. Singulis is plural, “each one separately”, given as “one alone”.
notes.other_reading: neither good fortune nor bad comes to each separately

notes.note: An impersonal passive, “there is living in common”, kept impersonal.
notes.other_reading: we live in common

notes.note: Alter is “the other” of two, or “another person”. The “you” is general, though it also falls on Lucilius.
notes.other_reading: you have to live for the other man

check.note: “Otherwise … unless” doubles the condition and is hard to follow in English.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the doubled “otherwise … unless” is replaced by “or else … if … is not mine”. “Mine” is kept for meum, where the suggestion added “concern too”.

check.note: Agitur can mean “is at stake” or simply “is being done, is going on”. The English chooses the first without sign.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “whatever matter concerns you”, which leaves agitur open between “is going on” and “is at stake”. The note gives both.

check.note: Vero corrects the question just asked. “In truth” does not show that Seneca is taking back the Epicurean-sounding remark.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “But in fact”, which shows the correction that vero makes. “No” is not added, because the Latin has no separate word of denial.

passages.latin: Dic quid natura necessarium fecerit, quid supervacuum, quam faciles posuerit, quam iucunda sit vita, quam expedita illas sequentibus, quam acerba et implicita eorum qui opinioni plus quam naturae crediderunt *** si prius docueris quam partem eorum levatura sint. Quid istorum cupiditates demit? quid temperat? Utinam tantum non prodessent! nocent. Hoc tibi cum voles manifestissimum faciam, comminui et debilitari generosam indolem in istas argutias coniectam.
passages.english: Say what nature has made necessary and what superfluous, how easy the [laws] are that it has laid down, how pleasant life is, how unencumbered, for those who follow them, how bitter and entangled is the life of those who have trusted opinion more than nature [gap in the Latin] if you have first shown what part of them they are going to relieve. Which of those things takes away desires? Which moderates them? I wish it were only that they do no good! They do harm. Whenever you like I will make this perfectly clear to you: that a well-born character is crushed and weakened when it is thrown into those quibbles.

notes.note: The imperative is singular. The “you” may be Lucilius or an imagined teacher of the quibbles named at the end; the passage alone does not settle it.
notes.other_reading: Tell me what nature has made necessary

notes.note: The Latin as given does not construe: faciles (“easy”, plural) has no noun, and a feminine plural has dropped out. From memory, unchecked, editions have leges (“laws”) here. The English puts “laws” in square brackets as a supplement.
notes.other_reading: how easy the things are that it has laid down

notes.note: Illas (“them”, feminine plural) refers to the missing noun. Expedita is “unencumbered”, said of a soldier without baggage, and is set against implicita (“entangled”) in the next clause.
notes.other_reading: how free of hindrance for those who follow them

notes.note: Opinio is “opinion”, as in the glossary: what people suppose, as against what nature shows.
notes.other_reading: who have put more trust in belief than in nature

notes.latin: *** si prius docueris quam partem eorum levatura sint
notes.note: The asterisks mark a gap in the text, so the main clause that this “if” depends on is lost, and the English says so in square brackets. The subject of levatura sint is neuter plural, probably the logical puzzles; eorum (“of them”) may be the troubles just described or the people who suffer them. Levare is “to lighten” or “to relieve”.
notes.other_reading: if you have first shown what share of those people’s burdens they will lighten

notes.note: Istorum is “of those things”, with a hint of “of yours”: the puzzles the person addressed deals in. Quid is the subject: which of them removes desires.
notes.other_reading: What is there in those things of yours that takes away desires?

notes.note: Literally “Would that they only failed to help! They harm.” Tantum is kept as “only”.
notes.other_reading: If only they merely did no good! They do harm.

notes.note: Indoles is inborn character or natural gift. Generosa is “of good stock”, given as “well-born” as in Ep. 44.5; “nature” is avoided because it stands for natura in this passage.
notes.other_reading: a noble nature

notes.note: Argutiae are clever fine points, said with scorn, so “quibbles”. Istas can carry “of yours”. Coniectam is “thrown into”, and the image is kept.
notes.other_reading: when it is cast into those subtleties of yours

check.note: The Latin as given has no noun for faciles and illas to agree with. The bracketed supplement is right to be marked, and a note should say the noun is missing.
check.decided: Accepted: “[laws]” stays in square brackets, and the note now says that the noun is missing from the Latin as given and that “laws” is a supplement (from memory, unchecked).

check.note: After the gap neither eorum nor the subject of the verb can be identified, and “these” suggests something nearer than the Latin does. Levare with a part is to relieve it or take it away.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “what part of them they are going to relieve”. “Them” replaces “these” and “relieve” replaces “lighten”; the subject stays “they”, because the Latin names none and the gap hides what it was.

check.note: “Nature” stands three times in this passage for natura, and using it again for indoles blurs that. Generosus is “well born” in Ep. 44.5.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a well-born character”, so that “nature” is kept for natura alone and generosus has the same English as in Ep. 44.5.

check.note: The sense is right but the English is hard to take in at first reading.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the sentence is recast as a plain wish that ends “it were only that they do no good!”. “Only” is kept for tantum, and “the worst of it”, which the Latin does not have, is not added.

check.note: Argutiae is a scornful word, quibbles or hair-splitting, and “subtleties” can be praise. Istas also points at the other party.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “those quibbles”, since argutiae is a scornful word. “Of yours” is not added, to match “those things” for istorum earlier in the passage; the note records it.

passages.latin: Adversus haec me doce aliquid; effice ut ego mortem non fugiam, vita me non effugiat. Exhortare adversus difficilia, [de aequanimitate] adversus inevitabilia; angustias temporis mei laxa. Doce non esse positum bonum vitae in spatio eius sed in usu posse fieri, immo saepissime fieri, ut qui diu vixit parum vixerit. Dic mihi dormituro 'potes non expergisci'; dic experrecto 'potes non dormire amplius'. Dic exeunti 'potes non reverti'; dic redeunti 'potes non exire'.
passages.english: Teach me something against these things. Bring it about that I do not flee from death, and that life does not escape me. Encourage me against what is hard, against what cannot be avoided; loosen the narrow limits of my time. Teach me that the good of life lies not in its length but in its use; that it can happen, indeed very often does happen, that a man who has lived long has lived too little. Say to me when I am about to sleep, “You might not wake up.” Say to me when I have woken, “You might not sleep again.” Say to me as I go out, “You might not come back.” Say to me as I come back, “You might not go out.”

notes.note: “These things” are the deadly things of the section before: death following and life fleeing.
notes.other_reading: Teach me something to meet this

notes.latin: ut ego mortem non fugiam, vita me non effugiat
notes.note: Fugere is “to flee” and effugere is “to flee out of reach”, “to escape”: two verbs from one root. The English reads “flee” and “escape”, so the step from one to the other is kept and the echo is lost.
notes.other_reading: that I do not flee from death, and that life does not flee from me

notes.note: A deponent imperative, “encourage”, with no object in the Latin. The English supplies the speaker as object here and again with the second “Teach”.
notes.other_reading: Give encouragement in the face of difficulties

notes.note: Square brackets in this copy mark words an editor cuts, here probably a reader’s heading that got into the text. The two words mean “on evenness of mind” and do not construe where they stand, so they are left out of the English. The rule: bracketed words are translated only where they construe and the sentence needs them, as in Ep. 41.2.
notes.other_reading: Encourage me against what is hard, [on evenness of mind] against what cannot be avoided

notes.note: Angustiae is a narrow place or tight squeeze, and laxare is “to loosen”, “to widen”. The English keeps the image of something tight being loosened.
notes.other_reading: widen the narrowness of my time

notes.latin: in spatio eius sed in usu posse fieri
notes.note: This copy has no stop after usu, but the sense needs one: the first clause ends at “use”, and posse fieri (“that it can happen”) begins a second thing to be taught. The English marks the break with a semicolon and adds no connective. Bonum vitae is “the good of life”.
notes.other_reading: that the good of life lies not in its length but in its use, and that it can happen

notes.note: Parum is “too little”, “not enough”.
notes.other_reading: has not lived enough

notes.note: Literally “you are able not to wake”, meaning it is possible that you will not. “Might not” is used in all four sayings because “may not” can be heard as a ban.
notes.other_reading: You may not wake up

notes.note: “To one going out”, with the speaker carried over from the first pair. Going out is leaving the house, with a hint of leaving life.
notes.other_reading: Say to a man as he leaves

check.note: The bracketed words are left out of the English with no sign in the text. Bracketed words in Ep. 41.2 are kept, so the reader should be told and one rule applied.
check.decided: Partly accepted: one rule is set for square brackets (see Ep. 41.2): words that do not construe where they stand are left out of the English and given in a note. These two words have no grammar in the sentence, so they stay out, and the note gives their meaning.

check.note: The Latin sets fugiam against effugiat, two different verbs. The English uses “flee” for both and loses the step from one to the other.
check.decided: Accepted: “escape” now stands for effugiat and “flee” for fugiam, so the two verbs are heard as two. The note explains that they share a root.

check.note: The Latin means it is possible that you will not. In all four sayings “You may not” reads in today’s English as a ban.
check.decided: Partly accepted: all four sayings now read “You might not”, which can only mean possibility. “Never” is not taken, because the Latin has a plain “not”, and “again” stands only where the Latin has amplius.

check.note: The Latin as given runs straight from usu to posse fieri with no stop or connective. “And that” is a fair reading but an addition.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the note on the missing stop is kept, and the added “and” is dropped. The English now sets the two clauses side by side with a semicolon: “in its use; that it can happen”.

passages.latin: Non tantum corpori sed etiam moribus salubrem locum eligere debemus; quemadmodum inter tortores habitare nolim, sic ne inter popinas quidem. Videre ebrios per litora errantes et comessationes navigantium et symphoniarum cantibus strepentes lacus et alia quae velut soluta legibus luxuria non tantum peccat sed publicat, quid necesse est?
passages.english: We ought to choose a place that is healthy not only for the body but also for our character. Just as I would not want to live among torturers, so I would not want to live among taverns either. To see drunk people wandering along the shores, and the revels of people out sailing, and the lakes noisy with the music of bands, and the other offences that self-indulgence, as if set free from the laws, not only commits but makes public: what need is there of that?

notes.note: Mores is habits, conduct, character or morals. The English reads “character” and gives it a possessive that the Latin does not have, to balance “the body”.
notes.other_reading: healthy not only for the body but also for morals

notes.note: Tortor is one who inflicts torture, often the public executioner’s man.
notes.other_reading: among executioners

notes.note: Popina is a cheap eating and drinking house with a low reputation, given as “tavern”. Ne … quidem is “not even” or “not … either”. The verb “live” is carried over from the first half.
notes.other_reading: so not even among cook-shops

notes.note: Comessatio is a drinking party that roams about after dinner. Navigantium is “of people sailing”, here pleasure parties on the water.
notes.other_reading: the carousing of boating parties

notes.note: Symphonia is a group of musicians playing or singing together, and cantus covers both song and playing. The lakes would be those by Baiae, which the section before names (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: the lakes ringing with the singing of choirs

notes.note: Luxuria is loose, extravagant living, given as “self-indulgence”; “luxury” today suggests comfort and costly goods. Soluta legibus is the phrase for being exempted from the laws, and it picks up the verb of loosening in the section before.
notes.other_reading: luxury, as though exempt from the laws

notes.note: A play on sound, peccat and publicat. The relative “which” is the object of both verbs: the wrongs it does and then displays. “Offences” gives that object of peccat.
notes.other_reading: the other things in which self-indulgence not only sins but advertises its sin

check.note: “Cook-shops” is an old word that a reader of today will not know. A popina is a cheap eating and drinking house with a low name.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “taverns”. “Cook-shops” is not a word of today, but a popina sold food as well as drink, which “bars” would lose.

check.note: Symphoniae are groups of musicians and cantus covers playing as well as song. “Singing” narrows it to voices.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the music of bands”, since cantus covers playing as well as song.

check.note: Luxuria is loose living, self-indulgence. “Luxury” today suggests comfort and costly goods, which do not commit offences.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “self-indulgence”. Luxuria here is loose living that commits offences, which “luxury” no longer suggests.

check.note: The Latin says only “other things which”, and “offences” is drawn forward from the verb. The addition is small and fair.
check.decided: Declined: “the other offences that self-indulgence … commits” stays. In the Latin “which” is the direct object of peccat, “does wrong”, so the things are named as wrongs done, and “offences” gives that; nothing is added.

passages.latin: Libertas proposita est; ad hoc praemium laboratur. Quae sit libertas quaeris? Nulli rei servire, nulli necessitati, nullis casibus, fortunam in aequum deducere. Quo die illam intellexero plus posse, nil poterit: ego illam feram, cum in manu mors sit?
passages.english: Freedom is what has been set as the goal; it is for this prize that the toil is done. You ask what freedom is? To be a slave to no thing, to no necessity, to no accidents; to bring Fortune down to level ground. On the day I understand that she has more power, she will have no power: am I to put up with her, when death is in my hand?

notes.note: Proposita is “set before” as an aim or as a prize put up in a contest. The Latin does not say by whom or for whom, and the English keeps it impersonal.
notes.other_reading: Freedom is the prize held out

notes.note: An impersonal passive: “there is toiling for this prize”, kept impersonal.
notes.other_reading: this is the reward I am working for

notes.note: Servire is “to be a slave to”. Res is any thing or circumstance, and “no thing” is written as two words to keep it wide.
notes.other_reading: To serve nothing

notes.note: Casus is what befalls, an accident or chance event. It is plural in the Latin, and the English reads “accidents”.
notes.other_reading: to no chances

notes.note: A military idiom: to bring an enemy down from high ground to the level, where the fight is on equal terms. The image is kept. Fortune has a capital here, by the glossary’s rule, because she is treated as an enemy in this section and the one before.
notes.other_reading: to meet Fortune on equal terms

notes.latin: Quo die illam intellexero plus posse, nil poterit
notes.note: As given, this says that on the day Fortune is found to be the stronger she will be able to do nothing, which the next clause explains: death is to hand. From memory, unchecked, editions print illa me for illam, so that the speaker is the stronger one. The English translates the Latin as given, with “power” for both posse and poterit.
notes.other_reading: On the day I understand that I have more power than she, she will have no power

notes.note: Feram can be future (“shall … bear”) or subjunctive (“am … to bear”). The sense is nearly the same, and the English takes the second.
notes.other_reading: Shall I endure her

notes.note: “In hand” means within one’s own power. The Latin has no possessive; English needs one with “hand”. The thought is that one can always choose to die.
notes.other_reading: when death is within reach

check.latin: Quo die illam intellexero plus posse, nil poterit
check.note: As given, the Latin makes Fortune the one with more power, which is said to turn the sentence against itself. The editions are recalled as reading illa me, so that the speaker is the stronger, and illam is taken for a slip of the copy.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps the Latin as given, in which illam is the subject of “has more power” and can only be Fortune. The sentence does not contradict itself: the clause after the colon gives the reason, that with death to hand the day Fortune proves stronger is the day she loses her hold. The reading of the editions is in the note (from memory, unchecked).

check.note: “To no chances” is not natural English. Casus are things that befall by chance.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “to no accidents”. Casus are things that befall, and the one plural noun is enough without “of chance”.

check.note: The Latin has a small f, and other letters in this set have “fortune” for the same word. The reader may also need help to see that the image means meeting Fortune on equal terms.
check.decided: Declined: the capital stays, by the glossary’s rule that Fortune has a capital where personified. Here she is led down like an enemy and is the “her” of the last sentence, while in Ep. 41.2 and 44.5 fortune is only something to rise above. “On equal terms” is not added, because the Latin says only “onto the level”; the note explains the image.

check.note: In manu also means “in one’s power, within reach”. The English keeps the literal image and supplies a possessive.
check.decided: Declined: the hand stays in the English, because the Latin has it (in manu) and images are to be kept as images. The possessive is supplied as English needs it, and the note gives “within reach” as the other reading.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft put a full stop where the Latin has a colon, which hid that the question gives the reason for the statement before it.
check.decided: Accepted: the colon is restored, and the two clauses are now one sentence.

passages.latin: 'Stultitia' inquis 'est cui nihil constat, nihil diu placet.' Sed quomodo nos aut quando ab illa revellemus? Nemo per se satis valet ut emergat; oportet manum aliquis porrigat, aliquis educat.
passages.english: “It is folly,” you say, “and for folly nothing holds firm, nothing pleases for long.” But how, or when, shall we tear ourselves away from it? No one is strong enough by himself to come up to the surface; someone must stretch out a hand, someone must draw him out.

notes.note: The word answers the question of the section before (what is it that pulls a person the wrong way?), so the English makes “folly” the answer: “It is folly”. The Latin can also be read as a definition with folly as its subject.
notes.other_reading: “Folly,” you say, “is the thing for which nothing holds firm, which nothing pleases for long.”

notes.note: “constat” covers “stands firm”, “is settled”, “is consistent” and “is agreed”. The English reads “holds firm”, and turns the relative clause (“for which”) into “and for folly” so that the sentence can be followed.
notes.other_reading: for which nothing is consistent

notes.note: “revellere” is to wrench off something that is stuck fast; the verb is a future (“shall”), not a wish. “illa” is folly.
notes.other_reading: how or when are we going to pull ourselves free of it?

notes.note: The verb is the opposite of “mergere”, to sink: to rise out of water or mud in which one is sunk. The image is kept with “come up to the surface”.
notes.other_reading: to get himself out

notes.note: After “oportet” this is the subjunctive of “educere”, to lead or draw out, not “educare”, to bring up. The Latin has no object; “him” is supplied. “Draw” keeps both the leading and the pulling that are in the verb.
notes.other_reading: someone must lead him out

check.note: Read on its own, “It is folly … for which nothing stays settled” is hard to parse, and “It is folly” may be taken as a judgement rather than as the name of the thing asked about. The Latin is a plain relative clause.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “It is folly,” you say, “and for folly nothing holds firm, nothing pleases for long.” The relative clause is unpacked so that folly is plainly the thing named, and “holds firm” gives the physical sense of constat.

check.note: After emergat and manum porrigat, educat is “draw out, pull out” of whatever he is sunk in. “Lead” loses the image of being hauled up by the offered hand.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “someone must draw him out”. Educere is to lead or draw out, and “draw” goes with the outstretched hand without making the verb stronger than it is, as “pull” would.

check.note: “To the surface” spells out water; emergat only says he gets himself up and out, and it could as well be mud.
check.decided: Declined: “come up to the surface” stands. Emergere is the opposite of mergere, to sink, so rising to a surface is in the verb itself, and a surface fits mud as well as water; “get himself out” would drop the image of rising.

passages.latin: Quosdam ait Epicurus ad veritatem sine ullius adiutorio exisse, fecisse sibi ipsos viam; hos maxime laudat quibus ex se impetus fuit, qui se ipsi protulerunt: quosdam indigere ope aliena, non ituros si nemo praecesserit, sed bene secuturos. Ex his Metrodorum ait esse; egregium hoc quoque, sed secundae sortis ingenium. Nos ex illa prima nota non sumus; bene nobiscum agitur, si in secundam recipimur. Ne hunc quidem contempseris hominem qui alieno beneficio esse salvus potest; et hoc multum est, velle servari.
