passages.english: Epicurus says that some people have come out to the truth without anyone’s help, that they themselves have made their own road; these he praises most, the ones whose drive came from themselves, who brought themselves forward. Others, he says, need another’s aid: they will not go if no one has gone ahead, but they will follow well. Metrodorus, he says, is one of these; this too is an outstanding talent, but of the second rank. We are not of that first grade; we are well treated if we are admitted to the second. Do not look down even on the man who can be safe through another’s good service; this too is a great deal, to want to be saved.

notes.note: Seneca reports Epicurus in indirect speech, so there are no quotation marks. From memory, unchecked: the saying is known only from this letter and comes from a lost writing of Epicurus.
notes.other_reading: According to Epicurus, some people

notes.note: Literally “have gone out”, which continues the image of emerging in the section before. From memory, unchecked: some editions may print a different verb here (“contendere”, to strive towards); the English follows the text as given.
notes.other_reading: have made their way to the truth

notes.note: “sibi” is “for themselves” and “ipsos” is “they themselves”, with no one’s help. The English gives the two as “they themselves” and “their own road”.
notes.other_reading: that they have made a road for themselves

notes.note: “proferre se” can be to bring oneself forward, to advance oneself, or to bring oneself out into view. The English takes it as moving forward under their own power, to match the road they made.
notes.other_reading: who brought themselves out into view

notes.note: Metrodorus of Lampsacus, the closest pupil and friend of Epicurus (from memory, unchecked).
“ingenium” is inborn ability or cast of mind; the English reads “talent” because the glossary keeps “mind” for animus. “sors” is literally a lot drawn, here a rank or class.
notes.other_reading: this too is an outstanding mind, but of the second lot

notes.note: “nota” is a mark or label, used of the grade marked on a wine jar, and so a class or quality. The English reads “grade”; the image of a stamped mark is lost. The same noun is understood with “the second”.
notes.other_reading: We do not bear that first stamp

notes.note: An idiom, literally “it is dealt well with us”. The English reads “well treated”: the luck lies in what is granted, not in a performance.
notes.other_reading: it goes well with us if we are let into the second

notes.note: “beneficium” is a good service or favour actually done, not a kindly disposition. “Help” and “aid” already stand for adiutorio and ope above, so the English reads “good service”.
notes.other_reading: by another’s kindness

notes.note: “salvus esse” is to be safe or sound; “servari” in the next clause is to be saved or kept safe. The two different words are kept apart as “safe” and “saved”.
notes.other_reading: who can be saved

check.note: “For themselves” renders sibi only; the emphatic ipsos (they did it themselves, with no one’s help) is lost.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “that they themselves have made their own road”, so that both the “themselves” of ipsos and the “for themselves” of sibi are heard.

check.latin: egregium hoc quoque, sed secundae sortis ingenium
check.note: “Kind of” is added, and ingenium is a cast of mind or nature rather than “talent” in the modern sense of a gift for something.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “kind of” is removed and the English reads “this too is an outstanding talent, but of the second rank”. “Talent” is kept for ingenium, in its sense of inborn ability, because the glossary keeps “mind” for animus; a note gives “mind” as the other reading.

check.note: The Latin is an impersonal passive: things go well for the people spoken of. The draft’s “doing well” suggests a performance, where Seneca means a piece of good luck.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “well treated” in place of “doing well”. The Latin idiom is of being dealt with well by someone else, which “treated” says directly; “well off” could be heard as a matter of money.

check.note: Beneficium is a service or favour actually done, not a disposition; “kindness” moves the point from the help received to the helper’s character.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “through another’s good service”. The point about beneficium holds, but “help” already stands for adiutorio and “aid” for ope earlier in the passage, so a third word is used for this third Latin word.

check.note: Salvus esse (to be safe) and servari (to be saved) are two different words in the Latin and both become “saved”, so the small step from being safe to wanting to be saved disappears.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “who can be safe” and then “to want to be saved”, one English word for each Latin word. “Can be safe” is the plain sense of esse salvus potest, without the added “come through”.

passages.latin: Nec ideo te prohibuerim hos quoque audire quibus admittere populum ac disserere consuetudo est, si modo hoc proposito in turbam prodeunt, ut meliores fiant faciantque meliores, si non ambitionis hoc causa exercent. Quid enim turpius philosophia captante clamores? numquid aeger laudat medicum secantem?
passages.english: Nor would I, on that account, forbid you to listen also to those whose habit it is to admit the public and lecture, provided that they come out before the crowd with this purpose, to become better and to make others better, if they do not practise this to court popularity. For what is more shameful than philosophy hunting for shouts? Surely a sick man does not praise the doctor who is cutting him?

notes.note: “On that account” points back to the advice just given: choose as a helper the man who teaches by his life rather than the fluent talker.
notes.other_reading: But that is no reason for me to stop you

notes.note: Literally “to admit the people and to discourse”: philosophers who give open lectures to anyone who comes. “disserere” is to set out an argument at length; the English reads “lecture” here and for the same verb in Ep. 52.11.
notes.other_reading: to let the public in and hold discourses

notes.note: The Latin has no object: “become better and make better”. “Others” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: to become better and make their hearers better

notes.note: “ambitio” is first a candidate’s going round for votes, then the courting of favour and applause. The English reads “to court popularity”, because the English word “ambition” now means wanting to get ahead.
notes.other_reading: for the sake of ambition

notes.note: “hoc exercent” is “practise this”, the public lecturing. It can also mean carrying it on as a profession.
notes.other_reading: if they do not make a trade of this to court popularity

notes.note: “clamores” are the shouts of an audience, here shouts of approval; “captare” is to hunt or angle for something. “Shouts” is used for this word in Ep. 52.11 and 52.12 as well.
notes.other_reading: philosophy fishing for cheers

notes.note: “numquid” expects the answer no, which “Surely … not” gives. “secantem” is the doctor cutting, that is, operating with the knife; the plain “cutting” is kept.
notes.other_reading: Does a sick man praise the surgeon who is operating on him?

check.note: “Holding discourses” is stiff and old. The same verb is “used to speak” in 52.11 (Disserebat populo), so the link between these lecturers and Fabianus is lost.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “whose habit it is to admit the public and lecture”, and the same verb is “used to lecture” in Ep. 52.11. “Habit” is used for consuetudo so that “practise” is free for exercent later in the sentence.

check.latin: si non ambitionis hoc causa exercent
check.note: The Latin has a second si with no connective, restating the condition from the other side; “and” makes it an added second condition.
check.decided: Accepted: “and” is removed, and the second condition now follows the first after a comma, as in the Latin: “if they do not practise this to court popularity”.

check.note: Ambitio is courting favour, playing to the crowd. English “ambition” means wanting to get ahead, which is not the charge here, as the next sentence shows.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “to court popularity”. Ambitio is the canvassing for favour that the next sentence describes, and “court” keeps the sense of going after it.

check.note: “Of applause” is an explanation folded into the text. Clamor is plain “shouts” and “shouting” in 52.11 and 52.12.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “philosophy hunting for shouts”, the same plain word as in the two sections that follow; a note says the shouts are an audience’s.

check.note: Numquid expects the answer no; the English leaves the question open.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Surely a sick man does not praise the doctor who is cutting him?”, which expects the answer no as numquid does.

passages.latin: Quanta autem dementia eius est quem clamores imperitorum hilarem ex auditorio dimittunt! Quid laetaris quod ab hominibus his laudatus es quos non potes ipse laudare? Disserebat populo Fabianus, sed audiebatur modeste; erumpebat interdum magnus clamor laudantium, sed quem rerum magnitudo evocaverat, non sonus inoffense ac molliter orationis elapsae.
passages.english: And how great is the madness of the man whom the shouts of the ignorant send away from the lecture hall cheerful! Why are you glad to have been praised by these people, whom you cannot yourself praise? Fabianus used to lecture to the public, but he was listened to with restraint; from time to time a great shout of praise would break out, but one that the greatness of what he was saying had called forth, not the sound of speech that had glided by without a stumble and softly.

notes.note: “imperiti” are those without knowledge or experience of the matter, the unqualified. The English reads “the ignorant”.
notes.other_reading: the shouts of people who know nothing about it

notes.note: “auditorium” can be the hall or the audience gathered in it. The English takes it as the place.
notes.other_reading: send away from his audience

notes.note: The “you” here is the applauded lecturer, addressed directly, or any such person; it need not be Lucilius. The second person is kept as it stands.
notes.other_reading: Why should a man be glad

notes.note: Papirius Fabianus, a philosopher and speaker whom Seneca heard when young (from memory, unchecked).
The adverb describes how the audience listened: within bounds, with self control. It could also be heard as “respectfully”.
notes.other_reading: but he was heard respectfully

notes.note: Literally “the greatness of the things”: the substance of what was said, as opposed to how it sounded.
notes.other_reading: the greatness of his subject

notes.latin: sonus inoffense ac molliter orationis elapsae
notes.note: Literally “the sound of speech that has slipped out without striking against anything and softly”. “elapsae” may be speech slipping out, slipping by or slipping away; the English reads “glided by”. “molliter” (softly) can carry a hint of effeminacy.
notes.other_reading: the sound of speech that had slipped out smoothly and effeminately

check.note: His is dropped. The Latin points at them (“these people”) with some contempt.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “by these people, whom you cannot yourself praise”.

check.note: The same verb is “holding discourses” in 52.9. Fabianus is the good example of exactly that practice, so the word should match.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Fabianus used to lecture to the public”, with the same “lecture” that renders the verb in Ep. 52.9.

check.note: “The greatness of the matter” is stiff and vague. Rerum is the content, what was being said, set against sonus, the mere sound of the words.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the greatness of what he was saying”, which sets the substance against the sound; a note gives the literal “things”.

check.note: “Slipping out” suggests words escaping by accident; elapsae is speech that has glided past. Inoffense is “without a stumble or hitch”, a little more exact than “smoothly”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “speech that had glided by without a stumble and softly”. “Glided by” is taken, the participle is put in the past as the Latin has it, and “without a stumble” keeps the image in inoffense of not striking against anything; the two adverbs stay in the Latin order.

passages.latin: Intersit aliquid inter clamorem theatri et scholae: est aliqua et laudandi elegantia. Omnia rerum omnium, si observentur, indicia sunt, et argumentum morum ex minimis quoque licet capere: impudicum et incessus ostendit et manus mota et unum interdum responsum et relatus ad caput digitus et flexus oculorum; improbum risus, insanum vultus habitusque demonstrat. Illa enim in apertum per notas exeunt: qualis quisque sit scies, si quemadmodum laudet, quemadmodum laudetur aspexeris.
passages.english: Let there be some difference between the shouting of the theatre and that of the school: there is a certain good taste in praising too. Everything is a sign of everything, if it is watched, and one may take evidence of character even from the smallest things: the lewd man is shown by his walk, by a movement of his hand, sometimes by a single answer, by a finger brought to his head, by the turn of his eyes; the wicked man is given away by his laugh, the madman by his face and bearing. For those traits come out into the open through their marks: you will know what each person is like if you look at how he praises and how he is praised.

notes.note: The “school” is a philosopher’s lecture room and the audience in it, set against the public theatre.
notes.other_reading: the shouting of the theatre and that of the lecture room

notes.note: “elegantia” is discrimination or fineness of taste rather than elegance of dress or style.
notes.other_reading: there is a kind of refinement even in giving praise

notes.latin: Omnia rerum omnium, si observentur, indicia sunt
notes.note: Literally “all things are signs of all things, if they are observed”. “Omnia” can also be taken with “indicia”: all things have their signs, if one watches for them. The English takes “omnia” as the subject.
notes.other_reading: There are signs of everything, if one watches for them

notes.note: “impudicus” is a man without sexual shame, and in Roman usage the word often points at a man thought effeminate or sexually passive, which the signs listed here suit. The English reads the general word “lewd”.
notes.other_reading: the effeminate man

notes.note: Literally “a finger carried back to the head”. From memory, unchecked: scratching the head with one finger was a proverbial sign of effeminacy at Rome. The literal gesture is kept.
notes.other_reading: scratching his head with one finger

notes.note: “flexus” is a bending or turning: a sideways or rolling glance.
notes.other_reading: by a sidelong glance

notes.note: “improbus” is the general word for a morally bad man, the opposite of “probus”, upright; it can lean towards “dishonest” or “shameless”. The English keeps the broad word “wicked”.
notes.other_reading: the dishonest man

notes.note: “habitus” covers bearing, physical condition and dress. The English reads “bearing”.
notes.other_reading: by his expression and his dress

notes.latin: Illa enim in apertum per notas exeunt
notes.note: “Illa” is a neuter plural with no noun: the English takes it as the hidden traits of character just named and supplies “traits”. “notae” are distinguishing marks, kept apart from “indicia”, “signs”, above.
notes.other_reading: For those things come out into the open through marks

check.note: “Unchaste” is archaic. Impudicus is a man without sexual shame.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the lewd man”. “Unchaste” is dropped as old, and “lewd” is a current single word for a man without sexual shame where “sexually shameless” would be heavy; a note gives the narrower Roman sense.

check.note: “Wicked” is broad and a little old. Improbus is the unprincipled, dishonest man.
check.decided: Declined: “the wicked man” stands. Improbus is the broad word for a morally bad man, the opposite of probus, so a broad English word is right, and “wicked” is still current; “scoundrel” is narrower and no plainer. A note records the narrower senses.

check.latin: Illa enim in apertum per notas exeunt
check.note: “Those things” can be read as the walk, laugh and face, though illa are the inner traits just listed. “Through marks” means little to a reader of today; notae are outward distinguishing marks, to be kept distinct from indicia, “signs”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “For those traits come out into the open through their marks”. “Traits” makes clear that illa are the inner qualities and not the walk or the laugh; “outward” is not added, because the Latin has only “marks” and “come out into the open” already says it.

passages.latin: Quare vitia sua nemo confitetur? quia etiam nunc in illis est: somnium narrare vigilantis est, et vitia sua confiteri sanitatis indicium est. Expergiscamur ergo, ut errores nostros coarguere possimus. Sola autem nos philosophia excitabit, sola somnum excutiet gravem: illi te totum dedica. Dignus illa es, illa digna te est: ite in complexum alter alterius. Omnibus aliis rebus te nega, fortiter, aperte; non est quod precario philosopheris.
passages.english: Why does no one confess his vices? Because he is still in them: to tell a dream is for a man who is awake, and to confess one’s vices is a sign of health. Let us wake up, then, so that we can expose our errors. But only philosophy will rouse us, only philosophy will shake off the heavy sleep: dedicate yourself wholly to her. You are worthy of her, she is worthy of you: go into each other’s embrace. Refuse yourself to all other things, bravely, openly; there is no reason for you to do philosophy by someone else’s leave.

notes.note: The glossary’s “vices” is kept. The section before treats them as diseases of the mind, so “faults” or “failings” is also possible.
notes.other_reading: Why does no one admit his faults?

notes.note: “sanitas” is both health of body and soundness of mind. The section before speaks of diseases of the mind, and “health” answers that image.
notes.other_reading: a sign of sanity

notes.note: “coarguere” is to prove something wrong or convict it by evidence; the English reads “expose”. “errores” is “errors”, but also “wanderings”, which suits the dream image.
notes.other_reading: to convict our wanderings

notes.note: “Philosophia” is feminine. Because the next sentence speaks of an embrace, the English reads “her” and “she” rather than “it”.
notes.other_reading: dedicate yourself wholly to it

notes.note: The command is plural, addressed to Lucilius and philosophy together: literally “go, the one into the embrace of the other”.
notes.other_reading: embrace one another

notes.note: Literally “deny yourself to all other things”: say no to every other claim on you.
notes.other_reading: Say no to everything else

notes.note: “fortiter” is “bravely”, and also “firmly, stoutly”. The English keeps the first sense.
notes.other_reading: firmly, openly

notes.note: A term from law: holding something only at another’s request and by his leave, which can be withdrawn at any moment. Here it means doing philosophy only when other business allows.
notes.other_reading: there is no reason for you to do philosophy on sufferance

check.note: Sanitas is both health and soundness of mind. The illness in question is of the mind, and the English keeps only the bodily word.
check.decided: Declined: “a sign of health” stands. The section before calls these states diseases of the mind, and sanitas is the plain opposite of disease; English “health” is said of mind as well as body, and “again” in the suggestion is not in the Latin. The note gives “sanity” as the other reading.

check.note: Coarguere is to show up, expose, convict. “Against ourselves” is not in the Latin, and the phrase as a whole is obscure.
check.decided: Accepted: the draft’s longer phrase is replaced by the single verb “expose”, which is what coarguere says; nothing is added.

check.note: With te nega and aperte, fortiter may be “firmly, resolutely” rather than “bravely”. Both are possible and the English has chosen silently.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “bravely” stays, as the first sense of fortiter and one that suits a refusal made in the open, but the choice is no longer silent: a note now gives “firmly” as the other reading.

check.note: “On sufferance” is a rare idiom now and many readers will not get it. Precario is “by someone else’s leave”, held only as long as it is allowed.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “by someone else’s leave”. This is the sense of precario in plain words; “only when” in the suggestion is not in the Latin, so it is left out.

passages.latin: Si aeger esses, curam intermisisses rei familiaris et forensia tibi negotia excidissent nec quemquam tanti putares cui advocatus in remissione descenderes; toto animo id ageres ut quam primum morbo liberareris. Quid ergo? non et nunc idem facies? omnia impedimenta dimitte et vaca bonae menti: nemo ad illam pervenit occupatus. Exercet philosophia regnum suum; dat tempus, non accipit; non est res subsiciva; ordinaria est, domina est, adest et iubet.
passages.english: If you were ill, you would have set aside the care of your property, and your business in the forum would have dropped out of your mind, and you would not think anyone worth so much that you would go down as his advocate during a remission; with your whole mind you would work at this, to be freed from the illness as soon as possible. Well then? Will you not do the same now too? Let go of everything that hinders you and make yourself free for a sound mind: no one reaches it while he is busy. Philosophy exercises her own royal power; she gives out time, she does not accept it; she is not a thing for leftover hours; she is a thing for the regular hours, she is the mistress, she is present and gives orders.

notes.note: The Latin moves from “would have” (set aside, dropped) to “would” (think, work); the shift is kept. “res familiaris” is one’s property, one’s private means.
notes.other_reading: you would have stopped looking after your estate

notes.note: “forensia” is “of the forum”, the place of the law courts and of public business in general.
notes.other_reading: your business in the courts

notes.note: “descendere” is the usual word for going down to the forum; an “advocatus” is one called in to stand by a party at law, by this date often the one who pleads. “remissio” is an abatement of the illness, a let up in the fever.
notes.other_reading: for whom you would go down to court to support him when the illness eased

notes.note: “impedimenta” are hindrances, and also the word for an army’s baggage. The plain sense is kept.
notes.other_reading: Send away all your baggage

notes.note: “vacare” is to be free or at leisure for something. “bona mens” is a sound or good mind; “mens” is a different word from “animus”, which is “mind” just before.
notes.other_reading: give your free time to good sense

notes.note: “occupatus” is “taken up”, busy with other affairs. In Seneca it is a set term for the man with no time of his own.
notes.other_reading: no one reaches it while preoccupied

notes.note: “regnum” is a king’s power or a kingdom: philosophy reigns in her own right. The English reads “royal power” so that the word is not taken for a regulation she follows.
notes.other_reading: Philosophy holds her own kingdom

notes.note: Literally “she gives time, she does not receive it”. It can mean that she hands time out to other things and takes none of what they leave over, or that she appoints the hours and has none appointed for her; “gives out” leans to the first. From memory, unchecked: the letter goes on to make philosophy refuse the time left over from other things.
notes.other_reading: she sets the time, she does not have it set for her

notes.latin: non est res subsiciva; ordinaria est
notes.note: “subsicivus” is used of land left over after a survey and then of odd spare moments. “ordinarius” is what belongs to the regular order, as opposed to the extra. The English gives the contrast as leftover hours and regular hours; the surveyor’s image is lost.
notes.other_reading: she is not an odd moments affair; she is a regular one

notes.note: “domina” is the mistress of a household who commands its slaves. This personification is why the English reads “she” for philosophy throughout the sentence.
notes.other_reading: it is the master

check.note: Res familiaris is one’s property, one’s private fortune. “Household affairs” suggests running the house.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the care of your property”.

check.note: “To court” is supplied; the Latin has only “go down” (that is, to the forum) with advocatus, “as a supporter at law”. It is a fair expansion, but it is an expansion.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “to court” is removed and the English now reads “go down as his advocate”, which is what the Latin has. “To the forum” is not supplied here either, because the forum is now named in the clause before, where forensia stands.

check.note: In English “her own rule” can be read as a regulation she follows. Regnum is kingly power: she reigns in her own right.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “Philosophy exercises her own royal power”. This removes the doubt about “rule” in plainer words than “sovereignty”, and “exercises” stays for exercet.

check.note: The English reads as though she grants time to people. The likelier sense is that she appoints the hours and does not take whatever hours are offered to her; the literal version leaves the reader to guess.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “she gives out time, she does not accept it”. The Latin verb is “gives”, not “sets”, and the sense may be that she hands time out to other things and takes none of what they leave; “gives out” shows that she is the one who allots it, and a note gives the suggested reading.

check.note: “Business” is added, and sits oddly beside “your business in the courts” and “busy”, which are what philosophy is set against. Ordinaria answers subsiciva: the regular, scheduled thing as against the spare time one.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “business” is removed and the English now reads “she is a thing for the regular hours”, answering “a thing for leftover hours”. It is “a thing”, not “the thing”, because the Latin does not say she is the only one.

check.note: Found while settling: “your business in the courts” narrows forensia, which is “of the forum”, where public business as well as lawsuits was done.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “your business in the forum”, which also tells the reader where the advocate of the next clause goes down to.

passages.latin: Rogo, non stultissimum dicas si quis existimet lucernae peius esse cum exstincta est quam antequam accenditur? Nos quoque et exstinguimur et accendimur: medio illo tempore aliquid patimur, utrimque vero alta securitas est. In hoc enim, mi Lucili, nisi fallor, erramus, quod mortem iudicamus sequi, cum illa et praecesserit et secutura sit. Quidquid ante nos fuit mors est; quid enim refert non incipias an desinas, cum utriusque rei hic sit effectus, non esse?
passages.english: I ask you, would you not call it most foolish if someone thought that a lamp is worse off when it has been put out than before it is lit? We too are both put out and lit: in the time between we go through something, but on either side there is deep freedom from care. For this, my Lucilius, unless I am mistaken, is where we go wrong: we judge that death follows, when it has both gone before and will follow. Whatever was before us is death; for what does it matter whether you do not begin or you cease, when the result of both is this, not to be?

notes.note: The form can be neuter (“a most foolish thing”) or masculine (“a complete fool”, said of the person who thinks so). The English takes it as neuter.
notes.other_reading: would you not call a man a complete fool if he thought

notes.note: Literally “that it is worse for the lamp”: an oil lamp is spoken of as if it could be well or badly off.
notes.other_reading: that things are worse for a lamp

notes.note: “pati” is to undergo, to have something happen to one, and also to suffer. “Go through” is chosen because it can be heard either way.
notes.other_reading: in the time between we suffer something

notes.note: “securitas” is the state of being without care or trouble; the glossary’s “freedom from care” is kept. “alta” is “deep”.
notes.other_reading: on either side there is deep peace

notes.note: “sequi” has no object: death “follows”, that is, comes after life. “iudicamus” is “judge”, kept apart from “thought” above.
notes.other_reading: we suppose that death comes afterwards

notes.note: The “you” is the general “you” (anyone), not Lucilius in particular; the second person is kept.
notes.other_reading: whether one never begins or one stops

check.note: Stultissimum can be neuter (“call it most foolish”) or masculine (“call him an utter fool”), with si quis as the person. The English takes the neuter; the sense is hardly affected.
check.decided: Declined: “would you not call it most foolish” stands. The form can be either gender and the Latin gives no “him” to decide it; the choice is recorded in a note with the other reading.

check.note: Patimur may be the neutral “undergo, feel” (in between something is felt, on either side nothing) rather than “suffer”. The English picks the stronger sense.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “go through something”. Pati is to undergo, which can be neutral or painful, and “go through” leaves that open as the Latin does; “feel” would be a different Latin verb.

passages.latin: Hoc tibi de me recipe: non trepidabo ad extrema, iam praeparatus sum, nihil cogito de die toto. Illum tu lauda et imitare quem non piget mori, cum iuvet vivere: quae est enim virtus, cum eiciaris, exire? Tamen est et hic virtus: eicior quidem, sed tamquam exeam. Et ideo numquam eicitur sapiens quia eici est inde expelli unde invitus recedas: nihil invitus facit sapiens; necessitatem effugit, quia vult quod coactura est. Vale.
passages.english: Be assured of this about me: I shall not tremble at the end, I am already prepared, I give no thought to a whole day. As for you, praise and imitate the man who is not sorry to die though he is glad to live: for what virtue is there in going out when you are being thrown out? Yet there is virtue here too: I am indeed being thrown out, but as though I were going out. And the reason the wise man is never thrown out is that to be thrown out is to be driven from a place you leave unwillingly: the wise man does nothing unwillingly; he escapes necessity, because he wants what it is going to force on him. Farewell.

notes.note: “recipere” is the word for giving or taking a guarantee. Literally “take this for yourself about me”, that is, accept it as assured.
notes.other_reading: Take this as my pledge about myself

notes.note: Literally “at the last things”: the final moments of life.
notes.other_reading: when the last moment comes

notes.note: Literally, no thought is given to “the whole day”. The likely sense is that he does not count on having a full day ahead of him; it could also be read as giving no thought to the day at all.
notes.other_reading: I do not count on a whole day

notes.note: “cum” is read as “although”: he is not unwilling to die even though living pleases him. Seneca sets this man against himself, old and ill, who is being pushed out anyway.
notes.other_reading: at a time when he enjoys living

notes.note: The glossary’s “virtue” is kept. The passage is close to the sense “courage”, and “what merit is there” would also be possible.
notes.other_reading: for what courage is there

notes.note: The argument rests on the pair “eici” (to be thrown out) and “exire” (to go out of one’s own accord). “Thrown out” and “going out” are kept throughout.
notes.other_reading: I am being evicted, it is true, but as if I were leaving

notes.note: Literally “because he wants what it is going to compel”. The subject of “coactura est” is necessity; “on him” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: because he wills what it would force him to do

check.note: “Pledge” is a little more than the Latin, which says “accept this about me”, “be assured of this”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Be assured of this about me”.

check.note: The English can be read as “for a whole day no plans are made”. The Latin means he gives no thought to having a whole day, that is, he does not count on one.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “give no thought to a whole day”, which cannot be taken as a day spent without plans. It keeps cogito as thinking rather than counting on; the note gives “do not count on a whole day” as the sense.

passages.latin: Nam qui res et homines fugit, quem cupiditatum suarum infelicitas relegavit, qui alios feliciores videre non potuit, qui velut timidum atque iners animal metu oblituit, ille sibi non vivit, sed, quod est turpissimum, ventri, somno, libidini; non continuo sibi vivit qui nemini. Adeo tamen magna res est constantia et in proposito suo perseverantia ut habeat auctoritatem inertia quoque pertinax.
passages.english: For the man who has run away from affairs and from people, whom the ill success of his own desires has banished, who could not bear to see others more successful, who has gone into hiding out of fear like a timid and sluggish animal: that man does not live for himself but, which is the most shameful thing, for his belly, for sleep, for lust; a man who lives for no one does not, just by that, live for himself. Yet steadiness, and persistence in one’s purpose, is so great a thing that even stubborn sluggishness carries weight.

notes.note: “res” is “things”, here the business of public and private life.
notes.other_reading: the world and its people

notes.note: The form can be present (“runs away”) or perfect (“has run away”). The other verbs in the series are perfect, so the English takes it as perfect.
notes.other_reading: the man who runs away from affairs and from people

notes.note: “infelicitas” is ill luck or failure: his ambitions came to nothing. It could also be the misery his desires brought him. “relegare” is the legal word for banishing someone to a distance; “ill success” lets “more successful” (feliciores) echo it.
notes.other_reading: whom the unhappiness of his own desires has sent into exile

notes.note: Literally “was not able to see”, meaning he could not stand the sight; “bear” is supplied. “feliciores” is “more fortunate, more successful”; “happier” is avoided because the glossary keeps “happy” for beatus.
notes.other_reading: who could not look at others more fortunate than himself

notes.note: The perfect of a verb meaning to hide oneself away, to go to ground.
notes.other_reading: has lain hidden

notes.note: “To live for oneself” is the phrase from the section before, where the crowd says it of any man of leisure and Seneca reserves it for the wise man.
notes.other_reading: does not live to himself

notes.note: “continuo” here is “as an immediate consequence”: it does not follow at once that he lives for himself.
notes.other_reading: it does not follow that a man who lives for no one lives for himself

notes.note: The glossary’s “steadiness”: holding to one course. The verb is singular, treating steadiness and persistence as one thing.
notes.other_reading: constancy

notes.note: “inertia” picks up “iners” said of the animal above, so the English reads “sluggish” and “sluggishness”. “pertinax” is “holding on obstinately”. “auctoritas” is weight or standing in others’ eyes.
notes.other_reading: even idleness, if it is obstinate, wins respect

check.note: Fugit can be present or perfect. The verbs beside it (relegavit, potuit, oblituit) are perfect, so “has run away” is at least as likely, and the English has chosen the present silently.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the man who has run away from affairs and from people”, in line with the three perfects that follow; a note records the present as the other reading.

check.note: “Idle animal” is odd English; “sluggish” is nearer. Iners and inertia are rightly kept as one word, so if one changes, both should.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a timid and sluggish animal” and “even stubborn sluggishness”, so that the echo of iners in inertia is still heard.

check.note: “Authority” may suggest power over others. The sense is that even this commands a certain respect.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “carries weight”. Auctoritas is weight or standing in the eyes of others, which “weight” gives without suggesting command; “wins respect” would say a little more than the Latin “has”.

passages.latin: Sed non multum ad tranquillitatem locus confert: animus est qui sibi commendet omnia. Vidi ego in villa hilari et amoena maestos, vidi in media solitudine occupatis similes. Quare non est quod existimes ideo parum bene compositum esse te quod in Campania non es. Quare autem non es? huc usque cogitationes tuas mitte.
passages.english: But place does not contribute much to calm: it is the mind that makes everything agreeable to itself. I have seen people gloomy in a cheerful and pleasant country house, I have seen people in the middle of solitude who were like busy men. So there is no reason for you to think that you are not well enough composed because you are not in Campania. But why are you not? Send your thoughts all the way here.

notes.note: The Latin has no article. The English takes the word generally (“place”), not as the particular villa just described.
notes.other_reading: But the place does not contribute much to calm

notes.note: “commendare” is to recommend or make something acceptable. The verb is subjunctive, which may carry a shade of “is the thing to” or “should”; the English gives a plain statement.
notes.other_reading: it is the mind that must commend all things to itself

notes.note: A “villa” is a country house or estate; “amoenus” is the usual word for a place with pleasant scenery.
notes.other_reading: in a bright and lovely villa

notes.note: Literally “like the occupied”: men taken up with business, Seneca’s set word for those with no leisure.
notes.other_reading: who looked like men with their hands full

notes.note: “compositus” can be “composed, in good order” in oneself or “well placed, settled” in a situation. The passage is about calm and the mind, so the English reads “composed”.
notes.other_reading: that you are not well enough placed

notes.note: The region around the Bay of Naples, where Seneca is writing from, near the villa of Vatia described in this letter.
notes.other_reading: here in Campania

notes.note: The verb “are” has nothing after it in the Latin: “But why are you not (in Campania)?” The next sentence answers it: he can be there in thought. It may also be a real question about why Lucilius has not come.
notes.other_reading: And yet why are you not here?

check.note: The Latin is general (where one is). “The place” can be read as the particular villa just described.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “But place does not contribute much to calm”, a general statement, as the general sentences that follow require; a note records the other reading.

check.note: Compositus is about the mind: composed, in good order. Next to “because you are not in Campania”, “settled” reads as settled in a place to live.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “that you are not well enough composed”. “Composed” is taken; “not well enough” is kept for parum bene, since “as you should be” is not in the Latin.

passages.latin: etiam nunc molestior est mihi sonus qui intermittitur subinde quam qui continuatur. Sed iam me sic ad omnia ista duravi ut audire vel pausarium possim voce acerbissima remigibus modos dantem. Animum enim cogo sibi intentum esse nec avocari ad externa; omnia licet foris resonent, dum intus nihil tumultus sit, dum inter se non rixentur cupiditas et timor, dum avaritia luxuriaque non dissideant nec altera alteram vexet. Nam quid prodest totius regionis silentium, si affectus fremunt?
passages.english: Besides, a sound that keeps breaking off is more of a nuisance to me than one that goes on without a break. But by now I have so hardened myself against all these things that I can listen even to a rowing-master giving the oarsmen their time in the harshest of voices. For I force my mind to be intent on itself and not to be called away to things outside. Let everything resound outside, so long as there is no uproar inside, so long as desire and fear do not brawl with each other, so long as greed and extravagance are not at odds and neither troubles the other. For what good is the silence of a whole district, if the passions are roaring?

notes.note: The section runs on from the list of noises before it. In Seneca these words often mean “furthermore” and not “even now”, and the English takes them so. The temporal sense is also possible, with “but by now” in the next sentence answering it.
notes.other_reading: Even now a sound that keeps breaking off is more of a nuisance to me

notes.note: The pausarius is the man on a galley who gives the rowers the time for the stroke. English has no exact word; “rowing-master” is used, though it may suggest a higher rank than the Latin intends.
notes.other_reading: the man who calls the stroke; the boatswain

notes.note: The same verb runs through the section before, where a voice “calls away” more than a noise does, so “called away” is kept and “distracted” is not used.
notes.other_reading: and not to be distracted by things outside

notes.note: Luxuria is the vice of lavish living and spending, set here against avaritia, the vice of getting and keeping. “Extravagance” keeps the opposition clear, though it narrows the word toward spending.
notes.other_reading: greed and luxury; greed and self-indulgence

notes.note: Regio can be a quarter of a city or a whole stretch of country. The English reads “district”.
notes.other_reading: the silence of the whole neighbourhood; of a whole region

notes.note: Affectus is the Stoic term for the passions. Fremere covers roaring, growling and a low angry murmur; the loud end is taken because it is set against silence.
notes.other_reading: if the passions are growling; if the feelings are in a roar

check.note: The English takes these words as “furthermore”. They can also be temporal, “even now”, and “but by now” in the next sentence could be read as answering them.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “Besides”. The sentence adds one more remark to the list of noises that ends the section before, which is where Seneca uses these words for “furthermore”; the temporal reading is recorded in a note.

check.note: Foris is paired with intus, outside and inside. “Out of doors” suggests the open air and blurs the plain pair.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Let everything resound outside, so long as there is no uproar inside”, so that the two plain words answer each other as foris and intus do.

passages.latin: Leve illud ingenium est nec sese adhuc reduxit introsus quod ad vocem et accidentia erigitur; habet intus aliquid sollicitudinis et habet aliquid concepti pavoris quod illum curiosum facit, ut ait Vergilius noster: et me, quem dudum non ulla iniecta movebant tela neque adverso glomerati e agmine Grai, nunc omnes terrent aurae, sonus excitat omnis suspensum et pariter comitique onerique timentem.
passages.english: It is a lightweight character, and one that has not yet withdrawn into itself, that starts up at a voice and at whatever happens. It has something of anxiety inside, and it has something of a dread that has formed in it, which makes the man watchful, as our Vergil says: “And I, who a little while ago was moved by no weapons hurled at me, nor by Greeks crowding out of the opposing ranks, am now frightened by every breeze; every sound startles me, on edge and afraid alike for my companion and for my burden.”

notes.note: “ingenium” is a person’s inborn character or temperament; the English reads “character”, keeping “mind” for animus and “nature” for natura. “Leve” is literally “light”, lacking weight and so easily moved; “lightweight” keeps the image of weight.
notes.other_reading: That is a light (unsteady, fickle) nature

notes.note: “introsus” is a spelling of introrsus, “inwards”. Literally “and has not yet led itself back inwards”; the English reads it as withdrawing into itself. The section before uses the military image of sounding the retreat, which “reduxit” may continue.
notes.other_reading: and has not yet drawn itself back inside

notes.note: “vocem” can be a voice, a cry or a spoken word. “accidentia” is things that happen, or more narrowly things that fall on the ear, that is, chance noises; the English takes the broader sense. “erigitur” is literally “is raised up”: it can mean is roused, pricks up its ears, or starts up, and the English reads “starts up”.
notes.other_reading: that pricks up its ears at a word and at every chance noise

notes.note: Literally “of conceived dread”: a dread that has formed inside, not one absorbed from outside. “pavoris” names something stronger than plain fear, and “dread” keeps it apart from the two other Latin words for frightening and fearing in the verse.
notes.other_reading: something of a fear that it has taken in

notes.note: “illum” is masculine and cannot agree with the neuter “ingenium”. The Latin slides from the character to the man who has it, or has the masculine word for mind, animus, in view, or the text is at fault. The English reads “the man” so that the shift is plain.
notes.other_reading: which makes it watchful

notes.note: “curiosum” ranges from “careful” through “inquisitive” to “nervously on the watch”. Here it is the state of attending to every sound, so the English reads “watchful”; the anxiety is already named earlier in the sentence by another word.
notes.other_reading: which makes the man inquisitive (or: prying, always on the alert)

notes.note: The lines are from Vergil’s Aeneid, book 2, about lines 726 to 729 (from memory, unchecked). Aeneas speaks as he flees burning Troy. The Latin as given has no quotation marks and runs the verse on as prose; the English uses quotation marks because “ut ait” marks the lines as quoted.
“dudum” can mean “a little while ago” or “for a long time before now”. The English takes the first, as the contrast with “now” suggests.
notes.other_reading: who for so long was moved by no weapons

notes.note: The Latin verb is a plain past and is active, with the weapons and the Greeks as its subject. The English turns it into “was moved by” to keep the sentence readable, and keeps “moved” for the image; the sense is “troubled” or “shook”.
notes.other_reading: whom no hurled weapons used to trouble

notes.note: Vergil’s line is remembered as having “ex” where this copy has “e”, and the metre needs it (from memory, unchecked); the sense is the same. The phrase is literally “Greeks massed out of the opposing column”: either Greeks gathering from the enemy line against him, or Greeks in massed enemy formation. The English takes the first.
notes.other_reading: nor by the Greeks packed together in their opposing ranks

notes.note: Literally “rouses” or “stirs up”. The English reads “startles”, which suits a man on edge.
notes.other_reading: every sound rouses

notes.note: Literally “hung up, in suspense”: anxious and uncertain. The English reads “on edge”.
notes.other_reading: in suspense

notes.note: In the Aeneid the companion is Aeneas’s small son Ascanius, walking beside him, and the burden is his old father Anchises, carried on his shoulders (from memory, unchecked). Seneca’s Latin does not name them, so the English does not either.
notes.other_reading: fearing equally for the one who walks beside and for the one who is carried

check.note: The Latin word means light in the sense of lacking weight or steadiness, easily moved. “A slight character” reads as small or insignificant, which is a different fault.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “a lightweight character”, since the Latin word means light, without weight and so easily moved, and “slight” suggested small. “Character” is kept for ingenium instead of the suggested “mind”, which this translation keeps for animus.

check.note: The first noun can be a voice, a cry or any utterance. The second is simply “things that happen”, probably incidental noises, so “chance” adds a colour the Latin word need not carry.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “at a voice and at whatever happens”, dropping “chance”, which the Latin word need not carry. The suggested “around it” is not taken because the Latin has no words for it; the narrower sense, chance noises, is recorded in the note.

check.note: The Latin is a fear conceived, one that has formed within, while “taken in” can be read as absorbed from outside or even as deceived. The noun is also stronger than plain fear, and “fear”, “frightened” and “afraid” stood for three different Latin words.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “something of a dread that has formed in it”. The Latin speaks of a dread conceived within, not absorbed from outside, and “dread” leaves “frightened” and “afraid” for the two other Latin words in the verse.

check.note: The pronoun is masculine and cannot agree with the neuter noun for character: the Latin slides from the character to the man who has it, or the text is at fault. “Him” after three uses of “it” leaves the reader with no one to refer it to.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “which makes the man watchful”, so that the reader has someone for the pronoun to point to. The Latin has only a masculine pronoun after a neuter noun, and the note records the shift and the other ways of taking it.

check.note: The Latin adjective is inquisitive, anxiously on the watch, prying into every noise. “Over-attentive” sounds like excessive politeness or diligence, and the “over-” is added.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “over-attentive” is replaced by “watchful”. “Anxiously” is not added, because anxiety is already named earlier in the same sentence by another Latin word and the adjective does not itself contain it; the note gives “inquisitive” and “always on the alert” as other readings.

check.note: The Latin is a plain past tense of continuing action (“were moving”, “used to move”). “Could” adds a notion of ability that is not there.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “could” is removed and the English now reads “was moved by no weapons”, a plain past with no idea of ability. “Moved” is kept instead of the suggested “troubled” because the Latin verb is literally “moved” and the image is kept; the note records the sense.

check.note: The sense is right, Greeks gathered in a mass out of the enemy column, but “massed from the opposing line” is not natural English and the reader has to work it out.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “nor by Greeks crowding out of the opposing ranks”, which is plainer English for the same sense. “Opposing” is kept for the Latin adjective, and the closing words of the suggestion are not taken because the Latin has nothing for them.

check.note: From memory, unchecked: Vergil’s line has “ex agmine” and the metre needs it, so “e” before a vowel is a slip in the digitised copy, with no effect on the sense. The verse is run on as prose without quotation marks, but the words introducing it mark it as quoted.
check.decided: Accepted: the English is unchanged, and the note on the phrase records that Vergil’s line is remembered as having “ex” (from memory, unchecked). The note on the source says why the English uses quotation marks.

passages.latin: Quemcumque ex istis felicibus elegeris, multa trahentibus, multa portantibus, videbis illum ‘comitique onerique timentem’. Tunc ergo te scito esse compositum cum ad te nullus clamor pertinebit, cum te nulla vox tibi excutiet, non si blandietur, non si minabitur, non si inani sono vana circumstrepet.
passages.english: Whichever you pick of those fortunate people, who drag much along and carry much, you will see him “fearing for both his companion and his load”. Know, then, that you are settled at the point when no shouting concerns you, when no voice shakes you out of yourself, not if it coaxes, not if it threatens, not if it is an empty voice making a din all round you with hollow sound.

notes.note: Felix is “lucky, prosperous”. The English reads “fortunate” and keeps “happy” for beatus, as the glossary has it. The word is ironic here.
notes.other_reading: of those prosperous people; those lucky ones

notes.note: The two verbs answer the two halves of the Vergil line: Aeneas leads a companion along by the hand and carries a load on his shoulders. “Drag” and “carry” are kept so the match shows.
notes.other_reading: who have much in tow and much on their backs

notes.note: Vergil, Aeneid 2.729 (from memory, unchecked): Aeneas afraid for the son he leads and the father he carries. The line is quoted in full in the section before, which is not among the passages given.
notes.other_reading: afraid alike for the one who walks with him and the one he bears

notes.note: Literally “put in order, set at rest”; the English reads “settled”. The Latin has “then” and “when”, with no “only”, so none is added.
notes.other_reading: that you are composed; that you are at peace

notes.note: Pertinere ad is “to reach” and also “to concern, to matter to”. The second is taken: the noise is still heard but is none of the hearer’s business, which is the letter’s point about living among noise.
notes.other_reading: when no shouting reaches you

notes.note: Literally “no voice will knock you away from yourself”. The image is kept as “shakes you out of yourself”.
notes.other_reading: when no voice robs you of yourself; makes you lose your self-possession

notes.note: Vana can be nominative, agreeing with vox (“an empty voice”), or a neuter plural object (“dins empty things around you”). The English takes it with vox.
notes.other_reading: not if it dins meaningless things around you with hollow sound

check.note: Pertinere ad can mean “concern” or “reach, get through to”. The English chooses “concerns”; “reaches you” is the other reading and sits well with the next clause about being shaken out of oneself.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “concerns”. Seneca has just said that he hears every noise and is not called away by it, so the test is that shouting does not matter to the hearer, not that it fails to arrive; “reaches you” is recorded in a note.

check.note: Found while settling: in the draft “who drag much along and carry much” followed “you pick” and could be taken with “you”. The participles belong to the fortunate people.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Whichever you pick of those fortunate people, who drag much along and carry much”, so that the clause stands next to the people it describes.

passages.latin: ‘Quid ergo? non aliquando commodius est et carere convicio?’ Fateor; itaque ego ex hoc loco migrabo. Experiri et exercere me volui: quid necesse est diutius torqueri, cum tam facile remedium Ulixes sociis etiam adversus Sirenas invenerit Vale.
passages.english: “What then? Is it not sometimes more comfortable to be without the racket as well?” I admit it; and so I shall move out of this place. I wanted to test myself and train myself. What need is there to be tormented any longer, when Ulysses found so easy a remedy for his comrades even against the Sirens? Farewell.

notes.note: The question in quotation marks is an imagined objector’s, as often in the letters; Seneca answers it with fateor, an admission.
notes.other_reading: “Well then,” you say,

notes.note: Et here is “also”: besides being able to bear the noise, to be free of it, hence “as well”. Convicium is a loud clamour and also abuse; here it is the din.
notes.other_reading: also to be free of the uproar; to be spared the abuse as well

notes.note: Commodus covers “convenient”, “comfortable” and “advantageous”. The English reads “more comfortable”.
notes.other_reading: more convenient; better

notes.note: The pronoun is the object of both verbs, so “myself” is repeated and neither verb is left hanging.
notes.other_reading: I wanted to make trial of myself and give myself practice

notes.note: Ulixes is the Latin name of Odysseus; the English gives the usual English form of the Latin name, Ulysses. The remedy is the wax with which he stopped his crew’s ears against the Sirens’ song (Odyssey 12, from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: Odysseus

notes.note: The copy has no stop between invenerit and the closing Vale. The sentence is plainly a question (“what need is there”), so the question mark in the English is supplied.

check.note: Et here is “also, as well”: the objector asks whether it is not sometimes more comfortable to be free of the noise too, besides being hardened to it. “Simply” is not in the Latin and turns the point into avoiding the noise instead.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “to be without the racket as well”. “Simply” is gone, and et keeps its sense of adding freedom from the noise to the hardening against it.

check.note: Sociis is dative, “for his comrades”. The draft’s word order could be read for a moment as if the comrades were the remedy.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “when Ulysses found so easy a remedy for his comrades even against the Sirens”, which makes plain who the remedy was for.

check.note: The Latin as given has no stop after invenerit. The sentence is a question, so a question mark has dropped out of the digitised text; the English punctuates rightly but the slip should be recorded.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps the question mark, and the note on these words now says that it is supplied because the copy has no stop there.

passages.latin: Aliquid tamen mihi illa obscuritas quod cogitarem dedit: sensi quendam ictum animi et sine metu mutationem quam insolitae rei novitas simul ac foeditas fecerat. Non de me nunc tecum loquor, qui multum ab homine tolerabili, nedum a perfecto absum, sed de illo in quem fortuna ius perdidit: huius quoque ferietur animus, mutabitur color.
passages.english: Still, that darkness gave me something to think about: I felt a kind of blow to the mind, and a change, without fear, which the newness and at the same time the foulness of an unfamiliar thing had brought about. I am not speaking to you now about myself, who am a long way from a tolerable man, let alone a perfect one, but about the man over whom Fortune has lost her authority: his mind too will be struck, his colour will change.

notes.note: The darkness is that of the road tunnel described in the section before, with its dust and torches.
notes.other_reading: that gloom

notes.note: Literally “a blow of the mind”, that is, a jolt the mind receives. The image is kept and is echoed below, where the mind “will be struck” (ferietur).
notes.other_reading: a kind of shock to the spirit; a certain mental jolt

notes.note: “A change without fear”: an alteration in him that was not fear. The Latin does not say what changed (mind, face or state), so the English leaves it open, and “change” is kept so that it answers “his colour will change” below.
notes.other_reading: an alteration of mood that was not fear

notes.note: Foeditas is foulness, ugliness, anything repulsive to the senses. “Foulness” suits the dust and murk of the tunnel.
notes.other_reading: the ugliness; the unpleasantness

notes.note: Literally “a man who can be put up with”, a passably good man. Perfecto after it is the finished, complete man, that is, the wise man.
notes.other_reading: far from a passable man, let alone a complete one

notes.note: Ius is a legal right or power over a person, and “authority” gives that sense in plain words. Fortune acts as a person here, so the word has a capital, as the glossary allows.
notes.other_reading: over whom fortune has lost its right; its jurisdiction

check.note: Ius in quem is legal power or authority over someone. “Lost her right” leaves the reader asking what the right was a right to.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “over whom Fortune has lost her authority”. Ius with in and a person is power over that person, and “authority” says so without leaving a question open.

passages.latin: Quaedam enim, mi Lucili, nulla effugere virtus potest; admonet illam natura mortalitatis suae. Itaque et vultum adducet ad tristia et inhorrescet ad subita et caligabit, si vastam altitudinem in crepidine eius constitutus despexerit: non est hoc timor, sed naturalis affectio inexpugnabilis rationi.
passages.english: For there are some things, my Lucilius, that no virtue can escape; nature reminds virtue of its own mortality. And so he will tighten his face at grim things, and shudder at sudden things, and his sight will go dim if he stands on the brink of a vast depth and looks down into it. This is not fear, but a natural feeling that reason cannot take by storm.

notes.note: Virtus is “virtue”, as in the glossary, and not only “courage”: the man in view is the perfect man of the section before, so the claim is that no degree of virtue gets a person clear of these reactions.
notes.other_reading: that no courage can escape

notes.note: Suae could strictly point back to natura, the subject, but the sense requires virtue’s own mortality: virtue is reminded that it lives in a mortal creature. The English names virtue again so that this is clear.
notes.other_reading: nature reminds it of nature’s own mortality

notes.note: The verbs have no stated subject. It is taken to be the man of the section before, over whom Fortune has lost her authority, because constitutus below is masculine and cannot go with virtus. Vultum adducere is to draw the face tight, to frown.
notes.other_reading: he will frown at sad things; it (virtue) will knit its brow at what is grim

notes.note: Caligare is to be in a mist or darkness: of the eyes, to grow dim; of the head, to turn giddy. The image of sight is kept.
notes.other_reading: he will grow dizzy

notes.latin: vastam altitudinem in crepidine eius constitutus despexerit
notes.note: Altitudo is height or depth alike; since he looks down, the English reads “depth”. Eius refers to the altitudo: he stands on its brink.
notes.other_reading: if, standing on its brink, he looks down from a vast height

notes.note: The word is affectio, not affectus, and no fault is implied, so the English reads “feeling” and not “passion”.
notes.other_reading: a natural affection; a natural state of being affected

notes.note: A siege image: a place that cannot be stormed, with reason as the one who fails to storm it. The image is kept.
notes.other_reading: unconquerable by reason; which reason cannot overcome

check.note: Virtus can be moral virtue in general or specifically courage. In a passage about flinching and fear, “no courage” is a live reading.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “no virtue”. The man in view is the perfect man of the section before, not merely a brave one, and the glossary keeps “courage” for passages that are about courage alone; “no courage” is recorded in a note.

check.note: By strict grammar suae refers to nature, the subject; by sense it refers to virtue, which lives in a mortal being. The draft’s “it” and “its own” left unclear whose mortality is meant.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “nature reminds virtue of its own mortality”, naming virtue so that the pronoun is clear. The noun “mortality” is kept as in the Latin, where the suggested “that it is mortal” would say more flatly that virtue dies.

check.note: “Its” pointed forward to “a vast depth”, which had not yet been named, so the phrase was hard to follow. “Set” is also stiff for constitutus, which is “standing”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “if he stands on the brink of a vast depth and looks down into it”, so that the depth is named before it is referred to.

passages.latin: Quintum genus est eorum quae communiter sunt; haec incipiunt ad nos pertinere; hic sunt omnia, homines, pecora, res. Sextum genus eorum quae quasi sunt, tamquam inane, tamquam tempus. Quaecumque videmus aut tangimus Plato in illis non numerat quae esse proprie putat; fluunt enim et in assidua deminutione atque adiectione sunt. Nemo nostrum idem est in senectute qui fuit iuvenis; nemo nostrum est idem mane qui fuit pridie. Corpora nostra rapiuntur fluminum more. Quidquid vides currit cum tempore; nihil ex iis quae videmus manet; ego ipse, dum loquor mutari ista, mutatus sum.
passages.english: The fifth kind is of the things that exist in the common way; these begin to concern us; here are all things: people, cattle, objects. The sixth kind is of the things that, so to speak, exist, such as the void, such as time. Whatever we see or touch, Plato does not count among the things that he thinks exist in the proper sense; for they flow, and are in constant loss and gain. None of us is the same in old age as he was when young; none of us is the same in the morning as he was the day before. Our bodies are swept along in the manner of rivers. Whatever you see runs with time; nothing of the things we see remains; I myself, while I say that these things are changing, have changed.

notes.note: This closes a list of six ways in which things are said to be, which Seneca gives as Plato’s. Genus is “kind” or “class”. “Exist” stands for esse all through, so that the argument can be followed.
notes.other_reading: The fifth class is of the things that are in the common way

notes.note: “Exist commonly”: in the ordinary, everyday sense of existing, as against existing “in the proper sense” (proprie) below. It could also be heard as “exist in common, generally”.
notes.other_reading: the things that exist in the ordinary sense; that exist generally

notes.note: After the higher kinds, these are the first that touch the world of human beings. Pertinere ad is “to concern, to have to do with”; it might also mean that these are the first to belong to the human level of reality.
notes.other_reading: with these the list begins to come to what has to do with us

notes.note: Homines is human beings of either sex, hence “people”. Pecora is strictly herd animals and here seems to stand for animals at large; res is the widest word for a thing.
notes.other_reading: human beings, animals, things

notes.note: “Exist as it were”: have a sort of existence. The Stoics classed void and time as things without body.
notes.other_reading: the things that quasi-exist; that have a kind of existence

notes.note: Literally “in constant lessening and adding”. The English reads “loss and gain”.
notes.other_reading: in constant decrease and increase; subtraction and addition

notes.note: Loquor with an accusative and infinitive: “while saying that these things change”. The present infinitive allows “change” or “are changing”.
notes.other_reading: while I speak of these things changing

check.note: Homines is human beings in general. “Men” reads as male to a reader of today.
check.decided: Accepted: the list now reads “people, cattle, objects”, since homines covers human beings of either sex.

check.note: The sense is right, but in “exist as it were, such as” the phrase “as it were” runs into “such as” and is hard to parse.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the things that, so to speak, exist, such as the void, such as time”. The qualifier is moved in front of “exist” as suggested, but “such as” is kept twice because the Latin repeats tamquam.

passages.latin: Hoc est quod ait Heraclitus: ‘in idem flumen bis descendimus et non descendimus’. Manet enim idem fluminis nomen, aqua transmissa est. Hoc in amne manifestius est quam in homine; sed nos quoque non minus velox cursus praetervehit, et ideo admiror dementiam nostram, quod tantopere amamus rem fugacissimam, corpus, timemusque ne quando moriamur, cum omne momentum mors prioris habitus sit: vis tu non timere ne semel fiat quod cotidie fit!
passages.english: This is what Heraclitus says: “Into the same river we go down twice and do not go down.” For the name of the river remains the same; the water has passed on. This is plainer in a river than in a human being; but a course no less swift carries us past too, and so I wonder at our madness, that we love so much a thing so quick to flee, the body, and fear that some day we may die, when every moment is the death of the state before it. Come, do not fear that what happens every day may happen once!

notes.latin: in idem flumen bis descendimus et non descendimus
notes.note: A saying of Heraclitus, the Greek philosopher of flux (a fragment known in Greek as well; from memory, unchecked). Bis, “twice”, may go with both verbs or only with the first, and the English leaves it placed as in the Latin.
notes.other_reading: we do and do not go down twice into the same river

notes.note: Literally “the water has been sent across, let through”: the water that was there has gone by.
notes.other_reading: the water has flowed past; has been carried through

notes.note: The Latin changes its word for the river here (amnis after flumen). Nothing turns on it, so “river” is kept.
notes.other_reading: This is plainer in a stream than in a human being

notes.note: Praetervehere is to carry past. The Latin does not say past what; the picture is of a current bearing its passengers by.
notes.other_reading: but a course no less swift sweeps us along too

notes.note: Dementia is being out of one’s mind, stronger than stultitia, which the glossary renders “folly”. The English reads “madness”.
notes.other_reading: our folly; our senselessness

notes.note: Habitus is the condition or state a thing is in. Each moment ends the state that held a moment before.
notes.other_reading: the death of our former condition

notes.note: Vis tu with an infinitive is an idiom of impatient urging, a command in the form of a question; the edition prints an exclamation mark. The English gives a brisk command, and “Come” stands for the tone, not for a Latin word.
notes.other_reading: Will you not stop fearing that what happens every day may happen once?

notes.note: “Once”, set against “every day”: the single final death against the daily ones.
notes.other_reading: may happen once and for all

check.note: The sense is right, but “carried past” leaves the reader asking past what. The Latin has the swift course as the active subject, doing the carrying.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now makes “a course no less swift” the subject of an active verb, as the Latin does. “Past” is kept because praeter means “past”, and “swept along” already stands for a different verb, rapiuntur, in the section before; the suggested wording is recorded in a note.

check.note: Found while settling: homine is a human being of either sex, and “a man” reads as male, the same point as was raised on the list in the section before.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “plainer in a river than in a human being”.

passages.latin: De homine dixi, fluvida materia et caduca et omnibus obnoxia causis: mundus quoque, aeterna res et invicta, mutatur nec idem manet. Quamvis enim omnia in sc habeat quae habuit, aliter habet quam habuit: ordinem mutat.
passages.english: I have spoken of man, matter that is flowing and perishable and at the mercy of every cause. The world too, an eternal and unconquerable thing, changes and does not remain the same. For although it has in itself all that it had, it has it otherwise than it had it: it changes its order.

notes.note: The phrase is in the ablative and is taken in apposition to homine; it could also be an ablative of description, “man, of flowing and perishable matter”. Fluvida picks up “they flow” from the earlier section; caduca is “apt to fall”, so “perishable”.
notes.other_reading: man, a thing of fluid and frail material

notes.note: Obnoxius is “liable to, exposed to, at the mercy of”. Causis is left bare: any cause at all can act on man.
notes.other_reading: exposed to every influence; liable to every accident

notes.note: Mundus is the ordered whole, world or universe. The English reads “world”.
notes.other_reading: the universe too

notes.note: Invictus is “unconquered” and by extension “unconquerable”. Beside “eternal”, and set against man who is at the mercy of every cause, the stronger sense is taken.
notes.other_reading: an eternal and unconquered thing

notes.note: The copy’s sc is a slip for se (“in itself”), and the English reads it so.

Ordo is order or arrangement. The world keeps the same contents but arranges them differently. The Latin has no “its” or “their”, so the order may be that of the contents and not of the world as a whole.
notes.other_reading: it changes the arrangement; it changes their order

check.note: “Exposed to every cause” is literal but opaque in English. The point is that anything at all can act on man and harm him.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “at the mercy of every cause”, which is what obnoxius means when a thing is liable to be acted on and harmed.

check.note: Invictus can be “unconquered” or “unconquerable”. Beside aeterna the stronger sense is a live reading.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “an eternal and unconquerable thing”. The word is set beside “eternal” and against man, whom anything can overcome, so the stronger sense fits; “unconquered” is recorded in a note.

check.note: Caduca is an adjective of disposition, liable to fall, perishable, parallel to fluvida. “Matter that perishes” turns it into an event.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “matter that is flowing and perishable and at the mercy of every cause”, three descriptions in a row as in the Latin.

passages.latin: Manent enim cuncta, non quia aeterna sunt, sed quia defenduntur cura regentis: immortalia tutore non egerent. Haec conservat artifex fragilitatem materiae vi sua vincens. Contemnamus omnia quae adeo pretiosa non sunt ut an sint omnino dubium sit.
passages.english: For all things remain, not because they are eternal, but because they are defended by the care of the one who governs them: immortal things would need no guardian. These things the craftsman preserves, overcoming the frailty of matter by his own power. Let us despise all the things that are so far from precious that it is doubtful whether they exist at all.

notes.note: Cuncta is “all things together”, the whole. Manent is the same verb as in the river passage, so “remain” is kept, though “last” would read more easily.
notes.other_reading: For the whole of things endures

notes.note: Literally “by the care of the one ruling”. This is the god of the section before, who defends from death what he could not make immortal. The Latin has no “them”.
notes.other_reading: by the care of their ruler

notes.note: Tutor is the legal guardian of a ward as well as a protector in general. “Guardian” keeps both.
notes.other_reading: would need no protector

notes.note: “These things” may be the same “all things” just mentioned, or more narrowly the things of this world. The Latin does not decide and the English leaves it open.
notes.other_reading: These things here below the craftsman preserves

notes.note: Artifex is a maker or craftsman; here it is the god as maker of the world. Vi sua is “by his own force”.
notes.other_reading: the maker; the artist, by his own strength

notes.latin: adeo pretiosa non sunt ut an sint omnino dubium sit
notes.note: Adeo non with ut is “so far from being that”. Sint is the bare verb “to be”, rendered “exist” as in the earlier sections of this letter, so the play between not being precious and perhaps not being at all is only half kept.
notes.other_reading: that are so little worth that it is in doubt whether they are at all

check.note: Found while settling: conservat is “preserves, keeps safe”. The draft’s “keeps in being” brought a word of being into a sentence that has none, in a letter whose argument turns on the verb “to be”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “These things the craftsman preserves”, so that words of being and existing appear only where the Latin has esse.

passages.latin: Noli me invitus audire, tamquam ad te iam pertineat ista sententia, et quid dicam aestima: non relinquam senectutem, si me totum mihi reservabit, totum autem ab illa parte meliore; at si coeperit concutere mentem, si partes eius convellere, si mihi non vitam reliquerit sed animam, prosiliam ex aedificio putri ac ruenti.
passages.english: Do not listen to me unwillingly, as though this pronouncement already applied to you; and weigh what I am saying. I shall not leave old age, if it keeps the whole of me for myself, the whole, that is, as regards that better part. But if it begins to shake my mind, if it begins to tear its parts loose, if it leaves me not life but breath, I shall leap out of a building that is rotten and falling down.

notes.note: Sententia is an opinion stated, and also a judge’s sentence or a vote in the senate. “Pronouncement” leaves both open; the legal colour would suit “already applied to you”.
notes.other_reading: as though this verdict already applied to you; this opinion

notes.note: The same verb returns below (reliquerit, “if it leaves”). “Leave” is used both times so the turn shows: old age will not be left unless it leaves only breath.
notes.other_reading: I shall not abandon old age; I shall not desert old age

notes.latin: totum autem ab illa parte meliore
notes.note: Ab here is “in respect of, on the side of”: whole as far as the better part goes. The better part is the mind, as against the body.
notes.other_reading: whole, I mean, in that better part of me

notes.note: The word is mens, the thinking faculty, not animus; English “mind” serves for both.
notes.other_reading: to shake the understanding; the reason

notes.note: Eius is the mind’s. Convellere is to wrench loose or tear up, so the parts may be its faculties pulled away one by one or the whole pulled apart. The verb “begins” is carried over from the clause before, as the Latin leaves coeperit to be understood.
notes.other_reading: if it begins to pull its faculties to pieces

notes.note: Anima is here the bare breath of life, set against vita, a life worth the name. The glossary allows “breath” where that is the sense.
notes.other_reading: if it leaves me not life but mere existence; not life but only a soul

notes.latin: prosiliam ex aedificio putri ac ruenti
notes.note: The body in old age is pictured as a rotten house coming down, and leaving life as jumping clear of it. The image is kept and is not explained in the text.
notes.other_reading: I shall jump clear of a building that is crumbling and collapsing

check.note: After “Do not listen” the reader could carry the “not” over to “weigh”. The Latin has a clear negative command followed by a positive one.
