check.decided: Partly accepted: a semicolon now stands before “and weigh”, so the “not” cannot carry over. “And” is kept for et, where the suggestion dropped it.

check.note: Sententia may be simply “opinion, statement” or a judge’s “sentence”. “Verdict” chooses the legal colour.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “this pronouncement”, which can be a stated view or a ruling, as sententia can. “Verdict” is recorded in a note as the other reading.

check.note: The Latin has three si clauses in a row. The draft dropped the second “if”, which weakened the build-up.
check.decided: Accepted: the second clause now reads “if it begins to tear its parts loose”, so that all three “if” clauses of the Latin stand in a row.

check.note: Ab parte is “in respect of, as regards”. “The whole on the side of that better part” is hard to understand in English.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the whole, that is, as regards that better part”, which gives the sense of ab with a part of something in plain words.

passages.latin: Iam docebo quemadmodum intellegas te non esse sapientem. Sapiens ille plenus est gaudio, hilaris et placidus, inconcussus; cum dis ex pari vivit. Nunc ipse te consule: si numquam maestus es, nulla spes animum tuum futuri exspectatione sollicitat, si per dies noctesque par et aequalis animi tenor erecti et placentis sibi est, pervenisti ad humani boni summam; sed si appetis voluptates et undique et cmnes, scito tantum tibi ex sapientia quantum ex gaudio deesse. Ad hoc cupis pervenire, sed erras, qui inter divitias illuc venturum esse te speras, inter honores, id est gaudium inter sollicitudines quaeris: ista, quae sic petis tamquam datura laetitiam ac voluptatem, causae dolorum sunt.
passages.english: I shall now show you how you may understand that you are not a wise man. The wise man is full of joy, cheerful and peaceful, unshaken; he lives with the gods as an equal. Now consult yourself: if you are never sad, if no hope makes your mind anxious with expectation of the future, if by day and by night the course of your mind, lifted up and pleased with itself, is even and level, you have reached the height of human good. But if you go after pleasures, from everywhere and all of them, know that you fall as far short of wisdom as you do of joy. This is what you long to reach, but you go wrong in hoping that you will get there among riches, among honours, that is, in looking for joy among anxieties: those things, which you go after as though they would give gladness and pleasure, are causes of pain.

notes.note: Ille marks the wise man as the well-known ideal figure, “that wise man”. The English reads “the wise man”, since “the” after “a wise man” already points back and “that” would suggest a particular person.
notes.other_reading: That wise man is full of joy

notes.note: Gaudium, “joy”, is in Stoic use the wise man’s settled gladness and is kept apart from voluptas, “pleasure”. The whole passage turns on that contrast, so “joy” and “pleasure” are held fixed.
notes.other_reading: full of gladness

notes.note: The English reads “peaceful” so as to keep “calm” for tranquillitas, as the glossary has it.
notes.other_reading: cheerful and calm; serene

notes.note: Ex pari is “on an equal footing”. The claim is strong and is not softened.
notes.other_reading: he lives on equal terms with the gods

notes.note: Consulere with a person is to ask for an opinion; ipse stresses that the asking is done by oneself.
notes.other_reading: Now question yourself; now ask your own self

notes.latin: nulla spes animum tuum futuri exspectatione sollicitat
notes.note: The Latin as given has no “if” before this clause; it rides on the one before, and the English supplies “if”. “Makes anxious” is used so that it answers sollicitudines, “anxieties”, further down.
notes.other_reading: if no hope troubles your mind with looking forward to what is to come

notes.latin: par et aequalis animi tenor erecti et placentis sibi
notes.note: Tenor is an unbroken course. Erecti is “raised, lifted up”, of a mind that is high and confident, and may also be “alert”; “upright” is avoided because in English it means honest. Placentis sibi, “pleased with itself”, is meant in a good sense here.
notes.other_reading: the even and steady tenor of a mind that is alert and content with itself

notes.note: Summa is the sum total and also the highest point; the English takes the second. Bonum is “the good” in the glossary.
notes.other_reading: the sum total of the good open to a human being

notes.note: The copy’s cmnes is a slip for omnes, and the English reads it so: pleasures from every quarter, and every one of them.
Hoc is joy, the nearest neuter noun. It could more loosely be the whole state just described.
notes.other_reading: It is this condition you long to reach

notes.note: Dolor is “pain” in the glossary. The Latin is plural, which English “pain” covers; here the pains are of mind as much as of body, so “sorrows” would also fit.
notes.other_reading: are sources of sorrows; causes of grief

check.note: Animus erectus is a mind lifted up, high and confident. “Upright” in English means morally honest, which is a different idea.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “lifted up and pleased with itself”. Erecti describes a mind raised and confident, not an honest one.

check.note: Consulere with a person is to consult, to ask for an opinion, and ipse stresses doing it oneself. “Question yourself” sounds like an interrogation.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Now consult yourself”, which is what consulere says and lets the reflexive carry the stress of ipse.

check.note: Ille points to the wise man as the known ideal figure, “that wise man”. The English drops it; the point is small.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “The wise man”. Coming straight after “a wise man”, the word “the” already points to the known figure as ille does, and “that wise man” would read as a particular person; the other reading is recorded in a note.

check.note: Summa here is the highest point or the whole. “The sum of the human good” is opaque to a reader of today.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “you have reached the height of human good”. The note records that summa can also be the sum total.

check.note: The plural “pains” is not natural English here and suggests bodily aches.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “are causes of pain”. English “pain” takes in the many pains of the Latin plural, and the note records the plural.

check.note: Found while settling: petis is the simple form of appetis, “go after”, used of pleasures earlier in the passage. The draft’s “chase” hid the echo and added a livelier picture than the Latin has.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “which you go after as though they would give gladness and pleasure”, so that the two related verbs are heard as one.

passages.latin: Hos itaque, ut ait Sallustius, ‘ventri oboedientes’ animalium loco numeremus, non hominum, quosdam vero ne animalium quidem, sed mortuorum. Vivit is qui multis usui est, vivit is qui se utitur; qui vero latitant et torpent sic in domo sunt quomodo in conditivo. Horum licet in limine ipso nomen marmori inscribas: mortem suam antecesserunt. Vale.
passages.english: So let us count these people, who are, as Sallust says, “obedient to the belly”, as animals, not as human beings, and some of them not even as animals, but as the dead. The one who is of use to many is alive; the one who makes use of himself is alive. But those who lie hidden and inert are in their house as they would be in a tomb. You may carve their name on marble at the very threshold: they have gone ahead of their own death. Farewell.

notes.note: From the opening of Sallust’s Catiline, where cattle are said to be made by nature bent downward and obedient to the belly (from memory, unchecked). Seneca fits the words to human beings.
notes.other_reading: slaves to the belly

notes.note: Literally “count in the place of animals”, that is, class them as animals. Animal is any living creature with breath.
notes.other_reading: let us reckon them among the living creatures, not among human beings

notes.note: Since animal is “a living creature”, the step from animals to the dead is sharper in Latin: not even among the living. “Animals” is kept so the word matches the clause before.
notes.other_reading: not even among living creatures, but among the dead

notes.latin: Vivit is qui multis usui est
notes.note: Vivit stands first in each clause and carries the weight. “Is alive” is used for it because the next step in the passage is to the dead.
notes.other_reading: He lives who is of use to many

notes.note: Se is ablative with utitur: “who uses himself”, puts himself to use. It answers “is of use to many” just before; the sense may be nearer “has command of himself”.
notes.other_reading: the one who has the use of himself; who is of use to himself

notes.note: Two verbs: to keep in hiding and to be torpid, without movement or activity. “Inert” is used for the second because it covers both idleness and the stillness of the dead that the tomb calls for.
notes.other_reading: those who skulk and are sluggish; who lie hidden and numb

notes.note: Conditivum is a burial place, a tomb. It is a rare word and the sense is given from memory, unchecked.
notes.other_reading: as in a burial vault

notes.latin: in limine ipso nomen marmori inscribas
notes.note: The picture is an epitaph cut over the house door, as over a tomb. Licet is “you may”, a permission, not a command.
notes.other_reading: You may as well inscribe their name on a marble slab right at the doorway

notes.note: Literally “they have gone before their own death”: they are dead before it arrives.
notes.other_reading: they have died before their death; they have anticipated their own death

check.latin: Vivit is qui multis usui est, vivit is qui se utitur
check.note: “He lives who” is an archaic word order. Plain English can keep the weight on being alive without it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “The one who is of use to many is alive; the one who makes use of himself is alive.” “Is alive” stands for vivit and ends each clause, so the weight stays on it and the contrast with the dead is plain.

check.note: “Count in the place of” is not natural English for loco numerare, which is to count as or class with. “Men” for hominum also blurs the contrast between animals and human beings.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “as animals, not as human beings, and some of them not even as animals, but as the dead”, and “these men” has become “these people” to match.

check.note: Torpere is to be sluggish, inert, doing nothing. “Numb” suggests loss of feeling and not idleness, which is the point here, set against being of use.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “those who lie hidden and inert”. “Inert” gives the idleness asked for and also the stillness of a body in a tomb, which “sluggish” would lose.

passages.latin: Desinamus quod voluimus velle. Ego certe id ago senex eadem velim quae puer volui. In hoc unum eunt dies, in hoc noctes, hoc opus meum est, haec cogitatio, imponere veteribus malis finem. Id ago ut mihi instar totius vitae dies sit; nec mehercules tamquam ultimum rapio, sed sic illum aspicio tamquam esse vel ultimus possit.
passages.english: Let us stop wanting what we have wanted. I at any rate am working at this: that as an old man I should not want the same things I wanted as a boy. To this one thing my days go, to this my nights; this is my work, this my thought: to put an end to old ills. I am working at this, that a day should be to me the equal of a whole life; and, by Hercules, I do not snatch at it as though it were my last, but I look at it as though it could even be my last.

notes.latin: id ago senex eadem velim quae puer volui
notes.note: The Latin as given has no “ne” or “ut” after “id ago” and does not construe; taken loosely it would say the opposite of the first sentence. From memory, unchecked: editions print a supplied “ne” before “senex”, which the digitised copy seems to have lost. The English translates with the negative.
notes.other_reading: I at any rate am working at this: that as an old man I should want the same things I wanted as a boy.

notes.note: “voluimus” is a perfect and can be a simple past or a past reaching into the present. The English takes it as reaching into the present.
notes.other_reading: Let us stop wanting what we once wanted.

notes.note: “mala” can be evils, ills or faults, and the Latin has no possessive here. The English reads “old ills”, a wide word that can cover his own long-standing failings; “fault” is kept in this project for “vitium”.
notes.other_reading: to put an end to my old faults

notes.note: “instar” with a genitive means the equivalent or image of something. The English reads “the equal of”.
notes.other_reading: that a day should count for me as a whole life

notes.note: A common Roman oath by Hercules, the hero made a god. It is kept as an oath.
notes.other_reading: and indeed

notes.note: Literally “to snatch” or “to seize”: the picture is of grabbing greedily at a day because it is the last. The image is kept.
notes.other_reading: I do not seize it in haste as though it were my last

notes.note: “vel” here strengthens: “even” or “actually”. It could also be taken more weakly as “perhaps”.
notes.other_reading: as though it could perhaps be my last

check.latin: id ago senex eadem velim quae puer volui
check.note: The Latin as given has no negative and no conjunction after “id ago”, yet the English says “should not want”. A “ne” has probably dropped out, but the gap must be declared; square brackets round “not” are suggested.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English keeps “should not want” without square brackets, because the published text is plain prose and the gap is declared in the note. The note now says outright that the Latin as given does not construe, that “ne” is supplied (from memory, unchecked) and what the words would say without it.

check.note: “malis” may be evils in general or, more likely here, his own long-standing faults or ills. “Old evils” reads as evils in the world at large and is heavy.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “old ills”, which is lighter and fits a man speaking of his own long-standing wants. “Faults” is not used because the Latin word is the wide “mala” and “fault” is kept for “vitium”, and no possessive is added because the Latin has none. The narrower reading is in the note.

passages.latin: Hoc animo tibi hanc epistulam scribo, tamquam me cum maxime scribentem mors evocatura sit; paratus exire sum, et ideo fruar vita quia quam diu futurum hoc sit non nimis pendeo. Ante senectutem curavi ut bene viverem, in senectute ut bene moriar; bene autem mori est libenter mori.
passages.english: I write you this letter in this frame of mind: as though death were going to call me away at the very moment of writing. I am ready to go, and I shall enjoy life for this reason, that I do not hang in too much suspense over how long this will last. Before old age I took care to live well; in old age I take care to die well. And to die well is to die willingly.

notes.note: “animus” is “mind” in the glossary; here it is a state of mind or mood. The English reads “frame of mind”, which keeps the glossary word.
notes.other_reading: In this spirit I write you this letter

notes.note: An idiom meaning “just now, at this very moment”, here with “scribentem”.
notes.other_reading: while I am actually writing

notes.note: “evocare” is to call out or summon, used of calling someone out of a place or calling up soldiers, and “exire”, “to go out”, answers it in the next clause. “Call out” and “go out” mean something else in English today, so the English reads “call away” and “ready to go”, and the shared “out” of the two Latin verbs is lost.
notes.other_reading: as though death were going to call me out at the very moment of writing. I am ready to go out

notes.note: The form can be future indicative or present subjunctive. The English takes it as future.
notes.other_reading: and so let me enjoy life, because

notes.note: “pendeo” is literally “to hang”: to be in suspense about something or to depend on it. The hanging image is kept, and “not too much” stays as the Latin has it, not “not at all”.
notes.other_reading: because I am not too anxious about how long this will be

notes.note: The Latin has one verb, the past “curavi”, for both halves, but the present subjunctive “moriar” shows that the care for dying well is going on now. The English supplies a present verb in the second half.
notes.other_reading: in old age, to die well

notes.note: “libenter” runs from “willingly” to “gladly”. The English reads “willingly” because the next section turns on willing and unwilling.
notes.other_reading: to die well is to die gladly

check.note: “With this mind” is not natural English today for a state of mind.
check.decided: Accepted: the sentence now begins with the letter and reads “in this frame of mind”, which is natural English and still keeps “mind” for “animus”.

check.note: In English today “call someone out” means to challenge or criticise, while the Latin has death summoning him away. “Go out” for “exire” has a similar problem, though the echo between the two verbs is worth keeping.
check.decided: Accepted: death now calls him “away” and he is “ready to go”. The echo of “out” in the two Latin verbs cannot be kept without the wrong modern sense, so it is explained in the note.

check.note: The Latin shifts tense: “viverem” follows a past “curavi”, but “moriar” is in present sequence, so the care is present. The English ellipsis put the second half in the past too.
check.decided: Accepted: the second half now has its own present verb, “take care to die well”, so that the care for living well is past and the care for dying well is present, as the tenses of the Latin show.

passages.latin: Da operam ne quid umquam invitus facias: quidquid necesse futurum est repugnanti, id volenti necessitas non est. Ita dico: qui imperia libens excipit partem acerbissimam servitutis effugit, facere quod nolit; non qui iussus aliquid facit miser est, sed qui invitus facit. Itaque sic animum componamus ut quidquid res exiget, id velimus, et in primis ut finem nostri sine tristitia cogitemus.
passages.english: Take care that you never do anything unwillingly. Whatever is going to be necessary for one who resists is no necessity for one who wants it. This is what I mean: the man who takes orders willingly escapes the bitterest part of slavery: doing what he does not want to do. It is not the man who does something under orders who is wretched, but the man who does it unwillingly. So let us set our mind in order so that we want whatever the situation demands, and above all so that we think of our own end without sadness.

notes.note: The section runs on one family of ideas: “invitus”, “volenti”, “libens”, “nolit”, “velimus”. The English uses “unwillingly” and “willingly” for “invitus” and “libens”, and “want” for every form of “velle” and “nolle”.
notes.other_reading: Take care that you never do anything against your will

notes.latin: quidquid necesse futurum est repugnanti, id volenti necessitas non est
notes.note: The point rests on “necesse” and “necessitas”, so “necessary” and “necessity” are kept. “necessitas” can also mean compulsion, which is the sharper sense here.
notes.other_reading: whatever will be forced on one who fights it is no compulsion for one who is willing

notes.note: As with “libenter” in the section before, this can be “willingly” or “gladly”. “Willingly” holds the contrast with “invitus”.
notes.other_reading: the man who takes orders gladly

notes.note: “miser” is wretched, pitiable or unhappy. The English reads “wretched”.
notes.other_reading: it is not the man who does something under orders who is unhappy

notes.note: “componere” is to put together, arrange or settle. The English reads “set in order”.
notes.other_reading: So let us compose our mind in such a way that

notes.note: “res” is very wide: the situation, circumstances, the matter in hand. The verb is future; English uses the present after “whatever”.
notes.other_reading: whatever circumstances will require

notes.note: The phrase means the end of the speakers themselves, that is, death. “End” is kept and “death” is not written, since the Latin avoids the word here.
notes.other_reading: that we think of our death without sadness

notes.note: “tristitia” is sadness or gloom. The English reads “sadness”.
notes.other_reading: without gloom

check.note: The draft’s wording for setting the mind “in such order that” is accurate but stiff. A small point of style only.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the clause now reads “in order so that”, which is plainer than the draft. The suggested wording, with “so order” before its object, is not taken because that word order is not the English of today.

passages.latin: Ante ad mortem quam ad vitam praeparandi sumus. Satis instructa vita est, sed nos in instrumenta eius avidi sumus; deesse aliquid nobis videtur et semper videbitur: ut satis vixerimus, nec anni nec dies faciunt sed animus. Vixi, Lucili carissime, quantum satis erat; mortem plenus exspecto. Vale.
passages.english: We must be prepared for death before we are prepared for life. Life is equipped well enough, but we are greedy for its equipment; something seems to us to be lacking, and always will seem so. That we have lived enough is brought about neither by years nor by days but by the mind. I have lived, dearest Lucilius, as much as was enough; having had my fill, I await death. Farewell.

notes.latin: Ante ad mortem quam ad vitam
notes.note: “ante” with “quam” can mean earlier in time or first in importance. The English reads “before”, which leaves both open.
notes.other_reading: We need preparing for death more than for life.

notes.latin: instructa vita est, sed nos in instrumenta eius avidi sumus
notes.note: The Latin plays on “instructa” and “instrumenta”, the same root, kept as “equipped” and “equipment”. “instrumenta” are the supplies and furnishings of life.
notes.other_reading: Life is well enough provided for, but we are greedy for its provisions

notes.note: “satis” comes three times in the section and is “enough” each time. The clause is the object of “faciunt”: what makes it the case that a life has been long enough.
notes.other_reading: Whether we have lived enough depends not on years or days but on the mind.

notes.note: “Mind”, as in the glossary. The sense is the state of the mind, its sense of having had enough.
notes.other_reading: but by the spirit

notes.note: A perfect, which can carry the tone of an epitaph: a life summed up as complete.
notes.other_reading: My living is done

notes.note: Literally “full”, as of someone who has eaten enough; it describes Seneca, not death. The English uses the idiom of having had one’s fill; the Latin does not say full of what.
notes.other_reading: full, I await death

check.note: In the draft the word “full” comes last and hangs oddly, so that a reader may take it with “death”. “plenus” describes Seneca as sated.
check.decided: Accepted: the clause now opens with the idiom of having had one’s fill and ends with awaiting death, so the fullness plainly belongs to Seneca. The bare “full” is given in the note as the more literal reading.

passages.latin: Mentiuntur qui sibi obstare ad studia liberalia turbam negotiorum videri volunt: simulant occupationes et augent et ipsi se occupant. Vaco, Lucili, vaco, et ubicumque sum, ibi meus sum. Rebus enim me non trado sed commodo, nec consector perdendi temporis causas; et quocumque constiti loco, ibi cogitationes meas tracto et aliquid in animo salutare converso.
passages.english: They are lying, those who want it to look as though a crowd of business stands between them and liberal studies: they feign occupations, they make more of them, and they are the ones who keep themselves occupied. I have time, Lucilius, I have time, and wherever I am, there I am my own. For I do not hand myself over to affairs but lend myself to them, and I do not go hunting for reasons to waste time. And in whatever place I have come to a stop, there I work over my own thoughts and turn something wholesome over in my mind.

notes.note: Literally “studies fit for a free person”, the higher studies, here chiefly philosophy. The traditional “liberal studies” is kept.
notes.other_reading: serious study

notes.latin: simulant occupationes et augent et ipsi se occupant
notes.note: The Latin plays on “occupationes” and “occupant”, kept as “occupations” and “occupied”. “augent” can mean that they add to their occupations or that they make them out to be bigger than they are; “make more of them” can be heard both ways.
notes.other_reading: they pretend to be busy, they exaggerate it, and they make themselves busy

notes.note: “vaco” is to be unoccupied, to have time, to be at leisure: the opposite of “occupant” just before. The English reads “have time” so that the contrast with being occupied is heard; “free” would suggest liberty in general.
notes.other_reading: I am free, Lucilius, I am free

notes.note: Literally “to be one’s own”: to belong to oneself, to be one’s own master. It is kept close.
notes.other_reading: there I am my own master

notes.note: “trado” is to hand over outright, “commodo” to lend something that stays one’s own. The contrast of handing over and lending is kept.
notes.other_reading: I do not surrender myself to affairs but put myself at their disposal

notes.note: “causa” here can be a reason, an occasion or a pretext for wasting time. The English reads “reasons”.
notes.other_reading: I do not chase after occasions for wasting time

notes.note: This is the first-person verb “converso”, “to keep turning over”, not a participle of “converto”. “salutare” is the adjective “wholesome, health-giving” going with “aliquid”.
notes.other_reading: and keep some health-giving thought revolving in my mind

check.note: “vaco” is the opposite of “occupant” just before: to have leisure, to have time. “Free” reads as liberty in general and loses the contrast with being occupied.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “have time” twice in place of “am free”, so that the word answers “occupied” in the sentence before. The other rendering is in the note.

check.note: “augent” can mean that they add to their occupations or that they exaggerate them, which sits well after “simulant”. “Multiply” chooses the first.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “they make more of them”, which can be heard as adding to them or as making them out to be bigger, as the Latin can. The note sets out both readings.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft put a semicolon where the Latin has “sed”, the same weakening that is corrected in the next section, and it began the last sentence without the “et” of the Latin.
check.decided: Accepted: the two verbs are now joined with “but”, and the last sentence begins with “And”, so that both connecting words of the Latin are in the English.

passages.latin: Cum me amicis dedi, non tamen mihi abduco nec cum illis moror quibus me tempus aliquod congregavit aut causa ex officio nata civili, sed cum optimo quoque sum; ad illos, in quocumque loco, in quocumque saeculo fuerunt, animum meum mitto.
passages.english: When I have given myself to my friends, I still do not take myself away from myself, and I do not linger with those with whom some occasion has thrown me together, or some cause arising from a citizen’s duty, but I am with all the best men. To them, in whatever place, in whatever age they lived, I send my mind.

notes.note: The verb has no object in the Latin as given; the object has to be carried over from the clause before, and the English supplies it.
notes.other_reading: I do not, for all that, withdraw from myself

notes.note: Literally “some time”: some occasion or passing circumstance. The English reads “occasion”.
notes.other_reading: those with whom some circumstance of the moment has brought me together

notes.note: “causa” may be a reason in general or a legal case; “officium civile” is the duty owed as a citizen, which could include appearing for someone in court. The general “cause” is kept.
notes.other_reading: or a case arising from public duty

notes.note: An idiom, “with each best one”, meaning all the best. The Latin is masculine and the English reads “men”; from what follows, they are the great minds of any place and age.
notes.other_reading: I am with the best people, every one of them

notes.note: Literally “they were”. The English reads “lived”, which is what being in a place and an age amounts to.
notes.other_reading: in whatever place, in whatever age they were

notes.note: “animus” is “mind”, as in the glossary. The image is of sending the mind off to keep company with them.
notes.other_reading: I send my thoughts to them

check.note: The “sed” that answers the clause about not lingering is replaced by a semicolon, so the contrast between those whom chance has brought together and the best is weakened.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “but” before the clause about the best men, so the contrast of the Latin is stated.

passages.latin: Itaque assidue cogitemus de nostra quam omnium quos diligimus mortalitate. Tunc ego debui dicere, ‘minor est Serenus meus: quid ad rem pertinet? post me mori debet, sed ante me potest’. Quia non feci, imparatum subito fortuna percussit. Nunc cogito omnia et mortalia esse et incerta lege mortalia; hodie fieri potest quidquid umquam potest.
passages.english: So let us think constantly about our own mortality as much as that of all those we love. I ought to have said then: “My Serenus is younger than I am: what has that to do with it? He ought to die after me, but he can die before me.” Because I did not, Fortune struck me suddenly and unprepared. Now I think this: all things are mortal, and mortal under an uncertain law. Whatever can happen at any time can happen today.

notes.note: As given, “quam” has nothing to answer it. From memory, unchecked: editions print a supplied “tam” before “de nostra”, which the digitised copy seems to have lost. The English translates the pair as “as much as”.
notes.other_reading: let us think constantly about our own mortality and that of all those we love

notes.note: “minor” here is “younger” in years, as the section before makes clear. English needs a second term of comparison to complete it.
notes.other_reading: My Serenus is the younger man

notes.note: Annaeus Serenus, the close friend whose death Seneca has just said he mourned beyond measure. From memory, unchecked: he is the man to whom several of Seneca’s shorter works are addressed.
notes.other_reading: my dear Serenus

notes.note: “debet” against “potest”: what ought to happen in the due order of things against what can happen. “Ought” and “can” are kept.
notes.other_reading: he is due to die after me, but he may die before me

notes.note: The object of the blow is understood with “imparatum”. “Fortune” has a capital because it is shown dealing a blow; “subito” is the adverb “suddenly”.
notes.other_reading: fortune struck a sudden blow and found me unprepared

notes.note: Literally “mortal by an uncertain law”: there is a law, but the order and the day it sets are not fixed, so that the young may die before the old. “lex” can also mean the terms of an agreement.
notes.other_reading: and mortal on uncertain terms

notes.note: The same verb as “cogitemus” in the first sentence, so “think” is kept in both places.
notes.other_reading: Now I reflect that

check.latin: de nostra quam omnium quos diligimus mortalitate
check.note: The Latin as given has “quam” with nothing for it to answer; a “tam” before “de nostra” seems to have dropped out. The English supplies “as much as”, and the gap should be declared.
check.decided: Accepted: the English stands, and the note says that “tam” is supplied (from memory, unchecked) and gives the sense without it.

check.note: The Latin says there is a law, but an uncertain one. “By no fixed law” can be read as “by no law at all”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “mortal under an uncertain law”, which keeps the law and its uncertainty as the Latin has them. The note gives “on uncertain terms” as the other reading.

passages.latin: In locum stili sermo successit, ex quo eam partem ad te perferam quae in lite est. Te arbitrum addiximus. Plus negotii habes quam existimas: triplex causa est. Dicunt, ut scis, Stoici nostri duo esse in rerum natura ex quibus omnia fiant, causam et materiam. Materia iacet iners, res ad omnia parata, cessatura si nemo moveat; causa autem, id est ratio, materiam format et quocumque vult versat, ex illa varia opera producit. Esse ergo debet unde fiat aliquid, deinde a quo fiat: hoc causa est, illud materia.
passages.english: Talk took the place of the pen, and from it I shall bring you the part that is in dispute. We have named you as arbiter. You have more work on your hands than you think: the case is threefold. Our Stoics say, as you know, that there are two things in the nature of things from which everything is made: cause and matter. Matter lies inert, a thing ready for everything, which will stay idle if no one moves it. But cause, that is, reason, shapes matter and turns it wherever it wishes, and brings varied works out of it. So there must be that from which a thing is made, and then that by which it is made: the second is cause, the first is matter.

notes.note: “stilus” is the writing tool, so writing; “sermo” is conversation. The friends who broke in on his writing in the section before stayed to talk.
notes.other_reading: Conversation took the place of writing

notes.note: Legal language: “addicere” is the formal word for assigning a judge or arbiter to a case. “lis”, just before, is a lawsuit as well as a dispute.
notes.other_reading: We have assigned the case to you as judge.

notes.note: A play on “causa”, which is both a case at law and a cause: “case” here and “cause” in every sentence that follows are one Latin word, the very word in dispute. The English takes the legal sense, which fits “arbiter”; three views of cause are in dispute, the Stoic, Aristotle’s and Plato’s.
notes.other_reading: the cause is threefold

notes.note: Seneca counts himself one of the school, and the possessive is kept.
notes.other_reading: we Stoics

notes.note: The phrase means in the whole of what exists, in the universe; it does not mean “inevitably”, as the English phrase can. The glossary rendering “the nature of things” is kept so that the phrase reads the same wherever it comes.
notes.other_reading: that there are two things in nature from which everything is made

notes.note: “fieri” is both “to be made” and “to come to be”. “Made” is used throughout, because the cause is later called the thing that makes.
notes.other_reading: from which all things come to be

notes.note: Literally “going to be idle”: matter will do nothing unless something moves it.
notes.other_reading: which will lie unused if no one sets it in motion

notes.note: “ratio” is “reason”, as in the glossary: the Stoic active principle, which the letter later equates with god.
notes.other_reading: that is, the rational principle

notes.note: “hoc” points to the nearer item (that by which a thing is made) and “illud” to the farther (that from which). The English reads “the second” and “the first” to keep the Latin order.
notes.other_reading: the latter is cause, the former matter

check.note: “causa” is the lawsuit here but is also the very word under dispute, translated “cause” in every sentence that follows. The English takes the legal sense, so the play is lost and the other reading, “cause is threefold”, is hidden.
check.decided: Accepted: “the case is threefold” stands, since the legal sense follows from the dispute and the arbiter just named. The note now says that “case” here and “cause” afterwards are one Latin word and gives the other reading.

check.note: “autem” marks the contrast with inert matter and is dropped.
check.decided: Accepted: the sentence now begins “But cause, that is, reason”, so the contrast with inert matter is stated. “But” does the work of the suggested “on the other hand” in fewer words.

check.note: “Two things in the nature of things” is clumsy, and “in the nature of things” suggests “inevitably” in English. The phrase means in nature, in the universe.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “all things” becomes “everything”, which removes one of the three uses of “things”, but “the nature of things” stays because the glossary settles that rendering for “rerum natura”. A new note says that the phrase means in the whole of what exists and gives “in nature” as the other reading.

passages.latin: Quaeris quod sit propositum deo? bonitas. Ita certe Plato ait: 'quae deo faciendi mundum fuit causa? bonus est; bono nulla cuiusquam boni invidia est; fecit itaque quam optimum potuit'. Fer ergo iudex sententiam et pronuntia quis tibi videatur verisimillimum dicere, non quis verissimum dicat; id enim tam supra nos est quam ipsa veritas.
passages.english: You ask what god’s purpose is? Goodness. So, at any rate, Plato says: “What cause did god have for making the world? He is good; one who is good begrudges nothing good; so he made it as good as he could.” Give your verdict, then, as judge, and declare who seems to you to say what is most like the truth, not who says what is truest; for that is as far above us as truth itself.

notes.note: “propositum” is literally “what is set before one”: an aim or purpose. In the section before it is the last in a list of causes, that for the sake of which god made the world, so the one word “purpose” is kept.
notes.other_reading: You ask what aim god set before himself?

notes.note: “certe” can limit (“at any rate”, “at least”) or affirm (“certainly”). The English takes it as limiting: this is Plato’s answer, which Lucilius is then asked to weigh as judge. The passage paraphrased is in Plato’s Timaeus, about 29d to 30a (from memory, unchecked); Seneca gives it in Latin of his own.
notes.other_reading: That is certainly what Plato says

notes.note: “causa” is the key term of this letter, which compares philosophers’ accounts of the causes of things, so “cause” is kept although “reason” would be more natural English here. “Reason” is also kept for ratio in this translation.
notes.other_reading: What was god’s reason for making the world?

notes.latin: bono nulla cuiusquam boni invidia est
notes.note: “invidia” is both envy and grudging; here it is grudging, the step that leads to the world being made as good as it could be. “cuiusquam boni” can mean “of any good thing” or “of anyone’s good”; the English takes the first, which also fits the Greek as remembered (from memory, unchecked). “Good” is repeated because the argument runs on the repeated word.
notes.other_reading: one who is good begrudges no one his good (or, with envy: one who is good envies nothing good)

notes.note: “optimum” is the superlative of “bonus” and describes the world: literally “he made it as very good as he could”. The English reads “as good as he could”, which keeps the word “good” running through the argument and speaks of the quality of the world, not of the effort.
notes.other_reading: so he made it the best that he could

notes.note: The phrase is the courtroom idiom for giving a vote or verdict, and “iudex” stands in apposition to the “you” of the command: “you, as judge”. Lucilius is asked to judge between the accounts of cause that Seneca has set out. “Verdict” is used, leaving “judgment” for iudicium.
notes.other_reading: So cast your vote as the judge in the case

notes.latin: quis tibi videatur verisimillimum dicere, non quis verissimum dicat
notes.note: The Latin plays on “verisimillimum” (most like the truth, most probable) and “verissimum” (truest), followed by “veritas” (truth). The word “truth” is kept visible in all three so the play can be followed, at the cost of the more usual “most probable”.
notes.other_reading: who seems to you to say what is most probable, not who says what is most true

notes.latin: id enim tam supra nos est quam ipsa veritas
notes.note: “id” (“that”) most naturally points back to deciding who says what is truest; it could also mean simply “what is truest”. The English leaves it as “that”, as open as the Latin.
notes.other_reading: for to settle that is as far beyond us as truth itself is

check.note: The word can be restrictive (“at least”, “at any rate”) or affirming (“certainly”), and the English chooses the restrictive sense. The choice should be confirmed.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps “at any rate”, as suggested. Seneca is reporting Plato’s answer and goes on to ask Lucilius to judge which account is most like the truth, so the limiting sense fits; the note gives “certainly” as the other reading.

check.latin: bono nulla cuiusquam boni invidia est
check.note: The Latin noun with a genitive of the thing is grudging: the good one begrudges no good thing, which is the step that leads to the world being made as good as possible. “Has no envy of anything good” reads as “does not covet good things”, and the choice between “any good thing” and “anyone’s good” was made without saying so.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “one who is good begrudges nothing good”. The Latin word covers both envy and grudging, and grudging is what leads to the next step, that god made the world as good as he could. The note records the other way of taking the two words in the middle, “begrudges no one his good”.

check.note: The adjective agrees with the world understood: he made the world as good as he could. “Made it the best he could” can be heard as “did his best at making it”, which is about the effort, not the quality of the world.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “so he made it as good as he could”. The Latin adjective describes the world, not the effort, and the new wording also keeps “good” running through the whole argument.

passages.latin: Sed nos nunc primam et generalem quaerimus causam. Haec simplex esse debet; nam et materia simplex est. Quaerimus quid sit causa? ratio scilicet faciens, id est deus; ista enim quaecumque rettulistis non sunt multae et singulae causae, sed ex una pendent, ex ea quae facit.
passages.english: But what we are asking about now is the first and general cause. This must be simple, for matter too is simple. Are we asking what the cause is? Reason that makes, of course: that is, god. For all those things you people have listed are not many separate causes, but hang from one, from the one that makes.

notes.note: “generalis” is “general” in the sense of belonging to the whole kind, the cause over all the particular ones. “General” is kept.
notes.other_reading: the first and universal cause

notes.note: “simplex” is simple in the sense of single and uncompounded, against the crowd of causes just listed.
notes.other_reading: This must be single; for matter too is single.

notes.note: This can be a question or a statement, and “quid sit causa” can be “what the cause is” (which thing it is) or “what cause is” (a definition). The English follows the copy’s question mark and takes the first sense, because the answer names the one cause that is sought. “quaerimus” is also the verb of the first sentence, so “asking” is used in both places.
notes.other_reading: We are asking what cause is.

notes.note: Literally “reason making”, reason as the thing that makes; “scilicet” is “plainly, of course”. The verb “make” is kept to match “the one that makes” at the end.
notes.other_reading: Plainly, creative reason

notes.note: The verb is second person plural: not Lucilius but those who put forward the many causes, Plato and Aristotle with their followers, or the friends arguing their side. The English reads “you people” so that the plural can be heard.
notes.other_reading: all those things you have listed

notes.note: Literally “many and single”: many causes each standing on its own. The English reads “many separate causes”.
notes.other_reading: are not many causes, each one independent

check.note: The same verb “quaerimus” was “looking for” in the first sentence and is “asking” here, so the echo is lost. Also “quid sit causa” may be “what cause is”, a definition, as well as “what the cause is”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: one verb is now used in both places, but it is “asking” and not the suggested “looking for”, since “asking about” a cause and “asking what the cause is” are both natural English. “What the cause is” stands because the answer names the one cause that is sought, and the definitional reading is recorded in the note.

check.note: The verb is plural: Seneca turns to those who list many causes, not to Lucilius, and English “you” hides this.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “you people”, so that the plural of the Latin can be heard and the words are not taken as said to Lucilius.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft put a semicolon where the Latin has “sed”, the same weakening that is corrected at Ep. 62.2.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “but hang from one”, so the contrast between the many causes and the one is stated.

passages.latin: Numquam me caro ista compellet ad metum, numquam ad indignam bono simulationem; numquam in honorem huius corpusculi mentiar. Cum visum erit, distraham cum illo societatem; et nunc tamen, dum haeremus, non erimus aequis partibus socii: animus ad se omne ius ducet. Contemptus corporis sui certa libertas est.
passages.english: Never will this flesh drive me to fear, never to a pretence unworthy of a good man; never will I lie to do honour to this little body. When it seems right, I shall break up my partnership with it. And even now, while we are stuck together, we shall still not be partners on equal shares: the mind will take all the rights for itself. Contempt for one’s own body is sure freedom.

notes.note: “ista” is a slighting demonstrative pointing at his own flesh. The English reads “this flesh”, which makes plain whose flesh it is but loses some of the scorn.
notes.other_reading: Never will that flesh drive me to fear

notes.note: “bono” is taken as masculine, the person who is good, not the abstract good. “simulatio” is pretence or putting on a false front.
notes.other_reading: to a hypocrisy unworthy of what is good

notes.note: A diminutive of “corpus”, used with contempt: “little body”, “poor body”.
notes.other_reading: this puny body

notes.note: Literally “when it shall have seemed good”. The Latin does not say to whom, and the English leaves it impersonal. It looks forward to leaving the body by death.
notes.other_reading: When I see fit

notes.note: “societas” is a partnership in the legal and business sense, and “distrahere” is the word for dissolving one. “socii aequis partibus” and “ius” carry the same legal image on.
notes.other_reading: I shall dissolve my association with it

notes.note: Literally “to stick” or “to be fastened”: mind and body fixed together. “Stuck” is used because “cling” would suggest fondness, against the contempt of the passage.
notes.other_reading: while we cling together

notes.latin: animus ad se omne ius ducet
notes.note: “animus” is “mind”, as in the glossary, though here it is set against the body. “ius” is legal right, here the rights of a partner in the joint concern, and “ducet” is literally “will draw”; “omne” is kept as “all”.
notes.other_reading: the mind will claim all the authority for itself

notes.note: “certa” is sure, assured, not in doubt.
notes.other_reading: is a sure way to freedom

check.note: “ista” here is dismissive and points at his own flesh. “That flesh” sounds like someone else’s or like flesh mentioned at a distance.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “this flesh”, which can only be his own. The suggested possessive is not added because the Latin has none; the scorn of “ista” is recorded in the note.

check.note: “haeremus” is being stuck or fastened together. “Cling” adds a note of attachment that goes against the contempt of the passage.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “stuck together” in place of “cling together”, so that no fondness is suggested.

check.latin: animus ad se omne ius ducet
check.note: “Take every right to itself” is literal but unclear. In the partnership image “omne ius” is the whole legal authority over the joint concern.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the mind will take all the rights for itself”, which is clearer and follows on from partners with equal shares. “Rights” is kept and “authority” is not used, because “ius” is the legal right of a partner; “authority” is given in the note.

passages.latin: Quem in hoc mundo locum deus obtinet, hunc in homine animus; quod est illic materia, id in nobis corpus est. Serviant ergo deteriora melioribus; fortes simus adversus fortuita; non contremescamus iniurias, non vulnera, non vincula, non egestatem. Mors quid est? aut finis aut transitus. Nec desinere timeo — idem est enim quod non coepisse —, nec transire, quia nusquam tam anguste ero. Vale.
passages.english: The place that god holds in this world, the mind holds in a human being; what matter is there, the body is in us. So let the worse serve the better. Let us be brave against the things of chance; let us not tremble at wrongs, at wounds, at chains, at want. What is death? Either an end or a crossing. I am not afraid of ceasing, for it is the same as not having begun; nor of crossing over, because nowhere shall I be so cramped. Farewell.

notes.note: “Mind” is kept, as in the glossary, because the comparison is with god as the reason that rules matter. The end of the section, on crossing over at death, would also bear “soul”.
notes.other_reading: the soul holds in a human being

notes.note: “mundus” is the world as the whole universe; “illic”, “there”, in the next clause points back to it.
notes.other_reading: in this universe

notes.note: Neuter plurals: “the worse things” and “the better things”, that is, body and matter under mind and god. “serviant” is the word for serving as a slave.
notes.other_reading: So let the lower be slaves to the higher

notes.note: The Latin has an echo of sound between “fortes” and “fortuita” that English loses. “fortuita” are things that happen by chance.
notes.other_reading: let us be brave against whatever fortune sends

notes.note: “iniuria” is a wrong done to a person, an injury or an insult. The English reads “wrongs”.
notes.other_reading: let us not tremble at injuries

notes.note: A passing across to somewhere else. “Crossing” and “crossing over” are used for “transitus” and “transire” so that the pair shows.
notes.other_reading: Either an end or a passage.

notes.note: The Latin has an adverb, “so narrowly”: nowhere will be as tight a lodging as the body is now. The Latin leaves “as here” unsaid and so does the English.
notes.other_reading: because nowhere shall I be in such narrow quarters as I am now

passages.latin: Hoc primo die quaesitum est, quomodo possint paria bona esse, si triplex eorum condicio est. Quaedam, ut nostris videtur, prima bona sunt, tamquam gaudium, pax, salus patriae; quaedam secunda, in materia infelici expressa, tamquam tormentorum patientia et in morbo gravi temperantia. Illa bona derecto optabimus nobis, haec, si necesse erit. Sunt adhuc tertia, tamquam modestus incessus et compositus ac probus vultus et conveniens prudenti viro gestus.
passages.english: On the first day this was the question asked: how can goods be equal, if their condition is threefold? Some, as our people think, are first goods, such as joy, peace, the safety of one’s country. Some are second goods, shaped in unlucky material, such as endurance of torture and self-control in a serious illness. The former goods we shall wish for ourselves outright, the latter if it proves necessary. There are also third goods, such as a restrained way of walking, a composed and decent expression, and gestures that suit a man of good sense.

notes.note: Impersonal passive: the Latin does not say who asked. “Hoc” points forward to the question. The first day is the first of the few days Seneca has just said he spent with Claranus.
notes.other_reading: This is what was inquired into on the first day

notes.note: “Bona” is read as the subject and “paria” as what is said of it: how goods can be equal. “Bona” is the Stoic term, rendered “goods” throughout the passage.
notes.other_reading: how there can be equal goods

notes.note: “Condicio” ranges over condition, situation, status and the terms on which a thing exists. The English keeps the neutral “condition”, because the passage is asking whether the three kinds differ in worth at all.
notes.other_reading: if their standing is of three kinds

notes.note: “Nostris” is “to our people”, meaning the Stoics, the school Seneca follows. The English keeps the Latin’s plain wording and leaves the explanation to this note.
notes.other_reading: as the Stoic school holds

notes.note: “Prima”, “secunda”, “tertia” are kept as “first”, “second”, “third” so the three classes stay visible. The Latin leaves open whether this is an order of rank or only of listing, and the question of the section turns on exactly that.
notes.other_reading: goods of the first rank, or primary goods

notes.note: In Stoic usage “gaudium” is the settled joy of the wise mind, kept apart from “voluptas” (pleasure). “Joy” keeps that distinction.
notes.other_reading: gladness

notes.note: “Expressa” is a craftsman’s word: pressed out, moulded, as a figure in wax or clay, and “materia” is the stuff worked on. The English keeps that image. “Infelici” is “unlucky” rather than “unhappy”, so that “happy” stays free for “beatus”. The phrase can also be read without the image, as goods that show themselves in bad circumstances.
notes.other_reading: shown in wretched circumstances

notes.note: The virtue of moderation or restraint. In the setting of an illness the English reads “self-control”.
notes.other_reading: moderation, or temperance, in a serious illness

notes.note: The Latin uses plain pointers here, “illa” (those, the ones named earlier) and “haec” (these, the ones just named), not the labels “prima” and “secunda”. “The former” and “the latter” keep them as pointers and keep the reference clear.
notes.other_reading: Those goods, and then: these

notes.note: Adverb: straight, directly. It is set against “si necesse erit”, so the English reads “outright”, that is, without a condition. It can also be taken as “directly, for their own sake”, a slightly different claim. Some editions print “directo”, with the same sense (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: directly, for their own sake

notes.note: “Optare” is to wish for, to choose, and also to pray for. The English keeps the plainer “wish for”.
notes.other_reading: pray for

notes.note: “Adhuc” here means “besides, in addition”, a use found in the Latin of Seneca’s time, not “up to now”.
notes.other_reading: There are still third ones

notes.note: “Modestus” is measured, kept within bounds, as well as unassuming. “Incessus” is a person’s manner of walking, not a walk taken.
notes.other_reading: a measured gait

notes.note: “Vultus” is the look on the face rather than the face itself. “Compositus” is set in order, settled; “probus” is upright or decent in a broad sense, not only truthful.
notes.other_reading: a composed and honest face

notes.note: “Prudens” is not “sapiens”. “The wise man” is kept for “sapiens”, and the English reads “a man of good sense” here.
notes.other_reading: a prudent man, or a wise man

notes.note: “Gestus” covers the carriage of the body in general and, more narrowly, the movements of hands and body. Walk and expression have just been named, so the English takes the narrower sense. The Latin is singular, used collectively.
notes.other_reading: a bearing that suits a man of good sense

check.note: “Condicio” is a neutral word: condition, situation, the terms on which a thing exists. “Standing” reads it as rank and so sharpens the puzzle a little beyond the Latin.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “if their condition is threefold”. The Latin word does not itself say rank, and the passage is asking whether the three kinds differ in worth, so the neutral word is kept and “standing” is recorded in the note.

check.note: The Latin says only “as our people think”. “School” is an explanation folded into the text, and “holds” is a shade firmer than “videtur”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “as our people think”. That the people meant are the Stoics is said in the note, not in the text.

check.note: “Unhappy material” is not clear English of today: “infelici” means unfortunate or wretched. “Expressa” is also open: moulded in a craftsman’s material, or brought out and shown.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “shaped in unlucky material”. “Unhappy” is given up, since it is unclear and collides with “happy” for “beatus”, but “shaped” stays because “expressa” with “materia” is a craftsman’s image and the image is to be kept. “Worked out” would lose it, and the reading without the image is given in the note.

check.latin: Illa bona derecto optabimus nobis, haec, si necesse erit
check.note: The Latin has plain pointers, “illa bona” and “haec” (those goods, these), not the labels “prima” and “secunda”, which the English reuses. “Optabimus” can also mean “pray for”, and the suggestion has “directly” for “derecto”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the sentence now begins “The former goods” and continues with “the latter”, so the pointers are back and the labels are not repeated. “Outright” stays for “derecto”, because the word is set against “if it proves necessary” and so means without a condition. “Directly” and “pray for” are recorded in notes.

check.note: In English of today “a modest walk” reads as a short stroll. The Latin means a restrained, well-governed manner of walking.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a restrained way of walking”. “Incessus” is how a person walks, and “modestus” is kept within measure.

check.note: “Vultus” is the look on the face rather than the face itself, and “probus” is decent or upright more broadly than “honest”. “An honest face” suggests looking trustworthy, which is narrower than the Latin.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “a composed and decent expression”. “Expression” and “decent” are taken from the suggestion. “Composed” stays, because “compositus” means set in order and “calm” is this translation’s word for “tranquillitas”.

check.note: “Gestus” can be general bearing or, more narrowly, gesture, the movements of hands and body. Gait and expression have already been named, so the third item may be gesture specifically. “Of good sense” for “prudenti” is acceptable.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “gestures that suit a man of good sense”. With walk and expression already named, the narrower sense gives three distinct examples, where “bearing” would overlap the first two. The broader reading is kept in the note, and “a man of good sense” stands.

passages.latin: Mortalia minuuntur cadunt, deteruntur crescunt, exhauriuntur implentur; itaque illis in tam incerta sorte inaequalitas est: divinorum una natura est. Ratio autem nihil aliud est quam in corpus humanum pars divini spiritus mersa; si ratio divina est, nullum autem bonum sine ratione est, bonum omne divinum est. Nullum porro inter divina discrimen est; ergo nec inter bona. Paria itaque sunt et gaudium et fortis atque obstinata tormentorum perpessio; in utroque enim eadem est animi magnitudo, in altero remissa et laxa, in altero pugnat et intenta.
passages.english: Mortal things dwindle and fall, are worn away and grow, are drained and filled; and so, in a lot so uncertain, there is inequality among them. Divine things have one nature. Now reason is nothing other than a part of the divine breath sunk into a human body. If reason is divine, and no good is without reason, then every good is divine. Further, there is no difference between divine things; so there is none between goods either. So joy and the brave, unyielding endurance of torture are equal; for in both there is the same greatness of mind, in the one slackened and loose, in the other fighting and taut.

notes.note: The other two pairs are opposites (worn away and grow, drained and filled), but “dwindle” and “fall” both point down, so the first pair is odd and the first verb may be corrupt in the transmitted text. The English translates what is given. From memory, unchecked: whether editors read something else here is not known.
notes.other_reading: Mortal things rise and fall

notes.latin: illis in tam incerta sorte inaequalitas est
notes.note: “sors” is a lot or allotted condition. The Latin says “in” so uncertain a lot, not “because of” it, and the English keeps that.
notes.other_reading: and so, their condition being so unsure, they are unequal

notes.note: “spiritus” is breath, the Stoic warm breath that runs through all things; “spirit” would be the other word. “Breath” keeps it physical. “mersa” is “plunged” or “sunk”.
notes.other_reading: a part of the divine spirit plunged into a human body

notes.note: “bonum” is “the good”, “a good”, as in the glossary. The argument is a syllogism, and “good”, “reason” and “divine” are kept fixed through it.
notes.other_reading: everything good is divine

notes.note: “gaudium” is joy, the wise man’s settled gladness, which the Stoics keep apart from “voluptas”, pleasure.
notes.other_reading: So gladness and

notes.note: Here in a good sense: firm, resolved, not giving way.
notes.other_reading: the brave and stubborn endurance of torture

notes.note: The glossary allows “spirit” for “animus” where the sense is courage. “Mind” is kept here because the same greatness is said to be present in joy as well as in endurance, and because “spiritus” stands a few lines above, so that “spirit” would blur which Latin word is meant.
notes.other_reading: the same greatness of spirit

notes.note: An image of tension, as in a string or a muscle: slack in joy, stretched tight (“intenta”) under torture. It is kept with “slackened and loose” and “taut”.
notes.other_reading: in the one relaxed and at ease

notes.note: As given, a finite verb (“it fights”) is joined to an adjective (“taut”), which breaks the match with the two adjectives before. From memory, unchecked: editions read “pugnax”, “given to fighting”, and the copy has a slip of one letter. The English reads the adjective, as “fighting”.
notes.other_reading: in the other it fights and is taut

check.note: The Latin as given joins a finite verb, “pugnat”, to an adjective, “intenta”, and breaks the parallel with “remissa et laxa”; “pugnat” is probably a slip for “pugnax”. The English follows the slip and smooths it over.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “in the other fighting and taut”, two describing words to match “slackened and loose”, on the reading “pugnax” (from memory, unchecked). “Fighting” is used and not “combative” so that the plain verb of the Latin is still heard; the note says that the Latin as given reads “pugnat”.

check.note: The other two pairs are opposites, but both verbs of the first pair point downward, so the first verb may be corrupt. The English renders the Latin as given and needs no change.
check.decided: Accepted: the English stands, and the note says that the first pair is not a pair of opposites and that the first verb may be corrupt.

check.note: “animus” is “mind” elsewhere in these passages but “spirit” here, in the paragraph where “spiritus” is “breath”, so a reader cannot tell which Latin word lies behind “spirit”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “greatness of mind”. The glossary would allow “spirit” for courage, but this greatness is said to be in joy as well as in endurance, and “spiritus” stands close by.

passages.latin: Distingue, mi Lucili, ista, et intelleges esse in iis aliquid optandum. Tormenta abesse a me velim; sed si sustinenda fuerint, ut me in illis fortiter, honeste, animose geram optabo. Quidni ego malim non incidere bellum? sed si inciderit, ut vulnera, ut famem et omnia quae bellorum necessitas affert generose feram optabo. Ton sum tam demens ut aegrotare cupiam; sed si aegrotandum fuerit, ut nihil intemperanter, nihil effeminate faciam optabo. Ita non incommoda optabilia sunt, sed virtus qua perferuntur incommoda.
passages.english: Draw distinctions among these things, my Lucilius, and you will understand that there is something in them to be wished for. I would want torture to be far from me; but if it has to be endured, I shall wish to carry myself in it bravely, honourably, with spirit. Why would I not prefer that war not break out? But if it does break out, I shall wish to bear wounds, to bear hunger and everything that the necessity of war brings, nobly. I am not so mad as to desire to be ill; but if I have to be ill, I shall wish to do nothing without self-control, nothing womanish. So it is not the hardships that are to be wished for, but the virtue by which the hardships are borne.

notes.note: “Make a distinction”: separate the hardship from the way it is borne. “ista” are the things Lucilius listed in the section before (being tortured bravely, being ill patiently).
notes.other_reading: Take these things apart, my Lucilius

notes.note: The argument turns on “optare” (“optandum”, “optabo” three times, “optabilia”): to wish for, to pray for, to choose. “Wish” is used every time. The usual philosophical word would be “desirable”, and the question in the section before ties it to prayers and vows.
notes.other_reading: that there is something in them to be desired

notes.note: A different verb from “optare”, so it has a different English word, “want”. The subjunctive is polite: “would want”.
notes.other_reading: I should like torture to be far from me

notes.note: The adverb of “honestum”, “what is honourable” in the glossary. “animose”, next to it, is “with spirit, with courage”.
notes.other_reading: bravely, nobly, with courage

notes.note: “bellum” is taken as the subject of “incidere”: that war should not befall or break out. It could also be read loosely as “not to fall into war”, though that would normally need “in”.
notes.other_reading: Why would I not prefer not to fall into a war?

notes.note: Literally “like one of good birth”: nobly, with a high spirit.
notes.other_reading: I shall wish to bear them like a man of breeding

notes.note: “Ton” is not a Latin word; it is a slip in the digitised copy for “Non”, and the English reads “Non sum”.
Literally “in a womanish way”, the Roman term of blame for softness in bearing pain. The literal word is kept.
notes.other_reading: nothing unmanly

notes.note: “incommoda” are disadvantages or discomforts, the Stoic word for things that are unwelcome but are not evils. The English reads “hardships”, which may be a little strong but fits torture, war and illness.
notes.other_reading: So it is not the inconveniences that are to be wished for

check.note: “Ton” is not a Latin word and is plainly a slip for “Non”. The English reads it rightly, and the point is recorded only so that the slip is on file.
check.decided: Accepted: the English stands, reading “Non” as the sense requires, and the note keeps the slip on record.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft wrote “unmanly” for a word that means “in a womanish way”, which softens the Roman term of blame.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “nothing womanish”, the literal sense, and “unmanly” is given in the note as the other reading.

passages.latin: ‘Et quando’ inquis ‘tibi proderit istud quod in exitu discis, aut in quam rem?’ In hanc, ut exeam melior. Non est tamen quod existimes ullam aetatem aptiorem esse ad bonam mentem quam quae se multis experimentis, longa ac frequenti rerum paenitentia domuit, quae ad salutaria mitigatis affectibus venit. Hoc est huius boni tempus: quisquis senex ad sapientiam pervenit, annis pervenit. Vale.
passages.english: “And when,” you say, “will what you are learning on your way out be of use to you, or for what purpose?” For this one: so that I may go out better. But you have no reason to think that any age is better suited to a good mind than the age that has tamed itself by many experiences, by long and frequent regret over what it has done, and has come, with its passions softened, to what heals. This is the time for this good: whoever has reached wisdom as an old man has reached it by his years. Farewell.

notes.note: “Exitus” is a going out, and so also the end of life. The plain image of leaving is kept because the answer picks it up with “exeam”.
notes.other_reading: what you are learning at the end of your life

notes.note: The Latin has only “better”, with no noun, and the English keeps it bare. “Go out” answers “on your way out” in the question.
notes.other_reading: so as to depart a better man

notes.note: “Bona mens” is Seneca’s set phrase for a mind in good order, close to wisdom. The English reads “a good mind” so that “this good” (“huius boni”) two sentences later can be heard to point back to it. The word here is “mens”, not “animus”.
notes.other_reading: a sound mind

notes.note: “Experimenta” are things tried: tests, and the experience gained from them. The English reads “experiences” because “trials” today suggests ordeals, which is darker than the Latin.
notes.other_reading: by many trials

notes.note: “Rerum” is a bare “of things”: regret for things done or chosen, or a wider dissatisfaction with how things are. The English narrows it to “what it has done”, since “regret for things” says little in English.
notes.other_reading: by long and frequent dissatisfaction with things

notes.note: “Tamed” continues an image from the section before, where the same root is used of the vices of youth.
notes.other_reading: has subdued itself

notes.note: Neuter plural, “things that bring health”. It can mean remedies in the medical sense or more generally what is good for one. “What heals” keeps the medical colour without naming medicines.
notes.other_reading: has come to what is good for it

notes.note: “Mitigare” is to make mild or soft. “Softened” is used and not “calmed” so that “calm” stays free for “tranquillitas”, as in the glossary.
notes.other_reading: with its passions calmed

notes.note: “Annis” is read as the means: his years are what brought him there. “Pervenit” is spelled the same in the present and the perfect, and the English takes both verbs as perfect.
notes.other_reading: whoever reaches wisdom as an old man reaches it through the years

check.note: The Latin “this good” points back to the good mind named a sentence earlier. With “sound mind” there and “this good” here, the reader cannot hear the link.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a good mind” and then “this good”, so that the second can be heard pointing back to the first, as it does in the Latin.

check.note: The Latin word means things tried, tests, experience gained by trying. “Trials” is likely to be heard today as ordeals, which is narrower and darker.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “by many experiences”. That removes the hint of ordeals in “trials” and keeps the Latin’s “many”, which “much experience” would lose. The sense of things tried is recorded in the note.

check.note: “Regret for things” is literal but hardly says anything in English. The Latin “of things” is the object of the regret and is left general.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “by long and frequent regret over what it has done”, since “regret for things” says almost nothing in English. The Latin word is the general “things”, and the note records the wider reading.

check.note: The Latin word means things that bring health or safety, in effect remedies. “Wholesome” today suggests clean and decent more than healing.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “to what heals”, because the Latin word means things that bring health, and “wholesome” today suggests decency more than healing.

check.note: The Latin has only “better”. “Man” is added: harmless, but not in the Latin.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “go out better”, with no “man”, because the Latin has only the one word “better”.

check.note: The verb can be present or perfect, and the English silently takes it as perfect. “By his years” adds “his” and is not quite clear, since the Latin means by means of the years.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the note now records that the verb can be present as well as perfect and gives the present reading. The English still reads “has reached it by his years”, because “through the years” would be heard as “as time went by”, while the Latin makes the years the means. English needs “his” or “the” here, and “his” is the clearer.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “with its passions calmed”, but the glossary keeps “calm” for tranquillitas, and the Latin participle means made mild or soft.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “with its passions softened”, which is closer to the Latin word and leaves “calm” for the one Latin word the glossary gives it to.

passages.latin: Scopulum esse illum putamus dementissimi: portus est, aliquando petendus, numquam recusandus, in quem si quis intra primos annos delatus est, non magis queri debet quam qui cito navigavit. Alium enim, ut scis, venti segnes ludunt ac detinent et tranquillitatis lentissimae taedio lassant, alium pertinax flatus celerrime perfert.
passages.english: We think that end is a rock, utter madmen that we are: it is a harbour, sometimes to be steered for, never to be refused, and if anyone has been carried into it within his first years, he should no more complain than a man who has made a quick voyage. For, as you know, sluggish winds toy with one man and hold him back and tire him out with the tedium of a very slow calm, while a persistent breeze carries another through very quickly.

notes.note: “Illum” points back to a masculine noun meaning “end” at the close of the section before, where it stands for death. “End” is supplied so that the sentence can stand alone.
notes.other_reading: that one is a rock

notes.note: A superlative, “most mad”, attached to the subject of “think”. The English gives it as an aside.
notes.other_reading: in utter madness

notes.note: “Aliquando” can be “sometimes” (on some occasions one should steer for it) or “at some time, one day”. The contrast with “never” and the letter’s subject, leaving life by choice, point to “sometimes”.
notes.other_reading: one day to be steered for

notes.note: Literally “within the first years”. It can mean the first years of life or, in the image, the first years of the voyage. The English keeps it literal, and “his” leans towards life.
notes.other_reading: in the first years of the voyage

notes.note: “Ludere” is to play with or make sport of someone, and also to cheat. The winds are taken as toying with the sailor.
notes.other_reading: mock one man

notes.note: “Tranquillitas” here is a literal calm at sea, not calm of mind; the glossary word “calm” fits both. “Lentissimae” is a superlative of “slow, dragging”, given as “very slow”, since “sluggish” already stands for “segnes” in the same sentence.
notes.other_reading: with the boredom of the most sluggish of calms

notes.note: “Flatus” is a blowing, a different word from the “venti” that hold the first sailor back, so the English reads “breeze”. “Pertinax” is holding on, persistent, sometimes stubborn: here a wind that does not drop.
notes.other_reading: an unrelenting blast

check.note: The Latin has only “that one”, and “end” is supplied from the section before. The supplement is correct and needed; the point is listed only so that it is known to be a supplement, with the advice to keep it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps “that end”, as advised, because without the supplied noun the section cannot stand alone. The note says that “end” is supplied.

check.note: The Latin word can mean “sometimes” or “at some time, one day”, and the English takes the first. “To be made for” is also awkward English.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “sometimes to be steered for, never to be refused”. “Sometimes” stays because it is set against “never” and the letter is about choosing when to leave life. “One day” is given in the note.

check.note: The Latin word is boredom or disgust, not weariness, and “wear out with the weariness” makes a repetition the Latin does not have. “The slowest calm” reads oddly; the superlative is “very” elsewhere in the passage, and the adjective means sluggish, dragging.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “tire him out with the tedium of a very slow calm”, which removes the doubled “wear” and “weariness” and gives the superlative as “very”. “Slow” is used and not “sluggish” because “sluggish” already stands for a different Latin word, said of the winds, in the same sentence.

check.note: The Latin has one word for the slack winds and another, a blowing or blast, for the one that drives the ship, but the English has “wind” for both. “Unrelenting” is harsher than the Latin, where this wind is the helpful one.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “a persistent breeze”, so that the helpful wind has its own word, as in the Latin, and loses the harsh colour of “unrelenting”. “Persistent” is used and not “steady” because the glossary keeps “steadiness” for constantia.

passages.latin: Idem evenire nobis puta: alios vita velocissime adduxit quo veniendum erat etiam cunctantibus, alios maceravit et coxit. Quae, ut scis, non semper retinenda est; non enim vivere bonum est, sed bene vivere. Itaque sapiens vivet quantum debet, non quantum potest.
passages.english: Consider that the same happens to us: life has brought some very quickly to the place that even those who hang back had to come to, and others it has soaked and stewed. Life, as you know, is not always to be held on to. For it is not living that is a good, but living well. So the wise man will live as long as he ought, not as long as he can.

notes.note: An imperative, “think” or “suppose”. It applies the image of the voyage to human lives.
notes.other_reading: Suppose the same happens

notes.note: The Latin is impersonal: “where there had to be a coming, even for those who hang back”. The English takes it as a general remark about everyone who delays. It can also be read of the same people who were brought quickly.
notes.other_reading: to the place they had to come to even if they hung back

notes.note: Both verbs are kitchen words (to soften by soaking, to cook) and both are also used of wearing down and tormenting. The English keeps the kitchen image, with “stewed” for its hint of slow suffering. The contrast with “very quickly” shows a long, slow process.
notes.other_reading: others it has worn down and tormented

notes.note: The relative picks up “vita”. The English begins a new sentence and repeats “life” for clarity.
notes.other_reading: which, as you know, is not always to be held on to

notes.latin: non enim vivere bonum est, sed bene vivere
notes.note: “Bonum” is the Stoic term, the good, and “bene” (well) plays on it. The English reads “a good”, not the glossary’s “the good”, because the word is a predicate here: living is not one of the goods.
