notes.other_reading: for the good is not living, but living well

notes.note: “Quantum” is “as much as”. Of a life it comes to “as long as”, though the Latin does not mention time.
notes.other_reading: as much as he ought, not as much as he can

check.note: Both verbs have a kitchen sense (soak, cook) and a common figurative sense (wear down, torment). “Steeped and cooked” gives only the kitchen sense and will puzzle a reader; the image should stay but the sense must come through.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “soaked and stewed”. Both are still kitchen words, as in the Latin, and “stewed” lets an English reader hear slow suffering as well. The note gives the plain sense.

check.note: The Latin is impersonal: the place that had to be reached, even by those who hang back. The draft’s “they” ties the hanging back to the people brought quickly, and can be misread as “brought them even if they hung back”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “to the place that even those who hang back had to come to”. The Latin is impersonal and general, and the draft’s “they” tied the hanging back to the people who were brought quickly. That other reading is kept in the note.

passages.latin: Citius mori aut tardius ad rem non pertinet, bene mori aut male ad rem pertinet; bene autem mori est effugere male vivendi periculum. Itaque effeminatissimam vocem illius Rhodii existimo, qui cum in caveam coniectus esset a tyranno et tamquam ferum aliquod animal aleretur, suadenti cuidam ut abstineret cibo, 'omnia' inquit 'homini, dum vivit, speranda sunt'.
passages.english: To die sooner or later does not matter; to die well or badly does matter. And to die well is to escape the danger of living badly. So I consider most unmanly the saying of that man of Rhodes who, when he had been thrown into a cage by a tyrant and was being fed like some wild animal, said to someone who advised him to refuse food: “A human being should hope for everything while he lives.”

notes.note: “Tardius” is “more slowly” or “later”. Paired with “citius” it means the timing of death, not how long the dying takes.
notes.other_reading: To die more quickly or more slowly

notes.note: An idiom, literally “does not bear on the matter”, that is, makes no difference. The phrase is repeated in the positive, so the English uses “does not matter” and then “does matter”.
notes.other_reading: is not to the point

notes.note: “Periculum” is danger or risk. “Male vivere” answers “bene mori” and could mean living wretchedly as well as living wrongly. “Badly” is kept to hold the pairing.
notes.other_reading: the risk of living in misery

notes.note: Literally “most effeminate” or “most womanish”, a superlative of a word that reproaches softness in a man. “Unmanly” is the plainer word today. “Vox” is a thing said, an utterance.
notes.other_reading: the most womanish of utterances

notes.note: “Illius” points to the man as one the reader is expected to know, and the English gives it as “that”. From memory, unchecked: this is Telesphorus of Rhodes, mutilated and caged by King Lysimachus, whose story Seneca also tells in On Anger.
notes.other_reading: of that famous man of Rhodes

notes.note: Literally “to abstain from food”. The adviser is recommending that he starve himself to death. “Refuse food” says as much without adding the word death, which the Latin does not have.
notes.other_reading: to starve himself

notes.note: “Homo” is a human being, not a male, and it stands against the wild animal the speaker was being fed like. “He” in “while he lives” follows the Latin singular.
notes.other_reading: A man should hope for everything while he lives.

notes.note: The form says what is to be done: “everything is to be hoped for”. It can also be heard more weakly as “may be hoped for”. The English takes the stronger sense, a rule of conduct, which is what Seneca calls unmanly.
notes.other_reading: A human being may hope for everything while he lives.

check.note: The form says what is to be done or ought to be done. “May hope” turns the saying into permission or possibility, which is weaker; the Rhodian is stating a rule for conduct, and that is what Seneca attacks.
check.decided: Accepted: the saying now reads “A human being should hope for everything while he lives.” The Latin form says what is to be done, so “may” was too weak. The weaker reading is kept in the note.

check.note: The Latin word is a human being, not a male. Coming straight after “unmanly”, “a man” makes an echo the Latin does not have and hides the contrast with being kept like a wild animal.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a human being”. The Latin word is not the word for a male, and this sets the speaker against the wild animal he was being fed like and removes the false echo of “unmanly”.

check.note: The Latin pointing word marks the man as that known Rhodian, but in the draft “that” belongs to the saying and the pointing is lost. “The Rhodian” may also be unclear to a reader of today; the name belongs in a note.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the saying of that man of Rhodes”, so the pointing word falls on the man and not on the saying. “Famous” is not added, because the Latin has only “that”. The name, from memory, is in the note.

check.note: The Latin is to abstain from food, here plainly to starve himself to death; “go without food” is weaker and could mean missing a meal. The verb is to advise or recommend, and “urging” is a little stronger.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “to someone who advised him to refuse food”. The Latin verb is to advise, and “refuse food” makes plain that deliberate starving is meant.

check.note: In today’s English “to the point” means relevant to what is being discussed, while the Latin means that the thing makes no difference. The repetition of the phrase is rightly kept.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “does not matter” and then “does matter”, one phrase used twice as in the Latin. “To the point” in today’s English is about relevance to a discussion, while the Latin says the thing makes no difference.

passages.latin: Quotiens quid fugiendum sit aut quid petendum voles scire, ad summum bonum, propositum totius vitae tuae, respice. Illi enim consentire debet quidquid agimus: non disponet singula, nisi cui iam vitae suae summa proposita est. Nemo, quamvis paratos habeat colores, similitudinem reddet, nisi iam constat quid velit pingere. Ideo peccamus quia de partibus vitae omnes deliberamus, de tota nemo deliberat.
passages.english: Whenever you want to know what is to be avoided or what is to be aimed at, look to the highest good, the purpose set before your whole life. For whatever we do ought to agree with it: no one will put the particulars in order unless he already has the whole of his life set before him. No one, though he has his colours ready, will produce a likeness unless it is already settled what he wants to paint. The reason we go wrong is that we all deliberate about the parts of life, and no one deliberates about the whole.

notes.latin: quid fugiendum sit aut quid petendum
notes.note: The verb petere comes back in the next section for the archer’s target and the sailor’s harbour. “Aim at” is used here and there so that the link shows.
notes.other_reading: what is to be fled or what is to be sought

notes.note: Propositum is literally “the thing set before”, and the same word returns as a verb in “proposita est”. The English reads “the purpose set before” here and “set before him” there, so that the echo can be heard.
notes.other_reading: the purpose of your whole life

notes.note: Summa can be the whole or sum of a thing, or its chief point, and it echoes summum bonum (the highest good). The English takes “the whole of his life”, set against the particulars and preparing the parts and whole at the end, though the Latin word there (tota) is a different one.
notes.other_reading: unless the chief end of his life is already set before him

notes.note: The Latin has no stated subject: literally “he will not arrange the particulars, except one for whom”. The English supplies “no one … unless”.
notes.other_reading: only a man who already has the whole of his life before him will arrange the particulars

notes.note: Quamvis can be a plain “although” or a matter of degree, “however ready”. The English takes the plain sense.
notes.other_reading: however ready he has his colours

notes.latin: nisi iam constat quid velit pingere
notes.note: Constat is impersonal, “it is settled”. It could be settled for the painter himself or simply settled; the impersonal form is kept.
notes.other_reading: unless he is already clear what he wants to paint

notes.note: Peccare ranges from making a mistake to doing wrong. “Go wrong” covers both.
notes.other_reading: This is why we make mistakes

check.note: The Latin uses one word twice, propositum in the first sentence and proposita est here. The draft gave “purpose” and then “set before him”, so the echo that ties the two sentences together was lost.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the purpose set before your whole life” and “set before him”, so the same words return. The suggested “aim” is not used because “aim at” already stands for another Latin verb (petere) in this section and the next.

check.note: “The sum of his life” sounds like a total. Summa is the whole or the main point of a life, set against the particulars and echoing the highest good.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the whole of his life”. Summa is set against singula, the particulars, and a note gives the other sense, “the chief end”.

check.note: “The single things” is awkward English; singula are the particular matters, the details, set against the whole.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the particulars”, which is what singula means when it is set against the whole.

check.note: The word order of “however ready he has his colours” copies the Latin and is hard to read. Quamvis here is simply “although”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “though he has his colours ready”. A note records the other sense of quamvis, “however ready”.

passages.latin: Scire debet quid petat ille qui sagittam vult mittere, et tunc derigere ac moderari manu telum: errant consilia nostra, quia non habent quo derigantur; ignoranti quem portum petat nullus suus ventus est. Necesse est multum in vita nostra casus possit, quia vivimus casu.
passages.english: The man who wants to shoot an arrow must know what he is aiming at, and then direct and guide the shaft with his hand: our plans go astray because they have nothing to be directed at; no wind is favourable to one who does not know what harbour he is aiming for. Chance is bound to have great power in our life, because we live by chance.

notes.note: The same verb as “petendum” in the section before and “quem portum petat” below. “Aim at” and “aim for” are kept so that the three uses read as one thought.
notes.other_reading: what he is seeking

notes.note: Telum is any missile or weapon; here it is the arrow, so the English has “shaft”. Derigere returns as “derigantur”, and “direct” is kept for both.
notes.other_reading: to point and control the weapon with his hand

notes.note: Errare is both to wander and to miss, so the plans stray like badly aimed arrows. Consilia can be plans, decisions or pieces of advice; the letter began from a request for advice, but here the word is general.
notes.other_reading: our counsels wander

notes.note: Literally “no wind is his own”. A wind that is “one’s own” is an idiom for a favourable wind, and the English gives the sense with “favourable”.
notes.other_reading: no wind is his own wind

notes.note: Casus is “chance” in both halves of the sentence, and one word is kept. The ablative could also be heard as “at random”.
notes.other_reading: because we live at random

check.latin: Necesse est multum in vita nostra casus possit
check.note: “Must” can be read as a guess (“surely it must”). The Latin states a necessity: it cannot be otherwise.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Chance is bound to have great power”. Necesse est says that it cannot be otherwise, and “must” could be taken as a guess.

check.note: The Latin runs the archer and the plans together in one sentence, so that the second reads as the application of the first. The full stop in the draft loosened that link.
check.decided: Accepted: the colon and the semicolon of the Latin are restored, so the archer, the plans and the harbour stand in one sentence. The harbour clause now reads “no wind is favourable to one who does not know what harbour he is aiming for”, so that no “for” after the semicolon can be taken as “because”.

passages.latin: Socrates, qui totam philosophiam revocavit ad mores et hanc summam dixit esse sapientiam, bona malaque distinguere, 'sequere' inquit 'illos, si quid apud te habeo auctoritatis, ut sis beatus, et te alicui stultum videri sine. Quisquis volet tibi contumeliam faciat et iniuriam, tu tamen nihil patieris, si modo tecum erit virtus. Si vis inquit 'beatus esse, si fide bona vir bonus, sine contemnat te aliquis.' Hoc nemo praestabit nisi qui omnia prior ipse contempserit, nisi qui omnia bona exaequaverit, quia nec bonum sine honesto est et honestum in omnibus par est.
passages.english: Socrates, who called the whole of philosophy back to conduct and said that this is the highest wisdom, to distinguish goods from evils, says: “Follow them, if I have any authority with you, so that you may be happy, and let yourself seem a fool to someone. Let anyone who wishes insult you and wrong you; you will still suffer nothing, so long as virtue is with you. If you want to be happy,” he says, “if you want to be truly a good man, let someone despise you.” No one will achieve this unless he has first despised all things himself, unless he has put all goods on one level, because there is no good without what is honourable, and what is honourable is equal in all.

notes.note: Mores is conduct, character, morals: the part of philosophy now called ethics. The English takes “conduct”.
notes.other_reading: brought the whole of philosophy back to morals

notes.note: Summam can be an adjective with sapientiam (“the highest wisdom”) or a noun (“the sum”). The English takes the adjective.
notes.other_reading: said that the sum of wisdom is this

notes.note: The pronoun (“those”, masculine plural) has no antecedent inside this section. In the section before, Seneca sets the people who discovered these teachings against those who only teach them, and “them” is taken to be the discoverers.
notes.other_reading: Follow those men

notes.note: The quotation marks in the Latin as given are defective here: a mark opens after “inquit” with none closed before it. The English treats everything from “sequere” to “aliquis” as one speech of Socrates, with “he says” put in twice. The words seem to echo the end of Plato’s Gorgias (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: “If you want,” he says, “to be happy …” as a second, separate saying

notes.note: Contumelia is an insult, an affront to a person’s standing; iniuria is a wrong or injury done. The English turns the two nouns into verbs.
notes.other_reading: Let whoever wishes do you insult and injury

notes.note: A legal phrase, literally “in good faith”, here meaning really and without pretence, so the English has “truly”. The verb “to be” is understood from the clause before.
notes.other_reading: if you want to be a good man in good faith

notes.note: The same verb as “contemnat” just before: he who is to bear being despised must first have despised everything. “Despise” is kept for both.
notes.other_reading: unless he has first looked down on all things himself

notes.note: Literally “has made all goods equal”, that is, has come to count every good as equal to every other. “Put on one level” shows that the levelling is in how he rates them.
notes.other_reading: has made all goods equal

notes.note: Honestum is the Stoic term for what is honourable, the morally fine. “In omnibus” can be “in all goods”, “in all things” or “in all cases”; the English “in all” leaves this open, though the goods just mentioned are the nearest sense.
notes.other_reading: what is honourable is equal in every case

check.note: The Latin as given has no closing quotation mark before this “inquit”, so the marks do not pair up. The English repairs this without saying so.
check.decided: Accepted: the English stands, with one speech of Socrates and “he says” put in twice. The note on these words records that the quotation marks in the Latin copy are defective here.

check.note: Fide bona here means genuinely, really and truly. “In good faith” in English means “with honest intent”, and “a good man in good faith” is hard to understand.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “if you want to be truly a good man”. Fide bona is a legal phrase used here for “really, without pretence”, and the English “in good faith” means honest intent, which is another thing.

check.note: In omnibus can mean “in all goods” or more widely “in all things, in every case”. The draft chose the narrower reading by adding “of them”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “what is honourable is equal in all”, without “of them”. The note gives the readings “in all goods” and “in every case”.

check.note: “Men” is added, and illos points back to people named in the section before, so a reader of the excerpt cannot tell who is meant.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Follow them”. The note says that the people meant are the discoverers of these teachings named in the section before.

check.note: “Do you insult and injury” is not English of today.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Let anyone who wishes insult you and wrong you”, which is English of today and keeps both Latin nouns.

check.note: Exaequare here is to put on one level, to count as equal. “Made equal” suggests that he changes the goods themselves.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “has put all goods on one level”. The reason that follows shows the levelling is in how he rates the goods, not a change in them.

passages.latin: Certis eunt cuncta temporibus: nasci debent, crescere, exstingui. Quaecumque supra nos vides currere et haec quibus innixi atque impositi sumus veluti solidissimis carpentur ac desinent; nulli non senectus sua est. Inaequalibus ista spatiis eodem natura dimittit: quidquid est non erit, nec peribit sed resolvetur.
passages.english: All things move through fixed periods: they must be born, grow, be extinguished. Whatever you see running above us, and these things on which we lean and have been set as though they were the most solid of things, will be worn away and will cease. There is nothing that does not have its own old age. Nature sends these things off to the same place after unequal spans: whatever is will not be, yet it will not perish but will be dissolved.

notes.note: Tempora can be times, seasons or set periods. The English takes “fixed periods”, with “move” for eunt (“go”), so that “run” is kept for currere in the next sentence.
notes.other_reading: All things go at fixed times

notes.note: The image is of a flame going out. “Be extinguished” keeps it; the plain sense is “die”.
notes.other_reading: die out

notes.note: This means the heavenly bodies, which “run” their courses overhead. The English leaves it as Seneca has it, without naming them.
notes.other_reading: whatever you see moving in its course above us

notes.latin: quibus innixi atque impositi sumus veluti solidissimis
notes.note: This is the earth underfoot. “Veluti solidissimis” is taken as “as though they were the most solid of things”; it could also be heard as a plain comparison.
notes.other_reading: on which we lean and are set as on the most solid of things

notes.note: Carpere is to pluck or wear away bit by bit. The English takes “worn away”.
notes.other_reading: will be plucked away and come to an end

notes.latin: Inaequalibus ista spatiis eodem natura dimittit
notes.note: Spatium is a stretch of distance or time, and also a lap of a racecourse; dimittere is to send off or dismiss. “Eodem” is “to the same place”, the same end. “Spans” can be heard of time or of distance.
notes.other_reading: Nature dismisses these things to the same end over courses of unequal length

notes.note: Nec here turns against what has just been said, so the English has “yet”. Resolvi is to be loosened or broken up into what a thing was made of; the next section of the letter turns on this word, so “dissolved” is used.
notes.other_reading: and it will not perish but be broken up

check.note: “Be put out” without a fire in view is unclear and can be misread as “be annoyed” or “be expelled”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “be extinguished”, which keeps the image of a flame without the other senses of “be put out”.

check.note: Spatia are stretches of a course or of time: things reach the same end after runs of different length. “At unequal intervals” suggests batches sent off with gaps between.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “after unequal spans”. Spatia are the stretches each thing covers before the same end, not gaps between departures.

check.note: Nec here corrects what has just been said (“will not be”): and yet it will not perish. A plain “and” weakens the turn.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “yet it will not perish but will be dissolved”. Nec here corrects the words just before, “will not be”.

check.note: “Go by fixed times” is not clear English. The sense is that everything moves through set periods.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “All things move through fixed periods”. “Move” is used, not the suggested “run”, because eunt is the plain verb “go” and “run” is needed for currere in the next sentence.

passages.latin: Itaque ut M. Cato, cum aevum animo percucurrerit, dicet, 'omne humanum genus, quodque est quodque erit, morte damnatum est; omnes quae usquam rerum potiuntur urbes quaeque alienorum imperiorum magna sunt decora, ubi fuerint aliquando quaeretur et vario exitii genere tollentur: alias destruent bella, alias desidia paxque ad inertiam versa consumet et magnis opibus exitiosa res, luxus. Omnes hos fertiles campos repentini maris inundatio abscondet aut in subitam cavernam considentis soli lapsus abducet. Quid est ergo quare indigner aut doleam, si exiguo momento publica fata praecedo?'
passages.english: And so, like Marcus Cato, when he has run through the ages in his mind, he will say: “The whole human race, both the part that is and the part that will be, is condemned to death. All the cities that anywhere hold supreme power, and all those that are the great ornaments of empires not their own: one day it will be asked where they were, and they will be done away with by one kind of destruction or another. Wars will pull some down; others will be eaten away by idleness and peace turned to sloth, and by a thing destructive to great wealth, luxury. All these fertile plains will be hidden by a sudden flood of the sea, or carried off into a sudden chasm by the slipping of the ground as it sinks. What reason is there, then, for me to be indignant or to grieve, if I go a brief moment ahead of the common fate?”

notes.latin: Itaque ut M. Cato, cum aevum animo percucurrerit, dicet
notes.note: The verb “dicet” has no stated subject; the section before speaks of the mind that would bear its end more bravely if it saw further. The English supplies “he”, a person of such a mind who speaks “like Marcus Cato”, because a mind running through time “in its mind” (animo) would be strange; “it will say” and “as Marcus Cato will say” are also possible. Cato is Cato the Younger, who killed himself rather than live under Caesar.
notes.other_reading: And so, as Marcus Cato will say when he has run through the ages in thought

notes.note: Aevum is time in its whole length, or an age. The English has “the ages”, without an “all” that the Latin does not have.
notes.other_reading: when he has run through time in his mind

notes.note: A legal phrase: sentenced, with death as the penalty. The English keeps “condemned to death”.
notes.other_reading: has been sentenced to death

notes.note: An idiom for being master of affairs, holding the highest power. The English has “hold supreme power”.
notes.other_reading: that anywhere are masters of the world

notes.note: Taken of cities that do not rule but are the glory of empires belonging to others. The phrase is compressed and could be read more loosely.
notes.other_reading: and those that are the great glories of foreign empires

notes.note: Impersonal in the Latin, and kept so. “Aliquando” is “one day”.
notes.other_reading: some day people will ask where they stood

notes.note: Opes is wealth, resources or power, and of ruling cities “great power” is possible. The English takes “great wealth”, the sense that goes most closely with luxury. “Exitiosa” picks up “exitii” (destruction) a line earlier, so the English has “destructive”.
notes.other_reading: and luxury, a thing ruinous to great power

notes.note: Literally “the flooding of a sudden sea”: the Latin attaches “sudden” to the sea. The English moves it to the flood.
notes.other_reading: the flood of a sudden sea

notes.note: Dolere is to feel pain or to grieve. Here it is the grief of a man facing his own end, so the English has “grieve”.
notes.other_reading: why I should be indignant or feel pain

notes.note: “Publica fata” is the fate shared by all people and all states; for Cato the word also suggests the fate of the republic. “Exiguo momento” is the small measure by which he goes first.
notes.other_reading: if I go before the fate of all by a tiny margin

check.note: The Latin gives “dicet” no subject. The English supplies “he”, though the subject carried over from the section before is the mind, and it is also open whether the clause about running through time belongs to Cato or to the speaker.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps “he”, and the note now says that the subject is supplied and gives “it will say” and “as Marcus Cato will say” as other readings. “He” is kept because the speaker runs through time “in his mind” (animo), which fits a person better than the mind itself.

check.note: “All” is added; the Latin has only aevum.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the ages”. Aevum is time in its whole length, and the Latin has no word for “all”.

check.note: Rerum potiri is to be master of affairs, to hold supreme power. “Hold power” is weaker, and the contrast with the cities that adorn the empires of others depends on the stronger sense.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “hold supreme power”. The idiom means to be master of affairs, and the contrast with cities that only adorn the empires of others needs the full sense.

check.note: Opes can be wealth, but also power or resources, and since these are cities that rule, “great power” is at least as likely. The point is that the choice should be stated.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “great wealth”. Opes is in the first place riches and resources, the phrase is a general remark attached to luxury, and the note on these words states the choice and gives “great power” as the other reading.

check.note: “Removed” is flat and slightly odd of cities; tollere here is to do away with.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “they will be done away with”. That is the sense of tollere named in the point; the suggested “swept away” would add an image of sweeping that the Latin does not have.

check.note: The English copies the Latin in attaching “sudden” to the sea, and “a sudden sea” reads oddly. The sense is a sudden flooding by the sea.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a sudden flood of the sea”. A note records that the Latin attaches “sudden” to the sea.

passages.latin: Magnus animus deo pareat et quidquid lex universi iubet sine cunctatione patiatur: aut in meliorem emittitur vitam lucidius tranquilliusque inter divina mansurus aut certe sine ullo futurus incommodo, si naturae remiscebitur et revertetur in totum. Non est ergo M. Catonis maius bonum honesta vita quam mors honesta, quoniam non intenditur virtus. Idem esse dicebat Socrates veritatem et virtutem. Quomodo illa non crescit, sic ne virtus quidem: habet numeros suos, plena est.
passages.english: Let a great soul obey god and undergo without hesitation whatever the law of the universe commands. Either it is sent out into a better life, to remain among divine things in greater light and greater calm, or at least it will be without any trouble, if it is mixed back into nature and returns into the whole. So Marcus Cato’s honourable life is not a greater good than his honourable death, since virtue cannot be stretched any further. Socrates used to say that truth and virtue are the same thing. As truth does not grow, so virtue does not either: it has its full complement, it is full.

notes.note: The glossary prefers “mind” for animus, with “soul” where it is what survives the body. That is exactly the question in this sentence, where the animus is sent out into a better life or mixed back into nature, so the English has “soul”.
notes.other_reading: Let a great mind obey god

notes.note: Pati is to suffer, bear, undergo. The English takes “undergo”, since the sentence is about accepting what is commanded.
notes.other_reading: and suffer without delay whatever the law of the universe orders

notes.note: The Latin has two comparative adverbs, “more brightly and more calmly”. The English turns them into nouns to be readable.
notes.other_reading: to stay more brightly and more calmly among divine things

notes.note: Incommodum is a mild and general word: inconvenience, disadvantage, trouble. “Trouble” keeps it mild without narrowing it to bodily feeling.
notes.other_reading: or at least it will be free of any harm

notes.latin: si naturae remiscebitur et revertetur in totum
notes.note: The “if” clause is attached to the second alternative only: the soul does not live on but is blended back into the whole.
notes.other_reading: if it is to be blended with nature again and go back into the universe

notes.note: The genitive can be “Cato’s” good or a good “for Cato”. The English attaches it to the life and the death.
notes.other_reading: So for Marcus Cato an honourable life is not a greater good than an honourable death

notes.note: Intendere is to stretch or tighten, as a string or a bow. The Stoic point is that virtue has no degrees and cannot be raised higher, which is why the next sentences say it does not grow. The English keeps the image with “stretched any further”.
notes.other_reading: since virtue cannot be increased

notes.note: An idiom: a thing that “has its numbers” has every element that makes it whole. The English gives the sense with “its full complement”, and keeps “full” for plena.
notes.other_reading: it has its numbers

check.note: “Is not stretched any tighter” keeps the image of a string, but a reader will not see the point, which is that virtue cannot be raised in degree.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “since virtue cannot be stretched any further”. “Stretched” keeps the image of a string, as the rule on images requires, and “any further” makes plain that the point is about degree; the note explains the doctrine.

check.note: Incommodum is harm, disadvantage or trouble in general. “Discomfort” is narrower and suggests bodily feeling.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “without any trouble”. Incommodum is trouble or disadvantage in general, not bodily discomfort.

check.note: “All” is added, and numeros (numbers, full complement) becomes “parts”. The Latin says only that it has its own full tally.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “it has its full complement, it is full”, without “all” and without “parts”. “Full” is kept for plena, not the suggested “complete”, because “complete” stands for another Latin word (perfectum) in the later sections of this letter.

check.note: Animus is “soul” here but “mind” in the other sections of this letter. The change is defensible, since the passage is about survival after death, but it should be decided on purpose.
check.decided: Accepted: “soul” is kept on purpose and the note says why. In this sentence the animus is what is sent out into a better life or mixed back into nature, which is the case where the glossary allows “soul”.

passages.latin: Non educo sapientem ex hominum numero nec dolores ab illo sicut ab aliqua rupe nullum sensum admittente summoveo. Memini ex duabus illum partibus esse compositum: altera est irrationalis, haec mordetur, uritur, dolet; altera rationalis, haec inconcussas opiniones habet, intrepida est et indomita. In hac positum est summum illud hominis bonum. Antequam impleatur, incerta mentis volutatio est; cum vero perfectum est, immota illi stabilitas est.
passages.english: I do not take the wise man out of the number of human beings, nor do I move pains away from him as from some rock that lets in no feeling. I remember that he is made up of two parts: one is without reason, and this part is bitten, burned, feels pain; the other has reason, and this part holds unshaken beliefs, is fearless and unconquered. In this part is placed that highest good of a human being. Before that good is brought to fullness, there is an unsure wavering of the mind; but when it has been made complete, the mind has a stability that does not move.

notes.note: Summovere is to clear away or keep at a distance. Seneca denies that he puts the wise man out of reach of pain.
notes.other_reading: nor do I fence pains off from him

notes.note: Sensus is feeling in the sense of sensation. “Feeling” is used here and for “sensus” in section 29.
notes.other_reading: that admits no sensation

notes.note: “Without reason” and “has reason” keep the glossary word “reason” (ratio) in view.
notes.other_reading: one is irrational … the other rational

notes.note: Two passives and then an active verb. The English keeps the change.
notes.other_reading: is stung, is scorched, hurts

notes.note: The glossary gives “opinion” for opinio and allows “belief” for a settled belief. These are the firm convictions of the rational part, so the English has “beliefs”.
notes.other_reading: holds unshaken opinions

notes.note: Indomita is “untamed, unconquered”, and such forms can also mean “not to be tamed, unconquerable”. The English keeps the first sense.
notes.other_reading: is fearless and unconquerable

notes.note: The subject is the highest good (the neuter “perfectum est” confirms it), and the English names it as “that good” so that “it” is not taken as the rational part. Impleri is to be filled up, brought to its full measure.
notes.other_reading: Before it is filled out

notes.note: Volutatio is a rolling or tossing about. Mens is “mind” here as animus is elsewhere.
notes.other_reading: there is an uncertain tossing of the mind

notes.note: “Illi” can be the mind, the good itself or the man. The English takes the mind, as the contrast with the wavering mind suggests.
notes.other_reading: it has an unmoved stability

check.note: Illi does not say whose stability it is: the mind, the good itself once perfected, or the man. The English names the mind as if the Latin did.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps “the mind”, and the note on these words flags the choice and gives “it has an unmoved stability”. The mind is the nearest sense because the clause answers “wavering of the mind” in the clause before.

check.note: Illud is dropped: “that highest good”, the one already spoken of.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “that highest good of a human being”, so that illud, which points to the good already spoken of, is kept.

check.note: “Filled out” is unclear, and “it” can be taken as “this part”. The neuter form that follows shows the subject is the good.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Before that good is brought to fullness”. Naming the good removes the doubt about “it”, and the note says that the subject is supplied from the neuter verb form that follows.

check.note: Indomita can be “unconquered” or “not to be tamed, unconquerable”. Beside intrepida the second is at least as likely.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English keeps “unconquered”, the first sense of the form, and a new note gives “unconquerable” as the other reading.

passages.latin: Itaque inchoatus et ad summa procedens cultorque virtutis, etiam si appropinquat perfecto bono sed ei nondum summam manum imposuit, ibit interim cessim et remittet aliquid ex intentione mentis; nondum enim incerta transgressus est, etiam nunc versatur in lubrico. Beatus vero et virtutis exactae tunc se maxime amat cum fortissime expertus est, et metuenda ceteris, si alicuius honesti officii pretia sunt, non tantum fert sed amplexatur multoque audire mavult 'tanto melior' quam 'tanto felicior'.
passages.english: And so the man who is only begun and is moving toward the heights, one who cultivates virtue, even if he is coming near to the complete good but has not yet put the finishing touch to it, will from time to time go backward and relax something of the exertion of his mind; for he has not yet crossed over the unsure ground and is still on slippery footing. But the happy man, whose virtue is perfected, loves himself most when he has put himself to the test most bravely, and the things the rest fear, if they are the price of some honourable duty, he not only bears but embraces, and he much prefers to hear “so much the better man” than “so much the more fortunate”.

notes.note: Literally “the begun one”: a person who is himself begun but not finished, like a piece of work, set against the man of perfected virtue below.
notes.other_reading: the man who is still unfinished

notes.note: Cultor is one who tends or cultivates, and also a worshipper.
notes.other_reading: and a devotee of virtue

notes.note: An idiom from the workshop: literally “put the last hand to it”.
notes.other_reading: has not yet put the last hand to it

notes.note: Interim can mean “meanwhile, for the time being” or, in Seneca’s time, “sometimes”. The English takes “from time to time”. Cessim is backward, giving ground.
notes.other_reading: will for the time being go backward

notes.note: Intentio is the tension of a stretched string, hence effort or concentration. “Exertion” is used here and for the same word in section 35.
notes.other_reading: something of the tension of his mind

notes.note: “Incerta” picks up the “unsure” wavering of the section before. “Ground” is supplied to go with the slippery footing that follows.
notes.other_reading: for he has not yet passed beyond what is uncertain

notes.note: A genitive of description: a man “of perfected virtue”. Exactus is finished off, brought to exactness; it is a different word from perfectum, which is “complete” in this letter.
notes.other_reading: the happy man of finished virtue

notes.note: The verb has no stated object. “Himself” is understood from “se … amat” just before; the trial could also be of fortune or of hardship, or the sense could be passive.
notes.other_reading: when he has been tried most bravely

notes.note: Literally “things to be feared by the rest”: things everyone else finds fearful, not things they are obliged to fear.
notes.other_reading: the things that others dread

notes.latin: si alicuius honesti officii pretia sunt
notes.note: Pretium is price or reward. The fearful things are taken as what an honourable duty costs.
notes.other_reading: if they are the reward of some honourable service

notes.note: A colloquial cry of approval, something like “well done” (from memory, unchecked). The English keeps the literal comparison so that it answers “tanto felicior”, where felix is “fortunate” and not the “happy” of beatus.
notes.other_reading: “well done” rather than “lucky you”

check.note: The Latin means things that are fearful to everyone else. “Must fear” makes it a duty or a necessity for them, which Seneca does not say.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the things the rest fear”. The Latin form says these things are fearful to the rest, not that the rest are obliged to fear them.

check.note: Interim can mean “sometimes” or “meanwhile, for the time being”, that is, until he reaches the complete good. Both fit, and the choice should be flagged.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps “from time to time”, and the note on these words flags the choice and gives “for the time being” as the other reading.

check.note: “Finished” can be read as “over and done with”. Exactae is “brought to completion, perfected”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “whose virtue is perfected”, so that it cannot be taken as “over and done with”.

check.note: English says “the finishing touch”; “the finishing hand” is a Latinism.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “put the finishing touch to it”. The note gives the literal “the last hand”.

check.note: Etiam nunc here is simply “still”. “Even now” puts a stress that the Latin does not have.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and is still on slippery footing”. Etiam nunc is the ordinary Latin for “still”.

check.note: The Latin has no object: “when he has most bravely made trial”. “Himself” is a reasonable supplement, but the trial may equally be of fortune or of hardship.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps “has put himself to the test”, and the note flags that “himself” is supplied from the “se” just before and that fortune or hardship could be meant.

check.note: Inchoatus is passive: the man who is himself begun but unfinished, like a work in progress, an image that continues in the finishing touch. The draft turned it into something he has done.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the man who is only begun”. This keeps the passive sense, a man begun like a piece of work, and keeps the root meaning “begun”; the suggested “unfinished” is given in the note.

passages.latin: Venio nunc illo quo me vocat exspectatio tua. Ne extra rerum naturam vagari virtus nostra videatur, et tremet sapiens et dolebit et expallescet; hi enim omnes corporis sensus sunt. Ubi ergo calamitas, ubi illud malum verum est? illic scilicet, si ista animum detrahunt, si ad confessionem servitutis adducunt, si illi paenitentiam sui faciunt.
passages.english: I come now to the point to which your expectation calls me. So that our virtue may not seem to wander outside the nature of things: the wise man will tremble, and feel pain, and turn pale, for all these are feelings of the body. Where, then, is the disaster, where is that true evil? There, of course: if these things drag the mind down, if they bring it to a confession of slavery, if they make it dissatisfied with itself.

notes.latin: illo quo me vocat exspectatio tua
notes.note: Literally “to that place where your expectation calls me”: the thing Lucilius has been waiting to hear.
notes.other_reading: I come now to what you are waiting for

notes.latin: Ne extra rerum naturam vagari virtus nostra videatur
notes.note: A purpose clause that explains why Seneca makes the admission that follows; the colon marks that loose link. “Virtus nostra” most likely means virtue as the Stoic school describes it, not the virtue that Seneca and Lucilius possess; the English keeps the bare possessive of the Latin.
notes.other_reading: Lest virtue as the Stoics teach it seem to stray beyond nature

notes.latin: et tremet sapiens et dolebit et expallescet
notes.note: The triple “et” piles the verbs up; the first could also be heard as “even”. Dolebit is physical pain here.
notes.other_reading: the wise man will even tremble and suffer and grow pale

notes.note: Sensus is sensation. “Feeling” is kept, as in section 27.
notes.other_reading: sensations of the body

notes.note: “Verum” is the adjective “true”, set after the noun for weight.
notes.other_reading: where is the real evil

notes.note: Detrahere is to pull down or to pull away. The English takes “drag down”, which fits the slavery that follows. The verb is slightly odd with this object and the text may be doubted (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: if these things pull the mind away

notes.note: “Illi” is the mind (or the wise man). Literally “produce in it regret of itself”: it becomes sorry to be what it is.
notes.other_reading: if they make him sorry to be what he is

check.note: “Regret itself” is not natural English. The sense is that the mind becomes dissatisfied with itself, sorry to be what it is.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “if they make it dissatisfied with itself”. Paenitentia sui is being displeased with what one is, and “regret itself” is not natural English.

check.note: Nostra most likely means the virtue of the Stoic school, virtue as the Stoics describe it. The plain possessive can be read as the virtue Seneca and Lucilius possess.
check.decided: Accepted: the possessive is kept as the Latin has it, and the note now says that it most likely means virtue as the Stoic school describes it, with that reading given as the alternative.

passages.latin: Sapiens quidem vincit virtute fortunam, at multi professi sapientiam levissimis nonnumquam minis exterriti sunt. Hoc loco nostrum vitium est, qui idem a sapiente exigimus et a proficiente. Suadeo adhuc mihi ista quae laudo, nondum persuadeo; etiam si persuasissem, nondum tam parata haberem aut tam exercitata ut ad omnes casus procurrerent.
passages.english: The wise man, it is true, conquers fortune by virtue, but many who have professed wisdom have at times been terrified by the slightest threats. Here the fault is ours, who demand the same thing of the wise man and of the man who is making progress. I am still urging on myself the things I praise; I have not yet convinced myself. Even if I had convinced myself, I would not yet have them so ready or so practised that they would run out to meet whatever happens.

notes.note: Fortune is an opponent here, but it is not addressed or described as a person, so it has no capital.
notes.other_reading: defeats Fortune by virtue

notes.note: Profiteri is to declare openly, and so to claim or to make a profession of something. These are people who announced themselves as philosophers.
notes.other_reading: many who have laid claim to wisdom

notes.note: The glossary gives “vice” for vitium, and “fault” where it is small. Here it is a mistake of judging, so “fault”.
notes.other_reading: On this point the vice is ours

notes.note: The proficiens is the Stoic term for one who is advancing toward wisdom but is not yet wise.
notes.other_reading: and of the learner

notes.latin: Suadeo adhuc mihi ista quae laudo, nondum persuadeo
notes.note: A play on suadeo (urge, advise) and persuadeo (urge with success, convince). English has no such pair on one root, so the English has “urging” and “convinced”. The Latin verb is a present, “do not yet convince”.
notes.other_reading: I am still recommending to myself what I praise; I do not yet persuade myself

notes.note: A military image: troops running forward to meet an attack. Casus is the word rendered “chance” in section 3; here, in the plural, it is the things that befall a person.
notes.other_reading: that they would run out to meet every chance

check.note: The Latin plays suadeo (urge) against persuadeo (succeed in convincing). The draft’s “am not yet persuading myself” is awkward and blurs the point, which is that the urging has not yet worked.
check.decided: Accepted: the clause now reads “have not yet convinced myself”, and “convinced” returns in the next sentence for the same verb. The note records the play on suadeo and persuadeo and that the Latin verb is a present.

check.note: “Every chance” is unclear in English and sounds like “every opportunity”. Casus here are the things that befall a person.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “run out to meet whatever happens”. Casus here are the things that befall a person, and the note records that the same word is “chance” in section 3.

check.note: English says “slightest threats”, not “lightest threats”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the slightest threats”, the English idiom for the same sense.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft turned the Latin relative clause (“who demand”) into a clause of reason beginning with “for”, a word the Latin does not have.
check.decided: Accepted: the clause now reads “who demand the same thing of the wise man and of the man who is making progress”, a relative clause as in the Latin.

passages.latin: Quemadmodum lana quosdam colores semel ducit, quosdam nisi saepius macerata et recocta non perbibit, sic alias disciplinas ingenia, cum accepere, protinus praestant: haec, nisi alte descendit et diu sedit et animum non coloravit sed infecit, nihil ex iis quae promiserat praestat.
passages.english: Just as wool takes on some colours in one go, and others it does not drink in fully unless it has been soaked and boiled again several times, so there are other branches of learning that intellects make good on at once, as soon as they have received them: this one, unless it has gone down deep and settled for a long time and dyed the mind rather than coloured it, makes good on nothing of what it had promised.

notes.note: Ducere colorem is to take on a colour; semel is “once”, at a single dyeing.
notes.other_reading: absorbs some colours at the first dipping

notes.note: Saepius is “rather often, repeatedly”. It is taken with both participles.
notes.other_reading: steeped again and again and boiled a second time

notes.note: The prefix per- means “through and through”, hence “drink in fully”.
notes.other_reading: does not soak up

notes.note: Disciplinae are branches of learning; “alias” (other) is answered by “haec” (this one) after the colon. Ingenium is inborn ability, and “intellects” is used so that “mind” stays free for animus later in the sentence.
notes.other_reading: so there are some studies which natural talents

notes.note: Praestare is to make good, deliver or show in practice; it returns in “praestat” at the end, and “make good on” is kept for both.
notes.other_reading: can show at once

notes.note: “This one” is the branch of learning Seneca has been speaking of, philosophy or wisdom. It is not named in this section and the name is not added.
notes.other_reading: but this branch of learning, philosophy

notes.note: Sedere is to sit or settle, as a dye sets.
notes.other_reading: has sunk deep and sat long

notes.note: The contrast is between colour on the surface and dye taken right through; literally “has not coloured the mind but dyed it”. Inficere is to dye or steep; it can also mean to stain, but there is no bad sense here.
notes.other_reading: has not tinted the mind but steeped it

check.note: Coming after “unless it has”, the words “has not coloured” read at first as a second, negative condition. The Latin means: unless it has dyed the mind through, rather than just tinting it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and dyed the mind rather than coloured it”, so that no “not” stands inside the “unless” clause. “Coloured” is kept, not “tinted”, because it answers the “colours” of the wool.

check.note: “Intellects deliver teachings” is hard to understand. Praestare here is to make good on, to show in practice, and the same verb returns at the end, so one English verb should serve both.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “make good on” now serves for the verb in both places, and the sentence reads “there are other branches of learning that intellects make good on at once”. “Intellects” is kept, not the suggested “minds”, because “mind” is needed for animus in the same sentence.

check.note: The prefix per- (through and through) is not rendered in “drink in”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “does not drink in fully”, which gives the force of the prefix per-, “through and through”.

check.note: Disciplinae are branches of learning, subjects of study, set against this one. “Other teachings” is vague, and “other” has nothing to refer to until the next sentence.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “other branches of learning”. “Other” is kept because the Latin alias is answered by “this one”, and the two now stand in one sentence joined by a colon, as in the Latin.

passages.latin: Imperfecta necesse est labent et modo prodeant, modo sublabantur aut succidant. Sublabentur autem, nisi ire et niti perseveraverint; si quicquam ex studio et fideli intentione laxaverint, retro eundum est. Nemo profectum ibi invenit ubi reliquerat.
passages.english: Things that are incomplete are bound to totter, and now go forward, now slip down or collapse. And they will slip down, unless they keep on going and striving; if they slacken anything of their zeal and faithful exertion, they have to go backward. No one finds his progress where he had left it.

notes.note: Neuter plural, “incomplete things”, though the sense is people who are not yet made perfect. The neuter is kept, and “incomplete” answers “complete” for perfectum in sections 27 and 28.
notes.other_reading: Those who are not yet perfect

notes.note: From labare, to totter or be unsteady, not from labi, to slip.
notes.other_reading: are bound to be unsteady

notes.note: Sublabi is to slip or sink down from under; a backward direction is stated only later, in “retro”. Succidere is to sink under oneself, as knees do. “Sublabentur” in the next sentence repeats the first verb, and “slip down” is repeated.
notes.other_reading: now slip back or give way

notes.note: Niti is to strain, push or climb with effort.
notes.other_reading: to go on and to struggle

notes.note: Intentio is tension, and “laxaverint” (slacken) keeps the image of a string. “Exertion” is used as in section 28. Studium is zeal or devoted study.
notes.other_reading: their eagerness and loyal tension

notes.note: An impersonal form, “there must be a going back”. The English gives it to the same subject, “they”, since no new subject is meant.
notes.other_reading: one has to go backward

notes.latin: Nemo profectum ibi invenit ubi reliquerat
notes.note: Profectus is progress, the noun of proficere, which the next section plays on.
notes.other_reading: No one picks up his progress at the point where he dropped it

check.note: The Latin is impersonal but still about the same subjects. The switch from “they” to “one” in the middle of the sentence reads like a new subject.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “they have to go backward”. The Latin is impersonal but speaks of the same subjects, and “one” read like a new subject.

check.note: Sublabi is to slip down or sink from under. “Back” is a direction the Latin gives only later, with retro, and the draft read the later word into this one.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “slip down” in both places. The verb itself gives only a sinking or loss of footing; the backward direction comes later, with retro.

check.note: Succidere is to collapse, to sink under oneself, a stronger step after slipping. “Give way” is weaker.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “or collapse”, the stronger step after slipping.

check.note: Found while settling: “must totter” can be read as a guess, as with the same Latin words for necessity in section 3.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “are bound to totter”, as in section 3, since necesse est says that it cannot be otherwise.

passages.latin: Instemus itaque et perseveremus; plus quam profligavimus restat, sed magna pars est profectus velle proficere. Huius rei conscius mihi sum: volo et mente tota volo. Te quoque instinctum esse et magno ad pulcherrima properare impetu video. Properemus: ita demum vita beneficium erit; alioquin mora est, et quidem turpis inter foeda versantibus. Id agamus ut nostrum omne tempus sit; non erit autem, nisi prius nos nostri esse coeperimus.
passages.english: So let us press on and persevere. More remains than we have got through, but a great part of progress is wanting to make progress. This I know of myself: I want to, and I want to with my whole mind. I see that you too have been roused and are hurrying with great force toward the finest things. Let us hurry: only so will life be a gift. Otherwise it is a delay, and a shameful one at that, for those who live among foul things. Let us see to it that all time is ours; but it will not be, unless we have first begun to be our own.

notes.note: Profligare is to strike down, and so to bring a task or a war near its end. The English takes the plain “got through”.
notes.other_reading: more is left than we have dispatched

notes.latin: magna pars est profectus velle proficere
notes.note: Profectus (genitive) and proficere are noun and verb of one root. “Progress” is kept for both.
notes.other_reading: a large part of advancing is the will to advance

notes.note: An ordinary Latin phrase for knowing something of oneself at first hand. The literal wording, “conscious to myself of this thing”, is stiff in English.
notes.other_reading: This I can vouch for in my own case

notes.note: Mens, not animus. “Mind” is used for both.
notes.other_reading: with all my heart

notes.note: Instinctus is goaded, fired, set in motion.
notes.other_reading: that you too have been spurred on

notes.note: Literally “toward the most beautiful things”, with a moral sense: the noblest aims. They are set against the “foul things” (foeda) below.
notes.other_reading: toward what is most beautiful

notes.note: Beneficium is a kindness or favour done to someone, a word Seneca uses with weight. Life will count as something given only on this condition; “gift” is used because “benefit” sounds like a mere advantage.
notes.other_reading: only so will life be a benefit

notes.note: The subject can be life (“it is a delay”, a mere waiting) or nothing (“there is delay”). The English takes life.
notes.other_reading: otherwise there is delay

notes.note: Versari is to move about in a place, to spend one’s days there. The participle has no pronoun: the English keeps the general “for those who”, though with “let us” on both sides it may well mean Seneca and Lucilius themselves.
notes.other_reading: for us who spend it among foul things

notes.note: Literally “that all time be ours”, with the possessive once. The sense is most likely all the time a person has, not all the ages.
notes.other_reading: that all our time is ours

notes.latin: nisi prius nos nostri esse coeperimus
notes.note: A play on the possessive: time will belong to a person only when he himself is “his own”, that is, belongs to himself.
notes.other_reading: unless we first begin to belong to ourselves

check.note: The Latin has the possessive once: “that all time be ours”. The draft added a second possessive, which narrows “all time” to the time a person has.
check.decided: Accepted: the second possessive is dropped, so the clause now reads “that all time is ours”, as the Latin has it. A new note says that the time a person has is the likely sense.

check.note: The participle has no pronoun. With “let us” on both sides it most likely means Seneca and Lucilius themselves, while the English makes it other people.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps the general “for those who live among foul things”, because the Latin participle has no pronoun, and the note now flags that it may mean “for us” and gives that reading.

check.note: Beneficium is a kindness done, a gift or favour. “A benefit” is flatter and sounds like an advantage.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “only so will life be a gift”. Beneficium is a kindness done to someone, and “benefit” sounds like an advantage.

check.note: “Conscious in myself” is stiff English; the Latin is an ordinary phrase for knowing something of oneself.
check.decided: Accepted: the stiff “conscious in myself” is replaced by the suggested plain wording, without “much”, which the Latin does not have. The phrase is an ordinary one for knowing something of oneself.

passages.latin: Non cum vacaveris philosophandum est, sed ut philosopheris vacandum est; omnia alia neglegenda ut huic assideamus, cui nullum tempus satis magnum est, etiam si a pueritia usque ad longissimos humani aevi terminos vita producitur. Non multum refert utrum omittas philosophiam an intermittas; non enim ubi interrupta est manet, sed eorum more quae intenta dissiliunt usque ad initia sua recurrit, quod a continuatione discessit. Resistendum est occupationibus, nec explicandae sed summovendae sunt. Tempus quidem nullum est parum idoneum studio salutari; atqui multi inter illa non student propter quae studendum est.
passages.english: It is not when you have time free that you are to do philosophy, but you are to make time free so that you may do philosophy. Everything else is to be neglected so that we may sit in attendance on philosophy, for which no time is long enough, even if life is drawn out from boyhood to the farthest limits of a human lifetime. It does not matter much whether you give philosophy up or leave it off for a time; for it does not stay where it was interrupted, but, like things stretched tight that spring apart, it runs back all the way to its beginnings, because it has left off being continuous. We must resist the things that keep us busy: they are not to be untangled but pushed out of the way. There is in fact no time that is ill suited to a study that brings health; and yet many do not study in the midst of the things on account of which one ought to study.

notes.latin: Non cum vacaveris philosophandum est, sed ut philosopheris vacandum est
notes.note: The sentence turns on one verb, vacare (to have time free, to be at leisure), used twice and crossed with “do philosophy” twice. Both duties are impersonal in the Latin (“philosophy is to be done”, “time is to be made free”), while the two other verbs are second person. The English makes both duties personal (“you are to”) so that it reads plainly, and keeps “time free” for vacare both times.
notes.other_reading: Philosophy is not to be done when you have leisure; leisure is to be made so that you may do philosophy.

notes.note: Assidere is to sit beside someone in attendance, as at a sickbed or beside a teacher. The image of sitting is kept. The Latin says only “this”, and the English names philosophy so that the reference is clear.
notes.other_reading: in order to attend closely to this

notes.note: Aevum is a span of life or an age. Here it is the length of a human life, so “a human lifetime”; the same word is “lifetime” in Ep. 74.10.
notes.other_reading: the farthest limits of the human span

notes.note: A play on two compounds of one verb: omittere (let go altogether) and intermittere (leave off for a time). English cannot keep the echo; “give up” and “leave off for a time” keep the difference between stopping for good and stopping for a while.
notes.other_reading: whether you drop philosophy or interrupt it

notes.note: The image is open: things under tension that “leap apart” may be things stretched tight that snap and fly back (a cord, a spring) or things strained that burst. The English takes them as stretched things springing apart, since the point is the recoil to the starting point.
notes.other_reading: like things that burst when they are strained

notes.note: Quod can be “because”, with philosophy still the subject, or “whatever”, starting a general statement with a new subject. The English takes it as “because”, since the sentence is built as “it does not stay…, but runs back…” and such a pair normally keeps one subject.
notes.other_reading: but, like things stretched tight that spring apart, whatever has broken its continuity runs back all the way to its beginnings

notes.note: The word picks up the busy days and the fresh business of the section before: whatever fills one’s time. “Occupations” is the nearer English word in form, but today it suggests jobs.
notes.other_reading: Occupations are to be resisted

notes.note: Explicare is to unfold, disentangle or sort out in order; summovere is to clear out of the way, the word used of clearing a crowd from someone’s path. Both are kept as physical images.
notes.other_reading: they are not to be settled one by one but removed

notes.latin: inter illa non student propter quae studendum est
notes.note: “The things” are not named. They are most likely the troubles and pressures that make the healing study necessary in the first place, though they could be the busy affairs themselves; the English leaves them unnamed as the Latin does. Studere and studium are “study” throughout, though the word also means earnest pursuit in general.
notes.other_reading: many fail to study in exactly the circumstances that make study necessary

notes.note: Salutaris is giving health or saving; the study meant is philosophy as a cure. The English reads “a study that brings health”.
notes.other_reading: a wholesome pursuit

check.latin: Non cum vacaveris philosophandum est, sed ut philosopheris vacandum est
check.note: “Become free” does not say free of what and may suggest liberty, while vacare is to have time free. The “but” (sed) that carries the reversal is reduced to a semicolon.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “It is not when you have time free that you are to do philosophy, but you are to make time free so that you may do philosophy.” “Time free” stands for vacare both times and “but” is restored. The suggested “should” is not used, since the Latin states a duty rather than advice.

check.note: Assidere is to sit by someone in constant attendance, as at a bedside or with a teacher. “Sit beside it” keeps the image, but a reader may not see that steady attendance is meant or that “it” is philosophy.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “sit in attendance on philosophy”, which keeps the sitting, brings out the attendance and names philosophy for the Latin “this”. “Constant” is left out because the Latin has no separate word for it.

check.note: “A human age” is not current English and could be taken for an era. Aevum here is a lifetime.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “to the farthest limits of a human lifetime”, since aevum here is the span of one life.

check.note: The Latin contrasts giving up for good (omittas) with leaving off for a while (intermittas). “Break it off” sounds as final as “drop”, so the contrast is blurred.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “whether you give philosophy up or leave it off for a time”. “Leave gaps in it” is not used, because intermittere is to stop for a while, which is what the next clause (“where it was interrupted”) takes up.

check.note: The English takes quod as “because”. It can equally be a relative and the subject of “runs back”, giving a general statement: “whatever has departed from continuity runs back to its beginnings”.
check.decided: Declined: “because it has left off being continuous” stands. The sentence has the shape “it does not stay…, but runs back…”, and such a Latin pair normally keeps one subject, here philosophy; quod as “because” needs no agreement in gender, so the neuter form does not count against it. The note records the other reading.

check.note: “Occupations” today suggests jobs or professions, while occupationes are whatever keeps one busy. A possessive is added that the Latin does not have.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “occupations”, which today suggests jobs, gives way to a plain phrase for whatever keeps a person busy, and the added possessive goes. “Resist” is kept rather than “stand up to”, because resistere is the plain word for resisting.

check.note: The Latin has only illa, with no word for “very”; the emphasis is added.
check.decided: Accepted: “very” is dropped and the English reads “in the midst of the things on account of which one ought to study”, since the Latin has only “those things”.

passages.latin: 'Incidet aliquid quod impediat.' Non quidem eum cuius animus in omni negotio laetus atque alacer est: imperfectis adhuc interscinditur laetitia, sapientis vero contexitur gaudium, nulla causa rumpitur, nulla fortuna; semper et ubique tranquillus est. Non enim ex alieno pendet nec favorem fortunae aut hominis exspectat. Domestica illi felicitas est; exiret ex animo si intraret: ibi nascitur.
passages.english: “Something will come up to get in the way.” Not, at any rate, in the way of the man whose mind is glad and lively in every piece of business. In those who are still imperfect, gladness is cut apart; but the wise man’s joy is woven in one piece: it is torn by no cause, by no fortune. He is calm always and everywhere. For he does not hang on what is not his own, and he does not wait for the favour of fortune or of a man. His happiness is home-grown: it would go out of the mind if it came into it. It is born there.

notes.note: An imagined objection, marked as quoted in the Latin; the speaker could be Lucilius or anyone. In the reply, “the man” is the object of “get in the way”, so the English repeats the phrase to make that clear.
notes.other_reading: “Something will happen to hinder you.” Not him, at least, whose mind…

notes.latin: imperfectis adhuc interscinditur laetitia, sapientis vero contexitur gaudium
notes.note: Seneca sets laetitia against gaudium, and the mind in the sentence before is called laetus. “Glad” and “gladness” stand for laetus and laetitia and “joy” for gaudium, so that the contrast shows. The verbs come from cloth: one is cut apart, the other woven together, which the English gives as “woven in one piece”.
notes.other_reading: the cheerfulness of the imperfect is interrupted, but the joy of the wise man is woven together

notes.note: Literally “those still not completed”: people who are making progress but are not yet wise. “Imperfect” is the same word in English dress and keeps the sense of something not yet brought to completion.
notes.other_reading: for those who are still unfinished

notes.note: Causa may be “cause” or “occasion, circumstance”; fortuna here is any turn of fortune and could be personified. The English keeps “cause” and “fortune” with a small letter. Rumpere is to break or burst; “torn” keeps the cloth of the verb before.
notes.other_reading: no circumstance breaks it, no stroke of Fortune

notes.note: Alieno can be neuter (what is another’s, what lies outside him) or masculine (another person). The English takes it as neuter, “what is not his own”, and keeps the image of hanging, where plainer English would say “depend on”.
notes.other_reading: he does not depend on another person

notes.note: Fortune stands beside “a man” as a giver of favour, so it is close to personified; the small letter is kept. Hominis is singular: “of a man” or “of any person”.
notes.other_reading: the favour of Fortune or of any human being

notes.note: Felicitas is good fortune, prosperity or happiness; domestica means belonging to his own house, produced at home. “Happiness” is used here so that “fortune” stands only for fortuna in this section; the same word is “good fortune” in Ep. 74.18 and 75.15. “Happy” is otherwise this project’s word for beatus, which does not occur in this section.
notes.other_reading: His good fortune is of his own household

notes.note: A compressed thought: what comes into the mind from outside can also leave it, so his happiness is not something that entered. The English is literal and leaves the inference to the reader, as the Latin does.
notes.other_reading: if it had come into the mind from outside, it would also leave it

check.note: Fortuna has just been “fortune” twice, and now felicitas, a different word, is “good fortune”. The English seems to say that the wise man does not wait on fortune and yet has good fortune at home, an echo the Latin does not have.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “His happiness”, so that “fortune” stands only for fortuna in this section. The note records that felicitas is “good fortune” in Ep. 74.18 and 75.15, where it means prosperity or luck.

check.note: “Of his own household” is stiff and suggests family or servants. Domestica here is “at home, home-grown”, as against brought in from outside.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “His happiness is home-grown”. Domestica means produced at home as against brought in from outside, which is the point of the next clause.

check.note: “Unfinished” is odd of people; the sense is “not yet perfect”. At the head of the sentence “For” can be misread as “because”, which the Latin does not say.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “In those who are still imperfect”. “Unfinished” is odd of people, and “In” removes the risk that the opening word is read as “because”.

check.note: “In the middle” is not in the Latin; the verb is simply “is cut apart”, as a fabric is.
check.decided: Accepted: “in the middle” is dropped and the English reads “gladness is cut apart”.

check.note: The image is of cloth (woven, then torn); “broken” lets the image go, and “by no cause” is stiff.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “it is torn by no cause, by no fortune”, which keeps the cloth of the verb before it. The two phrases stand side by side without “and”, as in the Latin.

check.note: “Hang on” is not clear English for “depend on”, and alienum is anything not one’s own, not only another person’s property.
check.decided: Partly accepted: alieno is now “what is not his own”, since the word covers anything outside him and not only another person’s property. “Hang on” stays, because pendet is an image of hanging and “depend” would let it go; the note gives the plainer wording.

check.note: Alacer is brisk, lively, in good spirits; “eager” suggests wanting something, which is not the point here.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “glad and lively”. Alacer is brisk and in good spirits, and “eager” suggests wanting something.

passages.latin: Quicumque beatus esse constituet, unum esse bonum putet quod honestum est; nam si ullum aliud existimat, primum male de providentia iudicat, quia multa incommoda iustis viris accidunt, et quia quidquid nobis dedit breve est et exiguum si compares mundi totius aevo.
passages.english: Whoever resolves to be happy should think that the only good is what is honourable. For if he considers anything else a good, first, he passes an unfavourable judgment on providence, because many troubles happen to just men, and because whatever it has given us is short and slight, if you compare it with the lifetime of the whole world.

notes.latin: unum esse bonum putet quod honestum est
notes.note: The Stoic thesis that what is honourable (honestum) is the only good (bonum). Unum is “one” and here amounts to “the only”, as the next clause (“anything else”) shows.
notes.other_reading: should think that there is one good, what is honourable

notes.note: Future tense in the Latin (“shall resolve”); English uses the present in such a clause. Constituere is to decide or settle on.
notes.other_reading: Whoever shall have made up his mind to be happy

notes.note: “First” opens a list whose next member falls outside this section, so the English “first” stands alone here as the Latin does.
notes.other_reading: in the first place

notes.note: Literally “judges badly about providence”: forms a low opinion of it. “Judgment” is kept because iudicat is the verb of iudicium. “Unfavourable” shows that the judgment is a low one and not a mistaken one, though the Latin could mean either.
notes.other_reading: he thinks ill of providence

notes.note: Incommoda is the Stoic word for disadvantages, the opposite of commoda (advantages): things that are unwelcome but not truly evils. “Troubles” is the plain English; the technical colour is lost.
notes.other_reading: many disadvantages befall just men

notes.note: The subject of “has given” is not stated; it is taken to be providence, carried over from the clause before, hence “it”.
notes.other_reading: whatever she has given us

notes.note: Aevum is a lifetime or an age; mundus is the world in the sense of the whole ordered universe, not the earth. “World” is kept for mundus so that it matches Ep. 74.20, where “universe” is needed for another word.
notes.other_reading: the lifetime of the entire universe

notes.note: The sentence moves from “he” to a general “you”. The second person is kept as the Latin has it.
notes.other_reading: if one compares it

check.latin: unum esse bonum putet quod honestum est
check.note: Unum here is “one only”. “There is one good” can be read as “there is a good”, which weakens the exclusive claim that the next clause depends on, and “namely” is a small addition.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “should think that the only good is what is honourable”, and “namely” is gone. The next clause (“anything else”) shows that unum shuts out every other good.

check.note: “Judges badly of” is not current English and could be taken as “judges inaccurately”. The sense is that he has a low opinion of providence.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “he passes an unfavourable judgment on providence”, which cannot be taken as “judges inaccurately”. “Thinks ill of” is not used because iudicat is the verb of iudicium, which this project keeps as “judgment”.

check.note: Incommoda is the mild word, disadvantages or troubles; “hardships” is somewhat heavier.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “many troubles”. Incommoda is the mild Stoic word for things unwelcome but not evil, and “hardships” is heavier than that.

check.note: “The age of the world” reads as “how old the world is” or as an era. Aevum is a whole span of life, and mundus is the universe rather than the earth.
check.decided: Partly accepted: aevum is now “lifetime”, as in Ep. 72.3. “World” is kept for mundus, because Ep. 74.20 has universi and mundi side by side and needs “universe” for the first; the note says that the whole ordered universe is meant.

passages.latin: Omnia ista nobis accedant, non haereant, ut si abducentur, sine ulla nostri laceratione discedant. Utamur illis, non gloriemur, et utamur parce tamquam depositis apud nos et abituris. Quisquis illa sine ratione possedit non diu tenuit; ipsa enim se felicitas, nisi temperatur, premit. Si fugacissimis bonis credidit, cito deseritur, et, ut deseratur, affligitur. Paucis deponere felicitatem molliter licuit: ceteri cum iis inter quae eminuere labuntur, et illos degravant ipsa quae extulerant.
passages.english: Let all those things come to us as additions and not stick fast to us, so that, if they are led away, they may leave without tearing us at all. Let us use them, not boast of them, and let us use them sparingly, as things deposited with us that are going to leave. Whoever has possessed them without the use of reason has not kept them long; for good fortune itself, unless it is kept within measure, bears itself down. If he has trusted in goods that are the quickest to run away, he is soon deserted, and, in order to be deserted, he is struck down. Few have been allowed to lay their good fortune down gently: the rest fall together with the things among which they stood high, and the very things that had lifted them up weigh them down.

notes.note: “Those things” are the advantages of the section before: things called goods by opinion, which Seneca has just said should be called advantages and treated as property, not as parts of a person.
notes.other_reading: All those advantages
