notes.note: Accedere is to come to, to be added; haerere is to stick or cling. “As additions” brings out the sense of something added on from outside, which a bare “come” would lose.
notes.other_reading: Let all these things come near us, not cling to us

notes.note: Abducere is to lead away, the verb used of taking off slaves or cattle; the section before has just called these things slaves. The verb is future: Seneca expects it to happen.
notes.other_reading: if they are taken away

notes.note: Literally “without any tearing of us”: the image is of something stuck to the flesh that tears it when pulled off. The image is kept, with a verb in place of the noun.
notes.other_reading: without any wound to us

notes.latin: tamquam depositis apud nos et abituris
notes.note: A legal image: a deposit is property left in one’s keeping, to be returned on demand. The same verb returns below in “lay down” good fortune (deponere), an echo English cannot keep with one word.
notes.other_reading: as things entrusted for safe keeping and soon to depart

notes.note: Ratio is “reason” in the glossary, and the neighbouring sections speak of reason as what moderates wealth. “The use of” is added so that the phrase is not read as “for no reason”. The Latin can also mean simply “without method”.
notes.other_reading: Whoever has possessed them without a plan

notes.latin: ipsa enim se felicitas, nisi temperatur, premit
notes.note: Felicitas is good fortune or prosperity; premere is to press hard on or weigh down. “Good fortune” is used here and in Ep. 75.15; in Ep. 72.4, where the word stands beside fortuna, it is “happiness”. Temperare is to keep in due measure.
notes.other_reading: for prosperity, unless it is moderated, crushes itself

notes.latin: Si fugacissimis bonis credidit, cito deseritur
notes.note: The subject is not stated. By grammar it could be good fortune, the subject just before; by sense and tense (the same past form as “has possessed”) it is the person, and the English takes it so. “Goods” is used loosely here, of things Seneca has just said are goods only in name.
notes.other_reading: If it has trusted in the most fleeting goods, it is soon deserted

notes.note: The clause is doubtful. The English takes ut as purpose: for the goods to leave him he is knocked down, which fits the next sentence about how few lay good fortune down gently. It can also be read as a concession.
notes.other_reading: and, even granted that he is deserted, he is struck down

notes.latin: cito deseritur, et, ut deseratur, affligitur
notes.note: As given, the second clause comes close to repeating the first, and the text may be at fault. A “not” (non) may have dropped out before deseratur; this is from memory, unchecked. The English follows the Latin as given.
notes.other_reading: he is soon deserted, and, even if he is not deserted, he is battered

notes.note: Deponere is to lay or set down, like a load, and echoes the “deposited” things above. Molliter is softly, gently, without a crash.
notes.other_reading: to put off their prosperity without a shock

check.note: The English takes ut as purpose (“so that he may be deserted, he is struck down”), which seems to make no sense. The second reader holds that only a concessive reading construes: “even supposing that he is deserted”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the clause is reworded as “in order to be deserted, he is struck down”, and the note marks it as doubtful and gives the concessive reading. The purpose reading stays, because ut with this verb form is the ordinary Latin for “in order to” and so does construe, and it fits the next sentence: few lay good fortune down gently, the rest fall.

check.latin: cito deseritur, et, ut deseratur, affligitur
check.note: As given, the second clause seems only to repeat the first. The second reader suspects that a “not” (non) has dropped out, which would give “and even if he is not deserted, he is battered”; this rests on memory of the usual text, unchecked.
check.decided: Partly accepted: a note now says that the clause is doubtful and gives the reading with “not” restored. The English does not restore it, because the Latin as given has no non and can be construed without one.

check.note: The English makes the man the subject. The nearest subject in the Latin is felicitas, which would give “if it has trusted in the most fleeting goods, it is soon deserted”; both construe.
check.decided: Declined: “he” stands. The verb is in the same past form as “has possessed” and “has not kept”, whose subject is the person, and it is a person who is “deserted” by his goods. The note records the other reading.

check.note: “Possessed them without reason” reads as “for no reason”. The Latin means without the use of reason, the faculty.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “without the use of reason”, which cannot be taken as “for no reason”. “Guidance” is not used because the Latin has only “without reason”, and “use” is the smaller addition.

check.note: “Again” is added; the Latin says only that they are going to leave.
check.decided: Accepted: “again” is dropped and the phrase now ends “that are going to leave”. “Deposited” is kept from the draft so that the legal image of a deposit stays.

check.note: “Tempered” in this sense is dated and may suggest steel; the meaning is “kept within measure”. “Crushes” is a little stronger than premit, which is to press or bear down on.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “unless it is kept within measure, bears itself down”. Temperare is to keep in due measure, and premere is to press or bear down on, which is less than crushing.

check.note: The draft’s phrase is accurate but awkward; a reader has to stop to see who is torn when the things go.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “without tearing us at all”. This is plainer than the draft, and it keeps the Latin image of the whole person being torn, where the suggestion speaks of a part torn away.

passages.latin: Nihil indignetur sibi accidere sciatque illa ipsa quibus laedi videtur ad conservationem universi pertinere et ex iis esse quae cursum mundi officiumque consummant; placeat homini quidquid deo placuit; ob hoc ipsum suaque miretur, quod non potest vinci, quod mala ipsa sub se tenet, quod ratione, qua valentius nihil est, casum doloremque et iniuriam subigit.
passages.english: Let him not be indignant at anything that happens to him, and let him know that the very things by which he seems to be harmed serve to preserve the universe and are among those that bring the course of the world and its task to completion. Let whatever has pleased god please man. For this very reason let him admire himself and what is his: that he cannot be conquered, that he holds evils themselves beneath him, that by reason, and nothing is stronger than reason, he subdues chance and pain and wrong.

notes.note: The subject “he” is the man of the section before, and these wishes answer the question there about what the inner equipment is. Nihil may be the subject of “happen” (“that anything happens to him”) or adverbial (“let him in no way resent what happens”). The sense is close either way.
notes.other_reading: Let him in no way resent what befalls him

notes.note: “Seems to be harmed”: the seeming may be his own impression or how it looks to others. The English leaves it as open as the Latin.
notes.other_reading: by which he thinks he is harmed

notes.note: Pertinere ad is to bear on or tend towards. The Latin has a noun, “the preservation of the universe”; the English turns it into a verb.
notes.other_reading: have to do with the preservation of the universe

notes.note: Officium is duty, function or appointed task; it is said here of the world itself. Consummare is to bring to a full total, to complete. Mundus is “world” and universi just before is “universe”; Seneca may mean no difference between them.
notes.other_reading: that fulfil the course and function of the universe

notes.note: One verb, placere, is used of god and of man; “please” is kept for both. Deus is singular, “god”, as in the glossary.
notes.other_reading: let man approve whatever god has approved

notes.note: As given, the Latin does not quite construe: the “and” in suaque has no first object to join. “Himself” is supplied on the assumption that se has dropped out before suaque; editions are believed to print se suaque (from memory, unchecked). If the Latin is read as it stands, ipsum has to serve as “himself” and “very” goes.
notes.other_reading: For this let him admire himself and what is his

notes.note: Mirari is to admire or to wonder at. “Admire” is used because the sense is to think highly of, not to be puzzled by.
notes.other_reading: let him wonder at himself and what is his

notes.note: “Evils themselves”, said from the ordinary point of view: for a Stoic these are not truly evils. The plain word is kept.
notes.other_reading: the very things called bad

notes.note: Casus is chance, accident or mishap; dolor is “pain” in the glossary and could be grief; iniuria is a wrong or injury done to one by another. The English reads “chance and pain and wrong”.
notes.other_reading: misfortune, grief and injustice

check.note: The Latin as given does not construe cleanly: the “and” attached to sua needs a first object, and there is none unless ipsum is made to serve as “himself”. The English uses ipsum for “this very” and also supplies “himself”; a se has probably dropped out (from memory, unchecked), and the supplied word should be declared.
check.decided: Accepted: “himself” is kept, and the note now says plainly that it is supplied on the assumption that se has dropped out, and gives the reading of the Latin as it stands. Either way the English has “himself and what is his”.

check.note: “Wonder at himself” suggests puzzlement in today’s English; mirari here is to admire, to think highly of.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “let him admire himself and what is his”. Mirari here is to think highly of, and “wonder at” suggests puzzlement.

check.note: “Belong to the preservation” is unclear; pertinere ad here is to bear on, to serve.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “serve to preserve the universe”. Pertinere ad is to bear on or contribute to, and “belong to the preservation” did not say that clearly.

check.note: “Than which” is bookish English.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “by reason, and nothing is stronger than reason,”. The sense is unchanged and “than which” is gone.

passages.latin: De hoc loco aliquid cogitemus: bene nobiscum agetur, si in hunc admittimur numerum. Magna felicitate naturae magnaque et adsidua intentione studii secundus occupatur gradus; sed ne hic quidem contemnendus est color tertius. Cogita quantum circa te videas malorum; aspice quam nullum sit nefas sine exemplo, quantum cotidie nequitia proficiat, quantum publice privatimque peccetur: intelleges satis nos consequi, si inter pessimos non sumus.
passages.english: Let us give some thought to this rank: it will go well with us if we are admitted to this group. The second step is won through great good fortune in one’s nature and through great and unremitting effort in study; but not even this third colour is to be despised. Think how much evil you see around you; look how there is no outrage without a precedent, how much progress wickedness makes every day, how much wrong is done in public and in private: you will understand that we attain enough if we are not among the worst.

notes.note: Locus is place or rank; here it is the third class of people making progress, described in the section before. It could also mean “topic”. Cogitare de can mean to think about or to set one’s mind on as an aim; “thought” is kept so that it matches “Think” below (cogita).
notes.other_reading: Let us aim at this rank

notes.note: An idiom, literally “it will be dealt well with us”: to be well treated, to be doing well.
notes.other_reading: it will be a good outcome for us

notes.note: Numerus is a number in the sense of a class or company. The verb is present tense in the Latin, where English also uses a present after “if”.
notes.other_reading: to be admitted to this number

notes.note: Felicitas is good fortune; with naturae it means a lucky natural endowment. “Good fortune” matches Ep. 74.18; “one’s” is added for plain English.
notes.other_reading: by great gifts of nature

notes.note: Intentio is a straining or stretching, so effort or application; studium is study or earnest pursuit, kept as “study”.
notes.other_reading: by great and constant application to study

notes.note: Occupare is to seize or take possession of; gradus is a step or rank. The English reads “is won”, with good fortune and effort as the means. The Latin has no “only”, though the sense leans that way, and none is added.
notes.other_reading: the second rank is reached

notes.note: Literally “third colour”, where “class” or “kind” would be expected: the third class of people making progress is meant. What the image is drawn from (a shade, a cast, a mark of rank) is not clear, and “colour” is kept as an image. The text may be doubted.
notes.other_reading: this third kind

notes.latin: quam nullum sit nefas sine exemplo
notes.note: Exemplum can be a precedent (every crime has been done before), an instance (every crime is in fact being committed) or a model to copy. Sine exemplo usually means “unprecedented”, so the English reads “without a precedent”. Nefas is a crime in the strong sense of something abominable.
notes.other_reading: how no abomination lacks its example

notes.note: Proficere, to make progress, is Seneca’s usual word for moral progress; here it is wickedness that progresses, which looks like deliberate irony. The English keeps “progress”.
notes.other_reading: how far wickedness advances every day

notes.note: An impersonal passive: “how much wrongdoing there is”. Publice and privatim can mean in public and in private, or by communities and by individuals. The English keeps the passive and takes the first.
notes.other_reading: how much wrong is done by states and by individuals

check.note: Locus here is a position or rank among the classes of people making progress; “this place” reads as a location.
check.decided: Accepted: “this place” becomes “this rank”. Locus here is a position among the classes of people making progress, not a location.

check.note: “Admitted to this number” is dated; numerus is the group or class.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “admitted to this group”. Numerus here is a class or company of people.

check.note: The two phrases name means, not doers: the second rank is reached through gifts of nature and through application. “Is taken by great good fortune” reads as if good fortune takes the step.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “The second step is won through”, so that good fortune and effort are the means and not the doers. “Won” is used rather than “reached” because occupare is to take possession of.

check.note: “Good fortune of nature” is unclear; the sense is being very fortunate in one’s natural gifts.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “through great good fortune in one’s nature”, as suggested. The second half keeps “effort” rather than “application”, because intentio is a straining.

check.note: A reader today will not know what a “third colour” of person is. Color is used here for a kind or shade.
check.decided: Declined: “this third colour” stands. The Latin word is color, and the translator’s brief keeps an image as an image; “kind” would drop it and “shade” would add a faintness the Latin does not have. The note says that the third class is meant.

check.note: Exemplum here is a precedent, a case already committed; “without its example” is unclear, and “its” is added.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “how there is no outrage without a precedent”. Sine exemplo is the usual Latin for “unprecedented”, and the added “its” is gone.

check.note: Nefas is stronger than a crime: something forbidden outright, an abomination.
check.decided: Accepted: “crime” becomes “outrage”. Nefas is an act forbidden outright, which is stronger than a breach of law.

check.note: Found while settling: the Latin repeats quantum (“how much”) three times, and the draft’s “how far wickedness advances” breaks the run. Proficere is also Seneca’s usual verb for making moral progress, which “advances” hides.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “how much progress wickedness makes every day”, which keeps the repeated “how much” and the word “progress”.

passages.latin: Pudet autem me generis humani quotiens scholam intravi. Praeter ipsum theatrum Neapolitanorum, ut scis, transeundum est Metronactis petenti domum. Illud quidem fartum est, et ingenti studio quis sit pythaules bonus iudicatur; habet tubicen quoque Graecus et praeco concursum: at in illo loco in quo vir bonus quaeritur, in quo vir bonus discitur, paucissimi sedent, et hi plerisque videntur nihil boni negotii habere quod agant; inepti et inertes vocantur. Mihi contingat iste derisus: aequo animo audienda sunt inperitorum convicia et ad honesta vadenti contemnendus est ipse contemptus.
passages.english: But I am ashamed of the human race every time I go into the school. As you know, anyone making for Metronax’s house has to pass right by the theatre of the Neapolitans. That place, to be sure, is packed, and with enormous eagerness judgment is passed on who is a good piper; a Greek trumpeter and a herald draw a crowd as well. But in the place where a good man is what is inquired into, where a good man is what is learned, very few sit, and to most people these seem to have no good business to be about; they are called silly and idle. May that mockery fall to me: the abuse of the ignorant must be heard with a calm mind, and one who is heading for what is honourable must hold contempt itself in contempt.

notes.note: Schola here is the philosopher’s lecture room, that of Metronax at Naples, whose house the next sentence names. The perfect with quotiens marks a repeated action, so the English has a present.
notes.other_reading: whenever I have entered the lecture hall

notes.note: A Greek word for a player of the pipe (aulos), by its make-up one who plays the Pythian piece; from memory, unchecked, it is also used of a solo piper in the theatre. The English narrows it to “piper”.
notes.other_reading: Pythian piper

notes.note: Impersonal passive, literally “it is judged who is a good piper”. Bonus is then repeated for the good man and for “good business”, so “good” is kept each time.
notes.other_reading: they decide who is a fine piper

notes.latin: habet tubicen quoque Graecus et praeco concursum
notes.note: Graecus agrees with tubicen, but it may be meant to colour the herald too. The English leaves it with the trumpeter only.
notes.other_reading: a Greek trumpeter and a Greek herald also draw a crowd

notes.latin: in quo vir bonus quaeritur, in quo vir bonus discitur
notes.note: Literally “where a good man is sought, where a good man is learned”. Quaeritur can mean “is looked for” or “is inquired into”; set against the theatre, where the question judged is who is a good piper, the English takes the second. Discitur leaves open whether what is learned is what a good man is or how to be one, and the English keeps that open and keeps the two clauses parallel.
notes.other_reading: where a good man is looked for, where one learns to be a good man

notes.latin: nihil boni negotii habere quod agant
notes.note: Literally “to have nothing of good business that they might do”. Boni carries on the play on “good”, so the word is kept.
notes.other_reading: to have nothing worthwhile to occupy them

notes.note: An idiom for taking something calmly, literally “with a level mind”. “Mind” is kept for animus, as the glossary prefers, and “calm” stands for aequus; the same phrase is given the same way at 76.23.
notes.other_reading: calmly

notes.note: Inperitus is one without knowledge or skill. “The ignorant” fits here, where the point is that they do not know what the school is for; at 76.34 the same word is “the inexperienced”.
notes.other_reading: the jeers of the inexperienced

notes.note: A play on contemnere and contemptus, kept with “contempt” twice.
notes.other_reading: being despised is itself to be despised

check.note: Quaeritur can mean “is looked for” or “is inquired into”. Beside the theatre’s judging of who is a good piper, the likelier sense is that the school asks what a good man is, and “is sought” reads as a hunt for one.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “where a good man is what is inquired into”, because the clause answers the theatre’s question of who is a good piper. The suggested wording is not used, so that “a good man” stays in first place as in the Latin and the next clause can match it.

check.note: The Latin is literally “where a good man is learned”. “Where one learns to be a good man” supplies words, decides that the learning is how to become one, and loses the parallel of the two clauses.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “where a good man is what is learned”, which adds no “one” or “to be” and leaves open whether the lesson is what a good man is or how to become one. The wording differs from the suggestion so that the two clauses run in parallel.

check.note: Quidem is dropped. It marks the concession that the later “at” answers.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “That place, to be sure, is packed”. Quidem grants the point that the “But” of the next sentence then answers.

check.note: “With an even mind” is not something a reader of today says. The same phrase occurs at 76.23, so the two should change together.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “with a calm mind” here and at 76.23. “Even mind” is not current English, but “mind” is kept for animus as the glossary prefers, so the phrase is not cut down to “calmly”.

passages.latin: Perge, Lucili, et propera, ne tibi accidat quod mihi, ut senex discas; immo ideo magis propera quoniam id nunc adgressus es quod perdiscere vix senex possis. 'Quantum' inquis 'proficiam?' Quantum temptaveris.
passages.english: Keep going, Lucilius, and hurry, so that what has happened to me does not happen to you: to be learning as an old man. Or rather, hurry all the more for this reason, that you have now taken on something you could hardly learn through to the end as an old man. “How much progress shall I make?” you say. As much as you attempt.

notes.latin: ne tibi accidat quod mihi, ut senex discas
notes.note: The ut clause spells out what has happened to Seneca: he is learning as an old man. The English sets it after a colon so that it attaches to the thing that happens and to nothing else.
notes.other_reading: so that it does not happen to you, as it has to me, that you learn as an old man

notes.note: Open: either the subject is so large that one can hardly finish learning it by the time one is old, or it is one that a man already old could hardly master. The English adds nothing and so leaves both readings standing, as the Latin does.
notes.other_reading: something that you could hardly learn thoroughly if you were an old man

notes.note: The form is either future indicative or present subjunctive; the English takes the future. Proficere is the usual word for a learner’s progress in philosophy.
notes.other_reading: How far am I to get?

notes.note: Future perfect, literally “as much as you will have attempted”. English uses a present in such a clause.
notes.other_reading: As far as you will have tried.

check.note: “Even” is not in the Latin, which says only that he could hardly learn it through as an old man.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “something you could hardly learn through to the end as an old man”. The Latin has no word for “even”, and without it the English is as open as the Latin.

check.note: The Latin is a clause that explains what has happened to Seneca. The participle “learning as an old man” dangles and can be attached to either person or to nothing.
check.decided: Accepted: the phrase now stands after a colon as “to be learning as an old man”. It explains the thing that happens, as the Latin clause does, and no longer dangles.

passages.latin: Omnia suo bono constant. Vitem fertilitas commendat et sapor vini, velocitas cervum; quam fortia dorso iumenta sint quaeris, quorum hic unus est usus, sarcinam ferre; in cane sagacitas prima est, si investigare debet feras, cursus, si consequi, audacia, si mordere et invadere: id in quoque optimum esse debet cui nascitur, quo censetur.
passages.english: Every thing rests on its own good. What recommends the vine is its fruitfulness and the flavour of its wine; what recommends the stag is speed. Of pack animals, whose one use is this, to carry a load, you ask how strong they are in the back. In a dog the first thing is keenness of scent if it has to track wild animals, running if it has to catch them, boldness if it has to bite and attack. In each thing, what ought to be best is that for which it is born, that by which it is rated.

notes.note: Constare with the ablative can mean “consist in”, “depend on” or “stand firm by”. The English takes it that each thing rests on the good that is its own, and “rests” keeps the sense of standing. Bonum is “good” as in the glossary.
notes.other_reading: All things consist in their own good.

notes.note: One verb serves both the vine and the stag, and the English repeats it. It means what makes a thing valued.
notes.other_reading: Fruitfulness and the flavour of its wine commend the vine, speed the stag

notes.latin: quam fortia dorso iumenta sint quaeris
notes.note: A general “you”, kept as the Latin has it. Iumenta are beasts of burden.
notes.other_reading: one asks how strong in the back beasts of burden are

notes.note: Of a dog this is keenness of scent; of a person it would be shrewdness.
notes.other_reading: sharpness

notes.note: Cui is a dative of purpose, “for which it is born”. Censeri is the word for being assessed in the census, so “rated”.
notes.other_reading: that for which it comes into being and by which it is valued

check.note: In English “stands by” means “stays loyal to”, which is not the sense. Constare with the ablative says that things consist in or depend on their own good.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “Every thing rests on its own good”. “Stands by” suggested loyalty; “rests on” gives the dependence the Latin verb expresses and keeps its root sense of standing, which “depend” would lose.

check.note: “Since” is added. The Latin is a plain relative clause.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Of pack animals, whose one use is this, to carry a load, you ask how strong they are in the back”. The Latin gives a relative clause and no “since”.

check.latin: id in quoque optimum esse debet cui nascitur, quo censetur
check.note: The sense is right but the sentence is hard to parse: “that” can be taken as a conjunction and the two relative clauses trail after the verb.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “In each thing, what ought to be best is that for which it is born, that by which it is rated”. The sentence is recast so that it parses at first reading, but “the quality” is not added, since the Latin has only “that”.

passages.latin: In homine quid est optimum? ratio: hac antecedit animalia, deos sequitur. Ratio ergo perfecta proprium bonum est, cetera illi cum animalibus satisque communia sunt. Valet: et leones. Formonsus est: et pavones. Velox est: et equi. Non dico, in his omnibus vincitur; non quaero quid in se maximum habeat, sed quid suum. Corpus habet: et arbores. Habet impetum ac motum voluntarium: et bestiae et vermes. Habet vocem: sed quanto clariorem canes, acutiorem aquilae, graviorem tauri, dulciorem mobilioremque luscinii?
passages.english: What is best in a human being? Reason: by this he goes ahead of the animals and comes next after the gods. So perfected reason is the good peculiar to him; everything else he has in common with animals and plants. He is strong: so are lions. He is handsome: so are peacocks. He is swift: so are horses. I say nothing of his being outdone in all these; I am not asking what he has in him that is greatest, but what is his own. He has a body: so do trees. He has impulse and voluntary movement: so do beasts and worms. He has a voice: but how much louder is the dogs’, how much shriller the eagles’, deeper the bulls’, sweeter and more supple the nightingales’?

notes.note: Homo is the human being as a kind, not the male. The English has “a human being” and then “he” for the pronouns.
notes.other_reading: In man

notes.note: Sequitur can mean “comes next after” in rank or “follows” as one follows a leader. Paired with going ahead of the animals, it is taken as rank.
notes.other_reading: by this he goes ahead of the animals and follows the gods

notes.latin: Ratio ergo perfecta proprium bonum est
notes.note: Ratio is “reason” (the Stoic term). Perfecta is reason brought to completion; “perfect” is used for this verb through 76.9 and 76.10 because the argument turns on it. Proprium is what belongs to him and to nothing else, so “peculiar to him”.
notes.other_reading: So reason brought to completion is his proper good

notes.note: Sata are literally “things sown”, that is crops or plants.
notes.other_reading: and with crops

notes.latin: Non dico, in his omnibus vincitur
notes.note: The Latin sets the plain statement that he is outdone beside non dico, with nothing joining them. The English takes this as passing over a point that is granted; it could be read as declining to make the claim.
notes.other_reading: I am not saying that in all these he is outdone

notes.note: Impetus is the Stoic term for the impulse that sets a living thing moving, and “impulse” is kept.
notes.other_reading: drive and movement at will

notes.note: Clarior can be “louder” or “clearer”; for dogs the English takes “louder”. Acutior is high and piercing.
notes.other_reading: how much clearer the dogs’, how much higher the eagles’

notes.note: A masculine form of the usual luscinia, nightingale. It is read as nominative plural, parallel to the other animals; it could be genitive singular.
notes.other_reading: the nightingale’s

check.latin: Non dico, in his omnibus vincitur
check.note: The Latin sets the indicative vincitur beside non dico with no construction. The natural reading passes the point over and so grants it, while the draft reads as declining to claim that he is outdone.
check.decided: Accepted: the clause now reads “say nothing of his being outdone in all these”, which passes the point over while granting it. The Latin states the outdoing as a fact, and the next clause, which asks not what is greatest in him but what is his own, fits that reading.

check.note: Sequitur can be rank or following as a guide. Paired with antecedit animalia, rank is likelier, and “follows the gods” suggests obedience.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “comes next after the gods”. Set beside going ahead of the animals, the verb gives a place in an order; the reading “follows the gods” is kept in a note.

passages.latin: Quid est in homine proprium? ratio: haec recta et consummata felicitatem hominis implevit. Ergo si omnis res, cum bonum suum perfecit, laudabilis est et ad finem naturae suae pervenit, homini autem suum bonum ratio est, si hanc perfecit laudabilis est et finem naturae suae tetigit. Haec ratio perfecta virtus vocatur eademque honestum est.
passages.english: What is peculiar to a human being? Reason: when this is right and brought to its full measure, it has made a human being’s happiness complete. So if every thing, when it has perfected its own good, is praiseworthy and has reached the goal of its nature, and if a human being’s own good is reason, then if he has perfected this he is praiseworthy and has touched the goal of his nature. This perfected reason is called virtue, and it is also what is honourable.

notes.note: Consummata is “brought to its sum”, finished off. It is kept distinct from perfecta, for which the English has “perfected”.
notes.other_reading: upright and consummate

notes.note: Felicitas, not beata vita; “happiness” is used all the same, since “good fortune” would mislead here. The perfect implevit states a general truth; literally “has filled up”.
notes.other_reading: fills up the measure of human good fortune

notes.note: Perficere is to carry through to completion. “Perfect” is used for it each time (perfecit, perfecit, perfecta) so that the chain of the argument shows.
notes.other_reading: when it has brought its own good to completion

notes.note: The subject is not stated; it is taken to be the human being, with hanc as reason.
notes.other_reading: if it has perfected this

notes.note: Finis is the end in the sense of goal, and “goal” is used both times so that it is not read as a stopping. Tetigit is literally “has touched”, and the image is kept.
notes.other_reading: has attained the end of his nature

notes.note: Literally “and the same thing is the honourable”. Honestum is “what is honourable”, as in the glossary.
notes.other_reading: and this same thing is what is honourable

check.note: “End” here means goal, but “the end of its nature” can be read as its nature coming to a stop. The same applies to the second finem in the sentence, and one word should serve both.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “has reached the goal of its nature” and, later, “the goal of his nature”. Finis here is the aim a nature is made for, and “end” could be read as that nature stopping.

check.note: Found while settling: “has attained” flattens tetigit, which is literally “has touched” and is a different verb from the pervenit (“has reached”) of the clause before.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “has touched the goal of his nature”. The image of touching the goal is in the Latin and is plain in English once “goal” is the noun.

passages.latin: Virum bonum concedas necesse est summae pietatis erga deos esse. Itaque quidquid illi accidit aequo animo sustinebit; sciet enim id accidisse lege divina qua universa procedunt. Quod si est, unum illi bonum erit quod honestum; in hoc enim positum et parere diis nec excandescere ad subita nec deplorare sortem suam, sed patienter excipere fatum et facere imperata.
passages.english: You must grant that the good man is a man of the highest piety towards the gods. So whatever happens to him he will bear with a calm mind; for he will know that it has happened by the divine law by which all things go forward. If that is so, the one good for him will be what is honourable; for in this lies obeying the gods, and not flaring up at sudden events or bewailing his lot, but patiently accepting fate and doing what is commanded.

notes.note: Pietas is dutiful devotion, wider than the English “piety”. “Piety” is kept because the gods are named.
notes.other_reading: of the greatest dutifulness towards the gods

notes.note: Aequo animo is an idiom for taking something calmly, literally “with a level mind”. The English has “with a calm mind”, keeping the glossary’s “mind” for animus, as at 76.4.
notes.other_reading: he will bear calmly

notes.note: Universa is “all things together”, close to “the universe”. Procedunt is “go forward, take their course”.
notes.other_reading: by the divine law under which the whole proceeds

notes.latin: unum illi bonum erit quod honestum
notes.note: Unum is “one” in the sense “the only”. Illi can be “for him” or “in his eyes”; the English has “for him”.
notes.other_reading: in his eyes the only good will be what is honourable

notes.note: The verb est is understood. Hoc may point back to what is honourable, or forward to the list of infinitives; it is taken as pointing back.
notes.other_reading: for what is honourable consists in this: to obey the gods

notes.note: Excandescere is literally “to grow white hot”, used of flaring up in anger. Subita are things that come suddenly.
notes.other_reading: to blaze up at the unexpected

notes.note: A phrase with a military ring, “to carry out orders”.
notes.other_reading: carrying out orders

check.note: The same phrase as at 76.4, where “with an even mind” was found not to be current English. The two places should change together.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “with a calm mind”, as at 76.4. The phrase is brought into current English but keeps “mind” for animus, as the glossary prefers, in place of the bare “calmly”.

check.latin: et parere diis nec excandescere ad subita nec deplorare sortem suam
check.note: The sense is right, but “both, and neither, nor” is heavy and hard to follow in English.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “for in this lies obeying the gods, and not flaring up at sudden events or bewailing his lot”. Nothing in the Latin is lost and the heavy run of “both, and neither, nor” is gone.

passages.latin: Sed ille quoque cui etiam hoc gaudium eripitur quod tractatio operis maximi et ultimi praestat, nihil cunctatus desiliet in mortem, facere recte pieque contentus. Oppone etiamnunc illi multa quae dehortentur, dic, 'factum tuum matura sequetur oblivio et parum grata existimatio civium'. Respondebit tibi, 'ista omnia extra opus meum sunt, ego ipsum contemplor; hoc esse honestum scio; itaque quocumque ducit ac vocat venio'.
passages.english: But even the man from whom this joy too is snatched away, the joy that the handling of his greatest and last work gives, will leap down into death without any hesitation, content to act rightly and dutifully. Go further and set against him many things to dissuade him; say: “Your deed will be followed by early oblivion and by a less than grateful verdict from your fellow citizens.” He will answer you: “All those things lie outside my work; I am looking at the work itself. I know that this is honourable; so wherever it leads and calls, I come.”

notes.note: “This joy” is the one in the section before: the pleasure a brave man takes in looking ahead to the deed he is about to do.
notes.other_reading: even this joy

notes.note: Tractatio is “handling”. It can be handling in thought, which the section before describes, or the actual carrying out of the deed; “handling” leaves both open.
notes.other_reading: dwelling on his greatest and last work; or, the carrying out of his greatest and last work

notes.note: The image is of jumping down, as from a height or a horse, and it is kept.
notes.other_reading: will plunge into death

notes.note: Pie is the adverb of pietas, acting as duty to gods, country and kin requires. The English has “dutifully”; “piously” would be too narrow here.
notes.other_reading: rightly and piously

notes.note: Etiamnunc is “even now” or “still further”. It is taken as adding a further test.
notes.other_reading: Even now set against him

notes.note: Existimatio is what the citizens think of the deed; “verdict” is used because the glossary keeps “judgment” for iudicium and “opinion” for opinio. Grata can be “grateful” or “favourable, pleasing”, and parum is “too little”; the English takes the citizens’ view as short of grateful.
notes.other_reading: a verdict from your fellow citizens that is far from favourable

notes.note: The subject of ducit and vocat is not stated: it is either what is honourable or the work, and “it” leaves that open. Venio is kept as “come”, in the present tense.
notes.other_reading: wherever what is honourable leads and calls, I go

check.note: Tractatio is “handling”, which can be handling in thought or the actual carrying out of the deed. “Dwelling on” silently chooses the mental sense.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the handling of his greatest and last work”. Tractatio does not say whether the handling is in thought or in the doing, and the note records both.

check.note: “Estimate” is the wrong word for existimatio, which is what people think of a person or deed, and “none too” is dated. Grata could also be “favourable”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “a less than grateful verdict from your fellow citizens”. “Estimate” and “none too” are gone, but “judgment” is not used because the glossary keeps it for iudicium; that grata may mean “favourable” is recorded in the note.

check.note: “Put him off” is ambiguous in English (delay him, or repel him). Dehortari is to dissuade.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “many things to dissuade him”. Dehortari is to argue someone out of a course, and “put him off” could also mean to delay him.

passages.latin: Nemo ex istis quos purpuratos vides felix est, non magis quam ex illis quibus sceptrum et chlamydem in scaena fabulae adsignant: cum praesente populo lati incesserunt et coturnati, simul exierunt, excalceantur et ad staturam suam redeunt. Nemo istorum quos divitiae honoresque in altiore fastigio ponunt magnus est. Quare ergo magnus videtur? cum basi illum sua metiris. Non est magnus pumilio licet in monte constiterit; colossus magnitudinem suam servabit etiam si steterit in puteo.
passages.english: None of those whom you see dressed in purple is happy, any more than any of those to whom the plays assign a sceptre and a cloak on the stage: when they have walked before the people with a broad swagger and in high boots, the moment they have gone off, their boots are taken off and they return to their own stature. None of those whom riches and offices set at a greater height is great. Why then does he seem great? You are measuring him together with his pedestal. A dwarf is not great though he has taken his stand on a mountain; a colossus will keep its greatness even if it stands in a well.

notes.note: Men in purple, that is courtiers and men of high rank, purple being the dress of kings and their courts.
notes.other_reading: the courtiers in purple

notes.note: Felix, not beatus. It leans towards “fortunate”, but “happy” is used to match “happiness” for felicitas at 76.10.
notes.other_reading: fortunate

notes.note: Fabulae is taken as nominative plural, the subject of adsignant. It could be genitive singular with scaena, leaving the verb with an unnamed “they”.
notes.other_reading: to whom they assign a sceptre and a cloak on the stage of a play

notes.note: A chlamys is a Greek cloak, here the mantle of a stage king. The English has only “cloak”, as the Latin does.
notes.other_reading: a royal cloak

notes.note: Lati is “broad”, of a walk and bearing that take up room, or of the padded figure of the tragic actor; the English takes it of the walk. From memory, unchecked, some editions print elati, “raised up”. Coturnati is “wearing the cothurnus”, the tragic actor’s boot with a thick sole.
notes.other_reading: have walked raised up and in high boots

notes.note: Fastigium is a gable or peak, and so high rank. The English keeps the image as “height”, and statura in the sentence before is “stature” so that the two are not confused.
notes.other_reading: on a higher summit

notes.note: Basis is the pedestal of a statue. The sentence answers the question and is taken as a statement.
notes.other_reading: Because you measure him pedestal and all.

notes.note: Magnus means both “great” and “big, tall”, and the passage moves from one to the other. “Great” and “greatness” are kept throughout so that the argument can be followed.
notes.other_reading: A dwarf is not tall

notes.note: A giant statue, like the one at Rhodes.
notes.other_reading: a giant statue

check.note: “Royal” is an explanation folded into the text. The Latin has only the cloak, and the sceptre already carries the idea of kingship.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a sceptre and a cloak”. The Latin names only the cloak; that it is a stage king’s is left to the sceptre and to a note.

check.note: “Broad” on its own is not clear English. The Latin means that they walked spreading themselves wide, which “strutted” already half says, so the image comes twice and the second time obscurely.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “when they have walked before the people with a broad swagger and in high boots”. “Broad” alone was unclear, and “strutted” said the same thing a second time.

check.note: “A higher summit” is odd English, since no other summit is in view. Fastigium here is height or elevation of rank.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “set at a greater height”, which keeps the image of elevation without the odd “higher summit”; “loftier” is not used because it is not plain English of today. Statura in the sentence before becomes “stature” so that “height” does not stand for two Latin words.

passages.latin: Hoc laboramus errore, sic nobis inponitur, quod neminem aestimamus eo quod est, sed adicimus illi et ea quibus adornatus est. Atqui cum voles veram hominis aestimationem inire et scire qualis sit, nudum inspice; ponat patrimonium, ponat honores et alia fortunae mendacia, corpus ipsum exuat: animum intuere, qualis quantusque sit, alieno an suo magnus.
passages.english: This is the error we suffer from, this is how we are taken in: we value no one by what he is, but add to him the things he is decked out with as well. Yet when you want to make a true valuation of a human being and to know what he is like, examine him naked; let him lay aside his estate, let him lay aside his offices and the other lies of fortune, let him strip off even his body: look at his mind, what it is like and how great, whether it is great by what is another’s or by what is its own.

notes.note: Impersonal passive of imponere with the dative, in the sense “to deceive, to impose on”.
notes.other_reading: this is the trick played on us

notes.note: A phrase from reckoning accounts, “to enter on a valuation”. “Value” and “valuation” are kept for aestimamus and aestimationem.
notes.other_reading: to arrive at a true estimate of a human being

notes.note: A man’s estate, often but not only property that has come down to him from his father. The English has “his estate” and does not press the inheritance.
notes.other_reading: his inherited wealth

notes.note: Mendacia are lies or shams. Fortune is close to being a person here; the English leaves it in lower case, and a capital would also be defensible.
notes.other_reading: Fortune’s other shams

notes.note: Exuere is to take off clothing; the body is treated as one more garment.
notes.other_reading: let him take off his very body

notes.note: Animus is set against the body here, but not as what survives it, so the glossary’s “mind” is kept. Intuere is “look at”, distinct from inspice (“examine”) earlier in the sentence.
notes.other_reading: look at his soul

notes.note: Alieno and suo are neuter ablatives, “by what belongs to another or by what is his own”. Magnus could agree with the mind (animus is masculine) or with the man; the English takes the mind.
notes.other_reading: whether he is great by another’s goods or by his own

check.note: Patrimonium is a man’s estate or property in general. “Inherited” narrows it and suggests a point about inheritance that Seneca is not making.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “his estate”. Patrimonium is a man’s property as a whole, and “inherited” brought in a point that the sentence does not make.

check.note: The Latin has two verbs, inspice here and intuere for the mind later, and both were given as “look at”. Inspice fits the image of examining goods before pricing them.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “examine him naked”, and “look at” is kept for intuere alone. The two Latin verbs now have two English verbs.

check.note: A point of consistency: homo is “a human being” at 76.9 and 76.10 of the same letter and “a man” here.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “a true valuation of a human being”, the same words as for homo at 76.9 and 76.10, in place of “a man”. The suggested “a person” would have brought in a third rendering.

passages.latin: Praecogitati mali mollis ictus venit. At stultis et fortunae credentibus omnis videtur nova rerum et inopinata facies; magna autem pars est apud inperitos mali novitas. Hoc ut scias, ea quae putaverant aspera fortius, cum adsuevere, patiuntur.
passages.english: When an evil has been thought out beforehand, its blow comes soft. But to fools and to those who trust fortune every face that events show seems new and unexpected; and for the inexperienced a great part of an evil is its newness. So that you may know this: the things they had thought harsh they bear more bravely once they have grown used to them.

notes.note: Malum is “an evil”, the opposite of bonum; here it is a misfortune that falls on someone. “Evil” is kept for both occurrences.
notes.other_reading: a trouble foreseen

notes.note: Those who trust fortune, that is, who count on their luck lasting.
notes.other_reading: those who put their faith in luck

notes.note: This takes up the words of the verse quoted in the section before, where no face of hardship rises new or unexpected (Vergil, Aeneid 6, about lines 103 to 105; from memory, unchecked). “Face”, “new” and “unexpected” are kept so that the echo shows, and rerum is given as “events”.
notes.other_reading: every turn of events seems strange and unforeseen

notes.note: At 76.4 the same word is “the ignorant”. Here the point is lack of experience of trouble, as the next sentence on growing used to things shows, so “the inexperienced” fits the argument better.
notes.other_reading: among the ignorant

notes.note: An idiom that introduces a proof, literally “so that you may know this”. The second person, which is Lucilius, is kept.
notes.other_reading: To see that this is so

notes.note: “More bravely” or “more firmly”.
notes.other_reading: with more strength

check.note: The reader first takes “an evil thought” as a noun phrase and has to start again. The sense is right but the sentence misleads on first reading.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “When an evil has been thought out beforehand, its blow comes soft”. The words “an evil thought” no longer run together, and “soft” stays an adjective of the blow as in the Latin.

check.note: The second person is dropped. Seneca addresses Lucilius: “that you may know this”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “So that you may know this:”. Scias is second person, addressed to Lucilius, and the draft had dropped it.

check.note: Inperiti can be the inexperienced or, more broadly, the ignorant or untrained; the word is “the ignorant” at 76.4 and stands parallel to stultis here. “Inexperienced” fits the point about newness but is a choice.
check.decided: Declined: “for the inexperienced” stands. The next sentence proves the point from people growing used to hardships, so want of experience is the sense the argument needs here, and the note records “the ignorant” as the other reading and as the rendering at 76.4.

check.latin: omnis videtur nova rerum et inopinata facies
check.note: “Face of things” is obscure in English. The phrase echoes the verse quoted in the section before, so the word used should match the rendering of that verse.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “every face that events show seems new and unexpected”. “Things” becomes “events” for clarity, but “face” is kept because the Latin word is an image and repeats the facies of the verse quoted just before.

passages.latin: Iter inperfectum erit si in media parte aut citra petitum locum steteris: vita non est inperfecta si honesta est; ubicumque desines, si bene desines, tota est. Saepe autem et fortiter desinendum est et non ex maximis causis; nam nec eae maximae sunt quae nos tenent.
passages.english: A journey will be incomplete if you stop in the middle of it or short of the place you were making for. A life is not incomplete if it is honourable; wherever you leave off, if you leave off well, it is whole. But often one must leave off both bravely and for reasons that are not the greatest; for the reasons that hold us are not the greatest either.

notes.note: “Not carried through”, unfinished. The English has “incomplete” both times; “imperfect” would suggest a flaw, which is not the point.
notes.other_reading: unfinished

notes.note: Literally “on this side of the place sought”.
notes.other_reading: before reaching your destination

notes.latin: ubicumque desines, si bene desines, tota est
notes.note: Desinere is “to stop, to leave off”, here to leave off living. Both verbs are future, and the English uses the present. The subject of tota est is the life.
notes.other_reading: wherever you will end, if you end well, it is a whole life

notes.latin: et fortiter desinendum est et non ex maximis causis
notes.note: The two et are taken as “both” and “and”, pairing “bravely” with “not for the greatest reasons”. The first et could instead mean “also”, adding bravely to the “well” of the sentence before.
notes.other_reading: But often one must leave off bravely too, and not for the greatest reasons

notes.latin: nec eae maximae sunt quae nos tenent
notes.note: Eae picks up causae: the reasons that hold a person in life are not the greatest either. The Latin does not say “in life” and the English does not add it.
notes.other_reading: for neither are those the greatest reasons that keep us here

check.latin: et fortiter desinendum est et non ex maximis causis
check.note: The paired et is most naturally “both” and “and”. The draft took the first et as “too”, adding bravely to the “well” before it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “one must leave off both bravely and for reasons that are not the greatest”. The paired et is most naturally “both” and “and”; the reading “bravely too” is kept in the note.

passages.latin: Amicus noster Stoicus, homo egregius et, ut verbis illum quibus laudari dignus est laudem, vir fortis ac strenuus, videtur mihi optime illum cohortatus. Sic enim coepit: 'noli, mi Marcelline, torqueri tamquam de re magna deliberes. Non est res magna vivere: omnes servi tui vivunt, omnia animalia: magnum est honeste mori, prudenter, fortiter. Cogita quamdiu iam idem facias: cibus, somnus, libido -- per hunc circulum curritur; mori velle non tantum prudens aut fortis aut miser, etiam fastidiosus potest.'
passages.english: Our Stoic friend, an outstanding person and, to praise him in the words in which he deserves to be praised, a brave and energetic man, seems to me to have urged him on best. For he began like this: “Do not torment yourself, my Marcellinus, as if you were deliberating about a great matter. Living is not a great matter: all your slaves live, all animals do. The great thing is to die honourably, sensibly, bravely. Think how long you have now been doing the same thing: food, sleep, lust. This is the circle one runs round. Not only a sensible man or a brave one or a wretched one can want to die, but also one who is fed up.”

notes.note: The friend is not named. Noster may mark him simply as a friend the two men share, or as a particular Stoic whom Lucilius will recognise; the English takes the second.
notes.other_reading: A Stoic friend of ours

notes.note: Seneca flags this as a set form of praise. From memory, unchecked, it is an old Roman formula of commendation for a soldier or citizen.
notes.other_reading: a gallant and vigorous man

notes.note: Illum is Tullius Marcellinus, the sick man of the section before, who was deliberating about death. Optime may be “best of them all” or “excellently”; cohortari is to urge on or exhort, so “urged him on”.
notes.other_reading: to have exhorted him excellently

notes.note: Mi with the name is the affectionate form of address. The English keeps the bare possessive and adds no “dear”, which the Latin does not have.
notes.other_reading: my dear Marcellinus

notes.note: Passive in form, “to be tormented”. It is taken in a reflexive sense.
notes.other_reading: do not be tormented

notes.note: With practical good sense and foresight. The English has “sensibly”, and “sensible” for prudens in the last sentence, since “prudent” now suggests caution.
notes.other_reading: prudently

notes.note: Sexual desire, given as “lust”.
notes.other_reading: sex

notes.note: Impersonal passive, literally “through this circle there is running”. It is kept impersonal with “one”.
notes.other_reading: this is the round we run

notes.note: One who has had too much and turns away in distaste; the word can also mean squeamish or hard to please. “Fed up” gives the first sense without supplying an object that the Latin leaves unsaid.
notes.other_reading: the fastidious man

check.note: In today’s English “prudent” means cautious or careful with money, while prudenter and prudens mean with good sense and foresight. Whatever is chosen must serve for prudens at the end as well.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “to die honourably, sensibly, bravely” and, at the end, “a sensible man”. Prudens is a person of good sense and foresight, while “prudent” today suggests caution; one word is kept for both places.

check.note: “Dear” is added; the Latin has only the possessive.
check.decided: Accepted: “dear” is removed and the address keeps only the possessive that the Latin has. A note records the fuller form of address.

check.note: Fastidiosus is a man who feels distaste from having had too much, and can also be squeamish. “Sick of it” supplies an object that the Latin leaves unsaid.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “one who is fed up”, which gives the distaste of having had too much and supplies no object. “Merely” is not added, since the Latin has only etiam, “also”.

check.note: Cohortari is to exhort or urge on. “Encouraged” suggests cheering him up, whereas the friend is urging him to a decision.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “to have urged him on best”. Cohortari is to urge someone on, not to cheer him up, but the verb stays a verb in place of “given him the best exhortation”.

passages.latin: 'Sed ego' inquit 'vivere volo, qui multa honeste facio; invitus relinquo officia vitae, quibus fideliter et industrie fungor.' Quid? tu nescis unum esse ex vitae officiis et mori? Nullum officium relinquis; non enim certus numerus quem debeas explere finitur.
passages.english: “But I,” he says, “want to live, I who do many things honourably; it is against my will that I am leaving the duties of life, which I carry out faithfully and diligently.” What? Do you not know that to die is also one of the duties of life? You are leaving no duty; for no fixed number is laid down that you must complete.

notes.note: An imagined objector, spoken of in the third person and then answered directly as “you”. Both persons are kept as the Latin has them.
notes.other_reading: someone says

notes.note: The relative clause may give his reason for wanting to live. It is kept as a plain relative and no “because” is added.
notes.other_reading: since I do many honourable things

notes.note: Relinquo states that he is leaving; invitus says that it is against his will. The English keeps the leaving as a fact, since the reply takes up the same verb.
notes.other_reading: I am unwilling to leave the duties of life

notes.note: Officium is a duty or function owed. “Duty” is kept for all three occurrences, since the reply turns on the word.
notes.other_reading: the tasks of life

notes.latin: unum esse ex vitae officiis et mori
notes.note: Et here is “also” or “even”.
notes.other_reading: that even dying is one of life’s duties

notes.latin: non enim certus numerus quem debeas explere finitur
notes.note: The Latin does not say a number of what. A number of duties follows from the sentence before, and a number of years is possible; the English leaves it unstated as the Latin does. Finitur is “is marked off, is fixed as a limit”.
notes.other_reading: for no definite number of years is set that you must complete

check.note: The Latin says that he is leaving the duties, against his will. “Unwilling to leave” reads as a refusal, and the reply takes up the plain statement of leaving.
check.decided: Accepted: the objector now says that it is against his will that he is leaving the duties of life. Relinquo states the leaving as a fact and invitus only says how he takes it, so “unwilling to leave” read as a refusal that the Latin does not make.

check.note: Seneca throws the objector’s own verb back at him (relinquo, relinquis). “Leave” followed by “leaving behind” blunts the echo.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “You are leaving no duty”. The reply throws back the objector’s own verb, and “leaving” now answers “leaving” with nothing added.

check.latin: non enim certus numerus quem debeas explere finitur
check.note: One does not “fill” a number in English. Explere numerum is to make it up or complete it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “for no fixed number is laid down that you must complete”. A number is completed or made up in English, not filled.

passages.latin: Saepe impetum cepi abrumpendae vitae: patris me indulgentissimi senectus retinuit. Cogitavi enim non quam fortiter ego mori possem, sed quam ille fortiter desiderare non posset. Itaque imperavi mihi ut viverem; aliquando enim et vivere fortiter facere est.
passages.english: I often had the impulse to break off my life: the old age of my most loving father held me back. For I thought not of how bravely I could die, but of how far he was from being able to miss me bravely. So I ordered myself to live; for sometimes even to live is to act bravely.

notes.note: Impetus is a sudden impulse more than a settled plan, and abrumpere is to break or snap off. The English keeps the impulse and the image of breaking.
notes.other_reading: formed the resolve to cut life short

notes.note: The word covers kind, tender and indulgent. The English takes the sense of affection, not of spoiling.
notes.other_reading: most indulgent father

notes.latin: quam ille fortiter desiderare non posset
notes.note: Desiderare is to miss someone who is gone; its object is not in the Latin and is supplied. Quam is taken as measuring how far he was from being able, and fortiter is “bravely” all three times in the section.
notes.other_reading: but of how bravely he could not miss me

notes.note: Fortiter can go with facere (to live is to act bravely) or with vivere (to live bravely is a deed). The English takes it with facere, which answers the bravery of dying in the sentence before.
notes.other_reading: sometimes even to live bravely is a deed

check.latin: quam ille fortiter desiderare non posset
check.note: The Latin has a measuring “how” in both halves, and the draft’s “how he could not” reads as a bare fact, so the parallel is weakened. Desiderare is simply “miss”, and “bear the loss” spells it out.
check.decided: Accepted: the clause now measures how far the father was from being able to miss his son bravely, with “miss” for desiderare. Quam is a measure in both halves of the Latin, and the draft’s wording read as a bare fact.

check.note: Impetum capere is to form or conceive a sudden impulse, a little more active than an urge that is merely felt. A small point.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “had the impulse”, with “impulse” for impetus. “Formed the impulse” is not said in English of today, and “had” leaves open, as cepi does, whether the impulse came or was taken up.

passages.latin: Ad illud nunc proprium incommodum revertamur: magnos cruciatus habet morbus, sed hos tolerabiles intervalla faciunt. Nam summi doloris intentio invenit finem; nemo potest valde dolere et diu; sic nos amantissima nostri natura disposuit ut dolorem aut tolerabilem aut brevem faceret.
passages.english: Now let us go back to that trouble which is illness’s own: illness has great torments, but intervals make them bearable. For the intensity of pain at its height finds an end; no one can be in pain both severely and for long; nature, who loves us most dearly, has so arranged us as to make pain either bearable or short.

notes.note: Proprium means “its own”, and “illness’s” is supplied. The section before listed three burdens of illness and said the fear of death belongs to nature, not to illness, so this is the trouble that is illness’s own, bodily pain.
notes.other_reading: that particular trouble

notes.note: Intentio is a stretching or tension, the pitch to which the pain is strained. “Intensity” is used so that the strain is clearly the pain’s own and not the sufferer’s.
notes.other_reading: the strain of pain at its height

notes.note: Literally “finds an end”. It can mean that the pain stops, or that it reaches a limit beyond which it cannot go; the literal phrase is kept.
notes.other_reading: reaches its limit

notes.note: Dolere is the verb of dolor, which the glossary gives as “pain”, so the English says “be in pain” where “suffer” would be more usual.
notes.other_reading: no one can suffer both severely and long

notes.note: Nature is personified as one who loves humankind. The superlative can be a true superlative or simply “very loving”.
notes.other_reading: nature, in her great love for us

check.note: The Latin says only “that trouble which is its own”, and “illness’s” is supplied. The supplement looks right in view of the section before, but it should be confirmed and recorded.
check.decided: Accepted: “that trouble which is illness’s own” stands, and the note now says plainly that “illness’s” is supplied. The section before lists three burdens of illness and hands the fear of death over to nature, so the trouble proper to illness is bodily pain.

check.note: Intentio is the stretching or pitch of the pain itself, its intensity. “The strain of pain” can be read as the strain that pain puts on the sufferer.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the intensity of pain at its height finds an end”. Intentio is the pitch to which the pain itself is stretched, and “the strain of pain” could be taken as strain on the sufferer.

check.latin: nemo potest valde dolere et diu
check.note: The draft follows the Latin word order and reads awkwardly. The point, severely and long both at once, is not clear at first reading.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “no one can be in pain both severely and for long”. “Both” makes the two conditions clear, and “pain” is kept, not “suffer”, because dolor and dolere run through the section as one word.

passages.latin: Hoc itaque solacium vasti doloris est, quod necesse est desinas illum sentire si nimis senseris. Illud autem est quod inperitos in vexatione corporis male habet: non adsueverunt animo esse contenti; multum illis cum corpore fuit. Ideo vir magnus ac prudens animum diducit a corpore et multum cum meliore ac divina parte versatur, cum hac querula et fragili quantum necesse est.
passages.english: So this is the consolation for immense pain: that you are bound to stop feeling it if you feel it too much. But what troubles the untrained when the body is in distress is this: they have not become used to being content with the mind; they have had much to do with the body. That is why a great and prudent man draws his mind apart from the body and spends much time with the better and divine part; with this complaining and fragile one, as much as is necessary.

notes.note: Vastus is huge, and can also suggest something that lays waste. The English takes size.
notes.other_reading: of devastating pain

notes.note: Literally those without skill or experience, here people with no training in philosophy. “The untrained” is used.
notes.other_reading: the inexperienced

notes.note: An idiom: to trouble or distress someone, to put someone in a bad way.
notes.other_reading: what puts the untrained in a bad way

notes.note: Animus is “mind” by the glossary. It is set against the body here and called the better and divine part, but not as what survives death, so “soul” is not used.
notes.other_reading: to be satisfied with the soul alone

notes.note: Literally “there has been much for them with the body”, an idiom for having dealings with someone. The same multum cum returns for the great man and the better part, so “much” is kept both times.
notes.other_reading: their dealings have been mostly with the body

notes.note: Prudens is a man of practical wisdom and foresight. “Prudent” is used, though the English word today leans toward caution; “wise” is kept for sapiens, which Seneca did not write here.
notes.other_reading: a great and wise man

notes.note: Diducere is to draw apart, to separate. The texts may vary here between diducit and deducit (from memory, unchecked); the English follows what is given.
notes.other_reading: leads his mind away from the body

notes.note: The Latin has no “only”; the limit is implied by the contrast with “much” and is left implied. Necesse est also stands in the first sentence, where it is “bound to”: there it is what is certain to happen, here what cannot be avoided.
notes.other_reading: only as far as he has to

check.note: Necesse est states what is bound to happen, not what one ought to do. “You must stop” can be read as an instruction.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “you are bound to stop feeling it”. Necesse est states what cannot fail to happen, and that certainty is the consolation.

check.note: Necesse est comes twice in the section and was given two different ways. The repeat carries no argument, but one phrase in both places would keep the echo.
check.decided: Declined: the second place keeps “as much as is necessary”. The first necesse est is about what is certain to happen and the second about what cannot be avoided, and no step of the argument rests on the repeat. One English phrase for both would turn the first into a command or the second into a prediction; the note records the repeat.

check.note: Male habere with a person is to trouble or distress that person. The draft shifted to what makes their affairs turn out badly.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “what troubles the untrained”. Male habere with a person as object is to trouble or distress that person, not to make things turn out badly.

check.note: The Latin sets the two halves side by side with no connective, as a contrast. The added “and” flattens the contrast into a list.
check.decided: Accepted: the added “and” is gone and a semicolon sets the halves against each other: “much time with the better and divine part; with this complaining and fragile one, as much as is necessary”. The Latin has no connective there.

check.note: “Sensible” is slight beside “great”. Prudens is the man of practical wisdom, and “wise” is suggested.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “sensible” becomes “prudent”, which is the Latin word’s own English form and carries more weight. “Wise” is not used because the glossary keeps it for sapiens, and Seneca wrote prudens here.

passages.latin: Noli mala tua facere tibi ipse graviora et te querelis onerare: levis est dolor si nihil illi opinio adiecerit. Contra si exhortari te coeperis ac dicere 'nihil est aut certe exiguum est; duremus; iam desinet', levem illum, dum putas, facies. Omnia ex opinione suspensa sunt; non ambitio tantum ad illam respicit et luxuria et avaritia: ad opinionem dolemus.
passages.english: Do not make your own ills heavier for yourself and load yourself with complaints: pain is light if opinion has added nothing to it. If, on the other hand, you begin to encourage yourself and to say, “It is nothing, or at least it is slight; let us hold out; it will stop soon”, you will make it light in thinking it so. Everything hangs on opinion; it is not only ambition and extravagance and greed that look to it: we feel pain according to opinion.

notes.note: Mala are bad things. In Stoic argument they are “evils”, but here they are a sick man’s sufferings, so “ills” is used here and in the next section.
notes.other_reading: your evils

notes.latin: levis est dolor si nihil illi opinio adiecerit
notes.note: Opinio is “opinion” by the glossary, meaning what one believes about the pain. The section runs on an image of weight (heavier, load, light), which is kept.
notes.other_reading: pain is slight if belief has added nothing to it

notes.note: Durare is to harden oneself and so to last out. The plural is the sick man talking to himself.
notes.other_reading: let us harden ourselves

notes.note: Dum with the present beside a future verb is normally “while”, here close to “by”: the pain is made light in the act of thinking it light. It can also be read as a limit of time.
notes.other_reading: you will make it light for as long as you think it so

notes.note: Literally “all things are hung from opinion”. The image of hanging is kept.
notes.other_reading: Everything depends on opinion

notes.note: Respicere ad is to look to, to have regard for. With ambition, extravagance and greed the opinion looked to may be other people’s, while with pain it is one’s own; the Latin uses the one word and so does the English.
notes.other_reading: it is not only ambition that has an eye on what people think

notes.note: Luxuria is the vice of showy, self-indulgent living, not the costly goods themselves. “Extravagance” is used.
notes.other_reading: luxury

notes.note: Ad here is “in accordance with, to the measure of”. Dolemus is the verb of dolor, so the English keeps “pain”.
notes.other_reading: our suffering is measured by our opinion

check.note: Dum with the present beside a future main verb can mean “while, in thinking it so”, so that the pain is made light by the act of thinking it light. The draft chose the limiting sense, which is a different point.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “you will make it light in thinking it so”. Dum with a present tense beside a future main verb normally means “while”, the time in which the thing is done, not “for as long as”, which would usually take the future. The limiting sense is recorded in the note.

check.latin: non ambitio tantum ad illam respicit et luxuria et avaritia
check.note: The trailing “and luxury and greed” copies the Latin order and reads like an afterthought. A reader may not see that all three are subjects of the one verb.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “it is not only ambition and extravagance and greed that look to it”. All three are subjects of the one verb, and the contrast of “not only” is with pain in the next clause.

check.note: Luxuria is the vice, set beside ambition and greed. “Luxury” today suggests the goods more than the disposition.
check.decided: Accepted: luxuria is now “extravagance”. It is named as a vice between ambition and greed, and “luxury” today suggests costly goods more than a way of living.

check.latin: Noli mala tua facere tibi ipse graviora
check.note: The draft is faithful to ipse and tibi, but its string of “yourself, your, yourself” is clumsy in English.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Do not make your own ills heavier for yourself”. The force of ipse, that the sick man is himself the one adding the weight, is carried by “your own” and “for yourself”.

passages.latin: Tam miser est quisque quam credidit. Detrahendas praeteritorum dolorum conquestiones puto et illa verba: 'nulli umquam fuit peius. Quos cruciatus, quanta mala pertuli! Nemo me surrecturum putavit. Quotiens deploratus sum a meis, quotiens a medicis relictus! In eculeum inpositi non sic distrahuntur.' Etiam si sunt vera ista, transierunt: quid iuvat praeteritos dolores retractare et miserum esse quia fueris? Quid quod nemo non multum malis suis adicit et sibi ipse mentitur? Deinde quod acerbum fuit ferre, tulisse iucundum est: naturale est mali sui fine gaudere. Circumcidenda ergo duo sunt, et futuri timor et veteris incommodi memoria: hoc ad me iam non pertinet, illud nondum.
passages.english: Everyone is as wretched as he has believed himself to be. I think complaints about past pains should be done away with, and these words too: “No one has ever had it worse. What torments, what great ills I have gone through! No one thought I would get up again. How many times my own people gave me up for lost, how many times the doctors abandoned me! Men put on the rack are not pulled apart like this.” Even if those things are true, they are over: what good does it do to go back over past pains and to be wretched because you have been? And what of the fact that there is no one who does not add a great deal to his own ills and lie to himself? Then again, what was bitter to bear is pleasant to have borne: it is natural to be glad at the end of one’s own ill. So two things must be cut away, both the fear of what is to come and the memory of old trouble: the old trouble no longer concerns me, what is to come does not yet.

notes.latin: Tam miser est quisque quam credidit
notes.note: Credidit is perfect and has no object, so “himself to be” is supplied. It could also be a general perfect, better put as a present.
notes.other_reading: Everyone is just as wretched as he believes he is

notes.note: Detrahere is to pull off or take away. The Latin is impersonal, and the English keeps it so with a passive.
notes.other_reading: complaints about past pains are to be stripped away

notes.note: Literally “would rise”, that is, get up from the sickbed.
notes.other_reading: No one thought I would recover

notes.note: Deplorare is to weep for someone as already lost, and so to give up hope of them. Mei are one’s own people, family and household; the Latin passive is turned into an active in English.
notes.other_reading: How many times I was wept over by my family as a dead man

notes.note: The eculeus (“little horse”) was a frame on which a person was stretched under torture. “Rack” is the nearest English.
notes.other_reading: Men set on the torture horse

notes.note: Literally to handle again. It can also suggest touching a wound again.
notes.other_reading: to reopen past pains

notes.note: An idiom that brings in a further point: “what of the fact that”.
notes.other_reading: Besides, everyone adds a great deal to his own ills

notes.note: Literally “to be cut round”, as in pruning or surgery. The cutting is kept.
notes.other_reading: So two things must be pruned back

notes.latin: hoc ad me iam non pertinet, illud nondum
notes.note: Hoc and illud are neuter and point to the things themselves, the nearer one just named (the old trouble) and the farther one (what is to come), not to the memory and the fear. The English names them so that this is plain.
notes.other_reading: this no longer concerns me, that does not yet

check.latin: hoc ad me iam non pertinet, illud nondum
check.note: The neuter hoc and illud cannot stand for the memory (feminine) and the fear (masculine). They point to the old trouble and to what is to come, and “the second, the first” makes Seneca say something else.
check.decided: Accepted: the last clause now names the things themselves, “the old trouble” and “what is to come”, in place of “the second” and “the first”. Hoc and illud are neuter, so they cannot point to the memory, which is feminine, or the fear, which is masculine.

check.note: Quisque is “each person”, and “man” is not in the Latin. Credidit may be a general perfect, and “himself to be” is necessarily supplied.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Everyone is as wretched as he has believed himself to be”. Quisque is “each person”; the note records that “himself to be” is supplied and that the perfect may be general.

check.note: The Latin is “those words”. “Like” turns them into examples of a type.
