check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and these words too”. Illa verba are particular words, the ones then quoted, not examples of a kind.

check.note: “Once” is added. The Latin is simply “because you have been”.
check.decided: Accepted: “once” is removed and the clause reads “because you have been”. The Latin has only the perfect fueris.

check.note: Found while settling: the Latin is impersonal (complaints “are to be taken away”), and the draft’s wording added a plural first person that is not there.
check.decided: Accepted: the sentence is now passive, “complaints about past pains should be done away with”, so that only Seneca’s own puto is in the first person, as in the Latin.

passages.latin: In ipsis positus difficultatibus dicat, forsan et haec olim meminisse iuvabit. Toto contra ille pugnet animo; vincetur si cesserit, vincet si se contra dolorem suum intenderit: nunc hoc plerique faciunt, adtrahunt in se ruinam cui obstandum est. Istud quod premit, quod inpendet, quod urguet, si subducere te coeperis, sequetur et gravius incumbet; si contra steteris et obniti volueris, repelletur.
passages.english: Set in the very midst of difficulties, let him say, “Perhaps one day it will be pleasant to remember even these things.” Let him fight back with his whole mind; he will be conquered if he gives way, he will conquer if he braces himself against his pain. As things are, what most people do is this: they pull down on themselves the collapse they ought to be standing against. That thing which presses, which hangs overhead, which bears down: if you begin to draw yourself out from under it, it will follow and weigh more heavily; if you stand against it and choose to push back, it will be driven back.

notes.note: The subject is not stated in this section, and ille follows in the next sentence. It is taken as the man in pain in general; the Latin then moves to “you” in the last sentence, and that shift is kept.
notes.other_reading: let a man say

notes.latin: forsan et haec olim meminisse iuvabit
notes.note: A line of Vergil, Aeneid 1.203 (from memory, unchecked). The Latin as given has no quotation marks; they are added because the line is direct speech after dicat.
notes.other_reading: let him say that perhaps one day it will be pleasant to remember even these things

notes.note: Iuvare is both “to please” and “to help”. “Pleasant” is taken, in line with “pleasant to have borne” in the section before, although quid iuvat there has the sense of use.
notes.other_reading: it will be of use

notes.note: Animus is “mind” by the glossary, though toto animo is also the ordinary phrase for “with all one’s heart”. Contra is an adverb with no object, so the English says “fight back”.
notes.other_reading: Let him fight against it with all his spirit

notes.note: Literally “has stretched, strained himself against his pain”. It is the verb behind intentio in 78.7.
notes.other_reading: if he strains every nerve against his pain

notes.note: Nunc is “as things are” here, not “at this moment”, and hoc points forward to what follows. The English begins a new sentence at this point.
notes.other_reading: but now most people do this

notes.latin: adtrahunt in se ruinam cui obstandum est
notes.note: Ruina is the falling of a building or wall. The image is of pulling down on oneself what should be stood against, and it is kept as a collapse.
notes.other_reading: they draw upon themselves the ruin they ought to resist

notes.latin: quod premit, quod inpendet, quod urguet
notes.note: The three verbs have no object in the Latin, and the English gives them none. Istud is “that thing of yours”, the pain or trouble at hand.
notes.other_reading: which presses on you, which hangs over you, which bears down on you

notes.note: Subducere is to draw away from underneath, as from under a weight.
notes.other_reading: if you begin to back away

notes.note: Volueris is an act of will: “choose to”, “make up your mind to”. “Are willing to” would be weaker.
notes.other_reading: if you stand against it and are willing to push back

check.latin: forsan et haec olim meminisse iuvabit
check.note: The Latin as given has no quotation marks around the line, which the English adds after “let him say”. It is a verse of Vergil, and a note should name it.
check.decided: Accepted: the quotation marks stay, since the words are direct speech after dicat. The note names Vergil, Aeneid 1.203 (from memory, unchecked) and says that the marks are added.

check.note: Iuvare is “to please” or “to help”, and “a joy” is stronger than either. The same verb was given as “what good does it do” in the section before.
check.decided: Accepted: the line now reads “Perhaps one day it will be pleasant to remember even these things”. “A joy” was stronger than either sense of iuvare, and “pleasant” answers “pleasant to have borne” in the section before; haec stays plural.

check.note: Contra is an adverb here with no object. “Them”, the difficulties, is supplied, while the next clause names the opponent as his pain.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Let him fight back with his whole mind”. Contra is an adverb with no object, and the next clause names the opponent as his pain, not the difficulties.

check.latin: quod premit, quod inpendet, quod urguet
check.note: “You” is supplied three times, though the Latin verbs have no object. It is harmless but it is an addition.
check.decided: Accepted: the three verbs now stand without “you”: “That thing which presses, which hangs overhead, which bears down”. The Latin order is also restored, with the two “if” clauses following, and incumbet is “weigh more heavily” with no object.

check.note: Volueris is “choose to” or “make up your mind to”. “Are willing” sounds like mere consent.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “choose to push back”. Volueris is an act of will, and “are willing” sounded like mere consent.

check.note: The image is of a mass pushed back by one who braces against it. “Driven off” suggests chasing something away.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “it will be driven back”. Repellere is to push back what presses forward, which fits a weight braced against.

passages.latin: Illud quoque proderit, ad alias cogitationes avertere animum et a dolore discedere. Cogita quid honeste, quid fortiter feceris; bonas partes tecum ipse tracta; memoriam in ea quae maxime miratus es sparge; tunc tibi fortissimus quisque et victor doloris occurrat: ille qui dum varices exsecandas praeberet legere librum perseveravit, ille qui non desiit ridere cum hoc ipsum irati tortores omnia instrumenta crudelitatis suae experirentur. Non vincetur dolor ratione, qui victus est risu?
passages.english: This too will help: to turn the mind away to other thoughts and to step away from the pain. Think of what you have done honourably, what you have done bravely; go over the good parts of your life in your own mind; scatter your memory across the things you have most admired; then let all the bravest men, the conquerors of pain, come before you: the man who went on reading a book while he offered his varicose veins to be cut out, the man who did not stop laughing while the torturers, angered by that very thing, tried every instrument of their cruelty. Will pain not be conquered by reason, when it has been conquered by laughter?

notes.note: Literally to walk away, to withdraw from the pain. The movement is kept.
notes.other_reading: to take your thoughts off the pain

notes.note: Honeste is the adverb of honestum, “what is honourable” in the glossary, so “honourably”.
notes.other_reading: what you have done nobly, what bravely

notes.note: Partes can be “parts, sides” (the good side of a life or a character) or a role in a play, and tractare can be “go over” or “play (a role)”. The English takes the first, supplies “of your life” from the sentence before, and gives tecum as “in your own mind”.
notes.other_reading: play the good role to yourself

notes.latin: memoriam in ea quae maxime miratus es sparge
notes.note: Spargere is to scatter or sprinkle. The image is kept, so that memory is sent out to many things at once.
notes.other_reading: let your memory range over the things you have most admired

notes.note: Literally “each bravest man and conqueror of pain”, one group. Victor, victus and vincetur are one word in the Latin, so “conquer” is used throughout.
notes.other_reading: every one of the bravest, every conqueror of pain

notes.latin: ille qui dum varices exsecandas praeberet legere librum perseveravit
notes.note: Seneca does not name this man or the one who laughed under torture, and the English does not identify them. A story of varicose veins cut without flinching is told of Marius, though without a book (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: the man who kept on reading his book while he held out his leg for the varicose veins to be cut away

notes.note: Hoc ipsum is taken with irati: angry at that very thing, his laughing.
notes.other_reading: the torturers, furious for that very reason

notes.latin: Non vincetur dolor ratione, qui victus est risu?
notes.note: Ratio is “reason” by the glossary. The relative clause gives the ground (“seeing that it has been”); the English has “when” and does not add “since”.
notes.other_reading: Shall pain, which laughter has conquered, not be conquered by reason?

check.note: The draft is unclear: good parts of what? The Latin can mean dwelling on the good side of one’s life or, in the stage sense, taking the good role, and “with yourself” is a Latinism.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “go over the good parts of your life in your own mind”. “Parts” is kept for partes, “of your life” is supplied from the sentence before about past deeds, and the stage sense is recorded in the note as the reading not taken.

check.note: The Latin is one group joined by et, all the bravest men who are conquerors of pain. The draft repeats “every” and makes two parallel groups.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “let all the bravest men, the conquerors of pain, come before you”. The Latin phrase is one group, each man both among the bravest and a conqueror of pain.

check.latin: memoriam in ea quae maxime miratus es sparge
check.note: “Spread your memory over” is not natural English. Spargere is “scatter” or “let range”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “scatter your memory across the things you have most admired”. “Scatter” is the plain sense of spargere and keeps Seneca’s image, which “let your memory range” would give up; “spread over” is gone.

check.note: “On him” is supplied. The Latin has only that they tried every instrument of their cruelty.
check.decided: Accepted: “on him” is removed. The Latin says only that the torturers tried every instrument of their cruelty.

passages.latin: 'Sed nihil' inquit 'agere sinit morbus, qui me omnibus abduxit officiis.' Corpus tuum valetudo tenet, non et animum. Itaque cursoris moratur pedes, sutoris aut fabri manus inpedit: si animus tibi esse in usu solet, suadebis docebis, audies disces, quaeres recordaberis. Quid porro? nihil agere te credis si temperans aeger sis? ostendes morbum posse superari vel certe sustineri.
passages.english: “But illness,” he says, “lets me do nothing; it has taken me away from all my duties.” Ill health holds your body, not your mind as well. So it slows the feet of a runner, it hampers the hands of a cobbler or a smith: if your mind is what you are used to using, you will advise and teach, listen and learn, inquire and remember. And another thing: do you believe you are doing nothing if you are self-controlled in your sickness? You will show that illness can be overcome, or at least borne.

notes.note: Third person: an imagined objector. The answer then turns to “you”, and both are kept as the Latin has them.
notes.other_reading: you say

notes.note: Officia are duties, including the social and public tasks of a Roman of rank. The Latin has a relative clause, which the English joins with a semicolon, and the object of “lets” in the first clause is supplied.
notes.other_reading: which has drawn me away from all my occupations

notes.note: Valetudo is state of health, here bad health. The Latin has morbus in the objection and valetudo in the answer, so the English has “illness” and “ill health”.
notes.other_reading: It is your body that sickness holds

notes.note: Literally “not also the mind”.
notes.other_reading: not your mind too

notes.note: “So”: because it holds the body alone, it stops those whose work is of the body. The Latin does not spell out that step, and the English does not add it.
notes.other_reading: That is why

notes.note: Faber is any worker in hard materials: a smith, a carpenter, a builder. “Smith” is chosen because the general word “craftsman” would take in the cobbler as well.
notes.other_reading: of a cobbler or a carpenter

notes.latin: si animus tibi esse in usu solet
notes.note: Literally “if the mind is usually in use for you”. Animus stands first in its clause, and the English stresses it against the feet and hands.
notes.other_reading: if you are in the habit of using your mind

notes.latin: suadebis docebis, audies disces, quaeres recordaberis
notes.note: Six verbs in three pairs with no “and”. “And” is added inside each pair, since bare pairs do not read as English.
notes.other_reading: you will advise, you will teach; you will listen, you will learn; you will inquire, you will remember

notes.note: A short question that moves on to a further point, literally “what further?”. The English gives it as a phrase leading into the next question.
notes.other_reading: What then?

notes.note: Temperans is the man who has temperantia, self-control or moderation. Aeger can be a noun (“a sick man”) or describe the state in which he is self-controlled; the English takes the second.
notes.other_reading: if you are a temperate patient

check.note: Porro moves on to a further point. “What then?” suggests an inference from what was just said.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “And another thing:” and runs on into the question. Porro moves forward to a further point, where “What then?” suggested a conclusion drawn from what came before.

check.note: “A self-controlled sick man” is heavy and unnatural in English.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “if you are self-controlled in your sickness”. The heavy noun phrase is gone, but “show” is not used, because the next sentence has ostendes, “you will show”, and the Latin does not have that verb here.

check.note: The relative clause was made a separate sentence, which loosens the link between the two halves of the objection. The sense is kept.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the objection is one sentence again, its two halves joined by a semicolon in place of the full stop. “Since” is not added, because the Latin has a bare relative clause and the rules for the English forbid a supplied reason. The note records that the object of the first clause is supplied.

check.note: Faber is a worker in hard materials such as a smith, carpenter or builder. “Craftsman” is wider and would include the cobbler just named.
check.decided: Accepted: faber is now “a smith”. “Craftsman” would take in the cobbler just named; the note records that the Latin word also covers a carpenter or builder.

passages.latin: Vitam enim occupare satietas sui non potest tot res varias, magnas, divinas percensentem: in odium illam sui adducere solet iners otium. Rerum naturam peragranti numquam in fastidium veritas veniet: falsa satiabunt.
passages.english: For a life that is surveying so many varied, great, divine things cannot be overtaken by the sense of having had its fill of itself: what usually brings it to hatred of itself is sluggish leisure. To one who ranges through the nature of things the truth will never become distasteful: it is false things that he will have his fill of.

notes.note: Satietas is having had enough, to the point of being sick of something. The last word, satiabunt, is the same root, so “fill” is used in both places; “the sense of” is added to make the phrase a noun.
notes.other_reading: satiety with itself cannot take hold of a life

notes.note: Agrees with vitam: it is the life that goes through these things one by one, reviews them. “Surveying” narrows the sense a little.
notes.other_reading: a life that is reckoning up so many varied, great, divine things

notes.latin: in odium illam sui adducere solet iners otium
notes.note: Otium is leisure, time free of business, and iners is sluggish, doing nothing. The Latin puts the phrase last for weight, and the English keeps that order.
notes.other_reading: it is idleness with nothing to do that makes life loathe itself

notes.note: Peragrare is to travel all through a country. “The nature of things” is the glossary’s rendering, meaning the natural world as an object of study.
notes.other_reading: For one who travels through the whole of nature

notes.note: Fastidium is the distaste of someone who has eaten too much. It carries on the image of having had one’s fill.
notes.other_reading: the truth will never come to disgust him

notes.note: Two words in the Latin, with no object: “false things will sate”. The English supplies “he”, the one who ranges through nature, and adds the emphasis of “it is” to bring out the contrast with truth.
notes.other_reading: false things will cloy

check.note: “Satiety” is a rare, bookish word today. The link to satiabunt at the end is rightly kept, but both English words are dated.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “satiety” is replaced and the clause reads “cannot be overtaken by the sense of having had its fill of itself”, with the life first as in the Latin order. “The sense of” is added so that the phrase can stand as a noun; “fill” returns at the end for satiabunt.

check.note: “Sate” with no object is hardly current English and the clause is unclear at first reading. Whatever is chosen should still echo the word used for satietas.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the clause now reads “it is false things that he will have his fill of”. “Fill” echoes the word used for satietas; “he” and not a general plural is supplied, since the unstated object is the one who ranges through nature in the same sentence.

check.note: “Idle leisure” is nearly a tautology in English. Iners is sluggish, doing nothing, as against leisure spent surveying great things.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “sluggish leisure”. Iners is doing nothing, and “idle leisure” said one thing twice.

passages.latin: Interim hoc tene, hoc morde: adversis non succumbere, laetis non credere, omnem fortunae licentiam in oculis habere, tamquam quidquid potest facere factura sit. Quidquid expectatum est diu, levius accedit. Vale.
passages.english: Meanwhile hold on to this, grip this with your teeth: not to give in to adversity, not to trust prosperity, to keep before your eyes all that Fortune is free to do, as though she were going to do whatever she can do. Whatever has been long expected is lighter when it comes. Farewell.

notes.note: Literally “bite this”: get the teeth into it and do not let go. The bite is kept.
notes.other_reading: bite on this

notes.latin: adversis non succumbere, laetis non credere
notes.note: Two neuter plurals: things that go against a person and things that gladden. The English uses the abstract nouns, and keeps the infinitives as “not to”.
notes.other_reading: not to give in to adverse things, not to trust glad ones

notes.note: Licentia is freedom to do as one pleases, unchecked power; the English word “licence” could be taken for a permit. Fortune acts as a person here (factura sit), so she has a capital, as the glossary allows.
notes.other_reading: the whole of Fortune’s licence

notes.latin: tamquam quidquid potest facere factura sit
notes.note: Literally “as if she is going to do whatever she is able to do”.
notes.other_reading: as though she will do everything that is in her power

notes.note: Accedit is “comes up, arrives”, and levius is “more lightly”, the weight image of the earlier sections. The verb is easily confused with accidit (“happens, falls”), which would also give sense; the English follows what is given.
notes.other_reading: falls less heavily

check.note: “Glad ones” is not natural English, since things are not glad. “Adversity” and “prosperity” are suggested.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “not to give in to adversity, not to trust prosperity”. The Latin words are neuter plurals, things that go against a person and things that gladden; the abstract nouns are natural English for them and the note records the literal sense.

check.note: “Fortune’s licence” may be read today as a permit. The sense is everything Fortune is free to do.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “to keep before your eyes all that Fortune is free to do”. Licentia is unchecked freedom, not a permit; “can take” is not used, because the next clause already says “whatever she can do”.

check.note: The image is of gripping with the teeth and not letting go. “Bite on this” may puzzle a reader.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “hold on to this, grip this with your teeth”. The bite of mordere is kept and “this” is repeated as hoc is.

check.note: “Arrives more lightly” is a little odd in English. The sense is that it comes with less weight.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “is lighter when it comes”. The odd adverb is gone and the weight image stays, but “falls” is not used, because the Latin as given has accedit, “comes”, not accidit, “falls”.

passages.latin: Nulla virtus latet, et latuisse non ipsius est damnum: veniet qui conditam et saeculi sui malignitate conpressam dies publicet. Paucis natus est qui populum aetatis suae cogitat. Multa annorum milia, multa populorum supervenient: ad illa respice. Etiam si omnibus tecum viventibus silentium livor indixerit, venient qui sine offensa, sine gratia iudicent. Si quod est pretium virtutis ex fama, nec hoc interit. Ad nos quidem nihil pertinebit posterorum sermo; tamen etiam non sentientes colet ac frequentabit.
passages.english: No virtue lies hidden, and to have lain hidden is not virtue’s own loss: a day will come to make public the virtue that was buried and held down by the spite of its own age. The man who thinks of the people of his own time is born for few. Many thousands of years, many thousands of peoples will come after: look to those. Even if envy has imposed silence on all who are alive with you, there will come those who judge without ill will, without favour. If virtue has any reward from fame, this does not perish either. The talk of those who come after will indeed not concern us at all; yet it will honour us and keep returning to us even though we do not feel it.

notes.note: A flat present, though the next clause grants that virtue may have been hidden for a time. The sense is that none stays hidden; the flat statement is kept because the Latin repeats the same verb in latuisse.
notes.other_reading: No virtue stays hidden

notes.note: Ipsius is “of virtue itself”: the loss is not virtue’s own, with the hint that it is the age’s. The hint is not added.
notes.other_reading: to have been hidden does it no harm

notes.latin: conditam et saeculi sui malignitate conpressam
notes.note: Condere is to put away, store or bury, and malignitas is ill will, grudging meanness. The two participles are given as a plain relative clause.
notes.other_reading: stored away and suppressed by the meanness of its own century

notes.note: “Born for few”: his life serves or reaches only a few people. The Latin has no “only”.
notes.other_reading: He is born for only a few

notes.note: Milia is taken as understood again: many thousands of peoples.
notes.other_reading: many generations of peoples

notes.note: Livor is the bluish colour of a bruise, and so envy. Indicere is the word for an official proclamation, so envy “decrees” silence.
notes.other_reading: even if spite has decreed silence

notes.note: Offensa is dislike or resentment, taken here as the judge’s own feeling, and gratia is favour, partiality. The phrase means with no bias either way.
notes.other_reading: without taking offence, without partiality

notes.latin: Si quod est pretium virtutis ex fama, nec hoc interit
notes.note: The “if” leaves open whether virtue gets any reward from fame at all. Nec hoc is “not even this” or “this, too, not”.
notes.other_reading: If there is any price paid to virtue by fame, not even that is lost

notes.note: No object in the Latin; the first person plural is supplied from non sentientes. Colere is to honour or pay court to, and frequentare is to visit often or in numbers.
notes.other_reading: it will pay us honour and throng about us

check.note: Frequentare is to visit often or attend in numbers. “Gather round”, said of talk, is a strained image and a little more than the Latin.
check.decided: Accepted: frequentabit is now “keep returning to”. Frequentare is to visit often, and talk that gathers round a person was a strained image.

check.latin: conditam et saeculi sui malignitate conpressam
check.note: The concessive “though it was” is added. The Latin has two plain participles describing the virtue that the day will make public.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a day will come to make public the virtue that was buried and held down by the spite of its own age”. The two participles simply describe the virtue, with no “though” in the Latin; “make public” is the plain sense of publicet.

check.note: The bare present is kept, but beside “to have lain hidden” it can look like a contradiction. The sense is “no virtue stays hidden”, and the literal present needs a decision.
check.decided: Declined: “No virtue lies hidden” stands. The Latin has the bare present latet and at once repeats the verb as latuisse, so the sharp statement followed by its concession is Seneca’s own; the note gives “stays hidden” as the sense.

check.note: “Without grudge” is not idiomatic. Offensa is ill will or dislike, the opposite of gratia.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “without ill will, without favour”. Offensa is dislike or resentment, the opposite of gratia.

check.note: “This too does not perish” is awkward English for nec hoc, which is “not even this” or “this not either”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “this does not perish either”. “Either” gives nec hoc in natural English, and “perish” is kept because interit is the verb for dying or being destroyed.

check.latin: Paucis natus est qui populum aetatis suae cogitat
check.note: Found while settling: “He is born for few who thinks” follows the Latin word order into an old-fashioned English turn.
check.decided: Accepted: the sentence now reads “The man who thinks of the people of his own time is born for few”. Nothing is added or dropped; only the order is that of English today.

passages.latin: Illud maxime revolvo mecum: si corpus perduci exercitatione ad hanc patientiam potest qua et pugnos pariter et calces non unius hominis ferat, qua solem ardentissimum in ferventissimo pulvere sustinens aliquis et sanguine suo madens diem ducat, quanto facilius animus conroborari possit ut fortunae ictus invictus excipiat, ut proiectus, ut conculcatus exsurgat. Corpus enim multis eget rebus ut valeat: animus ex se crescit, se ipse alit, se exercet. Illis multo cibo, multa potione opus est, multo oleo, longa denique opera: tibi continget virtus sine apparatu, sine inpensa. Quidquid facere te potest bonum tecum est.
passages.english: What I turn over most in my own thoughts is this: if the body can be brought by training to this endurance, by which it bears the fists and equally the kicks of more than one man, by which someone holding out under the most blazing sun in the most scorching dust, and drenched in his own blood, lasts out the day, how much more easily the mind can be strengthened so that it takes the blows of Fortune unconquered, so that thrown down, so that trampled on, it rises up. For the body needs many things in order to be in good condition: the mind grows from itself, feeds itself, trains itself. Those men need much food, much drink, much oil, and long labour besides: virtue will come to you without equipment, without expense. Whatever can make you good is with you.

notes.note: Literally “roll over with myself”. “Thoughts” is used and not “mind”, which in this section is the word for animus.
notes.other_reading: What I turn over with myself most is this

notes.note: Patientia is the capacity to bear things, endurance, not “patience” in the mild English sense. Hanc is kept as “this”, pointing to what is on show in the stadium; it could also be the “such” that prepares the clause after it.
notes.other_reading: to such a power of endurance that it bears

notes.latin: pugnos pariter et calces non unius hominis
notes.note: Calces are heels, so kicks, which points to a fighting contest in which both were allowed. “Not of one man” means of several opponents; pariter may be “alike” or “at the same time”.
notes.other_reading: the punches and at the same time the kicks of more than a single opponent

notes.note: Literally “draws out the day”: gets through the whole day.
notes.other_reading: spends the day

notes.note: The subjunctive depends on the opening verb of pondering. It is kept as a statement of what is being pondered, not a question to Lucilius.
notes.other_reading: how much more easily might the mind be strengthened

notes.note: Fortune is the opponent who lands blows here, so she has a capital as in 78.29. Invictus is “unconquered” or “unbeaten”.
notes.other_reading: so that it takes fortune’s blows unbeaten

notes.note: Ut is said three times in a row, and the English repeats “so that” to match. Exsurgat is “rises up”.
notes.other_reading: so that, thrown down and trampled on, it rises again

notes.note: Valere is both to be in health and to be strong. “In good condition” keeps both.
notes.other_reading: in order to be strong

notes.note: “Those men” are the athletes of the section before, whose noise from the stadium set off the thought.
notes.other_reading: The athletes

notes.note: Oil for rubbing the body before exercise, as athletes did.
notes.other_reading: much oil for rubbing down

notes.latin: Quidquid facere te potest bonum tecum est
notes.note: Bonum is taken with te: “make you good”. It is the adjective here, not “the good” of the glossary; tecum est is “is with you”, already in your possession.
notes.other_reading: Whatever can make you a good man you have with you

check.note: Hanc is dropped. Seneca points to this endurance, the kind on show in the stadium he can hear.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “to this endurance, by which it bears”. Hanc points to the endurance on show in the stadium Seneca can hear.

check.note: “With myself” copies mecum. English says “in my mind”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “with myself” is replaced by a phrase with “thoughts”, not “mind”. In this section “mind” is the word for animus, set against the body, and it should not also stand for mecum.

check.note: The repeated ut is merged into one clause and “again” is added, though exsurgat is “rises up”. A small point.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “so that thrown down, so that trampled on, it rises up”. The repeated ut is heard again and “again” is removed, since exsurgat is only “rises up”.

check.note: Valere is both “be in health” and “be strong”. The draft picks “strong”, and “be in good condition” would keep both.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “in order to be in good condition”. Valere covers both health and strength, and “strong” also made a false echo with “strengthened”, which translates a different Latin word.

check.note: A point of consistency across the passages: fortuna has a capital and “she” in 78.29 and is lower case here. One form should be chosen for the whole set.
check.decided: Accepted: “Fortune” has a capital here as in 78.29. She is the opponent who lands blows and tramples, which is the personified use the glossary marks with a capital.

passages.latin: Vides illum Scythiae Sarmatiaeve regem insigni capitis decorum? Si vis illum aestimare totumque scire qualis sit, fasciam solve: multum mali sub illa latet. Quid de aliis loquor? si perpendere te voles, sepone pecuniam, domum, dignitatem, intus te ipse considera: nunc qualis sis aliis credis. Vale.
passages.english: Do you see that king of Scythia or Sarmatia, adorned with the mark of rank on his head? If you want to value him and to know him whole, what he is like, undo the band: much that is bad lies hidden under it. Why do I speak of others? If you want to weigh yourself up, set aside money, house, standing; look at yourself within, for yourself: as it is, you take the word of others for what you are. Farewell.

notes.note: Scythia and Sarmatia are the lands north of the Black Sea, for a Roman the far edge of the world. “Or” shows that any such distant king is meant, not a particular one.
notes.other_reading: that Scythian or Sarmatian king

notes.note: Insigne capitis, “the mark of rank on the head”, is the diadem, a band of cloth tied round the head. Decorus is “adorned” or “handsome”.
notes.other_reading: splendid in his diadem

notes.note: Fascia is both the cloth band of a diadem and a bandage. The section before spoke of a buyer who has a bandaged leg or arm uncovered to see what the dealer is hiding, so the royal band is treated as one more bandage; “band” is kept to hold both senses.
notes.other_reading: untie the bandage

notes.note: The buyer’s word from the section before: to put a value on, to appraise.
notes.other_reading: If you want to appraise him

notes.note: Totum agrees with illum: to know him whole, what sort he is all through.
notes.other_reading: and to know the whole of what he is like

notes.note: Literally “much of bad”. It can be moral evil or, keeping the picture of the bandage, something unsound underneath; “much that is bad” leaves it open.
notes.other_reading: a great deal of evil

notes.note: Perpendere is to weigh carefully, a word of valuing like aestimare above. “Weigh yourself up” is used because the bare “weigh yourself” means the scales.
notes.other_reading: If you want to assess yourself

notes.note: Standing in public life, not “dignity” as a personal quality. “Standing” is used and not “rank”, which appears earlier in the section for another Latin word.
notes.other_reading: rank

notes.note: Ipse is “you yourself”, the one who is to do the looking, and is given as “for yourself”. The Latin has no “and” before this clause.
notes.other_reading: and look at yourself within

notes.note: Nunc is “as things are”. Literally “you believe others as to what you are like”.
notes.other_reading: at present you trust others to tell you what you are

check.note: Ipse is dropped. It says that the examining is to be done by the person himself, which is the foil to trusting others in the next clause.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “look at yourself within, for yourself”. Ipse says that the looking is to be done by Lucilius himself, against taking the word of others in the next clause.

check.note: In English of today “weigh yourself” means stepping on the scales.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “weigh yourself up”. Perpendere is to weigh carefully, and the bare “weigh yourself” means the scales.

check.note: Fascia is both the cloth band of a royal diadem and a bandage, and the next clause depends on the bandage sense. “Band” is neutral, and “headband” with a note is suggested.
check.decided: Declined: “undo the band” stands. Fascia is one word for the cloth of a diadem and for a bandage, and “headband” would keep only the first, while “band” after “on his head” can be heard both ways. The note explains the bandage.

check.note: Totum agrees with illum: to know him whole, what he is like. The difference from the draft is small.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “to know him whole, what he is like”. Totum agrees with illum, the king, not with the clause that follows.

check.note: Insigne capitis is the mark of rank worn on the head, that is the diadem. “Emblem” suggests a badge and does not prepare for “band”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “adorned with the mark of rank on his head”. Dignitatem later in the section becomes “standing”, so that “rank” is not used for two different Latin words.

check.note: Found while settling: aliis comes twice in the section, and the draft gave it as “others” the first time and “other people” the second.
check.decided: Accepted: the last clause now reads “you take the word of others for what you are”. The same English word answers the same Latin word, and the turn from other people as a subject to other people as judges can be heard.

passages.latin: Quereris incidisse te in hominem ingratum: si hoc nunc primum, age aut fortunae aut diligentiae tuae gratias. Sed nihil facere hoc loco diligentia potest nisi te malignum; nam si hoc periculum vitare volueris, non dabis beneficia; ita ne apud alium pereant, apud te peribunt. Non respondeant potius quam non dentur: et post malam segetem serendum est. Saepe quidquid perierat adsidua infelicis soli sterilitate unius anni restituit ubertas.
passages.english: You complain that you have run into an ungrateful man. If this is now the first time, give thanks either to fortune or to your own carefulness. But in this matter carefulness can do nothing except make you grudging; for if you want to avoid this risk, you will not give benefits; and in this way, so that they are not lost in someone else’s hands, they will be lost in yours. Let them fail to bring a return rather than fail to be given: even after a bad harvest one must sow. Often whatever had been lost through the persistent barrenness of a poor soil has been restored by the richness of a single year.

notes.note: The clause has no verb; “has happened” is understood. The command that follows, to give thanks (gratias), plays on the ungrateful man (ingratum) just named.
notes.other_reading: if this has happened now for the first time

notes.note: Diligentia here is carefulness in choosing whom to help, not hard work. One word, “carefulness”, serves for both occurrences.
notes.other_reading: to your own diligence

notes.note: Malignus can mean spiteful, but with giving it means stingy, grudging. The English takes the second sense, which the next clause explains.
notes.other_reading: except make you spiteful

notes.note: Beneficium is the key term of this letter: a kindness or favour done. It is “benefit” throughout the passages from letter 81.
notes.other_reading: you will not do favours

notes.note: Literally “they will perish at your house”: by never being given, the benefits are wasted in the giver’s own keeping. Apud is given as “in someone’s hands”, and “lost” is kept because the same verb (perire) returns in the last sentence.
notes.other_reading: they will go to waste with you

notes.latin: Non respondeant potius quam non dentur
notes.note: Respondere is used of a field or a loan that answers with a return, which prepares the image of sowing. The subjunctives express a preference.
notes.other_reading: Let them go unanswered rather than ungiven

notes.note: Infelix of soil means unfruitful; its common sense is “unlucky”. The English has “poor” so as not to say “barren” twice.
notes.other_reading: of an unlucky soil

check.note: The English drops nunc. The Latin says “now for the first time”, which carries the point that he has been lucky until now.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “If this is now the first time”. Nunc (“now”) is in the Latin and marks that he has been spared until today.

check.latin: ne apud alium pereant, apud te peribunt
check.note: “Lost with another, lost with you” is stiff and unclear in today’s English. Apud here means in someone’s hands.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “so that they are not lost in someone else’s hands, they will be lost in yours”. “Lost” is kept and not changed to “wasted”, because the same Latin verb (perire) comes back in the last sentence as “had been lost”.

check.note: “Care” alone is vague and could mean kindness or worry. Diligentia here is carefulness in choosing whom to help, in this sentence and the next.
check.decided: Accepted: both places now read “carefulness”, which is what diligentia means here: taking care over whom one helps.

passages.latin: Omnia facienda sunt ut quam gratissimi simus. Nostrum enim hoc bonum est, quemadmodum iustitia non est (ut vulgo creditur) ad alios pertinens: magna pars eius in se redit. Nemo non, cum alteri prodest, sibi profuit, non eo nomine dico, quod volet adiuvare adiutus, protegere defensus, quod bonum exemplum circuitu ad facientem revertitur (sicut mala exempla recidunt in auctores nec ulla miseratio contingit iis qui patiuntur iniurias quas posse fieri faciendo docuerunt), sed quod virtutum omnium pretium in ipsis est. Non enim exercentur ad praemium: recte facti fecisse merces est.
passages.english: We must do everything to be as grateful as we can. For this good is our own, in the same way that justice is not, as is commonly believed, something that has to do with others: a great part of it comes back to itself. There is no one who, when he does good to another, has not done good to himself. I do not say this for the reason that the man who has been helped will want to help and the man who has been defended will want to protect, or that a good example comes back round in a circle to the one who sets it (just as bad examples fall back on their authors, and no pity comes to those who suffer wrongs that they taught could be done, by doing them), but because the reward of all the virtues is in the virtues themselves. For they are not practised for a prize: the pay for a right deed is to have done it.

notes.note: “This good” is gratitude; nostrum says that it belongs to the grateful person, not to the one thanked. Bonum is “the good”, as in the glossary.
notes.other_reading: For this is a good thing for ourselves

notes.latin: quemadmodum iustitia non est (ut vulgo creditur) ad alios pertinens
notes.note: The comparison is compressed: gratitude belongs to the grateful in the same way that justice is not, as people think, a matter concerning others. The Latin has no “only”, and none is added, though the next clause (“a great part”) shows that is meant.
notes.other_reading: just as justice does not, as is commonly believed, concern other people only

notes.note: Se can be justice itself or, loosely, the just person. The English keeps the literal “itself”.
notes.other_reading: a great part of it comes back to the one who is just

notes.latin: Nemo non, cum alteri prodest, sibi profuit
notes.note: A double negative for “everyone”; the perfect profuit says the gain is already made at the moment of the act. Prodesse is given as “does good to”; it is a different word from bonum (“the good”) and beneficium (“benefit”).
notes.other_reading: Everyone who is useful to another has been useful to himself

notes.note: A bookkeeping phrase, “under that heading”, continuing the language of accounts from the section before. The English gives the plain sense, “for the reason”. The Latin sets the two reasons side by side with no joining word; “or” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: under this heading

notes.note: Literally “by a circuit”: the example goes round and returns to its source.
notes.other_reading: comes back by a roundabout way

notes.latin: virtutum omnium pretium in ipsis est
notes.note: Pretium can be price, worth or reward. With praemium (prize) and merces (pay) following, the English takes “reward” and gives each of the three its own word.
notes.other_reading: the worth of all the virtues is in themselves

notes.note: Merces is wages or pay. The Latin is very compressed: “of a thing rightly done, to have done it is the pay”.
notes.other_reading: the wages of a good deed is having done it

check.latin: virtutum omnium pretium in ipsis est
check.note: Pretium can mean “reward” or “worth”. The English has “reward”, which fits the prize and pay of the next sentence; the choice should be a knowing one.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps “reward”, as suggested, because the next sentence goes on with praemium (prize) and merces (pay). The note records “worth” as the other reading.

check.note: “On this score, that” is stiff and a little dated. Eo nomine is simply “for this reason”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “on this score” is gone and the sentence now runs “for the reason that” and closes with “but because”. Dico is given as “say”, which is the plain sense of the verb, and the note keeps the bookkeeping sense of eo nomine.

check.note: “Is useful to” is thinner than prodesse, which in a passage about benefits means to do good to someone.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “when he does good to another, has not done good to himself”. Prodesse is to do good or be of service, and “is useful to” was too thin for it here.

passages.latin: Itaque ingrati esse vitemus non aliena causa sed nostra. Minimum ex nequitia levissimumque ad alios redundat: quod pessimum ex illa est et, ut ita dicam, spississimum, domi remanet et premit habentem, quemadmodum Attalus noster dicere solebat, 'malitia ipsa maximam partem veneni sui bibit'. Illud venenum quod serpentes in alienam perniciem proferunt, sine sua continent, non est huic simile: hoc habentibus pessimum est.
passages.english: So let us avoid being ungrateful, not for another’s sake but for our own. The smallest and lightest part of wickedness spills over onto others: what is worst in it and, so to speak, thickest stays at home and presses on the one who has it, as our Attalus used to say: “Vice itself drinks the greatest part of its own poison.” That poison which snakes bring out for another’s destruction, and hold without destruction to themselves, is not like this one: this one is worst for those who have it.

notes.note: Seneca uses nequitia here and malitia in the saying, apparently for the same thing. Two English words, “wickedness” and “vice”, let the reader see that there are two Latin ones.
notes.other_reading: worthlessness

notes.latin: malitia ipsa maximam partem veneni sui bibit
notes.note: Malitia is the general opposite of virtue (virtus) in the section before, not only ill will, so the English has “vice”. The glossary gives “vice” to vitium, which does not occur in this section.
notes.other_reading: Malice itself drinks most of its own poison

notes.note: “Thickest” or “densest”: the image is of a liquid whose light part spills over while the dregs stay in the vessel. Seneca marks the image with “so to speak”.
notes.other_reading: most concentrated

notes.note: Literally “overflows”, of a liquid running over the rim. It belongs to the same image as “thickest”.
notes.other_reading: overflows onto others

notes.note: Attalus was a Stoic philosopher whose lectures Seneca attended when young (from memory, unchecked). Noster marks him as one of Seneca’s own school, or as his teacher.
notes.other_reading: Attalus of the Stoic school

notes.note: Elliptical: sua takes up perniciem, “without their own [destruction]”. The English supplies the noun again. Snakes hold their venom without harm to themselves.
notes.other_reading: and keep in without harm to themselves

notes.note: Premere is to press, weigh down or choke. The English keeps the plain “presses on”.
notes.other_reading: weighs down its owner

check.note: “And hold without their own” cannot be understood as it stands. Sua takes up perniciem, so the noun has to be given to the reader again.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and hold without destruction to themselves”. Sua looks back to perniciem (“destruction”), and English needs the noun repeated; “hold” is kept for continent, which is to hold in.

check.note: “Badness” sounds childish in English. Malitia is rightly kept apart from nequitia (“wickedness”), but a more natural word is needed.
check.decided: Accepted: the saying now begins “Vice itself”. In the section before, malitia stands as the opposite of virtus, which is what “vice” means in English; the glossary’s word for “vice”, vitium, does not occur in this section, and a note says so.

passages.latin: Malis una voluptas est et haec brevis, dum accipiunt beneficia, ex quibus sapienti longum gaudium manet ac perenne. Non enim illum accipere sed accepisse delectat, quod inmortale est et adsiduum. Illa contemnit quibus laesus est, nec obliviscitur per neglegentiam sed volens.
passages.english: Bad men have one pleasure, and that a short one, while they are receiving benefits; from those benefits a long joy, one that does not fail, stays with the wise man. For what delights him is not receiving but having received, which is undying and constant. He scorns the things that have hurt him, and he forgets not through carelessness but by choice.

notes.note: Dative plural of “the bad” (people), set against the wise man. It could in form be “for evils”, which makes no sense here.
notes.other_reading: For the wicked there is one pleasure

notes.note: Seneca sets voluptas (pleasure), which the bad have, against gaudium (joy), which the Stoics allow the wise man. The English keeps two distinct words.
notes.other_reading: a long gladness

notes.note: Literally “lasting the year through”, used of springs that never run dry.
notes.other_reading: and everlasting

notes.note: The relative refers to “having received”: a past fact cannot be taken away. It could loosely refer to the delight.
notes.other_reading: a delight that is undying and constant

notes.note: Contemnere is to think little of, to hold of small account; it does not mean to hate. “Scorn” is used here and for the same verb in Ep. 82.16.
notes.other_reading: He makes light of the things that have hurt him

notes.note: Literally “willing”: the forgetting is an act of will, not a lapse. The verb has no stated object.
notes.other_reading: but willingly

check.note: In today’s English “despises” suggests loathing. Contemnit is “thinks little of”, which fits with forgetting on purpose; a reader may take the English to mean that he hates his injuries.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “He scorns the things that have hurt him”. Contemnere is to hold of small account, not to hate, so “despises” goes; “scorns” is used and not “makes light of” so that one English verb can serve here and in Ep. 82.16, where death “ought to be scorned”.

passages.latin: Non vertit omnia in peius nec quaerit cui inputet casum, et peccata hominum ad fortunam potius refert. Non calumniatur verba nec vultus; quidquid accidit benigne interpretando levat. Non offensae potius quam offici meminit; quantum potest in priore ac meliore se memoria detinet, nec mutat animum adversus bene meritos nisi multum male facta praecedunt et manifestum etiam coniventi discrimen est; tunc quoque in hoc dumtaxat, ut talis sit post maiorem iniuriam qualis ante beneficium. Nam cum beneficio par est iniuria, aliquid in animo benivolentiae remanet.
passages.english: He does not turn everything to the worse, nor does he look for someone to blame for an accident, and he puts men’s wrongdoings down to fortune instead. He does not put a bad meaning on words or looks; whatever happens, he lightens it by interpreting it kindly. He does not remember an offence rather than a service; as far as he can he keeps himself in the earlier and better memory, and his mind does not change toward those who have done well by him unless the bad deeds far outstrip the good and the difference is plain even to one who shuts his eyes; and even then only this far, that after the greater wrong he is such as he was before the benefit. For when the wrong is equal to the benefit, some goodwill remains in the mind.

notes.note: Inputare is an accounting word, to enter something to a person’s account; the English gives the plain “blame”. Casus is a chance event. “He” throughout is the wise man of the section before.
notes.other_reading: someone to whose account he can put a mischance

notes.note: Referre ad is also used of entering an item under a heading. Human faults are booked to chance and not to the person.
notes.other_reading: he prefers to set men’s faults down to chance

notes.note: Calumniari is to bring a false or quibbling charge. Here it means reading ill will into what was said or how someone looked; the Latin does not name what comes of it.
notes.other_reading: He does not find fault with words or looks

notes.note: The two nouns are chosen for their like sound, which English cannot keep. Officium is a service or good turn.
notes.other_reading: a slight rather than a kindness

notes.latin: in priore ac meliore se memoria detinet
notes.note: “Earlier” because the benefit came before the offence. Literally “he holds himself in the earlier and better memory”.
notes.other_reading: he dwells on the earlier and better recollection

notes.note: Animus is “mind”, as in the glossary, and returns at the end of the passage. Here it is closer to attitude or feeling toward a person, so the English avoids the idiom of changing one’s mind, which means altering a decision.
notes.other_reading: he does not change his feeling toward

notes.note: Literally “those who have deserved well”, that is, who have earned thanks by what they did for him. “Service” is not used, because it already stands for officium in this sentence.
notes.other_reading: those who have done him good service

notes.note: Praecedunt is taken as “go ahead of, surpass”: the bad deeds far exceed the good, and “the good” is supplied as the thing surpassed. It can also mean “go before” in time, which fits the context less well.
notes.other_reading: unless many bad deeds have come first

notes.note: Conivere is to close the eyes, and so to overlook on purpose. The English keeps the image.
notes.other_reading: even to one willing to overlook it

notes.latin: talis sit post maiorem iniuriam qualis ante beneficium
notes.note: Even when the wrong is greater than the benefit, he only goes back to where he stood before the benefit, that is, to neutral, not to enmity.
notes.other_reading: that after the greater injury he is what he was before the kindness

check.note: “Charge with a mischance” is archaic and unclear. The sense is looking for someone to blame for an accident.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “someone to blame for an accident”. Casus is something that happens by chance, and the note records the account-book sense of inputare.

check.note: “Into a grievance” is added. Calumniari is to put a false or malicious sense on something; the Latin does not name the result.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “He does not put a bad meaning on words or looks”. “Into a grievance” is dropped because the Latin names no result; “meaning” is used in place of the suggested “construction” as the plainer word.

check.note: In English “change his mind” means to alter a decision or opinion. Animum here is his feeling or attitude toward those who have done him good.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “his mind does not change toward”, which avoids the idiom about decisions. “Mind” is kept for animus, as in the glossary, because the same word returns in the last sentence (“remains in the mind”) and the link should be heard; the note gives “feeling” as the sense.

check.note: “Go far beyond” is left hanging: beyond what? Praecedunt means the bad deeds surpass the good ones, and English needs the object stated.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “unless the bad deeds far outstrip the good”. The object is supplied as suggested; “outstrip” is used and not “outweigh” because praecedere is to go ahead of, and the Latin has no image of weighing.

check.note: “Deserved well of him” is an archaic idiom that many readers of today will not follow.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “those who have done well by him”. The old idiom is gone; the suggested “good service” is not used because “service” already stands for officium in the same sentence, and the two Latin words should not share one English word.

check.note: Conivere is literally to close the eyes, but also to overlook on purpose. The English takes the literal sense; the other reading is “even to one who is willing to overlook it”.
check.decided: Declined: “even to one who shuts his eyes” stands. Conivere is literally to close the eyes, and the English image already says that the looking away is deliberate; the note records the plainer “willing to overlook it”.

passages.latin: Quemadmodum reus sententiis paribus absolvitur et semper quidquid dubium est humanitas inclinat in melius, sic animus sapientis, ubi paria maleficiis merita sunt, desinit quidem debere, sed non desinit velle debere, et hoc facit quod qui post tabulas novas solvunt.
passages.english: Just as a defendant is acquitted when the votes are equal, and humane feeling always tips whatever is doubtful toward the better side, so the mind of the wise man, when the services are equal to the misdeeds, does indeed cease to owe, but does not cease to want to owe, and does what those do who pay after a cancellation of debts.

notes.note: Refers to the rule that a tied vote of the jurors acquits (from memory, unchecked). Sententiae are the jurors’ votes.
notes.other_reading: when the verdicts are evenly divided

notes.note: Humanitas ranges over human feeling, kindness and civilised decency. The English has “humane feeling”.
notes.other_reading: kindness

notes.note: “Toward the better”, that is, toward the more favourable view. “Side” is supplied by the English.
notes.other_reading: toward the more lenient view

notes.note: Merita are the good services a person has done, maleficia the bad deeds. They answer to beneficium and iniuria in the section before, but the Latin words are different, so the English has “services” and “misdeeds”, not “benefit” and “wrong”.
notes.other_reading: when the good turns balance the ill turns

notes.note: Literally “new account books”, the Roman term for a general cancellation of debts (from memory, unchecked). The English gives the sense so that the comparison can be followed.
notes.other_reading: those who pay after new account books

check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “injuries” for maleficiis, which a reader would take for iniuria, the word given as “wrong” in the section before.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “when the services are equal to the misdeeds”. Maleficium is literally a bad deed, and iniuria does not occur in this section.

passages.latin: Philosophia circumdanda est, inexpugnabilis murus, quem fortuna multis machinis lacessitum non transit. In insuperabili loco stat animus qui externa deseruit et arce se sua vindicat; infra illum omne telum cadit. Non habet, ut putamus, fortuna longas manus: neminem occupat nisi haerentem sibi.
passages.english: Philosophy must be set around us, a wall that cannot be stormed, which Fortune does not get past, though she has assailed it with many siege engines. The mind that has abandoned external things stands in a place that cannot be scaled, and claims its freedom in its own citadel; every missile falls below it. Fortune does not have the long hands we think she has: she seizes no one except the one who clings to her.

notes.note: The Latin does not say around whom. The English supplies the general first person plural of the section before.
notes.other_reading: One must put philosophy around oneself

notes.note: Fortune takes a capital and “she” where she acts as a person, as here with her siege engines and hands. Where fortuna is plain chance, as in Ep. 81.1 and 81.25, the word is in lower case.
notes.other_reading: which fortune does not get past

notes.note: The participle belongs to the wall: “the wall, though attacked with many engines”. The English makes Fortune the one attacking, which the Latin implies.
notes.other_reading: which, though it has been battered by many engines, Fortune does not cross

notes.note: Insuperabilis is “that cannot be climbed over” as well as “that cannot be defeated”. The English takes the first, since the image is of high ground below which the missiles fall.
notes.other_reading: on ground that cannot be conquered

notes.note: Se vindicare is a legal phrase, to claim oneself as free; it can also mean simply to protect oneself. The ablative arce sua can be “in” or “by means of” its citadel.
notes.other_reading: and defends itself in its own citadel

notes.note: The parenthesis gives the common belief, that Fortune has long hands, which Seneca denies. The English is worded so that it cannot be read as a belief that she has none.
notes.other_reading: Fortune does not, as people suppose, have long hands

notes.note: Long hands, that is, a long reach. A proverb said that kings have long hands; a line of Ovid has it (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: a long reach

notes.note: Sibi refers to Fortune: the one who clings to her. By form it could refer to the person, which gives poor sense.
notes.other_reading: except one who holds fast to her gifts

check.note: Se vindicare can be “claim oneself as free” or “defend oneself”, and arce sua can be “in” or “by means of” its citadel. The English has the legal sense; the other reading is “defends itself in its own citadel”.
check.decided: Declined: “claims its freedom in its own citadel” stands. Vindicare is at root to lay a legal claim, and with se it is to claim oneself as free, a sense Seneca uses elsewhere (from memory, unchecked); the note records “defends itself” as the other reading.

check.note: Ground is not “overcome” in English. Insuperabilis here is “that cannot be climbed over”, and the height matters because the missiles fall below it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “in a place that cannot be scaled”. The word means that the place cannot be got over, and the next clause, with missiles falling below, shows that height is the point.

check.latin: Non habet, ut putamus, fortuna longas manus
check.note: The English can be read as saying that people think she does not have long hands. The Latin means the opposite: they suppose she has them, and she has not.
check.decided: Accepted: the sentence is reworded as suggested, so that the belief reported by ut putamus is plainly that Fortune has long hands, which Seneca then denies.

check.note: Here and in Ep. 84.13 the English has “Fortune” with a capital and “she”; in Ep. 81.1 and 81.25 it has “fortune” in lower case, for the same Latin word. One usage should be settled.
check.decided: Declined: both forms stand, as the glossary lays down: a capital where fortune is personified. Here she attacks with siege engines and has hands, and in Ep. 84.13 she lowers herself, while in Ep. 81.1 and 81.25 fortuna is plain chance, named beside carefulness or as the cause of faults.

passages.latin: Est et horum, Lucili, quae appellamus media grande discrimen. Non enim sic mors indifferens est quomodo utrum capillos pares habeas: mors inter illa est quae mala quidem non sunt, tamen habent mali speciem: sui amor est et permanendi conservandique se insita voluntas atque aspernatio dissolutionis, * * * quia videtur multa nobis bona eripere et nos ex hac cui adsuevimus rerum copia educere. Illa quoque res morti nos alienat, quod haec iam novimus, illa ad quae transituri sumus nescimus qualia sint, et horremus ignota. Naturalis praeterea tenebrarum metus est, in quas adductura mors creditur.
passages.english: Among these things too, Lucilius, which we call middle, there is a great difference. For death is not a matter of indifference in the same way as whether you have an even number of hairs: death is among those things that are not indeed evils, yet have the look of an evil. There is love of self, and an inborn will to last and to preserve oneself, and a shrinking from dissolution, [gap in the Latin text] because it seems to snatch many goods away from us and to lead us out of this plenty of things to which we have grown used. This too estranges us from death, that we already know the things here, while we do not know what the things are like to which we are going to cross over, and we shudder at the unknown. Besides, there is a natural fear of the dark, into which, it is believed, death will lead us.

notes.note: Media, “middle things”, is the Stoic term for things neither good nor evil, also called indifferentia in the section before. The English keeps “middle” for media and “indifference” for indifferens.
notes.other_reading: which we call intermediate

notes.note: Indifferens is the Stoic term for what is in itself neither good nor evil. “A matter of indifference” is used, here and in Ep. 82.16, because “death is indifferent” would read as if death did not care.
notes.other_reading: For death is not indifferent in the same way

notes.note: Pares is taken as “even in number”, the stock Stoic example of something wholly indifferent (from memory, unchecked). It could also mean hairs of equal length. The Latin as given does not say “or odd”; later editions print words for it after pares (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: whether your hair is cut evenly

notes.note: Species is outward look or appearance. Malum is “an evil”, the opposite of “a good” (bonum).
notes.other_reading: the appearance of something bad

notes.note: Est is taken as “there is”. With the gap that follows, this clause stands without a link to what comes before or after, and the first shape of the sentence cannot be recovered.
notes.other_reading: it is love of self

notes.note: Voluntas is will or wish. Here it is an inborn drive to go on existing.
notes.other_reading: an implanted desire

notes.note: Dissolutio is a loosening or coming apart: here, the coming apart of the living creature at death. Aspernatio is a turning away or rejection.
notes.other_reading: a recoil from being broken up

notes.note: The edition marks a gap here: some words are lost. The gap is marked in the English and not filled.
notes.other_reading: (nothing supplied)

notes.note: After the gap the subject of “seems” is not stated. It is presumably death, and the English has “it”.
notes.other_reading: because death seems

notes.note: Literally “makes us strangers to death”, with death in the dative.
notes.other_reading: sets us against death

notes.note: A future participle, “going to lead to”, with no object stated; the English supplies the first person plural.
notes.other_reading: into which death, it is believed, will lead

check.note: “Indifferent” is the technical Stoic term, but to a reader of today “death is not indifferent” sounds as if death does not care. The same word recurs in Ep. 82.16.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “death is not a matter of indifference”, and the same phrase is used in Ep. 82.16. A note gives the Stoic sense of indifferens: neither good nor evil in itself.

check.note: Pares can mean even in number or equal, level. The English has chosen number, which is likely, and the choice should be on record.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps “an even number of hairs”, as suggested, and the note records the other reading, hair of even length, and that the Latin as given has no “or odd”.

check.note: The gap is rightly marked. Two things follow from it: the clause before it stands without a link to what precedes, and the subject of videtur after it is lost, so “it” is a guess (presumably death).
check.decided: Accepted: the marker is kept and nothing is filled in. One note says that “it” after the gap is presumably death, and another that the clause about love of self stands unlinked.

check.note: “Is believed to be going to bring” is clumsy. The object is supplied, which is acceptable, but the sentence can be made plain.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “into which, it is believed, death will lead us”. The future participle and the belief are both kept, and the note says that the object is supplied.

check.note: “Dissolution” is bookish and may not be understood as the breaking up of the self.
check.decided: Declined: “a shrinking from dissolution” stands. Dissolutio is a loosening or coming apart, which “being broken up” would turn into something violent, and the English word is the Latin’s own; a note now says that the coming apart of the living creature is meant.

passages.latin: Itaque etiam si indifferens mors est, non tamen ea est quae facile neglegi possit: magna exercitatione durandus est animus ut conspectum eius accessumque patiatur. Mors contemni debet magis quam solet; multa enim de illa credidimus; multorum ingeniis certatum est ad augendam eius infamiam; descriptus est carcer infernus et perpetua nocte oppressa regio, in qua ingens ianitor Orci ossa super recubans antro semesa cruento aeternum latrans exsangues terreat umbras. Etiam cum persuaseris istas fabulas esse nec quicquam defunctis superesse quod timeant, subit alius metus: aeque enim timent ne apud inferos sint quam ne nusquam.
passages.english: So even if death is a matter of indifference, it is still not a thing that can easily be disregarded: the mind must be hardened by much training to bear the sight of it and its approach. Death ought to be scorned more than it usually is; for we have believed many things about it; the talents of many have competed to increase its bad name; a prison in the underworld has been described, and a region weighed down by everlasting night, in which the huge doorkeeper of Orcus, lying on half-eaten bones in his bloody cave, barking for ever, frightens the bloodless shades. Even when you have persuaded people that these are stories and that nothing is left for the dead to fear, another fear comes up: for they are equally afraid of being in the underworld and of being nowhere.

notes.note: Indifferens is the Stoic term for what is neither good nor evil in itself, given as “a matter of indifference” as in Ep. 82.15.
notes.other_reading: even if death is indifferent

notes.note: Exercitatio is practice or drill, as of a soldier or athlete.
notes.other_reading: by long practice

notes.note: “Scorned” in the sense of held of small account, not hated. It is the same verb as in Ep. 81.24.
notes.other_reading: Death ought to be thought less of than it usually is

notes.note: Impersonal: “there has been a contest by the talents of many”. The poets are meant.
notes.other_reading: many gifted men have vied with one another

notes.latin: ingens ianitor Orci ossa super recubans antro semesa cruento aeternum latrans exsangues terreat umbras
notes.note: These words are verse, woven into Seneca’s sentence without being marked as a quotation, so the English has no quotation marks. They join lines of Vergil’s Aeneid about Cerberus, from book 8 and book 6 (from memory, unchecked), as a sample of what the talents of many have written. Orcus is the god, or the realm, of the dead.
notes.other_reading: the huge gatekeeper of the underworld, crouched over half-gnawed bones in a gory cave

notes.note: The subjunctive is carried over from the verse and may give the sense “is there to frighten”. The English has a plain “frightens”.
notes.other_reading: is to frighten the bloodless shades

notes.note: Second person singular with no object: a general “you”, or Lucilius. The following verbs are third person plural, so “people” is supplied. A less likely reading is that “you” have become convinced.
notes.other_reading: Even when you have convinced them

notes.note: Literally “those who have finished”, a usual word for the dead.
notes.other_reading: for those who have done with life

notes.latin: aeque enim timent ne apud inferos sint quam ne nusquam
notes.note: Literally “they fear being among those below equally as being nowhere”. The English keeps the Latin order and the even balance of the two fears.
notes.other_reading: for they fear being nowhere just as much as being in the underworld

check.latin: ingens ianitor Orci ossa super recubans antro semesa cruento aeternum latrans exsangues terreat umbras
check.note: From memory, unchecked: these words are verse adapted from Vergil’s Aeneid, books 8 and 6. The Latin as given does not mark them as quoted, so the English rightly adds no quotation marks, but the reader should be told that a poet is being quoted.
check.decided: Accepted: the wording is kept without quotation marks, since the Latin as given does not mark the words as quoted, and the note names Vergil’s Aeneid as the source (from memory, unchecked).

check.note: “People” is supplied; the Latin verb has no object. The plural verbs that follow support it, but it is an addition. A less likely reading is “when you have become convinced”.
check.decided: Accepted: “when you have persuaded people” is kept, as suggested, because the verbs that follow are in the third person plural and need someone to refer to. The note records that “people” is supplied and gives the other reading.

check.note: As in Ep. 81.24, “despised” suggests hatred in today’s English. Contemni is to be thought little of, the opposite of the fear the passage goes on to describe.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Death ought to be scorned more than it usually is”. Contemnere is to hold of small account, and “scorn” is the same verb used for it in Ep. 81.24.

check.note: The Latin is “the talents of many (people)”: it is the people who are many. “Many talents” loses the people.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the talents of many have competed”. Multorum is “of many people”, so the many are the writers, not their gifts.

check.note: The same technical term as in Ep. 82.15; “death is indifferent” reads as if death does not care.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “even if death is a matter of indifference”, the same phrase as in Ep. 82.15, with a note on the Stoic term.

passages.latin: Singulos dies tibi meos et quidem totos indicari iubes:bene de me iudicas si nihil esse in illis putas quod abscondam. Sic certe vivendum est tamquam in conspectu vivamus, sic cogitandum tamquam aliquis in pectus intimum introspicere possit: et potest. Quid enim prodest ab homine aliquid esse secretum? nihil deo clusum est; interest animis nostris et cogitationibus medius intervenit -- sic 'intervenit' dico tamquam aliquando discedat.
passages.english: You tell me to report to you each of my days, and the whole of each: you judge well of me if you think there is nothing in them that I would hide. Certainly we must live as if we were living in plain sight, and think as if someone could look into the inmost heart: and someone can. For what is the use of something being kept secret from a human being? Nothing is shut to god; he is present in our minds and comes into the midst of our thoughts. I say “comes into” as if he ever went away.

notes.note: “And whole ones at that”: Lucilius wants the entire day accounted for, not a selection.
notes.other_reading: and in full

notes.note: Certe can affirm (“certainly”) or limit (“at any rate”: whatever is true of Seneca’s own days, this is how one must live). The English takes the first. The gerundive is an obligation, “must”.
notes.other_reading: At any rate, this is how one must live

notes.note: “In view”, with no word saying whose. It may be in the sight of everyone or of some observer.
notes.other_reading: in public

notes.note: Two words: “and [someone] can”. The subject is the “someone” just mentioned, who turns out to be god.
notes.other_reading: and there is one who can

notes.note: Homo is a human being, set against god in the next sentence; the contrast is not between male and female.
notes.other_reading: from a man

notes.note: A spelling of clausum, “closed, shut”.
notes.other_reading: Nothing is closed off from god

notes.latin: interest animis nostris et cogitationibus medius intervenit
notes.note: Two verbs in inter-: interest, “is among, is present in”, and intervenit, “comes among”. Medius stresses that he comes right into the middle.
notes.other_reading: he is in our minds and steps in among our thoughts

notes.note: Seneca corrects his own word: to say that god “comes in” wrongly implies that he is sometimes away. The edition’s dash is rendered as a new sentence.
notes.other_reading: “comes in”, as though he sometimes withdrew

check.note: The gerundive is an obligation and is “must” elsewhere in the draft; “should” weakens it. Certe may also be “at any rate” and not “certainly”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the gerundive is now “must”, the same obligation as elsewhere in these passages. “Certainly” is kept for certe, which can also be “at any rate”; a note records that reading.

check.note: The contrast is human being against god, not male against female. “From a man” blurs that for a reader of today.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “from a human being”. Homo is the word for a human as such, and the next sentence sets it against god.

passages.latin: Faciam ergo quod iubes, et quid agam et quo ordine libenter tibi scribam. Observabo me protinus et, quod est utilissimum, diem meum recognoscam. Hoc nos pessimos facit, quod nemo vitam suam respicit; quid facturi simus cogitamus, et id raro, quid fecerimus non cogitamus; atqui consilium futuri ex praeterito venit.
passages.english: So I will do what you tell me, and I will gladly write to you what I do and in what order. I will watch myself at once and, what is most useful, I will review my day. This is what makes us very bad, that no one looks back at his own life; we think about what we are going to do, and that rarely; we do not think about what we have done; and yet a plan for the future comes from the past.

notes.note: Protinus can mean “at once” or “straight on, without a break”. The English takes “at once”.
notes.other_reading: without a break, from now on

notes.note: Recognoscere is to go over and inspect, as one checks accounts or musters troops.
notes.other_reading: go back over the day

notes.note: A superlative, which can be “the worst” or “very bad”. With nothing to compare it to, the English takes “very bad”.
notes.other_reading: the worst of men

notes.note: Literally “looks back at”. The image of turning round to look is kept.
notes.other_reading: no one reviews his own life

notes.note: Consilium is both a plan and advice. The genitive is “of the future”.
notes.other_reading: advice about what is to come

check.note: The superlative can be “very bad” or “the worst”. The English has the weaker sense; either is defensible.
check.decided: Declined: “very bad” stands. A Latin superlative with nothing to compare it to is most often “very”, and “so bad” would add a word of degree that is not in the Latin; the note records “the worst”.

check.note: “Counsel” is a little dated. The sense is a plan, or good judgement, about what is to come.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a plan for the future comes from the past”. Consilium is a plan as well as advice, and “plan” is the plain word of today; the note keeps “advice” as the other reading.

passages.latin: 'Quomodo' inquis 'hoc effici poterit?' Adsidua intentione:si nihil egerimus nisi ratione suadente, nihil vitaverimus nisi ratione suadente.
