Hanc si audire volueris, dicet tibi: relinque ista iamdudum ad quae discurritur; relinque divitias, aut periculum possidentium aut onus; relinque corporis atque animi voluptates, molliunt et enervant; relinque ambitum, tumida res est, vana, ventosa, nullum habet terminum, tam sollicita est ne quem ante se videat quam ne secum, laborat invidia et quidem duplici. Vides autem quam miser sit si is cui invidetur et invidet.
passages.english: “How,” you say, “will it be possible to bring this about?” By constant attention: if we do nothing except at reason’s urging and avoid nothing except at reason’s urging. If you are willing to listen to reason, it will say to you: leave at once those things that people run about after; leave riches, either a danger or a burden to those who own them; leave the pleasures of body and of mind, they soften and weaken; leave ambition, it is a swollen thing, empty, windy, it has no limit, it is as anxious not to see anyone ahead of it as not to see anyone level with it, it suffers from envy, and a double envy at that. And you see how wretched a man is if he who is envied also envies.

notes.note: “This” is the state described in the section before: a mind in which many arts, precepts and examples sound together as one. The verb is future, “will be able to be brought about”, which the English turns as “will it be possible”.
notes.other_reading: how can that be achieved

notes.note: Intentio is a stretching or straining of the mind, so attention or effort. The English takes “attention”. The “if” clauses that follow hang on it with no main verb.
notes.other_reading: By unremitting effort

notes.note: Literally “with reason advising”. Ratio is “reason”, as in the glossary; the phrase is repeated word for word, and so is the English.
notes.other_reading: unless reason advises it

notes.note: A feminine pronoun for reason. The English names reason again and then has “it”, not “her”. Reason’s speech has no quotation marks in the Latin, so none are added.
notes.other_reading: If you are willing to listen to her, she will tell you

notes.note: With an imperative iamdudum means “at once, without more delay”, and it stands here before the relative clause, beside the imperative. It could instead be taken with the relative clause in its usual sense of “for a long time now”.
notes.other_reading: leave those things that people have long been running after

notes.note: Pleasures of the mind as well as of the body are to be given up. Animus is “mind”, as in the glossary.
notes.other_reading: the pleasures of body and soul

notes.note: Literally “take the sinews out”.
notes.other_reading: they soften and unstring

notes.note: Ambitus is properly going round canvassing for office, and so the pursuit of position.
notes.other_reading: leave the chase after office

notes.note: Elliptical: “lest [it see anyone] with itself”, that is, alongside it as an equal. The English fills in the verb.
notes.other_reading: as not to see anyone beside it

notes.note: Invidia is both the envy one feels and the ill will one draws. “Double” is explained by the next sentence: the ambitious man envies and is envied.
notes.other_reading: it is troubled by ill will, and of two kinds

notes.latin: si is cui invidetur et invidet
notes.note: The Latin is slightly loose: “how wretched he is, if the one who is envied also envies”. The English supplies “a man” as the one who is wretched; it could also be ambition itself, spoken of as a person.
notes.other_reading: how wretched it is when the man who is envied is envious too

check.note: Intentio can be attention or straining, effort. The English has chosen attention; the other reading is “by unremitting effort”.
check.decided: Declined: “By constant attention” stands. Intentio is the mind held stretched toward something, and the two clauses that follow describe heeding reason in every act, which is attention; the note records “effort” as the other reading.

check.latin: relinque ista iamdudum ad quae discurritur
check.note: Iamdudum with an imperative can mean “at once”, as the English has it, but it stands next to the relative clause and may belong there: “those things people have long been running after”. The choice should be on record.
check.decided: Accepted: “leave at once” is kept, as suggested. Iamdudum stands before the relative ad quae, inside the main clause with the imperative, where it means “without more delay”; the note records the other reading.

check.note: The Latin is future (“will it be possible”); the English is present. The difference is slight.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the question now reads “will it be possible to bring this about?”. The future of poterit is kept, in plainer words than the suggested “will this be able to be brought about”.

passages.latin: Quaecumque videntur eminere in rebus humanis, quamvis pusilla sint et comparatione humillimorum exstent, per difficiles tamen et arduos tramites adeuntur. Confragosa in fastigium dignitatis via est; at si conscendere hunc verticem libet, cui se fortuna summisit, omnia quidem sub te quae pro excelsissimis habentur aspicies, sed tamen venies ad summa per planum. Vale.
passages.english: Whatever things seem to stand high in human affairs, though they are tiny and stand out by comparison with the lowest, are still reached by hard and steep paths. The road to the peak of rank is rough; but if you care to climb this summit, the one before which Fortune has lowered herself, you will indeed see beneath you everything that is counted as loftiest, and yet you will come to the top over level ground. Farewell.

notes.note: They rise above the surface only relative to what is lowest. The Latin has no “only”, and none is added. Humillimorum can be the lowest things or the lowest people.
notes.other_reading: and stand out by comparison with the humblest people

notes.note: Fastigium is a gable or peak; dignitas is rank or standing in public life.
notes.other_reading: to the height of high office

notes.note: “This summit” is wisdom, to which the section before has just directed Lucilius; it is not the peak of rank just named. The English adds “the one” so that the relative clause marks it off.
notes.other_reading: this peak of wisdom

notes.note: Literally “to which Fortune has lowered herself”, that is, has submitted. Fortune is treated as a person and so takes a capital.
notes.other_reading: to which Fortune has submitted

notes.note: “Over the level”: the paradox is that the true height is reached without a climb.
notes.other_reading: by a level road

notes.note: Summa is neuter plural, “the highest things”.
notes.other_reading: you will arrive at the highest things

check.note: Read on its own, “this summit” points back to the peak of rank just mentioned, which makes the sentence contradict itself. In the letter “this” points to wisdom, in contrast with rank, and the quoted section needs some sign of that.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English keeps “this summit” and now adds “the one before which Fortune has lowered herself”, so that the relative clause marks this summit off from the peak of rank. No word for wisdom is put into the text, since the Latin has none here; the note says that wisdom is meant.

passages.latin: Deinde, si das aliquid iuris tristitiae, timori, cupiditati, ceteris motibus pravis, non erunt in nostra potestate. Quare? quia extra nos sunt quibus inritantur; itaque crescent prout magnas habuerint minoresve causas quibus concitentur. Maior erit timor, si plus quo exterreatur aut propius aspexerit, acrior cupiditas quo illam amplioris rei spes evocaverit.
passages.english: Next, if you grant any rights to sadness, to fear, to desire, to the other wrong movements, they will not be in our power. Why? Because the things that provoke them are outside us; and so they will grow according to whether the causes that stir them up are great or lesser. Fear will be greater if it has seen more to terrify it, or seen it nearer; desire will be keener to the degree that the hope of a larger thing has called it out.

notes.note: A legal turn of phrase: literally “if you give anything of right”, that is, any legal standing. The legal colour is kept with “grant any rights”.
notes.other_reading: if you allow any authority to

notes.note: The word ranges from gloom to grief. The English reads “sadness” and leaves “pain” and “grief” for dolor, as the glossary does.
notes.other_reading: grief, or distress

notes.note: Motus is “movement”, here a movement of the mind, Seneca’s general word for an emotion; pravus is literally “crooked”. The Latin does not say “of the mind”, and the English does not add it.
notes.other_reading: the other crooked movements of the mind

notes.note: The Stoic phrase for what depends on a person. The subject of “will not be” is the passions just listed.
notes.other_reading: they will not be under our control

notes.note: The Latin sets a plain adjective beside a comparative, “great or lesser causes”, and the English keeps the pair. Literally “according as they have had great or lesser causes”.
notes.other_reading: in proportion as the causes that stir them up are large or small

notes.latin: si plus quo exterreatur aut propius aspexerit
notes.note: Very compressed: literally “if it has seen more by which to be terrified, or nearer”. Fear itself is the subject of “has seen”, and the English keeps that personification. Propius could also be “has looked more closely”.
notes.other_reading: if a person has seen more to terrify him, or seen it nearer at hand

notes.latin: quo illam amplioris rei spes evocaverit
notes.note: Quo answers the comparative acrior: literally “by as much as the hope of a larger thing has called it out”. The English keeps “the hope of a larger thing” as the subject.
notes.other_reading: the larger the thing that it has been roused to hope for

check.note: The Latin says only “the other wrong movements”. “Of the mind” is an explanation folded into the text.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “to the other wrong movements”, because the Latin has no words for “of the mind”. The note explains that movements of the mind are meant.

check.note: The connective is dated, and “great or smaller” copies the Latin mix of a plain adjective and a comparative in a way that reads oddly in English.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “they will grow according to whether the causes that stir them up are great or lesser”. The dated connective is gone; “great or lesser” still shows that the Latin sets a plain adjective beside a comparative, and reads more easily than “large or smaller”.

check.note: “Whose hope” reads as if the thing does the hoping. The Latin is “hope of a larger thing”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “desire will be keener to the degree that the hope of a larger thing has called it out”, so that the hope is of the thing, as in the Latin. “To the degree that” stands where the suggestion has “in proportion as”, to the same effect.

check.note: One Latin verb governs both halves; the English gives it twice with two different verbs.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “if it has seen more to terrify it, or seen it nearer”, with one verb for the one Latin verb. “Terrify” replaces “frighten” because exterreatur is the stronger word.

passages.latin: Illud vero cuius dementiae est, credere quarum rerum extra nostrum arbitrium posita principia sunt, earum nostri esse arbitri terminos! Quomodo ad id finiendum satis valeo ad quod prohibendum parum valui, cum facilius sit excludere quam admissa conprimere?
passages.english: But what madness this is: to believe that where the beginnings of things are placed outside our control, their limits are within our control! How am I strong enough to set a limit to a thing that I was not strong enough to prevent, when it is easier to shut things out than to hold them down once they have been let in?

notes.note: Literally “but that, of what madness it is”, an exclamation. Vero marks a step up in the argument and is given as “But”.
notes.other_reading: And how mad this is

notes.note: Arbitri is the short genitive of arbitrium, the same word as a few words earlier, not arbiter, “judge”. The English reads “control” both times so that the repetition shows; the word is literally a person’s say or decision. Terminos, literally boundary marks, is set against principia, “beginnings”.
notes.other_reading: that their limits are ours to decide

notes.note: Finire can mean to set a bound to something or to bring it to an end. Because the argument is about how large the passions grow, and terminos has just been used, the English reads “set a limit to”.
notes.other_reading: to put an end to a thing

notes.note: The same verb valere as in satis valeo just before: “am strong enough” against “was too little strong”. The English keeps “strong enough” in both halves.
notes.other_reading: that I had too little strength to prevent

notes.note: Admissa is a general neuter plural, “things let in”; conprimere is to press down, hold in check. No object is named for “shut out” either, so the English reads “things”.
notes.other_reading: to suppress them once admitted

check.note: “Placed outside our decision” is not natural English; arbitrium here is a person’s say or control. One word is rightly used for both occurrences, and any replacement should do the same.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “control” for arbitrium in both places. It is the natural English for a person’s say over a thing, and it stays distinct from “power”, which this translation keeps for potestas.

check.note: Finire can also mean “put an end to”. The English has chosen “set a limit”, which fits the “limits” of the sentence before; the other reading should at least be noted.
check.decided: Declined: “set a limit to” stands. The sentence before speaks of the limits (terminos) of the passions, and the last clause speaks of holding them down, not of removing them; the other reading, “put an end to”, is recorded in the note.

check.note: Vero marks a step up in the argument; “And” is flat.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now begins “But what madness this is”, because vero marks a turn to a stronger point, which “And” did not show.

passages.latin: Ego aliter respondendum iudico: nec artem gubernatoris deteriorem ulla tempestate fieri nec ipsam administrationem artis. Gubernator tibi non felicitatem promisit sed utilem operam et navis regendae scientiam; haec eo magis apparet quo illi magis aliqua fortuita vis obstitit. Qui hoc potuit dicere, 'Neptune, numquam hanc navem nisi rectam', arti satis fecit: tempestas non opus gubernatoris inpedit sed successum.
passages.english: I judge that a different answer should be given: that neither the helmsman’s art nor the actual practice of the art is made worse by any storm. The helmsman did not promise you good luck, but useful effort and the knowledge of how to steer a ship; this knowledge is all the more visible, the more some chance force has stood in his way. Anyone who has been able to say this, “Neptune, never this ship except on a straight course”, has done enough for his art: a storm hinders not the helmsman’s work but his success.

notes.note: Seneca has just reported and set aside another reply to the comparison of the wise man with a helmsman; here he gives his own. “Should be given” renders the impersonal gerundive.
notes.other_reading: that one must reply differently

notes.note: Administratio is the carrying out or handling of something; the word can also be used of steering. Ipsam goes with administrationem and sets the practice beside the art, so the English reads “the actual practice of the art”.
notes.other_reading: nor the exercise of the art itself

notes.note: Here a lucky result, not happiness of mind. “Happy” is kept for beatus and “fortune” for fortuna, so the English reads “good luck”.
notes.other_reading: a fortunate outcome

notes.note: Opera is effort or pains given to a task. “Effort” keeps it apart from opus, “work”, later in this section and from ministerium, “service”, in 85.36.
notes.other_reading: useful service

notes.note: Regere, “to steer”, is the root of rectam in the saying that follows and of rector in 85.38.
notes.other_reading: the science of guiding a ship

notes.latin: haec eo magis apparet quo illi magis aliqua fortuita vis obstitit
notes.note: Haec is the knowledge just named, so the English says “this knowledge”. Illi may be the helmsman or the knowledge itself; the English takes it as the helmsman because the pronoun changes.
notes.other_reading: the more some chance force has stood in its way

notes.latin: Neptune, numquam hanc navem nisi rectam
notes.note: The saying has no verb; something like “will you sink” is left unsaid, and the English keeps the gap. It is a helmsman’s saying, sometimes given to a Rhodian pilot (from memory, unchecked). Rectam agrees with the ship and can mean “straight, on course” or “upright”; the English takes the first, which suits the steering just mentioned.
notes.other_reading: Neptune, never this ship except upright

notes.note: Satis facere is to do enough for, to meet a claim, as one settles a debt. The art is treated as the thing he owed something to.
notes.other_reading: has met what his art requires

notes.note: The outcome, how it turns out, set against opus, the work itself. “Work” is kept for opus here and in the sections that follow.
notes.other_reading: the result

check.note: The quoted saying has no verb. Rectam agrees with the ship and means “upright” or “on a straight course”; the English adds “held”, turns it into a condition and picks “straight” without saying so.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “Neptune, never this ship except on a straight course”. “Held” and the conditional “unless” are gone and the verb is still left unsaid; “on a straight course” is kept over “upright” because rectam belongs to the verb for steering used just before, and the note gives the other reading.

check.latin: haec eo magis apparet quo illi magis
check.note: Haec is feminine and picks up the knowledge, but the English “this” reads as “this fact”. Illi can be the helmsman or the knowledge, and “and” is added.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “this knowledge is all the more visible, the more some chance force has stood in his way”, with no added “and” and with the knowledge named. The note records that “his way” could be “its way”.

check.note: “The very practice” is dated; ipsam simply sets the exercise of the art beside the art.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “nor the actual practice of the art”. “The very practice” is gone, but “the exercise of the art itself” is not used because in English “itself” would attach to the art, while ipsam goes with the practice.

check.note: Felicitas can be good luck or a successful outcome. With “success” closing the section, “a fortunate outcome” is the other reading.
check.decided: Declined: “good luck” stands. Felicitas is what the helmsman cannot promise because it rests on chance, and “success” is needed for successum at the end of the section; the other reading is in the note.

check.note: Hoc, “this”, is dropped, and “The man who has been able to say” is stiff.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Anyone who has been able to say this”, so that hoc is no longer dropped.

check.note: Opera is rendered “service” here and ministerium is also “service” in 85.36. These are two different Latin words, and “work” is already used for opus.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “useful effort”, so that “service” is left for ministerium in 85.36 and “work” for opus.

passages.latin: Deinde gubernatoris ars alienum bonum est: ad eos quos vehit pertinet, quomodo medici ad eos quos curat: commune bonum est: et eorum cum quibus vivit et proprium ipsius. Itaque gubernatori fortasse noceatur cuius ministerium aliis promissum tempestate inpeditur:
passages.english: Next, the helmsman’s art is a good that belongs to others: it is for those he carries, as the doctor’s is for those he treats. [The wise man’s] is a shared good: it is both the good of those he lives with and his own. And so the helmsman may perhaps be harmed, whose service, promised to others, is hindered by a storm.

notes.note: Literally a good that is another’s. The phrase comes back in 85.37, where it is rendered the same way.
notes.other_reading: another’s good

notes.note: Pertinere ad can mean to concern, to belong to or to be for the benefit of. The English reads “is for”, here and for the same verb in 85.37.
notes.other_reading: it concerns those he carries

notes.latin: quomodo medici ad eos quos curat
notes.note: “Art” is understood again with medici: “as the doctor’s [art is for] those he treats”.
notes.other_reading: just as medicine concerns the doctor’s patients

notes.latin: commune bonum est: et eorum cum quibus vivit et proprium ipsius
notes.note: The Latin as given has no subject for this clause and would say that the helmsman’s art is both a good that belongs to others and a shared one, which contradicts the sentence before. From memory, unchecked: editors supply sapientis (“the wise man’s”) before commune. 85.37 shows that wisdom is meant, and the supplied words stand in square brackets.
notes.other_reading: it is a shared good: both of those he lives with and his own

notes.note: Proprium is “one’s own” as against commune, “shared”; ipsius is “of the man himself”. The English reads simply “his own”.
notes.other_reading: and his own in particular

notes.note: An impersonal passive in the subjunctive of possibility: “harm may perhaps be done to the helmsman”. Seneca concedes the point without asserting it.
notes.other_reading: perhaps the helmsman would be harmed

notes.note: The relative clause may carry a reason (“since his service”); the English keeps the plain “whose” and adds no “because”. Ministerium is “service”, the work of one who serves.
notes.other_reading: since the service he promised to others

notes.note: The Latin sentence does not end here: after the colon it runs on into 85.37 (“the wise man is not harmed”). The English closes with a full stop so that the section can stand alone as a paragraph.
notes.other_reading: is hindered by a storm: the wise man is not harmed

check.note: The Latin as given has no subject for this clause; as it stands it would call the helmsman’s or doctor’s art both another’s good and a shared good. A word has evidently dropped out, and the reader needs to be told that the bracketed words are a supplement.
check.decided: Accepted: the bracketed “[The wise man’s]” stays, and the note says plainly that the Latin as given has no subject for this clause. “The wise man’s” is kept over “Wisdom” because “those he lives with” and “his own” need a person; the supplement rests on memory of the editions, unchecked.

check.note: After “another’s good”, pertinet ad more likely means “belongs to” or “is for”. “Concerns” is weaker and vaguer.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “it is for those he carries”, and “the work that is for others” in 85.37. “Concerns” was too weak, but “belongs to” would only repeat the clause before and would not suit the work spoken of in 85.37, so “is for” serves both places.

check.note: “Very” adds emphasis that the Latin does not have.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “very” is removed and the English reads “his own”. “In particular” is not added, since proprium ipsius means no more than “his own” as against “shared”, and “in particular” could be read as “especially”.

check.note: “Is another’s good” is a little obscure on first reading. Any change should be made in 85.37 as well.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a good that belongs to others”, here and in 85.37.

check.note: The Latin sentence runs on past the colon into the contrast with the wise man in 85.37. The full stop closes it and cuts the antithesis, which should at least be marked.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the full stop stays, because each section is printed as a paragraph of its own and a closing colon would leave it hanging. The note says that the Latin sentence runs on into 85.37 and gives the joined reading.

passages.latin: sapienti non nocetur a paupertate, non a dolore, non ab aliis tempestatibus vitae. Non enim prohibentur opera eius omnia, sed tantum ad alios pertinentia: ipse semper in actu est, in effectu tunc maximus cum illi fortuna se opposuit; tunc enim ipsius sapientiae negotium agit, quam diximus et alienum bonum esse et suum.
passages.english: The wise man is not harmed by poverty, nor by pain, nor by the other storms of life. For not all his work is prevented, but only the work that is for others: he himself is always in action, greatest in what he achieves at the time when fortune has set itself against him; for then he is doing the business of wisdom itself, which we said is both a good that belongs to others and his own.

notes.note: This begins in lower case because it finishes the sentence of 85.36 (“the helmsman may perhaps be harmed:”). The English begins a new sentence with a capital.
notes.other_reading: no harm is done to the wise man

notes.note: The image is kept: poverty and pain are “storms”, like the helmsman’s storm.
notes.other_reading: the other tempests of life

notes.note: Prohibere recurs through 85.38. The English uses “prevent” for it every time, and “hinder” for inpedire.
notes.other_reading: are blocked

notes.note: Opera is the plural of opus, “work”, the word used of the helmsman in 85.33 and of the wise man in 85.38. The English reads “all his work” in the singular, because “works” suggests finished products.
notes.other_reading: not all his works are prevented

notes.note: The same verb as in 85.36, rendered “is for” in both places.
notes.other_reading: only those that concern others

notes.latin: ipse semper in actu est, in effectu tunc maximus
notes.note: In actu is “in action, at work”; in effectu is “in what is brought about”, and the two words answer each other. The English takes in effectu with maximus (“greatest in what he achieves”); it could instead go with est.
notes.other_reading: he himself is always in action and in effect, and greatest then when

notes.note: Fortune is pictured as an opponent who stands in the way. The English keeps the small letter and “itself”, to match the plain “fortune” of 85.38 and 85.40; a capital and “herself” would press the personification further.
notes.other_reading: when Fortune has set herself against him

notes.note: Ipsius can go with sapientiae (“of wisdom itself”) or stand alone as “his own”. The English takes the first. Negotium agere is to carry on someone’s business.
notes.other_reading: he is doing the business of his own wisdom

notes.latin: quam diximus et alienum bonum esse et suum
notes.note: The verb of saying points back to 85.36, exactly where the Latin as given has lost its subject; this clause is the evidence that wisdom was meant there. Suum could be wisdom’s “its own” or a general “one’s own”; the English reads “his own”, the wise man’s, as in 85.36.
notes.other_reading: which, as we said, is both another’s good and one’s own

check.latin: et alienum bonum esse et suum
check.note: Suum grammatically goes back to wisdom (“its own”) or means loosely “one’s own”. “His” resolves it as the wise man’s, which fits 85.36 but is a choice.
check.decided: Declined: “his own” stands. In 85.36 the good was called the wise man’s own, and this clause refers back to that place; the note now records that suum could also be “its own” or “one’s own”.

check.note: The capital letter and “herself” personify more than the Latin as given, and fortuna is plain “fortune” in 85.38 and 85.40.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “fortune has set itself against him”, with a small letter, as in 85.38 and 85.40. The note gives the more strongly personified reading.

check.note: “Very” is added; the Latin is simply “then, when”.
check.decided: Accepted: “very” is removed and the English reads “at the time when”, which is all that tunc and cum say.

check.note: “Works are prevented” is odd English, and “works” suggests finished products; opera here are his activities.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “not all his work is prevented, but only the work that is for others”. “Work” in the singular replaces “works”, but “prevented” stays because the same Latin verb, prohibere, runs through 85.38 and needs one English word.

passages.latin: Praeterea ne aliis quidem tunc prodesse prohibetur cum illum aliquae necessitates premunt. Propter paupertatem prohibetur docere quemadmodum tractanda res publica sit, at illud docet, quemadmodum sit tractanda paupertas. Per totam vitam opus eius extenditur. Ita nulla fortuna, nulla res actus sapientis excludit; id enim ipsum agit quo alia agere prohibetur. Ad utrosque casus aptatus est: bonorum rector est, malorum victor.
passages.english: Besides, he is not prevented from being of use even to others at the time when some constraints press on him. Because of poverty he is prevented from teaching how the state should be handled, but he teaches this: how poverty should be handled. His work stretches through the whole of life. So no fortune, no circumstance shuts out the wise man’s actions; for he is busy with the very thing that prevents him from being busy with other things. He is fitted for either turn of events: he steers good things, he conquers bad ones.

notes.note: Necessitates are things that cannot be avoided and that force a person’s hand. The English reads “constraints”, because “necessities” today means things one needs. Premere is “press”, and the same verb is “pressed” in 85.40.
notes.other_reading: when some unavoidable circumstances weigh on him

notes.note: The same verb tractare is used of the state and then of poverty, so the English reads “handled” for both. Res publica may be “the state” or “public affairs”.
notes.other_reading: how public affairs should be managed

notes.latin: Per totam vitam opus eius extenditur
notes.note: Totam vitam can be “the whole of life” (every condition of it) or “his whole life” (its whole length). The English takes the first, which suits the argument.
notes.other_reading: His work extends over his whole life

notes.note: Actus is plural, “actions”, and picks up in actu of 85.37. Excludit is “shuts out”.
notes.other_reading: bars the wise man from acting

notes.latin: id enim ipsum agit quo alia agere prohibetur
notes.note: Agere is used twice, and the English reads “be busy with” both times. The sense is that his poverty, which stops other activity, is itself what he works on. The Latin is passive: literally “by which he is prevented”.
notes.other_reading: for he is doing the very thing by which he is prevented from doing other things

notes.note: Casus is what befalls, a chance or outcome; “either” means good fortune and bad.
notes.other_reading: for both kinds of chance

notes.note: Bonorum and malorum are taken as neuter, “good things” and “bad things”, not good and bad men. Rector and victor are nouns, “one who steers or rules” and “conqueror”; the English turns them into verbs. Rector is taken as the one who steers, from the verb used of the ship in 85.33.
notes.other_reading: he is the ruler of good things, the conqueror of bad ones

check.note: “Necessities” is not how English today says “things that cannot be avoided”. Also, premere is “press on” here but “pressed down” in 85.40.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “when some constraints press on him”. “Necessities” is gone; “constraints” is closer to necessitates than “unavoidable circumstances” and leaves “circumstance” free for res later in the section. Premere is “press” here and “pressed” in 85.40.

check.latin: id enim ipsum agit quo alia agere prohibetur
check.note: Accurate but heavy and hard to take in at one reading.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “for he is busy with the very thing that prevents him from being busy with other things”. The clause is lighter, as suggested, but one English verb is kept for the repeated agere, where the suggestion has “at work on” and “doing”.

check.note: Casus here are the things that befall him, good or bad. “Kinds of chance” is unclear.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “He is fitted for either turn of events”, since casus are the things that befall him, good or bad.

check.note: Rector is also the one who steers, and the whole argument runs on the helmsman. “Ruler” drops the echo, and “ruler of good things” is odd in itself.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “he steers good things, he conquers bad ones”, which keeps the link with the steering of the ship in 85.33. The note records that the Latin has nouns and that “ruler” is the other sense of rector.

passages.latin: Tu illum premi putas malis? utitur. Non ex ebore tantum Phidias sciebat facere simulacra; faciebat ex aere. Si marmor illi, si adhuc viliorem materiam obtulisses, fecisset quale ex illa fieri optimum posset. Sic sapiens virtutem, si licebit, in divitiis explicabit, si minus, in paupertate; si poterit, in patria, si minus, in exilio; si poterit, imperator, si minus, miles; si poterit, integer, si minus, debilis. Quamcumque fortunam acceperit, aliquid ex illa memorabile efficiet.
passages.english: You think he is pressed by bad things? He uses them. It was not only out of ivory that Phidias knew how to make statues; he made them out of bronze. If you had offered him marble, if you had offered him a still cheaper material, he would have made the best that could be made out of it. In the same way the wise man will display virtue in riches if he is allowed, and if not, in poverty; in his own country if he can, and if not, in exile; as a general if he can, and if not, as a soldier; able-bodied if he can, and if not, disabled. Whatever fortune he receives, he will make out of it something worth remembering.

notes.note: Premere is the verb used in 85.38 (“constraints press on him”), so the English keeps “pressed”. Malis is rendered “bad things”, to match “bad ones” in 85.38. The expressed Tu is emphatic, which the English shows by opening with “You think”.
notes.other_reading: Do you think he is crushed by evils?

notes.latin: Non ex ebore tantum Phidias sciebat facere simulacra
notes.note: Phidias was the Athenian sculptor of the fifth century BC, famous for statues of gods in gold and ivory. Simulacra are images, especially of gods; the English reads “statues”. Tantum, “only”, goes with “out of ivory”.
notes.other_reading: Phidias knew how to make images of the gods, and not from ivory alone

notes.note: The Latin has no “also”, and none is added. The imperfect may mean “he used to make them”.
notes.other_reading: he used to make them in bronze as well

notes.latin: quale ex illa fieri optimum posset
notes.note: Literally “such a thing as could be made best out of it”. Materiam, “material”, is also Seneca’s word in this letter for the material that virtue works on.
notes.other_reading: the best statue that material allowed

notes.note: Explicare is to unfold, unroll or deploy, as a general deploys a line of battle. The English reads “display”, which is clearer than “unfold” and comes from the same image.
notes.other_reading: will unfold virtue, or will deploy virtue

notes.note: Here a commanding general, set against the common soldier. In Seneca’s time it was also a title of the emperor, which is not the sense here.
notes.other_reading: as a commander

notes.note: Integer is whole, unimpaired; debilis is disabled or weakened in body. Both are about the body, though the Latin does not say “in body”.
notes.other_reading: whole if he can, and if not, maimed

notes.note: Worth recording or telling. The English reads “worth remembering”.
notes.other_reading: something notable

check.note: The expressed Tu is emphatic and the English loses it. Also premere is “press on” in 85.38 and “pressed down” here.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “You think he is pressed by bad things?”. “Pressed” matches “press on” in 85.38, and the emphatic Tu is shown by putting “You” first; “really” is not added because the Latin has no such word.

check.note: “Unfold virtue” is not clear English. Explicare here is to deploy or display.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “will display virtue”. The note records the literal “unfold” or “deploy”.

check.latin: si poterit, integer, si minus, debilis
check.note: “Whole” and “maimed” are dated, and “maimed” narrows debilis (disabled, weakened in body) to mutilation.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “able-bodied if he can, and if not, disabled”. “Maimed” narrowed debilis to mutilation; “able-bodied” gives integer in one word without a separate “in body”, which the Latin does not have.

check.latin: quale ex illa fieri optimum posset
check.note: “Thing” is vague; the Latin means the best of its kind that the material allows.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the best that could be made out of it”, without the added “thing”.

check.latin: Non ex ebore tantum Phidias sciebat facere simulacra
check.note: Found while settling: “did not know how to make statues only out of ivory” could be read as saying that Phidias lacked a skill. Tantum, “only”, limits “out of ivory”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “It was not only out of ivory that Phidias knew how to make statues”, so that “not only” falls on the ivory. No “also” is added in the next clause, since the Latin has none.

passages.latin: Quid enim, oro te, liberale habent isti ieiuni vomitores, quorum corpora in sagina, animi in macie et veterno sunt? An liberale studium istuc esse iuventuti nostrae credimus, quam maiores nostri rectam exercuerunt hastilia iacere, sudem torquere, equum agitare, arma tractare? Nihil liberos suos docebant quod discendum esset iacentibus. Sed nec hae nec illae docent aluntve virtutem; quid enim prodest equum regere et cursum eius freno temperare, adfectibus effrenatissimis abstrahi? quid prodest multos vincere luctatione vel caestu, ab iracundia vinci?
passages.english: For what is there that is liberal, I ask you, about those people who vomit on an empty stomach, whose bodies are stuffed fat and whose minds are thin and sluggish? Or do we believe that this is a liberal study for our youth, whom our ancestors trained upright, to throw javelins, to hurl a stake, to ride a horse, to handle weapons? They taught their children nothing that had to be learned lying down. But neither these arts nor those teach or nourish virtue; for what use is it to control a horse and moderate its pace with the bridle, yet be dragged away by the most unbridled passions? What use is it to beat many at wrestling or boxing, yet be beaten by a hot temper?

notes.note: The whole letter turns on this word: liberalis means befitting a free person (liber), and it gives “liberal arts” and “liberal studies”. It does not mean generous or politically liberal here. The English keeps “liberal” so that the argument about the word can be followed.
notes.other_reading: worthy of a free man

notes.note: These are the wrestlers and athletes dismissed just before. Literally “those fasting vomiters”: ieiuni is “on an empty stomach”, and it may point to a training regime of fasting, vomiting and heavy feeding, though the Latin does not say so. It could also be a slur, “starved” or “meagre”, in line with the thin minds that follow.
notes.other_reading: those starved vomiters

notes.latin: corpora in sagina, animi in macie et veterno
notes.note: Sagina is fattening or cramming, the word used of animals and of gladiators. Macies is leanness and veternus is torpor or drowsiness. The Latin has nouns in parallel, literally “bodies in fattening, minds in leanness and torpor”; the English uses adjectives.
notes.other_reading: whose bodies are in the feeding stall and whose minds are wasted and drowsy

notes.note: “That thing”, with a note of contempt: the athletes’ training just dismissed. The English reads “this”.
notes.other_reading: that pursuit of theirs

notes.note: Rectam agrees with the youth: “trained it upright”, that is, not on the ground. It is set against iacentibus, “lying down”, in the next sentence. It could also give the result, “trained to be upright”.
notes.other_reading: whom our ancestors trained to stand straight

notes.note: “Lying down” is not explained: it may be wrestling on the ground or reclining at ease. There may also be a play between iacere, “to throw”, just before and iacere, “to lie”; the English cannot show it.
notes.other_reading: nothing that could be learned by people reclining

notes.note: Liberi, “children”, is the same word as “the free”, so it echoes liberale. The echo is lost in English.
notes.other_reading: their freeborn children

notes.note: Feminine plural with no noun. “Arts” (artes) is supplied from the argument just before; the two groups are the athletes’ training and the ancestors’ military exercises.
notes.other_reading: neither the one kind nor the other

notes.note: Effrenatissimis plays on freno, kept as “bridle” and “unbridled”. The two infinitives stand side by side with no connecting word, as a contrast; the English adds “yet” to carry the contrast, here and before “be beaten”.
notes.other_reading: to moderate its pace with the bridle and be dragged away by passions utterly unbridled

notes.note: The caestus is the boxer’s strapping of leather thongs, so “with the caestus” means “at boxing”. Vincere and vinci are kept as one verb, “beat” and “be beaten”.
notes.other_reading: to defeat many in wrestling or with the boxing glove

notes.note: Iracundia is the disposition to anger, a hot temper, as distinct from ira, a fit of anger. Seneca does not always keep the two apart.
notes.other_reading: and be beaten by anger

check.note: “Fasting vomiters” is opaque to a reader today. Ieiuni most naturally means “on an empty stomach”; it could also be heard as “starved”, in line with the lean minds that follow.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “those people who vomit on an empty stomach”, and the sentence is recast as “what is there that is liberal about” so that the “whose” clause follows the people it describes. The note gives the literal “fasting vomiters” and the other sense of ieiuni.

check.note: “Liberal” on its own will be read as generous or political; here it means fit for a free person, and it plays against liberos, “children”, two sentences on. The word should stay the same in “liberal study”, with a note.
check.decided: Accepted: “liberal” is kept in both places for the chain, and the notes on liberale and on liberos suos explain the sense, fit for a free person, and the lost play on “children”.

check.latin: quorum corpora in sagina, animi in macie et veterno sunt
check.note: The Latin sets fat bodies against thin minds in parallel phrases. The English breaks the parallel, and “in leanness” is not English.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “whose bodies are stuffed fat and whose minds are thin and sluggish”, which sets fat bodies against thin minds in matching phrases.

check.note: Rectam agrees with the youth, but “standing upright” can be taken with the ancestors. It is set against “lying down” in the next sentence.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “whom our ancestors trained upright”. Without “standing” the word attaches to the youth and still answers “lying down”; “on their feet” is not used because riding a horse is among the exercises.

check.note: “The stake” with the definite article is puzzling; the sudis is a pointed stake thrown as a weapon.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “to hurl a stake”.

check.note: “Arts” is supplied. The feminine plural supports it and the section needs it to stand alone, so the suggestion is to keep it and to make clear that it is an addition.
check.decided: Declined: “arts” stays. The Latin pronouns are feminine plural and English needs a noun for them; the note says that the word is supplied and from where.

check.note: The Latin sets the two halves side by side with no link, as a contrast, and “and” weakens it, here and before “be beaten”. “Passions utterly unbridled” is ornate word order.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “yet be dragged away by the most unbridled passions”, and “yet be beaten” in the next sentence. The Latin has no linking word, as the note records, but the bare contrast cannot stand in English without one.

check.note: Iracundia is the disposition, a hot temper, more than a single fit of anger.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “yet be beaten by a hot temper”. Iracundia is the standing disposition, but “one’s own” is not in the Latin and is not added; the note gives “anger” as the other reading.

passages.latin: Discribitur in tribus populus, in centurias exercitus; quidquid in maius crevit facilius agnoscitur si discessit in partes, quas, ut dixi, innumerabiles esse et parvulas non oportet. Idem enim vitii habet nimia quod nulla divisio: simile confuso est quidquid usque in pulverem sectum est.
passages.english: The people is distributed into tribes, the army into centuries; whatever has grown large is more easily made out if it has separated into parts, which, as I said, ought not to be countless and tiny. For too much division has the same fault as none: whatever has been cut all the way down to dust is like a jumble.

notes.note: Tribus here is “tribes” (accusative plural), the divisions of the Roman people, not the number three. Discribitur is to mark off or distribute into classes; “distributed” keeps it apart from divisio, “division”, in the last sentence.
notes.other_reading: The people is marked off into tribes

notes.note: A century is a Roman army unit of nominally a hundred men, not a hundred years. The Roman term is kept, as “tribes” is.
notes.other_reading: the army into companies

notes.note: Literally “has grown into something larger”. No point of comparison is stated, and the English reads “has grown large”.
notes.other_reading: whatever has grown to a larger size

notes.note: To recognise, to come to know, to make out. The English reads “made out”, since the point is taking in something too big to see whole.
notes.other_reading: is more easily recognised

notes.note: Points back to what comes just before this section, where he promised to divide philosophy into parts and not into scraps.
notes.other_reading: as I have said

notes.note: Confusum is what has been poured together and not sorted. The thought is that dust is as hard to take in as an undivided heap.
notes.other_reading: is like what is mixed together

check.note: This is a different Latin verb from the “division” (divisio) of the last sentence; it means marked off or distributed into classes. “Divided” for both blurs the two.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “The people is distributed into tribes”, so that “division” is left for divisio in the last sentence.

check.note: A reader today will first take “centuries” as spans of a hundred years; “companies” is suggested.
check.decided: Declined: “centuries” stays. It is the name of the Roman unit, as “tribes” is of the divisions of the Roman people, and beside “the army” it can hardly be taken for years; the note explains it and gives “companies”.

check.note: “Has grown to a larger size” is stiff; the Latin is simply “has grown large”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “whatever has grown large”. The note gives the literal form.

check.note: “All” is added in “all mixed together”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “is like a jumble”, without the added “all”.

check.note: Found while settling: usque, “all the way”, was not rendered in “cut down to dust”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “cut all the way down to dust”.

passages.latin: Ergo cum tripertita sit philosophia, moralem eius partem primum incipiamus disponere. Quam in tria rursus dividi placuit, ut prima esset inspectio suum cuique distribuens et aestimans quanto quidque dignum sit, maxime utilis -- quid enim est tam necessarium quam pretia rebus inponere? -- secunda de impetu, de actionibus tertia. Primum enim est ut quanti quidque sit iudices, secundum ut impetum ad illa capias ordinatum temperatumque, tertium ut inter impetum tuum actionemque conveniat, ut in omnibus istis tibi ipse consentias.
passages.english: So, since philosophy has three parts, let us begin by setting out its moral part first. It has been held that this in turn is divided into three: the first is the examination that assigns to each thing its own and assesses how much each is worth, useful in the highest degree (for what is so necessary as putting prices on things?); the second is about impulse, the third about actions. For the first thing is that you judge how much each thing is worth; the second, that you take up toward those things an impulse that is ordered and moderated; the third, that your impulse and your action fit together, so that in all of these you agree with yourself.

notes.note: The three parts named earlier in the letter are the moral, the natural and the rational (ethics, physics, logic).
notes.other_reading: since philosophy is threefold

notes.note: Primum is “first”, slightly doubled by “let us begin”. The English keeps both. Disponere is to set out in order.
notes.other_reading: let us first begin to arrange

notes.note: Placuit is impersonal, “it has been held” or “it has been agreed”, the settled view of the school; Seneca does not say whose. The ut clause spells out the division, so the English uses a colon.
notes.other_reading: It has been decided to divide this in turn into three, so that the first is

notes.note: Inspectio is a looking into, the examining part of ethics. Suum cuique echoes the formula of justice, “to each his own”; cuique can be “to each thing” or “to each person”. The English takes “each thing” because the next words are about what each thing is worth.
notes.other_reading: the examination that gives each person his due

notes.note: Agrees with inspectio. It can mean “extremely useful” or “the most useful of the three”; the English reads “useful in the highest degree”, which leaves the comparison with the other two unstated, as the Latin does.
notes.other_reading: the most useful of the three

notes.note: Literally to put prices on things. The image of pricing is kept.
notes.other_reading: to set values on things

notes.note: Impetus is Seneca’s Latin for the Stoic term for the impulse toward action (Greek horme; from memory, unchecked). “Impulse” is used for it throughout 89.14 and 89.15.
notes.other_reading: about the drive to act

notes.latin: ut in omnibus istis tibi ipse consentias
notes.note: This second ut may give the aim or result of all three points (“so that”) or restate the third (“that is, that”). The English reads “so that”, because “in all of these” looks back over all three. Tibi consentias is to be in agreement with yourself.
notes.other_reading: that is, that in all of these you are consistent with yourself

check.note: This can be “the most useful (of the three)” or “extremely useful”. The English picks the second in a dated form and adds “part”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “useful in the highest degree”, which drops the dated “a most useful part” and the added “part”. It leaves open, as the Latin does, whether a comparison with the other two parts is meant; the note gives “the most useful of the three”.

check.latin: ut in omnibus istis tibi ipse consentias
check.note: The second ut may run parallel to the first and restate the third requirement, not give a result. “So that” chooses result without saying so.
check.decided: Declined: “so that” stands. “In all of these” (in omnibus istis) looks back over assessment, impulse and action together, which suits an aim of the whole better than a restatement of the third point; the other reading is in the note.

check.note: Placuit is the settled view of the philosophers, not a decision taken by an unnamed body. The ut clause spells out the division; it does not give its result.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “It has been held that this in turn is divided into three: the first is”, so that placuit is a settled view and the ut clause sets out the division.

check.note: This echoes the formula “to each his own”, where cuique is a person. The English takes it of things, which the following quidque supports, but it is a choice that should be kept or noted.
check.decided: Declined: “assigns to each thing its own” stands, because the words that follow are about what each thing is worth. The note already records the echo of “to each his own” and the reading with a person.

passages.latin: Quidquid ex tribus defuit turbat et cetera. Quid enim prodest inter aestimata habere omnia, si sis in impetu nimius? quid prodest impetus repressisse et habere cupiditates in sua potestate, si in ipsa rerum actione tempora ignores nec scias quando quidque et ubi et quemadmodum agi debeat? Aliud est enim dignitates et pretia rerum nosse, aliud articulos, aliud impetus refrenare et ad agenda ire, non ruere. Tunc ergo vita concors sibi est ubi actio non destituit impetum, impetus ex dignitate rei cuiusque concipitur, proinde remissus acrior prout illa digna est peti.
passages.english: Whichever of the three is missing throws the rest into disorder as well. For what use is it to have everything assessed, if you go too far in impulse? What use is it to have checked your impulses and to have your desires in your own power, if in the action itself you are ignorant of the timing and do not know when each thing should be done, and where, and how? For it is one thing to know the worth and the prices of things, another to know the critical moments, another to rein in impulses and to go to what has to be done, not rush at it. So a life is in harmony with itself when action does not desert impulse, and impulse takes its start from the worth of each thing, slack [or] keener in proportion as that thing is worth seeking.

notes.note: Literally “to have all things among things assessed”. Aestimare is the verb of 89.14, so “assess” is kept.
notes.other_reading: to hold everything at its assessed value

notes.note: Literally “if you are too much in impulse”.
notes.other_reading: if you are excessive in impulse

notes.note: Sua is third person because the infinitive is general (“to have desires in one’s own power”). The English reads “your own” to run on with the “you” of the if clauses.
notes.other_reading: to have desires in one’s own power

notes.note: Literally “in the very action of things”, that is, in the doing of deeds. The English reads “in the action itself”, keeping “action” for actio as elsewhere in 89.14 and 89.15.
notes.other_reading: in the actual doing of things

notes.note: Literally “you are ignorant of the times”, that is, of when to act. The English reads “the timing”.
notes.other_reading: you do not know the right times

notes.note: Dignitas, dignitate and digna all belong to one word family here, as does dignum in 89.14. “Worth” is used for all of them and “prices” for pretia.
notes.other_reading: the values and prices of things

notes.note: Articulus is a joint, and so a turning point in time, the exact moment. “To know” is carried over from the clause before. It answers the “timing” mentioned just above.
notes.other_reading: another to know the junctures

notes.note: Destituere is to abandon, to leave in the lurch, to fail someone. Action is pictured as a companion that might leave impulse stranded.
notes.other_reading: when action does not fall short of impulse

notes.note: To be conceived, to be taken up, to take its start. Impulse is to arise out of the worth of the thing.
notes.other_reading: is conceived from the worth of each thing

notes.latin: proinde remissus acrior prout illa digna est peti
notes.note: The Latin as given has no “or” between remissus and acrior and does not construe as it stands; a connective seems to have dropped out, and the English supplies “[or]” in square brackets. Remissus is a plain adjective and acrior a comparative, and the English keeps that difference. Proinde with prout is “correspondingly, according as”.
notes.other_reading: slacker or keener in proportion as that thing is worth seeking

check.note: The Latin as given sets remissus and acrior side by side with no “or”, and remissus is not a comparative. As it stands it does not construe; the English supplies “or” and makes both words comparative without saying so.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “slack [or] keener in proportion as that thing is worth seeking”. The supplied “or” is in square brackets, “slack” is no longer made a comparative, and the note says that the Latin as given has no connective.

check.note: “Right” is added; the Latin is “do not know the times”, that is, the timing.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “you are ignorant of the timing”, without the added “right”.

check.note: “Right” is added again. Articuli are the joints or critical points. The supplied “to know” is needed.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “another to know the critical moments”, without “right”. “Critical” gives the sense of articulus, a joint or turning point, and the note keeps the image.

check.note: Actio is “action” everywhere else in 89.14 and 89.15, and the argument turns on the triad of assessment, impulse and action. Here alone it becomes “doing”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “in the action itself”, so that actio is “action” throughout 89.14 and 89.15. The note gives the literal “in the very action of things”.

check.latin: impetus ex dignitate rei cuiusque concipitur
check.note: “Conceived from” is unclear in English.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “impulse takes its start from the worth of each thing”.

check.note: “If you are excessive in impulse” is stiff.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “if you go too far in impulse”.

passages.latin: 'Ego debebam dicere "quousque eadem peccabitis?" Remedia ante vultis quam vitia desinere? Ego vero eo magis dicam, et quia recusatis perseverabo; tunc incipit medicina proficere ubi in corpore alienato dolorem tactus expressit. Dicam etiam invitis profutura. Aliquando aliqua ad vos non blanda vox veniat, et quia verum singuli audire non vultis, publice audite.
passages.english: “I was the one who ought to be saying ‘How long will you keep doing the same wrong things?’ Do you want the remedies to stop before the vices do? I, for my part, will say it all the more, and because you refuse I will keep on; medicine begins to do good at the point when, in a body that has lost its feeling, a touch has forced out pain. I will say things that will help even the unwilling. Let some voice that does not flatter reach you at last, and because you are not willing to hear the truth each on your own, hear it all together.

notes.note: This opens the reply that Lucilius is told to give to people who complain “how long the same things?”. The speech runs on past this section, so the Latin has an opening quotation mark and no closing one, and the English quotation is left open too. Debebam is “it was for me to say”.
notes.other_reading: I should have been the one to say

notes.note: This throws the complaint “how long the same things?” back at the complainers, with peccare, to go wrong or commit a fault. “You” is plural here and through the whole passage: it is the complainers, not Lucilius.
notes.other_reading: How long will you keep making the same mistakes?

notes.latin: Remedia ante vultis quam vitia desinere?
notes.note: Both remedies and vices are subjects of “stop”: do you want the cure to give up before the disease does. Vitia is kept as “vices”.
notes.other_reading: Do you want remedies to cease before faults do?

notes.note: Dicam has no object in the Latin; the English supplies “it”, and keeps “say” for dicere all three times it comes in this section. It is taken as future, parallel to perseverabo.
notes.other_reading: I, for my part, will speak all the more

notes.note: Alienatus, “estranged”, is used of a body or limb that has lost sensation, gone dead (medical usage, from memory, unchecked). The English reads “that has lost its feeling”.
notes.other_reading: in a deadened body

notes.note: Literally “touch has pressed out pain”: the pain shows that feeling is coming back. Dolor is “pain”.
notes.other_reading: when a touch has drawn a cry of pain

notes.note: Etiam invitis, “even to the unwilling”, can go with the saying or with “things that will help”. The English takes it with the helping, because prodesse regularly takes such a dative and the medical image has just been used. The Latin is general and has no “you”.
notes.other_reading: I will say, even to unwilling hearers, things that will help

notes.latin: Aliquando aliqua ad vos non blanda vox veniat
notes.note: Aliquando can be “at last”, “for once” or “at some time”; the English reads “at last”. Non blanda is “not coaxing, not flattering”.
notes.other_reading: Let a voice that is not soothing reach you for once

notes.latin: quia verum singuli audire non vultis, publice audite
notes.note: Singuli is “each one separately, as individuals”, set against publice, “as a community, all together”. Publice can also be heard as “in public, openly”.
notes.other_reading: since you are not willing to hear the truth as individuals, hear it in public

check.note: Invitis is taken by the second reader with the saying: he will speak even to unwilling hearers. The English ties the unwillingness to being helped and adds “you” twice where the Latin is general.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “things that will help even the unwilling”, with no “you”, since the Latin is general. The unwillingness stays with the helping, because invitis stands next to profutura, a verb that takes such a dative, and the medical image has just been used; the note gives the reading with the saying.

check.note: Singuli means each on his own, as individuals, set against publice, all together. “Hear the truth one by one” reads as one after another, or even as truths taken one at a time.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “to hear the truth each on your own, hear it all together”, so that each alone is set against all together. The note records that publice can also be “in public”.

check.note: The Latin repeats et quia in two parallel clauses; the English has “and because” the first time and “and since” the second.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and because” both times, as the Latin repeats et quia.

check.note: Dicam is “speak” here and “say” two sentences later; the repetition is deliberate and picks up “ought to be saying”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “will say it all the more”, so that dicere is “say” all three times.

check.note: The English reads alienato as numbed, which fits the medical image, but it is an interpretation; the word is literally “estranged”.
check.decided: Declined: “in a body that has lost its feeling” stands. A touch that brings out pain makes sense only of a part that had gone numb; the note gives the literal “estranged” and marks the medical usage as unchecked.

check.note: The Latin “you” is plural throughout (the objectors), which English cannot show. A reader may take it as one person; “you all” once would mark it.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “all” is not added at this point, but the same sentence now ends “each on your own, hear it all together”, which shows that many are addressed. The note on the retort also says that “you” is plural throughout.

check.note: This can be “at last” or “for once”. Either fits; the English has chosen one.
check.decided: Declined: “at last” stands, since it suits a wish made to people who have long refused to listen. “For once” is given in the note.

check.note: Found while settling: “doing the same wrongs” is not natural English, and the retort should still echo the complaint about “the same things”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “How long will you keep doing the same wrong things?”.

passages.latin: Ad initia deinde rerum redit aeternamque rationem toti inditam et vim omnium seminum singula proprie figurantem. Tum de animo coepit inquirere, unde esset, ubi, quamdiu, in quot membra divisus. Deinde a corporibus se ad incorporalia transtulit veritatemque et argumenta eius excussit; post haec quemadmodum discernerentur vitae aut vocis ambigua; in utraque enim falsa veris inmixta sunt.
passages.english: Then it went back to the beginnings of things, to the eternal reason set within the whole, and to the force of all seeds, which shapes each single thing in its own way. Then it began to inquire about the soul: where it comes from, where it is, how long it lasts, into how many members it is divided. Then it moved from bodies to things without body, and examined truth and its proofs thoroughly; after that, how the ambiguities of life or of speech were to be told apart; for in both, false things are mixed in with true.

notes.note: The form can be a present (“goes back”) or a shortened perfect (“went back”). The English reads the perfect, because the verbs that follow are perfects and the questions that hang on them are in past sequence. The subject is not expressed; it is carried over from the earlier sections and is wisdom (sapientia), from memory, unchecked.
notes.other_reading: Then it goes back to the beginnings of things

notes.note: “ratio” is the Stoic reason that runs through the universe; “toti” is “the whole”, meaning the universe. The English keeps “the whole” and “set within”.
notes.other_reading: the eternal reason implanted in the universe

notes.latin: vim omnium seminum singula proprie figurantem
notes.note: This points to the Stoic teaching of principles like seeds that give each thing its form. “proprie” is rendered “in its own way”; it can also mean “specifically, each one separately”.
notes.other_reading: the power of all seeds, which gives each single thing its particular form

notes.note: The glossary prefers “mind” for “animus”. “Soul” is used here because the questions are about where it comes from and how long it lasts, which is the soul as what may survive the body.
notes.other_reading: about the mind

notes.note: Only “how long” stands in the Latin, with no verb. “It lasts” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: for how long

notes.note: “membra” is literally “limbs” and is used here for the divisions of the soul. “Members” keeps the bodily word, which suits the next sentence, where the soul is counted among bodies.
notes.other_reading: into how many parts it is divided

notes.latin: a corporibus se ad incorporalia transtulit
notes.note: For the Stoics the soul itself is a body, so the move “from bodies” includes leaving the topic of the soul. The plain words are kept.
notes.other_reading: it passed from corporeal things to incorporeal ones

notes.note: “argumenta” can be “proofs”, “signs” or “tests” of truth; “excussit” is literally “shook out”, meaning examined closely.
notes.other_reading: and shook out truth and the signs by which it is known

notes.latin: post haec quemadmodum discernerentur vitae aut vocis ambigua
notes.note: This clause has no main verb of its own; it hangs on the verb of examining before it. “vocis” can be “of a word”, “of speech” or “of language”; the ambiguities of life are things in life that can be taken two ways.
notes.other_reading: after this it examined how what is doubtful in life or in a word might be distinguished

check.note: The form as given is a present and can also be a shortened perfect. The section before is mostly in the present, while the verbs after it are perfects, so the past tense in the English is a choice.
check.decided: Declined: the English still reads “went back”. The verbs that follow (“began”, “moved”, “examined”) are plain perfects and the questions that hang on them are in past sequence, so the shortened perfect is the reading taken; the note records the present, “goes back”.

check.note: The Latin word is limbs or members, a bodily image applied to the soul. “Parts” flattens the image.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “into how many members it is divided”. The Latin word is the one for limbs, and the bodily word fits a passage that goes on to count the soul among bodies.

check.note: One adverb is given as “own” plus “proper”. The doubling adds nothing and “proper” sounds dated.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “in its own way”. One Latin adverb stands there, and one English phrase is enough for it.

passages.latin: Sed quamvis egregia illis vita fuerit et carens fraude, non fuere sapientes, quando hoc iam in opere maximo nomen est. Non tamen negaverim fuisse alti spiritus viros et, ut ita dicam, a dis recentes; neque enim dubium est quin meliora mundus nondum effetus ediderit. Quemadmodum autem omnibus indoles fortior fuit et ad labores paratior, ita non erant ingenia omnibus consummata. Non enim dat natura virtutem: ars est bonum fieri.
passages.english: But although their life was outstanding and free of deceit, they were not wise men, since that name now belongs to the greatest of works. Still, I would not deny that they were men of lofty spirit and, so to speak, fresh from the gods; for there is no doubt that the world brought forth better things when it was not yet worn out with bearing. But while all of them had an inborn character that was stronger and readier for toil, their natural abilities were not, in all of them, brought to completion. For nature does not give virtue: to become good is an art.

notes.note: “They” are the people of the earliest age, described in the sections before.
notes.other_reading: the life of those first people was

notes.note: “fraus” is first of all deceit, but it can also be wrongdoing or harm in general. The English keeps the first sense.
notes.other_reading: free of wrongdoing

notes.latin: quando hoc iam in opere maximo nomen est
notes.note: Literally “since this name is now in the greatest work”. The English takes it to mean that the name “wise” by now belongs to the greatest of works; “work” leaves open whether the task or its result is meant.
notes.other_reading: since that name is now given only for the greatest achievement

notes.note: Literally “fresh from the gods”, that is, newly sprung from them. The image is kept.
notes.other_reading: newly come from the gods

notes.note: “effetus” is used of a body worn out by bearing young, or of exhausted soil. The image of childbearing is kept.
notes.other_reading: the world, not yet exhausted

notes.note: “indoles” is inborn quality, set against “ingenia” later in the sentence. The English has “inborn character” for the one and “natural abilities” for the other.
notes.other_reading: a sturdier native constitution

notes.latin: ita non erant ingenia omnibus consummata
notes.note: The reach of “non” is open. The English follows the Latin order, “were not, in all of them”, which most naturally says that not all of them had finished abilities; the Latin can also say that none of them had, which fits “they were not wise men”. The pair of words that frames the sentence, literally “just as … so”, sets the two facts against each other, so the English has “while”.
notes.other_reading: so in none of them were the natural abilities brought to completion

notes.note: “bonum” here is “a good man”, not “the good”. “ars” is a skill that is learned, set against what nature gives.
notes.other_reading: becoming a good man is a skill

check.latin: ita non erant ingenia omnibus consummata
check.note: The “not” can deny the whole clause (in none of them) or only “all” (not in all of them), and the English takes the first. “ingenia” is probably minds or intellects, and “natural abilities” sits too close to “inborn character” just before.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “their natural abilities were not, in all of them, brought to completion”, which follows the Latin order and its plainer sense, “not in all”; the note gives the stronger reading, “in none”. “Natural abilities” stays, because “mind” is kept for animus and ingenium is an inborn gift that still needs finishing, which is the point of the sentence.

check.note: The “just as … so” pair here sets two facts against each other, stronger natures yet unfinished minds. As a parallel it is hard to follow in English.
check.decided: Accepted: the sentence now begins “But while all of them had an inborn character that was stronger and readier for toil”. The Latin pair of words often marks a contrast of this kind, and “while” says so without adding anything.

check.note: The Latin noun is deceit but also wrongdoing or harm in general. The English picks the narrower sense without saying so.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “free of deceit” stays, because deceit is the first sense of the Latin word, and a new note records the wider sense, “free of wrongdoing”.

check.note: The Latin noun is a work or task as well as its result. “Achievement” chooses the result, while the Latin may mean that the name is now kept for the greatest undertaking.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “since that name now belongs to the greatest of works”. “Work” covers both the task and its result, as the Latin word does; “belongs to” is kept because the Latin says only that the name is “in” that work, not that it is reserved for it.

passages.latin: Quid ergo ? Ignorantia rerum innocentes erant; multum autem interest utrum peccare aliquis nolit an nesciat. Deerat illis iustitia, deerat prudentia, deerat temperantia ac fortitudo. Omnibus his virtutibus habebat similia quaedam rudis vita: virtus non contingit animo nisi instituto et edocto et ad summum adsidua exercitatione perducto. Ad hoc quidem, sed sine hoc nascimur, et in optimis quoque, antequam erudias, virtutis materia, non virtus est. Vale.
passages.english: What then? They were innocent through ignorance of things; but it makes a great difference whether someone does not want to do wrong or does not know how. They lacked justice, they lacked prudence, they lacked self-control and courage. Their unschooled life had certain things that resembled all these virtues: virtue does not come to a mind unless that mind has been trained and taught thoroughly and brought to the highest point by constant exercise. We are born for this, it is true, but without it, and even in the best people, before you school them, there is the material of virtue, not virtue. Farewell.

notes.note: “innocentes” is both “harmless” and “guiltless”; “rerum” is “of things”, meaning of the world and of what there is to do wrong with.
notes.other_reading: They were harmless because they did not know the world

notes.latin: utrum peccare aliquis nolit an nesciat
notes.note: “nesciat” with the infinitive is “does not know how to”. “peccare” is to do wrong; “sin” is avoided.
notes.other_reading: whether a person is unwilling to do wrong or has no knowledge of it

notes.note: “Prudence” is the usual English name for this one of the four chief virtues, and it stays apart from “wisdom”, which the glossary keeps for “sapientia”. It means good sense in action, not caution.
notes.other_reading: practical wisdom

notes.note: With justice and prudence these make up the four chief virtues. “temperantia” could also be “temperance”.
notes.other_reading: temperance and bravery

notes.note: “rudis” is raw, unworked, unschooled. “Unschooled” is used so that the link with “erudias” at the end of the section can be heard: that verb means to take the rawness out.
notes.other_reading: their rough life

notes.latin: Ad hoc quidem, sed sine hoc nascimur
notes.note: “hoc” (“this”) is neuter and points loosely to virtue, or to the trained state just described.
notes.other_reading: We are born for virtue, certainly, but without virtue

notes.note: A general “you”, meaning anyone who teaches. The second person is kept, and “school” answers “unschooled” above.
notes.other_reading: before they are educated

check.note: “Prudence” today suggests caution, while the Latin word, as one of the four virtues, is practical wisdom or good sense. A reader may take it too narrowly.
check.decided: Declined: the English still reads “they lacked prudence”. “Practical wisdom” would bring in “wisdom”, which this translation keeps for sapientia, a different Latin word and the very thing these people are said not to have reached; the note gives the fuller sense.

check.note: The verb picks up “rudis vita” (the raw life): it means to take the rawness out. “Untaught” and “educate” do not echo each other, so the link is lost.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Their unschooled life” and “before you school them”. The Latin verb at the end is built on the adjective used earlier, and the pair of English words lets that be heard.

passages.latin: Haec omnia Liberalis nostri adfectum inclinant, adversus sua firmum et erectum. Nec sine causa concussus est: inexpectata plus adgravant; novitas adicit calamitatibus pondus, nec quisquam mortalium non magis quod etiam miratus est doluit.
passages.english: All these things bend the spirit of our friend Liberalis, a spirit firm and unbowed against his own troubles. And he has not been shaken without cause: what is unexpected weighs more heavily; newness adds weight to disasters, and no mortal has failed to feel more pain at what also took him by surprise.

notes.note: “All these things” are the circumstances told just before: the city of Lyon destroyed in a single night, in a time of peace.
notes.other_reading: All this

notes.note: The Latin names him with the possessive that marks a friend; “friend” is supplied in the English. He is Aebutius Liberalis, a friend of Seneca from Lyon (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: of our Liberalis

notes.note: “adfectus” here is his whole state of feeling, with no fault implied, and it is singular. The glossary’s word would be “feeling”, but a thing that is bent and that stands firm and unbowed is better called “spirit” in English. “inclinant” is to bend or tilt, and can also mean to sway.
notes.other_reading: sway the feeling

notes.note: The adjectives agree with “adfectum”. “sua” is only “his own things”; “troubles” is supplied, set against the disaster of his city. “erectum” is standing straight, the opposite of bent, so “unbowed”.
notes.other_reading: a feeling steadfast and upright where his own affairs are concerned

notes.note: “novitas” is newness, the fact that a thing has not been met before.
notes.other_reading: strangeness

notes.latin: nec quisquam mortalium non magis quod etiam miratus est doluit
notes.note: A double negative, which is kept. “miratus est” is “wondered at” or “was astonished at”. “doluit” is pain, and here also grief.
notes.other_reading: and every mortal has grieved more over what he also wondered at

check.note: The Latin noun is singular and means his state of mind or spirit, which is then called firm and unbowed. The plural “feelings that are firm and upright” is odd English and blurs this.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “bend the spirit” and then “a spirit firm and unbowed”, in the singular. “Bend” is kept instead of “weigh down”, because the Latin verb is to bend or tilt and is answered by “unbowed”; the weight comes only in the next sentence.
