check.note: “Upright” in English suggests moral honesty. The Latin word here is standing straight or unbowed, the opposite of the bending in the main verb.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “unbowed”. The Latin word is about standing straight, not about honesty, and it answers “bend”.

check.note: “Troubles” is supplied; the Latin says only “against his own”. Some noun is needed and this one is fair.
check.decided: Declined: “his own troubles” stays, since English needs a noun where the Latin has only “his own”, and the note says that the noun is supplied. “In the face of” has become “against”, which is the Latin preposition.

check.note: The Latin word is newness, the fact of not having met a thing before. “Strangeness” suggests oddness.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “newness adds weight to disasters”. The Latin word is about a thing not having been met before, not about its being odd.

passages.latin: Ideo nihil nobis inprovisum esse debet; in omnia praemittendus animus cogitandumque non quidquid solet sed quidquid potest fieri. Quid enim est quod non fortuna, cum voluit, ex florentissimo detrahat? quod non eo magis adgrediatur et quatiat quo speciosius fulget? Quid illi arduum quidve difficile est?
passages.english: That is why nothing ought to be unforeseen by us; the mind must be sent ahead to everything, and what must be thought of is not whatever usually happens but whatever can happen. For what is there that Fortune, when she has wished it, does not drag down from its fullest flowering? What is there that she does not attack and shake all the more, the more splendidly it shines? What is an uphill climb for her, or what is hard?

notes.note: Literally “the mind must be sent ahead into all things”, like a scout sent before an army.
notes.other_reading: the mind must be sent forward into everything

notes.note: An impersonal form (“it must be thought”). It is kept impersonal in the English.
notes.other_reading: and we must think

notes.note: Fortune is treated as a person who wills, so the English has a capital and “she”. The perfect “voluit” is “has wished”, “once she has decided”.
notes.other_reading: fortune, when it pleases her

notes.note: Literally “drags down out of the most flourishing”, a neuter used as a noun for the most flourishing state.
notes.other_reading: pulls down from the height of prosperity

notes.note: “speciosius” is “more showily”, with a hint of mere outward show.
notes.other_reading: the more brilliant its show

notes.note: “arduum” is literally steep, a hard climb. “An uphill climb” keeps the image beside the plain word “hard”.
notes.other_reading: What is steep for her

check.note: “To meet” is added; the Latin has only “sent ahead into everything”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the mind must be sent ahead to everything”. The Latin has only the sending ahead, with no word for meeting.

check.note: “Steep” is the literal image, but “what is steep for her” is not natural English and may puzzle a reader.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the last question now begins “What is an uphill climb for her”. “Uphill” keeps the image of the steep slope in ordinary English, and “climb” stays inside that image where “task” would step out of it.

passages.latin: Non est tamen quod istis qui te circumstrepunt credas: nihil horum malum est, nihil intolerabile aut durum. Ex consensu istis metus est. Sic mortem times quomodo famam: quid autem stultius homine verba metuente? Eleganter Demetrius noster solet dicere eodem loco sibi esse voces inperitorum quo ventre redditos crepitus. 'Quid enim' inquit 'mea, susum isti an deosum sonent?'
passages.english: Still, there is no reason for you to believe those people who make a din all around you: none of these things is an evil, none is unbearable or hard. Their fear comes from general agreement. You fear death in the same way that you fear what people say: but what is more foolish than a man who is afraid of words? Our friend Demetrius has a neat way of saying that the voices of the ignorant count for the same with him as the noises of the belly breaking wind. “For what is it to me,” he says, “whether those people make their sound up above or down below?”

notes.note: “These things” are the ones listed just before: pain, thirst, hunger, old age, illness, loss, death.
notes.other_reading: nothing of all this

notes.note: Literally “their fear is from agreement”: these things are feared because everyone agrees to fear them. “Opinion” is avoided, since this translation keeps it for another Latin word.
notes.other_reading: Their fear is a matter of common consent

notes.note: “fama” covers rumour, common talk and reputation. “What people say” is taken because the next clause speaks of fearing words. It could also be fear of a bad name.
notes.other_reading: You fear death as you fear for your reputation

notes.note: Demetrius the Cynic philosopher, a contemporary whom Seneca admired (from memory, unchecked). The possessive marks him as a friend.
notes.other_reading: our Demetrius

notes.note: An idiom: “to be in the same place for him”, that is, to be held in the same regard. The English gives the sense. The literal “place” may prepare the joke about above and below.
notes.other_reading: are in the same place for him

notes.note: Literally “noises given back by the belly”, a roundabout Latin phrase for farts. The English keeps the roundabout wording but says plainly what kind of noise it is.
notes.other_reading: farts

notes.latin: mea, susum isti an deosum sonent
notes.note: “mea” stands for a fuller phrase meaning that a thing matters to the speaker, with the verb left out. “susum” and “deosum” are everyday forms of the words for “upward” and “downward”, here “up above” and “down below”. “isti” is masculine and most likely the people, though it could be the noises.
notes.other_reading: what do I care whether those noises go upward or downward

check.note: The Latin word is what people say: talk, report, reputation, ill repute. “Rumour” narrows it to unverified news, while the next clause and the saying of Demetrius point to talk.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “you fear what people say”. The Latin word is talk in general, and the next clause, about a man afraid of words, shows that talk is meant.

check.note: The Latin means farts. “Noises let out by the belly” is coy and could be taken as a rumbling stomach, which spoils the joke about above and below.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the noises of the belly breaking wind”, which cannot be mistaken for a rumbling stomach. The Latin itself uses a roundabout phrase and not a blunt word, so “farts” is left to the note.

check.note: “isti” is taken as the ignorant people; it could also be the noises themselves. The two adverbs are everyday forms meaning “upwards” and “downwards”, which the English turns into “from above” and “from below”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “whether those people make their sound up above or down below”, which is nearer to the homely Latin adverbs. “Those people” stays, with the other reading in the note, and “that lot” and “top end” are not used because they add a slang the Latin does not have.

check.note: The Latin noun is general agreement or common opinion. “Agreeing with one another” can be read as a deliberate act of agreement, which is more than the Latin says.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “Their fear comes from general agreement”, which no longer suggests a deliberate act of agreeing. “Opinion” is not used, because this translation keeps that word for opinio and the Latin here is a different word.

passages.latin: Puto, inter me teque conveniet externa corpori adquiri, corpus in honorem animi coli, in animo esse partes ministras, per quas movemur alimurque, propter ipsum principale nobis datas. In hoc principali est aliquid inrationale, est et rationale; illud huic servit, hoc unum est quod alio non refertur sed omnia ad se refert. Nam illa quoque divina ratio omnibus praeposita est, ipsa sub nullo est; et haec autem nostra eadem est, quae ex illa est.
passages.english: I think you and I will agree that external things are acquired for the body, that the body is cared for in honour of the mind, that in the mind there are serving parts, through which we move and are nourished, given to us for the sake of the ruling part itself. In this ruling part there is something without reason, and there is also something with reason; the first serves the second, and the second is the one thing that is not referred to anything else but refers everything to itself. For that divine reason too is set over all things and is itself under nothing; and this reason of ours, which comes from that one, is the same.

notes.note: Two verbs stand side by side: a verb of thinking in the first person, then an impersonal “it will be agreed” between the two friends. The English joins them into one clause.
notes.other_reading: I suppose it will be agreed between me and you

notes.note: “externa” are external things such as possessions. “corpori” is “for the body”, for its sake.
notes.other_reading: that outward things are sought for the body’s sake

notes.note: “animus” here is the whole soul, including the powers of movement and nourishment. The glossary’s “mind” is kept, because nothing is said here of survival and the same word runs on into the next section. “Soul” would be the more natural English for this wider sense.
notes.other_reading: that in the soul there are servant parts

notes.note: “principale” is Seneca’s Latin for the Stoic term for the leading or commanding part of the soul. “The ruling part” is used throughout the passage.
notes.other_reading: the chief part itself

notes.latin: est aliquid inrationale, est et rationale
notes.note: “Without reason” and “with reason” are used so that the link with “reason” (ratio) in the next sentences shows in English.
notes.other_reading: there is something irrational, and there is also something rational

notes.latin: alio non refertur sed omnia ad se refert
notes.note: “referre” is to refer one thing to another as its end or measure. The same verb is used twice and one English verb is kept.
notes.other_reading: is not directed to something else but directs all things to itself

notes.note: “nullo” can be neuter (“under nothing”) or masculine (“under no one”). The English takes the neuter, to match “set over all things”.
notes.other_reading: is itself under no one

notes.latin: et haec autem nostra eadem est, quae ex illa est
notes.note: “eadem” (“the same”) can mean the same in kind as the divine reason, or the same in being set over all and under nothing. The relative clause is kept as a plain “which”; it may also be giving the ground.
notes.other_reading: and this reason of ours is the same, since it comes from that one

check.note: The Latin is a plain relative clause, “which is from that one”. “Since” turns it into a stated reason, which the Latin does not say.
check.decided: Accepted: the last clause now reads “which comes from that one” and no longer “since it comes from that one”. The Latin has a plain “which” clause and does not state a reason; the causal reading is kept in the note.

check.note: The Latin form can be masculine (“under no one”) or neuter (“under nothing”). The English chooses the neuter without saying so.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “under nothing” stays, to match “set over all things” in the same sentence, and a new note records that the Latin can also be “under no one”.

check.note: “Outward things” is slightly old-fashioned.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “external things”, the plain word of today for the same Latin.

passages.latin: Si de hoc inter nos convenit, sequitur ut de illo quoque conveniat, in hoc uno positam esse beatam vitam, ut in nobis ratio perfecta sit. Haec enim sola non summittit animum, stat contra fortunam; in quolibet rerum habitu ~servitus~ servat. Id autem unum bonum est quod numquam defringitur. Is est, inquam, beatus quem nulla res minorem facit; tenet summa, et ne ulli quidem nisi sibi innixus; nam qui aliquo auxilio sustinetur potest cadere. Si aliter est, incipient multum in nobis valere non nostra. Quis autem vult constare fortuna aut quis se prudens ob aliena miratur?
passages.english: If we agree on this, it follows that we also agree on that: the happy life rests on this one thing, that reason in us should be perfect. For it alone does not let the mind sink; it stands against fortune; in whatever state things are, it keeps [the next word is corrupt in the Latin]. And that alone is good which is never broken off. That man, I say, is happy whom nothing makes smaller; he holds the heights, and leans on no one at all except himself; for a man who is held up by some support can fall. If it is otherwise, things that are not ours will begin to have great power in us. But who wants to owe his standing to fortune, or what sensible man admires himself for things that are not his own?

notes.latin: ut in nobis ratio perfecta sit
notes.note: “perfecta” is both “perfect” and “brought to completion”. “Perfect” is kept, as the description of reason at its full growth.
notes.other_reading: that reason in us should be brought to completion

notes.note: Literally “does not lower the mind”. The phrase is the usual one for losing heart, so “spirit” would also be right. “Mind” is kept with the glossary.
notes.other_reading: does not let the spirit droop

notes.note: The copy marks “servitus” (“slavery”) as corrupt, and the words as given do not construe: “servat” (“it keeps”) has no object. The English leaves the gap and says so in square brackets. From memory, unchecked: editors have proposed a word meaning “safe” or “free from care” here.
notes.other_reading: in whatever state things are, it keeps us free from care (a guess at the lost word)

notes.latin: Id autem unum bonum est quod numquam defringitur
notes.note: This can be “that alone is good which …” or “the one good is that which …”. “defringitur” is “is broken off”, as a branch is. The image is kept.
notes.other_reading: But the one good is that which is never broken

notes.note: Literally “he holds the highest things”: the top, the summit.
notes.other_reading: he occupies the highest place

notes.latin: ne ulli quidem nisi sibi innixus
notes.note: “ulli” can be “anyone” or “anything”. The English takes “no one”, the commoner sense of the word standing alone and the one that matches “himself”; the “support” of the next clause would also suit “nothing”.
notes.other_reading: leaning on nothing at all except himself

notes.note: “constare” with the ablative can be “to stand firm by means of”, “to depend on” or “to consist of”. The English takes it as standing by fortune’s gift, which echoes “stands against fortune” earlier.
notes.other_reading: to be made up of what fortune gives

notes.note: “prudens” can be “a sensible man” or “knowingly, with his eyes open”.
notes.other_reading: or who, knowing what he does, admires himself for what is another’s

check.note: The tildes are the editor’s sign of corruption: “servitus” (“slavery”) makes no sense as it stands and “servat” has no object. The English does not smooth this over, but it leaves “it keeps” hanging and puts an editorial bracket inside the running text.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the bracket stays in the text, since the rule is to say so where the Latin does not construe, but it now reads “it keeps [the next word is corrupt in the Latin]”, so that the reader sees what is missing. The note explains the mark and gives the guessed sense, from memory, unchecked.

check.latin: ne ulli quidem nisi sibi innixus
check.note: “ulli” can be “anyone” or “anything”. The next clause speaks of “some support”, which favours the wider “nothing”, and the English narrows it to persons.
check.decided: Declined: the English still reads “leans on no one at all except himself”. Standing alone as it does here, the Latin word is more usually “anyone”, and it is paired with “himself”; the note records “nothing”.

check.note: The verb with this case can mean “stand firm by means of” or “consist of, be made up of”. The English takes the first; the other reading should be on record.
check.decided: Declined: the English still reads “owe his standing to fortune”, as the point itself advises. The verb echoes “it stands against fortune” earlier in the section, and the note records the other reading, “to be made up of what fortune gives”.

check.latin: ut in nobis ratio perfecta sit
check.note: The bare subjunctive “be” is stiff. The Latin participle is also “perfected, brought to completion”, not only “perfect”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “that reason in us should be perfect”, without the stiff bare “be”. “Perfect” is kept and not “perfected”, because the Latin describes the state of reason and not the process; the note gives “brought to completion”.

passages.latin: 'Quid ergo?' inquit 'si virtutem nihil inpeditura sit bona valetudo et quies et dolorum vacatio, non petes illas?' Quidni petam? non quia bona sunt, sed quia secundum naturam sunt, et quia bono a me iudicio sumentur. Quid erit tunc in illis bonum? hoc unum, bene eligi. Nam cum vestem qualem decet sumo, cum ambulo ut oportet, cum ceno quemadmodum debeo, non cena aut ambulatio aut vestis bona sunt, sed meum in iis propositum servantis in quaque re rationi convenientem modum.
passages.english: “What then?” he says. “If good health and rest and freedom from pains are not going to hinder virtue in any way, will you not seek them?” Why would I not seek them? Not because they are goods, but because they are according to nature, and because they will be taken by me with good judgment. What then will be good in them? This one thing: being well chosen. For when I take the kind of clothing that is fitting, when I walk as I ought, when I dine as I should, it is not the dinner or the walk or the clothing that is a good, but my purpose in them, the purpose of one who keeps, in each thing, the measure that agrees with reason.

notes.note: “He says”: an imagined objector, not a named person.
notes.other_reading: someone says

notes.note: “quies” is rest or quiet; the section before uses it for a state of repose.
notes.other_reading: quiet

notes.note: “bona” is neuter, while the three things named are feminine, so it is taken as the noun “goods” and not the adjective “good”. The same form at the end of the section is rendered the same way, “a good”.
notes.other_reading: Not because they are good

notes.note: A Stoic term: things “according to nature” are worth choosing without being goods. The literal phrase is kept.
notes.other_reading: they are in accord with nature

notes.note: “sumere” is “to take” and is the same verb used just below for putting on clothing. “Take” is used in both places so that the link shows.
notes.other_reading: they will be chosen by me with sound judgment

notes.note: A passive infinitive: “to be well chosen”. The good lies in the choosing, not in the thing chosen.
notes.other_reading: this alone, that they are chosen well

notes.note: “servantis” is a genitive that agrees with the speaker implied in “meum”, so the purpose is that of a person who keeps the measure; the English repeats “purpose” to make this plain. “propositum” is purpose, intention, or the plan one sets oneself.
notes.other_reading: my intention in them, as I keep

notes.note: “modus” is measure or limit; “convenientem” is “agreeing with”, “fitting”.
notes.other_reading: the limit that suits reason

check.note: The same Latin words at the end of the section are given as “is good”, while here they are “are goods”. The argument turns on this word, so one form throughout is safer.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the two places now agree, but as “goods” and “a good”, not as “good”. The Latin form is neuter while the things named are feminine, which marks it as the noun, so the first place stands and the last sentence now reads “that is a good”.

passages.latin: Etiamnunc adiciam: mundae vestis electio adpetenda est homini; natura enim homo mundum et elegans animal est. Itaque non est bonum per se munda vestis sed mundae vestis electio, quia non in re bonum est sed in electione quali; actiones nostrae honestae sunt, non ipsa quae aguntur.
passages.english: I will add this as well: the choice of clean clothing is something a human being should seek; for a human being is by nature a clean animal and one that chooses with care. And so clean clothing is not a good in itself, but the choice of clean clothing is, because the good is not in the thing but in a choice of a certain kind; it is our actions that are honourable, not the things themselves that are done.

notes.note: “Etiamnunc” here is “further, besides”, not “even now”.
notes.other_reading: Even now I will add

notes.note: “mundus” is clean, neat, well kept. “Clean” is used throughout the passage.
notes.other_reading: the choice of neat clothing

notes.note: “adpetenda” is “to be sought, to be reached for”; “homini” can be “by a human being” or “for a human being”.
notes.other_reading: is a thing for a human being to desire

notes.note: “elegans” is discriminating, having taste. It is related to the verb “to choose” and so answers “electio” (“choice”) beside it, as “mundum” answers “mundae”. “One that chooses with care” keeps that link.
notes.other_reading: a clean and discriminating animal

notes.latin: non est bonum per se munda vestis
notes.note: “per se” (“in itself”) can go with “a good” or with “clean clothing”. The English leaves it as open as it can: it says that clean clothing is not a good in itself and that the choice is a good, without settling whether the choice is a good in itself.
notes.other_reading: And so what is good in itself is not clean clothing but the choice of clean clothing

notes.note: Literally “in a choice of some sort”, that is, in what kind of choice it is. Read the other way, “quali” could mean “in the choice, such as it is”.
notes.other_reading: in the quality of the choice

notes.latin: actiones nostrae honestae sunt, non ipsa quae aguntur
notes.note: The noun “actiones” and the verb “aguntur” share a root: the acting is honourable, not what is acted. The English has “actions” and “done”.
notes.other_reading: it is our acts that are honourable, not the very things that are enacted

check.note: The Latin adjective is choosy in a good sense: discriminating, having taste. It is akin to the word for “choice”, on which the passage turns, and “fastidious” has a fussy colour and loses the link.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a clean animal and one that chooses with care”. The Latin adjective is formed from the verb “to choose”, and the sentence gives the reason why the choice of clean clothing is to be sought, so the link with “choice” has to be heard.

check.latin: non est bonum per se munda vestis
check.note: “In itself” can go with “a good” or with “clean clothing”. The English takes the first, which implies that the choice is good in itself; the second claims only that the choice is good.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “clean clothing is not a good in itself, but the choice of clean clothing is”. This no longer states that the choice is good in itself, which the Latin does not settle; a note records both ways of taking “in itself”.

passages.latin: Eodem modo virtuti opposita nihil detrahunt: non est minor, sed minus fulget. Nobis forsitan non aeque apparet ac nitet, sibi eadem est et more solis obscuri in occulto vim suam exercet. Hoc itaque adversus virtutem possunt calamitates et damna et iniuriae quod adversus solem potest nebula.
passages.english: In the same way, the things set in the way of virtue take nothing away from it: it is not smaller, but it shines less. To us, perhaps, it does not show and gleam as much; to itself it is the same, and like the sun when it is obscured it exerts its force out of sight. And so disasters and losses and wrongs have the same power against virtue that a mist has against the sun.

notes.note: This carries on the comparison in the section before, where clouds stand in front of the sun without hindering it.
notes.other_reading: In the same manner

notes.note: Literally “things placed opposite virtue”, as clouds are placed in front of the sun. It could also be heard as “things opposed to virtue”.
notes.other_reading: the things opposed to virtue

notes.note: “aeque” is “equally”, with the comparison (“as before, as when nothing is in the way”) left unsaid, and “ac” is taken as joining the two verbs. The two words together can also make a comparison of their own, “as much as”.
notes.other_reading: it does not show as much as it gleams

notes.note: “To itself” is set against “to us”: in itself, for its own part.
notes.other_reading: in itself it is the same

notes.note: “obscuri” is “obscured, hidden from view” by what stands in front, not dimmed in itself; “in occulto” is “in a hidden place, unseen”.
notes.other_reading: in the manner of a hidden sun, it works in secret

notes.note: “iniuriae” are wrongs done to a person; “injuries” in the older sense.
notes.other_reading: injuries

notes.note: “nebula” is mist, fog or thin cloud. The image is the same as the clouds in the section before.
notes.other_reading: a cloud

check.note: The Latin adjective here means hidden from view by what stands in front. “Darkened” suggests that the sun itself loses its light, which is what Seneca denies.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “like the sun when it is obscured”. This says that the sun is covered from view without losing its light, and it avoids “hidden” beside “out of sight” in the same clause.

passages.latin: Cum se in hanc sublimitatem tulit, corporis quoque ut oneris necessarii non amator sed procurator est, nec se illi cui inpositus est subicit. Nemo liber est qui corpori servit; nam ut alios dominos quos nimia pro illo sollicitudo invenit transeas, ipsius morosum imperium delicatumque est.
passages.english: When it has raised itself to this height, it is, towards the body too, as towards a necessary burden, not a lover but a manager, and it does not put itself under the thing it has been set over. No one is free who is a slave to the body; for, even if you pass over the other masters that too much anxiety on the body’s behalf finds, the body’s own rule is hard to please and fussy.

notes.latin: Cum se in hanc sublimitatem tulit
notes.note: The subject is not expressed. It is taken to be the mind (animus), which the section before is speaking of, so the English has “it”. The masculine forms would also fit “he”, a man.
notes.other_reading: When he has raised himself to this height

notes.note: A “procurator” manages property on another’s behalf: an agent or steward. He looks after a thing without being attached to it.
notes.other_reading: a steward

notes.latin: nec se illi cui inpositus est subicit
notes.note: A play on “under” and “over”: the one set over the body (as its overseer) does not place himself under it.
notes.other_reading: and does not subject itself to that which it has been put in charge of

notes.note: “servit” is “is a slave to”, stronger than “serves”. The slavery is kept because the sentence is about being free.
notes.other_reading: who serves the body

notes.latin: ut alios dominos quos nimia pro illo sollicitudo invenit transeas
notes.note: Literally “granted that you pass over the other masters”, with a general “you”, which the English keeps. “invenit” is “finds”, that is, comes upon or gets for itself; the form can be present or perfect. The other masters are those a person falls under through worrying about the body.
notes.other_reading: to leave aside the other masters that excessive worry about the body has found

notes.note: “morosus” is peevish, hard to please; “delicatus” is pampered, fussy, self-indulgent. Both describe a difficult master and are applied here to his rule.
notes.other_reading: its own command is peevish and pampered

check.note: Said of a “rule”, “spoiled” reads as “ruined”. The Latin adjective here is pampered, fussy or capricious, said of the body as master.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “hard to please and fussy”. “Spoiled” said of a rule could be read as “ruined”; “hard to please” stays for the first adjective, which is its plain meaning.

check.note: The Latin verb is in the second person, “though you pass over”. The English makes it impersonal, and the person of the Latin should be kept.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “even if you pass over the other masters”. The Latin verb is in the second person, a general “you”, and the English now keeps it.

passages.latin: Utrum, obsecro te, aequius iudicas, te naturae an tibi parere naturam? quid autem interest quam cito exeas unde utique exeundum est? Non ut diu vivamus curandum est, sed ut satis; nam ut diu vivas fato opus est, ut satis, animo. Longa est vita si plena est; impletur autem cum animus sibi bonum suum reddidit et ad se potestatem sui transtulit.
passages.english: Which, I beg you, do you judge the fairer: that you should obey nature, or that nature should obey you? And what does it matter how soon you leave a place that must be left in any case? What we must take care of is not that we live long but that we live enough; for to live long you need fate, to live enough you need the mind. A life is long if it is full; and it is made full when the mind has given back to itself its own good and has transferred to itself the power over itself.

notes.note: The word answers the fairness (aequitas) that Seneca said he missed in Lucilius in the section before, so “fairer” is kept. It can also mean more reasonable or more just.
notes.other_reading: more reasonable

notes.note: The Latin names no place, only “from where”; life is meant. The verb is impersonal, a leaving that falls on everyone, so the English reads “must be left” and not “you must leave”. “Utique” can be “in any case” or “without fail”.
notes.other_reading: from where one must go out without fail

notes.note: The verb is left to be supplied from the clause before. “Satis” is “enough”: the point is a life that is sufficient, not merely a fairly long one.
notes.other_reading: but that we live sufficiently

notes.note: Animus is “mind” by the glossary, and the next sentence speaks of the mind (animus) recovering its own good, so one word is kept. Here it also leans towards spirit or resolve.
notes.other_reading: to live enough you need spirit

notes.note: “Reddere” is to give back or to pay what is due. The English takes it as the mind restoring to itself the good (bonum) that belongs to it; it could be the weaker “has delivered”.
notes.other_reading: has rendered to itself the good that is its own

notes.note: The wording is that of a legal transfer of authority: the mind takes over control of itself from outside owners. “Transferred” and “power” are kept to show this.
notes.other_reading: has taken control of itself into its own hands

check.note: The Latin verb is an entreaty, stronger than “ask”, and the English phrase can be heard as an exclamation of exasperation that the Latin does not have.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “beg” in place of “ask”, which gives the force of the entreaty. The suggested “please tell me” is not used because it adds a verb of telling that the Latin does not have.

check.note: The Latin is impersonal, a necessity for everyone, and the English turned it into “you must leave”. A small point.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “a place that must be left in any case”. The first verb stays “you leave” because the Latin has the second person there, and the second is impersonal as in the Latin.

passages.latin: Nec ideo mihi plures annos accedere recusaverim; nihil tamen mihi ad beatam vitam defuisse dicam si spatium eius inciditur; non enim ad eum diem me aptavi quem ultimum mihi spes avida promiserat, sed nullum non tamquam ultimum aspexi. Quid me interrogas quando natus sim, an inter iuniores adhuc censear? habeo meum.
passages.english: I would not on that account refuse to have more years added to me; yet I will say that I lacked nothing for the happy life if its span is cut short; for I have not made myself ready for the day that greedy hope had promised me as my last, but there is no day I have not looked on as if it were my last. Why do you ask me when I was born, or whether I am still registered among the younger men? I have what is mine.

notes.note: “Not for that reason”: it looks back to the praise, in the section before, of a man whose short time was well spent. Seneca now speaks in the first person.
notes.other_reading: And yet I would not therefore refuse

notes.note: The form can be future or subjunctive. The English takes the future, “will say”, because the “if” clause that follows has a plain present, “is cut short”; after the mild “would not refuse” the subjunctive is also possible.
notes.other_reading: yet I would say

notes.note: “Eius” most naturally refers to the happy life just named, though it may mean life in general. The verb is present, “is cut short”, literally “is cut into”.
notes.other_reading: if the span of my life is cut short

notes.note: Literally “fitted myself to that day”: he did not arrange himself with a view to one far-off final day. The English reads “made myself ready for”, which is one plain sense of the verb.
notes.other_reading: I have not arranged myself around that day

notes.note: A double negative, “none not looked on as the last”, set against the single day that hope had promised. The English keeps both negatives; the possessive with “last” is carried over from the clause before.
notes.other_reading: but have looked on every day as if it were my last

notes.note: A term of the Roman census: the “iuniores” were the men of military age, up to about forty-five (from memory, unchecked). “Censear” is “be entered at the census”, so the English reads “registered” and keeps “the younger men” as the plain name of the class.
notes.other_reading: or whether I am still entered on the roll of the men of military age

notes.note: Two words: the verb “have” and a bare possessive with no noun. The noun is left open: a share, a due, what belongs to the speaker. The English is kept as open as the Latin.
notes.other_reading: I have my share

check.note: The form can be future or subjunctive, and after the potential “would not refuse” the subjunctive is at least as likely; the point is that the English chose the future.
check.decided: Declined: The English keeps the future, now worded “will say”. The “if” clause that depends on it has a plain present, “is cut short”, which goes more naturally with a future, and the note on the word records “would say” as the other reading.

check.note: The Latin has an emphatic double negative set against the one day that hope promised; “every day” is right in sense but flattens it.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now keeps both negatives, “there is no day” followed by “not looked on”, so that the contrast with the one promised day is heard.

check.note: The verb is the word for being entered at the census and the “iuniores” are a formal class, the men of military age; “counted among the younger men” loses the official register.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “registered among the younger men”. “Registered” gives the census verb; “the younger men” is kept because that is what the Latin word says, and the note explains that the class is the men of military age.

check.note: “Fitted myself to that day” is not clear English; the Latin means to arrange or prepare oneself with a view to something.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “made myself ready for the day”, which is a plain sense of the verb and keeps the reflexive. The literal “fitted myself to” is given in the note and the suggested “arranged myself around” is its other reading.

passages.latin: Quemadmodum in minore corporis habitu potest homo esse perfectus, sic et in minore temporis modo potest vita esse perfecta. Aetas inter externa est. Quamdiu sim alienum est: quamdiu ero, ut sim, meum est. Hoc a me exige, ne velut per tenebras aevum ignobile emetiar, ut agam vitam, non ut praetervehar.
passages.english: Just as a person can be complete in a smaller build of body, so too a life can be complete in a smaller measure of time. Years are among the external things. How long I am to be is not mine: to be, for as long as I will be, is mine. Demand this of me: that I do not travel the whole length of an obscure lifetime as if through darkness, that I lead my life, not that I am carried past it.

notes.note: “Habitus” is the build or condition of the body; with “smaller” it means a small stature.
notes.other_reading: in a body of smaller stature

notes.note: The word means finished, complete, and so perfect. “Complete” is used for both the person and the life, since the argument is about nothing being missing.
notes.other_reading: perfect

notes.note: “Aetas” is age or lifetime; here it means how many years one gets, and “years” says that without an added explaining word. “Externa” is the Stoic term for things outside a person and not in that person’s control.
notes.other_reading: Length of life is one of the externals

notes.note: “Alienum” is literally “belonging to another”, the set opposite of “meum”, “mine”, in the next clause. The English reads “not mine” so that a reader does not look for some particular other owner.
notes.other_reading: How long I am to be belongs to another

notes.latin: quamdiu ero, ut sim, meum est
notes.note: Very compressed: the verb “to be” stands twice, and the second time it seems to carry a full sense, to be truly alive and not merely to last, which is what the next sentence asks for. The English keeps the bare verb and adds no “truly”. Editors have doubted the wording here and a word may have dropped out (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: that I should truly be alive, for as long as I am alive, is in my power

notes.note: “Emetiri” is to measure out and so to travel the whole length of; with “through darkness” and the travel verb that follows, the English takes the travelling sense. “Ignobile” is unknown, obscure, without distinction.
notes.other_reading: that I do not measure out an inglorious span of years

notes.latin: ut agam vitam, non ut praetervehar
notes.note: A play of active against passive: “agere vitam” is the common phrase for living a life but literally “to drive” it, while “praetervehi” is to be carried past, as in a ship or a carriage. “Lead” keeps the active sense. The Latin does not say what one is carried past; “it” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: that I drive my life, not that I am carried along past

check.latin: quamdiu ero, ut sim, meum est
check.note: The Latin is extremely compressed and may be damaged (from memory, unchecked); the English settled it with an emphatic “do exist” where the weight may lie on really being alive, and the compression should be flagged.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now uses the bare verb “to be” throughout the sentence and adds neither the emphatic “do exist” nor the suggested “truly”, since the Latin has only the one verb. The note says that the clause is terse, that the second “be” seems to mean really living, and that the text has been doubted (from memory, unchecked).

check.note: The verb means “measure out” but also “travel across”; with “through darkness” and the travel verb that follows it is the second sense, and “measure out through darkness” gives no clear picture.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “travel the whole length of an obscure lifetime as if through darkness”. “Travel the whole length of” gives the journey and still holds the idea of measure; “obscure” is kept for “ignobile” because it suits the darkness.

check.note: The word is the plain opposite of “mine”, meaning outside one’s own control; “belongs to another” makes a reader look for some particular other person.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “is not mine”, the plain opposite of the “is mine” that follows. The suggested “to settle” is left out because the Latin has no such verb, and the literal “belongs to another” is in the note.

check.note: The word is “age” or “lifetime”; “Length of” is an explanation folded into the text.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “Years are among the external things”. “Years” carries the sense of a span without the added “length of”, and the suggested possessive is left out because the Latin has none.

check.note: The word is a human being, not specifically a male. A small point.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “a person can be complete”.

check.latin: ut agam vitam, non ut praetervehar
check.note: Found while settling: the Latin sets “that” against “not that”, and the draft joined the two halves with “and”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now keeps the Latin shape, “that” followed by “not that”. The “it” after “carried past” is supplied, and the note says so.

passages.latin: Scis amicitias sancte colendas esse, sed non facis. Scis inprobum esse qui ab uxore pudicitiam exigit, ipse alienarum corruptor uxorum; scis ut illi nil cum adultero, sic tibi nil esse debere cum paelice, et non facis. Itaque subinde ad memoriam reducendus es; non enim reposita illa esse oportet sed in promptu. Quaecumque salutaria sunt saepe agitari debent, saepe versari, ut non tantum nota sint nobis sed etiam parata. Adice nunc quod aperta quoque apertiora fieri solent.
passages.english: You know that friendships are to be cultivated religiously, but you do not do it. You know that a man is shameless who demands chastity of his wife while he himself is a seducer of other men’s wives; you know that, just as she ought to have nothing to do with an adulterer, so you ought to have nothing to do with a mistress, and you do not do it. So you must be brought back to remembering again and again; for these things ought not to be stored away but at hand. Whatever is wholesome ought to be often stirred, often turned over, so that it is not only known to us but also ready. Add now that even plain things usually become plainer.

notes.note: The “you” here is the general “you” of the argument about the use of reminders: anyone who knows the rule and does not keep it. It need not be Lucilius in particular. The second person is kept.
notes.other_reading: One knows

notes.note: “Sancte” is an adverb, “in a holy way”, and so scrupulously, faithfully; “religiously” keeps both the manner and the sacred colour. “Colere” is to cultivate, tend or honour.
notes.other_reading: that friendships are to be tended scrupulously

notes.note: The word ranges from dishonest to shameless to wicked. “Shameless” is chosen because the word is often used of someone who asks for more than is fair, which is the case described.
notes.other_reading: that a man is in the wrong

notes.note: “Illi” is the wife. The verb “ought to have” is supplied from the second half of the comparison.
notes.other_reading: as she has no business with a lover

notes.note: The “paelex” is a woman kept by a married man, the rival of the wife. “Mistress” is the nearest plain word.
notes.other_reading: a concubine

notes.note: “Subinde” can be “repeatedly” or “from time to time”. The English takes the stronger, since the next sentences say “often”. Literally “you must be led back to memory”.
notes.other_reading: from time to time you must be reminded

notes.note: “In promptu” is in view and within reach; “parata”, in the next sentence, is prepared for use. The English keeps the two apart as “at hand” and “ready”.
notes.other_reading: but ready to hand

notes.note: Two verbs of physical movement: to keep in motion or stir, and to turn over. They may be meant of discussion or of thinking over, and the English leaves that open.
notes.other_reading: ought to be often discussed, often dwelt on

notes.note: “Aperta”, things that lie open, answers the objector’s word in the section before. One English word, “plain”, is kept for both forms.
notes.other_reading: even what is obvious tends to become more obvious

check.note: “In promptu” was “ready to hand” and “parata” is “ready”, so two different Latin expressions share one English word and the step from within reach to prepared for use is blurred.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “at hand” for “in promptu” and keeps “ready” for “parata”, so the two Latin expressions have two English ones.

check.note: The verb is to keep in motion, stir or go over in thought or talk; “handled” is flat and suggests touching with the hands.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “often stirred, often turned over”. “Stirred” gives the sense of keeping a thing in motion; the suggested “stirred up” is not used because in English it suggests rousing trouble.

check.note: The word is broad (wicked, unprincipled, in the wrong) and the English picked the narrower “shameless”, where the point may be the unfairness of the double standard.
check.decided: Declined: The English keeps “shameless”. The Latin word is regularly used of a person who asks for more than is fair without blushing, which is exactly the husband described, and the note records the wider sense as the other reading.

check.note: The first word is an adverb of manner and the verb is “cultivate, tend”; the English turned the manner into a statement about what friendship is.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “are to be cultivated religiously”, so the adverb is an adverb of manner again. “Religiously” is used and not the suggested “scrupulously” because the Latin adverb comes from the word for holy, and “religiously” keeps that colour while still meaning with strict care.

passages.latin: Sit ergo aliquis custos et aurem subinde pervellat abigatque rumores et reclamet populis laudantibus. Erras enim si existimas nobiscum vitia nasci: supervenerunt, ingesta sunt. Itaque monitionibus crebris opiniones quae nos circumsonant repellantur.
passages.english: So let there be some guardian, and let him tug at our ear again and again, and drive off the common talk, and shout back against the praise of the crowds. For you are wrong if you think that vices are born with us: they have come upon us, they have been forced into us. So let the opinions that sound all around us be driven back by frequent reminders.

notes.note: A guard, keeper or watcher, the word used of a boy’s attendant as well as of a sentry. The English reads “guardian”.
notes.other_reading: some keeper

notes.note: Tugging the ear was a Roman gesture for reminding someone (from memory, unchecked). The Latin has only “the ear”; the possessive is supplied from the first person plural of the next sentence. “Subinde” is again “repeatedly” or “from time to time”.
notes.other_reading: and pluck the ear from time to time

notes.note: Not only false reports but what people in general are saying, popular talk and reputation.
notes.other_reading: drive away rumours

notes.note: Plural, literally “the peoples praising”; the plural of this word can mean whole peoples, as in the section before, or simply crowds. The English takes crowds and puts the weight on the praise, which is the crowd’s praise of the wrong things.
notes.other_reading: against the peoples as they praise

notes.note: The first verb is “came on top” or “came in addition”, set against being born with a person. The second is “were poured in”, “heaped on” or “forced upon”. Both say that vices arrive from outside.
notes.other_reading: they arrived later, they were heaped upon us

notes.note: “Monitio” is a reminder, a piece of advice or a warning. This letter defends the use of such reminders, so “reminders” is used.
notes.other_reading: by frequent warnings

notes.note: “Opinio” is “opinion” by the glossary: here the mistaken beliefs of the crowd. The verb is an image of noise on every side, and it is kept.
notes.other_reading: the beliefs that din around us

check.note: The plural here means crowds or the public; “the peoples as they praise” is stiff and leaves a reader unsure who is meant.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “shout back against the praise of the crowds”. “Crowds” is taken from the suggestion; “praise” is kept and not changed to “applaud” because the Latin verb is the ordinary word for praising.

check.note: The noun is the act of reminding or admonishing, the subject of this whole letter, not a warning of danger; “warnings” narrows it.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “by frequent reminders”.

check.note: “Afterwards” unpacks the prefix of the verb; it is a fair reading but an added word.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now drops “afterwards” and reads “come upon”, where “upon” gives the prefix of the verb, to the same effect as the suggested “on top of”.

passages.latin: Multi inveniuntur qui ignem inferant urbibus, qui inexpugnabilia saeculis et per aliquot aetates tuta prosternant, qui aequum arcibus aggerem attollant et muros in miram altitudinem eductos arietibus ac machinis quassent. Multi sunt qui ante se agant agmina et tergis hostium [et] graves instent et ad mare magnum perfusi caede gentium veniant, sed hi quoque, ut vincerent hostem, cupiditate victi sunt. Nemo illis venientibus restitit, sed nec ipsi ambitioni crudelitatique restiterant; tunc cum agere alios visi sunt, agebantur.
passages.english: Many are found who carry fire into cities, who lay low what the centuries could not storm and what had been safe through several generations, who raise a siege mound level with citadels, and with rams and engines batter walls that had been built up to an astonishing height. There are many who drive armies before them and press hard on the backs of the enemy and come to the great sea drenched in the slaughter of nations; but these too, in order to conquer the enemy, were conquered by desire. No one withstood them as they came, but neither had they themselves withstood ambition and cruelty; at the time when they seemed to be driving others, they were being driven.

notes.note: “Saeculis” can be a dative (“not to be stormed by the centuries”, with time itself as the besieger) or an ablative of time (“impregnable for centuries”). The English takes the dative, since the word stands without any “many” or “so many” and the phrase about generations that follows already speaks of length of time.
notes.other_reading: what had been impregnable for centuries

notes.note: The “agger” is the earth ramp a besieging army builds up against a wall. “Arx” is a citadel or a height.
notes.other_reading: a rampart as high as the strongholds

notes.note: “Agmina” are columns on the march. With the enemy’s backs in the next phrase they are taken to be enemy forces driven in flight, but they could be the conqueror’s own troops. The verb is the one played on at the end, so “drive” is used in both places.
notes.other_reading: who lead their columns before them

notes.note: The square brackets are the editor’s sign that this word should be deleted. It is left out; it would not change the sense.
notes.other_reading: and who also press hard on the backs of the enemy

notes.note: “The great sea” may mean the outer Ocean at the edge of the world, the goal of conquerors such as Alexander. The phrase is left as it stands.
notes.other_reading: to the Ocean

notes.note: Literally “drenched with the slaughter of nations”, slaughter standing for blood. The image is kept as it is.
notes.other_reading: soaked in the blood of slaughtered peoples

notes.latin: ut vincerent hostem, cupiditate victi sunt
notes.note: The same verb stands in active and passive, so “conquer” is used twice. “Ut” is taken as purpose: they had first to be beaten by desire in order to go out and beat the enemy; a looser “though they conquered” is possible. “Cupiditas” is desire or greed.
notes.other_reading: though they conquered the enemy, they were themselves conquered by greed

notes.latin: tunc cum agere alios visi sunt, agebantur
notes.note: Again active against passive of one verb, “agere”, to drive. The next section, 94.62, opens with the same verb, so “drive” is kept there as well.
notes.other_reading: when they seemed to be chasing others, they were themselves being chased

check.note: “Saeculis” can be ablative of time (“for centuries”) or dative (“that the centuries could not storm”); the dative avoids saying nearly the same thing twice with the phrase about generations.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “what the centuries could not storm and what had been safe through several generations”. The Latin word stands alone, with no “many” or “so many” such as usually goes with a length of time, which favours time as the attacker; the draft’s reading stays in the note as the other reading.

check.note: “Bring fire to cities” is not how English says it and could even sound helpful; the Latin is to set fire to, to carry fire into.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “carry fire into cities”, which keeps the Latin verb of carrying in and cannot be heard as a kindness. “Set fire to” would be plain but drops that verb.

check.note: The same noun was “the enemy” a line earlier and is now “an enemy”; the Latin sets the enemy outside against the one within, so the phrase should be kept the same.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “in order to conquer the enemy”.

passages.latin: Agebat infelicem Alexandrum furor aliena vastandi et ad ignota mittebat. An tu putas sanum qui a Graeciae primum cladibus, in qua eruditus est, incipit? qui quod cuique optimum est eripit, Lacedaemona servire iubet, Athenas tacere? Non contentus tot civitatium strage, quas aut vicerat Philippus aut emerat, alias alio loco proicit et toto orbe arma circumfert; nec subsistit usquam lassa crudelitas inmanium ferarum modo quae plus quam exigit fames mordent.
passages.english: Wretched Alexander was driven by a madness for laying waste what belonged to others, and it sent him off to unknown lands. Or do you think a man sane who begins first with the disasters of Greece, where he was educated? Who snatches from each the best thing it has: orders Sparta to be a slave, Athens to be silent? Not content with the overthrow of so many states, which Philip had either conquered or bought, he throws down others, some in one place and some in another, and carries his arms around the whole world; and his cruelty, like savage beasts that bite more than hunger demands, nowhere tires and comes to a halt.

notes.note: The same verb as at the end of 94.61 (“agebantur”), so “driven” again. The Latin is active, “madness drove Alexander”; the English is passive to keep Alexander first and the two verbs close to their subject.
notes.other_reading: A madness for laying waste what belonged to others drove wretched Alexander

notes.note: The opposite of “felix”, the word the crowd uses of such men just before: not fortunate, and so wretched or ill-starred. “Wretched” is used because “unhappy” today reads as merely sad.
notes.other_reading: Unhappy Alexander

notes.note: “Furor” is frenzy or madness. “Aliena” is what is another’s, which can also mean foreign lands.
notes.other_reading: a frenzy for devastating foreign lands

notes.latin: a Graeciae primum cladibus, in qua eruditus est
notes.note: “Clades” are disasters or defeats, here those he inflicted on Greece; the plural is kept. “In qua” refers to Greece. The allusion is probably to the destruction of Thebes and to his schooling under Aristotle (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: who starts with the defeats of Greece, where he had his schooling

notes.note: “Cuique” is “from each”, each city or people. The two examples follow with no linking word, so the English sets them after a colon: Sparta (in the Latin, Lacedaemon) loses its freedom, Athens its speech.
notes.other_reading: who robs each state of what it prizes most

notes.latin: quas aut vicerat Philippus aut emerat
notes.note: Philip is Philip II of Macedon, Alexander’s father. “Bought” refers to his winning cities by bribery (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: which Philip had either defeated or purchased

notes.note: Literally “he throws forth others in another place”, the idiom for “one in one place, another in another”. “Proicere” can be to throw down, to fling away or to cast out, and it is not certain which is meant.
notes.other_reading: he flings others aside, each in a different place

notes.note: “Lassa” (tired) can fall under the negative: his cruelty nowhere tires and stops. Or it can stand apart: his cruelty is tired and still does not stop. The English takes the first; the beast simile fits either.
notes.other_reading: and his cruelty, though worn out, nowhere comes to a halt

check.note: The Latin has no “and”: the freedom of Sparta and the speech of Athens are the examples of the best thing in each being taken, not further acts.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “Who snatches from each the best thing it has: orders Sparta to be a slave, Athens to be silent?” The added “and” is gone, and the colon shows that the two cities are the examples.

check.note: Placed after “come to a halt”, the comparison can be read as halting the way beasts do, the opposite of the point.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now puts the beasts before the verbs: “his cruelty, like savage beasts that bite more than hunger demands, nowhere tires and comes to a halt”. “Nowhere” is kept, and not the suggested “never”, because the Latin word is one of place.

check.note: The word here is ill-starred or wretched, a judgement on his condition; “unhappy” reads today as sad.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “Wretched Alexander was driven”. The note records that the Latin word is the opposite of the one the crowd uses of such men.

check.note: The Latin is plural, a series of disasters or defeats; “the ruin” makes it one total event. A small point.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “the disasters of Greece, where he was educated”. “Where” replaces “in which” so that the clause still points to Greece and not to the disasters.

passages.latin: Ne Gnaeo quidem Pompeio externa bella ac domestica virtus aut ratio suadebat, sed insanus amor magnitudinis falsae. Modo in Hispaniam et Sertoriana arma, modo ad colligandos piratas ac maria pacanda vadebat: hae praetexebantur causae ad continuandam potentiam.
passages.english: Gnaeus Pompeius, too, was urged to wars abroad and at home not by virtue or reason but by an insane love of false greatness. Now he was going into Spain and against the arms of Sertorius, now to bind the pirates and pacify the seas: these were the causes held out as a cover, in order to keep his power going without a break.

notes.note: “Ne” with “quidem” is “not even” or “not this one either”, and either way it stresses the man. After Alexander the English takes it as adding a second case, “Gnaeus Pompeius, too”. Gnaeus Pompeius is Pompey the Great, the Roman general and rival of Caesar.
notes.other_reading: Not even Gnaeus Pompeius was urged to wars abroad and at home by virtue or reason

notes.note: “Domestica” wars are wars at home, that is, civil wars.
notes.other_reading: foreign and civil wars

notes.note: “Virtus” could be courage in a passage about a general, but paired with reason (ratio) and set against a mad love it is the moral term, so “virtue”, as in the glossary. In the Latin these two are the subject of the verb; the English turns the sentence into the passive so that Pompeius comes first, as in the Latin.
notes.other_reading: courage or reason

notes.note: “Insanus” answers the question in 94.62 whether Alexander was sane, so “insane” is used and not “mad”.
notes.other_reading: a mad passion for a greatness that was not real

notes.note: Literally “the Sertorian arms”: the armed forces of Sertorius, the Roman commander who held Spain against the government at Rome (from memory, unchecked). “Against” is added, as the Latin preposition allows, so that “arms” cannot be heard as an embrace.
notes.other_reading: the war with Sertorius

notes.note: As given, the verb is “colligare”, to tie up or bind, and so to bring under restraint. A form differing by one letter, from “colligere”, would give “to gather”; which the editions prefer is not known here (from memory, unchecked). The English translates the text as given and keeps the image.
notes.other_reading: to round up the pirates

notes.latin: hae praetexebantur causae ad continuandam potentiam
notes.note: “Praetexere” is to weave a border in front, and so to put forward as a pretext: “held out as a cover”. “Causae” is “causes” here because “reason” is in use for “ratio” in the sentence before. “Continuare” is to make continuous: one command joined to the next, with no gap.
notes.other_reading: these were the pretexts put forward for prolonging his power

check.note: In English “off to the arms of Sertorius” reads as going to his embrace; the Latin means his armed forces, the war against him.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “into Spain and against the arms of Sertorius”. “Against” removes the false sense, and “arms” is kept because the Latin names the weapons, not the war, and the same word is “arms” in 94.62.

check.note: The verb is to tie up or restrain, and “bind the pirates” is literal and odd; the form is also one letter from a verb meaning to gather or round up, which would suit pirates.
check.decided: Declined: The English keeps “to bind the pirates”. To bind is what the verb as given says, and the image is kept as an image; the note records the looser sense of restraint and the one-letter variant that would give “round up”.

check.note: The Latin picks out Pompey himself (“not even Pompey”, “not Pompey either”); plain “Nor” keeps the link backwards but loses the stress on the man.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now begins “Gnaeus Pompeius, too, was urged to wars abroad and at home not by virtue or reason”, which puts the stress on the man. “Too” is used, not “not even”, because the sentence adds a second case after Alexander; “not even” is in the note.

check.note: Found while settling: “causae” was “reasons” one sentence after “ratio” was “reason”, so two different Latin words shared one English word in a passage where “reason” is a term of the argument.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “these were the causes held out as a cover”, and “reason” is left to “ratio” alone.

passages.latin: Quid illum in Africam, quid in septentrionem, quid in Mithridaten et Armeniam et omnis Asiae angulos traxit? infinita scilicet cupido crescendi, cum sibi uni parum magnus videretur. Quid C. Caesarem in sua fata pariter ac publica inmisit? gloria et ambitio et nullus supra ceteros eminendi modus. Unum ante se ferre non potuit, cum res publica supra se duos ferret.
passages.english: What dragged him into Africa, what into the north, what against Mithridates and into Armenia and every corner of Asia? Plainly a boundless desire to grow, since to himself alone he seemed not great enough. What sent Gaius Caesar headlong into his own doom and the state’s alike? Glory and ambition and no limit to standing out above the rest. He could not bear one man ahead of him, though the state was bearing two above it.

notes.note: “Him” is Pompey, carried on from 94.64.
notes.other_reading: What dragged Pompeius into Africa

notes.note: “Into the north”. Seneca does not say which campaign he means; the English is left as general as the Latin.
notes.other_reading: to the northern lands

notes.note: “Omnis” can be accusative plural with “corners” (“all the corners of Asia”) or genitive with “Asia” (“the corners of all Asia”). The English takes the first. Mithridates was the king of Pontus against whom Pompey fought (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: the corners of the whole of Asia

notes.note: “Scilicet” is “of course”, “plainly”, often with an edge of irony. “Cupido” is desire, close to the “cupiditas” of 94.61, so the same English word is used.
notes.other_reading: an endless craving to grow bigger, of course

notes.latin: cum sibi uni parum magnus videretur
notes.note: A play on Pompey’s surname Magnus, “the Great”: everyone called him great, and only he thought himself not great enough. “Cum” here gives the ground, “since”.
notes.other_reading: because he was the one man to whom he seemed too little “the Great”

notes.latin: in sua fata pariter ac publica inmisit
notes.note: “Fata” is “fate” by the glossary, but the plural here means death and ruin, Caesar’s own and the state’s, so “doom” is used. “Inmittere” is to let loose or launch, as a horse or a weapon. “Publica” is “of the public”, of the state; “the state’s” matches the next sentence.
notes.other_reading: What sent Gaius Caesar headlong into his own fate and the public fate alike?

notes.note: “Glory” here means the pursuit of glory. “Ambitio” is the striving for office and standing.
notes.other_reading: love of fame and ambition

notes.latin: Unum ante se ferre non potuit, cum res publica supra se duos ferret
notes.note: The same verb, “to bear”, stands twice, so one English word is used. “Cum” may be “though” or “at a time when”, and “res publica” could also be “the republic”. The “one” is Pompey; the “two” are presumably Pompey and Caesar himself as masters over the state, which the Latin does not say.
notes.other_reading: He could not endure one man in front of him at a time when the republic was enduring two over its head

check.note: The plural with this verb means doom or destruction, his own and the state’s; “fate” is neutral in English and loses the sense of death and disaster.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “into his own doom and the state’s alike”. The glossary word “fate” is set aside here because the Latin plural means a violent end, and the note says so.

check.note: “Commonwealth” is old-fashioned for a reader of today and is used twice; “was bearing two men above it” is also stiff, though keeping “bear” for both verbs is right.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “the state” in both places, and the last sentence reads “though the state was bearing two above it”, with “bear” kept for both verbs.

passages.latin: Omnes istae artes circa instrumenta vitae occupatae sunt, non circa totam vitam; itaque multa illas inhibent extrinsecus et inpediunt, spes, cupiditas, timor. At haec quae artem vitae professa est nulla re quominus se exerceat vetari potest; discutit enim inpedimenta et iactat obstantia. Vis scire quam dissimilis sit aliarum artium condicio et huius? in illis excusatius est voluntate peccare quam casu, in hac maxima culpa est sponte delinquere.
passages.english: All those arts are occupied with the equipment of life, not with the whole of life; and so many things check them from outside and hinder them: hope, desire, fear. But this one, which professes the art of life, cannot be prevented by anything from exercising itself, for it shatters hindrances and tosses aside what stands in its way. Do you want to know how unlike the condition of the other arts is to the condition of this one? In them it is more excusable to go wrong on purpose than by accident; in this one the greatest fault is to do wrong of one’s own accord.

notes.note: Ars is any skilled craft with rules, such as the helmsman’s in the section before. “Art” is kept throughout this passage and the next because the argument sets the “art of life” against the others.
notes.other_reading: All those crafts

notes.note: Instrumenta are tools, gear, the means one works with. The English has “equipment”; the contrast is with life as a whole.
notes.other_reading: the tools of life

notes.latin: multa illas inhibent extrinsecus et inpediunt, spes, cupiditas, timor
notes.note: Hope, desire and fear stand in apposition to “many things” and are said to act “from outside”, which is taken to mean from outside the art, not from outside the person. The bare list is kept as the Latin has it.
notes.other_reading: and so many things outside them hold them back and get in their way, such as hope, desire, fear

notes.latin: haec quae artem vitae professa est
notes.note: “This one” is wisdom (sapientia), named in the section before. Profiteri is what a teacher does when he announces his subject; the Latin form describes a claim that still stands, so the English has the present “professes”.
notes.other_reading: But this one, which has declared itself the teacher of the art of life

notes.latin: nulla re quominus se exerceat vetari potest
notes.note: Vetare is usually to forbid. Here nothing gives an order, so the English has “prevented”.
notes.other_reading: cannot be forbidden by anything to exercise itself

notes.latin: discutit enim inpedimenta et iactat obstantia
notes.note: Iactare is to toss or fling, often to toss about. It is taken here as tossing obstacles out of the way. “Hindrances” repeats “hinder” (inpediunt) from the sentence before, as the Latin does.
notes.other_reading: for it breaks up hindrances and flings obstacles about

notes.note: Peccare covers both a slip in a craft and a moral wrong, and the argument turns on that range. “Go wrong” is used for it here and in the next section. Voluntate is “by will”, that is, on purpose.
notes.other_reading: to make a mistake deliberately

notes.note: A different verb from peccare, so it has a different English phrase, “do wrong”. Delinquere is to fall short, to fail in what one ought to do.
notes.other_reading: to fail deliberately

check.latin: haec quae artem vitae professa est
check.note: The Latin form has present force, so “has professed” reads wrongly as a past event. “This one” may also be taken as “this art” when wisdom is meant.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “this one, which professes the art of life”, in the present, because the Latin describes a claim still being made. “Claims as its business” is not taken, since “business” is not in the Latin, and “this one” stays as bare as the Latin word, with a note saying that it is wisdom.

check.note: “By will” is not current English and is unclear. The sense is deliberate error as against accidental error.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “to go wrong on purpose than by accident”.

check.note: “Offend” today suggests hurting feelings. Delinquere is to do wrong, to fail in what one ought to do.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “to do wrong of one’s own accord”. This still differs from “go wrong”, the phrase used for the other verb, peccare, so the two Latin verbs stay apart.

check.latin: nulla re quominus se exerceat vetari potest
check.note: Found while settling: “cannot be forbidden by anything” is not natural English, since the Latin verb here means to stop or prevent, not to give an order.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “cannot be prevented by anything from exercising itself”, and a note gives the literal “forbidden”.

passages.latin: Quod dico tale est. Grammaticus non erubescet soloecismo si sciens fecit, erubescet si nesciens; medicus si deficere aegrum non intellegit, quantum ad artem magis peccat quam si se intellegere dissimulat: at in hac arte vivendi turpior volentium culpa est. Adice nunc quod artes quoque pleraeque -- immo ex omnibus liberalissimae -- habent decreta sua, non tantum praecepta, sicut medicina; itaque alia est Hippocratis secta, alia Asclepiadis, alia Themisonis.
passages.english: What I mean is this. A grammarian will not blush at a mistake in grammar if he made it knowingly; he will blush if he made it unknowingly. A doctor, if he does not realise that his patient is failing, goes wrong more, as far as his art is concerned, than if he pretends not to realise it. But in this art of living the fault of those who go wrong willingly is the more shameful. Add now the fact that most arts too, or rather the most liberal arts of them all, have their own doctrines, not only precepts, as medicine does; and so the school of Hippocrates is one, that of Asclepiades another, that of Themison another.

notes.note: The grammaticus is the teacher of language and literature. The Latin word is “solecism”, a fault in the construction of a sentence; the English says “a mistake in grammar” because “solecism” is no longer a common word.
notes.other_reading: A grammarian will not blush at a solecism

notes.note: Dissimulare is to hide what is in fact the case: he does realise it and acts as if he did not. The English puts this as “pretends not to realise it”.
notes.other_reading: than if he conceals that he realises it

notes.note: This limits the claim to the doctor’s skill, leaving aside the moral side. The limit is kept explicit.
notes.other_reading: so far as skill goes

notes.note: Literally “the fault of the willing is the more shameful”, the comparison being with those who go wrong unwillingly. The English supplies “those who go wrong”, the verb already used of the doctor, so that “the willing” is not misread.
notes.other_reading: the fault of the willing is the more shameful

notes.note: Plerique can mean “most” or, more loosely, “very many”. The English has “most”.
notes.other_reading: a great many arts too

notes.note: Liberalis is “worthy of a free person”, the word behind “liberal arts”. The English keeps “liberal” in that old sense and sets it beside “arts” so that the term can be heard. The Latin marks the phrase off as an aside; the English uses commas.
notes.other_reading: or rather those most worthy of a free person among them all

notes.note: The two technical terms of this letter. Decreta are the general tenets of a school (Seneca elsewhere in the letter equates them with the Greek dogmata; from memory, unchecked) and praecepta are particular instructions. The English uses “doctrines” and “precepts” and keeps “precept” in the later sections.
notes.other_reading: their own principles, not only rules

notes.latin: alia est Hippocratis secta, alia Asclepiadis, alia Themisonis
notes.note: Three Greek physicians treated as heads of rival medical schools: Hippocrates of Cos, Asclepiades of Bithynia, who practised at Rome, and his pupil Themison (from memory, unchecked). Secta is a school one follows; “school” is used here and in Ep. 97.14.
notes.other_reading: the sect of Hippocrates is one thing, that of Asclepiades another, that of Themison another

check.note: “Grammarian” and “solecism” are learned words that a reader of today may not know. The first is a teacher of language and literature, the second a mistake in grammar.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “solecism” becomes “a mistake in grammar”. “Grammarian” is kept, because it is still current English and lets the reader hear that the mistake falls within the man’s own art.

check.note: “The willing” is unclear in today’s English and suggests people who are ready to help. The Latin means those who do wrong because they want to.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the fault of those who go wrong willingly”. “Go wrong” is used and not “do wrong”, because it is the phrase already used for peccare in this passage.

check.note: “Liberal” will be read in its modern sense, generous or political. The Latin means the arts most worthy of a free person, the liberal arts in the highest degree.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the most liberal arts of them all”, which lets the reader hear the term “liberal arts”. The longer wording suggested adds “deserve to be called”, which is not in the Latin; the note explains the old sense of the word.

passages.latin: M. Brutus in eo libro quem peri kathekontos inscripsit dat multa praecepta et parentibus et liberis et fratribus: haec nemo faciet quemadmodum debet nisi habuerit quo referat. Proponamus oportet finem summi boni ad quem nitamur, ad quem omne factum nostrum dictumque respiciat; veluti navigantibus ad aliquod sidus derigendus est cursus.
passages.english: Marcus Brutus, in the book he titled “Peri kathekontos” (“On Duty”), gives many precepts to parents and to children and to brothers. No one will carry these out as he ought unless he has something to refer them to. We must set before us the goal of the highest good, towards which we may strive, towards which every deed and word of ours may look, just as those who sail must direct their course towards some star.

notes.note: Marcus Junius Brutus, the assassin of Caesar, who also wrote philosophical works (from memory, unchecked). The first name is written out.
notes.other_reading: M. Brutus

notes.note: Seneca gives the title in Greek, which this copy prints in Latin letters. The English keeps the Greek title and adds its meaning in brackets, which is not in the Latin. Kathekon is the Stoic term for what it is fitting to do, Latin officium.
notes.other_reading: the book he titled “On Appropriate Action”

notes.note: “These” are the precepts, or the things they prescribe. Facere here is to do what they say, so the English has “carry these out”.
notes.other_reading: no one will do these things in the way he should

notes.note: Literally “unless he has that to which he may refer (them)”, a fixed point of reference. No object is expressed; “them” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: unless he has a standard to measure them against

notes.note: The genitive can define (“the end that is the highest good”) or depend more loosely. “The goal of the highest good” keeps the Latin shape and leaves this open. Summum bonum is the Stoic term, “the highest good”.
notes.other_reading: We must set before us an end, namely the highest good

notes.note: English more often says that one steers “by” a star. “Towards” is used because the Latin has the same small word three times, for striving towards the goal, looking towards it and steering towards the star.
notes.other_reading: must direct their course by some star

check.note: The Latin gives the title in Greek. The English turns it silently into an English title, so the reader does not learn that Brutus gave his book a Greek name.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now keeps the Greek title, “Peri kathekontos”, and gives its meaning, “On Duty”, in brackets after it. The word “Greek” is left to the note, since the Latin does not say it.

check.note: The Latin has a genitive, “the end of the highest good”, which the English narrows to “an end, the highest good”. “An end” may also be read as “a finish”; “goal” is plainer.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the goal of the highest good”, which keeps the Latin shape and leaves open how the two nouns are joined. The note gives the reading “an end, namely the highest good”.

check.note: The Latin repeats ad three times and the comparison rests on it: actions look to the goal as a course is set to a star. “Towards which”, “to which” and “by” lose the link.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now has “towards” three times, for striving, for looking and for the course set “towards some star”, so that the repeated Latin word can be heard.

passages.latin: Quomodo sint dii colendi solet praecipi. Accendere aliquem lucernas sabbatis prohibeamus, quoniam nec lumine dii egent et ne homines quidem delectantur fuligine. Vetemus salutationibus matutinis fungi et foribus adsidere templorum: humana ambitio istis officiis capitur, deum colit qui novit. Vetemus lintea et strigiles Iovi ferre et speculum tenere Iunoni: non quaerit ministros deus. Quidni? ipse humano generi ministrat, ubique et omnibus praesto est.
