passages.english: It is usual to give precepts on how the gods are to be worshipped. Let us forbid anyone to light lamps on the sabbath, since the gods have no need of light and not even human beings take pleasure in soot. Let us forbid the performing of morning greetings and sitting at the doors of temples: it is human vanity that is won by such attentions; whoever knows god worships him. Let us forbid the bringing of towels and bath scrapers to Jupiter and the holding of a mirror for Juno: god does not look for servants. Why would he? He himself serves the human race; he is at hand everywhere and for everyone.

notes.note: Impersonal passive, “it is usual for precepts to be given”. The English stays impersonal and keeps the word “precepts”, since the letter’s argument is about them.
notes.other_reading: People usually lay down rules on how the gods are to be worshipped.

notes.note: This verb form, and the two that follow (vetemus), can be an exhortation or a concession, with the point, made in the next section, that such bans are not enough without a right idea of god. The English takes the exhortation, which is the plainer reading of the form.
notes.other_reading: We may forbid anyone to light lamps on the sabbath

notes.note: The Jewish sabbath, here in the plural (“on sabbaths”). Seneca is speaking of a foreign rite practised at Rome.
notes.other_reading: on sabbaths

notes.note: The salutatio, literally a greeting, was the morning call a Roman dependant had to pay at his patron’s house. Here the same attendance is paid to a god at his temple. Fungi is to carry out a duty, so “performing”.
notes.other_reading: Let us forbid the paying of morning calls

notes.note: Ambitio here is the wish to be courted and honoured, not the wish to rise, so “vanity”. Capitur is “is caught, won over”. Officia are the dutiful attentions just listed.
notes.other_reading: it is human ambition that is caught by such services

notes.note: The second verb has no object in the Latin; “god” is understood from the first. The English order is turned round for clarity.
notes.other_reading: he worships god who knows him

notes.latin: lintea et strigiles Iovi ferre et speculum tenere Iunoni
notes.note: Worshippers wait on the statues as slaves wait on a master at the bath and a mistress at her dressing. Lintea are linen towels, strigiles the scrapers used at the bath. Jupiter is the chief Roman god and Juno his wife.
notes.other_reading: to carry linen cloths and strigils to Jupiter and to hold up a mirror to Juno

notes.note: The Latin moves from “the gods” to “god” in the singular in this passage, and the English keeps that. “Servants” and “serves” render ministros and ministrat, one word repeated.
notes.other_reading: god does not need attendants

notes.note: Literally “why not?”, an idiom that confirms what has just been said. After a negative statement English needs the question turned round.
notes.other_reading: Of course not.

check.note: “Morning calls” sounds like social visits. The Latin is the morning attendance of Roman dependants at a great man’s door, here carried over to the gods, and fungi is to perform a duty.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the performing of morning greetings”. “Performing” is taken for fungi; “greetings” is used and not “attendance”, because salutatio is literally a greeting, and the note explains the Roman custom.

check.note: “Ambition” in English is the wish to rise and points to the worshipper. Here ambitio is the human love of being courted, which such attentions catch.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “it is human vanity that is won by such attentions”. “Vanity” and “attentions” are taken; “won” is kept and not “taken in”, because capitur here is to be won over, not to be deceived.

check.note: The word order of the English is old in style, and it is briefly unclear who knows whom.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “whoever knows god worships him”.

check.note: A reader of today will not know what “scrapers” are. These are the scrapers used at the bath, with towels, after oiling.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “towels and bath scrapers”, since a strigil is a scraper used at the bath.

check.note: Found while settling: homines are human beings, set here against the gods, and the same word is “human” in Ep. 95.53 and “human beings” in Ep. 95.54 as settled.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “not even human beings take pleasure in soot”.

passages.latin: Quae causa est dis bene faciendi? natura. Errat si quis illos putat nocere nolle: non possunt. Nec accipere iniuriam queunt nec facere; laedere etenim laedique coniunctum est. Summa illa ac pulcherrima omnium natura quos periculo exemit ne periculosos quidem fecit.
passages.english: What cause do the gods have for doing good? Nature. Anyone who thinks they are unwilling to do harm is mistaken: they are not able to. They can neither suffer a wrong nor do one, for to hurt and to be hurt are joined together. Those whom that nature, the highest and most beautiful of all, has taken out of danger it has not made dangerous either.

notes.latin: Quae causa est dis bene faciendi?
notes.note: Causa is “cause” or “reason, motive”. “Cause” is kept, since the answer is not a motive but nature.
notes.other_reading: What reason do the gods have for doing good?

notes.note: The answer is one bare word with no possessive. It can be the gods’ own nature or nature in general. The English leaves it bare, so that the last sentence can take it up as “that nature”.
notes.other_reading: Their nature.

notes.note: “To be unwilling to harm”, that is, to refrain by choice. The correction that follows is that it is not a matter of choice.
notes.other_reading: that they choose not to do harm

notes.latin: Nec accipere iniuriam queunt nec facere
notes.note: Iniuria is a wrong done to someone. The literal verb is “receive”; English says “suffer a wrong”.
notes.other_reading: They can neither receive an injury nor do one

notes.note: The thought is that the power to hurt and the liability to be hurt go together. “Hurt” is kept for laedere here and in Ep. 95.52, and “harm” for nocere.
notes.other_reading: for hurting and being hurt belong together

notes.latin: Summa illa ac pulcherrima omnium natura
notes.note: It is open whether this is the gods’ own nature or the nature of things that made them, and whether “of all” goes with the adjectives or with “nature”. The English keeps the phrase as open as the Latin.
notes.other_reading: That supreme and most beautiful nature of all things

notes.note: Ne … quidem is “not even” or “not … either”. Here the second fits: out of danger, and not dangerous either. The Latin plays on periculo and periculosos, kept as “danger” and “dangerous”.
notes.other_reading: it has not even made dangerous

check.latin: Quae causa est dis bene faciendi? natura.
check.note: The Latin answer is the bare word natura. “Their” is added and settles it as the gods’ own nature, though the last sentence takes the word up again without any possessive.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Nature.” with no possessive, as bare as the Latin word, so that the last sentence can take it up as “that nature”. The note gives “Their nature.” as the other reading.

check.note: “Injury” today means bodily hurt, and “do an injury” is dated. Iniuria is a wrong done to someone.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “They can neither suffer a wrong nor do one”.

passages.latin: Primus est deorum cultus deos credere; deinde reddere illis maiestatem suam, reddere bonitatem sine qua nulla maiestas est; scire illos esse qui praesident mundo, qui universa vi sua temperant, qui humani generis tutelam gerunt interdum incuriosi singulorum. Hi nec dant malum nec habent; ceterum castigant quosdam et coercent et inrogant poenas et aliquando specie boni puniunt. Vis deos propitiare? bonus esto. Satis illos coluit quisquis imitatus est.
passages.english: The first way to worship the gods is to believe in the gods; next, to give them the majesty that is theirs, to give them the goodness without which there is no majesty; to know that it is they who preside over the world, who govern all things by their power, who have the guardianship of the human race, sometimes without concern for individuals. They neither give evil nor have it; yet they chastise some people and restrain them and impose punishments, and sometimes they punish by what looks like a good. Do you want to win the favour of the gods? Be good. Whoever has imitated them has worshipped them enough.

notes.note: Literally “the first worship of the gods”. English needs a noun such as “way” or “act”; “first” is answered by “next”.
notes.other_reading: The first act of worship of the gods

notes.note: Credere with a plain object: to believe in the gods, to believe that they exist. The English takes the shorter form.
notes.other_reading: to believe that there are gods

notes.note: Reddere is to give what is owed, or to give back, and suam marks the majesty as their own. “Give” is repeated as the Latin repeats the verb.
notes.other_reading: to give them back their majesty

notes.latin: scire illos esse qui praesident mundo
notes.note: This can be “to know that they are the ones who preside” or “to know that there are those who preside”. The English takes the first, since the gods’ existence was the first point.
notes.other_reading: to know that there are beings who preside over the world

notes.note: Universa is “all things together”; temperare is to regulate, keep in due order. Vi sua is “by their own force”.
notes.other_reading: who regulate the universe by their own force

notes.note: As given the text says the gods are sometimes careless of individuals. Some editions are thought to read or conjecture “curiosi” here, without the negative, which gives the opposite sense (from memory, unchecked). The English translates the text as given.
notes.other_reading: and who sometimes take thought for individuals

notes.note: Malum is “evil” or “harm”. The two plain verbs, “give” and “have”, are kept.
notes.other_reading: They neither do harm nor suffer it

notes.note: Literally “under the appearance of a good”. The English takes it that the thing which looks like a good is itself the punishment. It could also mean that they punish while seeming to do a kindness.
notes.other_reading: sometimes they punish under a show of kindness

check.note: “The first worship” is not natural English. The Latin means the first act or first form of worship.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “The first way to worship the gods”. English needs a noun here, and a note gives the literal form.

check.note: Reddere is to give what is owed, and suam stresses that the majesty is their own. “Grant” sounds like a concession, in both places.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “to give them the majesty that is theirs, to give them the goodness without which there is no majesty”.

check.note: The English renders the Latin as given correctly. The phrase may have been doubted by editors, with a reading that says the opposite (from memory, unchecked), so the text is worth a look.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps the Latin as given, “sometimes without concern for individuals”. The text could not be checked here, so the note records, from memory, unchecked, that a reading without the negative has been proposed and what it would mean.

check.note: This can mean that the punishment looks like a good thing, or more loosely that the gods punish with a show of kindness. The English takes the first and is hard to follow.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “sometimes they punish by what looks like a good”, and the note gives the other reading, a show of kindness.

passages.latin: omne hoc quod vides, quo divina atque humana conclusa sunt, unum est; membra sumus corporis magni. Natura nos cognatos edidit, cum ex isdem et in eadem gigneret; haec nobis amorem indidit mutuum et sociabiles fecit. Illa aequum iustumque composuit; ex illius constitutione miserius est nocere quam laedi; ex illius imperio paratae sint iuvandis manus.
passages.english: All this that you see, in which things divine and human are enclosed, is one; we are limbs of a great body. Nature brought us forth as kin, since she begot us from the same things and for the same things. She planted in us love for one another and made us fit for fellowship. She established what is fair and just; by her arrangement it is more wretched to harm than to be hurt; by her command let our hands be ready for those who need help.

notes.note: The passage begins in lower case because it is the formula of human duty announced at the end of the section before. “You” is singular, the person to whom the formula is handed.
notes.other_reading: this whole that you see

notes.note: Membra are limbs or members. The bodily image is kept.
notes.other_reading: we are members of a great body

notes.note: Cognati are blood relatives. The English has “kin”.
notes.other_reading: Nature produced us as blood relatives

notes.latin: cum ex isdem et in eadem gigneret
notes.note: Literally “from the same things and into the same things”. The second half can mean for the same ends or back into the same elements; the English takes the ends and keeps the wording loose. Cum is taken as “since”; it could be “when”.
notes.other_reading: when she begot us from the same elements, to return into the same

notes.note: “Able to join in fellowship.” The English has “fit for fellowship” so that it links with societas, “fellowship”, in the next section.
notes.other_reading: and made us sociable

notes.note: Constitutio is how something has been set up, an arrangement or a ruling. The English has “arrangement”, beside “command” (imperio) in the next clause.
notes.other_reading: by her ruling

notes.note: Two different verbs, kept as “harm” and “be hurt”. Miser is “wretched”, the word also used in Ep. 96.1.
notes.other_reading: it is more pitiable to do harm than to suffer it

notes.note: Iuvandis has no noun: “for those (or the things) that are to be helped”. The English takes it of persons. The verb is a command, and the Latin has no possessive with “hands”; one is supplied.
notes.other_reading: let hands be ready to help

check.note: The phrase can be “for the same ends” or “into the same things”, that is, the same condition or elements, and the English chooses purpose. Cum is also given as “since” where it could be “when”.
check.decided: Declined: “for the same things” stands. In with this case commonly states an end, “into the same things” is not plain English, and the choice is recorded in a note, which now also says that cum can be “when” as well as “since”.

check.note: “Ordinance” is archaic and legal. Constitutio is how she has set things up.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “by her arrangement”.

check.note: The form is given as persons, “those who are to be helped”; it can equally be general, “for helping”. The English is heavy, and “hands” with no possessive is stiff.
check.decided: Partly accepted: a possessive is supplied with “hands” and the clause now ends “ready for those who need help”. Persons are kept, because iuvandis is a plural form meaning those who are to be helped, not the bare act of helping; the note gives the looser reading.

passages.latin: Ille versus et in pectore et in ore sit: homo sum, humani nihil a me alienum puto. Habeamus in commune: nati sumus. Societas nostra lapidum fornicationi simillima est, quae, casura nisi in vicem obstarent, hoc ipso sustinetur.
passages.english: Let that verse be both in the heart and on the lips: “I am human: I count nothing human foreign to me.” Let us have it in common: we have been born. Our fellowship is very like an arch of stones, which would fall if the stones did not block one another, and is held up by that very thing.

notes.latin: et in pectore et in ore
notes.note: Literally “both in the breast and in the mouth”. No possessive is expressed. The English uses the pair “heart” and “lips”.
notes.other_reading: both in the breast and in the mouth

notes.latin: homo sum, humani nihil a me alienum puto
notes.note: A line of the comic poet Terence, from his play Heauton Timorumenos (line 77; from memory, unchecked). Homo is a human being, not specifically a male, and the line plays on homo and humani, so the English has “human” twice.
notes.other_reading: “I am a man: nothing that concerns man do I think foreign to me.”

notes.note: As given the Latin does not construe: the first verb has no object and the statement of being born stands bare, making no point. The English is word for word, with “it” supplied, which may point back to the verse or forward. Editors are thought to supply a second “in commune” or to repunctuate so that “in common” goes with “born” (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: Let us hold to this: we were born for the common good.

notes.note: Societas is partnership, the bond between associates. The English has “fellowship”, matching “fit for fellowship” in Ep. 95.52.
notes.other_reading: Our society

notes.note: Fornicatio is an arching or vaulting, from fornix, an arch. It is an arch built of stones.
notes.other_reading: a vault of stones

notes.note: The verb is plural, so its subject is the stones. Obstare is to stand against something: each stone blocks its neighbour’s fall.
notes.other_reading: which would collapse if the stones did not hold one another back

notes.note: “By this very thing”, that is, by the stones blocking one another. The English is left as bare as the Latin.
notes.other_reading: is kept up by precisely this mutual pressure

check.note: The Latin as given does not construe cleanly: the first verb has no object and the last two words alone make no point. Printed editions may supply a second “in commune” (from memory, unchecked), and the English smooths this over without saying so.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the sentence is now flagged in a note as one that does not construe as given, with what editors are thought to print (from memory, unchecked). The English stays word for word, with “it” and not “this” for the missing object, because “it” can point back to the verse or forward, as the gap in the Latin allows.

check.note: “Things” is not in the Latin, and with it the English makes Seneca recommend common ownership. The object may be what follows the colon, or the verse just quoted.
check.decided: Accepted: “things” is removed, so the English no longer speaks of common ownership; the missing object is now a bare “it”.

check.note: To stand in someone’s way in English is to hinder them from getting somewhere. The stones of an arch bear against one another and so keep one another from falling.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “which would fall if the stones did not block one another, and is held up by that very thing”.

passages.latin: Post deos hominesque dispiciamus quomodo rebus sit utendum. In supervacuum praecepta iactabimus nisi illud praecesserit, qualem de quacumque re habere debeamus opinionem, de paupertate, de divitiis, de gloria, de ignominia, de patria, de exilio. Aestimemus singula fama remota et quaeramus quid sint, non quid vocentur.
passages.english: After gods and human beings, let us look into how things are to be used. We shall be tossing out precepts to no purpose unless this has come first: what opinion we ought to hold about each thing, about poverty, about riches, about glory, about disgrace, about homeland, about exile. Let us assess each thing one by one with its reputation set aside, and ask what they are, not what they are called.

notes.note: Uti is to use or to deal with. The same phrase was used of people in the section before Ep. 95.52. Res are “things” in the widest sense, such as the poverty and exile listed next.
notes.other_reading: how we should deal with things

notes.note: Iactare is to toss or fling about, the same verb as in Ep. 95.8. In supervacuum is “to no use”.
notes.other_reading: We shall be scattering precepts uselessly

notes.note: Opinio, the Stoic term for the view held of a thing’s worth. “Opinion” throughout.
notes.other_reading: what belief we ought to hold

notes.note: Patria is one’s native country. The Latin has no possessive in any item of the list, and the items are kept bare.
notes.other_reading: about one’s country

notes.note: Aestimare is to judge what a thing is worth, which may be little. Singula is “each thing one by one”. The Latin then moves to the plural (“what they are”), and the English follows it.
notes.other_reading: Let us value each thing singly

notes.note: Fama is what people commonly say of a thing, its repute. The English has “reputation”, kept apart from “glory” (gloria) in the list.
notes.other_reading: setting aside what is commonly said of them

check.note: Homines are human beings. The English has “human” for homo in Ep. 95.53 but “men” here and in Ep. 95.47.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “After gods and human beings”, in line with “human” for the same word in Ep. 95.53, and Ep. 95.47 is changed to match.

check.note: “Value” can be read as “prize”. Aestimare is to assess what a thing is worth, which may be little.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “assess each thing one by one”. “Assess” is used and not “weigh”, because aestimare is to judge what a thing is worth and the Latin has no image of scales.

passages.latin: Tamen tu indignaris aliquid aut quereris et non intellegis nihil esse in istis mali nisi hoc unum quod indignaris et quereris? Si me interrogas, nihil puto viro miserum nisi aliquid esse in rerum natura quod putet miserum. Non feram me quo die aliquid ferre non potero. Male valeo: pars fati est. Familia decubuit, fenus offendit, domus crepuit, damna, vulnera, labores, metus incucurrerunt: solet fieri. Hoc parum est: debuit fieri.
passages.english: Yet you are indignant at something, or complain, and do not understand that there is nothing evil in these things except this one thing, that you are indignant and complain? If you ask me, I think nothing is wretched for a man except that there is anything in nature which he thinks wretched. I shall not put up with myself on the day when I am not able to put up with something. I am in poor health: it is part of fate. The slaves have taken to their beds, the interest has gone wrong, the house has cracked, losses, wounds, hardships, fears have come rushing in: it commonly happens. That says too little: it had to happen.

notes.note: Malum is “evil” or simply “bad”. “Evil” is kept, as in Ep. 95.50. The letter opens with “yet” (Tamen), as if answering a complaint of Lucilius.
notes.other_reading: that there is nothing bad in these things

notes.note: Vir is a man in the full sense, with a hint of “a real man”. The plain “a man” is kept.
notes.other_reading: for a true man

notes.latin: nisi aliquid esse in rerum natura quod putet miserum
notes.note: The one wretched thing is his thinking anything wretched; the English keeps the Latin shape. In rerum natura is also the ordinary Latin for “in existence”. The project’s usual “in the nature of things” would mean “inherently” in English, so the English has “in nature”.
notes.other_reading: except that there is anything in the world which he thinks wretched

notes.latin: Non feram me quo die aliquid ferre non potero
notes.note: The sentence turns on ferre used twice, of bearing oneself and of bearing a hardship. “Put up with” is used both times.
notes.other_reading: I shall not bear myself on the day when I am not able to bear something.

notes.note: First person and a plain statement. It may be Seneca’s real state or a supposed case, like the list that follows. The plain statement is kept.
notes.other_reading: Suppose I am ill

notes.note: Familia is the household, chiefly its slaves. Decumbere is to take to one’s bed with illness. The Latin has no possessive here or with the interest and the house, and the English has none.
notes.other_reading: My household has fallen sick

notes.note: Fenus is interest, or money out at interest. Offendere is to stumble or meet a setback, or to give trouble. The English leaves open whether it is income from lending that has failed or interest owed that presses on him.
notes.other_reading: the money lent at interest has gone bad

notes.note: Literally “this is too little”. “This” is the phrase just used, that such things commonly happen, which Seneca then replaces with a stronger one.
notes.other_reading: That is too little

notes.note: Debuit can be necessity, “it was bound to happen”, or what is owed or right, “it was due, it ought to have happened”. The English takes necessity, in line with the opening of the next section, where such things are said to be decreed. The other sense would prepare the taxes of that section, things that are owed.
notes.other_reading: it ought to have happened

check.note: The phrase is the ordinary Latin for “in the world, in existence”. “In the nature of things” in English means “inherently”, which is a different claim.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “anything in nature which he thinks wretched”. “In the nature of things” is dropped because in English it means “inherently”; “nature” is kept and not “the world”, because rerum natura is a term of this letter’s argument about fate and god, and the note gives “in the world”.

check.note: “Bear myself” is unclear and suggests posture or conduct. The play on the repeated verb should be kept, but in words that read plainly.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the verb is now “put up with” in both places, so the play is kept in plain words. “Be able to” is not added to the first verb, which in the Latin is a plain future.

check.note: Familia is the body of slaves, and “household” will be read as “family”. The possessive here and in the next two items is not in the Latin.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “The slaves have taken to their beds”, and the possessive is dropped here and from the interest and the house, since the Latin has none.

check.note: Fenus is interest. It may be income from money lent that has failed, or interest owed that has become a trouble, and the English chooses the first.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the interest has gone wrong”, which leaves open, as the Latin does, whether the interest is owed to him or by him; the note gives both.

check.note: “Toils” is archaic.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “hardships”.

check.note: An object is added in the English; the Latin leaves the verb without one.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “have come rushing in”, with no object, as in the Latin.

check.note: It is not at once clear that Seneca means his own last words, “it commonly happens”, say too little.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “That says too little”, which keeps the Latin “too little” and makes plain that it is the words just used that fall short.

check.note: Debuit can be necessity, as in the English, or “it was due, it ought to have happened”. The second reading prepares the taxes of the next section, things that are owed.
check.decided: Declined: “it had to happen” stands. Debuit with “happen” most naturally states what was bound to be, and the next section opens by saying that such things are decreed; “due to happen” in English suggests a timetable. The note records the sense of something owed and its link with the taxes.

passages.latin: Decernuntur ista, non accidunt. Si quid credis mihi, intimos adfectus meos tibi cum maxime detego: in omnibus quae adversa videntur et dura sic formatus sum: non pareo deo sed adsentior; ex animo illum, non quia necesse est, sequor. Nihil umquam mihi incidet quod tristis excipiam, quod malo vultu; nullum tributum invitus conferam. Omnia autem ad quae gemimus, quae expavescimus, tributa vitae sunt: horum, mi Lucili, nec speraveris immunitatem nec petieris.
passages.english: These things are decreed; they are not accidents. If you trust me at all, I am at this very moment uncovering my inmost feelings to you: in all the things that seem adverse and hard, this is how I have been formed: I do not obey god but agree with him; I follow him from the heart, not because it is necessary. Nothing will ever befall me that I shall receive gloomily, that I shall receive with a sour face; I shall pay no tax unwillingly. And all the things at which we groan, at which we take fright, are the taxes of life: from these, my Lucilius, do not hope for exemption and do not ask for it.

notes.note: Decernere is to decree, as a senate or a judge does. Accidere is to befall, with a sense of chance. English “happen” alone loses the contrast, so the English has “are not accidents”, which is the same word in origin.
notes.other_reading: These things are decreed; they do not merely happen.

notes.note: Adfectus is usually “passion” in this project. Here no fault is implied, so “feelings”.
notes.other_reading: my inmost passions

notes.note: An idiom, “at this very moment, right now”.
notes.other_reading: just now

notes.note: Passive, “have been shaped thus”. It can imply that he has shaped himself by training. The passive is kept.
notes.other_reading: this is how I have trained myself

notes.note: Adsentiri is to agree, to give one’s assent, a word with a Stoic ring. The English has the plain “agree with him”.
notes.other_reading: I do not obey god but assent to him

notes.note: An idiom for “sincerely, willingly”. Animus is “mind” in this project, but English says “from the heart”.
notes.other_reading: with my whole mind

notes.note: Tributum is a levy paid to the state, and conferre is to pay in one’s share. The English has “tax”, repeated in “the taxes of life”.
notes.other_reading: I shall pay no tribute against my will

notes.note: A direct prohibition in the second person: do not hope, do not ask. Immunitas is the legal term for exemption from a tax, which carries on the image.
notes.other_reading: do not hope for immunity from these or seek it

check.note: The form is passive, formed by someone or something. It can also be read as having formed or trained oneself. A small point.
check.decided: Declined: the passive “have been formed” stands, because formatus sum is a passive of shaping, and “the frame of mind … reached” replaces that image with words the Latin does not have. The note records the reading in which he has trained himself.

check.note: The Latin is a direct prohibition. “You should neither” softens it to advice.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “do not hope for exemption and do not ask for it”, a direct prohibition as in the Latin.

passages.latin: Non gaudet navigio gubernator everso, non gaudet aegro medicus elato, non gaudet orator si patroni culpa reus cecidit, at contra omnibus crimen suum voluptati est: laetatur ille adulterio in quod inritatus est ipsa difficultate; laetatur ille circumscriptione furtoque, nec ante illi culpa quam culpae fortuna displicuit. Id prava consuetudine evenit.
passages.english: A helmsman does not rejoice when his ship has been overturned, a doctor does not rejoice when his patient has been carried out for burial, an orator does not rejoice if the defendant has lost through the advocate’s fault; but on the other hand to everyone his own offence is a pleasure. One man delights in an adultery to which he was provoked by its very difficulty; another delights in cheating and theft, and the fault does not displease him until the fault’s fortune does. This comes about through perverse habit.

notes.note: Evertere is to overturn or wreck. No possessive is expressed; “his” is supplied here and with the patient.
notes.other_reading: A helmsman does not rejoice when the ship is wrecked

notes.note: Efferre is the set word for carrying a body out to burial. “For burial” is added to make that plain.
notes.other_reading: when the sick man has been carried out

notes.latin: orator si patroni culpa reus cecidit
notes.note: The orator and the patronus (advocate) are the same man: he is not glad when his own mistake loses the case. The Latin has no possessive with “advocate”. Cecidit, “fell”, is the idiom for losing in court.
notes.other_reading: if the accused was convicted through the fault of his counsel

notes.note: Crimen is a charge and so the offence charged. “Everyone” keeps omnibus at full strength. Voluptas is “pleasure”.
notes.other_reading: all men take pleasure in their own guilt

notes.latin: in quod inritatus est ipsa difficultate
notes.note: Inritare is to goad or excite. The difficulty itself is what spurred him on.
notes.other_reading: to which the very difficulty of it incited him

notes.note: Circumscriptio is defrauding someone, especially by sharp practice. The English has the plain “cheating”.
notes.other_reading: in fraud and theft

notes.latin: nec ante illi culpa quam culpae fortuna displicuit
notes.note: Literally “nor has the fault displeased him before the fault’s fortune did”: he is sorry only when it turns out badly. The past form states a general truth, so the English uses the present. “Fortune” keeps fortuna; here it means how the thing turned out.
notes.other_reading: and he is not sorry for the fault until it turns out badly for him

notes.note: Pravus is crooked, perverse, stronger than “bad”. Consuetudo can be a person’s habit or general custom. The English takes habit.
notes.other_reading: from corrupt custom

check.note: The orator is himself the advocate, and the English can be read as if the advocate were a third person. The Latin leaves the same looseness, so this is only a caution.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “through the advocate’s fault”, without “his”, which the Latin does not have and which could suggest a third person. The clause order is kept, and the note says that orator and advocate are the same man.

check.note: “The fortune of the fault” is word for word but obscure. The sense is that he is not sorry for the wrong until it turns out badly for him.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “until the fault’s fortune does”. “Until” is taken as the plainer way to say “not before”; “fortune” is kept for fortuna, as in the glossary and in Ep. 97.14, and the note explains that it means how the thing turned out.

check.note: Found while settling: “bad habit” in English suggests a small personal quirk, while pravus is crooked or perverse, a stronger word than “bad”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “through perverse habit”.

passages.latin: Alioquin, ut scias subesse animis etiam in pessima abductis boni sensum nec ignorari turpe sed neglegi, omnes peccata dissimulant et, quamvis feliciter cesserint, fructu illorum utuntur, ipsa subducunt. At bona conscientia prodire vult et conspici: ipsas nequitia tenebras timet.
passages.english: Apart from that, so that you may know that a sense of the good lies underneath even in minds that have been drawn away into the worst things, and that what is shameful is not unknown but disregarded: all people conceal their wrongdoings and, however luckily these have turned out, enjoy the fruit of them while keeping the deeds themselves out of sight. But a good conscience wants to come forward and be seen; wickedness is afraid even of the darkness.

notes.note: “Otherwise, in other respects”, or more loosely “besides”. The section before ends by blaming perverse habit, and the English takes the word as “apart from that”.
notes.other_reading: Besides,

notes.note: A purpose clause hanging on the act of speaking: “(this is said) so that you may know”. The Latin shape is kept and the turn is marked with a colon.
notes.other_reading: As proof that

notes.note: Sensus is a perception or awareness; bonum is “the good”.
notes.other_reading: a feeling for what is good

notes.note: Turpe is what is shameful or base, the opposite of what is honourable. Neglegi is to be disregarded, not merely overlooked.
notes.other_reading: and that the base is not unrecognised but ignored

notes.note: The noun from peccare. In this letter the sense is moral, so “wrongdoings”, and “do wrong” in Ep. 97.14.
notes.other_reading: all people hide their sins

notes.note: Feliciter is “with good luck, successfully”. “Happy” is kept for beatus, so the English has “luckily”.
notes.other_reading: even though they have turned out successfully

notes.note: Two short clauses with no connective: they use the proceeds and withdraw the deeds from view. The English joins them with “while”.
notes.other_reading: they use the profit of them and hide the acts themselves

notes.note: Ipsas is emphatic and has the force of “even”: wickedness fears the very darkness that hides it. Nequitia is wickedness, worthlessness.
notes.other_reading: wickedness is afraid of the darkness itself

check.note: The word can be “apart from that”, “besides”, or “in general, otherwise”, that is, bad habit aside. The English chooses the first. A small point.
check.decided: Declined: “Apart from that” stands. The first sense of alioquin is “in other respects, otherwise”, which here sets what follows apart from the perverse habit just named, while “Besides” would make it a bare addition. The note records “Besides”.

check.note: Ipsas here has the force of “even”: wickedness fears even the dark that hides it. “The darkness itself” keeps the word but loses the point.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “wickedness is afraid even of the darkness”.

passages.latin: Hoc ego repugnare sectae nostrae si sic expediatur non iudico. Quare? quia prima illa et maxima peccantium est poena peccasse, nec ullum scelus, licet illud fortuna exornet muneribus suis, licet tueatur ac vindicet, inpunitum est, quoniam sceleris in scelere supplicium est. Sed nihilominus et hae illam secundae poenae premunt ac sequuntur, timere semper et expavescere et securitati diffidere. Quare ego hoc supplicio nequitiam liberem? quare non semper illam in suspenso relinquam?
passages.english: I do not judge that this conflicts with our school, if it is explained in this way. Why? Because the first and greatest punishment of those who do wrong is to have done wrong, and no crime, even if Fortune adorns it with her gifts, even if she protects and defends it, is unpunished, since the penalty of crime is in the crime. But nonetheless these second punishments too press hard upon that first one and follow it: always to be afraid, to take fright, and to have no trust in one’s own security. Why should I free wickedness from this penalty? Why should I not leave it always in suspense?

notes.note: “This” is the saying of Epicurus quoted in the section before, that a guilty man may stay hidden but cannot be confident of it. The school meant is the Stoic one, to which Epicurus was a rival.
notes.other_reading: I do not think this is at odds with our sect

notes.note: Expedire is to disentangle, set out. “In this way” may point back to the paraphrase in the section before or forward to the account that follows. The English leaves it open.
notes.other_reading: provided it is set out as follows

notes.latin: prima illa et maxima peccantium est poena peccasse
notes.note: The sentence repeats peccare, kept as “do wrong … have done wrong”. Poena is “punishment” throughout the passage and supplicium is “penalty”.
notes.other_reading: the first and greatest punishment of sinners is to have sinned

notes.latin: licet illud fortuna exornet muneribus suis
notes.note: Fortune is treated as a person who gives gifts and protects, so the English has a capital and “her”.
notes.other_reading: however much fortune decks it out with its gifts

notes.note: Vindicare is to claim as one’s own, to champion, or to rescue from a charge. The English has “defends”.
notes.other_reading: even if she protects it and takes its side

notes.note: Supplicium is a penalty exacted, often a severe one. It is kept distinct from poena.
notes.other_reading: the punishment of crime lies in the crime itself

notes.latin: et hae illam secundae poenae premunt ac sequuntur
notes.note: Illam is feminine singular and the word for crime is neuter, so it is taken as the first punishment, and “first” is supplied to say so: the second punishments follow close upon the first. It could instead look ahead to wickedness (nequitiam), named two sentences later. The two verbs together mean to follow hard upon.
notes.other_reading: these second punishments too press hard on wickedness and pursue it

notes.note: Securitas is “freedom from care” in this project’s glossary. Here the wrongdoer distrusts something he seems to have, and that phrase makes the clause hard to follow, so the English has “security”, which like the Latin word covers both safety and ease of mind. The section before, which breaks off in this copy, seems to set safe crimes against carefree ones (from memory, unchecked). The possessive is supplied.
notes.other_reading: and to put no trust in freedom from care

check.note: The bare forms “though Fortune adorn” and “though she protect” are archaic English.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “even if Fortune adorns it with her gifts, even if she protects and defends it”, in the ordinary present.

check.latin: et hae illam secundae poenae premunt ac sequuntur
check.note: Illam is taken as the first punishment, with “first one” added to say so, though it could be wickedness, as in the last sentence. The two verbs are one idea, “follow hard upon”, and “press upon and follow” reads oddly.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “press hard upon that first one and follow it”, which brings the two verbs closer to one idea. “First” stays, because a bare “it” would point to “crime”, and the Latin pronoun is feminine while the word for crime is neuter; the note records that it may instead be wickedness.

check.note: “To put no trust in freedom from care” is hard to make sense of. In this argument about escaping detection the word is the wrongdoer’s safety, which he may have but cannot rely on.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “to have no trust in one’s own security”. “Security” is used and not “safety”, because the Latin word covers ease of mind as well as safety, and the departure from the glossary is explained in a note.

passages.latin: Omnia quae fortuna intuetur ita fructifera ac iucunda fiunt si qui habet illa se quoque habet nec in rerum suarum potestate est. Errant enim, Lucili, qui aut boni aliquid nobis aut mali iudicant tribuere fortunam: materiam dat bonorum ac malorum et initia rerum apud nos in malum bonumve exiturarum. Valentior enim omni fortuna animus est et in utramque partem ipse res suas ducit beataeque ac miserae vitae sibi causa est.
passages.english: All the things that Fortune looks on become fruitful and pleasant on this condition: that the one who has them also has himself and is not in the power of his own things. For those people are wrong, Lucilius, who judge that Fortune gives us anything good or anything evil: she gives the material for goods and evils, and the beginnings of things that, in our keeping, will turn out for evil or for good. For the mind is stronger than any fortune, and itself leads its own things in either direction, and is for itself the cause of a happy life and of a wretched one.

notes.note: The verb means to look at or have regard to. It may mean everything in Fortune’s field of view, or the things she looks on with favour. The English keeps the plain image of looking.
notes.other_reading: All the things that Fortune looks on with favour

notes.latin: ita fructifera ac iucunda fiunt si
notes.note: The pair ita ... si is restrictive: “on these terms, if”. The English reads “on this condition” so as not to add an “only” that is not a separate word in the Latin.
notes.other_reading: become fruitful and pleasant only if

notes.note: Literally “also has himself”, meaning he is in possession of himself. “Has” is kept because the sentence turns on the repeated verb habet.
notes.other_reading: is also master of himself

notes.note: Res is wide: things, possessions, circumstances, affairs. It is “things” all three times in this passage (rerum suarum, initia rerum, res suas), so that the answer at the end can be heard: the owner must not be in the power of his things, and the mind leads its things.
notes.other_reading: and is not under the control of his own possessions

notes.note: Materia is raw stuff or timber, what a thing is made from. Bonum and malum are “good” and “evil” throughout this passage so the chain can be followed.
notes.other_reading: she supplies the raw stuff of good things and bad things

notes.latin: apud nos in malum bonumve exiturarum
notes.note: Apud nos is “with us”, “at our house”, “in our possession”. It says where the outcome is decided. The English reads “in our keeping”, the wording used for the same preposition in 98.10.
notes.other_reading: things that in our hands will end as an evil or as a good

notes.note: Omni can be “every” or “any”. The noun is the same fortuna as before, but with omni it means any kind of fortune, good or bad, which fits “in either direction”, so it has no capital here.
notes.other_reading: For the mind is stronger than anything Fortune can do

notes.note: Ducit is “leads” or “draws”. Ipse stresses that the mind does this itself, not Fortune. Res suas would more naturally be “its own affairs” in English; “things” is kept for the echo of rerum suarum.
notes.other_reading: it steers its own affairs itself to one side or the other

check.note: Set off by commas, “with us” is hard to follow. The sense is that what Fortune gives becomes good or evil once it is in our hands.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the beginnings of things that, in our keeping, will turn out for evil or for good”. Apud nos is “with us” or “in our possession” and has no hands in it, and “keeping” is the word used for the same preposition in 98.10.

check.note: “They are wrong who judge” is a dated English word order, though nothing is mistranslated.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “For those people are wrong, Lucilius, who judge”. The word order is changed as suggested, but “judge” is kept because iudicant is the verb of judgment, which the glossary keeps apart from thinking and opinion.

check.note: “Every fortune” reads oddly after “Fortune” twice as a person. The reader should still hear the same word.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “stronger than any fortune”. It stays without a capital because omni makes it any kind of fortune, good or bad, and a note says so.

check.note: Found while settling: res was “things” twice and then “affairs”, which hides that the res suas the mind leads answer the rerum suarum in whose power the owner must not be.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “itself leads its own things in either direction”, so that res is “things” all three times in the passage.

passages.latin: Immo mehercules, ut carmen fortius ac iustius petam quo animum tuum magis fulcias, hoc dicito quotiens aliquid aliter quam cogitabas evenerit: 'di melius'. Sic composito nihil accidet. Sic autem componetur si quid humanarum rerum varietas possit cogitaverit antequam senserit, si et liberos et coniugem et patrimonium sic habuerit tamquam non utique semper habiturus et tamquam non futurus ob hoc miserior si habere desierit.
passages.english: Or rather, by Hercules, so that I may reach for a line that is braver and more just, one with which you may prop up your mind more, say this whenever something has turned out otherwise than you had reckoned: “The gods decided better.” Nothing will happen to one so settled. And he will be so settled if he has reckoned, before he has felt it, with what the changeableness of human affairs can do, if he has children and wife and property as one who will not necessarily have them always, and as one who will not be more wretched on that account if he stops having them.

notes.note: Immo corrects what was just said: the section before recommended a line of verse about the gods seeing a matter otherwise. Mehercules is the everyday oath by Hercules.
notes.other_reading: No, indeed

notes.note: Carmen can be a verse, a chant, a set form of words or a charm. The section before quoted a line of Vergil (Aeneid 2, from memory, unchecked) and the replacement is two bare words, not verse, so the English reads “line”, which covers both. Fortius is “braver” or “stronger”; iustius is “more just”, that is, fairer to the gods.
notes.other_reading: a formula (or charm) that is stronger and fairer

notes.latin: ut carmen fortius ac iustius petam
notes.note: Petam is first person: the one who goes for the better line is Seneca, and the one who is to say it is Lucilius. Petere is to make for a thing, to go and get it.
notes.other_reading: to look for a line that is braver and more just

notes.note: Magis is “more”. The English avoids “better” here so that it is not confused with the “better” of the two quoted words, which is a different Latin word (melius). Fulcire is to prop or shore up.
notes.other_reading: with which you may better support your mind

notes.note: Two words with no verb. In ordinary use they are a wish (“may the gods grant better”, almost “heaven forbid”). Here they answer the line of verse in the section before, in which the gods saw the matter otherwise, and are offered as braver and more just, so the English makes them a statement and supplies the verb “decided”.
notes.other_reading: “May the gods grant better.”

notes.note: Composito has no noun: it may be a person or the mind (animus, also masculine); the English reads “one so settled” and means a person, because what follows speaks of having wife and children. Accidet is “will happen to”, with the sense of something falling on a person as an accident. The Latin shifts here from “you” to “he”, and the English keeps that.
notes.other_reading: To a mind so composed nothing will come as an accident.

notes.note: The same verb as cogitabas above: to think over, to plan, to count on. “Reckon” is used in both places so the link can be heard. Senserit is to feel or experience.
notes.other_reading: if he has thought about it before he has experienced it

notes.note: Varietas is variety, here in the sense of shifting and change.
notes.other_reading: the vicissitudes of human affairs

notes.note: Non utique is “not necessarily”, “not for certain”: keeping them always is not guaranteed. It does not say that they will certainly be lost.
notes.other_reading: as one who is not sure to have them for ever

notes.note: Strictly the estate inherited from a father; more loosely one’s property.
notes.other_reading: inheritance

check.note: Non utique means “not necessarily”. “Not in any case going to have them always” reads as a certainty of loss, where Seneca says only that keeping them is not guaranteed.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “as one who will not necessarily have them always”. Non utique denies only that the thing is certain, and the draft’s wording could be read as saying the loss is certain.

check.note: The Latin has no verb and the English supplies “decided”, making a statement. The two words are also a common wish, “may the gods grant better”, so the choice should be confirmed and noted.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps “The gods decided better.” and the note now says plainly that the verb is supplied and gives the wish as the other reading. Seneca offers the two words as braver and more just than the line before, in which the gods saw the matter otherwise, and a wish for something better would be neither.

check.note: Carmen can be a set form of words or a line of verse. A line of poetry has just been quoted, and “formula” drops that link.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a line”, which can be a line of verse or a set line to say. The link with the verse quoted just before is kept without calling two bare words a verse.

check.latin: ut carmen fortius ac iustius petam
check.note: Petam is first person: it is Seneca who goes to fetch the better line. The bare infinitive in the English can be read as if Lucilius were to look for it.
check.decided: Accepted: the clause is now a first person purpose clause with “reach for”, as suggested. The one fetching the line is plainly Seneca and the one saying it is Lucilius.

check.note: The Latin has no noun. A person suits what follows, but “a man” is an addition.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “one so settled”. The Latin has no noun, and “he” in the next sentence is enough to show that a person is meant.

check.note: “Befall” is archaic.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Nothing will happen to one so settled.” The note records that the verb also carries the sense of an accident.

check.note: Cogitare here is to plan or count on, and “were thinking” is vague. The same verb returns in cogitaverit, so any change should keep one English word for both.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “otherwise than you had reckoned” and, below, “if he has reckoned, before he has felt it, with what the changeableness of human affairs can do”. One English verb still serves both places.

check.note: Found while settling: “prop up your mind better” put a “better” (for magis) two lines before the “better” of the quoted words (melius), which suggests an echo the Latin does not have.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “prop up your mind more”. Magis is “more”, and “better” is left to the quoted words alone.

passages.latin: Egregie itaque videtur mihi Metrodorus dixisse in ea epistula qua sororem amisso optimae indolis filio adloquitur: 'mortale est omne mortalium bonum'. De his loquitur bonis ad quae concurritur; nam illud verum bonum non moritur, certum est sempiternumque, sapientia et virtus; hoc unum contingit inmortale mortalibus.
passages.english: So I think Metrodorus put it excellently in the letter in which he consoles his sister after the loss of her son, who was of the finest promise: “Every good of mortals is mortal.” He is speaking of these goods that people rush to in crowds. For that true good does not die; it is sure and everlasting: wisdom and virtue. This is the one immortal thing that falls to mortals.

notes.note: A close friend and follower of Epicurus (from memory, unchecked). The sentence quoted is a fragment of a letter of his, which would have been in Greek.
notes.other_reading: Metrodorus the Epicurean

notes.note: The verb is “speaks to”, “addresses”, and is regularly used of words of comfort after a death. The English reads “consoles”.
notes.other_reading: in which he addresses his sister

notes.note: The Latin does not say whose son. Latin often leaves out “his” or “her” with family words, and the English takes the son to be the sister’s. Indoles is inborn quality, and of the young it means promise.
notes.other_reading: after the loss of a son of the finest character

notes.note: Mortalium can be “of mortals” (people) or “of mortal things”. The English takes people, because the passage ends with mortalibus, “to mortals”.
notes.other_reading: Every good that belongs to mortal things is mortal.

notes.note: An impersonal passive: “to which there is a running together”. English needs a subject, so “people” is supplied, and “in crowds” stands for the “together” of the verb.
notes.other_reading: the goods the crowd rushes after

notes.note: Illud, “that”, sets the true good apart from “these goods” (his bonis) of the sentence before.
notes.other_reading: For the true good does not die

notes.note: Certum is sure, fixed, to be relied on.
notes.other_reading: it is fixed and lasts for ever

notes.note: Two nouns set beside the singular “true good” with no connecting word. The English keeps that with a colon.
notes.other_reading: that is, wisdom and virtue

notes.note: Contingit is “falls to the lot of”. Unum is “one” or “alone”.
notes.other_reading: This alone comes to mortals as something immortal.

check.note: After a death, adloqui is to speak words of comfort. “Addresses” is flatter and loses the fact that this is a letter of consolation.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “in which he consoles his sister”. After a death this verb is the regular one for speaking words of comfort, and the plain “addresses” is kept in the note.

check.note: The Latin does not say whose son, and the natural sense is the sister’s own. “A son” can sound like some unrelated son.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “after the loss of her son”. Latin leaves out the possessive with family words, and the phrase is attached to the sister; the note records that “her” is supplied.

check.note: Indoles is inborn quality, and of the young it means promise. “Character” suggests a formed moral character.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “who was of the finest promise”. Indoles is what a young person is born with and may grow into, not a character already formed.

check.note: “Run together to get” is literal and awkward. The sense is goods that the crowd rushes for.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “these goods that people rush to in crowds”. “To get” is dropped as suggested, and “in crowds” is added to the suggestion because the verb is a running together from all sides.

check.note: Illud is dropped. It sets “that true good” against “these goods” just before.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “For that true good does not die”, and the sentence before has “these goods” for his bonis, so that the contrast of this and that can be heard.

passages.latin: Ceterum tam inprobi sunt tamque obliti quo eant, quo illos singuli dies trudant, ut mirentur aliquid ipsos amittere, amissuri uno die omnia. Quidquid est cui dominus inscriberis apud te est, tuum non est; nihil firmum infirmo, nihil fragili aeternum et invictum est. Tam necesse est perire quam perdere et hoc ipsum, si intellegimus, solacium est. Aequo animo perde: pereundum est.
passages.english: But they are so shameless, and so forgetful of where they are going, of where each single day is pushing them, that they are surprised to lose anything themselves, though on one day they are going to lose everything. Whatever it is that you are written down as owner of is in your keeping; it is not yours. Nothing is firm for one who is not firm, nothing eternal and unconquerable for one who is fragile. It is as necessary to perish as to lose, and this very fact, if we understand it, is a comfort. Lose with an even mind: one must perish.

notes.note: “They” has no noun here; it picks up the mortals of the sentence before (98.9). Inprobi ranges over shameless, unreasonable, greedy beyond bounds; the English reads “shameless”.
notes.other_reading: Yet people are so presumptuous

notes.note: A future participle: “being about to lose”. Uno die is “on one day” or “in a single day”.
notes.other_reading: when in a single day they will lose it all

notes.note: The language of a title or register: the thing has your name entered as owner. The form can be present or future; the English takes the present.
notes.other_reading: Whatever you will be registered as master of

notes.note: “Is with you”, “is at your house”: the language of a thing left in someone’s keeping, set against owning it. The English reads “in your keeping”.
notes.other_reading: is with you

notes.note: A play on firmum and infirmo (firm, weak). The English keeps the echo with “firm” and “not firm”.
notes.other_reading: nothing is solid for the weak

notes.note: Invictus can be “unconquered” or “unconquerable”. Beside “eternal” the English takes the second.
notes.other_reading: nothing eternal and unconquered

notes.note: A play that English cannot keep in full: perire (to perish) serves in Latin as the passive of perdere (to lose). The same pair returns in the last sentence.
notes.other_reading: It is as necessary to be lost as to lose

notes.note: The set phrase for calm acceptance. The glossary’s “mind” is kept for animus.
notes.other_reading: Lose calmly

notes.note: An impersonal form: “there must be perishing”. The English keeps it impersonal with “one”, though the command before it is addressed to “you”.
notes.other_reading: you must perish

check.note: Correct, but “is with you” is weak for the contrast between holding a thing and owning it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “is in your keeping; it is not yours”. Apud te is the language of a thing lodged with someone, and the new wording marks the contrast with owning it.

check.note: Invictus can be “unconquered” or “unconquerable”. Beside aeternum the second fits better.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “nothing eternal and unconquerable”. The form covers both senses, and beside “eternal” the claim is about what can never be overcome.

passages.latin: Quid ergo adversus has amissiones auxili invenimus? hoc, ut memoria teneamus amissa nec cum ipsis fructum excidere patiamur quem ex illis percepimus. Habere eripitur, habuisse numquam. Peringratus est qui, cum amisit, pro accepto nihil debet. Rem nobis eripit casus, usum fructumque apud nos relinquit, quem nos iniquitate desiderii perdidimus.
passages.english: What help, then, do we find against these losses? This: that we hold in memory the things lost, and do not let the fruit we gathered from them drop away along with the things themselves. Having is snatched away; having had, never. It is a thoroughly ungrateful man who, when he has lost a thing, owes nothing for having received it. Chance snatches the thing from us; the use and the fruit of it chance leaves with us, and this we ourselves have lost by the unfairness of our longing.

notes.note: A rare noun, “losings”. English “lose” covers two Latin verbs in this passage: amittere (to let go, lose) and, in the last clause, perdere (to lose by ruining or wasting).
notes.other_reading: these bereavements

notes.note: The form is the same for present and perfect. The English takes the present.
notes.other_reading: What help, then, have we found

notes.note: Fructus is fruit, yield, enjoyment; “fruit” is kept because the legal pair “use and fruit” follows. Excidere is to fall out, and is also used of things slipping from memory.
notes.other_reading: nor allow the enjoyment to slip from our minds

notes.note: Two infinitives used as nouns. No person is named, and none is added.
notes.other_reading: To have can be taken from us, to have had never can.

notes.note: Bookkeeping language: acceptum is what is entered as received. “Owes nothing” means he behaves as if he owed nothing.
notes.other_reading: counts himself as owing nothing for what he was given

notes.note: “Chance”, not fortuna, so not “Fortune”.
notes.other_reading: accident

notes.note: A legal term, usus fructus: the right to use a thing and take its yield without owning it. The two plain words are kept so that “fruit” repeats.
notes.other_reading: the usufruct

notes.note: Quem is singular and picks up the fruit (or use and fruit as one thing). The perfect is kept as it stands, though it may be meant generally. Desiderium is longing for what is gone; iniquitas is unfairness, the opposite of an even mind.
notes.other_reading: which we throw away by the injustice of our regret

check.note: The form is both present and perfect. The perfect is equally possible and makes little difference to the sense.
check.decided: Declined: the present stands. The Latin form serves for present and perfect alike, the answer that follows is framed in the present, and the note gives the perfect as the other reading.

check.note: Found while settling: “A man is thoroughly ungrateful who” has the same dated word order that the second reader marked in 98.2.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “It is a thoroughly ungrateful man who, when he has lost a thing, owes nothing for having received it.” Nothing is added, and “ungrateful” still comes first as in the Latin.

passages.latin: Quare defecimus? quare desperamus? Quidquid fieri potuit potest, nos modo purgemus animum sequamurque naturam, a qua aberranti cupiendum timendumque est et fortuitis serviendum. Licet reverti in viam, licet in integrum restitui: restituamur, ut possimus dolores quocumque modo corpus invaserint perferre et fortunae dicere 'cum viro tibi negotium est: quaere quem vincas'.
passages.english: Why have we given up? Why do we despair? Whatever it has been possible to do, it is possible to do. Only let us cleanse our mind and follow nature: one who strays from her must desire and fear and be a slave to the things of chance. We may return to the road, we may be restored to our original condition. Let us be restored, so that we can bear pains to the end, in whatever way they invade the body, and say to Fortune: “It is a man you have to deal with. Look for someone you can conquer.”

notes.note: A perfect beside the present desperamus. The verb ranges over failing, giving out, losing heart and deserting.
notes.other_reading: Why have we failed?

notes.note: Potuit is past and potest present: what it was possible to do then is possible now. The past looks back to the examples in the section before (Fabricius, Tubero, Sextius). Fieri can also be “to happen”.
notes.other_reading: Whatever was able to happen is able to happen.

notes.note: Modo with the subjunctive can be an exhortation (“only let us”) or a proviso (“provided that”). The English takes the exhortation and splits the sentence.
notes.other_reading: provided only that we cleanse our mind

notes.note: Impersonal forms of necessity with a dative: “for one who strays there must be desiring and fearing”. No objects are given.
notes.other_reading: for anyone who wanders from it, craving and fear are unavoidable

notes.note: Fortuita are things that come by chance. Servire is to be a slave.
notes.other_reading: and must serve accidents

notes.note: A legal phrase (from memory, unchecked): a magistrate’s order putting a person back in the position he held before a loss. Integer is “whole”, “untouched”. The English gives the legal sense plainly and repeats “restored” as the Latin repeats its verb.
notes.other_reading: we may be made whole again

notes.note: The form looks forward: in whatever way pains shall have invaded. English puts this in the present. Invadere is to invade or attack.
notes.other_reading: in whatever way they have attacked the body

notes.note: Vir is “man” in the strong sense, the word behind virtus. Negotium is business, dealings.
notes.other_reading: “Your business is with a real man.”

notes.note: Literally “look for one whom you may conquer”, implying: not this one.
notes.other_reading: “go and find someone to defeat”

check.note: Potuit is past: what it was once possible to do is possible now. “Could be done” also reads as “might be done”, which makes the sentence a near tautology.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Whatever it has been possible to do, it is possible to do.” Potuit is past and potest present, and the draft’s “could” was open to being read as “might”.

check.note: This is the legal phrase for being put back in one’s original position. “Our whole state” is unclear English.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “we may be restored to our original condition”. This gives the legal sense of the phrase plainly, and “restored” still repeats in the next sentence as the Latin verb does.

check.note: The Latin looks forward and generalises. “Have invaded” ties it to pains already present.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “in whatever way they invade the body”. The tense looks forward as the Latin does, but “invade” is kept rather than “attack”, since invadere is exactly that image.

passages.latin: Hoc est, mi Lucili, philosophiam in opere discere et ad verum exerceri, videre quid homo prudens animi habeat contra mortem, contra dolorem, cum illa accedat, hic premat; quid faciendum sit a faciente discendum est.
passages.english: This, my Lucilius, is learning philosophy in action and training on the real thing: seeing how much spirit a man of good sense has against death, against pain, when the one is coming near and the other is pressing on him. What is to be done must be learned from one who is doing it.

notes.note: “This” points back to the example in the section before, the man who goes on living under torment.
notes.other_reading: This is what it means

notes.note: Literally “in the work”: on the job, in the doing, as against in the lecture room. “In practice” is avoided because the next verb is itself about practising.
notes.other_reading: at the work itself

notes.note: “To be exercised against the real”: training on the real thing, not in practice bouts. Verum can also be “the truth”.
notes.other_reading: to be trained by the truth

notes.note: Animi depends on quid: “what of spirit”, that is, how much. The glossary prefers “mind” for animus, but the sense here is courage, so the English reads “spirit”. Prudens is a man of good sense, not the technical “wise man” (sapiens).
notes.other_reading: how much courage a sensible man has

notes.note: Illa is death and hic is pain. Premat has no object in the Latin; “on him” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: when death approaches and pain bears down

notes.note: A present participle: from someone in the act of doing it.
notes.other_reading: from the doer

check.note: “At the work itself” is unclear, and “itself” is added. The sense is learning philosophy in practice, as against in words.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “learning philosophy in action”. “Itself” is dropped and the phrase made plain, but “in practice” is avoided because the next verb, exerceri, is about practising and the two would blur.

check.note: Quid animi is a question of amount: how much courage. “What spirit” reads as what kind of spirit.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “how much spirit a man of good sense has against death, against pain”. “How much” is taken, along with the two bare “against” phrases of the Latin; “spirit” is kept as the glossary’s word for animus where the sense is courage.

passages.latin: Sed plerique non conputant quanta perceperint, quantum gavisi sint. Hoc habet inter reliqua mali dolor iste: non supervacuus tantum sed ingratus est. Ergo quod habuisti talem amicum, perit opera? Tot annis, tanta coniunctione vitae, tam familiari studiorum societate nil actum est? Cum amico effers amicitiam? Et quid doles amisisse, si habuisse non prodest? Mihi crede, magna pars ex iis quos amavimus, licet ipsos casus abstulerit, apud nos manet; nostrum est quod praeterit tempus nec quicquam est loco tutiore quam quod fuit.
passages.english: But most people do not reckon up how much they have received, how much they have rejoiced. Among its other evils that grief has this one: it is not only needless but ungrateful. So then, that you had such a friend: is it wasted effort? In so many years, in so close a sharing of life, in so intimate a partnership of pursuits, was nothing achieved? Do you carry the friendship out to burial along with the friend? And why do you grieve at having lost him, if having had him does you no good? Believe me, a great part of those we have loved stays with us, even though chance has taken the people themselves away. The time that has gone by is ours, and nothing is in a safer place than what has been.

notes.note: An accounting word: to add up, to reckon.
notes.other_reading: do not count

notes.note: Percipere is to take in or receive, and is the regular verb for gathering crops or income. With “fruit” in 98.11 it is “gathered”; here and in 99.5, where no fruit is its object, the English reads “received”.
notes.other_reading: how much they have gathered

notes.note: “Grief”, since the subject is mourning. Iste points at the person addressed or at the kind just mentioned. From memory, unchecked: most of letter 99 is a copy of a letter Seneca wrote to Marullus on the death of his small son, so “you” in this section is Marullus, and the lost friend is a supposed case.
notes.other_reading: this grief of yours

notes.note: The idiom for wasted effort or trouble. Perit can be present or a shortened perfect.
notes.other_reading: has it all gone to waste?

notes.note: Vitae is singular and has no “your”: one life joined or shared.
notes.other_reading: in so close a joining of your lives

notes.note: Studia can be studies or, more widely, the things a person gives himself to. “Pursuits” covers both.
notes.other_reading: so intimate a partnership in studies

notes.note: The usual verb for carrying a body out to burial. The image is kept.
notes.other_reading: Do you bury the friendship with the friend?

notes.latin: magna pars ex iis quos amavimus
notes.note: This can mean a great part of each person, or a great many of them. The English leaves the wording open.
notes.other_reading: much of those we have loved

notes.note: As spelled, praeterit is present (“passes”); it can also be a shortened perfect (“has passed”). The English takes the perfect, because “what has been” follows.
notes.other_reading: the time that is passing is ours

check.note: Operam perdere is the ordinary idiom for wasted trouble. “Is that effort lost?” leaves the reader asking what effort.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “So then, that you had such a friend: is it wasted effort?” The idiom is made plain, but “effort” is kept because opera is a word of the Latin and the suggestion leaves it out.

check.note: Without the word “fruit”, “gathered” suggests piling things up. Percipere here is to receive or enjoy.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “how much they have received”. With no fruit named here the harvest sense of “gathered” does not carry, and the note records the link with 98.11.

check.note: “Your” is added and vitae is singular, a life shared. “A joining of lives” is also stiff.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “in so close a sharing of life”. Vitae is singular and the Latin has no “your”.

check.note: Studia can be studies or, more widely, pursuits and interests. The English picks the narrower sense and adds “your”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “so intimate a partnership of pursuits”. “Your” is dropped, and “pursuits” is used rather than “interests” because it covers both studies and the wider sense of studia.

check.note: “Them themselves” is clumsy.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “even though chance has taken the people themselves away”. “People” stands for the suggested “persons” as the plainer word of today.

check.note: As spelled, the form is present. The English takes it as a contracted perfect, which fits the end of the sentence but is a choice.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps “has gone by”, and the note now records that the form as spelled is present and gives “is passing” as the other reading.

passages.latin: Ingrati adversus percepta spe futuri sumus, quasi non quod futurum est, si modo successerit nobis, cito in praeterita transiturum sit. Anguste fructus rerum determinat qui tantum praesentibus laetus est: et futura et praeterita delectant, haec expectatione, illa memoria, sed alterum pendet et non fieri potest, alterum non potest non fuisse. Quis ergo furor est certissimo excidere? Adquiescamus iis quae iam hausimus, si modo non perforato animo hauriebamus et transmittente quidquid acceperat.
passages.english: We are ungrateful for what we have received, out of hope for what is to come, as if what is to come, if it does turn out well for us, were not going to pass quickly into what is past. Whoever is glad only at what is present sets narrow bounds to the fruits of things. Both what is to come and what is past give delight, the one by expectation, the other by memory; but the one is in suspense and may not come about, while the other cannot not have been. What madness is it, then, to lose hold of what is surest? Let us rest in the things we have already drawn in, provided that we were not drawing them in with a mind full of holes, one that let through whatever it had received.

notes.note: Futuri is taken as “of the future”, depending on spe, and sumus goes with ingrati. The words could be read together as “are going to be”, but then spe hangs loose.
notes.other_reading: We are going to be ungrateful for what we have received, through hope

notes.note: The verb of 99.4, here again “received”. It is the regular verb for gathering fruit, and “fruits” follows in the next sentence. The last word of the section, acceperat, is a related verb and is also “received”.
notes.other_reading: ungrateful for what we have gathered

notes.note: Succedere with a dative of the person is to turn out well for someone; it can also be simply to come next. The English takes “turn out well”, the usual sense when a thing hoped for is the subject.
notes.other_reading: if indeed it comes to us at all

notes.note: The “fruit” of 98.11, here plural: yield or enjoyment. Determinat is to mark out boundaries.
notes.other_reading: the enjoyment of things

notes.note: By the usual rule haec would be the nearer word (the past) and illa the further (the future), but the sense requires the reverse: the future by expectation, the past by memory. The English follows the sense.
notes.other_reading: the latter by expectation, the former by memory

notes.note: Pendet is “hangs”, is in suspense; there are no scales in the Latin. Non goes with fieri: “is able not to happen”. It does not mean “cannot happen”.
notes.other_reading: is still hanging and can fail to happen

notes.note: Excidere with the ablative is to fall out of a thing, to be put out of possession of it. The English gives the sense with “lose hold of”. It is the verb used of the fruit in 98.11.
notes.other_reading: to fall away from what is surest

notes.note: To come to rest in a thing, to be content with it.
notes.other_reading: Let us be content with

notes.note: Haurire is to draw a liquid and also to drink it up. With a mind full of holes that lets through what it receives, the picture is of drawing water in a leaking vessel, so the English reads “drawn in” and “drawing them in”.
notes.other_reading: the things we have already drunk in

notes.note: The mind as a vessel pierced with holes, so that what is poured in runs out. The image recalls the leaking jar of the Danaids (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: with a punctured mind

check.note: Succedere can be “turn out well” or simply “come to us in its turn”. The second would suit the point that the future is uncertain.
check.decided: Declined: the draft’s “if it does turn out well for us” stands. With a dative of the person and a thing hoped for as subject, succedere is the ordinary Latin for turning out well, and the sentence is about hope; the other reading is in the note.

check.note: As in 99.4, “gathered” without “fruit” suggests accumulating. The sense is what has been received.
check.decided: Accepted: percepta is now “received”, as in 99.4. The related verb at the end of the section (acceperat) is “received” too, which suits two verbs from one root.

check.note: “In the balance” brings in a pair of scales that the Latin does not have. Pendet is just “hangs”, “is in suspense”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the one is in suspense and may not come about”. Pendet is only “hangs”, and the scales are gone.

check.note: Excidere with the ablative is to lose hold of, to forfeit. “Fall away from” is unclear and could be read as deserting.
