check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “to lose hold of what is surest”. “Lose hold of” is used rather than “let slip” because in the Latin it is the person who falls out of the thing, not the thing that slips away.

check.note: Haurire is to draw water as well as to drink. With a mind full of holes the picture is of drawing into a leaky vessel, and “drunk in” chooses the other sense.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the verb is now “drawn in” and “drawing them in”. The vessel full of holes points to drawing water, as the second reader says; “in” is added because “things drawn” alone is not clear English.

check.note: Found while settling: “He sets narrow bounds ... who is glad” has the same dated word order that the second reader marked in 98.2.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Whoever is glad only at what is present sets narrow bounds to the fruits of things.” Nothing is added or dropped.

passages.latin: 'Innumerabilia sunt exempla eorum qui liberos iuvenes sine lacrimis extulerint, qui in senatum aut in aliquod publicum officium a rogo redierint et statim aliud egerint. Nec inmerito; nam primum supervacuum est dolere si nihil dolendo proficias; deinde iniquum est queri de eo quod uni accidit, omnibus restat; deinde desiderii stulta conquestio est, ubi minimum interest inter amissum et desiderantem. Eo itaque aequiore animo esse debemus quod quos amisimus sequimur.
passages.english: There are countless examples of men who carried out their children, young men, to burial without tears, who went back from the pyre to the senate or to some public duty and at once turned to other business. And not without reason. For first, it is needless to grieve if you gain nothing by grieving. Next, it is unfair to complain of a thing that has happened to one and is waiting for all. Next, the complaint that longing makes is foolish where very little lies between the one lost and the one who longs for him. So our mind ought to be all the more even, because we are following those we have lost.

notes.note: The Latin as given opens with a quotation mark that is not closed in this section. It marks the passage as part of the letter to Marullus that Seneca is copying out (from memory, unchecked), so “you” here is the reader of that letter. In every section of letter 99 the English leaves this outer mark out, because it is never closed inside a section.
notes.other_reading: The same sentence with an opening quotation mark left open

notes.note: Iuvenes are young adults, not small children: sons who were grown.
notes.other_reading: their young children

notes.note: The verb for carrying a body out to burial, as in 99.4.
notes.other_reading: who buried

notes.note: Literally “at once did something else”.
notes.other_reading: and immediately attended to something else

notes.note: A general “you”, kept as in the Latin.
notes.other_reading: if one gains nothing by grieving

notes.note: “One” is a single person, set against “all”. Accidit can be present or perfect, and the English takes the perfect. Restat is “remains”, is still to come.
notes.other_reading: what happens to one man and is in store for everyone

notes.note: Literally “the complaint of longing is foolish”. The genitive can be the source (the complaint that longing makes) or the thing complained of (a complaint about one’s longing). The English takes the source, and keeps “complaint” to match “complain” (queri) just before.
notes.other_reading: it is foolish to complain of longing

notes.note: “The least lies between”: the gap may be of time (the mourner follows soon) or of condition.
notes.other_reading: where the difference is very slight

notes.note: Eo ... quod with a comparative is “all the more ... because”. “Even mind” is kept for aequus animus, as in 98.10. The same root is in iniquum, “unfair”, two clauses earlier, an echo the English does not keep.
notes.other_reading: So we ought to be all the calmer because

check.note: The Latin opens with a single quotation mark that is not closed within the section, as 99.10 does, and the English drops it without notice. One treatment for the outer quotation is needed across the letter 99 sections.
check.decided: Accepted: one treatment is fixed for letter 99. The outer mark of the copied letter is left out of the English in every section, because it is opened and never closed inside a section; the marks round an objector’s words are kept, and notes at 99.6 and 99.10 say so.

check.note: “Already” is added. The Latin says only that the children were in their youth, that is, grown and not infants.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “who carried out their children, young men, to burial without tears”. “Already” was not in the Latin.

check.note: Accidit is present or perfect, so “happens to one” is equally possible. A small point.
check.decided: Declined: “has happened to one” stands. The form is both present and perfect, the perfect suits a complaint about a death that has taken place, and the note now records the present.

check.note: The genitive can be the thing complained of or the source of the complaint. “Complain of longing” is odd English, and the second reading fits the argument better.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the complaint that longing makes is foolish”. The genitive is taken as the source, as suggested, but “complaint” and “longing” are kept so that the links with queri just before and desiderantem just after can be heard, and “the dead” is not added.

check.latin: Eo itaque aequiore animo esse debemus quod
check.note: Correct but stiff. Eo ... quod with a comparative is “all the more ... because”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the sentence now begins “So our mind ought to be all the more even, because”. “All the more ... because” is taken as suggested, and “even mind” is kept for aequus animus, as in 98.10, rather than “calmer”.

passages.latin: '"Sed puer decessit." Nondum dico melius agi cum eo qui vita defungitur: ad eum transeamus qui consenuit: quantulo vincit infantem! Propone temporis profundi vastitatem et universum conplectere, deinde hoc quod aetatem vocamus humanam compara immenso: videbis quam exiguum sit quod optamus, quod extendimus.
passages.english: “But he died a boy.” I am not yet saying that the one who is done with life is better off. Let us pass to the one who has grown old: by how little he beats the infant! Set before yourself the vastness of deep time and take in the whole; then compare this thing we call a human lifetime with the immeasurable. You will see how small a thing it is that we wish for, that we stretch out.

notes.note: An imagined objection. The Latin as given has an outer opening mark (the letter being copied, as in 99.6) and inner marks round these words; the English keeps only the marks round the objection. Puer is a boy or a child.
notes.other_reading: “But it was a child who died.”

notes.latin: melius agi cum eo qui vita defungitur
notes.note: As given there is no word for “early” or “quickly”, and the English translates what stands. From memory, unchecked, printed editions have cito (“quickly”) here, which answers the objection more directly. Melius agi cum is the idiom for being better off; defungi is to be done with a thing, as with a duty.
notes.other_reading: that the one who is quickly done with life is better off

notes.note: Quantulo is “by how tiny an amount”. Infans is a baby not yet speaking.
notes.other_reading: how small the margin by which he outdoes the baby

notes.note: Profundi is taken as an adjective with temporis: deep, bottomless time. It can also be a noun (“the abyss of time”). Vastitas is vastness, with a shade of emptiness.
notes.other_reading: the vastness of the abyss of time

notes.note: Conplectere is an imperative: “embrace”, “take in”. Universum is taken as the whole of time; it can also mean the universe.
notes.other_reading: and embrace the universe

notes.note: Aetas is an age or a span of life.
notes.other_reading: what we call the age of man

notes.note: Immensum is the unmeasured, the boundless.
notes.other_reading: compare it with infinity

notes.note: “What we stretch out”: what people try to make longer. The image is kept.
notes.other_reading: what we try to prolong

check.note: As given, the clause covers anyone who dies, which is no direct answer to the objection. From memory, unchecked, the usual text has cito before vita, and the edition should be checked.
check.decided: Declined: the English follows the Latin as given, which construes and makes sense without the word. The edition cannot be checked here, so the recollection of cito stays in the note, marked “from memory, unchecked”, with the English it would give.

check.note: “It goes better with one” is a literal copy of the Latin idiom. Plain English is “is better off”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “that the one who is done with life is better off”. This is the plain English for the Latin idiom.

check.note: Profundi is an adjective with temporis: the vastness of deep time. The English turns it into the “depth” of time and moves “vast” onto “expanse”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the vastness of deep time”. Profundi goes with “time” and “vastness” is given back to its own noun; “deep” is used rather than “bottomless” as the first sense of the word.

passages.latin: Illud quoque dicamus ei qui deflet ac desiderat in aetate prima raptum: omnes, quantum ad brevitatem aevi, si universo compares, et iuvenes et senes, in aequo sumus. Minus enim ad nos ex aetate omni venit quam quod minimum esse quis dixerit, quoniam quidem minimum aliqua pars est: hoc quod vivimus proximum nihilo est; et tamen, o dementiam nostram, late disponitur.
passages.english: Let us also say this to one who weeps and longs for someone snatched away in his earliest years: all of us, as far as shortness of lifetime goes, if you compare it with the whole of time, both young and old, are on a level. For less comes to us out of all time than what anyone would call the least, since the least is at any rate some part. This span that we live is next to nothing; and yet, oh our madness, it is planned out on a wide scale.

notes.note: The object is an unnamed masculine “one snatched”. Aetas prima is the earliest age, childhood or first youth.
notes.other_reading: a child carried off in infancy

notes.note: “As far as concerns”. Aevum is a lifetime or span.
notes.other_reading: so far as the brevity of life is concerned

notes.note: Universo is taken as the whole of time, as in 99.10, since aevi stands just before and “all time” just after; it can also mean the universe. What is compared is left unsaid, and “it” is supplied for the lifetime. The “you” is general.
notes.other_reading: if you compare us with the universe

notes.note: Aetas here is time at large, not an age of life.
notes.other_reading: out of the whole of eternity

notes.latin: quam quod minimum esse quis dixerit
notes.note: “Than what anyone would say is the least.” The next clause gives the ground: the least is still a part, and the human share is less than that.
notes.other_reading: than the smallest thing one could name

notes.note: Literally “this which we live”. English needs a noun, so “span” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: This that we live

notes.note: An exclamation in the accusative, set inside the sentence.
notes.other_reading: how mad we are

notes.note: Disponere is to set out, arrange, plan; late is “widely”. The sense is that this next to nothing is planned as if it were a broad space. The passive is kept.
notes.other_reading: it is laid out far and wide

check.note: The meaning is hard to get from “it is laid out on a wide scale”. Disponere is to arrange or plan out, and the passive hides that this is the doing of the people whose madness is named.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “it is planned out on a wide scale”. “Planned” makes the sense plain; the passive is kept because the Latin is passive, and “far and wide” is not used because in English it means “everywhere”.

check.note: “This that we live” is stiff English.
check.decided: Accepted: “span” is supplied as suggested, since English needs a noun after “this”. The note gives the literal wording.

check.note: “In the first of his years” is an unusual phrase and can be read as “in his first year”. The Latin means in earliest youth.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “snatched away in his earliest years”. The draft’s phrase could be read as “in his first year”, which the Latin does not say.

check.note: “The whole” is vague. Universum may be the whole of time or the universe, and the first is much the likelier here.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “if you compare it with the whole of time”. Aevi stands just before and “all time” just after, so time is the whole that is meant; the note records “the universe”.

passages.latin: Quid autem stultius quammirari id ullo die factum quod omni potest fieri? Stat quidem terminusnobis ubi illum inexorabilis fatorum necessitas fixit, sed nemo scit nostrumquam prope versetur a termino; sic itaque formemus animum tamquam ad extremaventum sit. Nihil differamus; cotidie cum vita paria faciamus.
passages.english: But what is more foolish than to be surprised that something has happened on any one day which can happen on every day? A boundary does stand for us, where the necessity of the fates, which no plea can move, has fixed it; but none of us knows how near he is to the boundary. So let us shape our mind as though the end had been reached. Let us put nothing off. Let us balance our account with life every day.

notes.note: Read as “quam mirari” (two words run together in the copy). “Mirari” ranges from “wonder at” to “be surprised”; the English takes “be surprised”, since the section before speaks of brief astonishment at other people’s deaths.
notes.other_reading: than to marvel that something has happened

notes.latin: ullo die factum quod omni potest fieri
notes.note: “Ullo die” is “on any day at all”, set against “omni”, “on every (day)”. The English reads “on any one day” so that the contrast with “every day” is heard.
notes.other_reading: that a thing has happened on some day which can happen on every one

notes.note: “Terminus” is a boundary mark, the stone that fixes the edge of a piece of land; “stat” (“stands”) and “fixit” (“has fixed”) keep that picture. “Boundary” is used for both occurrences in the passage.
notes.other_reading: A limit is indeed set

notes.note: “Fatorum” is plural and the English keeps “the fates” (lower case), though it may be no more than “fate”. “Inexorabilis” is literally “not to be moved by entreaty”, given as “which no plea can move”.
notes.other_reading: the inexorable necessity of fate

notes.note: Read as “nostrum quam”: “nostrum” goes with “nemo” and “quam” with “prope”. “Versetur” is “moves about, finds himself”; the English narrows it to “is”.
notes.other_reading: how close to the boundary he is moving

notes.note: Read as “ad extrema ventum sit”, an impersonal passive: literally “as though it had been come to the last things”. The English keeps it impersonal.
notes.other_reading: as though we had arrived at the very end

notes.note: “Paria facere” is a bookkeeping idiom: to make the two sides of an account equal, to settle up. The English keeps the accounting image.
notes.other_reading: let us be quits with life every day

check.note: “Stat” is only “stands”. The draft added “fixed” here and then gave “fixit” as “planted”, so the Latin’s one word of fixing appeared twice in two forms.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “A boundary does stand” and, for “fixit”, “has fixed it”. “Stat” says only “stands”, and the one Latin word of fixing now appears once.

check.note: “Ullo die” is “on any day”, set against “omni”, “on every (day)”. “On some one day” is awkward and blurs the contrast of any and every.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “on any one day which can happen on every day”, so that “any” answers “every” as “ullo” answers “omni”.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “that boundary”, but the Latin has no word for “that”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “how near he is to the boundary”.

passages.latin: Maximumvitae vitium est quod inperfecta semper est, quod [in] aliquid ex illadiffertur. Qui cotidie vitae suae summam manum inposuit non indiget tempore;ex hac autem indigentia timor nascitur et cupiditas futuri exedens animum.Nihil est miserius dubitatione venientium quorsus evadant; quantum sitillud quod restat aut quale sollicita mens inexplicabili formidine agitatur.
passages.english: The greatest fault of life is that it is always unfinished, that some part of it is put off. The man who has put the finishing touch to his life every day is not in need of time. But from this need fear is born, and a craving for the future, one that eats away the mind. Nothing is more wretched than doubt about where the things that are coming will end up. The mind, anxious about how much is left or what kind of thing it is, is driven about by a fear that cannot be untangled.

notes.note: The glossary prefers “vice” for “vitium”, but this is a defect in life itself, not a moral failing, so the English has “fault”. The Latin also has a play of sound between “vitae” and “vitium” that English loses.
notes.other_reading: The greatest vice of life

notes.note: “Inperfecta” is “not brought to completion”, given as “unfinished”; it does not mean morally imperfect here.
notes.other_reading: it is always incomplete

notes.note: Read as “ex illa differtur”. The square brackets around “in” mark a word the edition deletes, and the English is translated without it. With “in” the clause would say that life is put off to something.
notes.other_reading: that something of it is always being postponed to some later point

notes.note: “Summa manus”, literally “the last hand”, is the craftsman’s idiom for the final touch on a finished work. The English keeps the image as “the finishing touch”.
notes.other_reading: has laid the last hand on his life

notes.note: “Indigentia” picks up “indiget” just before, and “need” is used for both. “This need” is the need for more time, which the man just described does not have and everyone else does.
notes.other_reading: but from this want

notes.note: “Futuri” (“of the future”) is taken with the craving only, as the word order suggests, and “exedens” (“eating away”) with the craving too. “Futuri” could also depend on “timor”, and “exedens” could be felt with the fear as well. “Animus” is “mind” as in the glossary.
notes.other_reading: fear of the future and a craving for it, which eat away the mind

notes.note: “Venientium” is “of things that are coming”, taken as events, not persons. “Quorsus evadant” is literally “in what direction they will come out”, given as “where they will end up”.
notes.other_reading: than uncertainty about how what is coming will turn out

notes.latin: quantum sitillud quod restat aut quale
notes.note: Read as “quantum sit illud”. The two indirect questions have no governing verb of their own; the English hangs them on “sollicita” (“anxious about”). They could depend loosely on the whole clause.
notes.other_reading: How much is left, and of what kind: over this the anxious mind is driven about

notes.note: “Inexplicabilis” is literally “that cannot be unfolded or disentangled”; it can also mean “from which there is no way out” or “that cannot be explained”. The English keeps the image of something knotted and names no one who fails to untangle it.
notes.other_reading: by a dread that has no way out

check.note: “Futuri” can depend on both nouns (fear of the future and craving for it), while the draft tied it to the craving only. In the draft “that eats away” could also be read with “the future”, though “exedens” goes with “cupiditas”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “fear is born, and a craving for the future, one that eats away the mind”, so that the eating away can only belong to the craving. “Of the future” stays with the craving alone, as the Latin word order has it (fear, then the verb, then craving for the future), and a note records the other reading.

check.note: “Inexplicabilis” is “that cannot be unravelled” or “from which there is no way out”, and could be heard as “that cannot be explained”. The draft picked the first and added the mind as the one who cannot untangle it.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “by a fear that cannot be untangled”. The Latin adjective names no one who fails to untangle the fear, and the note records the other senses.

check.note: The square brackets mark a word the edition deletes, and the draft follows the deletion, which is the reading that construes. No change is asked for.
check.decided: Accepted: The English is unchanged, “that some part of it is put off”, and the note on the bracketed word records that the deletion is followed.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft had “come” for “nascitur”, which is “is born”; the image is easy to keep.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “fear is born”.

check.note: Found while settling: “where the things that are coming will end” could be taken as when they will stop, while “quorsus evadant” asks which way they will come out.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “where the things that are coming will end up”.

passages.latin: Ideo propera, Lucili mi, vivere, et singulos dies singulas vitas puta. Qui hoc modo se aptavit, cui vita sua cotidie fuit tota, securus est: inspem viventibus proximum quodque tempus elabitur, subitque aviditas et miserrimus ac miserrima omnia efficiens metus mortis. Inde illud Maecenatis turpissimum votum quo et debilitatem non recusat et deformitatem et novissime acutam crucem, dummodo inter haec mala spiritus prorogetur:
passages.english: So hurry to live, my Lucilius, and count each single day as a single life. The man who has fitted himself in this way, for whom his life has been whole every day, is free from care. From those who live looking towards hope, each moment slips away as it comes nearest, and in come a greedy hunger and the fear of death, most wretched itself and making everything most wretched. Hence that most shameful prayer of Maecenas, in which he does not refuse crippling, or deformity, or last of all the sharp cross, provided that among these evils his breath is prolonged:

notes.note: The repeated “singulos” and “singulas” pair one day with one life each time. “Single” is repeated to keep the pairing.
notes.other_reading: think of each day as a separate life

notes.latin: cui vita sua cotidie fuit tota
notes.note: Literally “for whom his own life has every day been whole”. It can mean that each day’s life was complete, or that each day was his whole life; the English keeps the literal order, which leaves both open.
notes.other_reading: for whom each day has been his entire life

notes.note: The glossary gives “freedom from care” for “securitas”, so “securus” is “free from care”, not “safe”.
notes.other_reading: is secure

notes.note: Read as “in spem viventibus”, literally “those living into hope”, that is, with their life directed at what they hope for. The dative is taken with “elabitur”: time slips away from them.
notes.other_reading: for those who live on hope

notes.note: “Proximum quodque tempus” is “each nearest time”: either the moment immediately at hand or each next period as it arrives. The English reads “each moment as it comes nearest”, which narrows “tempus” (“time”) to “moment”.
notes.other_reading: each next stretch of time slips away

notes.note: “Subit” is “comes up from below, steals in”, often “takes the place of”. “Aviditas” is greedy wanting with no object stated; from the context it is hunger for more time or more life, and “greed” alone would suggest money.
notes.other_reading: and greed for life takes its place

notes.latin: miserrimus ac miserrima omnia efficiens metus mortis
notes.note: The Latin repeats the same superlative: the fear of death is “most wretched” and makes all things “most wretched”. The English repeats the word.
notes.other_reading: the fear of death, the most miserable of things and the thing that makes everything else most miserable

notes.note: Maecenas was the friend of Augustus and patron of poets, who also wrote verse himself. “Votum” is a prayer or vow; the verses that the colon introduces follow in the next section of the letter and are not part of this passage.
notes.other_reading: that most disgraceful wish of Maecenas

notes.note: “Crux” is the instrument of execution, whether a cross with a beam or a single stake, and “acuta” is “sharp, pointed”. A pointed stake on which a man is set may be meant (the verses that follow in the letter speak of sitting on it: from memory, unchecked). The English keeps the literal words.
notes.other_reading: the pointed stake

notes.note: “Spiritus” is breath, and so life; “prorogare” is the official word for extending a term of office or a deadline. The English keeps “breath” and adds nothing to it.
notes.other_reading: provided his life is given an extension

check.note: Read “in spem viventibus”. At the head of the sentence “For” reads as “because”, but the Latin has only a dative; and “live for hope” is unclear, since “in spem” is living with one’s eyes on what is hoped for.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “From those who live looking towards hope”. The dative goes with “slips away”, and “looking towards” gives the direction in “in spem” without the false “because”.

check.note: “Each nearest stretch of time” is hard to follow. The Latin means each moment in turn as it becomes the nearest one.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “each moment slips away as it comes nearest”. A note records that “tempus” is “time” in general and that “moment” narrows it.

check.note: “Aviditas” here is greedy wanting of more time or life. To a reader of today “greed” suggests money.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “a greedy hunger”, which keeps the greed and turns it away from money. “For more” is not added, because the Latin gives “aviditas” no object; the note says what the hunger is for.

check.note: “Crux” can be any stake of execution, and “acuta” (“pointed”) suggests a stake for impaling. “The sharp cross” is literal but puzzling, and the other reading should be weighed.
check.decided: Declined: The English keeps “the sharp cross”. “Crux” is the Latin’s own word and covers both a cross and a stake, so “stake” would settle in the text what the Latin leaves to its context; the note gives “the pointed stake” as the other reading.

check.note: “Prorogare” is to prolong or extend a term. “Breath drawn out” suggests one long breath, and “longer” is added.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “his breath is prolonged”, with “longer” removed. “Of life” is not added, since the Latin has only “spiritus”, “breath”; the note says that breath stands for life.

passages.latin: Negas me epistula prima totam quaestionem explicuisse in qua probareconabar id quod nostris placet, claritatem quae post mortem contingit bonumesse. Id enim me non solvisse quod opponitur nobis: 'nullum' inquiunt 'bonumex distantibus; hoc autem ex distantibus constat'.
passages.english: You say that in my earlier letter I did not work through the whole inquiry in which I was trying to prove what our school holds: that the renown which comes after death is a good. For, you say, I did not resolve the objection that is made against us: “No good,” they say, “is made up of things that stand apart; but this one is made up of things that stand apart.”

notes.note: Literally “in the first letter”. It is taken as the first of the letters on this question, that is, the earlier one, so that a reader does not think of the first letter of the collection; the passage does not say which letter is meant.
notes.other_reading: in the first letter

notes.latin: totam quaestionem explicuisse in qua probareconabar
notes.note: Read as “probare conabar”. “In qua” (“in which”) can refer to “quaestionem”, the nearer word, or to “epistula”. The English takes the nearer word and gives “quaestio” as “inquiry”, since one proves something in an inquiry, not in a question.
notes.other_reading: in my earlier letter, in which I was trying to prove what our school holds, I did not work through the whole question

notes.note: “Nostris” is the dative of the word for those on one’s own side, here the Stoics. “Placet” is the regular word for a school’s settled doctrine.
notes.other_reading: the view that our people accept

notes.note: Later sections of this letter set “claritas” apart from “fama” and “gloria”, so the three need three English words: “renown” for “claritas” throughout, “fame” for “fama” and “glory” for “gloria”.
notes.other_reading: distinction

notes.note: Read as “bonum esse”. The question is whether renown counts as “a good” in the Stoic sense, so the English has “a good”, not “good”.
notes.other_reading: is good

notes.latin: Id enim me non solvisse quod opponitur nobis
notes.note: The accusative and infinitive carries on what Lucilius says, so “you say” is repeated in the English though the Latin does not repeat it. “Solvere” is to untie a knot, and so to resolve an objection.
notes.other_reading: For the knot that is put in the way has not, you say, been untied

notes.note: “Ex distantibus” is a Stoic technical phrase for a whole whose members are physically separate, such as an army or a people (from memory, unchecked). The first clause has no verb in the Latin; “is made up” is supplied from the second, and the same rendering of “constat” returns in section 17 of this letter.
notes.other_reading: consists of separate things

check.note: “Prima” can mean the earlier letter on this question rather than the first of all. “First letter” makes a reader think of Letter 1 of the collection, and the possessive is added.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “earlier letter”. The letter meant is the first of those on this question, not the first of the collection; the possessive stays because English needs it where the Latin’s subject already shows whose letter it is. The note gives the literal “first”.

check.note: “In qua” can refer to “epistula” as easily as to “quaestionem”. The draft attached it to the question, which reads oddly, since one does not prove something in a question.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “the whole inquiry in which”, with no comma. “In qua” is left with “quaestionem”, the nearer word, and “quaestio” is given as “inquiry” so that the clause reads naturally; a note records that the letter may be meant instead.

check.note: “You say” is not repeated in the Latin; the accusative and infinitive simply continue the reported speech. The addition is fair and no change is asked for.
check.decided: Accepted: The English is unchanged and keeps the second “you say”, which shows that the reported speech goes on. The note on these words records that the Latin does not repeat it.

passages.latin: Fama vocem utique desiderat, claritas potest etiam citra vocem contingerecontenta iudicio; plena est non tantum inter tacentis sed etiam inter reclamantis.Quid intersit inter claritatem et gloriam dicam: gloria multorum iudicisconstat, claritas bonorum.
passages.english: Fame in any case needs a voice; renown can come even without a voice, content with a judgment. It is complete not only among people who are silent but even among people who cry out against it. I will say what the difference is between renown and glory: glory is made up of the judgments of the many, renown of the judgments of the good.

notes.note: “Fama” is what is said about someone, talk, and is related to the Latin verb for speaking; that is why it needs a voice. “Utique” is a word of necessity, “in any case, without exception”, not of time.
notes.other_reading: Talk about a man necessarily requires speech

notes.note: “Citra” is literally “on this side of”, that is, stopping short of. The English gives it as “without”.
notes.other_reading: even short of any utterance

notes.note: “Iudicium” is “judgment” as in the glossary: here a verdict held in the mind, even if it is never spoken. The Latin does not say whose judgment.
notes.other_reading: satisfied with a favourable opinion

notes.note: “Plena” is literally “full”, taken as “complete, lacking nothing”.
notes.other_reading: it is at its full

notes.note: “Reclamantis” (accusative plural) is “those who shout back, cry out in protest”. The Latin gives no object; “against it” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: even among those who shout in opposition

notes.note: Read as “iudiciis constat”: as printed, “iudicis” looks like “of a judge”, but the ablative plural of “iudicium” is needed. “Multorum” is “of many people”, given as “the many” because it is set against “the good”. “Constat” is “is made up of”, as in section 3 of this letter, where the objection turns on what a good is made up of.
notes.other_reading: glory rests on the judgments of many people

notes.note: “Bonorum” is “of good men”, persons, not “of good things”. “Judgments” is repeated in the English where the Latin leaves it understood.
notes.other_reading: renown on those of good men

check.note: “Utique” is “in any case, necessarily”, not a word of time. The same word is “at any rate” in 102.18.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “Fame in any case needs a voice”. “Always” is gone because “utique” is a word of necessity, not of time; “must” is not added, since “desiderat” is simply “needs”.

check.note: Bare “judgment” is unclear in English. The point is that renown is satisfied with an opinion held, even if it is never spoken.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “content with a judgment”. The article shows that a verdict held by someone is meant, not the faculty of judging.

check.note: In 102.3 of the same letter “constat” is “is made up of”, and the objection there turns on what renown is made up of. Here the same verb became “rests on”, which loses the link.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “glory is made up of the judgments of the many, renown of the judgments of the good”. The link is restored with the very words used in section 3, where “consists in” would still have been a different phrase.

check.note: As printed, “iudicis” looks like “of a judge”. It must be read as “iudiciis”, and the draft reads it so.
check.decided: Accepted: The English is unchanged in reading “the judgments of the many”, and the note on these words now says that “iudicis” is read as “iudiciis”.

passages.latin: 'Cuius' inquit 'bonum est claritas, id est laus bono a bonis reddita?utrum laudati an laudantis?' Utriusque. Meum, qui laudor; quia natura meamantem omnium genuit, et bene fecisse gaudeo et gratos me invenisse virtutuminterpretes laetor. Hoc plurium bonum est quod grati sunt, sed et meum;ita enim animo compositus sum ut aliorum bonum meum iudicem, utique eorumquibus ipse sum boni causa.
passages.english: “Whose good,” he says, “is renown, that is, praise rendered to a good man by good men? Is it the good of the one praised or of the one praising?” Of both. It is mine, as the one who is praised: because nature bore me as someone who loves all people, I both rejoice to have done good and am glad to have found grateful interpreters of the virtues. That they are grateful is a good of several people, but it is mine too. For my mind is so made that I judge the good of others to be mine, at any rate the good of those for whom I am myself the cause of the good.

notes.note: “He says”: an imagined objector, in the singular, and the English keeps the singular.
notes.other_reading: someone says

notes.note: “Reddita” is “rendered, paid as something due”, which looks ahead to the argument in the next section about justice paying what is owed.
notes.other_reading: praise given to a good man by good men

notes.note: Read as “me amantem”. The “because” clause is taken with what follows (the copy has a semicolon before it); it could go with the words before it. “Omnium” can be “of all people” or “of all things”, and the argument that the good of others is one’s own points to people.
notes.other_reading: because nature bore me as a lover of all things

notes.note: “Bene fecisse” can be “to have acted well” or “to have done a kindness”. The gratitude that follows points to the second, and “done good” leaves both audible.
notes.other_reading: to have acted well

notes.note: Read as “virtutum interpretes”; the Latin has only “of virtues”, with no word for whose. An “interpres” is one who explains or reads the meaning of a thing, here people who read virtuous acts rightly. “Judges” is not used, because “judge” is kept for “iudicare” in this letter.
notes.other_reading: to have found people who gratefully understand my virtues

notes.latin: Hoc plurium bonum est quod grati sunt
notes.note: “Plurium” is “of several, of more than one”: the gratitude is a good belonging to a number of people. It could also be pressed to “of the majority”.
notes.other_reading: This, their being grateful, is the good of the greater number

notes.note: Literally “for in mind I am so put together”. The English makes the mind the subject for the sake of natural English; “animus” is “mind” as in the glossary.
notes.other_reading: for such is the disposition of my mind

notes.note: “Boni causa” is taken as “the cause of (their) good”, with “causa” nominative. In other contexts “boni causa” could mean “for the sake of good”, which does not fit the dative here.
notes.other_reading: those whose good has its source in me

check.note: “Reddita” is “paid” or “rendered” as something due. “Given” loses that, and the idea of paying what is owed returns in 102.19.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “praise rendered to a good man by good men”. “Rendered” keeps the sense of something due, which the next section takes up when justice pays what is owed.

check.note: The draft’s wording for these words, with a relative clause hung on “mine”, is archaic English.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “It is mine, as the one who is praised”, which says the same in English of today.

check.note: “Omnium” can be “of all people” or “of all things”. The draft left it open, and “a lover of all” is stiff; the argument points to people.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “someone who loves all people”. The argument that follows is about the good of other people, and the note records “all things” as the other reading.

check.note: The Latin has “virtutum” without a possessive; it may mean the speaker’s virtues or virtues in general. “Interpreters” copies the Latin word; “interpretes” here are people who understand and judge virtue.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “grateful interpreters of the virtues”, with the possessive removed because the Latin has none. “Interpreters” stays: “judges” would bring in the word kept in this letter for “iudicare”, and an interpreter in English is still one who reads a thing’s meaning.

check.note: The draft’s “so made in mind” is not natural English.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “For my mind is so made that”. The mind becomes the subject, to the same effect as the suggestion, and the note gives the literal order.

check.note: Found while settling: “made” for “genuit” drops the picture of birth; the word is “begot, bore”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now has “bore” where it had “made”.

passages.latin: Est istud laudantium bonum; virtute enimgeritur; omnis autem virtutis actio bonum est. Hoc contingere illis nonpotuisset nisi ego talis essem. Itaque utriusque bonum est merito laudari,tam mehercules quam bene iudicasse iudicantis bonum est et eius secundumquem iudicatum est. Numquid dubitas quin iustitia et habentis bonum sitet autem sit eius cui debitum solvit? Merentem laudare iustitia est; ergoutriusque bonum est.
passages.english: That is a good of those who praise, for it is done by virtue, and every act of virtue is a good. This could not have come to them unless I were such a man. So to be praised deservedly is a good of both, just as much, by Hercules, as to have judged well is a good of the one who judges and of the one in whose favour judgment was given. Surely you do not doubt that justice is both a good of the one who has it and also a good of the one to whom it pays what is owed? To praise one who deserves it is justice; therefore it is a good of both.

notes.note: “Istud”, “that”, is the praising, or the gratitude just spoken of; this sentence takes the praisers’ side after the last section took the side of the one praised.
notes.other_reading: It is the praisers’ good as well

notes.note: Read as “enim geritur”. “Geritur” is “is carried on, performed”; “virtute” is ablative of means.
notes.other_reading: for it is an action carried out through virtue

notes.note: “Talis”, “of such a kind”, means a man who deserves the praise. The Latin leaves that unstated and so does the English.
notes.other_reading: if I were not the kind of man I am

notes.note: “Merito” is taken as the adverb “deservedly”. It could be felt as “for a merit”.
notes.other_reading: to be praised for what one has deserved

notes.note: An everyday oath by Hercules, used for emphasis. The name of the god is kept, as the translator’s brief asks for the names of gods.
notes.other_reading: just as surely as

notes.note: Read as “secundum quem”. This is the courtroom idiom for a verdict given in someone’s favour.
notes.other_reading: the one on whose side the verdict went

notes.note: “Numquid” marks a question that expects the answer no, given as “Surely you do not doubt”.
notes.other_reading: Do you doubt at all

notes.note: Read as “sit et autem sit”. The Latin as given does not construe naturally: “autem” cannot follow “et” in this way, and the text is likely faulty here. The English gives the sense, which is not in doubt, as “both” and “and also”, with no separate weight on “autem”.
notes.other_reading: is a good of the one who has it and, on the other hand, is a good of the one

check.note: “Et autem” does not construe naturally: “autem” cannot follow “et” in this way. The draft smooths it to “and also”; the sense is not in doubt, but the fault in the Latin as given should be recorded.
check.decided: Accepted: The English is unchanged, as suggested, and the note on these words now says plainly that the Latin as given does not construe and that “autem” is suspect.

check.note: “By Hercules” is literal and correct, but in plain English of today the oath reads as period costume.
check.decided: Declined: The English keeps “by Hercules”. The Latin names the god, and the translator’s brief keeps the names of gods as they are; a bare oath would drop him.

passages.latin: Dic potius quam naturale sit in immensum mentem suam extendere.Magna et generosa res est humanus animus; nullos sibi poni nisi communeset cum deo terminos patitur. Primum humilem non accipit patriam, Ephesumaut Alexandriam aut si quod est etiamnunc frequentius accolis laetiusvetectis solum: patria est illi quodcumque suprema et universa circuitu suocingit, hoc omne convexum intra quod iacent maria cum terris, intra quodaer humanis divina secernens etiam coniungit, in quo disposita tot numinain actus suos excubant.
passages.english: Say rather how natural it is to stretch one’s mind out into what has no measure. The human soul is a great and noble thing. It lets no boundaries be set for it except those it shares with god as well. First, it does not accept a lowly homeland, Ephesus or Alexandria or any ground there may be that is still more crowded with inhabitants or richer in buildings. Its homeland is whatever encloses the highest things and the whole of things in its circuit: this entire vault within which the seas and the lands lie, within which the air, while it separates the divine from the human, also joins them, in which so many divine powers are posted and stand watch, ready for their own work.

notes.note: A singular imperative, “say rather”, set against the quibbling arguments dismissed in the section before. The English keeps it as a command to the one addressed.
notes.other_reading: Speak instead of

notes.note: The glossary gives “mind” for “animus” and allows “soul” where it is set against the body as what survives. That is the case here: in the next section this “animus” leaves the body and returns to the gods. “Mind” is kept for “mens” in the sentence before, so the two Latin words stay apart.
notes.other_reading: The human mind

notes.note: “Generosus” is “of good birth, noble”, not “generous” in the modern sense.
notes.other_reading: high-born

notes.latin: nullos sibi poni nisi communeset cum deo terminos patitur
notes.note: Read as “communes et cum deo”. “Et” is “also”: the only boundaries it accepts are ones that god has too. “Terminos” is the boundary mark again, as in Ep. 101.7.
notes.other_reading: it allows no limits to be set for it other than those common to it and to god

notes.note: “Humilis” is literally “low, near the ground”, and so “humble”. Both senses work here, since the true homeland turns out to be the sky; “lowly” keeps both.
notes.other_reading: it does not accept a homeland down on the ground

notes.note: Read as “laetiusve tectis”. “Accolae” are those who live in or near a place; “tecta” are literally roofs, and so houses or buildings; “laetius” is “more flourishing, richer”. Ephesus and Alexandria stand for the great crowded cities of the day.
notes.other_reading: any soil more thickly settled or more richly roofed

notes.latin: quodcumque suprema et universa circuitu suocingit
notes.note: Read as “suo cingit”. Because the verb is singular, “quodcumque” is taken as its subject and “suprema et universa” as its objects: the homeland is the outermost thing that goes round everything. The forms would also allow “suprema et universa” as subject, but the verb does not agree with that.
notes.other_reading: whatever the highest and the whole enclose in their circuit

notes.note: The air lies between earth and heaven, so it both divides and links them. “Humanis” is taken as ablative, “from human things”.
notes.other_reading: the air, which parts things divine from things human, yet also unites them

notes.latin: disposita tot numinain actus suos excubant
notes.note: Read as “numina in actus suos”. “Numina”, divine powers, probably means the stars and planets. “Disposita” and “excubant” are military words (posted, keeping night watch); “in actus suos” with the accusative is “towards, for their own actions”, so the powers stand ready for their work and the work is not the thing guarded.
notes.other_reading: stand watch over their own tasks

check.note: “Mentem” in the sentence before and “animus” here were both “mind”. This “animus” is what in 102.22 leaves the body and returns to the gods, so “mind” is narrow for it and the two Latin words were merged.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “The human soul is a great and noble thing”. The glossary allows “soul” for “animus” where it is set against the body as what survives, which is what the next section does; “mind” stays for “mens”.

check.note: Read “communes et cum deo”. “Et” is “also”: boundaries that it has in common with god too. “Even” adds a note of surprise.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “except those it shares with god as well”. “Et” here is a plain “also”, and the surprise that “even” brought in is gone.

check.note: Read “laetiusve tectis”. “Tecta” are buildings or houses and “laetius” is “more flourishing”; “covered” was added and “roofs” is too literal.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “or richer in buildings”. “Covered” had no word in the Latin, and “tecta” is the ordinary word for houses; the note gives the literal “roofs”.

check.note: “In actus suos” with the accusative is “for” or “ready for” their own operations. “Watch over their tasks” made the tasks the thing guarded.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “are posted and stand watch, ready for their own work”. “Each” is left out, since the Latin has only “suos”, “their own”.

passages.latin: Deinde artam aetatem sibi dari non sinit: 'omnes' inquit 'anni mei sunt; nullum saeculum magnis ingeniis clusum est, nullum non cogitationi pervium tempus. Cum venerit dies ille qui mixtum hoc divini humanique secernat, corpus hic ubi inveni relinquam, ipse mediis reddam. Nec nunc sine illis sum, sed gravi terrenoque detineor.'
passages.english: Next, it does not let a narrow span of life be given to it. “All the years are mine,” it says. “No age is closed to great intellects, and there is no time that is not open to thought. When that day comes which is to separate this mixture of the divine and the human, I will leave the body here where I found it, and myself I will give back to the gods. Even now I am not without them, but I am held back by what is heavy and earthly.”

notes.note: “Aetas” is a lifetime or a period of time; “artam” is “tight, narrow”. This answers the “lowly homeland” of the section before: first no narrow place, now no narrow time.
notes.other_reading: a cramped stretch of time

notes.note: The speaker is the human soul (“animus”) of the section before, so the English has “it says”.
notes.other_reading: he says

notes.note: “Ingenium” is inborn talent or intellect. “Minds” is avoided because “mind” is this project’s word for “mens” and, elsewhere, for “animus”.
notes.other_reading: to great minds

notes.note: A double negative, “no time not passable to thought”, and the English keeps the two negatives. “Pervius” is “that can be travelled through”.
notes.other_reading: every time can be travelled by thought

notes.latin: qui mixtum hoc divini humanique secernat
notes.note: The subjunctive “secernat” gives the day its purpose or character, “which is to separate”. “Secernat” picks up “secernens” in the section before, and “separate” is used in both.
notes.other_reading: the day that will part this blend of divine and human

notes.note: As printed, “mediis” would mean “to the middle things”, which gives no good sense and leaves “reddam” without an object. The English reads “me diis” (“myself to the gods”), two words run together in the copy; the “them” of the next sentence then refers to the gods. “Ipse” sets the speaker against the body left behind, which is why “myself” comes first in its clause.
notes.other_reading: will give it back to those in between

notes.note: “Illis”, “them”, is the gods of the sentence before, on the reading taken there.
notes.other_reading: without those

notes.note: “Gravi terrenoque” are taken as neuter adjectives used as nouns, “what is heavy and earthly”. They could instead be felt with an unexpressed “body”.
notes.other_reading: held down by a heavy and earthly body

check.note: As printed, “mediis” is one word (“to the middle ones”), which gives no object for “reddam” and nothing for “illis” to refer to. It must be read as “me diis”, two words run together, as the draft reads it.
check.decided: Accepted: The English keeps this reading, “to the gods”, and the note on these words records the slip in the copy.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft passed over “ipse”, which sets the speaker’s self against the body just mentioned.
check.decided: Accepted: The clause now begins with “and myself”, so that the self is set against the body as “ipse” sets it.

passages.latin: Quid ista circumspicis quae tibi possunt fortasse evenire sed possuntet non evenire? Incendium dico, ruinam, alia quae nobis incidunt, non insidiantur:illa potius vide, illa [vide] vita [illa] quae nos observant, quae captant.Rari sunt casus, etiamsi graves, naufragium facere, vehiculo everti: abhomine homini cotidianum periculum. Adversus hoc te expedi, hoc intentisoculis intuere; nullum est malum frequentius, nullum pertinacius, nullumblandius.
passages.english: Why do you look about for those things that can perhaps happen to you but can also not happen? I mean fire, the collapse of a building, other things that fall on us but do not lie in wait for us. Look rather at those, avoid those: the things that watch us, that try to catch us. Being shipwrecked, being overturned in a carriage: these are rare accidents, even if serious ones; from man to man the danger is daily. Make yourself ready against this, and keep your eyes fixed on this. No evil is more frequent, none more persistent, none more ingratiating.

notes.note: “Circumspicere” is to look around on all sides, here anxiously, for dangers that may or may not come. “Look about for” keeps both the looking round and the fact that the things are not yet present.
notes.other_reading: Why do you keep an anxious watch for

notes.note: “Ruina” is a fall or collapse, in this context the collapse of a building. The Latin says only “collapse”; “of a building” narrows it.
notes.other_reading: a collapse

notes.note: A play of sound and sense: “incidunt” (fall upon, befall) against “insidiantur” (lie in ambush). The English keeps the two images and loses the echo.
notes.other_reading: things that befall us but do not plot against us

notes.latin: illa potius vide, illa [vide] vita [illa] quae nos observant
notes.note: The square brackets mark words the edition deletes. The English follows the text without them: “illa potius vide, illa vita”, “look rather at those, avoid those”. With the bracketed words the sentence repeats itself and does not run; the text is disturbed here and another restoration is possible.
notes.other_reading: look rather at those, look at those, avoid those that watch us

notes.note: “Captare” is to try to catch, as a hunter or a trapper does.
notes.other_reading: that hunt us

notes.note: An idiom: “to make shipwreck” means to suffer one, not to cause one.
notes.other_reading: to be wrecked at sea

notes.note: Read as “ab homine homini”. There is no verb in the Latin; “is” is supplied. “Homo” is a human being, not a male; “man” keeps the short form of the saying.
notes.other_reading: the danger that comes to one human being from another is an everyday thing

notes.note: “Se expedire” is to free oneself of baggage and get ready for action, a soldier’s phrase.
notes.other_reading: strip for action against this

notes.note: “Blandus” is coaxing, caressing, winning one over: this evil comes with a friendly face. “Ingratiating” is used because “flattering” today mostly means “showing to advantage” and “smooth-tongued” would narrow it to speech.
notes.other_reading: none more coaxing

check.note: “Circumspicere” here is to look about for, to be on the watch for, things that may or may not come. “Look around at” suggests they are already present.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “Why do you look about for those things”. “For” shows that the things are not yet present; “keep” is not added, since the Latin verb is a plain present.

check.note: The brackets mark words the edition deletes, leaving “illa potius vide, illa vita quae”. The draft follows that reading but adds “and”, and its word order is heavy.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “Look rather at those, avoid those:” and then gives the two relative clauses side by side with no “and”, as the Latin has them. “Those” is kept for “illa”, which points away from the speaker, where the suggestion had “these”.

check.note: “Blandus” is coaxing, smooth, winning one over. Today “more flattering” mostly means “showing one to better advantage”, which is not the sense.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “none more ingratiating”. “Flattering” is gone for the reason given; “smooth-tongued” is not used because “blandus” covers manner and looks as well as speech.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft added “such as” and gave “everti” as “thrown from”; the Latin sets the two infinitives beside “casus”, and “everti” is “to be overturned”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “Being shipwrecked, being overturned in a carriage: these are rare accidents, even if serious ones”.

check.note: Found while settling: “the other things” implies a fixed list, where “alia” is simply “other things”.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “other things” with no article and no added “and” before it.

passages.latin: Tu tamenita cogita quod ex homine periculum sit ut cogites quod sit hominis officium;alterum intuere ne laedaris, alterum ne laedas. Commodis omnium laeteris,movearis incommodis, et memineris quae praestare debeas, quae cavere.
passages.english: For your part, however, think about what danger comes from man in such a way that you think about what the duty of man is. Keep your eyes on the one so that you are not harmed, on the other so that you do not harm. Be glad when things go well for anyone, be moved when they go badly, and remember what you ought to fulfil and what you ought to guard against.

notes.note: “Tamen”, “however”, answers the section before, which says that people take pleasure in destroying one another. “Tu” is emphatic, given as “for your part”.
notes.other_reading: Even so, you

notes.note: “Quod” can be “what” (an indirect question, “what danger there is from man”) or “that” (“that there is danger from man”). It is taken as “what”, parallel to “what the duty of man is” in the next clause.
notes.other_reading: think that there is danger from man

notes.note: “Officium” is duty, what it is fitting for someone to do; “hominis” is “of a human being”, the same word as in “danger from man”. “Man” is kept in both so that the pairing shows.
notes.other_reading: what a human being’s proper part is

notes.latin: alterum intuere ne laedaris, alterum ne laedas
notes.note: “The one” is the danger and “the other” is the duty. “Intuere” is the verb of Ep. 103.1 (“keep your eyes fixed on”), so “keep your eyes on” is used here. “Laedere” appears in the passive and then the active, with “harm” for both.
notes.other_reading: look to the first so as not to be injured, to the second so as not to injure

notes.note: “Commodis” and “incommodis” are a matched pair in Latin, things that suit and things that do not; the English keeps a matched pair with “go well” and “go badly”. “Omnium”, “of all”, is given as “anyone”, each person whoever it is. The verbs are subjunctives used as mild commands.
notes.other_reading: Be glad at the advantages of all, be moved by their disadvantages

notes.note: “Praestare” ranges over “provide, perform, make good, answer for”; “fulfil” is used as the plain word for a duty owed. “Cavere” is to beware of or guard against: it may mean what must not be done to others or what one must protect oneself from, and the Latin does not say which.
notes.other_reading: what you owe to others and what you must beware of from them

check.note: “Commoda” and “incommoda” here are people’s good fortune and their troubles. “Advantages” and “disadvantages” are the wrong register and make the sentence unclear.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “Be glad when things go well for anyone, be moved when they go badly”. The stiff pair is gone, but “go well” and “go badly” keep a matched pair as the Latin has one, and “fortune” is avoided because it is this project’s word for “fortuna”, which is not in the passage.

check.note: “Also” is not in the Latin. It is harmless and brings out the pairing of “ita” and “ut”, but it is added.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “in such a way that you think about what the duty of man is”. “Also” had no word in the Latin, and “in such a way that” already carries the pairing.

check.note: The same imperative in 103.1 of this letter is “keep your eyes fixed on”. The verb is repeated on purpose, and “keep in view” weakened the echo.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “Keep your eyes on the one so that you are not harmed, on the other so that you do not harm”, so that the verb of 103.1 is heard again.

check.note: “Praestare” can be “provide”, but also “make good, perform, answer for” a duty owed. “Provide” is the narrower choice.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “what you ought to fulfil”. This is the sense of a duty owed and performed; “make good” is not used because in English of today it suggests repairing a loss.

check.note: Found while settling: “cogita” is an imperative, and the draft’s “should think” softened it to advice.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “For your part, however, think about what danger comes from man”; “for your part” gives the emphatic “tu”.

passages.latin: Sic vivendo quid consequaris? non te ne noceant, sed ne fallant. Quantumpotes autem in philosophiam recede: illa te sinu suo proteget, in huiussacrario eris aut tutus aut tutior. Non arietant inter se nisi in eademambulantes via.
passages.english: What would you gain by living this way? Not that they will not harm you, but that they will not deceive you. But withdraw into philosophy as far as you can: she will shelter you in her bosom, and in her shrine you will be either safe or safer. People do not ram into one another unless they are walking on the same road.

notes.note: A subjunctive of possibility, “what would you achieve”. It could also be read as a plain question about the result.
notes.other_reading: what do you get by living so?

notes.latin: non te ne noceant, sed ne fallant
notes.note: The Latin is compressed, and “te” sits oddly, since “noceant” would take a dative; it may belong by anticipation to “fallant”. The sense taken is: the gain is not that people will not harm you, but that they will not deceive you. “Fallant” can also mean “catch you unawares”.
notes.other_reading: Not that they will do you no harm, but that they will not take you by surprise

notes.note: “Sinus” is literally the fold of a garment over the chest, where something is held close and sheltered, and so “bosom” or “lap”. Philosophy is personified here (she has a bosom and a shrine), so the English has “she” and “her”, here and in the next section.
notes.other_reading: she will shelter you in the fold of her robe

notes.note: Read as “in huius sacrario”, “in the shrine of this one”, that is, philosophy’s. A “sacrarium” is a place where sacred things are kept.
notes.other_reading: in her sanctuary

notes.note: The same adjective appears in the plain and then the comparative form: “safe, or (at least) safer”. The English keeps the bare pairing without adding “at least”.
notes.other_reading: either safe or at any rate safer

notes.note: “Arietare” comes from “aries”, a ram: to butt, to crash into. “Ram into” keeps the animal in the verb. The Latin names no subject; “people” is supplied.
notes.other_reading: People do not knock into one another

check.note: “Fallere” is also “to catch off guard, to escape one’s notice”. After advice to keep one’s eyes on the danger, “that they do not take you unawares” is equally possible.
check.decided: Declined: The English keeps “deceive you”. That is the first sense of “fallere”, and it fits the warning in the section before against trusting the faces of the people one meets; the note gives “catch you unawares” as the other reading.

check.note: “Sinus” is the bosom, lap or fold. “Of her robe” is an explanation worked into the text.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “she will shelter you in her bosom”. The robe had no word in the Latin, and the note gives the literal fold of a garment.

check.note: “Arietare” is to butt like a ram. “Knock into” keeps the sense but loses the image.
check.decided: Partly accepted: The English now reads “People do not ram into one another”. “Ram” keeps the animal that the Latin verb is made from; “butt into” is not used because in English of today it means to interrupt.

passages.latin: Ipsam autem philosophiam non debebis iactare; multisfuit periculi causa insolenter tractata et contumaciter: tibi vitia detrahat,non aliis exprobret. Non abhorreat a publicis moribus nec hoc agat ut quidquidnon facit damnare videatur. Licet sapere sine pompa, sine invidia. Vale.
passages.english: But philosophy herself you must not show off. To many she has been a cause of danger when handled arrogantly and defiantly. Let her strip vices from you, not reproach others with theirs. Let her not be at odds with the ways of people at large, nor make it her business to seem to condemn whatever she does not do. One may be wise without parade, without ill will. Farewell.

notes.note: “Iactare” is literally to toss about, and so to flaunt or boast of something.
notes.other_reading: you must not boast of philosophy

notes.note: “Insolenter” is “arrogantly, immoderately”; “contumaciter” is “stubbornly, defiantly”, the manner of someone who will not bend to others. The participle “tractata” has no “when” in the Latin; it is supplied.
notes.other_reading: handled with insolence and obstinacy

notes.note: “Tibi” is the person from whom the vices are pulled away; “exprobrare” is to cast something in someone’s teeth. “With theirs” is supplied: the Latin says only “not reproach others”, with “vices” understood.
notes.other_reading: let it take away your faults, not throw other people’s in their faces

notes.note: “Abhorrere a” is literally to shrink back from, and so to be at odds with, out of keeping with. The second sense is taken, since the point is that philosophy should not stand apart from common ways. “Publici mores” are the ways of people in general.
notes.other_reading: Let her not shrink from the customs of the public

notes.latin: nec hoc agat ut quidquidnon facit damnare videatur
notes.note: Read as “quidquid non facit”. “Hoc agere ut” is “to make it one’s aim that”, and the English keeps the idea of aim. It could be weakened to a result, behaving so as to seem to condemn.
notes.other_reading: nor act in such a way that she seems to condemn everything she does not do

notes.note: “Pompa” is a public procession, and so show or display; “parade” keeps the picture.
notes.other_reading: without display

notes.note: “Invidia” can be the ill will one feels or the ill will one attracts. After the warning that philosophy has brought danger to many, ill will attracted is the likelier sense, but the Latin is bare and the English leaves it bare.
notes.other_reading: without malice

check.note: “Abhorrere a” is as often “be at odds with, be out of keeping with” as “shrink from”, which suggests fear or disgust. “Customs of the public” is also awkward.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “Let her not be at odds with the ways of people at large”. The point of the clause is that philosophy should not stand apart from common ways, and the note keeps “shrink from” as the other reading.

check.note: “Drawing” is added and settles “invidia” as ill will incurred from others. That is likely, but the Latin is bare; “and” is added too.
check.decided: Accepted: The English now reads “without parade, without ill will”, as bare as the Latin and without the added “and”. “Parade” stays for “pompa” because it keeps the picture of a procession; the note records both senses of “invidia”.

passages.latin: Indulgendum est enim honestisadfectibus; et interdum, etiam si premunt causae, spiritus in honorem suorumvel cum tormento revocandus et in ipso ore retinendus est, cum bono virovivendum sit non quamdiu iuvat sed quamdiu oportet: ille qui non uxorem,non amicum tanti putat ut diutius in vita commoretur, qui perseverabitmori, delicatus est. Hoc quoque imperet sibi animus, ubi utilitas suorumexigit, nec tantum si vult mori, sed si coepit, intermittat et suis commodet.
passages.english: For one must indulge honourable feelings; and sometimes, even if there are pressing reasons, the breath must be called back, even with torment, out of regard for one’s own people, and held back in the very mouth, since the good man must live not as long as it pleases him but as long as he ought. The man who thinks neither a wife nor a friend worth so much that he would stay longer in life, who will persist in dying, is soft. This too the mind should command of itself, when the interest of its own people demands it: not only if it wants to die but if it has begun to, it should pause and oblige its own people.

notes.note: Two words run together in the copy (honestis adfectibus). The glossary gives “passion” for adfectus, with “feeling” where no fault is implied; here they are called honourable, so the English reads “feelings”. The feeling meant is Seneca’s care for his wife Paulina, from the section before.
notes.other_reading: honourable passions

notes.note: The Latin does not say reasons for what. From what follows they are reasons for dying, such as age or illness. The English leaves this as open as the Latin.
notes.other_reading: even if there are pressing reasons to die

notes.note: Spiritus is breath, and so life. “Breath” is kept because the next words picture it as already in the mouth.
notes.other_reading: life

notes.note: Vel here is “even”. Tormentum is torture or severe pain; the pain is that of the one who goes on living.
notes.other_reading: even at the cost of suffering

notes.note: The image is of the last breath leaving through the mouth and being held back there. Os is “mouth”, and the English keeps it.
notes.other_reading: and held at the very lips

notes.note: Sui are a person’s own family and friends. The word comes three times in the section (suorum, suorum, suis) and “own people” is kept each time, even where the grammatical subject is the mind.
notes.other_reading: in honour of those who are his

notes.note: Delicatus is pampered, soft, fond of his own comfort. The point is that insisting on death can itself be a form of self-indulgence. “Soft” is also used for the same word at Ep. 107.2.
notes.other_reading: is self-indulgent

notes.note: Neither verb has an object in the Latin. The dying is taken to be what is paused. Commodare with a dative is to oblige or do a service to someone; it could also be “lend”, with “itself” understood.
notes.other_reading: let it break off and lend itself to its own people

check.note: The Latin is elliptical: the reasons are reasons for letting life go. “Reasons press” is not idiomatic English, and a reader cannot tell which reasons are meant.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “even if there are pressing reasons”. “To go” is not added, because the Latin does not say what the reasons are for; a note says that they are reasons for dying.

check.note: The repeated non is emphatic (not a wife, not a friend), and the English flattens it into a plain “or”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “who thinks neither a wife nor a friend worth so much that he would stay longer in life”, so that each of the two is denied in turn, as in the Latin.

check.note: Quoque goes with hoc, “this too”. In the English “also” floats and can be read as “the mind as well”, and the word order is awkward.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “This too the mind should command of itself”, so that “too” stands with “this”, where the Latin puts it.

check.note: The Latin verb is to interrupt or suspend for a time, and “break off” sounds like stopping for good. A small point.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “it should pause”. The Latin verb means to leave off for a time, and “break off” could be heard as stopping for good.

check.note: The Latin has no object. The verb can be “oblige, do a service to” or “lend itself”, and the English chooses the second; “its own people”, said of a mind, also reads oddly.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “oblige its own people”, the plain sense of the verb when it is used with a person, and “lend itself” moves to the note as the other reading. “Own people” stays, because it renders one Latin word used three times in the section.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft wrote “held at the very lips”, but the Latin has the mouth and a verb of holding back.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “held back in the very mouth”, which keeps the image as the Latin has it. “Lips” is recorded in the note.

passages.latin: Non multum ad hoc locus confert nisi se sibi praestat animus,qui secretum in occupationibus mediis si volet habebit: at ille qui regioneseligit et otium captat ubique quo distringatur inveniet. Nam Socraten querenticuidam quod nihil sibi peregrinationes profuissent respondisse ferunt,'non inmerito hoc tibi evenit; tecum enim peregrinabaris'.
passages.english: Place does not contribute much to this unless the mind puts itself at its own disposal; the mind will have seclusion in the midst of business if it wants it. But the man who picks out regions and chases after leisure will find everywhere something to pull him this way and that. For they say that Socrates, when someone complained that his travels had done him no good, answered: “This has happened to you, and not undeservedly, for you were travelling with yourself.”

notes.note: “This” points back to the end of the section before, where Seneca says he is beginning to study with his whole mind after leaving the city.
notes.other_reading: to this purpose

notes.note: Latin has no articles. The sentence is taken as a general remark about place, which the contrast with the man who picks out regions supports; it could also be said of the one place Seneca has just gone to.
notes.other_reading: The place does not contribute much to this

notes.note: Praestare se can mean to make oneself available, to show oneself, or to answer for oneself. The English takes it as the mind being present and available to itself.
notes.other_reading: unless the mind answers for itself to itself

notes.note: Secretum is a place or state apart: privacy, retreat, solitude.
notes.other_reading: a retreat

notes.note: Captare is to snatch at or hunt for. Otium is leisure, time free of business.
notes.other_reading: hunts for free time

notes.note: Distringere is to pull in different directions, and so to distract or keep busy. The English keeps the physical image without making it violent.
notes.other_reading: something to distract him

notes.note: A reported saying of Socrates. Seneca tells much the same story in an earlier letter on travel (Ep. 28, from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: is said to have replied

notes.note: Literally “you were travelling abroad with you”. The imperfect covers the whole time of the travels.
notes.other_reading: for you took yourself along on your travels

check.note: The Latin verb is to be pulled in different directions, kept busy, distracted. “Pull him apart” suggests being torn to pieces or breaking down, which is stronger than the Latin.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “to pull him this way and that”. This keeps the Latin image of being pulled in different directions, which “distract” would drop, without suggesting that the man is torn to pieces.

check.note: The phrase can also be read as “is present to itself” or “makes itself answer for itself”. The English choice is reasonable, but it is a choice.
check.decided: Declined: “puts itself at its own disposal” stands. The Latin phrase is regularly used of making oneself available to someone, so the draft’s choice is a fair reading, and the note records the other one.

check.note: With the article the English points to one particular place. The Latin is general: place as such.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Place does not contribute much to this”. The Latin speaks of place in general, as the contrast with the man who picks out regions shows, and “not much” keeps the Latin negative.

check.note: “It is not undeserved that this has happened to you” is a clumsy construction in English. The understatement can be kept more simply.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “This has happened to you, and not undeservedly”, which keeps the understatement of the Latin in plainer English.

passages.latin: At quanto ego de illis melius existimo! ipsi quoque haec possunt facere,sed nolunt. Denique quem umquam ista destituere temptantem? cui non facilioraapparuere in actu? Non quia difficilia sunt non audemus, sed quia non audemusdifficilia sunt.
passages.english: But how much better I think of them! They too can do these things, but they do not want to. And after all, whom have those things ever failed when he tried them? To whom have they not appeared easier in the doing? It is not because things are difficult that we do not dare; it is because we do not dare that they are difficult.

notes.note: “They” are the people of the section before, who say that what they cannot do cannot be done. Seneca thinks better of them than they do of themselves. “Opinion” is avoided, since the glossary keeps it for opinio.
notes.other_reading: how much higher an opinion I have of them

notes.note: Nolle is to be unwilling or to refuse. The English takes the milder sense.
notes.other_reading: but they refuse

notes.note: Destituere is here the short perfect (destituerunt), “have let down”, not an infinitive. Ista, “those things”, are the things said to be beyond human nature, toil and death from the section before. Denique before it is taken as “and after all”.
notes.other_reading: whom did those things ever leave in the lurch when he attempted them?

notes.note: Literally “in the act”, that is, once one is actually doing them.
notes.other_reading: in practice

notes.latin: Non quia difficilia sunt non audemus
notes.note: The sentence turns the same words round (difficult, not dare; not dare, difficult). The Latin has no noun and the English supplies “things”.
notes.other_reading: We do not fail to dare because they are hard; they are hard because we do not dare.

check.note: Haec and ista are both given as “these things”, though ista points to the things the objectors shrink from. Very small.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “whom have those things ever failed when he tried them?”, so that the two Latin pronouns are kept apart.

passages.latin: Si tamen exemplum desideratis, accipite Socraten, perpessiciumsenem, per omnia aspera iactatum, invictum tamen et paupertate, quam gravioremilli domestica onera faciebant, et laboribus, quos militares quoque pertulit. Quibus ille domi exercitus, sive uxorem eius moribus feram, lingua petulantem, sive liberos indociles et matri quam patri similiores +sivere+ aut in bellofuit aut in tyrannide aut in libertate bellis ac tyrannis saeviore.
passages.english: If, however, you people want an example, take Socrates, a long-suffering old man, tossed through every hardship, yet unconquered both by poverty, which his household burdens made heavier for him, and by toils, which he bore in military service as well. By these he was harassed at home, whether [one thinks of] his wife, with her savage ways and abusive tongue, or [of] his children, unteachable and more like their mother than their father; [the text is damaged here] he lived either in war or under tyranny or in a freedom crueller than wars and tyrants.

notes.note: Both verbs are plural. Seneca is speaking to the objectors of the section before, not to Lucilius alone. “People” is added only to show the plural, which English “you” cannot.
notes.other_reading: If, however, you want an example, take Socrates

notes.note: A rare word, from perpeti, to endure to the end: one who has borne much, or one who is inured to bearing.
notes.other_reading: an old man hardened to endurance

notes.note: Literally “which he bore military ones too”: among his toils were those of a soldier.
