notes.other_reading: including the toils of a soldier, which he also endured

notes.note: Quibus can be a linking relative (“by these”, the toils) or an exclamation (“by what things!”); the English takes the first. Exercitus is a participle, “harassed, kept hard at it”, perhaps with a glance at the military word just before. Latin often leaves out “was” with such a participle, and the English supplies it.
notes.other_reading: What trials he had at home!

notes.latin: sive uxorem eius moribus feram, lingua petulantem
notes.note: “Wife” and “children” are accusatives with no verb in the Latin as given, so the sentence does not construe. The words in square brackets, “one thinks of” and “of”, are supplied to carry them. The wife is Xanthippe.
notes.other_reading: whether his wife, wild in character and aggressive in speech

notes.note: The edition marks this word as corrupt, and the English marks the place in square brackets instead of translating it. It may hide the verb that governed “wife” and “children”, or a phrase setting public life against “at home”, or both. From memory, unchecked: editors have proposed supplements of both kinds, and none is certain.
notes.other_reading: if you judge truly, he lived either in war …

notes.note: Two words run together in the copy (in bello fuit). Literally “he was in war”, that is, his life fell in a time of war; the English writes “lived” so that it is not read as “he was fighting”.
notes.other_reading: he was either at war

notes.latin: in libertate bellis ac tyrannis saeviore
notes.note: The “freedom” is the restored democracy at Athens, which put Socrates to death, as the next section tells. Tyrannis here is “tyrants”, not “tyrannies”.
notes.other_reading: in a liberty more savage than wars and tyrants

check.note: Both verbs are plural: Seneca turns to the objectors, or to people in general, not to Lucilius. The English “you” will be read as Lucilius.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “If, however, you people want an example, take Socrates”. Both Latin verbs are plural, so the words are spoken to the objectors of the section before and not to Lucilius alone.

check.note: The word means one who has endured much. “Hardened to endurance” is odd English and says something a little different, toughened and not long-suffering.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a long-suffering old man”. The word is formed from the verb for enduring to the end and describes one who has borne much, which “long-suffering” says in ordinary English.

check.note: Exercitus is harassed, worn, kept hard at it, and “tried”, said of Socrates, suggests a court trial. The Latin is also a participle with no finite verb, and the English makes it a complete sentence.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “By these he was harassed at home”, since “tried” could suggest a court. It stays a full sentence, because Latin regularly leaves out “was” with such a participle and the damaged text that follows makes any closer join to the next clause uncertain.

check.note: The Latin is marked as corrupt here and does not construe: the two sive clauses have no verb, and the join to what follows is broken. The English fills the gap with a guess, a contrast with “at home”, and does not say that the text is damaged.
check.decided: Accepted: “[outside his home]” is removed and the English now reads “[the text is damaged here]” at that point. The Latin word is marked corrupt and cannot be translated, and the note says so.

check.note: The accusatives have no governing verb in the Latin as given, and “one thinks of” is the translator’s supplement. The brackets are also inconsistent: “of” before “his children” stands outside them.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “[one thinks of] his wife” and “[of] his children”, so that every supplied word is inside brackets. The note says that the two nouns have no verb in the Latin as given.

check.note: “Insolent in her tongue” is not idiomatic English. The Latin word is aggressive or abusive, where “insolent” suggests an inferior answering back.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “with her savage ways and abusive tongue”. “Abusive” replaces “insolent”, but “ways” is kept for moribus, which means character and habits and not temper, and “tongue” is kept because the Latin has it.

check.note: The Latin is “he lived in a time of war”. “He was at war” can be read as “he was personally fighting”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “he lived either in war or under tyranny”. The Latin places his life in a time of war and does not say that he was fighting.

passages.latin: Viginti et septem annis pugnatum est; post finita arma triginta tyrannisnoxae dedita est civitas, ex quibus plerique inimici erant. Novissime damnatioest sub gravissimis nominibus impleta: obiecta est et religionum violatioet iuventutis corruptela, quam inmittere in deos, in patres, in rem publicamdictus est. Post haec carcer et venenum. Haec usque eo animum Socratisnon moverant ut ne vultum quidem moverint. <O> illam mirabilem laudemet singularem! usque ad extremum nec hilariorem quisquam nec tristioremSocraten vidit; aequalis fuit in tanta inaequalitate fortunae.
passages.english: There was fighting for twenty-seven years. After the war was ended the city was given up to be harmed by thirty tyrants, most of whom were his enemies. Last of all, his condemnation was carried through under the gravest charges: he was accused both of violating religion and of corrupting the young, whom he was said to be letting loose against the gods, against their fathers, against the state. After this, prison and poison. So far had these things been from moving the mind of Socrates that they did not move even his face. What a wonderful and unique distinction that is! To the very end no one saw Socrates more cheerful or more gloomy; he was unvarying amid such great variation of fortune.

notes.latin: Viginti et septem annis pugnatum est
notes.note: Impersonal: “it was fought”. This is the Peloponnesian War between Athens and Sparta.
notes.other_reading: The war lasted twenty-seven years.

notes.note: Noxae dedere is a legal phrase: to surrender the one who did a wrong to the injured party. Noxa is also simply harm, and the English takes that plainer sense, since “for punishment” would imply that the city deserved it.
notes.other_reading: the city was surrendered to thirty tyrants for punishment

notes.note: These are the oligarchs who ruled Athens after its defeat, usually called the Thirty Tyrants or the Thirty. The Latin says only “thirty tyrants”.
notes.other_reading: to the Thirty Tyrants

notes.note: The Latin does not say whose enemies. “His” is supplied, since inimicus is a personal enemy and the passage is about Socrates. Plerique is “most”, and can also be “very many”.
notes.other_reading: very many of whom were hostile

notes.note: Nomina here are the heads or titles of a charge. Impleta is “filled up, completed”; it may mean that the condemnation crowned his troubles.
notes.other_reading: the measure was filled by his condemnation on the most serious counts

notes.note: By grammar quam could go with either noun, but by sense it is the youth that he is said to let loose against gods, fathers and state. Inmittere is to send against or let loose, as one sets a dog on someone.
notes.other_reading: a corruption which he was said to be letting loose on the gods

notes.note: The same verb, movere, is used of his mind and of his face. “Move” is kept for both.
notes.other_reading: they did not even change his expression

notes.note: The “O” is an editor’s addition, shown by the angle brackets; with or without it the phrase is an exclamation. Laus is praise, or the merit that earns it; the English takes the second, since what follows describes the merit itself.
notes.other_reading: What wonderful and singular praise that is!

notes.latin: aequalis fuit in tanta inaequalitate fortunae
notes.note: A play on aequalis and inaequalitas, “even” and “unevenness”. “Unvarying” and “variation” keep the echo in natural English.
notes.other_reading: he was even amid such great unevenness of fortune

check.note: The Latin is a legal phrase for surrendering someone to make good a wrong, and it can also be simply “handed over to be harmed”. “For punishment” implies that the city was paying a deserved penalty.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “given up to be harmed by thirty tyrants”. “For punishment” is dropped, since the Latin phrase need not mean a deserved penalty, and the legal sense is recorded in the note. “Thirty tyrants” now stands as the Latin has it, without the later title.

check.note: “His” is supplied: the Latin does not say whose enemies, though Socrates is the likely sense. Plerique can also be “very many” and not “most”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “most of whom were his enemies”, a relative clause as in the Latin. “His” stays without brackets, which this translation keeps for damaged text, because the Latin word means a personal enemy and the passage is about Socrates. The note says that “his” is supplied and that plerique can also be “very many”.

check.note: Quam can refer to the youth, as the English takes it, or to the corruption. “Setting on” is also not clear to a reader today.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “whom he was said to be letting loose against the gods, against their fathers, against the state”. “Letting loose” is clearer than “setting on” and keeps the Latin image of sending something against a target, which “inciting” would drop. The reading with “corruption” stays in the note.

check.note: Laus here may be merit or a title to glory, not praise spoken by someone, and “singular” is dated. The O before illam is an editor’s supplement and the sense does not depend on it.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “What a wonderful and unique distinction that is!”. “Distinction” takes the Latin word as the merit that earns praise, and “unique” replaces the dated “singular”. The exclamation is put in the English of today without “O”, which is an editor’s addition in any case.

passages.latin: Illud, ne timearis, praestabit tibi et fortunae mediocritaset ingeni lenitas: eum esse te homines sciant quem offendere sine periculopossint; reconciliatio tua et facilis sit et certa. Timeri autem tam domimolestum est quam foris, tam a servis quam a liberis: nulli non ad nocendumsatis virium est. Adice nunc quod qui timetur timet: nemo potuit terribilisesse secure.
passages.english: As for not being feared, both a middling fortune and a gentle disposition will secure that for you. Let people know that you are someone they can offend without danger; let reconciliation with you be both easy and sure. To be feared, on the other hand, is as troublesome at home as outside it, by slaves as much as by free men: there is no one who does not have strength enough to do harm. Add now that he who is feared fears: no one has been able to be terrifying and free from care.

notes.note: This is one item in a list. The section before deals with how to avoid being the object of others’ hopes, envy and hatred; this one turns to fear.
notes.other_reading: That other thing, that you not be feared

notes.note: Fortuna here is one’s means and standing. Mediocritas is a middle measure, with no slight intended.
notes.other_reading: a moderate station in life

notes.note: Offendere is to offend, cross or wrong someone. The danger is to the offender: Lucilius is to be known as one who does not take revenge.
notes.other_reading: whom they can cross without risk

notes.note: Literally “your reconciliation”. The English takes it as others winning back the good will of Lucilius after a quarrel; it could also be his own readiness to forgive.
notes.other_reading: let your forgiveness be easy and dependable

notes.latin: tam a servis quam a liberis
notes.note: Liberi can mean “free men” or “children”. Set against servis it is taken as “free men”, but with “at home” just before, “children” is possible.
notes.other_reading: by your slaves as much as by your children

notes.note: A double negative, “to no one is there not”. The English keeps the negative form.
notes.other_reading: everyone has strength enough to do harm

notes.note: Secure is “without care”, and can shade into “in safety”. The English follows the glossary’s “freedom from care” for securitas; the clause before, that he who is feared fears, points the same way.
notes.other_reading: no one has been able to inspire terror in safety

check.note: Autem marks the turn from not being feared to being feared (“but”, “now”). “Moreover” makes it an added point and not a contrast.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “To be feared, on the other hand, is as troublesome at home as outside it”. The Latin particle marks a turn from not being feared to being feared, not an added point.

check.note: The word can be “free men”, set against the slaves, or “children”, which would also fit “at home”. The English chooses “free men” and should record the other reading.
check.decided: Accepted: “free men” stays, as suggested, because the word is paired with “slaves”. The note records “children” as the other reading.

check.note: “To be feared from” someone is not English; the agent needs “by”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “by slaves as much as by free men”. The Latin names those who do the fearing, and English needs “by” for that.

check.note: “Has not strength” is archaic.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “there is no one who does not have strength enough to do harm”. The archaic “has not” is gone, but “enough” is kept, since the Latin has satis and the suggested wording dropped it.

check.note: The adverb can mean “without anxiety” or “in safety”. “Free from care” may be heard as “carefree”, which is lighter than the Latin.
check.decided: Declined: “free from care” stands. It is the glossary’s rendering of the related noun, and the clause before, “he who is feared fears”, shows that the adverb is about the feared man’s own fear. “In safety” is recorded in the note.

check.note: Found while settling: the Latin has et … et, “both … and”, and the draft gave only “and”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “both a middling fortune and a gentle disposition will secure that for you”, which keeps the Latin pairing.

passages.latin: Nihil horum insolitum, nihil inexpectatum est; offendirebus istis tam ridiculum est quam queri quod spargaris in publico aut inquineris in luto. Eadem vitae condicio est quaebalnei, turbae, itineris: quaedam in te mittentur, quaedam incident. Nonest delicata res vivere. Longam viam ingressus es: et labaris oportet etarietes et cadas et lasseris et exclames 'o mors!', id est mentiaris. Alioloco comitem relinques, alio efferes, alio timebis: per eiusmodi offensasemetiendum est confragosum hoc iter.
passages.english: None of these things is unusual, none is unexpected. To be jolted by such things is as ridiculous as to complain that you are splashed in public or dirtied in the mud. The terms of life are the same as those of a bathhouse, a crowd, a journey: some things will be thrown at you, some will fall on you. Living is not a soft business. You have set out on a long road: you are bound to slip, and knock into things, and fall, and grow tired, and cry out “O death!”, that is, tell a lie. In one place you will leave a companion behind, in another you will carry one out for burial, in another you will be afraid of one. Through jolts of this kind this rough journey has to be travelled to its end.

notes.note: “These things” are the troubles of the section before: the slaves of Lucilius ran away while he was busy.
notes.other_reading: Nothing of this kind

notes.note: Offendi is to be knocked against and so to be annoyed. The related noun offensas at the end of the section means knocks, stumbles or annoyances. “Jolted” and “jolts” are used so that the echo can be heard and so that the second fits the image of a rough road.
notes.other_reading: To be upset by such things … through upsets of this kind

notes.note: The next sentence names three settings (bathhouse, crowd, journey) while this one has only two complaints, so something may have dropped out. From memory, unchecked: later editions print a fuller text here, with splashing in the bath and jostling in public. The English translates what is given, with “in public” for in publico.
notes.other_reading: that you are splashed in the bath or jostled in public or dirtied in the mud

notes.latin: quaedam in te mittentur, quaedam incident
notes.note: The contrast is between things aimed at you and things that land on you by chance.
notes.other_reading: some things will be aimed at you, some will just happen to you

notes.note: Delicatus is soft, dainty, for the pampered. “Soft” is used as in Ep. 104.3.
notes.other_reading: Living is no dainty affair.

notes.note: Oportet with these verbs states what is bound to happen on such a road, not a duty.
notes.other_reading: you must slip

notes.note: A verb here, from arietare, to butt like a ram: to collide with things or people.
notes.other_reading: and stumble against things

notes.note: The cry “O death!” is a call for death to come. Seneca calls it a lie because the one who cries it does not really want to die.
notes.other_reading: and cry “Oh, for death!”, in other words, lie

notes.note: Efferre, “carry out”, is the usual Latin word for taking a body out to its funeral. The English keeps the carrying and adds “for burial” to make that plain.
notes.other_reading: in another you will bury one

notes.note: The verb has no object. “Companion” is carried through all three verbs (leave, carry out, fear). It could be a bare “you will be afraid”.
notes.other_reading: in another you will be afraid

check.note: Oportet with the subjunctive here states what is bound to happen, not a duty. “You must” can be read as an obligation.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “you are bound to slip, and knock into things, and fall”. The Latin states what cannot fail to happen on a long road, and “must” could be read as a duty.

check.note: The contrast seems to be between things aimed at you and things that simply happen to hit you. “Fall on you” is possible but blurs the point.
check.decided: Declined: “some will fall on you” stands. The Latin verb is literally “fall on”, and the Latin has no word answering to the suggested “just”. The contrast between what is aimed and what lands by chance is explained in the note.

check.note: “For burial” spells out what the Latin verb implies. It is within the meaning of the word, but it is an expansion.
check.decided: Declined: “carry one out for burial” stands. The Latin verb is literally “carry out” and is the set word for taking the dead to their funeral, so “bury” would drop the carrying, which the English keeps.

check.note: “Upsets” rightly echoes “upset” earlier in the section, but the Latin noun is also a physical knock or stumble, which carries on the image of the road. That sense is lost.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “To be jolted by such things” and “Through jolts of this kind”. One word serves for both Latin words and works both for a shock to the mind and for a knock on a rough road.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft wrote “in the street”, which is narrower than the Latin “in public”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “splashed in public”, which is what the Latin says and leaves room for the crowd named in the next sentence.

passages.latin: Nemo non fortius ad id cui se diu composuerat accessit et duris quoque, si praemeditata erant, obstitit: at contra inparatus etiam levissima expavit. Id agendum est ne quid nobis inopinatum sit; et quia omnia novitate graviorasunt, hoc cogitatio adsidua praestabit, ut nulli sis malo tiro.
passages.english: There is no one who has not gone more bravely to meet what he had long braced himself for and stood up even to hard things if they had been thought over beforehand; the unprepared man, on the other hand, has taken fright at even the lightest things. We must see to it that nothing is unexpected for us; and because all things are heavier for being new, constant thought will secure this: that you meet no trouble as a new recruit.

notes.note: A double negative, “no one has not”, which amounts to “everyone”. The English keeps the negative form, said once for both verbs.
notes.other_reading: Everyone has gone more bravely

notes.note: Se componere is to set oneself in position, as a fighter takes his stance. “Braced himself” keeps that; “prepared himself” would make an echo with “unprepared” that the Latin does not have.
notes.other_reading: what he had long prepared himself for

notes.note: This is the Stoic practice of rehearsing troubles in thought before they come (praemeditatio).
notes.other_reading: if they had been rehearsed in advance

notes.note: The three perfects (accessit, obstitit, expavit) state what has always been found to happen. The English keeps them as “has” and does not turn them into a general present.
notes.other_reading: the unprepared man panics at even the slightest things

notes.note: Literally “all things are heavier by newness”.
notes.other_reading: everything is harder to bear when it is new

notes.note: Tiro is a new recruit in the army, and the military image is kept. Malum is anything bad, an ill or a trouble, not only a moral evil; the Latin is literally “a recruit to no ill”, and the English supplies “meet”. The Latin moves from the first person plural to the second person singular here and the English keeps that.
notes.other_reading: that you are a raw recruit to no evil

check.note: The double negative carried through two clauses is heavy in English. The Latin simply means “everyone”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the negative form is kept, since the Latin is an emphatic “no one … not”, as it is at Ep. 105.4, but it is now said only once. The English reads “There is no one who has not gone more bravely … and stood up even to hard things”.

check.note: The Latin phrase is to set or ready oneself, like a fighter taking his stance. “Composed himself” in English means calmed himself.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “what he had long braced himself for”. “Composed himself” wrongly suggests calming down, and “braced” gives the fighter’s stance that is in the Latin verb. “Prepared” is avoided because it would echo “unprepared”, which is a different Latin word.

check.note: “The lightest” with no noun is hard to read. “Light” should be kept for the pairing with “heavier”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “at even the lightest things”, with “light” kept to answer “heavier” later in the section.

check.note: The Latin malum here is trouble or misfortune, and “evil” sounds moral. The phrase is also hard to follow, and “raw” adds a little to tiro.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “that you meet no trouble as a new recruit”. “Trouble” replaces “evil” and “raw” is dropped. “Trouble” is preferred to “misfortune” as the plainer and wider word for the Latin, which covers anything bad.

passages.latin: Nihil miremur eorum ad quae nati sumus, quae ideo nulli querenda quiaparia sunt omnibus. Ita dico, paria sunt; nam etiam quod effugit aliquispati potuit. Aequum autem ius est non quo omnes usi sunt sed quod omnibuslatum est. Imperetur aequitas animo et sine querella mortalitatis tributapendamus.
passages.english: Let us be surprised at none of the things we were born to; no one should complain of them, for this reason, that they are equal for all. I mean it: they are equal, for even what someone has escaped he could have suffered. And an even-handed law is not the one that all have come under but the one that has been passed for all. Let the mind be commanded to keep an even temper, and let us pay the taxes of mortality without complaint.

notes.note: Mirari is to wonder at or be surprised at. The English takes surprise, since the things in question are troubles.
notes.other_reading: Let us wonder at none of the things

notes.note: Ita dico insists on the word just used. Paria is “equal, the same”; the claim is that these things stand over everyone alike, not that everyone actually suffers the same.
notes.other_reading: Yes, I say, they are the same for all

notes.note: Aequum is both “equal” and “fair”, and aequitas in the next sentence picks it up. The English uses “even-handed” here and “even temper” there so that the link can be heard, and keeps “equal” for paria.
notes.other_reading: And a fair law is not the one

notes.note: Literally “which all have used”, that is, which has actually been applied in everyone’s case.
notes.other_reading: the one that all have experienced

notes.note: Aequitas with animus is the usual Latin for an even, calm mind, but here it also echoes the even-handed law just before, so that fairness may be meant as well. The English takes the first sense and keeps the echo in the word “even”.
notes.other_reading: Let fairness be commanded of the mind

notes.note: Tributum is a tax or levy paid to the state. The image is of the troubles of mortal life as dues owed.
notes.other_reading: the tribute of our mortal condition

check.note: The Latin verb here is to be surprised. “Wonder at” can be heard as “marvel at, admire”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “be surprised at”. The things in question are troubles, and “wonder at” could be heard as admiring them.

check.note: The sense is right, but “the one that all have had applied to them” is heavy. The Latin idiom is to come under a law, to experience it.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “not the one that all have come under but the one that has been passed for all”. “Come under” is lighter than the draft’s wording. “Actually” is not added, since the Latin has no such word, and “passed” is kept because the Latin verb is the one used for passing a law.

check.note: “Fairness” keeps the link with the fair law, but said of the mind the Latin word normally means evenness, calm acceptance. The reader gets “be fair” where Seneca probably means “be even-tempered”, and “commanded of the mind” is stilted.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “an even-handed law” and “Let the mind be commanded to keep an even temper”. Said of the mind, the Latin word normally means evenness, and the pair keeps the echo of the law in the word “even”. The note records “fairness” as the other reading.

passages.latin: Ad hanclegem animus noster aptandus est; hanc sequatur, huic pareat; et quaecumquefiunt debuisse fieri putet nec velit obiurgare naturam. Optimum est patiquod emendare non possis, et deum quo auctore cuncta proveniunt sine murmurationecomitari: malus miles est qui imperatorem gemens sequitur.
passages.english: Our mind must be fitted to this law; let it follow this, let it obey this; and let it think that whatever happens ought to have happened, and not wish to scold nature. It is best to bear what you cannot correct, and, without grumbling, to go along with the god by whose doing all things come about: he is a bad soldier who follows his commander groaning.

notes.note: Two words run together in the copy (hanc legem). “This law” is the one in the section before: nature governs the world by changes, and lasting things are made of opposites.
notes.other_reading: To this rule

notes.note: Debuisse can mean “ought to have happened” (rightness) or “was bound to happen” (necessity). The English takes rightness, because the next words forbid scolding nature, but both may be meant.
notes.other_reading: let it think that whatever happens had to happen

notes.note: Emendare is to free from fault, to correct. The same verb returns at Ep. 107.12 and “correct” is used in both places. The “you” is general.
notes.other_reading: what you cannot mend

notes.note: Auctor is an originator and also one on whose authority a thing is done. Proveniunt is “come forth, come about”.
notes.other_reading: the god on whose authority all things come forth

notes.note: To go as a companion. The verb returns in the verses at Ep. 107.11 and “go along” is used in both places.
notes.other_reading: to accompany

notes.note: Imperator is the commanding general. “Groaning” returns in the verses at Ep. 107.11.
notes.other_reading: who follows his general with a groan

check.note: The Latin can mean “was bound to happen” (necessity) or “ought to have happened” (it was right). The English chooses necessity, but with the words about not scolding nature the second sense is at least as likely.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “ought to have happened”. The Latin verb is first of all “ought”, and the words that follow, about not scolding nature, are about finding no fault and not only about necessity. “Had to happen” is kept in the note.

check.note: The Latin word is an originator, but also one on whose authority or at whose prompting a thing is done. The English is acceptable; the other shade is “on whose authority”.
check.decided: Declined: “by whose doing” stands. The Latin word is first of all the originator of a thing, which the English gives, and the note records “on whose authority”.

check.note: The word order of the English invites the reading “grumbling with the god”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and, without grumbling, to go along with the god by whose doing all things come about”, so that “grumbling with the god” can no longer be read.

passages.latin: Duc, o parens celsique dominator poli, quocumque placuit: nulla parendi mora est; adsum inpiger. Fac nolle, comitabor gemens malusque patiar facere quod licuit bono. Ducunt volentem fata, nolentem trahunt.
passages.english: Lead me, O father and ruler of the high heaven, wherever you have decided: there is no delay in obeying; I am here, and eager. Suppose I am unwilling: I shall go along groaning, and as a bad man I shall be made to do what I was allowed to do as a good one. The fates lead the willing; the unwilling they drag.

notes.note: These are five lines of verse, Seneca’s own Latin version of lines by the Stoic Cleanthes addressed to Jupiter, as the section before says. The copy gives them as running text with no quotation marks, so the English sets them as prose without marks. The verb has no object in the Latin and the English supplies one.
notes.other_reading: Lead, O parent

notes.note: Polus is the pole of the sky, and so the sky. Dominator is a master or ruler.
notes.other_reading: and master of the lofty sky

notes.note: Literally “wherever it has pleased”, with “you” understood.
notes.other_reading: wherever it has pleased you

notes.note: Parendi (“of obeying”) may echo parens (“father”) in the line before. The echo cannot be kept in English.
notes.other_reading: I obey without delay

notes.note: Inpiger is “not sluggish”: brisk, energetic, ready to act. “Eager” is used here and for the same word at Ep. 107.12; “unhesitating” would only repeat “no delay” from the clause before.
notes.other_reading: I am here, unhesitating

notes.note: Fac with an infinitive is “suppose that”. The subject of “be unwilling” is not expressed and is taken to be the speaker.
notes.other_reading: Make me unwilling

notes.latin: malusque patiar facere quod licuit bono
notes.note: Patiar facere is hard: literally “shall suffer to do”, with suffering set against doing, and the English takes it as being made to do. From memory, unchecked: some editions read a second pati in place of facere, which would give “shall suffer as a bad man what could have been suffered as a good one”. The English translates the text as given.
notes.other_reading: and, as a bad man, I shall bear doing what I was allowed to do as a good one

notes.note: “Lead” repeats the first word of the verses, and “unwilling” repeats nolle from two lines before; both echoes are kept. From memory, unchecked: this last line has no counterpart in the Greek lines of Cleanthes preserved elsewhere and may be Seneca’s own.
notes.other_reading: Fate leads the one who is willing and drags the one who is not.

check.note: The whole section is verse, a prayer whose author the section before names, but the English runs as plain prose with no sign that it is quoted verse. The Latin as given has no quotation marks; the supplied object of “lead” is needed.
check.decided: Partly accepted: a note says that these are five lines of verse, Seneca’s Latin version of Cleanthes. Quotation marks are not added, because the Latin as given has none and the lines are spoken as the writer’s own prayer. The supplied object of “lead” stays.

check.note: The Latin word is not sluggish, brisk, energetic. “Unhesitating” narrows it to “without delay”, which the clause before has just said, and the same applies at Ep. 107.12.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “eager” here and for the same word at Ep. 107.12. The Latin word means not sluggish, brisk, and “unhesitating” only repeated “no delay” from the clause before.

check.note: Patiar is set against facere, suffering against doing: he will be made to do what he could have done freely. “Bear doing” sounds like “put up with doing” and blurs the contrast.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “shall be made to do” replaces “shall bear doing”, so that suffering is set against doing, as in the Latin. “Was allowed to do” is kept in place of the suggested “was free to do”, because the Latin verb is about what was permitted.

passages.latin: Sic vivamus, sic loquamur; paratos nos inveniat atque inpigros fatum.Hic est magnus animus qui se ei tradidit: at contra ille pusillus et degenerqui obluctatur et de ordine mundi male existimat et emendare mavult deosquam se. Vale.
passages.english: Let us live this way, let us speak this way; let fate find us ready and eager. This is a great spirit, the one that has handed itself over to fate; the small and ignoble one, on the other hand, is the one that struggles against it and thinks ill of the order of the world and would rather correct the gods than itself. Farewell.

notes.note: “This way” points back to the verses of Cleanthes just quoted (Ep. 107.11): the speaking meant is speaking to the god as he does.
notes.other_reading: let us speak so

notes.note: The same word as in the verses at Ep. 107.11, and “eager” is used in both places. Literally “not sluggish”.
notes.other_reading: ready and unhesitating

notes.note: The glossary prefers “mind” for animus and allows “spirit” where the sense is courage or greatness of spirit, as here, where it is set against the “small” one that follows. “A great mind” would suggest intellect. It is the same Latin word that is “mind” at Ep. 107.9.
notes.other_reading: This is a great mind

notes.note: Ei is “to it”, taken as fate, the last noun, and the English repeats the noun for clarity. The form could also be “to him”, the god.
notes.other_reading: that has surrendered itself to him

notes.note: Pusillus is very small, the opposite of magnus. Degener is “fallen away from its stock”, here from the mind’s high origin; “ignoble” gives that without the modern sense of “degenerate”.
notes.other_reading: small and unworthy of its birth

notes.note: Mundus is the world as an ordered whole, the universe. Ordo is its arrangement or sequence.
notes.other_reading: has a low view of the arrangement of the universe

notes.note: The same verb as at Ep. 107.9 (“what you cannot correct”), and “correct” is kept. “Itself” follows the grammar, since the subject is the animus.
notes.other_reading: would rather reform the gods than himself

check.note: “Live so” and “speak so” are slightly stiff word order for the English of today. Very small.
check.decided: Accepted: “so” becomes “this way” in both halves of the sentence, which gives the same sense in the word order of today’s English.

check.note: “A great mind” in English suggests intellect, while the Latin is about greatness of spirit. “Mind” is the rendering of animus throughout, so changing it here breaks consistency.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “a great spirit”. The glossary allows “spirit” for animus in just this kind of phrase, and “a great mind” would be heard as a matter of intellect. The note says that it is the same word as “mind” at Ep. 107.9.

check.note: The pronoun ei is replaced by its noun. The reference to fate is right and the change helps the reader; it is noted only because a word is supplied, and the suggestion is to keep it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps “has handed itself over to fate”, as suggested. The pronoun points to “fate” in the sentence before, and the note says that the noun is written out and that “to him” is possible.

check.note: Pusillus is the opposite of magnus, small against great, and “petty” loses the plain contrast. The “that one … which” construction is also stiff.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the small and ignoble one, on the other hand, is the one that struggles against it”. “Small” answers “great” plainly, as the two Latin words answer each other.

check.note: The Latin word is fallen away from its stock, ignoble, base. “Degenerate” today suggests depravity, which is not in the Latin.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “ignoble”. The Latin word means fallen away from one’s stock, and “degenerate” now suggests depravity, which the Latin does not say.

passages.latin: Indemihi quaedam permansere, Lucili; magno enim in omnia impetu veneram, deindead civitatis vitam reductus ex bene coeptis pauca servavi. Inde ostreisboletisque in omnem vitam renuntiatum est; nec enim cibi sed oblectamentasunt ad edendum saturos cogentia (quod gratissimum est edacibus et se ultraquam capiunt farcientibus), facile descensura, facile reditura.
passages.english: From that, some things have stayed with me, Lucilius; for I had come at everything with a great rush, and then, brought back to the life of a citizen, I kept few of the things I had begun well. From that, oysters and mushrooms were given up for life; for they are not foods but treats that force people who are full to eat (which is what the greedy, and those who stuff themselves beyond what they hold, like best), things that will go down easily, come back up easily.

notes.note: This is “Inde mihi” run together. “Inde” can mean “from that source” (the teaching described in the section before) or “from that time”. It opens five sentences across this section and the next, and the English keeps one rendering, “From that”, because what follows are things that came out of that teaching.
notes.other_reading: Since then, some things have stayed with me

notes.latin: magno enim in omnia impetu veneram
notes.note: “impetus” here is the ordinary word for a rush or burst of eagerness, not the Stoic technical term “impulse” of Ep. 113.18.
notes.other_reading: for I had come to it all with great eagerness

notes.note: “civitas” is the body of citizens, the state, not the town as a place. The English reads “the life of a citizen”, set against the life of the philosopher’s school; whether a public career or simply the way citizens live is meant is left open.
notes.other_reading: brought back to public life

notes.note: The Latin is an impersonal passive with no “by me”. The English keeps the impersonal form, though Seneca clearly means himself.
notes.other_reading: I gave up oysters and mushrooms for life

notes.note: Literally “for all of life”. English “for life” already means for the whole of it, so no separate word for “all” is added.
notes.other_reading: for the whole of life

notes.note: “boletus” is a particular prized mushroom, a luxury dish like the oysters, not mushrooms in general. English has no plain single word for it, so the English reads “mushrooms”.
notes.other_reading: oysters and choice mushrooms

notes.note: The word means things that delight, set against “cibi”, real foods. The English reads “treats”.
notes.other_reading: they are not foods but amusements

notes.note: “quod” can look back (being made to eat when already full is what the greedy like best) or forward to the last words (that these things go down and come back up easily). The English takes it as looking back, following the brackets of the edition.
notes.other_reading: and, what the greedy like best, they will go down easily, come back up easily

notes.note: Future participles: these things will slip down and will return, that is, be vomited up. The English keeps the plain image without naming vomiting, and keeps the abrupt pairing without “and”.
notes.other_reading: sure to go down easily and to come back easily

check.note: “civitas” is the body of citizens, the state, not the town as a place, so “the life of the city” reads as town against country, which is not the contrast here.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “brought back to the life of a citizen”. “civitas” is the community of citizens, and the contrast is with the life of the philosopher’s school, not with the countryside.

check.note: “pauca” stresses how little was kept after the great rush; “a few” sounds like a modest success.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “kept few of the things”. “pauca” with nothing added is “few”, and the sentence is explaining why only some things stayed.

check.note: Said of things eaten, “amusements” is odd English; the word means things that give delight, here treats or titbits.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “they are not foods but treats”. The Latin word means things that give delight, and “treats” says that of things eaten in plain English.

check.note: “boletus” is one prized kind of mushroom, a luxury dish; plain “mushrooms” loses the point that these are delicacies, unless a note says which kind.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “mushrooms”. The Latin has one noun and no adjective, so “choice” would add a word; that a prized kind is meant is said in the note.

check.note: “For the whole of life” is stiff where plain English says “for life”; the impersonal passive is rightly kept. The phrase comes twice more in Ep. 108.16.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “were given up for life”, here and twice in Ep. 108.16. “For life” already means for the whole of it, so the “all” of the Latin is not lost, and the impersonal passive stays.

check.note: “Inde” can mean “from that source” or “from that time”. The English chooses the first, and with the section standing alone “that” points at nothing; “Since then” is suggested in all places.
check.decided: Declined: “From that” stays in all five places. The sentences list things that came out of the teaching described just before (no oysters, no perfume, no wine), so “from that source” is a sound reading of “Inde”; the note records “Since then” as the other reading.

check.note: The future participles say only “that will go down, that will come back”; “sure to” is a little stronger, the added “and” removes the abrupt pairing, and “come back” may not be understood as “come back up”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “things that will go down easily, come back up easily”. The participles say only what will happen, the Latin has no “and”, and “come back up” makes the return plain without naming it.

passages.latin: Indein omnem vitam unguento abstinemus, quoniam optimus odor in corpore estnullus. Inde vino carens stomachus. Inde in omnem vitam balneum fugimus;decoquere corpus atque exinanire sudoribus inutile simul delicatumque credidimus.Cetera proiecta redierunt, ita tamen ut quorum abstinentiam interrupi modumservem et quidem abstinentiae proximiorem, nescio an difficiliorem, quoniamquaedam absciduntur facilius animo quam temperantur.
passages.english: From that, we keep away from perfume for life, since the best smell on a body is none. From that, a stomach that goes without wine. From that, we avoid the bath for life; we came to believe that boiling the body down and emptying it out by sweating is both useless and self-indulgent. The other things I threw off have come back, but in such a way that, where I have broken off my abstinence, I keep to a limit, and one in fact nearer to abstinence, and perhaps harder, since for the mind some things are more easily cut off than kept within limits.

notes.note: The verb is first person plural, used by Seneca of himself, as are two more verbs in the section before the singular returns. The English keeps the person and number of the Latin.
notes.other_reading: I keep away from perfume for life

notes.note: The Latin has no verb: literally “From that, a stomach lacking wine”. The English keeps it as a fragment.
notes.other_reading: That is why my stomach goes without wine.

notes.note: The next clause shows that the hot bath that makes one sweat is meant, not washing in general.
notes.other_reading: the hot bath

notes.note: The form can be a present (“avoid”), in line with “abstinemus”, or a perfect (“have shunned”), in line with “credidimus”. The English reads the present; the sense hardly changes.
notes.other_reading: From that, the bath has been shunned for life

notes.note: “decoquere” is to boil down or cook away. The English keeps the cooking image.
notes.other_reading: to stew the body

notes.note: “delicatus” covers soft, pampered, effeminate. The English reads “self-indulgent”, as for the same word in Ep. 114.24.
notes.other_reading: both useless and soft

notes.note: This is “modum servem” run together. “modus” is a measure or limit; the English reads “keep to a limit” and picks the word up again in “kept within limits” for “temperantur” at the end.
notes.other_reading: keep a measure, and one in fact nearer to abstinence

notes.note: Literally a statement of not knowing whether it is harder. In classical usage the phrase leans towards yes, so the English reads “perhaps harder”.
notes.other_reading: and I do not know whether it is harder

notes.note: “animo” can be “for the mind” (the one that finds it easier), “by the mind” (the one that cuts) or “from the mind” (what the things are cut away from). The English takes it as “for the mind”, since the comparison covers both cutting off and keeping within limits.
notes.other_reading: since some things are more easily cut off from the mind than kept within limits

check.note: “animo” is read as “from the mind”, but it can also be “by the mind” or “for the mind”: the mind finds it easier to cut some things off than to use them in moderation, which fits wine and baths better.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “since for the mind some things are more easily cut off than kept within limits”. “animo” is taken as the one for whom it is easier, which covers both halves of the comparison, but the Latin passive is kept; the note gives “from the mind” as the other reading.

check.note: “fugimus” can be present or perfect (“have shunned”). The English chooses the present without saying so; the sense hardly changes.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps the present, “avoid the bath”, in line with “abstinemus”, and a note now says that the form can also be a perfect.

check.note: “Keep a measure” and “kept in measure” are not English of today; the sense is a limit, moderation.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “keep to a limit” and, at the end, “kept within limits”. “modus” is a limit or due measure, and “limit” says it in English of today.

check.note: The plural “sweats” follows the Latin plural but is odd in English; “draining it by sweating” is suggested.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “emptying it out by sweating”. The odd plural is gone, but “emptying out” is kept because that is what “exinanire” says.

check.note: As in Ep. 108.15, “for the whole of life” is stiff; it comes twice in this section.
check.decided: Accepted: both places now read “for life”, as in Ep. 108.15.

passages.latin: Itaque iudicium quidem tuum sustine, ceterum omnia tibi in integro serva. Si vera suntista, abstinuisse animalibus innocentia est; si falsa, frugalitas est. Quod istic credulitatis tuae damnum est? alimenta tibi leonum et vulturum eripio.'
passages.english: “So hold back your judgment, but keep everything open for yourself. If those things are true, to have abstained from animals is freedom from guilt; if they are false, it is frugality. What does your credulity lose you in that case? I am taking from you the food of lions and vultures.”

notes.note: The speaker is Sotion, whose quoted speech began in the section before and ends here. The English opens with a quotation mark to show that the speech is continuing. “You” is the young Seneca and the speaker is Sotion.
notes.other_reading: (the same words with only the closing quotation mark, as in the Latin)

notes.note: “sustinere” here is to hold up or suspend. The hearer is asked not to decide yet.
notes.other_reading: So suspend your judgment

notes.note: A legal idiom: to keep a matter “whole”, that is, undecided and not prejudiced. The English reads “keep everything open”.
notes.other_reading: but keep the whole question untouched for yourself

notes.note: Literally “doing no harm”, and so being clear of guilt. If souls do pass into animals, not eating them keeps one clear of bloodshed. The English reads “freedom from guilt” because “innocence” can suggest naivety.
notes.other_reading: to have abstained from animals is innocence

notes.note: The word covers thrift and sober living generally, not only saving money.
notes.other_reading: it is thrift

notes.note: Literally “the loss of your credulity”, with “istic”, “there, in that case”. The genitive is taken as the loss that believing causes, and the case meant is the one just named, that the doctrine is false. “credulitas” is given its plain sense, “credulity”.
notes.other_reading: What loss does your readiness to believe bring you there?

notes.latin: alimenta tibi leonum et vulturum eripio
notes.note: “The food of lions and vultures” is flesh. The present tense is kept.
notes.other_reading: All that is snatched from you is what lions and vultures feed on.

check.note: “istic” is “there”, “in that case”, not “here”, and the Latin asks what loss there is in that for the hearer’s credulity; the English makes the credulity the agent and adds “you”.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “What does your credulity lose you in that case?”. “istic” points back to the case just named, that the doctrine is false, so “in that case” replaces “here”. The loss is still said to fall on the hearer, as the next sentence shows.

check.note: “innocentia” is doing no harm, being free of guilt, here of killing a creature that may hold a human soul; “innocence” can suggest naivety.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “is freedom from guilt”. “innocentia” is doing no harm and so being clear of guilt, here the guilt of killing; a noun phrase is kept so that it stands level with “frugality” in the other half.

check.note: Found while settling: “readiness to believe” softens “credulitas”, which is the ordinary word for believing too easily.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “your credulity”. The question is asked of the case where the doctrine is false, and there the belief would be credulity, so the plain word fits.

passages.latin: Malus malo nocet facitque peiorem, iram eius incitando, tristitiaeadsentiendo, voluptates laudando; et tunc maxime laborant mali ubi plurimumvitia miscuere et in unum conlata nequitia est. Ergo ex contrario bonusbono proderit. 'Quomodo?' inquis.
passages.english: A bad man harms a bad man and makes him worse, by stirring up his anger, by going along with his gloom, by praising his pleasures; and bad men suffer most when they have mixed their vices most and their wickedness has been brought together into one. So, conversely, a good man will benefit a good man. “How?” you say.

notes.note: The Latin is masculine and general. The English reads “a bad man” to match “the wise man” elsewhere in the project.
notes.other_reading: A bad person harms a bad person

notes.note: This is “tristitiae adsentiendo” run together. “tristitia” ranges from sadness to sourness, and “adsentiri” is to agree with or fall in with.
notes.other_reading: by agreeing with his sadness

notes.note: “laborare” is to be in distress, to be afflicted, often to be ill. The English reads “suffer”.
notes.other_reading: bad men are sickest

notes.note: This is “plurimum vitia” run together. “plurimum” is taken as an adverb of degree, “most”. It is not said with what the vices are mixed, presumably with each other’s.
notes.other_reading: when they have blended very many of their vices

notes.note: Literally “wickedness has been carried together into one”. The image is of pooling or contributing to a common stock.
notes.other_reading: and their wickedness has been pooled

notes.note: The same verb as in the question the section before asks (what good one wise man will do another). The English reads “benefit”.
notes.other_reading: a good man will be of use to a good man

notes.note: Seneca imagines Lucilius breaking in. The Latin has “you say”, not “you ask”.
notes.other_reading: “How?” you ask.

check.note: “ex contrario” means “by the opposite case”, “conversely”. English “on the contrary” denies what has just been said, which is not what happens here.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “So, conversely, a good man will benefit a good man.” “ex contrario” draws the opposite case from the same reasoning; it does not deny what was just said.

check.note: “laborare” is to suffer or be afflicted, as with an illness; “in trouble” suggests difficulties from outside.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “bad men suffer most when they have mixed their vices most”. “laborare” is to be afflicted, as by an illness, not to meet difficulties from outside.

passages.latin: Ex Nomentano meo te saluto et iubeo habere mentem bonam, hoc est propitios deos omnis, quos habet placatos et faventes quisquis sibi se propitiavit. Sepone in praesentia quae quibusdam placent, unicuique nostrum paedagogum dari deum, non quidem ordinarium, sed hunc inferioris notae ex eorum numero quos Ovidius ait 'de plebe deos'. Ita tamen hoc seponas volo ut memineris maiores nostros qui crediderunt Stoicos fuisse; singulis enim et Genium et Iunonem dederunt.
passages.english: From my place at Nomentum I greet you and tell you to have a good mind, that is, all the gods well disposed; and whoever has made himself well disposed to himself has them appeased and favouring him. Set aside for now what some hold, that each one of us is given a god as a minder, not one of the regular rank, to be sure, but this one of a lower grade, from the number of those whom Ovid calls “gods from the common people”. Yet I want you to set this aside in such a way that you remember that our ancestors, who believed it, were Stoics; for to individuals, one by one, they gave both Genius and Juno.

notes.note: Literally “from my Nomentan”, that is, his estate at Nomentum, a town not far from Rome (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: From my Nomentan estate

notes.note: This plays on the usual greeting, which tells the other to be well. “mens bona” is a good or sound mind, and was also worshipped as a goddess (from memory, unchecked), which leads into the talk of gods. The word is “mens”, not “animus”, but “mind” is the natural English for both.
notes.other_reading: and tell you to be of sound mind

notes.note: The verb repeats the adjective “propitios” used of the gods just before. The English reads “well disposed” for both so that the echo shows.
notes.other_reading: whoever has made his peace with himself

notes.note: A “paedagogus” was the slave who minded a boy and walked him to school, not a teacher. The English reads “minder”.
notes.other_reading: a god as a guardian

notes.note: “ordinarius” is “of the regular order”, as of a regular magistrate. The contrast is with “inferioris notae”, “of a lower mark”, a phrase used of grades of goods such as wine.
notes.other_reading: not indeed a god of the first rank, but one of an inferior brand

notes.note: “hunc” (“this one”) is slightly odd here. It is taken as pointing to the minder god under discussion, and the English reads “this one”.
notes.other_reading: but one of a lower grade

notes.note: The phrase is from Ovid, Metamorphoses book 1, where Jupiter says he is no god from the common crowd (from memory, unchecked). “plebs” is the common people of Rome.
notes.other_reading: “plebeian gods”

notes.latin: maiores nostros qui crediderunt Stoicos fuisse
notes.note: The clause is taken as describing the ancestors as a whole: they believed it, and in that they were Stoics before the name. It could also be limited to those of the ancestors who believed it. “It” is supplied as the object of “believed”.
notes.other_reading: that those of our ancestors who believed this were Stoics

notes.latin: singulis enim et Genium et Iunonem dederunt
notes.note: In Roman belief each man had a Genius and each woman a Juno, a personal guardian spirit (from memory, unchecked). The Latin says that to individuals they gave “both Genius and Juno” without dividing them by sex, and the English keeps that, so that it can be heard as both for everyone or as one apiece.
notes.other_reading: they gave every man a Genius and every woman a Juno

check.note: The verb chosen for “iubeo” is archaic English.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “and tell you to have a good mind”. “iubeo” is the plain verb for telling someone to do something, and the older English verb is gone.

check.latin: quos habet placatos et faventes quisquis sibi se propitiavit
check.note: The relative clause is cut off from “anyone”, so the sentence has to be read twice. The content and the echo of “propitios” in “propitiavit” are right.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “and whoever has made himself well disposed to himself has them appeased and favouring him”. The order is changed as suggested so that the sentence reads at once; “favouring” is kept for “faventes” because the next section speaks of the gods’ “favour” with the same word.

check.latin: maiores nostros qui crediderunt Stoicos fuisse
check.note: Without commas the English says that only those ancestors who believed it were Stoics. The Latin more naturally speaks of the ancestors as a whole: they believed this, so in this they were Stoics.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “that our ancestors, who believed it, were Stoics”. The commas make the clause describe the ancestors as a whole, which is what the reason given next, about what they gave to individuals, requires; the limiting reading is in the note.

check.latin: singulis enim et Genium et Iunonem dederunt
check.note: The English says every person got both. The Latin says that to individuals they gave both Genius and Juno, which can equally mean one apiece, and “each single person” is awkward.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “for to individuals, one by one, they gave both Genius and Juno”. Without “each single person” the English no longer says outright that everyone had both, and “both” is kept for the Latin “et” twice over.

check.note: “hunc” (“this one”) is dropped. It is a small pointing word, but it marks the minder god as the one under discussion.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “but this one of a lower grade”. “hunc” is in the Latin and points to the god under discussion, so it is no longer dropped.

passages.latin: Postea videbimus an tantum dis vacet ut privatorum negotia procurent: interim illud scito, sive adsignati sumus sive neglecti et fortunae dati, nulli te posse inprecari quicquam gravius quam si inprecatus fueris ut se habeat iratum. Sed non est quare cuiquam quem poena putaveris dignum optes ut infestos deos habeat: habet, inquam, etiam si videtur eorum favore produci.
passages.english: We shall see later whether the gods have so much leisure that they manage the affairs of private persons. For the present know this: whether we have been assigned or neglected and given over to fortune, you can call down on no one anything worse than if you call down on him that he should have himself angry with him. But there is no reason for you to wish on anyone you think deserving of punishment that he should have the gods hostile: he has them so, I say, even if he seems to be carried forward by their favour.

notes.note: Literally “whether there is so much free time for the gods”.
notes.other_reading: whether the gods are so unoccupied

notes.note: “procurare” is to act as someone’s agent or steward. “privati” are individuals as opposed to the state or the world at large.
notes.other_reading: that they act as stewards of individuals’ business

notes.note: “Assigned” means assigned to a guardian god, as in the section before. The Latin does not say to whom, and nothing is added.
notes.other_reading: whether each of us has been allotted to a god

notes.note: To pray something down on someone, usually a curse. The verb comes twice and the English reads “call down” both times.
notes.other_reading: you can curse no one with anything worse

notes.note: Literally “that he may have himself angry”. It is modelled on the phrase for having the gods angry with one, and answers “made himself well disposed to himself” in the section before. The English keeps “have” and one “himself”, and supplies “with him” so that the phrase is not read as “make himself angry”.
notes.other_reading: that he should be at enmity with himself

notes.note: The object, “the gods hostile”, is understood from the clause before, and the English supplies “them so”.
notes.other_reading: he does have them hostile, let it be said

notes.note: “produci” is to be led forward, and so to be advanced or promoted.
notes.other_reading: even if he seems to be advanced by their favour

check.note: The Latin has one “se”: “that he should have himself angry”, on the pattern of having the gods angry or appeased. The English doubles “himself” and is hard to follow, though keeping “have” is right.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “that he should have himself angry with him”. There is one “himself” for the one “se”, and “have” is kept for the run of “habet” and “habeat”; “with him” is supplied because “have himself angry” alone would be read as “make himself angry”.

check.note: Of a curse, “heavier” is not natural English; “worse” or “graver” is suggested.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “anything worse”. “gravius” of a curse is “more grievous”, and “heavier” is not said of curses in English.

check.note: “putaveris” is the subjunctive of a general case, “anyone you may think”; “you have thought” points to a past judgment that the Latin does not have.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “anyone you think deserving of punishment”. “putaveris” is a subjunctive of the general case and does not point to a past judgment.

passages.latin: Sed ipsum illud cadere non habet in se mali quicquam si exitum spectes, ultra quem natura neminem deiecit. Prope est rerum omnium terminus, prope est, inquam, et illud unde felix eicitur et illud unde infelix emittitur: nos utraque extendimus et longa spe ac metu facimus. Sed, si sapis, omnia humana condicione metire; simul et quod gaudes et quod times contrahe. Est autem tanti nihil diu gaudere ne quid diu timeas.
passages.english: But that falling itself has no evil in it, if you look to the end, beyond which nature has thrown no one down. The limit of all things is near; near, I say, is both that from which the fortunate man is thrown out and that from which the unfortunate man is let go: we stretch both out and make them long by hope and fear. But, if you are wise, measure all things by the human condition; draw in together both what you rejoice at and what you fear. And it is worth the price to rejoice at nothing for long, so that you may not fear anything for long.

notes.note: “That falling” picks up the fall from a height spoken of in the section before.
notes.other_reading: But the fall itself

notes.note: “exitus” is a way out, an end, an outcome, and often death. The next clause shows that death is meant, but the English keeps the wider word “end”.
notes.other_reading: if you look to death

notes.latin: et illud unde felix eicitur et illud unde infelix emittitur
notes.note: “illud unde” is left vague: the state, span or place the fortunate man is thrown out of and the one the unfortunate man is released from. The two verbs differ on purpose (thrown out against his will, let out as a release). “Fortunate” is used for “felix” to keep “happy” for “beatus”.
notes.other_reading: both the point at which the lucky man is cast out and the point at which the unlucky man is set free

notes.note: “longa” is taken as agreeing with “utraque” (“make both long”), with “spe ac metu” as the means. It could be read as “by long hope and fear”, but then “facimus” has nothing to complete it.
notes.other_reading: stretch both out, and do so by long hope and fear

notes.note: An everyday phrase, “if you have sense”, but the verb is the one behind “sapiens”, the wise man, so the English reads “if you are wise”.
notes.other_reading: if you have any sense

notes.note: This can be divided two ways: “measure all things by the human condition” or “measure all human things by their condition”, that is, by the terms on which they are held. The English takes the first, since “condicione” alone would not say whose condition is meant.
notes.other_reading: measure all human things by their condition

notes.note: The opposite of “extendimus” (“stretch out”) just before, so the English reads “draw in” to keep the pair. “simul” with it is “together”, “at the same time”.
notes.other_reading: shorten at the same time both what you rejoice at and what you fear

notes.note: “tanti est” is an idiom of price: it is worth that much, it is worth it.
notes.other_reading: And it is worth while to rejoice at nothing for long

check.note: “humana” can go with “condicione” (“by the human condition”) or with “omnia” (“all human things by their condition”). The English chooses the first, and the other reading should be flagged.
check.decided: Accepted: the English is unchanged, “measure all things by the human condition”, and the note gives the other division of the words. “humana condicione” is taken together because “condicione” alone would not say whose condition is meant.

check.note: “simul” means “together”, “at the same time”; “at once” will be read by many as “immediately”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “draw in together both what you rejoice at and what you fear”. “simul” is “at the same time”, and “at once” could be read as “immediately”.

check.note: “That from which” is correct but vague; the Latin points to a place or point one leaves, and “the point from which” would be clearer.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “that from which”. The Latin has only the bare pronoun “illud”, and the next clause says that both are stretched out and made long, which suits a span as well as a point; “the point” would add a noun and settle what the Latin leaves open, as the note says.

passages.latin: Quidquid nobis bono futurum erat deus et parens noster in proximo posuit; non expectavit inquisitionem nostram et ultro dedit: nocitura altissime pressit. Nihil nisi de nobis queri possumus: ea quibus periremus nolente rerum natura et abscondente protulimus. Addiximus animum voluptati, cui indulgere initium omnium malorum est, tradidimus ambitioni et famae, ceteris aeque vanis et inanibus.
passages.english: Whatever was going to be for our good, our god and parent placed close at hand; he did not wait for us to search and gave it of his own accord: the things that would harm us he pressed down very deep. We can complain of nothing but ourselves: the things we were to perish by we have brought out, though the nature of things was unwilling and was hiding them. We have bound the mind over to pleasure, and to indulge pleasure is the beginning of all evils; we have handed it over to ambition and reputation, and to the rest, things equally empty and hollow.

notes.note: Literally “was going to be for a good”, that is, to do good to those it was given to. “Good” is kept because the passage sets it against the “evils” below.
notes.other_reading: Whatever was going to be of benefit to us

notes.note: “noster” can go with both nouns or only with “parens”. The English takes it with both, “our god and parent”. “parens” can also be “father”.
notes.other_reading: god, who is our father

notes.note: “ultro” means unasked, of his own motion.
notes.other_reading: and gave it unasked

notes.note: Literally “things going to harm he pressed down most deeply”. The section before speaks of digging in the earth, so buried metals are meant. The superlative can be “very deep” or “deepest”.
notes.other_reading: what would do harm he buried deepest

notes.note: The subjunctive gives purpose or destiny: things meant to bring ruin on those who dug them up, not merely things that did.
notes.other_reading: the things that would destroy us

notes.note: The glossary gives “the nature of things” for the two-word phrase. Here it acts almost as a person, unwilling and hiding things, and plain “nature” would also be possible.
notes.other_reading: though nature was unwilling and was hiding them

notes.note: “addicere” is a legal word: to make a person or thing over to another by a ruling, as a debtor was handed to his creditor. The English reads “bound over” so that the bondage can be heard.
notes.other_reading: the mind has been made over to pleasure

notes.note: “ambitio” is literally canvassing for office, and so the pursuit of standing. “fama” is what people say of one.
notes.other_reading: to the pursuit of office and to fame

notes.note: The two words are near synonyms, both meaning empty. Two English words are used to keep the pair.
notes.other_reading: equally vain and empty

check.note: “et” is dropped and the pair is turned into an apposition. The Latin has two titles joined, with “noster” probably covering both.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “our god and parent”. The Latin joins two titles with “et”, and “noster” most naturally covers both.

check.note: “rerum natura” is simply nature, here acting as a person who is unwilling and hides things. “The nature of things” sounds like an abstract quality, and Ep. 110.4 has plain “nature”.
check.decided: Declined: the English keeps “the nature of things”. The Latin here has the two-word phrase “rerum natura”, not “natura” alone as in Ep. 110.4, and the glossary gives “the nature of things” for it; a note records plain “nature” as possible.

check.note: “addicere” is the legal word for assigning a person to a master or creditor. “Made over” keeps the legal note faintly but loses the bondage.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “bound the mind over to pleasure”. “addicere” is the word for a ruling that hands a debtor to his creditor, and “bound over” lets the bondage be heard.

passages.latin: Hoc itaque ipse mihi dico quotiens tale aliquid praestrinxerit oculos meos, quotiens occurrit domus splendida, cohors culta servorum, lectica formonsis inposita calonibus: "quid miraris? quid stupes? pompa est. Ostenduntur istae res, non possidentur, et dum placent transeunt".
passages.english: So this is what I say to myself whenever something of that kind has dazzled my eyes, whenever I come upon a splendid house, a well-groomed troop of slaves, a litter set on handsome bearers: “Why do you marvel? Why are you struck dumb? It is a procession. Those things are shown, not owned, and while they please they pass by.”

notes.note: From memory, unchecked: this section stands inside a long speech of the philosopher Attalus that Seneca is reporting, so the speaker here would be Attalus and not Seneca. Nothing in the Latin given settles it, and the English reads the same either way.
notes.other_reading: (no difference in the English)

notes.note: “praestringere oculos” is to dazzle or dull the eyes. The tense is “shall have dazzled”, which English gives as “has dazzled”.
notes.other_reading: whenever something of the kind blinds my eyes

notes.note: “cohors” is a troop or retinue. “culta” is well cared for in dress and grooming.
notes.other_reading: a smartly dressed retinue of slaves

notes.note: “formonsis” is a spelling of “formosis”, handsome. “calones” are drudges or porters, here the men who carry the litter. Literally the litter is “placed upon” them.
notes.other_reading: a litter resting on the shoulders of good-looking porters

notes.note: “mirari” is to wonder at or admire, and the English reads “marvel”, as in Ep. 115.9. “stupere” is to be stunned or to gape.
notes.other_reading: “Why do you admire? Why do you gape?”

notes.note: “pompa” is a formal procession, the image carried over from the section before. It is not “pomp” in the English sense.
notes.other_reading: It is a parade.

notes.note: “istae” points away from the speaker, to the things the one addressed is staring at, so the English reads “Those things”.
notes.other_reading: These things are shown, not owned

notes.note: “transeunt” is “pass by”, as a procession does, and also “pass away”. The English keeps the procession image.
notes.other_reading: and even while they please they are gone

check.note: From memory, unchecked: this section is part of a speech by Attalus that Seneca reports, so the speaker may not be Seneca, and the double quotation marks suggest a quotation inside a quotation. A note may be needed.
check.decided: Accepted: the text is unchanged and the note on the speaker is kept. The wider letter is not among the Latin given, so the note still says “from memory, unchecked”, and the English reads the same whoever speaks.

check.note: “istae” points away from the speaker: “those things” that the one addressed is gaping at.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Those things are shown, not owned”. “istae” points away from the speaker, to the things the one addressed is staring at.

passages.latin: Omne rationale animal nihil agit nisi primum specie alicuius rei inritatum est, deinde impetum cepit, deinde adsensio confirmavit hunc impetum. Quid sit adsensio dicam. Oportet me ambulare: tunc demum ambulo cum hoc mihi dixi et adprobavi hanc opinionem meam; oportet me sedere: tunc demum sedeo. Haec adsensio in virtute non est.
passages.english: No rational living being does anything unless it has first been stirred by the impression of some thing, then has formed an impulse, and then assent has confirmed this impulse. I will say what assent is. I ought to walk: only then do I walk, when I have said this to myself and approved this opinion of mine; I ought to sit: only then do I sit. This assent is not found in virtue.

notes.latin: Omne rationale animal nihil agit nisi
notes.note: Literally “Every rational animal does nothing unless”. The English turns it as “No … does anything unless”, which says the same, and reads “living being” for “animal” because the argument counts gods as well as men under the word.
notes.other_reading: Every rational animal does nothing unless

notes.note: “species” is the Stoic technical term for what appears to the mind, the Greek phantasia. The English reads “impression”.
notes.other_reading: by the appearance of some thing

notes.note: “impetus” is here the Stoic technical term for the movement towards action, the Greek horme, and the English reads “impulse”. In Ep. 108.15 the same word is the ordinary “rush”. “cepit” is literally “has taken”.
notes.other_reading: then has felt an urge

notes.note: “adsensio” is the Stoic technical term for the mind’s agreeing to an impression, the Greek synkatathesis. The English reads “assent” throughout the section.
notes.other_reading: then agreement has ratified this impulse

notes.note: This is the thought to which assent is given. The Latin does not mark it as quoted, so the English uses a colon and no quotation marks. “oportet” is “it is right or fitting that”.
notes.other_reading: “It is fitting for me to walk”

notes.note: “opinio” is “opinion” by the glossary. The approving of it is the assent being defined.
notes.other_reading: and have endorsed this belief of mine

notes.latin: Haec adsensio in virtute non est
notes.note: Literally “this assent is not in virtue”. The point is taken to be that a virtue does not itself give assent, so cannot act as a living being does. The Latin could also be heard as “this assent does not belong to virtue”.
notes.other_reading: This assent is no part of virtue.

check.note: “Taken an impulse” is not English; “felt an impulse” is suggested.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “then has formed an impulse”. “Taken an impulse” is not English; “formed” is nearer than “felt” to “cepit”, which is an act of taking up, not a feeling.

check.note: “Is not in virtue” is literal but unclear. The sense is that no such assent is found in virtue: a virtue does not assent.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “This assent is not found in virtue.” The sense is that a virtue has no such assent of its own, and “found in” makes that clear.

passages.latin: Doceat me quam sacra res sit iustitia alienum bonum spectans, nihil ex se petens nisi usum sui. Nihil sit illi cum ambitione famaque: sibi placeat. Hoc ante omnia sibi quisque persuadeat: me iustum esse gratis oportet. Parum est. Adhuc illud persuadeat sibi: me in hanc pulcherrimam virtutem ultro etiam inpendere iuvet; tota cogitatio a privatis commodis quam longissime aversa sit. Non est quod spectes quod sit iustae rei praemium: maius in iusto est.
passages.english: Let him teach me how sacred a thing justice is, which looks to another’s good and asks nothing from itself except to be put to use. Let it have nothing to do with ambition and reputation: let it win its own approval. Let each person convince himself of this before everything: I ought to be just without payment. That is too little. Let him convince himself of this as well: let me be glad to go further and even spend on this most beautiful virtue; let all thought be turned as far as possible away from private advantages. There is no reason for you to look to what the reward of a just act is: there is a greater one in what is just.

notes.note: The subject of “let him teach” is not named in this section or in the one given before it; it must come from earlier in the letter. The English keeps an open “him”.
notes.other_reading: Let someone teach me

notes.note: “bonum” is “the good” by the glossary: justice looks to the good of someone else. “spectare” comes back in the last sentence, so the English reads “look to” in both places.
notes.other_reading: having regard to the good of others

notes.note: Literally “except the use of itself”: justice wants nothing from itself but to be exercised. The English reads “except to be put to use”.
notes.other_reading: except its own exercise

notes.note: Literally “let it please itself”, that is, have its own approval and not look for other people’s. The English reads “let it win its own approval”, since “pleased with itself” would mean smug.
notes.other_reading: let it be pleased with itself

notes.note: “gratis” is without payment. The next sentences build on the money image (spending, reward), so the English reads “without payment” and keeps “reward” for “praemium”.
notes.other_reading: just for nothing

notes.latin: me in hanc pulcherrimam virtutem ultro etiam inpendere iuvet
