notes.note: “me” can be the one who is glad to spend or the thing spent (“to spend myself”); the English takes the first, as in “me iustum esse” just before, which leaves “spend” without a stated object. “ultro etiam” is read as “going further, even”: not only unpaid but paying out. It can also be “of my own accord”.
notes.other_reading: let it be my delight even to spend myself, of my own accord, on this most beautiful virtue

notes.note: Literally “the reward of a just thing”. The English reads “a just act”.
notes.other_reading: what the prize for a just deed is

notes.note: “maius” (“greater”) is neuter: the English understands “reward” with it, but it can also stand alone as “something greater”. “iusto” can be neuter (“in what is just”) or masculine (“in the just man”); the English takes it as neuter, following “iustae rei”.
notes.other_reading: there is something greater in the just man

check.note: “gratis” is “without payment”. “For nothing” can also be read as “to no purpose”, which would reverse the point.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “just without payment”. “For nothing” could be read as “to no purpose”; “payment” is used and not “reward”, so that “reward” is kept for “praemium” in the last sentence.

check.note: “Pleased with itself” means smug in English. The Latin means that justice should seek its own approval and not that of others.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “let it win its own approval”. “sibi placeat” means that justice should be approved by itself and not by others, and the new wording says so without the sense of smugness.

check.note: “ultro” can be “of my own accord”, as the English has it, or “over and above”, “into the bargain”: not merely unpaid but actually paying out. After “That is too little” the second fits the step up well.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “let me be glad to go further and even spend on this most beautiful virtue”. After “That is too little”, “ultro etiam” marks the step beyond being unpaid, to paying out; “of my own accord” is kept in the note as the other reading.

check.note: The English supplies “reward” with “maius” and takes “iusto” as neuter. Both are reasonable, but “maius” could be “something greater” and “in iusto” could be “in the just man”, and these should be flagged.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English keeps “there is a greater one in what is just”, and the note now gives both other readings. “maius” is neuter and can agree with “praemium”, so “a greater reward” is a sound reading, greater than whatever reward was being looked for.

check.note: “The use of itself” is literal and opaque. The sense is that justice asks only to be practised.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “asks nothing from itself except to be put to use”. The point holds that “the use of itself” is opaque; “use” is kept for “usum”, with the phrase turned so that it reads as English.

passages.latin: Illud adhuc tibi adfige quod paulo ante dicebam, nihil ad rem pertinere quam multi aequitatem tuam noverint. Qui virtutem suam publicari vult non virtuti laborat sed gloriae. Non vis esse iustus sine gloria? at mehercules saepe iustus esse debebis cum infamia, et tunc, si sapis, mala opinio bene parta delectet. Vale.
passages.english: Fix this in yourself as well, what I was saying a little earlier: that it is nothing to the point how many people know of your fairness. Anyone who wants his virtue made public is working not for virtue but for glory. Are you unwilling to be just without glory? But, by Hercules, you will often have to be just with a bad name, and then, if you are wise, let a bad reputation well won delight you. Farewell.

notes.note: Literally “fix it onto yourself”, as one pins or nails something on so that it stays.
notes.other_reading: Fasten this to yourself as well

notes.note: This looks back to the remark in the section before that justice should have nothing to do with ambition and reputation.
notes.other_reading: the thing said just now

notes.note: “aequitas” is fairness or even-handedness, a different word from “iustitia”. The English keeps them apart.
notes.other_reading: how many know of your justice

notes.note: “publicare” is to make public property. It can carry a harsher tone, of putting something up for common use, which the English does not bring out.
notes.other_reading: Anyone who wants his virtue advertised

notes.latin: Non vis esse iustus sine gloria?
notes.note: Literally “Do you not wish to be just without glory?”, that is, do you refuse to be just unless glory comes with it.
notes.other_reading: You do not want to be just without glory?

notes.note: An everyday oath, “by Hercules”, used for emphasis. The name is kept.
notes.other_reading: But truly

notes.note: “infamia” is ill repute, the opposite of “gloria”. It answers “without glory”: not merely without it, but with its opposite, and the English keeps “with” for that reason.
notes.other_reading: you will often have to be just and be ill spoken of

notes.note: A play on “bad” and “well”: a bad opinion, well got. “opinio” here is what others think of one, so the English reads “reputation” and not the glossary’s “opinion”, which would be heard as one’s own. “Well won” means won by acting well, not deserved.
notes.other_reading: let a bad opinion, well got, delight you

check.note: The image is kept, but “Fasten this to yourself” is odd English. The sense is to fix it firmly in oneself so that it stays.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Fix this in yourself as well”. “adfigere” is to fix or fasten something on so that it stays, and “fix” keeps that image in natural English.

check.note: “infamia” is ill repute, a bad name, which “mala opinio” picks up in the next clause. “Disgrace” suggests shame that is deserved, and “just with disgrace” is hard to read.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “you will often have to be just with a bad name”. “infamia” is ill repute, not deserved shame; “with” is kept so that it answers “without glory”, as “cum” answers “sine” in the Latin.

check.note: “bene” is only “well”, set against “mala”: a bad opinion well earned. “Honourably” explains the point and loses the play of bad against well.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “let a bad reputation well won delight you”. The Latin sets “bene” (“well”) against “mala” (“bad”), and “honourably” explained the play away.

passages.latin: Quoniam hac similitudine usus sum, perseverabo. Animus noster modo rex est, modo tyrannus: rex cum honesta intuetur, salutem commissi sibi corporis curat et illi nihil imperat turpe, nihil sordidum; ubi vero inpotens, cupidus, delicatus est, transit in nomen detestabile ac dirum et fit tyrannus. Tunc illum excipiunt adfectus inpotentes et instant; qui initio quidem gaudet, ut solet populus largitione nocitura frustra plenus et quae non potest haurire contrectans;
passages.english: Since I have used this comparison, I will keep to it. Our mind is at one time a king, at another a tyrant: a king when it looks to what is honourable, cares for the welfare of the body entrusted to it and gives it no command that is shameful, none that is sordid; but when it is uncontrolled, greedy, self-indulgent, it passes over to a hateful and dreadful name and becomes a tyrant. Then uncontrolled passions take hold of it and press on it; and at first, indeed, it rejoices, as a people commonly does when it is filled to no purpose with a handout that will harm it and paws at what it cannot swallow;

notes.note: The comparison is the one made in the section before, of the mind to a king.
notes.other_reading: this likeness

notes.note: “honesta” is the neuter plural, “honourable things”. The English reads the glossary’s “what is honourable”.
notes.other_reading: when it keeps its eyes on honourable things

notes.note: “salus” is both safety and health, what a king owes those in his charge. The English reads “welfare”, which covers both.
notes.other_reading: cares for the health of the body entrusted to it

notes.note: “sordidus” is dirty, and so low or base. The English keeps the Latin word in its English form, “sordid”.
notes.other_reading: none that is base

notes.note: The word means lacking power over oneself, not “powerless”. It returns in the plural of the passions in the next sentence, and the English reads “uncontrolled” both times.
notes.other_reading: when it has no command of itself

notes.note: Soft, pampered, given to luxury. The English reads “self-indulgent”, as in Ep. 108.16.
notes.other_reading: soft

notes.latin: transit in nomen detestabile ac dirum
notes.note: Literally “it crosses over into a name”. “dirus” is ill-omened, dreadful.
notes.other_reading: it takes on a name that is hated and accursed

notes.note: “excipere” is to catch, receive or take over next in turn. It may suggest the passions taking the mind over as attendants or captors.
notes.other_reading: Then uncontrolled passions receive it

notes.note: “largitio” is a public distribution of food or money, often a political bribe. “frustra” is taken with “plenus”, “full to no purpose”.
notes.other_reading: stuffed in vain with a largess that will do it harm

notes.note: “haurire” is to drain or gulp down, and “contrectare” is to handle or finger. The section as given stops in mid-sentence at a semicolon: “quidem” (“at first, indeed”) expects an answering clause that comes only in the next section, so the English ends on a semicolon too.
notes.other_reading: and fingers what it cannot consume;

check.note: “Mean” today is first of all “unkind”. “sordidum” is base, low, sordid.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “none that is sordid”. “Mean” would be heard as “unkind”; “sordid” is the English form of the Latin word and keeps its sense of dirt and lowness.

check.note: “salus” is health but also safety or welfare, the word for what a king owes those in his charge. “Health” suits the body but narrows the king image a little.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “cares for the welfare of the body entrusted to it”. “salus” is safety as well as health, and “welfare” suits both the body and the king who has it in his charge.

check.note: The section as given stops in mid-sentence: “quidem” (“at first, indeed”) expects an answering clause that is not here. The English rightly keeps the semicolon, and a note may be wanted.
check.decided: Accepted: the English is unchanged and still ends on a semicolon. The note on the last words now says that the sentence runs on into the next section and that “quidem” waits for an answering clause that is not here.

passages.latin: Miramur parietes tenui marmore inductos, cum sciamus quale sit quod absconditur. Oculis nostris inponimus, et cum auro tecta perfudimus, quid aliud quam mendacio gaudemus? Scimus enim sub illo auro foeda ligna latitare. Nec tantum parietibus aut lacunaribus ornamentum tenue praetenditur: omnium istorum quos incedere altos vides bratteata felicitas est. Inspice, et scies sub ista tenui membrana dignitatis quantum mali iaceat.
passages.english: We marvel at walls coated with thin marble, though we know what sort of thing it is that is being hidden. We cheat our own eyes, and when we have flooded ceilings with gold, what else are we rejoicing in but a lie? For we know that under that gold ugly timber is lurking. Nor is it only over walls or panelled ceilings that a thin ornament is stretched: the good fortune of all those you see striding loftily along is overlaid with gold leaf. Look inside, and you will know how much evil lies under that thin skin of rank.

notes.note: “mirari” is to wonder at or admire. The English reads “marvel”, as in Ep. 110.17.
notes.other_reading: admire walls coated with thin marble

notes.note: Literally “overlaid with thin marble”, a veneer. “tenuis” comes three times in the section and the English keeps “thin” each time.
notes.other_reading: walls veneered with a thin layer of marble

notes.note: “imponere” with a dative is an idiom for deceiving or imposing on someone.
notes.other_reading: impose on our own eyes

notes.note: “tecta” is taken as the noun, roofs or ceilings, the thing covered. “perfundere” is to drench or pour over.
notes.other_reading: with our roofs drenched in gold

notes.note: “lacunaria” are ceilings divided into sunken panels.
notes.other_reading: over walls or coffered ceilings

notes.note: “incedere” is to walk with a stately step. “altos” is high or lofty, of their bearing or their position; the English reads “loftily”.
notes.other_reading: whom you see walking tall

notes.note: “brattea” is metal beaten thin, gold leaf, and “bratteata” is “covered with gold leaf”: their good fortune is a surface layer only. The English reads “good fortune” for “felicitas” to keep “happy” for “beatus”.
notes.other_reading: all of them have a gilded happiness

notes.note: “membrana” is a thin skin or film. “dignitas” is rank or standing.
notes.other_reading: that thin film of high position

notes.note: Literally “how much of bad”. The English reads “evil” for “malum” as elsewhere in these passages.
notes.other_reading: how much that is bad lies beneath

check.note: “bratteata” is “covered with gold leaf”, plated, not “gold leaf” itself. The Latin says the good fortune is overlaid, with something else beneath.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “is overlaid with gold leaf”. “bratteata” is an adjective, “covered with gold leaf”, so the good fortune has a thin layer over something else; “gold leaf” is kept and not “plated” because the thinness is the point.

check.note: “Men” is added; the Latin is “all those people”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “all those you see”. The Latin “omnium istorum” does not say “men”.

check.note: “Walking tall” is a modern idiom with an approving tone. The Latin is a stately, lofty gait seen from outside, without approval.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “striding loftily along”. “incedere” is a stately gait and “altos” is said of how they look from outside, without the approving tone of the modern idiom.

passages.latin: Utrum satius sit modicos habere adfectus an nullos saepe quaesitum est. Nostri illos expellunt, Peripatetici temperant. Ego non video quomodo salubris esse aut utilis possit ulla mediocritas morbi. Noli timere: nihil eorum quae tibi non vis negari eripio. Facilem me indulgentemque praebebo rebus ad quas tendis et quas aut necessarias vitae aut utiles aut iucundas putas: detraham vitium. Nam cum tibi cupere interdixero, velle permittam, ut eadem illa intrepidus facias, ut certiore consilio, ut voluptates ipsas magis sentias: quidni ad te magis perventurae sint si illis imperabis quam si servies?
passages.english: It has often been asked whether it is better to have moderate passions or none. Our school drives them out; the Peripatetics temper them. For my part, I do not see how any moderate degree of a disease can be wholesome or useful. Do not be afraid: I am taking from you none of the things that you do not want denied to you. I will show myself easy and indulgent towards the things you are aiming at and that you think either necessary for life or useful or pleasant: I will take away the vice. For when I have forbidden you to crave, I will allow you to want, so that you may do those same things unafraid, so that you may do them with a surer purpose, so that you may feel the pleasures themselves more. Why should they not reach you more if you command them than if you are their slave?

notes.note: The Stoic term for the passions, which the school treats as faults of the mind and not as neutral feelings. The glossary word “passions” is kept because the next sentences call them a disease.
notes.other_reading: moderate feelings or none

notes.note: A possessive used as a noun, meaning the people of Seneca’s own side, the Stoics. The English says “school” so that the contrast with the Peripatetics, the followers of Aristotle, is seen.
notes.other_reading: The Stoics drive them out

notes.note: The verb can mean to moderate, to mix in the right proportion, or to keep within bounds. The plain “temper” is used.
notes.other_reading: the Peripatetics keep them within limits

notes.note: The noun is the Latin word for the Peripatetic “mean” or middle state, and it answers “moderate” in the first sentence. “Moderate” is used in both places so that the echo shows, at the cost of the technical colour of “mean”.
notes.other_reading: any mean of a disease, or: any middling amount of illness

notes.note: Short and abrupt in the Latin: the things are granted and only what is wrong in the wanting is removed, as the next sentence explains. “Vice” is the glossary word and is the word used for the same noun at the end of this letter; “fault” is possible.
notes.other_reading: the fault is what will be taken away

notes.note: The argument rests on two verbs of wanting: the first names desire as a passion, the second reasoned wanting. English “desire” and “want” are too close to show this, so the pair is “crave” and “want”; “crave” is a little stronger than the Latin verb.
notes.other_reading: forbidden to desire, allowed to will

notes.note: The clause has no verb of its own; “do them” is supplied from the clause before. The noun can mean purpose, plan or deliberation; “purpose” is taken.
notes.other_reading: so that you may do them with firmer deliberation

notes.note: Literally “be going to come through to you more”. “More” may mean more fully or more surely; the English leaves it as open as the Latin.
notes.other_reading: why should they not come home to you more fully

check.note: “Making for” is a dated idiom that a reader of today may stumble on. The sense, what you are heading for, is right.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “the things you are aiming at”. The Latin verb means to stretch or head towards something, and “aim at” says that in today’s English.

check.note: “The vice” can sound like one particular moral vice and leave the reader asking which; the Latin means what is faulty in the wanting. The suggestion is “only the fault in them” or “what is wrong”.
check.decided: Declined: “the vice” stands. The Latin is two bare words, the verb “take away” and the noun the glossary renders “vice”, with neither “only” nor “in them”; the next sentence says at once what the vice is, and the same noun is “vices” at the end of the letter. The note records “fault”.

check.note: Found while settling: the Latin writes out the pronoun, which it does only for stress, setting Seneca’s own view beside the two schools just named. The draft had the bare verb.
check.decided: Accepted: the sentence now opens with a phrase that marks the view as Seneca’s own, which is all the stressed pronoun does; no claim is added.

passages.latin: Scis quare non possimus ista? quia nos posse non credimus. Immo mehercules aliud est in re: vitia nostra quia amamus defendimus et malumus excusare illa quam excutere. Satis natura homini dedit roboris si illo utamur, si vires nostras colligamus ac totas pro nobis, certe non contra nos concitemus. Nolle in causa est, non posse praetenditur. Vale.
passages.english: Do you know why we cannot do those things? Because we do not believe that we can. Or rather, by Hercules, the fact of the matter is something else: we defend our vices because we love them, and we would rather excuse them than shake them off. Nature has given man strength enough, if we would use it, if we would gather our powers and rouse all of them on our own behalf, or at any rate not against ourselves. Not wanting to is the cause; not being able to is put forward as the pretext. Farewell.

notes.note: “Those things” are the Stoic demands that the objector in the section before calls too great and too hard. The pronoun has a second-person colour, “those things you speak of”.
notes.other_reading: the things you mention

notes.latin: Immo mehercules aliud est in re
notes.note: Seneca corrects the answer just given: the first is the polite one, the second the true one. “By Hercules” is an everyday Roman oath, kept as it is; “the fact of the matter” expands two short words, literally “in the thing”.
notes.other_reading: No, in truth the real case is different

notes.note: A play on two verbs that sound alike. The second means to shake out or shake off, and can also mean to search or examine closely; “shake off” is taken as the opposite of defending.
notes.other_reading: excuse them than examine them

notes.note: A fallback inside the sentence: use all the powers on one’s own behalf or, failing that, at least do not turn them against oneself.
notes.other_reading: certainly not against ourselves

notes.latin: Nolle in causa est, non posse praetenditur
notes.note: Two infinitives used as nouns: “to be unwilling” and “to be unable”. The second verb means to hold something out in front as a cover. “Not wanting” keeps the word used for the reasoned verb of wanting at the start of the letter.
notes.other_reading: Unwillingness is the reason; inability is the excuse held up in front of it

passages.latin: Omnes autem male habet ignorantia ueri. Tamquam ad bona feruntur decepti rumoribus, deinde mala esse aut inania aut minora quam sperauerint adepti ac multa passi uident; maiorque pars miratur ex interuallo fallentia, et uulgo bona pro magnis sunt.
passages.english: But ignorance of the truth afflicts everyone. Deceived by common talk, they are carried towards things as if towards goods; then, when they have got them and have suffered much, they see that these are bad, or empty, or smaller than they had hoped. And most people admire things that deceive from a distance, and commonly goods count as great things.

notes.note: An idiom, literally “has (someone) badly”: to trouble, distress or do harm to. “Afflicts” is used.
notes.other_reading: ignorance of the truth does harm to everyone

notes.note: The genitive can be “of the truth” in general or “of what is true” in the particular case, that is, of what these things really are. The general sense is taken.
notes.other_reading: not knowing what is true

notes.note: The Latin gives the rush no object of its own: literally “they are carried as if towards goods”. “Things” is supplied so that what is got and then found bad has a name; “goods” is the glossary word and returns in the last clause.
notes.other_reading: they are carried along as if towards goods

notes.note: Not “rumours” in the narrow sense but what people commonly say, the general report about what is worth having.
notes.other_reading: deceived by rumours

notes.note: Two participles. The Latin does not say whether the suffering comes before or after the getting; the English keeps the Latin order and leaves it open.
notes.other_reading: having gained them at the cost of much suffering

notes.note: “From a distance” can go with “admire” or with “deceive”. It is attached to “deceive”, in line with the section before, where things look high to someone lying far from them.
notes.other_reading: most people admire from a distance things that deceive

notes.note: The word can be the adverb “commonly” or a dative, “for the crowd”. The adverb is the usual use and is taken; the sense differs little.
notes.other_reading: and with the crowd goods count as great things

notes.note: As given, the words say that goods count as great things, and the English follows them. The run of thought would lead one to expect the reverse, that great things are taken for goods; some editions may print the two words the other way round (from memory, unchecked).
notes.other_reading: and commonly great things count as goods

check.note: As given, the Latin says that goods count as great things, while the argument leads one to expect the reverse. The two words may have changed places (from memory, unchecked), so the order should be kept and the doubt flagged in a note.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps the order of the Latin as given, “goods count as great things”, and a note gives the reverse reading and the doubt about the text, marked as from memory and unchecked.

check.note: “Stand for” is unclear in today’s English, where it can mean represent or put up with. The Latin means to count as, to be taken for.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “count as great things”. The Latin phrase means to be reckoned as something, and “count as” says that plainly.

check.note: The word can be the adverb “commonly” or a dative, “for the crowd”. The draft took the second without a note, and the adverb is at least as likely.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “commonly”, the usual sense of this form, and a note gives “with the crowd” as the other reading.

check.note: “From a distance” can go with “deceive” or with “admire”. The draft took the first, and the other reading should be recorded.
check.decided: Accepted: the English keeps “things that deceive from a distance”, which matches the section before, where things look high to one who lies far from them. The note gives the other reading.

check.note: The same word is “goods” in the second sentence and “good things” in the last. The passage turns on what counts as a good, so one English word should serve for both.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now has “goods” in both places, so that a reader can see it is one Latin word.

check.note: Two “they” in a row refer first to the people and then to the things. The Latin is clear because the things are neuter plural; the English is not.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “they see that these are bad”, so that the people and the things are kept apart.

check.note: “The greater part” with no noun is stiff and leaves the reader to guess that people are meant.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “most people admire”. The Latin phrase means the larger share of the “everyone” named in the first sentence.

passages.latin: Sic maxime coarguitur animus inprudens: alius prodit atquealius et, quo turpius nihil iudico, inpar sibi est. Magnam rem puta unumhominem agere. Praeter sapientem autem nemo unum agit, ceteri multiformessumus. Modo frugi tibi uidebimur et graues, modo prodigi et uani; mutamussubinde personam et contrariam ei sumimus quam exuimus. Hoc ergo a te exige,ut qualem institueris praestare te, talem usque ad exitum serues; efficeut possis laudari, si minus, ut adgnosci. De aliquo quem here uidisti meritodici potest 'hic qui est?': tanta mutatio est. Vale.
passages.english: This above all is how an unwise mind is shown up: it comes forward now as one, now as another, and it does not match itself, and I judge nothing more shameful than that. Count it a great thing to play one man. But no one except the wise man plays one; the rest of us are many-shaped. At one moment we will seem to you thrifty and serious, at another spendthrift and frivolous; we change our mask again and again and put on the opposite of the one we have taken off. So demand this of yourself: keep yourself, right to the end, such as you set out to show yourself. Bring it about that you can be praised, or, failing that, that you can be recognised. Of someone you saw yesterday it can rightly be said, “Who is this?”: the change is so great. Farewell.

notes.note: The adjective means lacking practical good sense, and can also mean unaware or off guard. “Unwise” is used so that the contrast with the wise man two sentences later is heard, though the Latin word is not formed from the word for “wise”.
notes.other_reading: a mind without foresight, or: a mind off its guard

notes.note: The verb form can be from “to come forward”, as an actor does, or from “to betray, reveal”, which would need an object. “Comes forward” is taken, which suits the stage language that follows; the paired pronouns mean different at different times and agree with “mind”, so no noun is added. Two words are run together in the copy.
notes.other_reading: it gives itself away as now one thing, now another

notes.note: Literally “unequal to itself”: not matching itself from one time to the next. The aside about shamefulness, which comes before this clause in the Latin, is moved to the end of the sentence to keep the English readable.
notes.other_reading: it is inconsistent with itself

notes.note: The verb is the stage word for playing a part. The point is to play a single character throughout, where most people play many. Two words are run together in the copy.
notes.other_reading: to act the part of one man

notes.note: A word of broad praise: thrifty, sober, decent. Since it is set against the spendthrift, “thrifty” is used.
notes.other_reading: sober and serious

notes.note: The first adjective is literally “heavy” and the last literally “empty”. Said of people they mean serious or steady and frivolous or unreliable, and the English gives those senses.
notes.other_reading: weighty, at another spendthrift and empty

notes.note: The actor’s mask, and so a role or character. The image of the mask is kept because it is put on and taken off like clothing in the same sentence.
notes.other_reading: the role is changed again and again

notes.note: The noun means a way out and so an end: the end of life, and also the end of a play. English “end” covers both.
notes.other_reading: right up to your death

notes.note: The same verb is understood: “that you can be recognised”. It is taken as being known for the same person as before; it could also mean being acknowledged.
notes.other_reading: or, if not, at least acknowledged

notes.note: A plain question of identity. The pronoun form could also ask what sort of man this is. The word for “yesterday” in the same sentence is an old spelling.
notes.other_reading: “What kind of man is this?”

check.note: In English “not equal to” suggests not being up to a task. The Latin means uneven, not matching itself, which is the point of the whole passage.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “it does not match itself”. The Latin adjective means unlike or uneven, here of a mind that differs from itself from one time to the next.

check.note: The subject is the mind and the Latin says only “one and then another”, so “man” is added. The paired pronouns also suggest change again and again, where “and then as another” sounds like a single change.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “it comes forward now as one, now as another”. “Man” is removed and the repeated change is shown, but “thing” is not added either, because the Latin pronouns are masculine only to agree with the word for “mind”.

check.note: “Weighty” and “empty” said of people are literal and unclear to a reader of today. The Latin pair means serious or steady against frivolous or shallow.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “thrifty and serious, at another spendthrift and frivolous”. The two Latin adjectives are ordinary words of character here, and a note records their literal senses, heavy and empty.

check.note: “Without sense” is stronger than the Latin and loses the contrast with the wise man two sentences later. The word means lacking good judgment, unwise.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “an unwise mind”. The Latin word means lacking practical good sense, and a note says that it is not formed from the word for “wise”.

check.note: The inverted order of “so great is the change” is literary. A small point.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “the change is so great”, in plain order. The suggested “that great” is looser than the Latin, which says only “so great”.

passages.latin: Quod autem hoc bonum? Dicam: liber animus, erectus, alia subicienssibi, se nulli. Hoc bonum adeo non recipit infantia ut pueritia non speret,adulescentia inprobe speret; bene agitur cum senectute si ad illud longostudio intentoque peruenit. Si hoc est bonum, et intellegibile est.
passages.english: But what is this good? I will tell you: a free mind, standing tall, putting other things under itself and itself under none. Infancy is so far from being able to take in this good that boyhood does not hope for it and youth hopes for it presumptuously; old age is doing well if it has reached it by long and concentrated effort. If this is the good, it is also a thing grasped by the understanding.

notes.note: The second adjective means raised up, standing straight, not bowed. “Upright” would say this but is heard as “honest” when said of a mind, so the English has “standing tall”.
notes.other_reading: a free mind, unbowed

notes.note: The form most often means “to no one”, but after “other things” it can as well mean “to no other thing”. “None” leaves the choice as open as the Latin.
notes.other_reading: and itself under no one, or: and itself under nothing

notes.note: Literally “does not receive”: cannot take in, has no room for. The sentence climbs through the ages of life: infancy, boyhood, youth, old age.
notes.other_reading: infancy is so far from being capable of this good

notes.note: The adverb means beyond what is proper: shamelessly, greedily, unreasonably. “Presumptuously” is taken, a hope beyond what one has a right to.
notes.other_reading: youth hopes for it shamelessly

notes.note: An idiom, literally “it is dealt well with old age”: old age is fortunate, has no cause for complaint.
notes.other_reading: old age is fortunate if

notes.note: The form can be present, “reaches”, or perfect, “has reached”. The perfect is taken: old age is doing well if by then it has arrived.
notes.other_reading: if it reaches it

notes.note: The noun is application, zeal or study, and “effort” is used as the widest of these; the second adjective means stretched tight, intent. Two words are run together in the copy.
notes.other_reading: by long and strenuous study

notes.note: A technical word: an object of the understanding as opposed to an object of the senses, and the surrounding letter argues over which of the two grasps the good. It is spelled out because “intelligible” in English today mostly means “clear”.
notes.other_reading: it is also intelligible

notes.note: Latin has no articles. “The good” is written because the section before speaks of man’s own good; “a good” is possible.
notes.other_reading: If this is a good

check.note: Said of a mind, “upright” in English means honest. The Latin word is about posture, standing tall and not bowed, and goes with “free” and with putting other things beneath itself.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “standing tall”. The Latin word describes something raised and not bowed, and “upright” would be heard as “honest”, a different quality.

check.note: The form can be neuter, “to nothing”, matching “other things”, or masculine, “to no one”. The draft’s English fixed it as “nothing”.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “itself under none”, which can be heard of persons or of things as the Latin form can. The note gives both narrower readings.

check.note: The draft’s future of “say” is stiff in English. The Latin is the ordinary way of announcing that an answer is coming.
check.decided: Accepted: the verb is now “tell you”, the ordinary English for this Latin way of announcing an answer.

check.note: The form can be present, “reaches”, or perfect, “has reached”. With the idiom about old age the perfect is at least as natural.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “if it has reached it”. The verdict on old age looks back on a road already travelled, and a note gives the present as the other reading.

check.note: The noun here is effort or application in general, wider than “study” as book-learning, and the second adjective is concentrated or intent more than strenuous.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “by long and concentrated effort”. The Latin noun covers any earnest application, and the adjective means stretched towards one thing.

check.note: “Admitting this good” can be read as confessing it. The Latin means to have room for it, to be capable of it.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “so far from being able to take in this good”. “Admitting” goes, but “take in” is used instead of “capable of” because the Latin verb is literally “receive”.

passages.latin: Quo nunc pertineat ista disputatio quaeris, et quid animo tuoprofutura sit? Dico: et exercet illum et acuit et utique aliquid acturumoccupatione honesta tenet. Prodest autem etiam quo moratur ad praua properantes. Sed illud dico: nullo modo prodesse possum magis quam si tibi bonumtuum ostendo, si te a mutis animalibus separo, si cum deo pono.
passages.english: Do you ask what this discussion now leads to, and what use it will be to your mind? I say: it exercises the mind and sharpens it, and it keeps the mind, which will be doing something in any case, in an honourable occupation. And it is also of use in that it delays those who are hurrying towards what is wrong. But I say this: I can in no way be of more use than if I show you your own good, if I separate you from the mute animals, if I place you with god.

notes.note: Literally “where this discussion now reaches to”: what it bears on, what its point is. The noun is a reasoned argument or debate.
notes.other_reading: what the point of this argument now is

notes.note: The verb “to benefit” comes three times in the section and is “be of use” each time. “Good” is kept for the different Latin word in “your own good”, the key term of the letter.
notes.other_reading: what good it will do your mind

notes.note: The participle goes with the mind: it will be busy with something, so let it be this. The adverb is taken with the participle, “in any case”; it could go with the main verb instead. Two words are run together in the copy.
notes.other_reading: and at the very least keeps it, which will be doing something, in an honourable occupation

notes.note: The first word is taken as “also”, a further benefit, though it can be “even”. The second is read as “in that”; it could be “in so far as”, which would limit the claim.
notes.other_reading: it is of use even in so far as it delays

notes.note: The adjective is literally “crooked” and so wrong or bad; “wrong” is used because “crooked” today suggests dishonest dealing. The people are general, “those who hurry”, not Lucilius alone.
notes.other_reading: those hurrying towards what is crooked

notes.note: Animals without speech, which for the Stoics goes with being without reason. “Mute” is the nearest English word and avoids “dumb”, which is now heard as “stupid”.
notes.other_reading: from the animals that cannot speak

notes.note: Singular, with no article in Latin: “with god” or “with a god”. “God” is written without a capital, as the glossary has it; the preposition says alongside, in the same class.
notes.other_reading: beside a god

check.note: The adverb can go with the participle, “bound to be doing something anyway”, or with the main verb, “at the least it keeps the mind busy”. The draft also turns the participle into a reason with “since”, which the Latin does not state.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “it keeps the mind, which will be doing something in any case, in an honourable occupation”. “Since” is gone, because the Latin describes the mind and gives no reason, and the note records the other placing of the adverb.

check.note: The first word may be “also”, a further benefit, and not “even”. “By this, that” is also heavy English.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “it is also of use in that it delays”. “Also” and “in that” are taken, but “delays” stays where “holds back” was suggested, because the Latin verb means to make someone late, not to stop them.

check.note: “Crooked” is literal and in today’s English suggests dishonest dealing. The Latin means wrong or bad things in general.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “towards what is wrong”. The Latin word is an ordinary word for wrong or bad, and the note records the literal “crooked”.

check.note: The inverted order of “But this I say” sounds biblical.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now puts “this” after the verb, in the plain order of today’s speech. The Latin phrase is not solemn.

check.note: Two different Latin words, the verb “to benefit” and the noun for “the good”, both come out as “good” in one clause. This blurs the term the argument depends on.
check.decided: Accepted: the verb is now “be of use” in all three places, and “good” is kept for the noun alone. The two Latin words are unrelated, so the echo in the draft was the English’s own.

check.note: “Dumb” today is read first as “stupid”. The Latin means without speech.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “dumb” goes and the English now reads “the mute animals”. “Mute” is the English word nearest the Latin one, while the suggested “speechless” today mostly describes a person lost for words.

check.latin: et exercet illum et acuit et
check.note: “Both” is used for a list of three, and the run of “it” is hard to follow, since the word refers first to the discussion and then to the mind.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “it exercises the mind and sharpens it, and it keeps the mind”. “Both” is gone, the mind is named, and the three verbs stay joined by “and” as in the Latin.

passages.latin: Quid,inquam, uires corporis alis et exerces? Pecudibus istas maiores ferisquenatura concessit. Quid excolis formam? cum omnia feceris, a mutis animalibusdecore uinceris. Quid capillum ingenti diligentia comis? cum illum ueleffuderis more Parthorum uel Germanorum modo uinxeris uel, ut Scythae solent,sparseris, in quolibet equo densior iactabitur iuba, horrebit in leonumceruice formonsior. Cum te ad uelocitatem paraueris, par lepusculo noneris.
passages.english: Why, I say, do you feed and exercise the strength of your body? Nature has granted that strength in greater measure to farm animals and wild beasts. Why do you cultivate your beauty? When you have done everything, you will be beaten in looks by the mute animals. Why do you dress your hair with enormous care? When you have let it flow in the manner of the Parthians, or tied it up in the way of the Germans, or, as is the habit of the Scythians, spread it loose, a thicker mane will toss on any horse you like, and a more beautiful one will bristle on the neck of lions. When you have trained yourself for speed, you will not be the equal of a little hare.

notes.note: A verb of saying in the first person, dropped into the question: Seneca picks up his own speech and presses the point of the section before. The first person is kept.
notes.other_reading: ask, where the English has “say”

notes.note: The first verb is “you feed, nourish”, not the noun for wings. The pair is feeding up and training, as an athlete does.
notes.other_reading: do you build up and train

notes.note: The pronoun is the thing granted, “that strength”, with a second-person colour, and “greater” describes it: literally “has granted that, greater”. The first noun is herd or farm animals, set against wild ones.
notes.other_reading: Nature has given greater strength than yours to livestock and wild beasts

notes.note: Outward shape, and so good looks or beauty. “Beauty” is used here and “more beautiful” for the related adjective said of the lion’s mane, which is in an old spelling; the different word in the next sentence is “looks”.
notes.other_reading: Why do you cultivate your looks?

notes.note: The verb form could be present, “you are beaten”, or future, “you will be beaten”; the futures around it decide for the future. The noun, grace or handsomeness, is a different word from the one for beauty and is “looks”.
notes.other_reading: you are beaten in beauty

notes.note: Literally “bound” it: taken as hair tied up or knotted, a style reported of some German peoples (from memory, unchecked). The Parthians are the eastern empire beyond the Euphrates, the Scythians the nomads north of the Black Sea.
notes.other_reading: or bound it as the Germans do

notes.note: Literally “scattered”: hair left loose and unarranged. How this differs from the flowing Parthian style is not clear from the Latin alone; two different English verbs are kept.
notes.other_reading: left it dishevelled

notes.note: The verb means to stand stiff, to bristle, and the image is kept.
notes.other_reading: a finer one will stand up on the necks of lions

notes.note: A diminutive, “little hare”, which makes the comparison more belittling. “Little” is kept.
notes.other_reading: a match for a hare

check.note: “Dumb” today is read first as “stupid”. The Latin means without speech.
check.decided: Partly accepted: “dumb” goes and the English now reads “the mute animals”, as in the section before. “Mute” is the English word nearest the Latin one, while “speechless” today mostly describes a person lost for words.

check.note: Today “cattle” means cows and bulls. The Latin word covers farm or herd animals in general, set beside wild ones.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “farm animals and wild beasts”. The Latin noun takes in all herd animals, not cows alone.

check.note: The verb means “are in the habit of” and is flattened to “do”. A small loss.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “as is the habit of the Scythians”. The habit is restored, but with “habit” and not “usually”, because the Latin verb speaks of custom and not of how often.

check.note: The noun is “looks”, but the adjective from the same root, said of the lion’s mane, is “more beautiful”, and a different word is “beauty”. The English ties the mane to the wrong word.
check.decided: Partly accepted: one root now serves the pair, but the other way round from the suggestion: “your beauty” and “a more beautiful one”, with “looks” for the different word between them. “More beautiful” is the plain sense of the adjective and reads more easily than “better-looking”.

check.note: Found while settling: the draft’s “greater strength than that” makes the pronoun a term of comparison. In the Latin the pronoun is the thing granted, “that strength”, and “greater” describes it.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Nature has granted that strength in greater measure to farm animals and wild beasts”. The sense is close to the draft’s, but nothing in the Latin says “than”.

passages.latin: Vis tu relictis in quibus uinci te necesse est, dum in alienaniteris, ad bonum reuerti tuum? Quod est hoc? animus scilicet emendatusac purus, aemulator dei, super humana se extollens, nihil extra se suiponens. Rationale animal es. Quod ergo in te bonum est? perfecta ratio. Hanc tu ad suum finem hinc euoca, in quantum potest plurimumcrescere.
passages.english: Will you not leave the things in which you are bound to be beaten while you strive for what is not your own, and go back to your own good? What is this? A mind, of course, freed from faults and pure, striving to equal god, lifting itself above human things, placing nothing of its own outside itself. You are a rational animal. What, then, is the good in you? Perfected reason. Summon it from here to its own goal, as far as it can possibly grow.

notes.note: Literally “do you want to”. With the pronoun this is a set way of urging someone, and English makes such an urging with a negative question, so “Will you not” is written although the Latin has no “not”.
notes.other_reading: Are you willing to leave the things

notes.note: “What is not your own” answers “your own good” and here means the goods of animals: strength, beauty, speed. The clause is taken as plain time, “while”; it could also give the reason for being beaten. Two words are run together in the copy.
notes.other_reading: because you strain at things that belong to others

notes.note: The first word means freed of faults, as a text is corrected. “Corrected” said of a mind sounds like a marked exercise, so the sense is spelled out. Two words are run together in the copy.
notes.other_reading: a mind corrected and clean

notes.note: One who strives to equal: the word covers both “rival” and “imitator”. “Striving to equal” keeps both and avoids the hostility that “rival” can suggest in English.
notes.other_reading: a rival of god, or: an imitator of god

notes.note: Literally “placing nothing of its own outside itself”: counting nothing external as its own. The literal image is kept. Two words are run together in the copy.
notes.other_reading: reckoning nothing outside itself as its own

notes.note: The adjective is a participle, “brought to completion”. “Perfected” is written because the last sentence shows something finished by growth, not a fixed quality.
notes.other_reading: perfect reason

notes.note: The noun is end in the sense of goal and also of limit; “goal” is written because “end” can be heard as ceasing. The adverb “from here” may mean from this point on or away from the bodily pursuits just listed, and the English leaves it as open as the Latin.
notes.other_reading: call it away from these things to its own limit

notes.note: Construed as a clause of extent hanging on the command: as far as it can possibly grow. It reads a little abruptly, and some editors may supply a verb meaning “allow” before it (from memory, unchecked). Two words are run together in the copy.
notes.other_reading: and let it grow as great as it can

check.note: The Latin is an impatient urging with a stressed “you”. “Will you leave” reads as a plain question about the future.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Will you not leave”. The Latin has no negative, but this set phrase urges, and English urges with a negative question; the note says so.

check.note: The conjunction with a present verb is “while”, and “so long as” can be read as a condition. The neuter plural is set against “your own”: things not yours, here the animals’ advantages, which “what belongs to others” narrows to other people’s property.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “while you strive for what is not your own”. “While” is the plain sense of the conjunction, and “not your own” answers “your own good” at the end of the sentence as the Latin pair does; “strive” is kept from the draft for the verb.

check.note: The word can mean a rival or one who strives to be like. “Rival” in English suggests opposition to god, which does not fit the passage.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “striving to equal god”. This drops the hostile colour of “rival” but keeps the aim of equalling, which the Latin word carries and which “lifting itself above human things” supports.

check.note: “A corrected mind” sounds like a marked exercise. The Latin means freed from faults.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “freed from faults”, which is what the Latin participle literally says.

check.note: The participle can be “perfect” or “perfected, brought to completion”. The next sentence, about growing to its end, favours the second.
check.decided: Accepted: the English now reads “Perfected reason”. The Latin word is a participle, and the next sentence speaks of reason growing to its goal.

check.latin: Hanc tu ad suum finem hinc euoca
check.note: “Call this on” is not clear English. The adverb may mean from this point or away from these things, and “end” can be read as termination where the sense is goal.
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “Summon it from here to its own goal”. “Summon” and “goal” are taken, but “from here” stays, because it is as open as the Latin adverb and “away from these things” would close it; the note gives both senses.

check.note: The draft’s wording is clumsy and the reader has to work out the sense. The clause construes as a loosely attached clause of extent, and an edition may have an added imperative here (from memory, unchecked).
check.decided: Partly accepted: the English now reads “as far as it can possibly grow”. This is plainer and keeps the Latin’s verb “grow” and its clause of extent, where the suggestion turns the verb into a noun; the note keeps the doubt about the text.
